## <a id="introduction"></a>Introduction

This book describes the worship and the church life of the evangelical churches of the
Reformation in Germany and the neighbouring lands, as their own church orders laid them down. A
church order (*Kirchenordnung*) is the law that a prince or a city council gave its church. It
says who shall preach and what, how the Lord's Supper, baptism and marriage are to be held,
which feasts are kept, how ministers are examined and bound, and how the schools and the poor
are provided for. The orders read here are those printed in Emil Sehling's edition, *Die
evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century): 2,581 texts, dated from 1521 to 1620.

The book is written chiefly for Lutherans who want to know what the first Lutheran churches did:
which parts of the Mass they kept and which they dropped, what they sang, how they prayed,
preached and kept the church year, and how they ordered their ministries. The orders are left to
speak for themselves. Each chapter quotes them in a close English translation and cites
every passage to its page in Sehling. This edition gives the English alone; the full edition
also prints each quotation in its original language ([Conventions](#conv-quotations)). Orders of other traditions are used
where they show the practice of their time, and they are always marked as such
([Conventions](#conv-traditions)).

### <a id="intro-sources"></a>The source: Sehling's edition

Emil Sehling, professor of law at Erlangen, began the edition in 1902. By 1913 he had published
five volumes at Leipzig, covering Saxony and Thuringia, Brandenburg, Lusatia and Silesia,
Prussia, Poland and Pomerania, and the Baltic lands, Mecklenburg, Lübeck, Lauenburg and Hamburg.
The Institute for Evangelical Church Law of the Evangelical Church in Germany, at Göttingen,
took up the work again in 1955. The Heidelberg Academy of Sciences carried it on, publishing its
volumes from 2004, and completed it in 2017. The edition runs to 24 volumes in 30 parts, with
two volumes of registers.

Each volume treats a group of territories: principalities and counties, bishoprics, imperial
cities and towns, from the North Sea to Transylvania. For each territory an editor's
introduction tells the history of its reformation and describes its orders. The orders follow,
with their variants and notes. Sehling took "church order" in the widest sense
([§1.2.1](#s1-2-1)), so the set holds visitation articles, mandates, consistory and school
orders, marriage and poor-law orders, agendas and confessions as well as the great church
orders.

Of the 2,581 texts, 1,950 are Lutheran. The rest are Reformed, Moderate Reformed and Philippist,
with a few of other traditions ([§1.3](#s1-3)). Sehling meant to print no orders made for the
Augsburg Interim of 1548, and only four are in the set ([§1.4](#s1-4)). The texts run from
Breslau's beggars' order of 1521 to the orders of 1620 for Stade, Limpurg and the Transylvanian
Saxons. One later text, a report of 1635 on the consistory of Henneberg, stands outside that
range.

### <a id="intro-arrangement"></a>How the book is arranged

[Chapter 1](#ch1) is an inventory of every order in the edition, volume by volume and territory
by territory, with its date, its kind, its confessional tradition and whether it belongs to the
Interim. Each of the other chapters takes one subject through the whole edition:
- the Mass: its order as a whole ([Chapter 2](#ch2)), the preliminaries, confession and
  exhortation ([Chapter 3](#ch3)), the propers ([Chapter 4](#ch4)), the collects
  ([Chapter 5](#ch5)), the general prayer ([Chapter 6](#ch6)), and the Canon in the German
  Masses ([Chapter 7](#ch7));
- music: hymns ([Chapter 8](#ch8)), and the organ, other instruments and bells
  ([Chapter 9](#ch9));
- the daily office ([Chapter 10](#ch10)), preaching ([Chapter 11](#ch11)) and the church year
  ([Chapter 12](#ch12));
- the occasional and extraordinary rites, from baptism to the Litany ([Chapter 13](#ch13));
- the furnishing of worship: art, architecture, paraments and vestments ([Chapter 14](#ch14));
- the duties of ministers, officers and people ([Chapter 15](#ch15)), and the ministries
  themselves: minor orders, deacons and elders ([Chapter 16](#ch16));
- confessional subscription ([Chapter 17](#ch17)).

Most chapters open with a summary of findings and a section on scope, sources and method. They
then set out the evidence subject by subject, quoting the orders and translating them. Tables by
order follow, and every chapter ends with a concordance of the orders it quotes.

Sections are numbered within their chapter, with the chapter number first: §2.3.2 is section 3.2
of Chapter 2. Every reference to a section is a link, and so is every entry in the
[Contents](#contents). The [Scripture index](#scripture-index) and the
[Index of persons](#index-of-persons) list the sections where each passage of Scripture and each
person is cited, and the [Glossary](#glossary) explains the rarer terms.

### <a id="intro-repository"></a>The repository and its methods

The book was made from a digital copy of Sehling's edition and from databases built from it.
They are kept, with the programs that built them, in a public repository:
<https://github.com/sethkasten/sehling-corpus>. The chapters sometimes name these files. This
section describes them, so that the book can be read without the repository.

#### <a id="repo-corpus"></a>The digital corpus

The corpus is the text of all 24 volumes, in their 30 parts, and of the two register volumes. It
was taken from the digitized edition of the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences (digi.hadw-bw.de) and
divided into documents. Each document carries:
- Sehling's citation, for example "Sehling 7, I/Bremen Nr. 3";
- its heading, with place and year;
- its range of printed pages;
- its full text, as read by optical character recognition (OCR).

Two limits of the corpus matter for the quotations in this book. Sehling's footnotes, variant
readings and editorial brackets stand in the text as printed, mixed with the order itself,
because OCR loses the type that tells them apart. They are left out when a passage is quoted
([Conventions](#conv-quotations)). And the OCR is not corrected in the corpus, so a quotation
can keep a misreading, as the Conventions describe.

Three pairs of half-volumes, 7/1 and 7/2.2, 17/1 and 17/2, and 20/1 and 20/2, were bound as
separate books that each number their pages from the beginning. A page number alone is therefore
ambiguous in these volumes, and this book always names the half-volume.

#### <a id="repo-ekodb"></a>The corpus database (`eko.db`)

`eko.db` is a SQLite database built from the corpus. It holds 2,368 records, one for each
document, from the 32 digitized volumes and half-volumes, register volumes included. Each record
gives the citation, heading, place, title, year and pages of its document, a link to the
facsimile page images, and the full text, which can be searched word by word. The database also
holds Sehling's registers of persons, places and subjects, 24,168 entries in all, each linked to
the documents it points to. The registers find mentions that a word search would miss, such as
older spellings and Latin forms.

The "Doc" numbers in the tables and concordances of this book are the record numbers of
`eko.db`. Every quotation is preceded by an invisible note naming the record it was checked
against. A record is a unit of the digitized edition, not always one order: one record may hold
several short orders, and a long order may run over several records. The database's year and
heading for a record are sometimes wrong, so this book names every order from Sehling's running
heads instead (see, for example, [§8.2.3](#s8-2-3)).

The database is about 120 MB. It is not kept in the repository, but is rebuilt from the corpus
by the program `build_database.py`.

#### <a id="repo-methods"></a>How the chapters were made

Each chapter was made in the same way.
- **Search.** The whole corpus was searched in `eko.db` for the words of the subject in High
  German, Low German, Dutch and Latin, in their period spellings, and, where useful, through
  Sehling's registers. Each hit was read in its context.
- **Findings.** What each order prescribes was recorded order by order. Where a thing was looked
  for and not found, the chapter says so. These negative findings are part of the evidence.
- **Quotations.** Every quotation was checked against the text of its record in `eko.db`, and
  its page against the edition's page markers ([Conventions](#conv-quotations)).
- **Translations** were made from the original, in the idiom of the Authorized Version
  ([Conventions](#conv-translations)).
- **Traditions.** Each order's confessional tradition and Interim status was fixed once, in the
  inventory of Chapter 1. The other chapters mark the orders they cite by that inventory
  ([Conventions](#conv-traditions)).

Each chapter's own section on scope, sources and method gives its searches, its sources and its
cautions: [§1.2](#s1-2), [§2.2](#s2-2), [§3.2](#s3-2), [§4.2](#s4-2), [§5.2](#s5-2),
[§6.2](#s6-2), [§7.1.3](#s7-1-3), [§8.2](#s8-2), [§9.2](#s9-2), [§10.2](#s10-2),
[§11.2](#s11-2), [§12.2](#s12-2), [§13.2](#s13-2), [§14.2](#s14-2), [§15.2](#s15-2),
[§16.2](#s16-2) and [§17.2](#s17-2).

#### <a id="repo-hymns"></a>The hymn database (`hymns.db`)

`hymns.db`, with its workbook `hymns.xlsx`, holds the **chief-hymn prescriptions**: the places
where a church order, a hymnal or a later list assigns a hymn to a particular Sunday, feast or
occasion. [Chapter 8](#ch8) treats where and how hymns were sung. The database holds the tables
of hymns by day, and [Appendix 8.A](#s8-a) condenses its "Compare by day" sheet.

The database holds 4,144 prescriptions from 48 witnesses, in two layers that must be kept apart:
- **The church orders.** 466 prescriptions come from the eight orders in Sehling that carry a
  table of hymns: Pomerania 1569, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1565, Hof 1592, Weissenfels 1578, Mansfeld
  1580, Hohenlohe 1596, Nördlingen 1579 and Heilbronn 1543. All are Lutheran. Weissenfels comes
  nearest to the later table of one hymn for each Sunday. The word *Hauptlied* does not occur in
  the corpus. It is later terminology.
- **The hymnals and compilations.** 3,678 prescriptions come from later books and lists:
  - Liliencron's concordance of fifteen hymnals of 1545–1694, Sunday by Sunday;
  - Ludecus's *Ordo cantionum Germanicarum* (1589);
  - Selnecker's own account of the scheme he kept;
  - a modern Hymn of the Day table, which collates the schemes of Selnecker, Carpzov and others
    with those of modern hymnals;
  - Krusemark's *Hymns ABC* (2018), of which only the hymns of the day are taken.

An order commands what shall be sung. A hymnal records what was sung, sometimes long after.

**Witnesses, not books, are counted.** A witness is counted once, whichever compilation it was
read from. Selnecker, for instance, appears in Liliencron, in the Hymn of the Day table and in
his own account, and he counts once. One overlap could not be resolved. A column of Krusemark's,
taken from Jason Thompson's dissertation, collates Ludecus with twelve other lists of the
sixteenth century without saying which list each hymn came from. Where that column and Ludecus
agree, Ludecus may be counted twice.

**Titles.** Each hymn is named by its German or Latin incipit as printed, with a literal English
rendering. Where the hymn has a received English title, that title is given as well. For 36
hymns with no received title, the title of Matthew Carver's translation is given, from
*Walther's Hymnal* (2012) or from his *Hymnoglypt*. 38 hymns have no English title at all. Where
a hymn has rival English titles, the choice between them is an editorial judgment, not a fact.

**Assignments.** On five days where no hymn has three old witnesses, the editor of the database
assigns one. These are marked "Assigned" and never counted as witnesses.

#### <a id="repo-prayers"></a>The general-prayer workbook and database (`general_prayers.db`)

`general_prayers.db`, with its workbook `general_prayers.xlsx`, holds the general prayer of the
Sunday service ([Chapter 6](#ch6)) from every order in Sehling that prints one: 57 orders, dated
1526–1618. The orders give 455 petitions, which fall into 18 families of text and 28 standard
categories of intention. Their languages are High German, Low German, Low Dutch and Latin.

Each petition is divided into its rubric (the heading or marginal note), its bid (the words
addressed to the people) and its prayer (the words addressed to God). Each part is given in English here; the workbook and the full edition also give the original.

**How the texts were made.** The original is Sehling's base text with his editorial matter
stripped out: sigla, footnote numbers, the variant readings of later editions, page and folio
markers, running heads, and words interleaved from the second column by the OCR. The spelling of
the print is kept, and obvious OCR slips are corrected. Every rubric, bid and prayer was found
again in its record in `eko.db`, with at least nine-tenths of its words. Where one order copies
another, the source's English was taken over and corrected wherever the German differs. Each
witness is dated as Sehling edits it, not by the year of its record in `eko.db`, which is wrong
for several of them.

**The sheets of the workbook.**
- The **Compare** sheet sets the orders side by side, petition by petition.
- The **Prayers** sheet gives every witness's own text.
- The **Archetypes** sheet and four **Critical** sheets collate each family's witnesses into one
  text for each category, with every variant in square brackets.
- Four **Representative** sheets give one clean text for each family and category. Chapter 6
  prints these, family by family.

##### <a id="repo-prayers-scope"></a>What counts as the general prayer

**Included.** The prayer of intercession for all estates and needs in the chief Sunday service.
It is normally after the sermon, from the pulpit. In family L it is in the Mass itself, and in
Norden 1528 (Reformed) it stands in the place of the Prone. The following count as part of it:
- an exhortation or preface to it;
- confession and absolution, when the order places them inside the prayer;
- the Our Father, the Creed or the Decalogue, when printed as its close.

Two orders that *prescribe the contents* of the prayer in indirect speech are also included:
Magdeburg 1562 and Osnabrück 1543.

**Excluded, deliberately:**
- **Collect banks**, even when they supply the texts for the prayer: Wittenberg 1536,
  Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, Mansfeld 1562, Lippe 1566, Grubenhagen, Hoya, the Prussian collects
  and Hanau-Lichtenberg's "XII Collecten" (Twelve Collects).
- **The Litany.** It is often the alternative form, and it is a genre of its own.
- **Prayer-day, occasional and emergency prayers**, such as the three prayers of the Wild- and
  Rhinegraves and the variant in the Nassau *Agende* of 1618.
- **Afternoon, weekday and Vespers forms**, such as the afternoon forms of Henneberg, Strasbourg
  1598 and Kurpfalz 1563 (Reformed).
- **Orders that only mention the prayer, or give it by reference**: Strasbourg 1577, Hessen 1574
  (Philippist), Mecklenburg 1552, Sponheim 1590, Emden 1594 (Reformed; free prayer), Saxony 1539
  (Luther's paraphrase, by reference only), and the references to Veit Dietrich's collects.
- **Orders that Sehling prints only as variants of another order.** Kurpfalz 1601 (Reformed) is
  identical to 1563.

##### <a id="repo-prayers-rules"></a>Representative texts

The representative texts give one clean text for each family and category, with no brackets.
They are built from the same collation as the critical texts, by five rules.
1. **Layout.** A representative cell is filled exactly where the critical cell is.
2. **Majority.** A petition is kept if at least half the family's witnesses to that category
   have it. Within a petition, a rubric, bid or prayer is kept if at least half its witnesses
   have it. Word by word:
   - a variant replaces the parent's reading only if at least half the witnesses to that text
     have it, and more have it than have the parent's reading;
   - an addition is kept if at least half the witnesses to that text have it.
3. **Moved words.** A transposition appears in the collation as an omission at one place and an
   addition at another. Both are decided by the votes above, so the order that more witnesses
   have wins. On a tie the parent's order is kept: an addition that exactly half the witnesses
   have is dropped when its words already stand in the parent close by.
4. **Consistent openings and endings.** Within each family one pattern is applied, taken from
   the family's own majority:
   - **A (Brenz):** bids end "Bittend also:" (*Pray ye thus:*). Collects end bare, as in
     Schwäbisch Hall 1526. The mediation formula and Amen that two collects carry are removed.
   - **B1 (Württemberg long form):** bids end "Bittend also:". Collects end "through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen." wherever they carry a
     mediation formula or lack a closing Amen.
   - **L (Brandenburg):** collects end "through thy Son Jesus Christ. Amen.", in place of the abbreviation "through our Lord etc.".

   The other families' texts are continuous prayers or exhortations whose openings and endings
   are already consistent.
5. **Divergent texts.** Where no reading has half the witnesses, the parent's reading stands.
   The parent is the earliest witness: the archetype, or, for an added petition, the earliest
   witness that has it. The same applies when no petition, or no group of related texts, has
   half the witnesses.

The English is not voted on separately. Each English variation takes the reading of the
witnesses whose reading the original chose at the same place. Where only the English varies, as
when two translations render the same words, the parent's English is kept. The original and the
English therefore give the same text. Sehling's editorial brackets are removed.

##### <a id="repo-prayers-findings"></a>What the comparison shows

- **Civil authority is the one universal intention.** It appears in all 57 orders, and in some
  it is prayed for twice. The Lüneburg family (J) has one petition for the Emperor and all
  magistrates, and another for the princess of the land and the young lordship.
- **The Church, then the magistrates, is the normal Lutheran sequence.** It comes from Brenz
  1526 through Württemberg 1553, and so reaches roughly half the orders. The typical series is:
  exhortation > the Church > magistrates > the afflicted > peace > enemies > women with child >
  fruits of the earth > the Our Father. The Reformed Heidelberg prayer begins elsewhere:
  confession > thanksgiving > the Word > magistrates > all men > the persecuted > the afflicted.
  Its petition for **all men** (1 Tim. 2) is a Reformed and Upper German feature. It occurs only
  in Heidelberg (R1, with the Lutheran Schaumburg 1614, which borrows the Heidelberg prayer), in
  Calvin (R3) and in Augsburg 1537 (Moderate Reformed).
- **The Word and its fruit is named in almost every family except the Brenz and Württemberg
  line.** There it is folded into the petition for the Church, and only two witnesses of that
  line add it: Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 (long form) and Magdeburg 1562. It opens the prayer in the
  Nürnberg exhortation (D), in Bugenhagen and Osnabrück (H), in the Lower Saxon *notel* (J) and
  in Heidelberg (R1, R2; Reformed).
- **Women with child are prayed for almost everywhere.** They are named in 42 of the 57 orders:
  in a petition of their own in the Brenz and Württemberg long forms, and within the petition
  for the afflicted in the short form and most other families. They are absent from the Mass
  intercessions (L); from Calvin, à Lasco and the Heidelberg paraphrase (all Reformed); from
  Veit Dietrich's exhortation (Nürnberg 1545 and Waldeck 1556); and from Osnabrück, Magdeburg,
  Leipzig, Hessen (Moderate Reformed), Worms and Norden (Reformed).
- **Brandenburg 1540 and its followers (family L) put the intercessions in the Mass, under the
  Sanctus.** These are collects for the ministers, the magistrates and peace, standing where the
  Roman Canon had its prayers of intercession (Sehling's note on Pfalz-Neuburg 1543). They are
  the closest evangelical survival of the Canon's intercessions in the corpus.
- **The Württemberg short form is the most copied prayer in the corpus.** Its 17 witnesses run
  from 1553 to 1618 and reach Electoral Saxony (1580), Magdeburg, Strasbourg and the Wetterau
  counts. Their local changes include the name of the ruling house, heretics among the enemies,
  the fallen-away and daily bread.

## <a id="conventions"></a>Conventions

These conventions hold throughout the book.

### <a id="conv-citations"></a>Citations and references

- **Sehling.** Citations are in the form "Sehling volume, page", for example
  "(Sehling 8, p. 245)". The half-volumes of the edition are written 6/1, 6/2, 7/1, 7/2.1,
  7/2.2, 17/1, 17/2, 19/1, 19/2, 20/1 and 20/2, following the digitized volumes. Where a passage
  comes from the editor's introduction, notes or apparatus rather than from the text of an
  order, this is said.
- **Orders** are named by place, title and date as Sehling's running heads give them, for
  example "**Hessen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566**". These names sometimes differ from the headings
  of the records in `eko.db` ([Introduction](#repo-ekodb); see, for example, [§8.2.3](#s8-2-3)).
- **Doc** in the tables and concordances is the number of the record in `eko.db` that holds the
  page cited ([Introduction](#repo-ekodb)). Each quotation is preceded by a note, invisible in
  print, that names the record it was checked against.
- **Sections** are numbered within their chapter, with the chapter number first: §2.3.2 is
  section 3.2 of Chapter 2. Appendices are lettered: Appendix 4.A has the sections 4.A.1, 4.A.2
  and so on. In Chapter 6 the petitions of each family keep the family's own numbering (A.1,
  B1.13) under the numbered family sections. Every reference to a section or a chapter is a
  link.
- **Concordances.** Each chapter ends with a concordance of the orders it quotes or cites. Its
  "§" or "Quoted in §" column gives the sections where each order is cited, and each number is a
  link. In Chapters 4 and 5, "A" in that column means the chapter's appendix.

### <a id="conv-quotations"></a>Quotations

- **This edition gives the quotations in English.** The full edition,
  `LITURGICAL_AND_ECCLESIASTICAL_LIFE.md`, prints each quotation from the orders in its own
  language, German, Latin, Low German or Low Dutch, as it stands in `eko.db`, the database built
  from the digitized edition ([Introduction](#repo-ekodb)), and follows it with an English
  translation. Here the original is left out, and the translation follows the citation of the
  order. Shorter quotations in the running text are given in English as well.
- **Terms and titles.** A term that the book keeps in its original language, such as the name of
  a liturgical text or of an office, is followed by its English the first time it occurs in a
  section. The titles of orders and of other works are left as Sehling prints them, so that they
  can be found in his edition.
- **Square brackets** in a translation enclose words supplied in English to complete the sense,
  and the signs of Sehling's editors, such as "[!]" and "[sic]", and the Scripture references
  they supply. A reference that the editors supplied inside a quotation is kept in its English.
- **Omissions.** "[…]" marks an omission. In Chapter 7 it also stands for a hymn or lesson that
  the order prints in full, or for text given in another section.
- **Checking.** Every quotation was checked against the database text before it was translated,
  allowing for OCR noise: at least 90 per cent of its words must be found there in order. Its
  page has been checked against the edition's page markers.
- **The Canon texts (Chapter 7)** are translated from Sehling's base text. A cross (✠) marks
  where the print has a sign of the cross over the elements, and rubrics are in italics. They are
  compared with the standard text of the late-medieval and Tridentine Roman Mass, given here in
  English. The diocesan missals of the 1520s–40s differ in small details. Where a German text
  follows a wording that the Tridentine missal does not have, this is noted, but the wording is
  not attributed to a particular missal.
- **The general-prayer texts (Chapter 6)** are translated from Sehling's text with his apparatus
  removed. "N." stands where the order leaves a name to be filled in, and "etc." where it gives
  only the opening of a well-known text, such as the Our Father or the Creed. Each petition is
  given as its **rubric** (a heading or direction printed with it), its **bid** (the words
  addressed to the people, "Let us pray for …") and its **prayer** (the words addressed to God).
  The **witnesses** are the orders that carry a family's text, named by place and year as in the
  workbook ([Introduction](#repo-prayers)).
- **Texts from outside Sehling.** Where a German collect renders a prayer of the Missal (Chapter
  5), the Missal's prayer is cited from the Roman Missal of the period. Where Sehling's editors
  identify the source, this is said, and where the identification is this book's own, that is
  said too. The English of the Common Service and the later American Lutheran books, given in
  [§3.4.5](#s3-4-5) for comparison, has not been checked against the corpus.

### <a id="conv-translations"></a>Translations

- The English is formal-equivalence, in the idiom of the Authorized Version (thee and thou,
  -eth). Word order and clause structure are kept where English allows, and nothing is smoothed
  away. Words the translation supplies are in square brackets.
- Liturgical names keep their customary Latin or English forms: Kyrie, Gloria, *Et in terra*,
  *Patrem*, Sanctus, *Benedicamus*, Matins, Lauds, Prime, Vespers, *Benedictus*, *Magnificat*,
  *Te Deum*, the Our Father. Stock liturgical phrases are given in their familiar English: *Vere
  dignum et iustum est* is "It is very meet and right", and *Oremus* and "Last uns bitten" are
  "Let us pray". Scripture quoted in a prayer is given in the wording of the Authorized Version
  where the German follows the same text.
- Book titles are given in their usual English form ("the Augsburg Confession", "the Smalcald
  Articles"). *Corpus doctrinae* and *norma doctrinae* are left in Latin.
- Hymn incipits are translated literally and put in quotation marks, so that the reader can see
  what the words say. They are not given under the titles of the English hymnals. Thus "Nun
  bitten wir den heiligen Geist" is "Now pray we the Holy Ghost", and "Erhalt uns, Herr, bei
  deinem Wort" is "Keep us, Lord, by thy word". In the running text the German incipit is used,
  and in this edition its English follows it the first time it occurs in a section.
- Stock terms are rendered the same way throughout:

### <a id="conv-traditions"></a>Traditions and the Interim

Most of the orders cited are Lutheran, and they are not marked. Every order of another tradition
is marked where it is cited, by its name in brackets after the order, as "Kurpfalz 1563
(Reformed)" or "Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed)". Orders made under or for the Augsburg Interim
of 1548 are marked as Interim orders. The traditions and the Interim orders are those of the
inventory in Chapter 1 ([§1.3](#s1-3), [§1.4](#s1-4)):
- **Reformed**: the Swiss, Calvinist and Heidelberg churches, among them the German territories
  that turned Reformed after 1560 and the French and Dutch stranger churches;
- **Moderate Reformed**: the Bucerian and related orders that stood between the Lutheran and the
  Swiss Reformed: Bucer's Strasbourg and the Upper German cities before the Interim, Philip of
  Hesse's church to 1566, Hermann von Wied's Cologne order, Rothmann's Münster, East Frisia
  under John a Lasco, and Colmar after 1578;
- **Philippist**: the churches that held to Melanchthon's later teaching and his *Corpus
  doctrinae* and refused the Formula of Concord: the joint Hessian synods and orders of
  1568–1598, Bremen 1556–1575, Nassau-Dillenburg 1575 and Anhalt 1590–1594;
- **Anglican**: the English exile congregation at Frankfurt;
- **Bohemian Brethren** (Hussite): the Unity of the Brethren in Greater Poland;
- **Sandomierz consensus**: the Polish synods at which Lutherans, Reformed and Brethren met
  together;
- **Roman Catholic humanist**: the Erasmian orders of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, which reform the old
  church without leaving it;
- **Roman Catholic**: the Bishop of Münster's edict of 1534 against the Anabaptists;
- **Radical Reformation**: Thomas Müntzer's Allstedt orders;
- **Anabaptist**: the Münster council's mandate of January 1534, which tolerated the
  Anabaptists;
- **Reformed–Lutheran treaty**: the East Frisian settlements of 1595 and 1599;
- **Multi-confessional**: the decrees of the Transylvanian diets, which received the Catholic,
  Lutheran, Reformed and Unitarian religions side by side. The Transylvanian Saxons' own orders,
  chapters and synods are Lutheran.

**The mark follows the order cited, not the territory**, since a territory could change its
tradition:
- Strasbourg is Moderate Reformed until the Interim of 1548 and Lutheran after it. Its German
  Masses of 1524–1525 are Moderate Reformed, and Marbach's order of 1553 is Lutheran.
- Kurpfalz is Lutheran in 1546 and 1556 and under Ludwig VI (1576–1583), and Reformed in
  1563–1576 and from 1583. Johann Casimir's Pfalz-Lautern stayed Reformed under Ludwig VI.
- Hesse is Moderate Reformed under Philip (to 1566) and Philippist under his sons. After the
  division, Hessen-Kassel turned Reformed (1605) and Hessen-Darmstadt stayed Lutheran.
- Bremen is Philippist from 1556 to 1575 and Reformed from 1582.
- Nassau-Dillenburg is Lutheran to 1570, Philippist in 1575 and Reformed from 1581.
- Anhalt is Philippist in 1590–1594 and Reformed from 1596.
- Pfalz-Zweibrücken is Lutheran until 1588, and Pfalz-Simmern until it fell to the Electoral
  Palatinate in 1598.

Where an order could be counted either Moderate Reformed or Philippist, it is counted Moderate
Reformed. Some further distinctions:
- "Philippist" also names a party within the Lutheran churches, as in Electoral Saxony before
  1574. An order is marked "(Philippist)" only where the inventory counts it so.
- The family names of the Mass in Chapter 2 ([§2.4](#s2-4)) are names of liturgical shape.
  "Upper German" there means the south-western Lutheran service of Württemberg and its copies,
  not the Moderate Reformed Upper German Reformation of Bucer's circle.
- The orders that took over Müntzer's German propers (Erfurt 1525, Calenberg-Göttingen 1542,
  Lippe 1571) are Lutheran. Only Müntzer's own Allstedt orders are marked.
- Some Lutheran orders took the Reformed line on images, vestments or vessels: Lichtenberg 1579,
  Sponheim 1590/91, the Upper Palatine visitation of 1579 and Nassau-Weilburg 1617. They are
  Lutheran orders, and the text says where they agree with the Reformed.
- Swiss sources outside the corpus (Zürich 1525, Basel 1526, Geneva) are Reformed.

### <a id="conv-abbreviations"></a>Abbreviations

- **Confessional writings** (Chapter 17 and elsewhere): CA = the Augsburg Confession (1530); CA
  *variata* = Melanchthon's altered edition of 1540; Apol = the Apology of the Augsburg
  Confession; SA = the Smalcald Articles; SC and LC = Luther's Small and Large Catechisms; FC =
  the Formula of Concord (1577); BoC = the Book of Concord (1580); *CPhil* = the *Corpus
  doctrinae Philippicum* (1560); KO = *Kirchenordnung*, church order.
- **The parts of the Mass**, in the tables of Chapter 2: Intr. (the introit, or the hymn in its
  place), Ky. (Kyrie), Gl. (Gloria), Coll. (collect), Ep. (epistle), Grad. (gradual, alleluia,
  sequence, or the hymn after the epistle), Gosp. (gospel), Cr. (creed), Serm. (sermon), Exh.
  (exhortation to the communicants), Pref. (Preface), San. (Sanctus), PN (Lord's Prayer), Verba
  (Words of Institution), Agn. (Agnus Dei), Comm. (distribution), Thanks. (postcommunion collect
  or thanksgiving), Bl. (blessing). Brackets mark a part that the order allows but does not
  require, and "→" separates the parts.
- **Traditions**, in the tables of Chapter 1: L = Lutheran; R = Reformed; MR = Moderate Reformed
  (Bucerian and Upper German); PH = Philippist; A = Anglican; H = Hussite (Unity of the Bohemian
  Brethren); C = Sandomierz consensus (Lutheran, Reformed and Brethren together); R/L = Reformed
  and Lutheran (treaty between the two); RCH = Roman Catholic humanist (Erasmian reform); RC =
  Roman Catholic; RAD = Radical Reformation (Müntzer); ANA = Anabaptist (civic toleration of the
  Anabaptists); T = multi-confessional diet decree (Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Unitarian
  received side by side).

### <a id="conv-inventory"></a>The inventory tables of Chapter 1

- **No.** is the number Sehling, or the later editor, gives the text within its territory.
  Volumes 1–5 number their registers in their own way, and their numbers are given as they
  stand.
- **Order** is the title as Sehling's tables of contents give it. For volumes 1–5 the titles
  come from the chronological register at the end of each volume. Long titles are shortened, and
  "…" marks the cut. Spelling is as printed, including OCR errors.
- **Date** is the year in the title or in the register. A few undated texts are dated from the
  text or from the editor's introduction or notes, as the notes column says. "n.d." means no
  single year is known.
- **Sehling** gives the volume and the page where the text begins. For volume 14 it is sometimes
  the introduction page where Sehling only describes the order.
- **Doc** is the record in `eko.db` that holds that page ([Introduction](#repo-ekodb)).
- **Kind** is assigned from the words of the title ([§1.2.4](#s1-2-4)).
- **Trad.** gives the tradition, in the codes listed under [Abbreviations](#conv-abbreviations).
- **Interim / notes** marks the Interim orders and texts tied to the Interim ([§1.4](#s1-4)),
  and adds notes such as the reigning prince.

<div style="page-break-before: always;"></div>

## <a id="ch1"></a>Chapter 1. The Church Orders: An Inventory by Tradition


This chapter lists every order that Sehling's *Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI.
Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century) prints, volume by volume and territory by territory: 2,581 texts in 24 volumes (30
parts). For each order it gives:
- its number in Sehling, its title, and its date;
- the page in Sehling and the [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) document that holds the text;
- what kind of order it is (church order, agenda, visitation order, mandate, and so on);
- the confessional tradition it belongs to: Lutheran, Reformed, Moderate Reformed (Bucer's
  circle and the Upper German cities), Philippist, Anglican, Hussite, and a few others;
- whether it is an Interim order, or otherwise tied to the Augsburg Interim of 1548.

**Confessional traditions and Interim orders**

Sehling's title calls these the *evangelical* church orders, and most of them are Lutheran:
1,950 of the 2,581 texts. The rest belong to other traditions:

- **Reformed** (340): the Swiss, Calvinist and Heidelberg churches, among them the German
  territories that turned Reformed after 1560 and the French and Dutch stranger churches;
- **Moderate Reformed** (198): the Bucerian and related orders that stood between the Lutheran
  and the Swiss Reformed: Bucer's Strasbourg and the Upper German cities before the Interim,
  Philip of Hesse's church to 1566, Hermann von Wied's Cologne order, Rothmann's Münster, East
  Frisia under John a Lasco, and Colmar after 1578;
- **Philippist** (33): the churches that held to Melanchthon's later teaching and his *Corpus
  doctrinae* (body of doctrine) and refused the Formula of Concord: the joint Hessian synods and orders of
  1568-1598, Bremen 1556-1575, Nassau-Dillenburg 1575 and Anhalt 1590-1594;
- a few others: Anglican (the English exile congregation at Frankfurt), the Bohemian Brethren
  (Hussite), the Sandomierz consensus of Lutherans, Reformed and Brethren in Poland, the Roman
  Catholic humanist orders of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, Thomas Müntzer's orders (Radical Reformation),
  one Roman Catholic and one Anabaptist-toleration text from Münster, two Reformed-Lutheran
  treaties in East Frisia, and the multi-confessional Transylvanian diet decrees.

A territory's tradition can change from one order to the next: Kurpfalz is Lutheran in 1556 and
Reformed in 1563, and Strasbourg Moderate Reformed before the Interim of 1548 and Lutheran after
it. This chapter gives the tradition of every order ([§1.3](#s1-3) defines them). Where an order could be
counted either Moderate Reformed or Philippist, it is counted Moderate Reformed. The chapter also
lists the few Interim orders and the texts tied to the Augsburg Interim ([§1.4](#s1-4)).

The other chapters mark every order of another tradition, and every Interim order, where they
cite it ([Conventions](#conv-traditions)).

**Layout**

- [§1.1](#s1-1) summarizes the findings.
- [§1.2](#s1-2) sets out the scope, the method and the cautions.
- [§1.3](#s1-3) defines the traditions and says where each is found.
- [§1.4](#s1-4) lists the Interim orders and the other texts tied to the Interim.
- [§1.5](#s1-5) is a table of the territories at a glance.
- §§[1.6](#s1-6)-[1.35](#s1-35) are the inventory itself, one section per volume. Each territory has a short note on
  its confessional history, followed by a table of its orders.

The columns of the inventory tables and the codes for the traditions are explained in the
[Conventions](#conv-inventory).

### <a id="s1-1"></a>1.1 Summary of findings

**1. The set holds 2,581 orders.** Sehling took "church order" in the widest sense ([§1.2.1](#s1-2-1)). The
set therefore includes far more than the great church orders and agendas:

| Kind | Texts |
|---|---|
| Church order | 333 |
| Agenda / liturgy | 271 |
| Visitation | 346 |
| Mandate / decree | 436 |
| Consistory / synod / government | 265 |
| Discipline / police | 178 |
| Marriage | 90 |
| Poor relief | 82 |
| School / university | 65 |
| Catechism / instruction | 44 |
| Monastery / chapter | 46 |
| Appointment / oath | 59 |
| Treaty / agreement | 77 |
| Articles / statutes | 45 |
| Local order | 59 |
| Confession / doctrine | 31 |
| Property / endowment | 6 |
| Other | 148 |

The full church orders (**333**) and the agendas and other liturgical orders (**271**) together
make up about a quarter of the set. Many of the rest are visitation orders, mandates, consistory
and synod orders, and orders on marriage, discipline, schools and the poor.

**2. Most of the orders are Lutheran.** By tradition:

| Tradition | Code | Texts |
|---|---|---|
| Lutheran | L | 1950 |
| Reformed | R | 340 |
| Moderate Reformed (Bucerian and Upper German) | MR | 198 |
| Philippist | PH | 33 |
| Anglican | A | 1 |
| Hussite (Unity of the Bohemian Brethren) | H | 3 |
| Sandomierz consensus (Lutheran, Reformed and Brethren together) | C | 6 |
| Reformed and Lutheran (treaty between the two) | R/L | 2 |
| Roman Catholic humanist (Erasmian reform) | RCH | 18 |
| Roman Catholic | RC | 1 |
| Radical Reformation (Müntzer) | RAD | 3 |
| Anabaptist (civic toleration of the Anabaptists) | ANA | 1 |
| Multi-confessional diet decree (Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Unitarian received side by side) | T | 25 |

- **Lutheran** (1,950): Saxony, Brandenburg, Prussia, Pomerania, the Baltic, Mecklenburg, the
  Hanse towns, Lower Saxony, Franconia, Württemberg, Hohenlohe and most of the imperial cities
  after 1552.
- **Reformed** (340): above all the Electoral Palatinate (from 1561/63) and the "Second
  Reformation" counties of the Wetterau and the Rhine (Nassau-Dillenburg, Hanau-Münzenberg,
  Ysenburg, Solms-Braunfels, Sayn, Wied, Wittgenstein, Moers, Bentheim-Tecklenburg),
  Pfalz-Zweibrücken (1588), Pfalz-Simmern (1598, under the Electoral Palatinate), Hessen-Kassel
  (1600/1605), Lippe (1600), Anhalt (1596), Bremen (from 1580), Emden and the East Frisian
  Reformed congregations, the London Dutch church, Mülhausen (Mulhouse), and the French refugee
  churches of Frankfurt, Wetzlar and the Lebertal.
- **Moderate Reformed** (198): Bucer's Strasbourg and the Upper German cities before the Interim
  (Konstanz, Ulm, Esslingen, Augsburg, Memmingen, Lindau, Isny, Biberach, Gengenbach, Landau,
  Worms, early Frankfurt); Philip's Hesse to 1566; Hermann von Wied's Cologne Reformation
  (1543-1546); Rothmann's Münster (1532/33); East Frisia under Countess Anna; Colmar after 1578,
  whose pastors came from Basel.
- **Philippist** (33): the joint Hessian synods and orders of 1568-1582 and the Hessian orders
  that followed them to 1598; Bremen (1556-1575); Nassau-Dillenburg (1575); Anhalt (1590-1594).
- **Anglican** (1): the order of the English exile congregation at Frankfurt, the "Old
  Discipline" and "New Discipline" of 1557 ([§1.3.4](#s1-3-4)).
- **Hussite** (3): the order of the Unity of the Bohemian Brethren (synod of Zerawitz, 1616) and
  the privileges for the Brethren's congregations at Ostroróg (1569) and Lissa (1580), in
  Greater Poland ([§1.3.5](#s1-3-5)). Six more Polish texts belong to the **Sandomierz consensus** of 1570,
  in which Lutherans, Reformed and Brethren joined.
- **Others**, each labelled with its own affiliation ([§1.3.6](#s1-3-6)):
  - **Roman Catholic humanist (Erasmian)** (18): the church orders of Jülich-Cleves-Berg;
  - **Roman Catholic** (1): the Bishop of Münster's edict against the Anabaptists (1534);
  - **Radical Reformation** (3): Thomas Müntzer's Allstedt orders;
  - **Anabaptist** (1): the Münster council's mandate of January 1534 that let each keep his
    faith and so recognized the Anabaptists;
  - **Multi-confessional** (25): the decrees of the Transylvanian diets;
  - **Reformed and Lutheran** (2): two East Frisian treaties between the Lutheran count and
    Reformed Emden.
- **Not in the set**: no order of the Waldensians, Lollards, Utraquists, Schwenckfelders,
  Hutterites, Mennonites or Antitrinitarians. Anabaptists, Schwenckfelders, Davidjorists,
  Mennonites and "Sakramentierer" appear only as the targets of some thirty mandates, which are
  coded by the authority that issued them.

**3. Almost no Interim orders.** Sehling deliberately left out the orders made under the
Augsburg Interim of 1548 ([§1.2.2](#s1-2-2)). Only four Interim orders proper are in the set ([§1.4](#s1-4)):
- the Brandenburg-Ansbach "Mehrung der vorigen kirchenordnung" ("augmentation of the former church order", the "Auctuarium") of 1548,
  printed "because of its special importance";
- the East Frisian Interim order of 16 July 1549, printed in the editor's introduction;
- the Württemberg Interim mandate of 1548;
- the Biberach council's mandate after accepting the Interim (1548).

16 further texts are tied to the Interim in other ways: issued under it, about it, or ending it
([§1.4](#s1-4)).

**4. Tradition followed the ruler, and changed with him.** Many territories changed tradition
within the century, and their orders change with them:
- **Electoral Palatinate**: Lutheran → Reformed (1561/63) → Lutheran (1577) → Reformed (1583).
- **Upper Palatinate**: Lutheran → Reformed (1559) → Lutheran (1577) → Reformed (1583).
- **Nassau-Dillenburg**: Lutheran → Philippist (1573) → Reformed (1578).
- **Bremen**: Lutheran → Philippist (1562) → Reformed (1580).
- **Hanau-Münzenberg** (1595), **Sayn** (1605), **Lippe** (1600), **Pfalz-Zweibrücken** (1588),
  **Wittgenstein** (about 1574), **Moers** (1578) and **Bentheim-Tecklenburg** (1580s): Lutheran
  → Reformed.
- **Ysenburg**: Ronneburg-Kelsterbach was Reformed 1584-1597, then Lutheran again; Birstein
  became Reformed in 1596.
- **The Upper German cities**: Upper German before the Interim, Lutheran afterwards.

### <a id="s1-2"></a>1.2 Scope, sources and cautions

#### <a id="s1-2-1"></a>1.2.1 What Sehling counted as a church order

Sehling took the term in its widest sense, to cover every ordinance that regulated church
affairs. **Sehling, preface to vol. 1, 1902** (Sehling 1, p. VIII):

<!-- doc 1 -->

We therefore take the term "church order" for our collection in the widest sense of the word,
and understand by it all ordinances made for the regulation of church affairs (excepting, of
course, those orders that served merely passing and particular ends).

#### <a id="s1-2-2"></a>1.2.2 What he left out: half measures and the Interim

Sehling also excluded orders that were never in force, and the "half measures" of wavering
rulers. **Sehling, preface to vol. 1, 1902** (Sehling 1, p. XV):

<!-- doc 1 -->

Furthermore, only the truly evangelical church orders will be given. Excepted are the half
measures that wavering authorities made to calm men's minds, or perhaps in an effort to bring in
reforms, without their ever becoming truly evangelical orders. In particular I do not intend to
print the Interim church orders.

He held to this for Saxony, where the great Interim agenda of 1549 is only described. **Sehling,
introduction to Albertine Saxony** (Sehling 1, p. 102):

<!-- doc 7 -->

The period of the Interim is only touched on in our collection, and so the great order that
falls in that period is not treated further here either: a product of necessity and of yielding,
it cannot be called a purely evangelical order.

His successors kept the rule, with one deliberate exception. **Brandenburg-Ansbach-Kulmbach,
editor's introduction** (Sehling 11, p. 291):

<!-- doc 274 -->

Although Interim orders are in general not to be taken into this edition, this one is
nevertheless printed as no. IV 4 because of its special importance.

Later volumes also print Reformed, Erasmian and multi-confessional orders: the Reformed
Palatinate and the Wetterau counties, the Jülich orders, the Transylvanian diets. The inventory
follows the volumes as they stand.

#### <a id="s1-2-3"></a>1.2.3 How the list was made

- **The list of texts.** It is taken from each volume's own table of contents (volumes 6-24) or
  chronological register (volumes 1-5).
  - Where the scanned contents page is unusable, the titles were read from the running heads of
    the texts. This applies to Oldenburg and Jever in vol. 7/2.1.
  - The registers of volumes 1-5 list orders printed "ganz oder theilweise", in whole or in
    part. They therefore include some orders printed only in extract within an introduction.
  - Volume 14 (Kurpfalz) lists, among its texts, some orders that Sehling only describes in his
    introduction. These are marked "described in the introduction only".
  - Introductions, registers and editorial chapters are left out.
- **Tradition.** It is assigned by territory and date, following the editors' introductions.
  Each territory's note in §§[1.6](#s1-6)-[1.35](#s1-35) gives its confessional history and the dates of change; each
  order takes the tradition of its territory at its date. Where an order belongs to a group with
  another tradition, it is marked individually. Examples:
  - a refugee congregation in a Lutheran city;
  - Hessen-Darmstadt orders within divided Hesse;
  - Solms-Braunfels within Solms;
  - the Lemgo recess of 1617, which guaranteed the town's Lutheran confession within Reformed
    Lippe.
- **Interim.** Texts are marked from their titles and from the editors' introductions ([§1.4](#s1-4)).

#### <a id="s1-2-4"></a>1.2.4 Kinds

The **Kind** column sorts the orders by the main word of the title. The kinds are:
- *Church order*: Kirchenordnung (church order), Agenda das ist Kirchenordnung (agenda, that is, church
  order), Reformation, ordinatio (ordinance);
- *Agenda / liturgy*: Agende (agenda), Messe (Mass), Gottesdienst (divine service), Taufe (baptism),
  Trauung (wedding), Abendmahl (Supper), Gesang (song), Gebet (prayer), Litanei (litany), Vesper
  (Vespers), Beichte (confession), Busse (penance), Ordination;
- *Visitation*: visitation orders and recesses, general articles;
- *Consistory / synod / government*: consistory, synod, church council, superintendent, classis,
  presbytery, ministerium, church officers;
- *Marriage*, *School / university*, *Poor relief*, *Monastery / chapter*, *Appointment / oath*,
  *Confession / doctrine*, *Catechism / instruction*, *Treaty / agreement*, *Property /
  endowment*;
- *Articles / statutes*: articles, instructions, leges (laws), statutes;
- *Discipline / police*: Zucht (discipline), Polizei (police), Sonntag (Sunday), Feiertag (holy day),
  Täufer (Anabaptists), Landordnung (territorial order);
- *Mandate / decree*: Mandat (mandate), Edikt (edict), Befehl (command), Ausschreiben (circular),
  Verordnung (ordinance);
- *Local order*: an "Ordnung für" ("order for") a town or village without further description;
- *Other*.

Large church orders contain agendas, catechisms and much else besides. The Kind column gives
only the leading character of the title. Search the text in [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) for the parts of a large
order.

#### <a id="s1-2-5"></a>1.2.5 Cautions

- **Coding by territory.** The tradition codes follow the territory and its ruler. They do not
  judge each text's theology; a Lutheran territory's marriage or poor-law order is coded L.
- **Moderate Reformed and Philippist.** The orders that stood between the Lutheran and the
  Reformed are divided into two groups ([§1.3.3](#s1-3-3)):
  - **Moderate Reformed**: Bucer's Strasbourg and the Upper German Zwinglian-Bucerian cities;
    Philip of Hesse's church, which stood within the Wittenberg Concord but bore Bucer's stamp;
    Hermann von Wied's Cologne order; and the other orders of Bucer's sphere;
  - **Philippist**: the churches that held to Melanchthon's later teaching and his *Corpus
    doctrinae* (body of doctrine) and would not accept the Formula of Concord: the joint Hessian synods, Bremen,
    Nassau-Dillenburg and Anhalt, each on its way to the Reformed.

  Where an order could be placed in either group, it is counted as Moderate Reformed. Use the
  territory notes for the finer distinctions.

- **Early orders** (1522-1530) come before the confessional lines were fixed. They are coded by
  what the territory became; Müntzer's orders are coded as radical.
- **Pages and dates.** Some come from OCR of contents pages and registers. Where a register's
  page was plainly wrong, it was checked against the text; a few may still be out by a page or
  two.
- **Doc** is the [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) document holding the start page. One database record may hold several
  orders, and one order may run over several records.

---

### <a id="s1-3"></a>1.3 The traditions

#### <a id="s1-3-1"></a>1.3.1 Lutheran (L)

Orders of territories and cities that held to the Augsburg Confession in its Lutheran reading,
from the Wittenberg orders of the 1520s to the Formula of Concord and after. 1,950 texts.
Volumes 3, 5, 6/1, 6/2, 7/2.1, 11, 15, 16 and 23 are wholly Lutheran, and volume 1 is too, save
Müntzer's three orders. Lutheran orders are a minority only in volumes 8 (Hesse, coded Moderate
Reformed and Philippist), 10 (Nassau, Hanau, Ysenburg), 14 and 19/2 (Kurpfalz), 20/1
(Strasbourg) and 20/2 (Alsace).

#### <a id="s1-3-2"></a>1.3.2 Reformed (R)

Orders of churches that took the Reformed (Swiss, Calvinist or Heidelberg) confession. Most
belong to the "Second Reformation" of German territories that turned from Lutheran to Reformed
after 1560. The rest are refugee and stranger churches (French, Dutch, Walloon) and the
Swiss-allied city of Mülhausen.

- Principality of Anhalt (Sehling 2, [§1.7](#s1-7)): 3 texts, 1596-1599.
- Greater Poland (Posen): synods, the Bohemian Brethren and the towns (Sehling 4, [§1.9](#s1-9)): 3 texts,
  1560-1561.
- East Frisia: Reformed orders of limited range (Norden, Emden, Leer, Lütetsburg; London)
  (Sehling 7/1, [§1.13](#s1-13)): 15 texts, 1528-1606.
- City of Bremen (Sehling 7/2.2, [§1.15](#s1-15)): 13 texts, 1582-1616.
- Divided Hesse (1582-1618) (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 11 texts, 1600-1618.
- County of Solms (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 7 texts, 1582-1616.
- Imperial city of Frankfurt (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 2 texts, 1554-1585.
- Imperial city of Wetzlar (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 2 texts, 1586-1596.
- Nassau-Dillenburg (Sehling 10, [§1.18](#s1-18)): 14 texts, 1581-1618.
- County of Hanau-Münzenberg (Sehling 10, [§1.18](#s1-18)): 24 texts, 1596-1614.
- County of Ysenburg (Sehling 10, [§1.18](#s1-18)): 12 texts, 1580-1614.
- Upper Palatinate (Electoral Palatinate) (Sehling 13, [§1.21](#s1-21)): 13 texts, 1566-1615.
- Electoral Palatinate (Kurpfalz) (Sehling 14, [§1.22](#s1-22)): 67 texts, 1561-1615.
- Duchy of Pfalz-Zweibrücken (Sehling 18, [§1.27](#s1-27)): 13 texts, 1588-1617.
- County of Sayn (Sehling 19/1, [§1.28](#s1-28)): 3 texts, 1606-1619.
- County of Wied (Sehling 19/1, [§1.28](#s1-28)): 8 texts, 1564-1619.
- Electoral Palatinate (supplement to vol. 14) (Sehling 19/2, [§1.29](#s1-29)): 65 texts, 1577-1610.
- Principality of Pfalz-Simmern (Sehling 19/2, [§1.29](#s1-29)): 2 texts, 1598.
- Lordship of Rappoltstein (Sehling 20/2, [§1.31](#s1-31)): 10 texts, 1558-1569.
- Imperial city of Mülhausen (Mulhouse) (Sehling 20/2, [§1.31](#s1-31)): 27 texts, 1523-1582.
- County of Lippe (Sehling 21, [§1.32](#s1-32)): 1 text, 1600.
- Archbishopric of Cologne (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 2 texts, 1583.
- County of Wittgenstein (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 10 texts, 1579-1611.
- County of Moers (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 3 texts, 1581-1603.
- County of Bentheim-Tecklenburg (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 10 texts, 1601-1619.

#### <a id="s1-3-3"></a>1.3.3 Moderate Reformed (MR) and Philippist (PH)

Between the Lutheran and the Swiss Reformed stood two groups of orders. They are coded apart,
and where an order could belong to either, it is counted as Moderate Reformed.

**Moderate Reformed (MR)**, 198 texts: the Bucerian and Upper German orders, and others close to
them:
- the Upper German Reformation of Bucer, Capito, Blarer and Zwick in the southern imperial
  cities before the Interim;
- Philip of Hesse's church, which bore Bucer's stamp. Bucer had a decisive share in the orders
  of 1539, and Philip's testament gave the Wittenberg Concord, Bucer's work, almost confessional
  weight. The editors place the Kirchenordnung of 1566 in the Strasbourg sphere;
- Hermann von Wied's Cologne order (written by Bucer and Melanchthon);
- a few early evangelical orders that moved toward Zurich (Rothmann's Münster) or took their
  pastors from Basel and ended Reformed (Colmar after 1578), and East Frisia under Countess Anna
  and John a Lasco.

- East Frisia: comital orders (Sehling 7/1, [§1.13](#s1-13)): 1 text, 1545.
- Landgraviate of Hesse under Philip (to 1567) (Sehling 8, [§1.16](#s1-16)): 21 texts, 1526-1566.
- Imperial city of Frankfurt (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 4 texts, 1530-1533.
- Imperial city of Augsburg (Sehling 12, [§1.20](#s1-20)): 13 texts, 1523-1548.
- Imperial city of Lindau (Sehling 12, [§1.20](#s1-20)): 3 texts, 1533-1539.
- Imperial city of Memmingen (Sehling 12, [§1.20](#s1-20)): 4 texts, 1528-1542.
- Imperial city of Konstanz (Sehling 17/1, [§1.25](#s1-25)): 19 texts, 1524-1548.
- Imperial city of Isny (Sehling 17/1, [§1.25](#s1-25)): 2 texts, 1533-1544.
- Imperial city of Gengenbach (Sehling 17/1, [§1.25](#s1-25)): 8 texts, 1538-1545.
- Imperial city of Ulm (Sehling 17/2, [§1.26](#s1-26)): 15 texts, 1528-1544.
- Imperial city of Esslingen (Sehling 17/2, [§1.26](#s1-26)): 34 texts, 1531-1547.
- Imperial city of Biberach an der Riß (Sehling 17/2, [§1.26](#s1-26)): 3 texts, 1531-1548.
- Imperial city of Landau (Sehling 19/1, [§1.28](#s1-28)): 5 texts, 1526-1554.
- Imperial city of Worms (Sehling 19/1, [§1.28](#s1-28)): 3 texts, 1524-1543.
- Imperial city of Strasbourg (Sehling 20/1, [§1.30](#s1-30)): 46 texts, 1523-1548.
- Imperial city of Colmar (Sehling 20/2, [§1.31](#s1-31)): 12 texts, 1578-1615.
- Archbishopric of Cologne (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 1 text, 1546.
- City of Münster (Sehling 22, [§1.33](#s1-33)): 4 texts, 1532-1533.

**Philippist (PH)**, 33 texts: churches that held to Melanchthon's later teaching and his
*Corpus doctrinae* (body of doctrine) of 1560, and would not accept the Formula of Concord. Most of them later
turned Reformed:
- the joint synods of the Hessian landgraviates (1568-1582), which took the Wittenberg *Corpus
  doctrinae* as their norm, and the Hessian orders that followed to 1598;
- Bremen, from Albert Hardenberg's dispute (1556) to the Reformed turn of 1580;
- Nassau-Dillenburg's Agende of 1575, which binds the pastors to the Augsburg Confession and the
  *Examen* (examination) of Philip Melanchthon;
- Anhalt under Prince Johann Georg before the Reformed turn of 1596.

- Principality of Anhalt (Sehling 2, [§1.7](#s1-7)): 2 texts, 1590-1594.
- City of Bremen (Sehling 7/2.2, [§1.15](#s1-15)): 9 texts, 1556-1575.
- The Hessian landgraviates: joint synods and orders (1567-1582) (Sehling 8, [§1.16](#s1-16)): 16 texts,
  1568-1582.
- Divided Hesse (1582-1618) (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 5 texts, 1574-1598.
- Nassau-Dillenburg (Sehling 10, [§1.18](#s1-18)): 1 text, 1575.

#### <a id="s1-3-4"></a>1.3.4 Anglican (A)

One order in the set is Anglican: the "Old Discipline" and "New Discipline" of the English exile
congregation at Frankfurt (1557). It was founded in 1554 by Marian exiles under Whittingham and
John Knox. In 1555 a second group under Richard Cox, loyal to the Book of Common Prayer, took
the lead and drove Knox out. **Frankfurt, editor's introduction** (Sehling 9, p. 492):

<!-- doc 2331 -->

Although, after the departure of Knox's faction, the English congregation was thoroughly
Anglican in character, the New Discipline shows traits of congregational development within the
existing framework of the Second Book of Common Prayer.

- Imperial city of Frankfurt (Sehling 9, [§1.17](#s1-17)): 1 text, 1557.

Sehling calls the congregation "englisch-reformiert". It is coded A here because the editor
shows that its order was framed within the Prayer Book.

Two related orders are coded R:
- the order of John a Lasco's Dutch stranger church in London under Edward VI, in Micron's
  German abridgement (Sehling 7/1, p. 579);
- the French Reformed congregation's *Liturgia sacra* (Sacred Liturgy) of 1554 at Frankfurt (Sehling 9, p. 562).
  Frankfurt also required the English congregation to use it.

#### <a id="s1-3-5"></a>1.3.5 Hussite: the Bohemian Brethren (H), and the Sandomierz consensus (C)

The Hussite tradition reaches the set through the Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum) in
Greater Poland. **Greater Poland, Sehling's introduction** (Sehling 4, p. 248):

<!-- doc 1845 -->

In Poland both the Lutheran and the Reformed teaching spread at the same time. Alongside them
arose congregations of the Bohemian Brethren in large numbers.

The Brethren had united with the Little Polish Reformed at Koźminek in 1555. In 1570, at
Sandomierz, they joined with the Reformed and the Lutherans in a common Consensus. Sehling
prints the Ostroróg privilege because of the town's place in the Unity. **Greater Poland,
Sehling's introduction** (Sehling 4, p. 254):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

Since Ostroróg was the chief congregation of the Unity and the seat of the senior, this
privilege shall be printed from a translation kindly placed at my disposal.

The Brethren (H):
- Greater Poland (Posen): synods, the Bohemian Brethren and the towns (Sehling 4, [§1.9](#s1-9)): 3 texts,
  1569-1616.
  - Kirchenordnung der Böhmischen Brüder (1616; Sehling 4, p. 273).
  - Privileg für Lissa (1580; Sehling 4, p. 298).
  - Privileg für Ostrorog (1569; Sehling 4, p. 299).

The Sandomierz consensus and its general synods (C):
- Synode von Sendomir (1570; Sehling 4, p. 257).
- Synode von Posen (1570; Sehling 4, p. 258).
- Synode von Krakau (1573; Sehling 4, p. 260).
- Synode von Petrikau (1578; Sehling 4, p. 262).
- Synode von Wladislaw (1583; Sehling 4, p. 263).
- Synode von Thorn (1595; Sehling 4, p. 265).

The synods of Xions (1560) and Pińczów (1561) belong to the Little Polish Reformed church united
with the Brethren, and are coded R. The Lutheran synod of Gostyń (1565) and the town orders of
Fraustadt are coded L.

The Brethren's order of 1616 was adopted by their general synod at Zerawitz in Moravia; Sehling
prints it for the Polish congregations. No Utraquist order is in the set.

#### <a id="s1-3-6"></a>1.3.6 Others

- **Roman Catholic humanist, Erasmian reform (RCH).** The church orders of Duke Johann III of
  Jülich-Cleves-Berg (1532/33) and their successors. They reform the old church on humanist
  lines without leaving it (Sehling 21; [§1.32.1](#s1-32-1)).
- **Multi-confessional diet decrees (T).** The decrees of the Transylvanian diets (1552-1619)
  regulate a principality that received the Lutheran, Reformed, Unitarian and Catholic religions
  side by side. The Transylvanian Saxons' own orders are Lutheran. The *Consensus doctrinae* of
  1557 is also coded L (Sehling 24; [§1.35](#s1-35)).
- **Radical Reformation (RAD).** Thomas Müntzer's German church office, German evangelical Mass
  and order of the German service at Allstedt (1523/24). They are coded apart from the Lutheran
  orders around them in vol. 1.
- **Anabaptist (ANA).** The Münster council and guild masters' mandate of 31 January 1534, three
  weeks before the Anabaptist council was elected. It bound the citizens to let each keep his
  faith, and so recognized the Anabaptists as a religious group in the city
  (Sehling 22, p. 363). It is not an order made by Anabaptists: no Anabaptist church order is in
  the set.
- **Roman Catholic (RC).** Bishop Franz von Waldeck's edict of 3 February 1534 against the
  "damned heresy and sect of the Anabaptists" (Sehling 22, p. 364).
- **Groups with no order in the set.** There are no orders of the Waldensians (named only in
  passing, by Luther and in the editors' notes), the Lollards, the Utraquists, the
  Schwenckfelders, the Hutterites, the Mennonites or the Antitrinitarians. Mandates against
  Anabaptists, Schwenckfelders, Davidjorists, Mennonites and "Sakramentierer" are coded by the
  authority that issued them: Lutheran, Reformed, Moderate Reformed or, in Jülich, Roman
  Catholic humanist.
- **Treaty (R/L).** The East Frisian Delfzijl settlement of 1595 and the Concordats of 1599,
  between the Lutheran count and Reformed Emden.

### <a id="s1-4"></a>1.4 The Interim orders

The Augsburg Interim of 1548 imposed a largely Catholic order on the Protestant estates until a
final council, allowing only the chalice and clerical marriage. The Leipzig Interim (1548/49)
was Electoral Saxony's milder version. As [§1.2.2](#s1-2-2) shows, Sehling meant to print no Interim orders.
Those in the set fall into four groups:
- **Interim order**: an order made to put the Interim into effect, or to adapt a territory's
  order to it;
- **under the Interim**: a text issued while the Interim was in force, not itself an Interim
  order;
- **on the Interim**: a text about the Interim, such as a response, a settlement or a protest;
- **after the Interim** or **end of the Interim**: a text that ends or repairs it.

Several orders of the set are **described but not printed** because they are Interim orders:
- the Saxon (Leipzig) Interim agenda of 1549 (Sehling 1, p. 102; Sehling 2, pp. 501-505);
- the planned Hamburg Interim church order (Sehling 5, p. 484);
- the Brandenburg Interim order (Sehling 3, pp. 12, 177);
- the Göttingen "church order under the Interim" of 1550 (Sehling 6/2, p. 904);
- the Nuremberg Interim agenda (Sehling 11, pp. 328, 482);
- the Augsburg Interim forms (Sehling 12, p. 28);
- the draft of a Prussian church order "on the basis of the Interim" (Sehling 4, p. 22).

Some cities kept Interim usages long after 1552. Schwäbisch Hall kept its Interim order until
1559 (Sehling 17/1, p. 34), and in Ansbach-Kulmbach the Mass vestment stayed "as a remnant of the Interim time" (Sehling 11, p. 292).

## <a id="ch2"></a>Chapter 2. The Order of the Mass


This chapter compares the **order of the Mass** (*ordo missae*, *Ordnung des Amts*, *Ordnung des
Nachtmahls*) in the evangelical church orders printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen
Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century). Other chapters of this book treat the parts of the
Mass one by one. This chapter puts them back together. It asks:
- **The whole ordo.** What sequence of parts did each order prescribe, from the opening to the
  dismissal? Which orders kept the shape of the Roman Mass, and which built a new service around
  the sermon?
- **Families.** Which orders copied which? Where do the main types of evangelical Mass come
  from?
- **The ordinaries.** What happened to the fixed parts (the Kyrie, Gloria, Creed, Sanctus and
  Agnus Dei), and to the fixed dialogues and formulas around them (the salutation, the Preface
  dialogue, the Pax, the *Ite missa est* [Go, it is the dismissal])? In particular:
  - Was the Kyrie sung three, four or nine times? Were the old seasonal Kyrie chants kept?
  - Who intoned the Gloria and the Creed? Which creed was sung?
  - Was the Sanctus sung with or without the Benedictus, and where did it fall?
  - How many times was the Agnus Dei sung, and how did it end?
  - What took the place of the *Ite missa est*?
- **The service without communicants.** What remained of the Mass when nobody came to the Lord's
  Table?

**How the chapter is laid out.**
- [§2.1](#s2-1) summarizes the findings, and [§2.2](#s2-2) sets out the scope, the method and what was not found.
- [§2.3](#s2-3) sets the baselines: the Roman ordo, and Luther's *Formula missae* (1523) and *Deutsche
  Messe* (1526).
- [§2.4](#s2-4) describes the families of evangelical ordo, and [§2.5](#s2-5) compares them in a table.
- §§[2.6](#s2-6)–[2.13](#s2-13) take the ordinaries and fixed formulas in order: Kyrie ([§2.6](#s2-6)), Gloria ([§2.7](#s2-7)), salutation,
  collect and Pax ([§2.8](#s2-8)), Creed ([§2.9](#s2-9)), Preface and Sanctus ([§2.10](#s2-10)), the Lord's Prayer and the Words
  of Institution ([§2.11](#s2-11)), Agnus Dei ([§2.12](#s2-12)), and the dismissal and blessing ([§2.13](#s2-13)).
- [§2.14](#s2-14) deals with the Sunday service when nobody communicated.
- [§2.15](#s2-15) gathers the ceremonial: the sign of the cross, kneeling, bowing, hats, hands, turning,
  places at the altar, the kiss of peace and incense.
- [§2.16](#s2-16) is a concordance of the orders quoted.

**Related chapters.** This chapter refers to the others constantly. They hold the detail:
- the opening versicles, the confession and absolution, and the exhortation to communicants:
  [Chapter 3](#ch3);
- the introit, the lessons, the gradual, alleluia and sequence, the offertory, the Proper
  Prefaces and the communion chant: [Chapter 4](#ch4);
- the collect, the secret and the postcommunion: [Chapter 5](#ch5);
- the hymns sung in each slot, including the German, troped and paraphrased ordinaries ("Allein
  Gott", "Wir glauben all", "Jesaia dem Propheten", "Christe du Lamm Gottes"):
  [Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.6](#s8-6)–[8.15](#s8-15);
- the canon, the Words of Institution and the elevation, order by order, in the early German
  Masses and their successors: [Chapter 7](#ch7);
- the sermon, its place and its length: [Chapter 11](#ch11);
- the general prayer of the church: [Chapter 6](#ch6);
- the Litany and the bidding prayers at the Mass:
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22](#s13-22);
- the organ in alternation with the choir:
  [Chapter 9](#ch9), [§9.3](#s9-3);
- vestments, lights and the elevation as marks of the feast:
  [Chapter 14](#ch14) and
  [Chapter 12](#ch12), [§12.10](#s12-10).

### <a id="s2-1"></a>2.1 Summary of findings

**1. Two baselines, not one** ([§2.3](#s2-3)). Luther left two Masses, and the orders descend from both.
- **The *Formula missae* (1523)**: the Latin Mass with the offertory and canon cut and the Words
  of Institution sung in the Preface; the ordinaries kept "with various melodies for the various
  seasons"; *Benedicamus* for *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal).
- **The *Deutsche Messe* (1526)**: German hymns for the introit and the chants; the Kyrie three
  times "and not nine"; no Gloria; a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer and an exhortation for the
  Preface; the bread and cup given separately after their words.

**2. Seven families of ordo** ([§2.4](#s2-4)).
- **Saxon** (Wittenberg 1533, Saxony 1539, 1580): the Latin school Mass with German pieces
  grafted on; Preface only on feasts or not at all.
- **Bugenhagen's northern Mass** (Braunschweig 1528 to Mecklenburg 1552): Latin and German side
  by side; Preface, Sanctus and exhortation optional; "after the Amen nothing more is sung".
- **Franconian** (Nürnberg 1533, Hof 1592): no Preface; the epistle and gospel read as chapters
  in course; **the Sanctus after the Words of Institution**, then the Lord's Prayer and the Pax.
- **Prussian** (1525): the Words of Institution sung in the Preface; Kyrie in three tongues;
  Agnus Dei twice.
- **The Latin frame** (Brandenburg 1540, Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, the Palatinate 1546, Breslau 1557):
  Preface dialogue, Pax and threefold Agnus kept; Breslau even kept *Ite missa est*.
- **Upper German** (Württemberg 1553, Strasbourg 1598, both Lutheran): the sermon service with
  the Supper added; no Kyrie, Gloria, Preface, Sanctus or Agnus.
- **Reformed** (Palatinate 1563, Bentheim-Tecklenburg 1588, both Reformed): the Supper form read
  at the table, the Apostles' Creed, the breaking of bread.

**3. Kyrie: three, four or nine; never seven** ([§2.6.1](#s2-6-1)). Luther's "three times and not nine"
became the parish norm. Nine survived for feasts and choirs (Wittenberg 1533; Pomerania 1542). A
fourfold Kyrie (Kyrie, Christe, Kyrie, Kyrie) comes from Müntzer (1524, Radical Reformation) and
survives in Calenberg-Göttingen 1542 and the Hessian *Agende* of 1574 (Philippist).
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel (1543) allows "three times, four times or nine times" in figured music
"at the schoolmaster's pleasure", but three plainly "in the name of the Father and of the Son
and of the Holy Ghost". No sevenfold Kyrie is found.

**4. The seasonal Kyrie chants survived** ([§2.6.2](#s2-6-2)). The orders with Latin schools kept the
medieval cycle by name: *dominicale* (Sunday [Kyrie]), *angelicum* (angelic [Kyrie]), *paschale* (Easter [Kyrie]), *Fons bonitatis* (Fount of goodness), *Magne Deus* (Great God),
*summum* (the highest [chant]), *minus summum* (the lesser summum), *apostolicum* (apostles' [Kyrie]), *de martyribus* (of martyrs), *de virginibus* (of virgins; Buxtehude 1565;
Pomerania 1542; Nördlingen 1544; Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557; Hof 1592, with the matching Gloria,
Sanctus and Agnus "of the season").

**5. Gloria: the festal companion of the Kyrie** ([§2.7](#s2-7)). Not after "the plain Kyrie" (Wittenberg
1533); "at times and not always" (Pomerania 1535). Where kept, the priest intoned, the scholars
sang *Et in terra* (And on earth) "and no more", the people sang "Allein Gott" (To God alone), and the scholars and organ
finished the Latin (Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543).

**6. Creed: three layers, and two creeds** ([§2.9](#s2-9)). The priest intoned *Credo in unum Deum* (I believe in one God), the
scholars sang the Latin *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), and the people "Wir glauben all" (We all believe; Wittenberg 1533 and most
Saxon and northern orders). Prussia (1525) forbade the priest's intonation. Which creed ([§2.9.4](#s2-9-4)):
- **Nicene only**: the Saxon, Bugenhagen and Franconian orders, in Latin, in German verse by
  verse (Braunschweig 1528, Hamburg 1529), or as "Wir glauben" (We believe).
- **Apostles' only**:
    - Strasbourg 1524 (Moderate Reformed), sung after the sermon, "the great *Patrem* … sung by
      some";
  - the Goslar foundation 1534;
  - the Upper German pulpit (Württemberg 1553);
    - the Reformed Supper (Frankfurt's French church 1554 and the Palatinate 1563, both
      Reformed).
- **A free choice**: Hesse 1574 (Philippist; the Apostles' Creed, Luther's paraphrase, or the
  Nicene); Kurland 1570.
- **By occasion**:
    - Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed): the Apostles' Creed every Sunday, the Nicene or Athanasian
      on the feasts of Christ;
  - Rothenberg 1618: "Wir glauben" on Sundays, the Apostles' Creed on other feasts;
  - Prussia 1568 and Feuchtwangen 1563: the Latin Nicene and the German creed on alternate
    Sundays.

**7. The Preface was optional; the Sanctus moved** ([§2.10](#s2-10)). The Preface was required in only a few
orders, festal or optional in most, absent in the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass), Nürnberg, Albertine Saxony
1580 and Württemberg. The Sanctus stood in five places: before the Verba, after the Verba with
or without a Preface, during the distribution, or nowhere. The Latin Sanctus kept its
*Benedictus*; Luther's "Jesaia dem Propheten" (To Isaiah the prophet) lost it; the Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel Trinitarian
Sanctus kept it with the Hebrew *Hosianna* (Hosanna).

**8. The Lord's Prayer and the Verba in seven sequences** ([§2.11](#s2-11)): the Lord's Prayer before the
Verba, after them, paraphrased in the exhortation, sung as a hymn before the confession, or said
inside a prayer before the creed. The bread and cup were given separately after their own words
in the *Deutsche Messe*, Prussia 1544 and the Saxon villages.

**9. Agnus Dei: three, two or one** ([§2.12](#s2-12)). Three, as of old (Brandenburg 1540; Regensburg;
Luther's German "Christe du Lamm Gottes" [Christ, thou Lamb of God] with "Give us thy peace" the third time). **Two**
in Prussia 1525 and Livonia 1533, "for brevity's sake", the first ending *miserere nobis* (have mercy upon us) and
the second *dona nobis pacem* (grant us peace). **Once** in the Albertine *Cellische Ordnungen* (1545). It stood
before, during or after the distribution.

**10. No *Ite missa est*; Benedicamus or nothing; Aaronic, Trinitarian or both** ([§2.13](#s2-13)).
- **The *Ite missa est***: kept only at Breslau (1557, beside the *Benedicamus*) and in the
  Ansbach visitation of 1536.
- **The *Benedicamus***, in its place:
  - in Latin, in the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) and the Franconian, Pfalz-Neuburg, Regensburg, Hohenlohe,
    Henneberg and Transylvanian orders;
    - in German, in the early German Masses (Müntzer (Radical Reformation), Erfurt, Lippe, Worms
      and Strasbourg (both Moderate Reformed)) and at Hof in 1592.
- **Neither**: the *Deutsche Messe* and most Saxon, Bugenhagen and Upper German orders end with
  the collect and the blessing.
- **The blessing**:
  - the Aaronic blessing is the rule;
    - Worms and Strasbourg (1524, both Moderate Reformed) and Regensburg (1542) used a
      Trinitarian blessing alone;
    - Strasbourg (1524, Moderate Reformed) put both together;
  - Brandenburg-Nürnberg (1533) offered four forms (Numbers 6, Psalm 67 and two Trinitarian), a
    set copied by a dozen orders;
  - Prussia (1525) sang Psalm 67 on feasts and the Aaronic blessing on ordinary days;
  - Strasbourg (1598) closed the sermon with the Trinitarian blessing and the Supper with both.

**11. Without communicants, no Mass** ([§2.14](#s2-14)). The service stopped after the sermon with a psalm,
a collect and the blessing (Pomerania 1535; Mecklenburg 1552; Saxony 1580), or fell back to an
office of psalm, chapter, creed and suffrages (Transylvania 1547). Hof kept a Mass-shaped daily
service for its schoolboys, with the Kyrie, Sanctus and Agnus of the season and no communion.

**12. Few rubrics, and kneeling the chief gesture** ([§2.15](#s2-15)).
- **Sign of the cross.** It was still printed in the early German Masses: over bread and cup at
  Allstedt 1523 (Müntzer, Radical Reformation), and at the greeting and the blessing at
  Strasbourg 1524 (Moderate Reformed). Hof printed it at the Pax and the blessing in 1592.
  Elsewhere it was let go: "so many crosses" at Hannover 1536, and "without all papistical
  crossing" at Danzig 1557.
- **Kneeling, never genuflection.** No order knows the Roman genuflection. The priest kneels at
  the preparation and after communion. The people kneel at the Kyrie (Schwäbisch Hall 1527), at
  the Lord's Prayer before the Verba (Hall 1535) and at the thanksgiving. Communicants kneel at
  the altar. The Polish synods of the Sandomierz consensus (1578, 1583) allowed standing or
  kneeling but forbade sitting. Calvinizing Nassau (1575, Philippist) warned against "folded
  hands and bending of the knee" as to an idol.
- **Other gestures.**
  - Bows survive only in the Latin canons (Brandenburg 1540).
    - Men are bareheaded and women covered (Hesse 1566, Moderate Reformed).
  - Nothing is said of the celebrant's hands beyond what they hold.
  - The minister turns to the altar to pray and to the people to read, greet and exhort. Döber
    (1525) said everything toward the people.
- **Not found.** No epistle or gospel horn, no turn over the right shoulder, no *orans* or
  joined hands, no kiss of altar, book or deacon, no biretta rubric, no incense and no *Lavabo*.
  Strasbourg (1542, Moderate Reformed) replaced the kiss of peace with a reading on
  reconciliation.

---

### <a id="s2-2"></a>2.2 Scope, sources and method

#### <a id="s2-2-1"></a>2.2.1 Sources and searches

The chapter draws on the full text of the Sehling edition in [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb). Two searches were made:
- **Full ordos.** Every passage was found in which, within about 5,000 characters, the order
  names at least thirteen of the parts of the Mass (introit, Kyrie, Gloria, collect, epistle,
  gradual or sequence, gospel, creed, sermon, exhortation, Preface, Sanctus, Lord's Prayer,
  Words of Institution, Agnus Dei, distribution, thanksgiving, blessing). These passages, about
  forty in all, were read in full, and the representative ones are compared in §§[2.4](#s2-4)–[2.5](#s2-5).
- **The ordinaries.** The corpus was searched for:
  - the Kyrie near the words for numbers (*drei*, *dreimal*, *neun*, *vier*, *sieben*, *ter*,
    *novies*, *semel*, *einmal*), and for runs of printed acclamations, which were counted;
  - the named Kyrie chants (*dominicale*, *angelicum*, *paschale*, *Fons bonitatis*, *Magne
    Deus*, *summum*, *apostolicum*, *de martyribus* and the rest);
  - the Agnus Dei near the same number words and near *dona nobis pacem* (grant us peace), *miserere nobis* (have mercy upon us), *gib
    uns deinen Frieden* (give us thy peace);
  - *Benedictus qui venit* (Blessed is he that cometh), *Osanna* (Hosanna), *Hosianna* (Hosanna);
  - *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal), *Benedicamus*;
  - *symbolum apostolicum* (Apostles' Creed), *Nicenum* (Nicene [Creed]), *Athanasii* (Athanasius's [creed]) near the Mass and its parts.

Pages were checked against Sehling's running heads, which often correct the database's record
headings. One attribution was corrected in the course of the
work: the Breslau account of the Sunday Mass and of the hours of the Passion is a report of
1557, not an order of 1550 (Sehling 3, pp. 404–405), and [Chapter 10](#ch10)
has been amended accordingly.

#### <a id="s2-2-2"></a>2.2.2 What was not found

- **No sevenfold Kyrie.** The counts in the corpus are three, four and nine ([§2.6.1](#s2-6-1)). No order
  prescribes seven or six acclamations.
- **No order that kept the offertory or the canon** as the priest's prayer of sacrifice. What
  the Latin-frame orders kept is described in
  [Chapter 7](#ch7).
