- **No evangelical Mass without communicants** ([§2.14](#s2-14)), except the Hof schoolboys' daily exercise,
  which has no consecration.
- **No fixed Lutheran ordo.** Even within a family the orders allow the minister to drop the
  Gloria, the Preface, the Sanctus or the exhortation "when it will grow too long". The tables
  give the full form each order prescribes; few churches will have sung all of it every Sunday.

---

### <a id="s2-3"></a>2.3 The baselines: the Roman ordo and Luther's two Masses

#### <a id="s2-3-1"></a>2.3.1 The Roman ordo in outline

**What the reformers inherited.** The orders measure themselves against the late medieval Roman
Mass, which they call *die messe* (the Mass), *das ampt* (the office) or *die hohe messe* (the high Mass). In outline it ran:
1. the priest's preparation at the altar (*Introibo*, Psalm 43, *Confiteor*);
2. introit, Kyrie (nine acclamations), Gloria;
3. salutation and collect(s);
4. epistle, gradual, alleluia or tract, sequence;
5. gospel, Nicene Creed (intoned by the priest, continued by the choir);
6. offertory and offertory prayers, the secret;
7. Preface dialogue (*Dominus vobiscum*, *Sursum corda*, *Gratias agamus*), Preface, Sanctus
   with Benedictus;
8. the canon, with the Words of Institution said silently and the elevation;
9. Lord's Prayer with its introduction (*Praeceptis salutaribus*) and embolism (*Libera nos*),
   the fraction, the Pax ("The peace of the Lord be always with you"), Agnus Dei (three times, the third
   ending *dona nobis pacem* [grant us peace]);
10. communion, communion chant, postcommunion;
11. *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal; or *Benedicamus Domino* [Let us bless the Lord] when there was no Gloria), blessing.

The sermon had no fixed place in the Roman Mass. Every evangelical order gave it one.

#### <a id="s2-3-2"></a>2.3.2 *Formula missae*, 1523: the Latin Mass purged

**Keep the ordinaries, cut the sacrifice.** Luther's Latin order of 1523 kept almost everything
before the creed "because it is ours and free". It cut the offertory and the canon, and moved
the Words of Institution into the Preface. The ordinaries stayed, sung by the choir "with
various melodies for the various seasons". **Wittenberg, Luther, *Formula missae*, 1523**
(Sehling 1, p. 5):

<!-- doc 2 -->

Secondly, the Kyrie eleison, as it hath been celebrated hitherto, with various melodies for the
various seasons, we embrace, together with the angelic hymn following, *Gloria in excelsis*; yet
it shall stand in the bishop's judgment how often he will have it left out.

The rest of the order is described in [Chapter 7](#ch7),
[§7.3](#s7-3). In outline (Sehling 1, pp. 5–6):
- introit, Kyrie, Gloria, one collect, epistle;
- a gradual of two verses with the alleluia; no sequences but *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks), *Sancti
  Spiritus* and *Veni sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit), at the bishop's pleasure;
- gospel, the Nicene Creed ("not displeasing" if sung, but at the bishop's choice), and the
  sermon either after the creed or before the introit;
- the preparation of bread and wine "during the creed or after", in the
  accustomed manner;
- *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you), *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts), the Preface, and the Words of Institution sung in the
  Preface tone;
- the Sanctus, with the elevation during the Benedictus;
- the Lord's Prayer, without the *Libera nos* (Deliver us), the fraction or the commixture, then at once *Pax
  Domini* (The peace of the Lord), "a kind of public absolution";
- the communion during the Agnus Dei; the postcommunion *Quod ore sumpsimus* (What we have taken with our mouth) or *Corpus tuum* (Thy body);
- *Benedicamus Domino* (Let us bless the Lord) for *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal), and the blessing.

The last item is Luther's replacement for the dismissal. **Wittenberg, Luther, *Formula missae*,
1523** (Sehling 1, p. 6):

<!-- doc 2 -->

In the place of *Ite missa* let *Benedicamus Domino* be said, with alleluia added (where and
when it pleaseth) in its melodies; or let the *Benedicamus* be borrowed from Vespers. Eighthly,
let the accustomed blessing be given. Or let that of Numbers 6 be taken, which the Lord himself
set in order, saying: "The Lord bless us and keep us, the Lord show us his face and have mercy
upon us, the Lord turn his face unto us and give us peace." Or that of Psalm 96 [67]: "God, even
our own God, shall bless us; God shall bless us, and all the ends of the earth shall fear him.
Amen."

#### <a id="s2-3-3"></a>2.3.3 *Deutsche Messe*, 1526: the German Mass for the people

**Three Kyries, German hymns, the Verba with the distribution.** The *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) made a
different shape, for the parishes. A German psalm or hymn stood for the introit; the Kyrie was
cut to three acclamations; the Gloria was gone; a German hymn followed the epistle and "Wir
glauben all" (We all believe) the gospel; the Preface was replaced by a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer and an
exhortation; the Words of Institution were sung, the bread given after the words over the bread
and the cup after the words over the cup, with German hymns during each; and the service ended
with a collect and the Aaronic blessing (Sehling 1, pp. 14–16). Of the Kyrie it says.
**Wittenberg, Luther, *Deutsche Messe und ordnung gottis diensts*, 1526** (Sehling 1, p. 14):

<!-- doc 3 -->

Thereupon the Kyrie eleison, also in the same tone, three times and not nine times, as
followeth: Kyrie eleison.

The German Sanctus "Jesaia dem Propheten" (To Isaiah the prophet) and "Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) belong to the
distribution and its close (§§[2.10](#s2-10), [2.12](#s2-12); [Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.12](#s8-12),
[8.15](#s8-15)).

#### <a id="s2-3-4"></a>2.3.4 The three side by side

| Part | Roman Mass | *Formula missae* 1523 | *Deutsche Messe* 1526 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opening | *Introibo* (I will go in), *Confiteor* (I confess) | (priest's private preparation, unregulated) | — |
| Introit | Latin antiphon and psalm | Latin, Sunday and feast introits | German psalm or hymn |
| Kyrie | ninefold, seasonal chant | "various melodies for various seasons" | threefold, "not nine times" |
| Gloria | Sundays and feasts | kept; bishop may omit | omitted |
| Collect | one or more | one only | one, in German |
| Epistle | sung | sung | read facing the people |
| Between the readings | gradual, alleluia, tract, sequence | gradual of two verses, alleluia; few sequences | German hymn |
| Gospel | sung | sung | read facing the people |
| Creed | Nicene, Latin | Nicene, at the bishop's choice | "Wir glauben all" (We all believe) |
| Sermon | — | after the creed or before the introit | after the creed |
| Offertory, secret | yes | cut | cut |
| Preface | yes | yes, with the Verba in the Preface tone | replaced by paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer and exhortation |
| Sanctus | with Benedictus, before the canon | after the Verba, elevation during Benedictus | German Sanctus during the distribution |
| Canon | yes | cut | cut |
| Lord's Prayer | after the canon | after the Sanctus | paraphrased before the Verba |
| Pax | before the Agnus | after the Lord's Prayer, as absolution | — |
| Agnus Dei | three times, before communion | during communion | German Agnus after the cup |
| Postcommunion | yes | *Quod ore* (What with our mouth) or *Corpus tuum* (Thy body) | German collect |
| Dismissal | *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal) | *Benedicamus Domino* (Let us bless the Lord) | — |
| Blessing | yes | usual, or Num 6, or Ps 67 | Num 6 |

---

### <a id="s2-4"></a>2.4 The families of evangelical ordo

**Seven shapes.** The orders fall into families. Within each, later orders copy earlier ones,
often word for word. The families differ less in what they cut than in where they put what they
kept: the sermon, the Preface and Sanctus, the Lord's Prayer and the Words of Institution.

#### <a id="s2-4-1"></a>2.4.1 The Saxon Mass: Latin and German together

**Wittenberg and the Albertine orders.** The Wittenberg town order of 1533, Duke Henry's order
of 1539 and the Albertine *Kirchenordnung* (church order) of 1580 keep the Latin Mass of the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass)
for the school and graft the German pieces of the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) on to it. The common pattern:
- introit (Latin, or a German psalm), Kyrie, Gloria with the Latin *Et in terra* (And on earth);
- a German collect, the epistle sung or read in German facing the people;
- an alleluia, sequence or German hymn;
- the gospel in German; the priest intones *Credo in unum Deum* (I believe in one God), the scholars sing the Latin
  *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), and the people "Wir glauben all" (We all believe);
- the sermon; then, for the communicants, the paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer and the
  exhortation from the *Deutsche Messe* (Saxony 1539, 1580), or the Lord's Prayer sung
  (Wittenberg 1533);
- the Words of Institution sung in German;
- the distribution, with the Latin Agnus Dei and the German Sanctus, "Jesus Christus unser
  Heiland" (Jesus Christ our Saviour), "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) and Psalm 111;
- "Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God), a German collect, the Aaronic blessing.

The Preface survives here only for the feasts. At Wittenberg "the Preface may well often be left
out, that we may the more diligently attend to the Lord's Supper, for that alone is the matter"
(Sehling 1, p. 704). Duke Henry's order allows a Latin Preface "on the feasts, and now and then
on Sundays" (Sehling 1, p. 274). The Albertine order of 1580 has none (Sehling 1, pp. 368–369).
On the Saxon Kyrie and Creed see §§[2.6](#s2-6), [2.9](#s2-9).

#### <a id="s2-4-2"></a>2.4.2 Bugenhagen's northern Mass

**Braunschweig, Hamburg, Lübeck, Pomerania, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, Mecklenburg.**
Bugenhagen's orders (Braunschweig 1528, Hamburg 1529, Lübeck 1531, Pomerania 1535, Denmark 1537,
Schleswig-Holstein 1542, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543) and the Mecklenburg order of 1552 make
the Mass of the northern towns. Its marks:
- a confession and absolution, or a prayer at the altar, before the introit (Mecklenburg 1552,
  Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543: [Chapter 3](#ch3),
  [§3.4](#s3-4));
- Kyrie and Gloria in Latin or German, the Gloria "at times and not always" (Pomerania 1535);
- the creed intoned by the priest, the Latin *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed) sung "*dominicaliter*, in full", then "Wir
  glauben" (We believe; Pomerania 1535, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543, Mecklenburg 1552);
- the sermon, with the general prayer at its end;
- a Preface and Sanctus that are allowed but not required;
- the exhortation to the communicants, the Lord's Prayer and the Words of Institution sung
  together;
- the distribution with "O Lamm Gottes" (O Lamb of God), "Jesus Christus" (Jesus Christ [our Saviour]), "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) or Psalm 111;
  "Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) after it; a collect and the Aaronic blessing.

The Pomeranian order puts the Preface, the Sanctus and the exhortation at the minister's
discretion, and allows him to go straight from the sermon hymn to the Lord's Prayer "as is also
done at Wittenberg". **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 341):

<!-- doc 1856 -->

Then the Preface is sung in Latin, but not always, rather when one will, especially at the high
feasts, with the Sanctus in Latin or German; and thereafter the exhortation concerning the
sacrament is read, briefly. Long singing, wherein some priests have pleasure, shall for this
cause be avoided: that such Christian and wholesome ceremonies may remain pleasant to the people
and not grow wearisome, and that the people also be exhorted to remain there gladly until the
last benediction or blessing. Therefore, when the people after the sermon have sung the German
song, the priest may at times and often let all the rest stand over, even the exhortation or
confession, that this be not too long and wearisome, and begin straightway: Let us pray, Our
Father, etc., as is also kept at Wittenberg.

The Mecklenburg order of 1552 is the fullest of the family, and gives the Latin text and notes
of the creed and the Preface (§§[2.9](#s2-9), [2.10](#s2-10)).

#### <a id="s2-4-3"></a>2.4.3 The Franconian Mass: Nürnberg and Brandenburg-Ansbach

**A Mass without a Preface.** The Brandenburg-Nürnberg order of 1533 and its descendants (the
Nürnberg agendas, Hof 1592) keep the Latin ordinaries for the schools but make the communion its
own action, "the order of the Lord's Supper", after the sermon. Its marks:
- the priest says a *Confiteor* (I confess) privately and reads the introit, the Kyrie and the *Et in
  terra* (And on earth), which the scholars sing in Latin or the people in German;
- *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) and one or more German collects;
- the epistle and gospel read as chapters in course, "the first chapter of the epistle to the
  Romans" and so on, not the Sunday pericopes ([Chapter 4](#ch4), [§4.5](#s4-5));
- the Credo sung in Latin by the scholars, or "Wir glauben" (We believe) by the people; the sermon;
- no Preface: the exhortation, then the Words of Institution sung;
- **the Sanctus after the Words of Institution**, then the Lord's Prayer with its old Latin
  introduction, and the Pax;
- the distribution during the Agnus Dei; collect; *Benedicamus*; one of several blessings.

**Brandenburg-Nürnberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1533** (Sehling 11, pp. 196–197):

<!-- doc 270 -->

Thereafter followeth the Sanctus in Latin or German. Thereupon straightway: *Oremus, praeceptis
salutaribus moniti et divina institutione formati, audemus dicere: Pater noster.* (Let us pray. Taught by saving precepts and formed by divine institution, we make bold to say: Our Father.) […] Thereafter
straightway: *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you), etc., or else in German, as it is noted
hereafter.

The order of Hof (1592) keeps the Franconian shape, but moves the Lord's Prayer and the Pax
before the Words of Institution, and sings the Sanctus and Agnus Dei of the season during the
distribution (Sehling 11, pp. 425–426).

#### <a id="s2-4-4"></a>2.4.4 The Prussian Mass of 1525: the Words of Institution in the Preface

**The *Formula missae* in German.** The Prussian articles of 1525 follow the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) in
setting the Words of Institution inside the Preface, sung in German, with the elevation, the
Sanctus after it, and the Pax as an absolution. They add three peculiarities: the Kyrie sung in
Greek, Latin and German, the creed not intoned by the priest, and the Agnus Dei sung only twice
(§§[2.6](#s2-6), [2.9](#s2-9), [2.12](#s2-12)). **Prussia, *Artikel der ceremonien und anderer kirchen ordnung*, 1525**
(Sehling 4, p. 32):

<!-- doc 1832 -->

Then followeth the Preface, which the priest singeth in German, together with the evangelical
words of the blessing or consecration of bread and wine (for the offertory, the secret, the
lesser and greater canon are of necessity left out). When the Preface and consecration are
ended, a sign is given with the bell; then straightway the priest elevateth both parts of the
sacrament, one after the other, without delay. Meanwhile, and as soon as the Preface together
with the evangelical benediction is ended, the choir singeth the Sanctus in German or Latin as
occasion serveth, with few notes.

The Livonian towns took over the Prussian order at Wolmar in 1533 (Sehling 5, pp. 15–16).

#### <a id="s2-4-5"></a>2.4.5 The Mass that kept the Latin frame

**Brandenburg, Pfalz-Neuburg, the Palatinate before 1556.** A group of orders of the 1540s kept
more of the Latin Mass than Wittenberg did: the Preface dialogue, the Pax, the Agnus Dei three
times, even the old prayers before communion. The Brandenburg order of 1540 and the
Pfalz-Neuburg order of 1543 are treated in
[Chapter 7](#ch7), §§[7.12](#s7-12), [7.14](#s7-14). The provisional order of the
Palatinate (1546, Lutheran; not an Interim order) even kept the tail of the secret, *per omnia
saecula* (world without end), before the Preface dialogue. **Palatinate, *Gemaine maß, die kirchen- und gottesdinst
anzurichten*, 1546** (Sehling 14, pp. 96–97):

<!-- doc 472 -->

After the sermon there shall be made an exhortation to the communicants out of Duke
Ottheinrich's church order, or the like, before the altar; and then [the priest] beginneth to
sing: *Per omnia saecula* (World without end); the choir: *Amen*; the priest: *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you); the choir: *Et cum
spiritu tuo* (And with thy spirit); the priest: *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts); the choir: *Habemus ad Dominum* (We lift them up unto the Lord); the priest: *Gratias
agamus Domino Deo nostro* (Let us give thanks unto the Lord our God); the choir: *Dignum et iustum est* (It is meet and right); the priest: *Vere dignum et iustum
est* (It is very meet and right), etc. And on the high feasts the priest singeth the whole Preface, and the choir thereafter
the Sanctus as far as the Agnus Dei; thereafter the priest beginneth to sing in German the Our
Father in the common tone.

The Breslau churches went further still. A report of 1557 says that the Sunday high Mass was
sung by a chaplain "in his habit, as of old", through the gospel and the *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed); then came the
sermon; "the sermon ended, the chaplain singeth the Preface; after the sermon he elevateth the
sacrament"; and the Mass closed with the Sanctus, Agnus Dei and communion chant, the
postcommunion, "and with the *Benedicamus* or *Ite missa est*" (Sehling 3, p. 404).

#### <a id="s2-4-6"></a>2.4.6 The Upper German preaching service with communion

**Württemberg, Baden, Strasbourg and their neighbours.** These are Lutheran orders: "Upper
German" here names the south-western shape of service, not the Moderate Reformed tradition. The
Württemberg order of 1553 (and its copies in Baden 1556, Mömpelgard 1560 and the Palatinate of
1556) has no introit, Kyrie, Gloria, epistle, Preface, Sanctus or Agnus Dei. The service is the
sermon service of every Sunday, to which the communion is added:
1. a German hymn ("Komm heiliger Geist", "Nun bitten wir" or a psalm "agreeable to the season");
2. the sermon, which on communion days includes "a short instruction" on the Supper;
3. the creed sung in German;
4. the exhortation to the communicants, read at the altar;
5. the general prayer, then "the church shall sing the Our Father in German together";
6. the public confession and absolution;
7. the Words of Institution read "with loud, understandable voice";
8. the distribution, with "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised), "Jesus Christus unser Heiland" (Jesus Christ our Saviour) or another hymn;
9. a thanksgiving prayer and the blessing, in one of three forms.

(Sehling 16, pp. 252–255.) The opening rubric is quoted in
[Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.3.4](#s8-3-4). Strasbourg in 1598 keeps the same
shape: the ordinary Sunday service "until the hymn after the sermon"; then the pastor goes to
the altar while the church sings the German *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks), and reads the Württemberg
exhortation (Sehling 20/1, pp. 611–612).

#### <a id="s2-4-7"></a>2.4.7 The Reformed Supper

**The Palatinate after 1563.** The Palatine order of 1563 (Reformed), and the Reformed orders
that copied it (Bentheim-Tecklenburg 1588, Ysenburg-Birstein 1598), keep nothing of the
ordinaries. After the sermon on the Supper and the Sunday prayer, the minister reads at the
table the "Form for holding the holy Supper":
- the Words of Institution from 1 Corinthians 11, with the self-examination and the list of
  those excluded;
- the doctrine of the Supper; a prayer ending in the Lord's Prayer;
- the Apostles' Creed, "with mouth and heart";
- a lifting up of hearts "into heaven, where Christ Jesus is", in place of the *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts);
- the breaking of the bread with the words of 1 Corinthians 10:16;
- singing, or the reading of John 14–18 or Isaiah 53, during the distribution;
- a thanksgiving from Psalm 103 and a closing prayer. Bentheim-Tecklenburg (Reformed) adds:
  "After all this the psalm is sung, and thereafter the blessing of the Lord spoken"
  (Sehling 22, p. 275).

The breaking replaced the distribution formula. **Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563**
(Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 386):

<!-- doc 504 -->

Here shall the minister of the church break of the bread of the Lord to every one, and in giving
it say: The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ. And the other minister
of the church, in giving the cup, [shall] say: The cup of thanksgiving, wherewith we give
thanks, is the communion of the blood of Christ.

The Bentheim-Tecklenburg order of 1588 (Reformed) has the same form and the same words
(Sehling 22, pp. 271–275).

#### <a id="s2-4-8"></a>2.4.8 The early German Masses

**Before the territorial orders.** The German Masses of 1522–1526 (Kantz at Nördlingen, Müntzer
at Allstedt (Radical Reformation), the Strasbourg and Worms Masses (Moderate Reformed),
Volprecht and Döber at Nürnberg, the Low German Masses of Bremen, Lippe and Kiel) are compared
part by part in [Chapter 7](#ch7), §§[7.2](#s7-2)–[7.11](#s7-11). They keep the
Roman shape and translate it, the canon included, before the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) set the pattern
for the parishes. Two of their ordinaries recur below: Müntzer's fourfold Kyrie ([§2.6.1](#s2-6-1)) and
Volprecht's *Benedicamus* "and never *Ite missa est*" ([§2.13](#s2-13)).

---

### <a id="s2-5"></a>2.5 The ordos compared

**How to read the table.** Each row gives the sequence of the Sunday Mass with communicants, in
the shorthand set out in the [Conventions](#conv-abbreviations). Brackets mark a part the order allows but does not
require. "→" separates the parts. Details of each ordinary are in §§[2.6](#s2-6)–[2.13](#s2-13); the propers, hymns and
prayers in the chapters named at the head of this chapter.

| Order | Sehling | Family | Ordo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Luther, *Formula missae*, 1523 | 1, pp. 5–6 | Latin, purged | Intr → Ky (seasonal) → Gl (bishop may omit) → one Coll → Ep → Grad + Alleluia → Gosp → Nicene Cr (optional) → Serm (or before the Intr) → Pref with Verba → San with Benedictus (elevation) → PN → Pax → Comm with Agn → *Quod ore* (What with our mouth) → *Benedicamus* → Bl |
| Luther, *Deutsche Messe*, 1526 | 1, pp. 14–16 | German | German psalm → Ky ×3 → Coll → Ep → German hymn → Gosp → "Wir glauben" (We believe) → Serm → paraphrase of PN + Exh → Verba (bread) → Comm with German San → Verba (cup) → Comm → German Agn → Thanks → Bl (Num 6) |
| Prussia, *Artikel der ceremonien*, 1525 | 4, pp. 31–33 | Prussian | Intr → Ky ×3 (Greek, Latin, German) → Gl → Coll → Ep (a chapter) → Alleluia with German psalm → Gosp (a chapter) → Cr in German, not intoned → Pref with Verba → bell, elevation → San → PN → Agn ×2 → Pax → Exh → Comm with hymns → Thanks → Bl |
| Brandenburg-Nürnberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1533 | 11, pp. 188–198 | Franconian | private *Confiteor* (I confess) → Intr → Ky + *Et in terra* (And on earth) → *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) → Coll(s) → Ep (a chapter) → Alleluia or Grad → Gosp (a chapter) → Cr → Serm → Exh → Verba → San → *Oremus praeceptis* + PN → Pax → Comm with Agn → Thanks → *Benedicamus* → Bl |
| Wittenberg, town order, 1533 | 1, pp. 704–705 | Saxon | German Benedictus → Intr → Ky ×3, or ×9 on feasts → [Gl] → German Coll → Ep → Alleluia/Grad, German hymn, sequence → Gosp → *Credo* intoned, *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), "Wir glauben" → Serm → *Da pacem* (Give peace) → versicle + Coll → [*Dominus vobiscum* + Pref on feasts] → PN → Verba (elevation) → Comm with hymns, Latin Agn → German Agn ×3 → Thanks → Bl (Num 6) |
| Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535 | 4, p. 341 | Bugenhagen | German psalm or Intr → Ky → [Gl] → German Coll → Ep → psalm, alleluia, sequence → Gosp → *Credo* intoned, *Patrem*, "Wi löven" (We believe) → Serm + general prayer → hymn → [Pref + San] → [Exh] → PN + Verba → Comm with Agn and hymns → German Agn → Coll → Bl (Num 6); "after the Amen nothing more is sung" |
| Albertine Saxony, *Kirchenordnunge zum anfang* (Duke Henry), 1539 | 1, pp. 274–275 | Saxon | Intr → Ky (seasonal, or ×3) → Gl + *Et in terra* → Coll → Ep → Gosp → Latin *Patrem* + "Wir glauben" → Serm → [Latin Pref on feasts] → paraphrase of PN + Exh (or PN sung) → Verba → Comm with Latin Agn or German hymns → German Agn → Coll → Bl → "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) |
| Brandenburg, *Kirchen-ordnung*, 1540 | 3, pp. 68–70 | Latin frame | Intr → Ky → Gl + *Et in terra* → *Dominus vobiscum* + Coll → Ep → Alleluia + sequence → Gosp → *Credo*, *Patrem* (German in parishes) → *Dominus vobiscum* without *Oremus* → offertory chant → Pref → Latin San (prayers said under it) → Verba (German, elevation) → PN (German) → Pax → Agn ×3 → Exh → Comm with *Discubuit Jesus* (Jesus sat at table) → Thanks → *Quod ore* |
| Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543 | 6/1, pp. 54–56 | Bugenhagen | German Benedictus → German psalm → Ky ×3 (prayer at the altar) → Gl intoned, *Et in terra*, "Allein Gott" (To God alone), *Laudamus* → one Coll → Ep → Alleluia, German psalm, [sequence] → Gosp → *Credo* intoned, *Patrem*, "Wy geloven" (We believe) → Serm → Exh → … (as Pomerania) |
| Palatinate, *Gemaine maß*, 1546 | 14, pp. 96–97 | Latin frame | versicle + Coll → Intr → Ky (each once) → *Et in terra* → Coll → Ep → Alleluia + sequence or tract → Gosp → *Credo* intoned, Latin Nicene Cr, "Wir glauben" → Serm → Exh → *Per omnia saecula* (World without end), *Dominus vobiscum*, *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts) → [whole Pref on high feasts] → San to the Agn → PN (German) → Verba → Pax → Comm … |
| Transylvania, *Kirchenordnung* (German), 1547 | 24, p. 244 | Saxon | German Benedictus (or *Salve festa dies* [Hail, festal day]) → Intr → Ky + *Et in terra* → Coll → Ep → sequence or tract → Gosp → "Wir glauben" or Latin *Credo* → *Dominus vobiscum*, Pref, San → PN → Verba → Agn, hymns during Comm → *Dominus vobiscum*, Coll → *Benedicamus* → Trinitarian Bl; the sermon is held before the Mass, after Matins, and again after dinner |
| Mecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552 | 5, pp. 198–199 | Bugenhagen | confession and absolution → Intr → Ky → Gl or "Allein Gott" → *Dominus vobiscum* → German Coll → Ep → sequence or hymn → Gosp → *Credo* intoned, *Patrem*, "Wir glauben" → Serm (about an hour) + prayer → [*Dominus vobiscum* + Pref + San] → [Exh] → PN + Verba sung (no elevation) → Comm with hymns, Agn, Isaiah → "Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) → Thanks → Bl (Num 6) → "Erhalt uns" (Keep us) |
| Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553 | 16, pp. 252–255 | Upper German | German hymn → Serm → German Cr → Exh → general prayer → "Vater unser" (Our Father) sung → confession and absolution → Verba read → Comm with hymns → Thanks → Bl |
| Breslau, report on the order of the churches, 1557 | 3, p. 404 | Latin frame | high Mass sung "as of old" to the Gosp and *Patrem* → Serm → Pref → elevation → Comm → San, Agn, communion chant → postcommunion → *Benedicamus* or *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal) |
| Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563 (Reformed) | 14, pp. 383–387 | Reformed | Serm on the Supper → Sunday prayer → the Form: Verba (1 Cor 11), self-examination, exclusion → prayer + PN → Apostles' Cr → hearts lifted up → breaking of bread (1 Cor 10:16) → Comm with singing or reading → Thanks (Ps 103) + prayer |
| Hesse, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566 (Moderate Reformed) | 8, pp. 237–254 | Hessian | confession and absolution, or Ps 51 → German Ky + Gl → Coll → Ep → psalm or sequence → Gosp → Apostles' Cr sung by all → Serm → general prayer → confession → notices and alms → Supper |
| Albertine Saxony, *Ordnung* of Duke August, 1580 | 1, pp. 368–369 | Saxon | Intr → Ky → Latin Gl + *Et in terra* → Coll → Ep (German) → sequence or psalm → Gosp (German) → *Credo*, Latin *Patrem*, "Wir glauben" → Serm → paraphrase of PN + Exh → Verba sung → Comm with Latin Agn, Isaiah, Ps 111, hymns → Coll → Bl (Num 6) |
| Bentheim-Tecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1588 (Reformed) | 22, pp. 271–275 | Reformed | as the Palatinate 1563 → psalm → Bl |
| Hof, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1592 | 11, pp. 425–426 | Franconian | Intr → Ky de tempore (three choirs) → Gl intoned, *Et in terra* in alternation → epistle prayer + Ep → German psalm → gospel prayer + Gosp → "Wir glauben" → "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we) kneeling → Serm → *Dominus vobiscum* + Coll → Exh → PN → Pax → Verba → Comm with San and Agn de tempore, Isaiah, hymns |
| Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598 | 20/1, pp. 610–612 | Upper German | Sunday sermon service to the prayer after the Serm → German *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks) while the bread and wine are set out → Exh (Württemberg text) → … |

**What the table shows.**
- **Everyone kept the readings, the sermon, the Verba and a closing blessing.** The epistle and
  gospel (or chapters in course), a sermon, the Words of Institution, a distribution with
  singing, a thanksgiving and a blessing are in every row.
- **The ordinaries divide the families.** The Saxon, Bugenhagen, Franconian, Prussian and
  Latin-frame orders keep Kyrie, Gloria and Creed, and some form of Sanctus and Agnus Dei. The
  Upper German (Lutheran) and Reformed orders keep only a creed: the German "Wir glauben" in
  Württemberg, the Apostles' Creed in the Reformed Palatinate.
- **The Preface was the first casualty.** Only the Prussian, Franconian-Hof, Latin-frame and
  Transylvanian orders require it. The Saxon and Bugenhagen orders make it optional or festal;
  the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass), Albertine Saxony 1580, Nürnberg 1533 and Württemberg drop it ([§2.10](#s2-10)).
- **The Verba and the Lord's Prayer travel.** The Lord's Prayer comes before the Verba (Saxony,
  Bugenhagen, Transylvania, Hof), after them (*Formula missae*, Prussia, Nürnberg 1533,
  Brandenburg 1540), as a paraphrase in the exhortation (*Deutsche Messe*, Saxony 1539, 1580),
  as a hymn before the confession (Württemberg), or inside the prayer before the creed
  (Palatinate, Reformed) ([§2.11](#s2-11)).
- **The sermon has two homes.** It follows the gospel and creed almost everywhere. The *Formula
  missae* allowed it before the introit, and Transylvania (1547) held the first sermon after
  Matins, before the Mass began (Sehling 24, p. 244).

---

### <a id="s2-6"></a>2.6 The Kyrie

The hymns sung as or with the Kyrie, the troped German Kyries and the Kyrie in three tongues are
treated in [Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.6](#s8-6). This section asks how many
acclamations were sung, and which of the old Kyrie chants survived.

#### <a id="s2-6-1"></a>2.6.1 Three, four or nine

**The medieval norm was nine.** The Roman Kyrie had nine acclamations: Kyrie three times,
Christe three times, Kyrie three times. The Hannover order of 1536 repeats the common
attribution: "To sing the Kyrie eleison nine times, Gregory the Great set up in the Roman
church, as Platina writeth; yet it came first from the Greek church" (Sehling 6/2, p. 1005).

**Luther: three, not nine.** The *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) cut the Kyrie to three acclamations, "three
times and not nine times" ([§2.3.3](#s2-3-3)). The threefold Kyrie became the norm of the German parish
service:
- Duke Henry's Saxony (1539): "on ordinary Sundays and in the villages one may sing it plain …
  only three times" (Sehling 1, p. 274);
- the visitation articles for Gnandstein (1539) and the *Gemeine Artikel* (Common Articles) for the see of Wurzen
  (1542): "Kyrie eleison three times" (Sehling 1, p. 564; 2, p. 98);
- Prussia (1525, 1544 and 1568): "since it is sung three times", in three tongues (1525); "the
  Kyrie eleison only three times, according to the former order" (1544, 1568)
  (Sehling 4, pp. 32, 64, 81);
- the Palatinate (1546): "the Kyrie eleison, each only once" (Sehling 14, p. 96);
- the Henneberg parishes of Suhl (1562) and Obermaßfeld (1563): "the German Kyrie three times"
  (Sehling 2, pp. 352, 346);
- Waldeck (1556): "a Kyrie eleison three times" (Sehling 9, p. 247).

**Nine on the feasts.** The ninefold Kyrie survived where there was a choir, and especially on
feasts. At Wittenberg the plain threefold Kyrie was "the right Kyrie", the ninefold the festal
one (Sehling 1, p. 704; quoted in [§2.7.1](#s2-7-1)). The Pomeranian order of 1542 gives the Sunday Kyrie
"three or nine times, or the Kyrie of the feast" (Sehling 4, p. 358). The
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel order of 1543 gives the reason for three, and leaves the festal number
to the schoolmaster. **Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Christlike kerken-ordeninge*, 1543**
(Sehling 6/1, p. 54):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

It is not needful to repeat the *eleison* or Kyrie nine times; it is enough to sing it three
times, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, without the organ. Yet
the scholars may well sing another Kyrie on the feasts, especially when they sing in figured
music, three times, four times or nine times, at the schoolmaster's pleasure; yet so that one
make it not too long with the singing and the organ, that the sermon be not hindered thereby.

**Four.** A fourfold form, Kyrie, Christe, Kyrie, Kyrie, appears in three places:
- Müntzer's *Deutsch evangelisch Messe* (German Evangelical Mass) of 1524 (Radical Reformation): "Kyrie leyson, Christe
  leyson, kyrie leyson, kyrie leyson" (Sehling 1, p. 499);
- the German Masses of the Calenberg-Göttingen order of 1542, which take the chants of Müntzer
  (Radical Reformation): some have the fourfold form, others the threefold
  (Sehling 6/2, pp. 812, 817, 825, 827, 829; three: pp. 820, 823, 832);
- the song appendix of the Hessian *Agende* of 1574 (Philippist), after the German introit for
  Trinity: "Kyrie eleison. Christe eleison. Kyrie eleison. Kyrie eleison" (Sehling 8, p. 465).

The fourth acclamation is the closing Kyrie of the chant, sung to its own melody, kept when the
middle repetitions were cut. Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel's "four times" in figured music (above)
is the same shape set polyphonically.

**One, by three choirs.** At Hof (1592) the German Kyrie was divided among three choirs, one
acclamation each: "the first choir singeth Kyrie eleison in German, the second Christe eleison,
the third, or the girls' choir, Kyrie eleison". In figured music the organ played each of the
three before the choir answered; otherwise the organ "preludeth once only before the *Et in
terra*" (Sehling 11, p. 425).

**Not found.** No order prescribes a sevenfold Kyrie, and none a sixfold one. The counts in the
corpus are three, four and nine, with the "each once" of the Palatinate (1546) amounting to
three.

#### <a id="s2-6-2"></a>2.6.2 Which Kyrie: the seasonal chants

**The old melodies kept.** The *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) kept the Kyrie "with various melodies for the
various seasons" ([§2.3.2](#s2-3-2)). The northern and Franconian orders name the chants they meant, by their
medieval titles. **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542** (Sehling 4, p. 356):

<!-- doc 1859 -->

Thereupon the *Kyrie dominicale*; or one may also sing on the Sundays the *Kyrie angelicum*, *de
martyribus* (of martyrs), or *confessoribus*, or *virginibus*, as they have been named; the *dominicale* (Sunday [Kyrie]) in
Advent and in Lent, the *paschale* (Easter [Kyrie]) between Easter and Whitsun, the *summum* (the highest [chant]) on the higher
feasts, or the *minus summum* (the lesser summum).

The fullest scheme is the Hof order of 1592, for the boys' daily Mass-shaped service sung from
the "great missal". **Hof, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1592** (Sehling 11, p. 472):

<!-- doc 294 -->

Next, secondly, there is sung out of the great missal the Kyrie of the proper season: either the
*angelicum* (angelic [Kyrie]) in the Advent of the Lord, or the Kyrie *Magne Deus potentiae* (O God of great power) of the Nativity of
Christ, to which the angelic *Et in terra* (And on earth) is joined; or the greater *dominicale* from the
Sunday Septuagesima until Easter; or the *paschale*; or the Kyrie *Fons bonitatis* (Fount of goodness) with the
angelic *Et in terra*; or the lesser *dominicale* after the feast of Trinity; or that of the
apostles, martyrs, etc., as the season requireth and the order of the book showeth.

The same order assigns, Sunday by Sunday, a "Kyrie angelicum seu feriale" (angelic or ferial Kyrie) in Advent, a "Kyrie
paschale" (Easter Kyrie) from Easter to the Ascension, and a "Kyrie dominicale" from the fourth Sunday after
Trinity to Advent, with the Sanctus and Agnus Dei of the same set (Sehling 11, pp. 432–450).

**Other lists.**
- **Buxtehude 1565**: a table of the Kyries by occasion: "On the highest feasts and Trinity Sunday … the lesser *summum*", "On the feasts of the blessed Virgin Mary", "*Kyrie paschale*",
  "*Dominicale*" (Sunday [Kyrie]), "*In Adventu Domini*" (In the Advent of the Lord), "*Angelicum*", "*Kyrie apostolicum*" (apostles' Kyrie)
  (Sehling 7/1, p. 123).
- **Nördlingen 1544**: German Kyries "according to the season, of which we have three at this
  time": the *paschale* from Easter to Whitsun, *Fons bonitatis* from Whitsun to Christmas,
  *Magne Deus* (Great God) from Christmas to Easter; and the "*Kyrie summum* with the *Et in terra*" at
  Whitsun and Trinity, with the "*Sanctus summus*" (Sehling 12, pp. 318, 321–322).
- **Mecklenburg, *Ordeninge der misse*, 1540/1545**: the Kyrie "according to the season, as hath
  been kept hitherto"; in the villages the pastors are to teach the people "the German *Kyrie summum* (highest Kyrie), *Ach vader, alder högeste godt* (Ah Father, God most high)" (Sehling 5, p. 151).
- **Schleswig-Holstein 1542**: "The Kyrie eleison may be sung with manifold notes according to
  the difference of the season, as hath been kept hitherto" (Sehling 23, p. 90).
- **Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557**: the song index lists a *Kyrie paschale*, a Kyrie "*in adventu
  domini*" (in the Advent of the Lord), an *angelicum* and an *apostolicum* (apostles' [Kyrie]), each with its Gloria (Sehling 18, p. 255). The
  hymn plan of 1565 marks "the second Kyrie" for ordinary Sundays (Sehling 18, p. 337).
- **Schweinfurt 1576**: the organ begins "the Latin *Kyrie dominicale*, which the choir
  repeateth" (Sehling 11, pp. 647–648).
- **Nördlingen 1579**: the Latin Kyries of the weekday office: the *Fons bonitatis* in Advent,
  the *Magne Deus* at Christmas and in Lent, the *dominicale* from Septuagesima and at
  Pentecost, the *paschale* from Easter, and on the other Sundays the Kyrie "without the text"
  (Sehling 12, pp. 377–380; [Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.6.4.7](#s8-6-4-7)).

So the old cycle of Kyrie chants, *Lux et origo* (Light and origin; the Easter Kyrie), *Fons bonitatis* (Fount of goodness), *Magne Deus*
(Great God), *Cunctipotens* (Almighty; the apostles' Kyrie), *Orbis factor* (Maker of the world; the
Sunday Kyrie) and the rest, survived in the
Lutheran churches that had Latin schools, assigned to the seasons as before. Where the orders
print a text, it is the plain Kyrie, or a new German trope set to the old melody. The old Latin
tropes are named by their opening words (Nördlingen 1579), or left out by Sehling's editor
(Buxtehude 1565), and are printed in full only once, in Hof's Holy Week office
([Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.6.4.7](#s8-6-4-7)).

#### <a id="s2-6-3"></a>2.6.3 Which language

**Latin, German, Greek.** The Kyrie is the one ordinary the orders most often leave
untranslated. The Homberg synod of 1526 (Moderate Reformed) kept "these accustomed little words,
*Kyrie eleyson*, *Hallelujah*, *Hosiannah*, *Sabaoth*, *Amen*", to be explained to the people
(Sehling 8, p. 45). Bugenhagen defended the Greek at length
(Braunschweig 1528, Sehling 6/1, p. 438; [Chapter 8](#ch8),
[§8.6.3](#s8-6-3)). Prussia sang it in three languages, "since it is sung three times". **Prussia, *Artikel
der ceremonien und anderer kirchen ordnung*, 1525** (Sehling 4, p. 32):

<!-- doc 1832 -->

Of the Kyrie eleison it is thought good, since it is sung three times, that it be sung in three
tongues, as is the custom here also: Greek, Latin and German. *Gloria in excelsis* and *Et in
terra* (And on earth) may be sung in German or Latin, as is convenient.

The Livonian towns took the same rule in 1533 (Sehling 5, p. 15).

---

### <a id="s2-7"></a>2.7 The Gloria

The German Gloria hymns ("Allein Gott in der Höh", "All Ehr und Lob"), the alternation of Latin
and German Sunday by Sunday, and the omission of the Gloria in Advent, Lent and winter are
treated in [Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.7](#s8-7). Three further points belong
to the ordo.

#### <a id="s2-7-1"></a>2.7.1 The Gloria belongs to the festal Kyrie

**Not after the plain Kyrie.** In the medieval Mass the Gloria went with a festal Kyrie and was
silent on ferias and penitential days. Wittenberg kept the rule. **Wittenberg, *Kirchen-Ordnung
für die Stadt Wittenberg*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 704):

<!-- doc 148 -->

Thereafter the right Kyrie three times; or at times, especially on the feasts, another one nine
times, as is customary. After the plain Kyrie one singeth not the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (Glory to God in the highest), but
after the others, when one will, and especially on the feasts.

The Brandenburg order of 1540 ties the two together: the Kyrie "according to occasion", then the
Gloria, "which together with the *Et in terra* belongeth to the Kyrie" (Sehling 3, p. 68). The
*Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) left it to the bishop "how often he will have it left out" ([§2.3.2](#s2-3-2)), and the
*Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) left it out altogether.

#### <a id="s2-7-2"></a>2.7.2 Intonation, *Et in terra*, and the divided Gloria

**The priest intones.** Where the Gloria was sung, the priest (or a deacon, or at Hof a boy)
intoned *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (Glory to God in the highest), and the choir continued *Et in terra pax* (And on earth peace). In the German
orders the priest sang "Glory be to God on high" and the people answered with "Allein Gott" (To God alone).
The orders of the north divided the Latin Gloria between the scholars, the people and the organ.
**Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Christlike kerken-ordeninge*, 1543** (Sehling 6/1, p. 55):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

After the Kyrie the priest singeth: *Gloria in excelsis Deo*. The scholars' choir answereth and
singeth: *Et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis* (And on earth peace to men of good will), no more. Straightway the whole church
singeth "To God alone on high be glory," etc., in full.

The scholars and the organ then continue the Latin *Laudamus te* (We praise thee) "in full" (Sehling 6/1, p. 55).
So the Gloria was sung twice over: once in its Latin form, divided between the priest, the
scholars and the organ, and once as Decius's hymn by the people. The Pomeranian order of 1542
allows either half to be dropped "when it will grow too long" (Sehling 4, p. 356).

**At Hof**, the minister intoned a Gloria "suited to the Mass and answering to the season"; the
organ began the *Et in terra* (And on earth), "divided into certain portions", which the three choirs finished
in alternation with the organ. In the hardest frost the organ only began it and the choir sang
the rest (Sehling 11, p. 425).

#### <a id="s2-7-3"></a>2.7.3 The Gloria and the Kyrie as one piece

**One unit.** Because the Gloria followed the Kyrie and shared its chant, several orders treat
the two as a single piece: "the Kyrie and the *Et in terra*" (Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533;
Kurpfalz 1546; Transylvania 1547; Nördlingen 1544), "Kyrie eleison with the *Gloria in excelsis
et in terra pax*, as it is put into German and printed in the song-books"
(Hesse 1566, Moderate Reformed, Sehling 8, p. 239). The Hof order of 1592 assigns to each
seasonal Kyrie its own *Et in terra* (And on earth): "the Kyrie *Magne Deus potentiae* … to which the angelic
*Et in terra* is joined" ([§2.6.2](#s2-6-2)). In East Frisia (1535) the Kyrie and Gloria together were sung
"as it is sung in the song *Allein Gott in der Höh sei Ehr*"
([Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.6.5](#s8-6-5)).

---

### <a id="s2-8"></a>2.8 Salutation, collect and Pax

The collect and postcommunion are treated in [Chapter 5](#ch5). Here the
fixed formulas around them.

**The salutation.** *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) before the collect survived in most of the Latin-shaped
orders, often given in German beside the Latin:
- Mecklenburg 1552: the salutation *Dominus vobiscum*, answered *Et cum spiritu tuo* (And with thy spirit), each with its German (Sehling 5, p. 198);
- Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533: *Dominus vobiscum* or its German
  (Sehling 11, p. 188);
- Hof 1592: "The Lord be with you! Chorus: And with thy spirit", sung "either chorally or
  figurally" (Sehling 11, p. 425);
- Transylvania 1547: before the Preface and again before the postcommunion collect
  (Sehling 24, p. 244).

Bugenhagen's Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel order dropped it: "*Dominus vobiscum*, or *De Here sy mit
ju*, is not needful to say" (Sehling 6/1, p. 55). The *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) and the Württemberg and
Reformed orders have no salutation.

**The Pax.** The *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) kept *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you) after the Lord's Prayer
as "a kind of public absolution from sins … the one and most worthy preparation for the Lord's
Table" (Sehling 1, p. 6). The Pax stayed where the Lord's Prayer stayed near the altar:
- Prussia 1525: "the priest turneth to the people and giveth them the evangelical absolution, or
  the peace, and singeth in German *Pax domini*" (Sehling 4, p. 32);
- Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, after the Lord's Prayer: "*Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum*, or else
  in German" ([§2.4.3](#s2-4-3));
- Brandenburg 1540: "*The peace of the Lord be with you all*. Let all the people say *Amen*"
  (Sehling 3, p. 69);
- the Palatinate 1546, after the Verba: "the peace of the Lord be with you all. The choir answereth: Amen" (Sehling 14, p. 97);
- Hof 1592: "The peace of the Lord be with you all" (Sehling 11, p. 426).

The *Deutsche Messe*, the Saxon orders of 1539 and 1580, the Pomeranian and Mecklenburg orders
and Württemberg have no Pax.

**The Preface dialogue** is treated with the Preface ([§2.10](#s2-10)).

---

### <a id="s2-9"></a>2.9 The Creed

The German creed-hymn "Wir glauben all" (We all believe) and its places in the service are treated in
[Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.9](#s8-9). This section asks which creed was used,
and who began it.

#### <a id="s2-9-1"></a>2.9.1 Intoned by the priest, sung by the choir, then by the people

**Three layers.** In the Saxon and Bugenhagen orders the creed was sung three times over: the
priest intoned the Nicene Creed in Latin at the altar, the scholars sang the Latin *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed) to
the end, and the people then sang "Wir glauben all" (We all believe). **Wittenberg, *Kirchen-Ordnung für die
Stadt Wittenberg*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 704):

<!-- doc 148 -->

Thereafter the priest singeth the gospel turned toward the people, thereafter, [turned] again
toward the altar, *Credo in unum Deum* (I believe in one God). Thereupon the scholars sing the *Patrem* in Latin, then
with the people "We all believe in one God". But often the schoolmaster beginneth "We believe",
etc., straight after the gospel, for brevity's sake.

The same three layers are in Pomerania 1535 ("the *Patrem* in full, *dominicaliter*"),
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543, Duke Henry's Saxony 1539 ("the Latin *Patrem* in full, after the
common notes"), Mecklenburg 1552 (with the Latin text and notes), the Palatinate 1546 and Saxony
1580 (Sehling 4, p. 341; 6/1, p. 55; 1, p. 274; 5, p. 198; 14, p. 96; 1, p. 368). Brandenburg
(1540) sang the Latin *Patrem* "in cathedrals and foundations", and "Wir glauben" (We believe) in the
parishes (Sehling 3, p. 68).

**Not intoned.** Prussia (1525) abolished the priest's intonation: "The *Credo* or creed the
priest shall not begin as heretofore, but it shall be sung in German by the choir and the
people" (Sehling 4, p. 32).

#### <a id="s2-9-2"></a>2.9.2 Nicene, Apostles' or Athanasian

**The Nicene Creed in the Lutheran Mass.** The Latin *Credo* of the Mass is the Nicene Creed,
and "Wir glauben all" (We all believe) is Luther's paraphrase of it. Sangerhausen (1555) calls the people's
German creed "the customary *Symbolum Nicaenum* in German" (Sehling 1, p. 658). Weissenfels
(1578) sometimes sang "the *Symbolum Nicenum*" in figured music before the German creed
(Sehling 1, p. 693).

**The Apostles' Creed in Hesse and the Reformed orders.** The Hessian order of 1566 (Moderate
Reformed) put the Apostles' Creed in the Mass, sung by everyone every Sunday, and kept the
Nicene and Athanasian Creeds for the feasts of Christ. **Hesse, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, pp. 242–243):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

But this creed and confession of faith is sung by the whole church every Sunday with clear voice
after the reading of the gospel, and that for the following causes […] But on the feasts of
Christ one may sing or read the Nicene Creed or that of Athanasius, which are very profitable
for the strengthening of our faith and for withstanding the heretics who in manifold ways have
assailed and blasphemed the honour and the two natures of Christ, the Son of God.

The Palatine order of 1563 (Reformed) has the communicants confess the Apostles' Creed "with
mouth and heart" inside the Supper form ([§2.4.7](#s2-4-7)). Nördlingen (1579) had "an article of the
Apostles' Creed with the short exposition of Luther's catechism" read before the German creed on
feast days (Sehling 12, p. 366).

**The Athanasian Creed** was read or sung on Trinity Sunday in some places: as the text of the
early sermon at Schweinfurt (1543) and at Altenburg (1554) (Sehling 11, p. 638; 1, p. 519). Its
place was otherwise the morning office ([Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.7](#s10-7)).

#### <a id="s2-9-3"></a>2.9.3 Where the creed fell

After the gospel nearly everywhere; after the sermon in Württemberg, where the creed was sung
"in German" when the sermon was over (Sehling 16, p. 252); and inside the Supper form in the
Reformed Palatinate. The places of the creed-hymn as offertory, as cover for the preacher's
movement to the pulpit, and as a substitute for "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we) are in
[Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.9.1](#s8-9-1)–[8.9.4](#s8-9-4).

#### <a id="s2-9-4"></a>2.9.4 Which creed, order by order

**Four practices.** A search of the corpus for the creeds named in or near the Mass (*Credo in
unum Deum*, *Patrem*, *symbolum Nicenum*, *symbolum apostolicum*, *Credo in Deum Patrem*, "Ich
glaub in Gott Vater", *Athanasii*) gives four practices:
- **The Nicene Creed only**, in Latin, in German verse by verse, or as Luther's "Wir glauben
  all" (We all believe). This is the rule of the Saxon, Bugenhagen and Franconian orders.
- **The Apostles' Creed only**, sung or said: Strasbourg (1524, Moderate Reformed), the
  foundation Mass at Goslar, the Upper German pulpit, the Reformed Supper.
- **A choice left open**, Nicene or Apostles', Latin or German, with no rule for when.
- **A choice by occasion**: one creed on Sundays, another on feasts.

**Strasbourg: the Apostles' Creed sung, the Nicene by some.** The Strasbourg German Mass of 1524
(Moderate Reformed) prints the Apostles' Creed with notes after the sermon, in Matthäus
Greiter's setting, and leaves the Nicene to those who want it. **Strasbourg, *Ordenung und
inhalt Teutscher Mess*, 1524** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, p. 138):

<!-- doc 1279 -->

Then followeth the sermon. Thereafter the Creed: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of
heaven and earth" […] The great *Patrem*, which is called the Nicene Creed, is sung by some.

The earlier Strasbourg Mass of Theobald Schwarz (1524, Moderate Reformed) had the Nicene Creed
in German, "I believe in one God, the almighty Father" (Sehling 20/1, p. 121).

**By occasion: Sundays and feasts.** Hesse (1566, Moderate Reformed) gave the Apostles' Creed to
every Sunday and the Nicene or Athanasian to the feasts of Christ ([§2.9.2](#s2-9-2)). The Rothenberg
ministers of 1618 reversed the scheme: "Wir glauben" (We believe) on Sundays, the Apostles' Creed word for
word on the other feasts. **Rothenberg, *Christliche vereinigung* of the ministers, 1618**
(Sehling 13, p. 548):

<!-- doc 460 -->

After the boys have stepped down, let the customary creed be sung on the Sundays: "We all
believe in one God", etc. But on the other holy days the Apostles' Creed in German, word for
word: "I believe in God the Father Almighty", etc.

**A free choice of three.** The Hessian *Agende* of 1574 (Philippist) lets the Apostles' Creed,
Luther's creed-hymn or the Nicene be sung after the gospel. On occasion the Nicene or the
Athanasian Creed might instead be read aloud at the altar. **Hesse, *Agende*, 1574**
(Philippist; Sehling 8, p. 411):

<!-- doc 2272 -->

Upon the reading of the gospel is sung the Apostles' Creed in German, word for word, or as
Doctor Luther hath set it in the manner of a song by way of paraphrase, or the Nicene Creed in
German. One may also now and then, after the gospel, sing the German *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks), or
another short song, and thereupon read the Nicene or Athanasian Creed with a clear voice to the
people before the altar.

The Hessian *Agende* (Philippist) counts "Wir glauben all" as a paraphrase of the Apostles'
Creed, not of the Nicene. The Corvey order for Bruchhausen (1603) does the same: "the Apostles'
Creed, as Dr Luther set it in German in the manner of a song", where Sehling's editors identify
the song as "Wir glauben all" (Sehling 21, p. 244). Most orders, and the modern editors, take it
as the Nicene.

**The table.** The orders that say which creed belongs in the Sunday Mass or service:

| Order | Sehling | Creed | By occasion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Luther, *Formula missae*, 1523 | 1, p. 5 | Nicene, Latin, at the bishop's choice | — |
| Volprecht, Nürnberg, 1524 | 11, p. 41 | Nicene in German, "I believe in one God" | — |
| Schwarz, Strasbourg, 1524 (Moderate Reformed) | 20/1, p. 121 | Nicene in German | — |
| Strasbourg, *Ordenung und inhalt*, 1524 (Moderate Reformed) | 20/1, p. 138 | Apostles' Creed, sung after the sermon | Nicene "by some" |
| Luther, *Deutsche Messe*, 1526 | 1, p. 14 | "Wir glauben all" | — |
| Braunschweig 1528; Hamburg 1529 | 6/1, p. 440; 5, p. 531 | priest intones "I believe in one God"; people sing the whole Nicene in Low German verse by verse; then "Wy gelöven" (We believe) | — |
| Goslar, town order, 1528 | 7/2.2, p. 242 | "the Nicene Creed or the German *Patrem*, Wir glauben" | — |
| Goslar, foundation of St. Simon and Jude, 1534 | 7/2.2, p. 263 | *Credo in Deum Patrem* (Apostles') after the gospel | — |
| Wittenberg 1533 and the Saxon and Bugenhagen orders | [§2.9.1](#s2-9-1) | *Credo in unum Deum* intoned, Latin *Patrem*, "Wir glauben" | "Wir glauben" alone for brevity |
| Northeim 1539 | 6/2, p. 925 | "the Nicene Creed or Wir glauben in German" | — |
| Brandenburg 1540 | 3, p. 68 | Latin *Patrem* | in cathedrals and foundations; "Wir glauben" in parishes |
| Schwäbisch Hall, 1543 (1615 revision) | 17/1, p. 163 | a hymn "with the Apostles' Creed, as a mark of the Church", or "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we), at the start of the Sunday service | — |
| Württemberg 1553 | 16, pp. 239, 252 | German creed sung after the sermon; the Apostles' Creed said from the pulpit every Sunday with the Decalogue and Lord's Prayer | — |
| Frankfurt, French Reformed church, 1554 (Reformed) | 9, p. 567 | Apostles' Creed sung by the people while the bread and wine are brought | — |
| Sangerhausen 1555 | 1, p. 658 | "the customary Nicene Creed in German" | — |
| Hamburg, Latin account, 1556 | 5, p. 543 | *symbolum apostolorum* (Apostles' Creed) after the gospel, before the Latin Preface | — |
| Ritzebüttel (Hamburg), 1556 | 5, p. 559 | Apostles' Creed after the gospel | on apostles' days and lesser holy days |
| Feuchtwangen 1563 | 11, p. 399 | *Credo in unum Deum Patrem omnipotentem* one Sunday, the German creed the next | alternating Sundays |
| Palatinate 1563 (Reformed) | 14, p. 386 | Apostles' Creed within the Supper form ([§2.4.7](#s2-4-7)) | — |
| Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed) | 8, pp. 242–243, 254 | Apostles' Creed every Sunday; "Wir glauben" or the Apostles' Creed in the shorter service | Nicene or Athanasian on the feasts of Christ |
| Prussia 1568 | 4, p. 81 | Latin Nicene in the cathedral | elsewhere alternating Sunday by Sunday with "Wir glauben" |
| Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569 | 4, p. 438 | Nicene in Latin or Low German, or "Wi gelöven" (We believe) | — |
| Kurland 1570 | 5, p. 88 | Latin *Patrem*, or the Apostles' Creed sung, or "Wir gleuben" (We believe) | — |
| Hesse, *Agende*, 1574 (Philippist) | 8, p. 411 | Apostles' word for word, Luther's paraphrase, or Nicene in German | Nicene or Athanasian sometimes read aloud |
| Weissenfels 1578 | 1, p. 693 | figured Nicene before the German creed | some days |
| Corvey (Bruchhausen) 1603 | 21, p. 244 | "Wir glauben all", called the Apostles' Creed | — |
| Rothenberg 1618 | 13, p. 548 | "Wir glauben all" on Sundays | Apostles' word for word on other feasts |

**What the table shows.**
- The Nicene Creed, sung in Latin by the choir and in German by the people, is the Lutheran norm
  north and east.
- The Apostles' Creed entered the Mass from three directions:
  - the Upper German sermon service (Strasbourg 1524, Moderate Reformed; Schwäbisch Hall and
    Württemberg's pulpit, Lutheran);
  - the Reformed Supper (Frankfurt's French church, the Palatinate; both Reformed);
  - Hesse (Moderate Reformed), where it was the creed of the whole congregation every Sunday.
- The Athanasian Creed was never the Sunday creed. It was read on the feasts of Christ in Hesse
  (Moderate Reformed) and on Trinity Sunday in a few places ([§2.9.2](#s2-9-2)), and otherwise belonged to
  the morning office.
- The weekday offices of Naumburg (1537) and Nördlingen (1544, 1579) gave the Nicene Creed its
  own day, Friday or Thursday, in a weekly round of canticles
  (Sehling 2, p. 72; 12, pp. 326, 377); that is office, not Mass.

---

### <a id="s2-10"></a>2.10 The Preface and the Sanctus

The Proper Prefaces, their texts and the days they were used, are in
[Chapter 4](#ch4), [§4.8](#s4-8) and [Appendix 4.A](#s4-a); the German Sanctus hymns ("Jesaia dem
Propheten", the Trinitarian "Heilig ist Gott der Vater") in
[Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.12](#s8-12).

#### <a id="s2-10-1"></a>2.10.1 The Preface: required, optional, festal or gone

**Four answers.** The orders give four answers to the question whether the Preface was sung:
- **Required.** The *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass), Prussia 1525, Brandenburg 1540, Transylvania 1547 and the
  Breslau Mass of 1557 have it in the ordo, with the dialogue (§§[2.4.4](#s2-4-4)–[2.4.5](#s2-4-5)).
- **If time allows.** Mecklenburg (1552) makes it the priest's choice "if the time permit".
- **Festal.** Wittenberg 1533 (feasts, and Trinity on Sundays "if one will"), Duke Henry's
  Saxony 1539 ("on the feasts and now and then on Sundays"), Pomerania 1535 ("not always …
  especially at the high feasts"), the Palatinate 1546 (the whole Preface "on the high feasts",
  the dialogue always) and the boys' daily service at Hof (from Lossius's book "on the chief
  festivals") (Sehling 1, pp. 704, 274; 4, p. 341; 14, p. 97; 11, p. 473).
- **Gone.** The *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass), Nürnberg 1533, Albertine Saxony 1580, Württemberg and the
  Reformed orders. The Palatinate's Reformed form (1563) keeps only the idea of the *Sursum
  corda*, as an exhortation to lift up the heart "into heaven, where Christ Jesus is" ([§2.4.7](#s2-4-7)).

The Mecklenburg rubric shows the whole Preface section made optional. **Mecklenburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 5, p. 199):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

If then the time permit, the priest may sing the Preface, in German or in Latin, beginning with
these words: *Dominus vobiscum*, or "The Lord be with you". And thou findest the Prefaces also
set down together hereafter in their place with the customary notes. Thereupon the Sanctus is
sung in Latin, as it is also set after the daily Preface, or in German, "Isaiah the prophet, it
befell", as it standeth in the song-book. If there be time, the priest may also read to the
people an exhortation and instruction concerning the most worthy sacrament, as is also set down
after the Prefaces. After the exhortation, or, when for shortness of time the exhortation and
Preface are left out, straightway after the sermon, let the priest sing [the Our Father and the
Words of the Testament].

#### <a id="s2-10-2"></a>2.10.2 Where the Sanctus fell

**Five places.** The Sanctus is the ordinary that moved most:
1. **After the Preface, before the Verba** (the Roman place): Mecklenburg 1552, Pomerania 1535,
   Brandenburg 1540, the Palatinate 1546, Transylvania 1547.
2. **After the Verba**, which were sung in the Preface: the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass; "with the
   elevation during the Benedictus") and Prussia 1525 ([§2.4.4](#s2-4-4)).
3. **After the Verba, without a Preface**: Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, followed by the Lord's
   Prayer and the Pax ([§2.4.3](#s2-4-3)).
4. **During the distribution**, in German: the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass), Duke Henry's Saxony 1539,
   Albertine Saxony 1580, Mecklenburg 1552 (as an alternative), Hof 1592 (the Latin Sanctus and
   Agnus "of the season" sung during the communion), Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 ("at another
   time, or at all times, under the communion").
5. **Nowhere**: Württemberg and the Reformed orders.

#### <a id="s2-10-3"></a>2.10.3 With or without the Benedictus

**The Latin Sanctus kept its Benedictus.** Where the Latin Sanctus was sung, it was sung whole,
with the *Benedictus qui venit* (Blessed is he that cometh) and its *Hosanna*. The *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) had the elevation "under
the singing of the *Benedictus*" (Sehling 1, p. 6). The Palatinate order of 1546 has the choir
sing "the Sanctus as far as the Agnus Dei", that is, through the *Benedictus*
(Sehling 14, p. 97), and the Amberg hospital church in 1544 "the Sanctus as far as the Agnus
Dei" before the German Lord's Prayer (Sehling 13, p. 283).

**Luther's German Sanctus dropped it.** "Jesaia dem Propheten" (To Isaiah the prophet) paraphrases Isaiah 6 only, and so
has no *Benedictus* and no *Hosanna*. Where it replaced the Latin Sanctus, the *Benedictus* went
with it.

**The other German Sanctus kept it.** The prose German Sanctus of the early German Masses, and
the Trinitarian Sanctus of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, keep the *Benedictus* and the Hebrew
*Hosianna* (Hosanna):
- Kantz (Nördlingen 1522): "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; full are heaven and earth of thy
  glory. Hosanna in the highest! Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Luck and
  salvation in the highest!" (Sehling 12, p. 286), with *Hosanna* rendered "luck and salvation";
- Bremen 1525, in Low German, the same (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 406);
- Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543: "Holy is God the Father, holy is God the Son, holy is God the
  Holy Ghost … *Hosianna* in the highest. Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord.
  *Hosianna* in the highest" (Sehling 6/1, p. 59);
- Dortmund 1554, Low German, with the gloss "*Hosianna* (ah, make us blessed)"
  (Sehling 21, p. 211);
- the Neuenrade order of 1564 prints two Low German Sanctus texts, both with "Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord" (Sehling 22, p. 532);
- Volprecht and Döber at Nürnberg (1524–1525) rendered *Hosanna* "make us blessed in the highest"
  (Sehling 11, pp. 41, 54; [Chapter 7](#ch7), §§[7.7](#s7-7)–[7.8](#s7-8)).

---

### <a id="s2-11"></a>2.11 The Lord's Prayer and the Words of Institution

The Words of Institution, their wording, their chant and the elevation are treated order by
order in [Chapter 7](#ch7); the people's Lord's Prayer
hymn in [Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.13](#s8-13). This section compares their
order.

**Seven sequences.**

| Sequence | Orders |
|---|---|
| Preface with Verba → Sanctus → Lord's Prayer → Pax → communion | *Formula missae* 1523; Prussia 1525 (with the Agnus before the Pax) |
| Exhortation → Verba → Sanctus → Lord's Prayer → Pax → communion | Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 |
| Preface → Sanctus → Verba → Lord's Prayer → Pax → Agnus → exhortation → communion | Brandenburg 1540 |
| (Preface → Sanctus →) Lord's Prayer → Verba → communion | Wittenberg 1533; Pomerania 1535; Mecklenburg 1552; Transylvania 1547; Palatinate 1546 (Verba → Pax); Hof 1592 (Lord's Prayer → Pax → Verba) |
| Paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer + exhortation → Verba → communion | *Deutsche Messe* 1526; Duke Henry's Saxony 1539; Albertine Saxony 1580; Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 (at times) |
| Lord's Prayer hymn → confession → Verba read → communion | Württemberg 1553 |
| Prayer ending in the Lord's Prayer → creed → breaking of bread | Palatinate 1563; Bentheim-Tecklenburg 1588 (both Reformed) |

**The bread and the cup apart.** The *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) gave the bread after the words over the
bread and the cup after the words over the cup. Albertine Saxony (1580) required this "in the
villages, where this sacrament is given out by one person only" (Sehling 1, p. 369), and Prussia
(1544) followed it (Sehling 4, pp. 65–66). Elsewhere both words were said or sung before the
distribution.

**The elevation.** Kept with the Verba in the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass), Prussia 1525, Wittenberg 1533,
Brandenburg 1540 and Breslau 1557; abolished in the Palatinate 1546 and in Mecklenburg 1552,
"that the inequality bring not contention" (Sehling 5, p. 199). See
[Chapter 7](#ch7) and
[Chapter 12](#ch12), [§12.10.6](#s12-10-6).

---

### <a id="s2-12"></a>2.12 The Agnus Dei

The German Agnus hymns ("Christe du Lamm Gottes", "O Lamm Gottes unschuldig") and their place
after the communion are in [Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.14](#s8-14)–[8.15](#s8-15).

#### <a id="s2-12-1"></a>2.12.1 How many times

**Three, as of old.** The Latin Agnus Dei three times, the third ending *dona nobis pacem* (grant us peace), is
printed in full in Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 and Brandenburg 1540 (Sehling 13, p. 75; 3, p. 69).
Regensburg had the schoolmaster sing it "three times slowly" during the distribution, and more
songs if the three were not enough (1542 and 1553: Sehling 13, pp. 393, 420). Luther's German
"Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) kept the threefold form: "*Christ, thou Lamb of God … have mercy upon us*. The third time thus: *give us thy peace, amen*"
(Wittenberg 1533, Sehling 1, p. 705). Hamburg (1529) and Neuenrade (1564) say the same in Low
German (Sehling 5, p. 529; 22, p. 532). Hof sang "O Lamm Gottes unschuldig" (O Lamb of God, innocent) three times, "the
last time with these words added: *Gib uns dein fride, o Jesu*" (Sehling 11, p. 429). Müntzer's
Allstedt (Radical Reformation) order had the people sing the Baptist's witness "three times",
the third ending "Give us thy peace" (Sehling 1, p. 506).

**Twice.** The Prussian order of 1525 cut the Agnus Dei to two, "for brevity's sake", so that
the people's hymns during the communion should have more room. **Prussia, *Artikel der
ceremonien und anderer kirchen ordnung*, 1525** (Sehling 4, p. 32):

<!-- doc 1832 -->

Straightway thereupon the choir singeth the Agnus Dei with few notes, in German or Latin as
occasion serveth, yet for brevity's sake only twice, that the Christian songs of the
congregation following may have the more room; and to conclude the first time with the *miserere
nobis* (have mercy upon us), the second with the *dona nobis pacem*.

The Livonian towns copied it: "the Agnus Dei with few notes, twice … first, *Be gracious to us*;
second, *Give us thy peace*" (Wolmar 1533, Sehling 5, p. 16).

**Once.** The Albertine *Cellische Ordnungen* (Celle orders) of 1545 had the choir sing the Latin Agnus Dei
once, after the communion, while the people knelt and gave thanks. **Albertine Saxony, *Die
Cellischen Ordnungen*, 1545** (Sehling 1, p. 301):

<!-- doc 33 -->

then shall the choir begin to sing the Latin Agnus Dei only once; meanwhile the people kneel and
make their thanksgiving to God.

The single German strophe "Christ, thou Lamb of God … have mercy upon us. Give us thy peace",
printed once as the close of the communion, is the form of Duke Henry's Saxony (1539) and the
Calenberg-Göttingen Masses (1542) (Sehling 1, p. 275; 6/2, pp. 819, 824), and Kantz's Mass of
1522 has one strophe combining both endings (Sehling 12, p. 286).

#### <a id="s2-12-2"></a>2.12.2 Where it fell

**Before or during the communion.** In the Roman place, before the communion, in Prussia 1525
and Brandenburg 1540; during the distribution in the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass), Nürnberg 1533, Pomerania
1535, Mecklenburg 1552, Transylvania 1547, Albertine Saxony 1580 and Hof 1592.

**After the communion.** The German Agnus "Christe du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) after the communion as its
close in Wittenberg 1533 ("when the communion is ended"), Hamburg 1529 ("when they have all
communicated and are in their places"), Pomerania 1535 and Mecklenburg 1552. Pomerania limits
the Latin Agnus and the hymns during the communion: "but not longer than the communion lasteth"
(Sehling 4, p. 341).

---

### <a id="s2-13"></a>2.13 The dismissal and the blessing

The Roman Mass ended with *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal; or *Benedicamus Domino* [Let us bless the Lord] in Masses without the
Gloria), and then the priest's blessing, "May almighty God bless you, the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost", a Trinitarian blessing (Sehling 11, p. 42, note 21). The evangelical orders
changed both. The *Benedicamus* in the offices, its seasonal melodies and its German forms are
treated in [Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.16.8](#s8-16-8)–[8.16.10](#s8-16-10); the closing hymns
in [§8.15](#s8-15) of the same chapter.

#### <a id="s2-13-1"></a>2.13.1 *Ite missa est*, *Benedicamus*, or neither

**Three practices.** A search of every *Ite missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal) and every *Benedicamus* near the end of
the Mass gives three practices:
- **The *Ite* kept.** Only two places:
  - the Breslau report of 1557: "with the *Benedicamus* or *Ite missa est* the Mass is closed"
    (Sehling 3, p. 404);
  - the Brandenburg-Ansbach visitation of 1536, which kept the old order "from the *Confiteor*
    to the end of the Mass, *Ite missa est*", so far as it was not against Scripture
    (Sehling 11, p. 326). The Ansbach *Auctuarium* of 1548, an Interim order, then put "the
    *Benedicamus* for the *Ite missa*" (Sehling 11, p. 327).
- **The *Benedicamus* in its place**, in Latin or in German (lists below).
- **Neither.** Luther's *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) and most Saxon, Bugenhagen, Upper German and Reformed
  orders end with the thanksgiving collect and the blessing, and at most a hymn after it.
  Pomerania (1535): "after the Amen nothing more is sung" (Sehling 4, p. 341).

**Never *Ite missa est*.** Volprecht's Nürnberg Mass makes the rule explicit. **Nürnberg,
*Deutsche Messe* of the Prior Volprecht, 1524** (Sehling 11, p. 39):

<!-- doc 247 -->

The blessing: this is said, and never is *Ite missa est* said; in its place is said *Benedicamus
Domino* (Let us bless the Lord); response: *Deo gratias*.

**The Latin *Benedicamus*:**
- Luther, *Formula missae* (1523): in the place of the *Ite*, "with alleluia added (where and
  when it pleaseth)", or with the vesper melodies ([§2.3.2](#s2-3-2); Sehling 1, p. 6);
- Nürnberg, *Form und Ordnung einer christlichen Messe* (1525): "*Benedicamus Domino*,
  *dominicaliter*", then "Es woll uns Gott genädig sein" (May God be gracious to us; Sehling 11, p. 57);
- Goslar (1528): the collect "with the *Benedicamus*" sung by the boys in the choir after the
  distribution (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 242);
- Brandenburg-Nürnberg (1533), followed by the blessing (quoted below, Sehling 11, p. 198);
- Regensburg (1542): the gospeller sings *Deo dicamus gratias* (Let us say thanks to God); Regensburg (1553): the second
  minister sings *Benedicamus Domino*, the choir *Deo dicamus gratias*
  (Sehling 13, pp. 393, 421);
- Pfalz-Neuburg (1543): sung by the priest or the deacons "in the tone in which the Kyrie was
  sung", the choir answering in the same tone *Deo dicamus gratias* (Sehling 13, p. 76);
- Transylvania (1547): *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you), collect and *Benedicamus*, all concluded "with the
  blessing of the people in the name of the Holy Trinity" (Sehling 24, pp. 223, 244);
- Hohenlohe (1553): "the collect with *Benedicamus Domino*", then the Aaronic blessing
  (Sehling 15, p. 73); the Öhringen foundation (1556) prints its melody with the Mass
  (Sehling 15, p. 104);
- Suhl in Henneberg (1562): "Collect. *Benedicamus*. The blessing out of Moses"
  (Sehling 2, p. 351);
- Wolfstein (1574): "the thanksgiving, the *Benedicamus*, the choir answereth *Deo gratias*, and
  the blessing" (Sehling 13, p. 577);
- Chemnitz (1578): "the collect which is called the *complenda*, and the *Benedicamus* together
  with the benediction, as is customary" (Sehling 1, p. 542).

**The German *Benedicamus*.** The early German Masses put the versicle into German, and Hof kept
it with its own melody in 1592:
- Müntzer, Allstedt (1524, Radical Reformation): each German Mass ends with a prayer and the
  *Benedicamus*, "Let us bless the Lord, alleluia. God be thanked for ever"
  (Sehling 1, pp. 497, 502);
- Erfurt, *Deutsches Kirchenamt* (1525), after Müntzer (Radical Reformation): "Let us bless the Lord. God be thanked for ever", then the Aaronic blessing (Sehling 2, p. 380);
- Lippe (1525), in Low German: "Let us bless the Lord; to God be thanks for ever", then the
  Aaronic blessing (Sehling 22, p. 569);
- Volprecht's German Mass (1524), after the blessing: "Let us give the Lord praise and thanks! Answer: God be thanked" (Sehling 11, p. 42);
- Worms (1524, Moderate Reformed): "Let us bless God", then a Trinitarian blessing
  (quoted below);
- Strasbourg (1524, Moderate Reformed): "Give thanks unto the Lord", then the blessing
  (Sehling 20/1, pp. 133, 139);
- Hof (1592): the deacon "addeth the German *Benedicamus*": "Let us bless the Lord. Chorus: God be thanked", then the Aaronic blessing (Sehling 11, pp. 426–427).

**Before or after the blessing.** In most orders that kept it the *Benedicamus* came before the
blessing, as in the Roman Mass. Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1528 put it after: "for the conclusion the
benediction of Numbers 6 in German, thereafter *Benedicamus Domino* sung" (Sehling 11, p. 137).
So did Volprecht's German Mass, and Nürnberg 1525, where the *Benedicamus* is followed by a
hymn.

#### <a id="s2-13-2"></a>2.13.2 The blessing: Aaronic, Trinitarian, or both

**Five practices.** The blessings at the end of the Mass were searched in every form: Numbers 6,
Psalm 67, the Trinitarian formulas ("God the Father, Son and Holy Ghost", "May … bless you, the Father and the Son"), and 2 Corinthians 13:13. They give five practices:
- **The Aaronic blessing alone.** This is the rule, from the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) onward. It is in
  the singular ("The Lord bless thee") in the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) and the Saxon orders, and in the
  plural ("The Lord bless you") in Nürnberg and the south. Examples:
  - Luther's *Deutsche Messe* (1526);
  - Wittenberg (1533);
  - Pomerania (1535);
  - Mecklenburg (1552);
  - Albertine Saxony (1580);
  - Volprecht (1524) and Döber (1525) at Nürnberg;
  - Lippe and Erfurt (1525);
  - Weißenburg and Brandenburg-Nürnberg (1528);
  - Hohenlohe (1553);
  - Suhl (1562);
  - Hof (1592);
  - the Palatinate's Sunday service (1563, Reformed, Sehling 14, p. 391).
- **A Trinitarian blessing alone**: the early German Masses of Worms and Strasbourg (1524, both
  Moderate Reformed), and Regensburg (1542), all quoted below. Transylvania (1547) blesses "in
  the name of the Holy Trinity" without printing the words (Sehling 24, p. 223).
- **The Aaronic and the Trinitarian together**, the second following the first: Strasbourg's
  *Ordenung und inhalt Teutscher Mess* (1524, Moderate Reformed): "The Lord bless you … The blessing of God, the Father and the Son, etc." (Sehling 20/1, p. 140); and the Strasbourg Supper of
  1598 (quoted below).
- **A choice of forms**: the Brandenburg-Nürnberg set of four, and its descendants (below).
- **Different blessings for different occasions**: Prussia (1525) and Strasbourg (1598) (below).

**The Nürnberg set of four.** Brandenburg-Nürnberg gave four blessings to choose from: Numbers
6; a paraphrase of Psalm 67; and two Trinitarian forms. **Brandenburg-Nürnberg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1533** (Sehling 11, p. 198):

<!-- doc 270 -->

*Benedicamus Domino. Deo gratias.* Thereafter let him bless the people thus: "The Lord bless you
and keep you! The Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious unto you! The Lord lift up
his countenance upon you and give you peace! Amen." Or thus: "God be gracious and merciful unto
us and give us his divine blessing! May he cause his face to shine upon us and give us his
peace! Amen." Or thus: "Bless and keep us, God the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost! Amen."
Or thus: "The blessing of God the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost be with you and
abide alway with us all! Amen."

The set passed, whole or shortened, into these orders:

| Order | Sehling | Forms offered |
|---|---|---|
| Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 | 11, p. 198 | Aaronic; Ps 67; "Bless and keep us, God the Father …"; "The blessing of God the Father …" |
| Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 | 13, p. 76 | the same four |
| Schwäbisch Hall 1543 | 17/1, p. 135 | Aaronic; the two Trinitarian forms |
| Strasbourg 1553 (Marbach) | 20/1, p. 415 | the same four |
| Württemberg 1553 | 16, p. 255 | Aaronic (singular); Ps 67; "Bless and keep us, God …" |
| Kurpfalz 1556 | 14, p. 150 | as Württemberg, in the plural |
| Worms, *Agendbüchlein*, 1560 | 19/1, p. 210 | the same four |
| Leiningen-Westerburg 1566 | 19/1, p. 253 | Aaronic; Ps 67; "Bless and keep us, God …" |
| Regensburg 1567 | 13, p. 463 | Aaronic (singular), or "God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Ghost bless and keep you" |
| Hanau-Lichtenberg 1573 | 20/2, p. 67 | Aaronic; Ps 67; "Bless and keep us, God …" |
| Oldenburg 1573 | 7/2.1, p. 1145 | Aaronic (singular); Ps 67; the two Trinitarian forms |
| Pfalz-Veldenz 1574; Lützelstein 1605 | 18, pp. 504, 607 | Aaronic with "Go forth; the Spirit of the Lord lead you unto eternal life", or "The blessing of God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost … and his Holy Spirit strengthen and preserve us unto eternal life" |

**A Trinitarian blessing alone.** The first German Mass of Worms (Moderate Reformed) closed with
a German *Benedicamus* and the Trinitarian blessing only. **Worms, *Deutsche Messe*, 1524**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 19/1, p. 129):

<!-- doc 1066 -->

Let us bless God. Thanks, laud, honour and praise be to God through Christ our Lord, Amen. The
blessing: "The blessing of Almighty God, Father, Son and Holy Ghost, be with you and abide alway
with you. Amen."

The Nunc dimittis followed. The two Strasbourg Masses of 1524 (Moderate Reformed) by Theobald
Schwarz and in the *Teutsche Meß und Tauff* (German Mass and Baptism) end the same way: "The blessing of God, the Father [+] and the Son [+] and the Holy Ghost [+], be with us and abide alway", with three signs of
the cross (Sehling 20/1, pp. 123, 133). At Regensburg in 1542 the priest blessed with the
Trinitarian form alone. **Regensburg, *Wahrhaftiger Bericht*, 1542** (Sehling 13, p. 393):

<!-- doc 432 -->

Thereafter the priest turneth about toward the people and blesseth them with these words: "Bless
and keep us God the Father, Son and Holy Ghost. Amen."
