**By occasion: feasts and weekdays.** Prussia assigned a sung blessing from Psalm 67 to the
feasts, and the Aaronic blessing to ordinary days, at the end of matins, vespers and the Mass
alike. **Prussia, *Artikel der ceremonien und anderer kirchen ordnung*, 1525**
(Sehling 4, pp. 37–38):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

There follow the benediction or closing chant at the end of matins, vespers and Mass. On feast
days: "God give us his blessing, our God bless us." Response: "And all the ends of the world
shall fear him, Amen." The daily benediction: "The Lord make his face shine upon us and be
gracious unto us."

**By occasion: the sermon and the Supper.** Strasbourg in 1598 closed the plain preaching
service with the Trinitarian blessing alone, "The blessing of God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost, be now and at all times with us all" (Sehling 20/1, p. 589). It
closed the Supper with the Aaronic and the Trinitarian together. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*,
1598** (Sehling 20/1, p. 613):

<!-- doc 1344 -->

"The Lord bless you and keep you. The Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious unto
you. The Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace. The benediction of God, of
the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, be now and at all times with us all, Amen." Go
hence in the peace of the Lord.

**2 Corinthians 13:13.** The apostolic blessing, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God, together with the communion of the Holy Ghost", appears in two places:
- Hesse (1566, Moderate Reformed) gives it as the alternative to Numbers 6 when the minister
  dismisses the congregation (Sehling 8, p. 248);
- Nördlingen (1579) closes the pulpit prayers with it (Sehling 12, p. 368).

**Psalm 67** stands beside the blessing in three forms:
- Luther's third option in the *Formula missae*;
- the second form of the Nürnberg set;
- the sung feast-day blessing of Prussia.

Where it was sung as Luther's hymn, "Es wolle uns Gott genädig sein" (May God be gracious to us), it closed the service
after the blessing: Nürnberg 1525 (Sehling 11, p. 57), Strasbourg 1525
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, p. 147), and Hoya 1571, in a service without the Supper
(Sehling 6/2, p. 1152; [Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.15](#s8-15)).

**After the blessing.**
- Pomerania (1535) ended there (Sehling 4, p. 341).
- Mecklenburg (1552) added "Erhalt uns, Herr, bei deinem Wort" (Keep us, Lord, by thy word) or "Verleih uns Frieden" (Grant us peace)
  (Sehling 5, p. 199).
- Duke Henry's Saxony (1539) added "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised), "and so go home" (Sehling 1, p. 275).

---

### <a id="s2-14"></a>2.14 When nobody communicated

**The Mass without the Supper.** No evangelical order allowed a Mass without communicants. When
nobody had announced himself for the Supper, the Mass stopped after the sermon. What was left
was the first half of the ordo, closed with prayers. The postcommunion substitutes and the
Litany in this place are treated in [Chapter 5](#ch5), [§5.6](#s5-6), and
[Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22](#s13-22); the change of vestments in
[Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.7](#s14-7).

**The forms.**
- **Pomerania 1535**: "everything is sung, as is ordered, until the sermon; but after the sermon
  one or two German psalms" (Sehling 4, p. 341).
- **Mecklenburg 1552**: confession and absolution; a German psalm or two, or "Allein Gott" (To God alone);
  collect; epistle; psalm; gospel; *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed); "Wir glauben" (We believe); the sermon with the prayer
  (Sehling 5, p. 199).
- **Albertine Saxony 1580**: "after the sermon, or a chapter of holy Scripture read, it shall be
  concluded with a Christian collect and the customary benediction" (Sehling 1, p. 369).
- **Transylvania 1547**: no Mass, but a German psalm, collect, sequence or tract, a chapter of
  the New Testament in course, "Wir glauben", and the suffrages.

The Transylvanian rubric shows how far the service fell back toward the office. **Transylvania,
*Kirchenordnung* (German), 1547** (Sehling 24, p. 244):

<!-- doc 1669 -->

But where there are no communicants for this office, no Mass at all is held; but in its stead
there is sung first a German psalm, thereupon the collect, further a Christian sequence or
tract, or what the season bringeth. Thereafter is read, in order from the beginning of the New
Testament to the end, always one chapter in German; only that in Lent the German epistles and
gospels are kept, as they are appointed for the days. After the reading of the same chapter is
sung "We all believe", with the versicle and collect of the Holy Trinity. Thereafter follow also
the other suffrages, namely for the king, for the forgiveness of sins and for peace, with their
versicles and collects; which also is concluded with the *Benedicamus* and the blessing of the
people.

**The boys' daily Mass at Hof.** One order kept a Mass-shaped service with no communion at all,
as a school exercise. At Hof (1592) the boys' "*actus diurnus*" (daily act) ran: the seasonal Kyrie and *Et
in terra* (And on earth) from the great missal; the gospel in Latin; sequence, tract or gradual; the gospel in
German; "the Sanctus of the season", with the Preface on the chief feasts; the Lord's Prayer
sung by a boy "in the deacon's place"; "the Agnus Dei of the season"; and a collect
(Sehling 11, pp. 472–473).

---

### <a id="s2-15"></a>2.15 Ceremonial: gestures, postures and places

Several gestures are treated elsewhere:
- where the minister stands, and whether he faces the people:
  [Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.5.2](#s14-5-2);
- vestments: [Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.7](#s14-7);
- the elevation, the signs of the cross printed over the elements, and the bows of the
  Latin-frame canons: [Chapter 7](#ch7) (e.g. §§[7.12.3](#s7-12-3),
  [7.12.8](#s7-12-8));
- the priest kneeling at the preparation and after the Mass:
  [Chapter 3](#ch3), §§[3.3.2](#s3-3-2)–[3.3.4](#s3-3-4), [3.6.3](#s3-6-3);
- kneeling during *Veni sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit), "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we) and the hymn in the place of the
  offertory: [Chapter 8](#ch8), §§[8.4.1](#s8-4-1), [8.11.3](#s8-11-3), [8.13.2](#s8-13-2);
- deacons, subdeacons and ministrants at the altar:
  [Chapter 16](#ch16), [§16.4.2](#s16-4-2).

This section gathers what the orders prescribe for the body during the Mass, gesture by gesture.

#### <a id="s2-15-1"></a>2.15.1 What the orders say, and what they do not

**The searches.** The corpus was searched, near the Mass and the Supper, for each of the
following:
- the sign of the cross ("creutz machen", *signum crucis*, "segnen", and the † and [+] marks the
  editions print in the text);
- genuflection (*genuflexio*, "kniebeugen", *flexis genibus*);
- kneeling, bowing (*inclinatio*, "neigen", "bücken") and standing or sitting;
- hats and bare heads ("hut", "baret", *capite aperto* [with bare head], "bloßes haupt" [bare head]);
- the hands (*manibus iunctis*, *extensis*, "gefaltene hände", "aufgehobene hände");
- turning ("kert sich zum volk", *conversus ad populum*), the sides and horns of the altar
  (*cornu*, "rechte seite", "epistelseite");
- the kiss and the pax, incense and the washing of hands.

**Few rubrics.** The orders prescribe little. Where they say anything, it is usually one of
three things:
- kneeling, for prayer and for communion;
- turning, toward the altar to pray and toward the people to read, greet and exhort;
- a warning against the old gestures.

Much was left to custom. Nassau (1575, Philippist) keeps "the customary old form of the
administration" of the Supper, but drops the "rites and gesticulations" (Sehling 10, p. 151).

**Not found.** No order in the corpus prescribes any of the following:
- the Roman genuflection on one knee. *Flexis genibus* (On bended knees) and "mit gebogenen knien" (with bent knees) always mean
  kneeling;
- the epistle and gospel horns of the altar, or carrying the book from one side to the other;
- turning over the right shoulder, or any rule for the direction of a turn;
- the hands of the celebrant joined, raised in the *orans* position, or extended toward the
  people;
- the kiss of the altar, of the book, of the paten, or of the deacon's hand. Nor are there any
  honours paid to the deacon;
- the celebrant's biretta, or taking it off and putting it on at the altar;
- incense at the Mass;
- the *Lavabo*.

#### <a id="s2-15-2"></a>2.15.2 The sign of the cross

**Kept in the early German Masses.** The first German Masses still print the crosses:
- **Allstedt** (Radical Reformation). Müntzer's *Ordnung und berechnunge des teutschen ampts*
  (1523) marks the bread and the cup at the Words of Institution: "blessed † it and brake it", "gesegnete † den" (blessed † it). The minister raises his hand at "This is my body", and turns to the people with the cup (Sehling 1, p. 506).
- **Strasbourg** (Moderate Reformed). In Schwarz's German Mass of 1524 the places "where the
  cross is to be made" are marked [+], according to the editors (Sehling 20/1, p. 120). The
  priest, turned to the people, says "God be gracious and have mercy upon us all [+]" at the
  beginning. He blesses with three crosses at the end, "The blessing of God, the Father [+] and the Son [+] and the Holy Ghost [+]" (Sehling 20/1, pp. 120, 123). The *Teutsche Meß und
  Tauff* (German Mass and Baptism) and the *Ordenung und inhalt* (order and content) of 1524 do the same (pp. 130, 133, 137).
- **Hof.** As late as 1592 the order prints a † after the deacon's Pax, "The peace of the Lord be with you all. †", and after the blessing (Sehling 11, pp. 426–427).

The Latin-frame orders keep the signs over the elements at the Verba. They are printed in
[Chapter 7](#ch7) with ✠.

**Rejected.** Hannover (1536) lets go of what is not needful, among it "so many crosses" and
"such gestures" (Sehling 6/2, pp. 1007–1008). Danzig (1557), as Sehling quotes it, makes the
point at the Words of Institution. **Danzig, first order of the Sunday Mass, 1557**
(Sehling 4, p. 168):

<!-- doc 1844 -->

The priest taketh the paten with the appointed host into his hand without all papistical
crossing and other gestures; so also, when he singeth the words "he took the cup", he taketh the
cup into his hand.

**Outside the Mass.** The sign of the cross stayed in baptism, at the exorcism ("Receive the sign of the holy cross", Luther's *Taufbüchlein* [baptism booklet], Sehling 1, p. 18). It also stayed in the
household prayers of the Small Catechism: "In the morning … thou shalt bless thyself with the
holy cross and say: The will of God, Father, Son and Holy Ghost be done" (Kurpfalz 1556, Sehling
14, p. 141).

#### <a id="s2-15-3"></a>2.15.3 Kneeling, not genuflecting

**The priest kneels.** The priest kneels at these points:
- for his preparation or *Confiteor* (I confess) at the foot of the altar (Pfalz-Neuburg, Mecklenburg,
  Regensburg, Hildesheim and others;
  [Chapter 3](#ch3), §§[3.3.2](#s3-3-2)–[3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). At Solms (1603) he
  does so "on the stool" before the altar (Sehling 9, p. 359);
- for the Kyrie and the prayers at Schwäbisch Hall (1535, below);
- through "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we) at Soest (1609), where the pastor "remains sitting on his knees"
  (Sehling 22, p. 489);
- after communion. At Hildesheim (1544) he kneels again before the altar and "thanketh God
  secretly for himself" (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 855). In Mecklenburg (1540/1545) the priest kneels
  before the altar and "the whole congregation shall do likewise", and they sing "Erhalt uns,
  Herr, bei deinem Wort" (Keep us, Lord, by thy word; Sehling 5, p. 155).

**The congregation kneels.** The Brenz order for Schwäbisch Hall makes the whole church kneel at
the Kyrie, and says why. **Schwäbisch Hall, *Kirchenordnung*, 1527** (Sehling 17/1, p. 49):

<!-- doc 755 -->

After the psalm the Kyrie eleison shall be sung, as hath been customary. But since it is an
earnest, humble prayer, the whole church shall kneel thereto; not that anything toward God lieth
in the kneeling, but that there may be a common discipline in the church, and every thing its
order.

The Hall draft of 1535 kneels everyone for the Lord's Prayer before the Verba, and lets the
pastor alone stand up to say them. **Schwäbisch Hall, draft order of service, 1535**
(Sehling 17/1, p. 102):

<!-- doc 760 -->

At the end of the announcement it shall be concluded with an Our Father, which every man shall
pray secretly, kneeling down also. After the prayer the pastor alone standeth up and saith the
words of consecration, "For in the night in which the LORD," etc., aloud, in German.

Other orders kneel the congregation at these points:
- from the Lord's Prayer to the end of the communion: Hatzkerode (1534): "the whole church shall
  kneel devoutly until the end of the communion" (Sehling 2, p. 587);
- at the Lord's Prayer of the preparation for the Supper, after the examination and the
  declaration of forgiveness: the Palatinate (1563, Reformed): "Kneel down and pray, as the Lord hath taught us: Our Father" (Sehling 14, p. 383). The Palatine order of 1601
  (Reformed) copied the preparation but struck the kneeling out
  ("the kneeling at the prayer is struck out", Sehling 14, p. 574);
- at the thanksgiving: Heilbronn (1543): "Kneel down and lift up your hearts unto God"
  (Sehling 17/1, p. 316); Lützelstein (1605): "Kneel and make the thanksgiving"
  (Sehling 18, p. 606);
- at the prayers: in the penitential service of Wittgenstein (1555) the ministers kneel and bid
  the people "also sit upon their knees" (Sehling 22, p. 139); Ulm (1556): the preachers asked
  that the people, who sat through the common prayer "out of the convenience of the pews", be
  taught to kneel, "as is customary in other churches" (Sehling 17/2, p. 213);
- in the place of the offertory: Celle (1545) and Anhalt (1548)
  ([Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.11.3](#s8-11-3)).

**Boys kneeling before the altar.** The singers of certain pieces knelt:
- *Da pacem* (Give peace), three times, in the Pomeranian Mass (1569, Sehling 4, p. 438);
- "Kom, heiliger Geist" (Come, Holy Ghost) at Corvey's Bruchhausen (1603, Sehling 21, p. 244);
- the litany at Marggrabowa in Prussia (1581, Sehling 4, p. 149);
- *Veni sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) and "Nun bitten wir" at Hof, with the whole choir kneeling
  ([Chapter 8](#ch8), [§8.4.1](#s8-4-1)).

**At "and was made man".** One custom is reported only later. At Mansfeld, as a memorial against
the Flacian error of Cyriacus Spangenberg, four choirboys knelt before the altar during the
Creed. They sang alone "is born a true man" and touched the altar steps with their
foreheads; the custom lasted into the eighteenth century
(Sehling 2, p. 183, after Leopold's chronicle of 1817).

**Communicants kneel.** Most orders that say how communion was received have the communicants
kneel at the altar:
- Regensburg (1542): the men on the right of the altar, the women on the left, "that at the end
  of the *Patrem* they kneel down there" (Sehling 13, pp. 392–393);
- Hohenlohe (1553): two honourable men set out a silk cloth and "little benches, on which the
  communicants kneel" (Sehling 15, p. 71);
- Lippe (1566): the men on one side, the women on the other (Sehling 21, p. 388);
- Marienhafe in East Frisia (1593): "kneeling, at one end of the altar or table the blessed
  bread, at the other the cup" (Sehling 7/1, p. 710);
- Solms (1603): the communicants kneel in the choir while the pastor, turned toward them, reads
  the exhortation (Sehling 9, p. 361);
- Ermsleben (1564): "they kneel down devoutly; then I pray before them, and they pray after me
  secretly; thereafter I do the consecration" (Sehling 2, p. 485).

After receiving, the communicants in Bugenhagen's orders went back to their places and "sit on
their knees or stand, until the last blessing" (Hamburg 1529, Sehling 5, p. 529; Wolfenbüttel
1543, Sehling 6/1, p. 58).

**Standing allowed, sitting forbidden.** In Poland the Lutheran, Reformed and Brethren churches
of the Sandomierz consensus had to settle the posture together. **Synod of Petrikau, 1–3 June
1578** (Sandomierz consensus; Sehling 4, p. 263):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

We grant the ceremonies to Christian liberty, and permit that the godly receive the sacrament of
the body and blood of Christ standing or kneeling. But the sitting at the Lord's table, since,
besides the rites commonly used in all evangelical churches throughout Europe, those were the
first authors of it among us who […] became faithless deserters from us to Arianism […] we
reject as a ceremony.

The synod of 1583 repeated the rule. Communion was to be given "to those standing or kneeling
(with a protestation against the bread-worship customary among the papists)"
(Sehling 4, p. 264). The Bohemian Brethren (Hussite) received kneeling. Their *Ordo
ecclesiasticus* (Church Order), as Sehling prints it, explains that their forebears had brought in standing in
1494 and gave it up under persecution (Sehling 4, p. 284). In Reformed Emden a Lasco still
received kneeling over a towel; the custom was abolished by 1546 at the latest
(editors' note, Sehling 7/1, p. 377).

**Reverence, not adoration.** The Calvinizing Nassau order of 1575 (Philippist) warned the
people off the old gestures. **Nassau-Dillenburg, *Agende*, 1575**
(Philippist; Sehling 10, p. 151):

<!-- doc 182 -->

Moreover the people shall be exhorted that they show themselves modest and reverent indeed, but
not as though they would worship an idol with folded hands and bending of the knee (as is done
in the papacy, and some of ours are still wont). After the exhortation "Dearly beloved in God",
etc. has been read, the ministers shall remain standing thus with their face turned toward the
people.

#### <a id="s2-15-4"></a>2.15.4 Bowing

**Only in the Latin canons.** The bows that survive are the priest's, in the orders that kept a
Latin canon:
- Brandenburg (1540) lifts the host "with a slight bow", and has the priest bow for the ablution prayer *Corpus tuum, Domine* (Thy body, O Lord)
  (*Deinde inclinet se et dicat*) (Sehling 3, pp. 69–70);
- Pfalz-Neuburg (1543) copies the second (Sehling 13, p. 76).

The texts are in [Chapter 7](#ch7), §§[7.12.3](#s7-12-3), [7.12.8](#s7-12-8).

**The name of Jesus.** No order prescribes a bow at the name of Jesus. The words of Philippians
2:10, "In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow", are sung as the introit of the Passion Mass
by Müntzer (Radical Reformation) and those who copied him
(Sehling 1, p. 502; 6/2, p. 825; 2, p. 379), but no rubric turns them into a gesture.

#### <a id="s2-15-5"></a>2.15.5 Hats and heads

**Men uncovered, women covered.** Hesse (Moderate Reformed) puts the old rule of 1 Corinthians
11 into the church order. **Hesse, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 231):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

It belongeth also to seemliness and Christian discipline, that in the common assembly of the
Christians the women appear with covered head, but the men with bare heads, whereof the apostle
Paul [speaketh], 1 Corinthians 11.

A bare head appears elsewhere as a mark of humility:
- the public penitent at Limpurg (1596) sits through the whole sermon "with bare head" on a
  stool set before the altar or pulpit (Sehling 16, p. 609);
- at an ordination the superintendent lays his hand "on the bare head" of the new pastor
  (Württemberg 1559, Sehling 16, p. 356).

No order regulates the clergy's caps at the altar. Clerical caps appear only as dress outside
the service ([Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.8](#s14-8)).

#### <a id="s2-15-6"></a>2.15.6 Hands

**No rule for the celebrant's hands.** The orders say only what the hands hold:
- Müntzer (Radical Reformation): "raising the hand" at the bread (*Elevando manu*), and taking
  the cup "before the people" (Sehling 1, p. 506);
- Brandenburg (1540): "take the chalice with both hands"
  (Sehling 3, p. 69);
- Transylvania (1547): the minister, turned to the people, says the Lord's Prayer and then the
  Verba "from the book over the bread and the wine, holding each in turn in his hands" (*per
  vices utrunque tenens in manibus*) (Sehling 24, p. 223).

**Folded hands.** Folded hands appear only for children at the table prayers (Sayn, Solms), and
in Nassau's warning against folded hands (1575, Philippist) before the sacrament (above). The
laying on of hands belongs to ordination, confirmation, absolution and the reconciliation of
penitents, outside the Mass.

#### <a id="s2-15-7"></a>2.15.7 Turning: toward the altar, toward the people

**The common rule.** Where the minister stood at an altar against the wall, the orders turn him
to the altar to pray and to the people to read, greet and exhort. Wittenberg (1533) sets the
pattern: "the priest readeth a German collect turned toward the altar, and singeth the epistle
turned toward the people"; the gospel "turned toward the people", then "again toward the altar"
for *Credo in unum Deum* (I believe in one God; Sehling 1, p. 704). Other orders follow it:
- Prussia (1544): "the priest turneth to the people and singeth: Der herre sei mit euch, and
  turneth again to the altar" for the collect (Sehling 4, p. 66);
- Mecklenburg (1552): the collect "toward the altar", then "he turneth himself again toward the
  people" for the epistle (Sehling 5, p. 202), followed by Lüneburg (1564, Sehling 6/1, p. 553);
- Schwarzburg (1574): the gospel toward the people, the creed toward the altar
  (Sehling 2, pp. 132–133);
- Osnabrück (1613): the salutation toward the people, the collect and the thanksgiving toward
  the altar (Sehling 7/1, pp. 268, 270).

**Turned for the Pax.** The minister turns to the people for the Pax:
- Regensburg (1542): "he turneth about toward the people and singeth: *Pax vobiscum*"
  (Sehling 13, p. 393);
- Pfalz-Neuburg (1543): "Thereafter let him turn to the people" (Sehling 13, p. 75);
- Hof (1592): *Diaconus spectans populum* (the deacon facing the people; Sehling 11, p. 426).

**Turned for the Verba, or away.** The orders divided over the Words of Institution:
- **toward the people:**
  - Müntzer (Radical Reformation; "the minister turning … before the people");
  - Transylvania (*minister conversus ad populum*);
  - Nassau (1575, Philippist, above). Brandenburg (1540) turns to the people for the exhortation
    and the thanksgiving ("turning to the people", Sehling 3, pp. 69–70);
- **toward the altar:**
  - Limpurg (1610): "he turneth himself toward the altar and saith with distinct voice the words
    or institution of the Supper" (Sehling 16, p. 620);
  - Sponheim (1607): the minister is to face the people always, "except when, in the action of
    the Holy Supper, they speak the words of blessing over the elements standing on the altar
    and pray the Our Father"; then they turn to the altar. But where the altar allows it, he
    shall stand behind it and say the whole preface, prayer and consecration there, facing the
    people (Sehling 18, p. 674).

**Everything toward the people.** Döber's German Mass at the Nürnberg hospital went furthest.
**Nürnberg, *Deutsche Messe* of Andreas Döber, 1525** (Sehling 11, p. 51):

<!-- doc 249 -->

First, when the priest cometh to the altar and hath taken the chalice out of the bag, he turneth
himself to the people and speaketh aloud as followeth (also all the words that are in the whole
Mass), so that he be understood by the hearers.

Heilbronn's draft of 1532 has the minister standing at the altar "by the cross", not in the Mass
vestment, turn to the people to read the German collect (Sehling 17/1, p. 301). Hesse (1566,
Moderate Reformed) has the collect read "after he hath turned himself to the people"
(Sehling 8, p. 239). The visitations that rebuilt altars so that the minister should face the
people throughout, and the condemnation of standing behind the table, are in
[Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.5.2](#s14-5-2).

#### <a id="s2-15-8"></a>2.15.8 Places at the altar

**No horns.** The orders do not speak of the epistle and gospel sides. The sides of the altar
appear instead as the places of the communicants and of the two elements:
- **Men right, women left.** Regensburg 1542 (above), Wertheim about 1555 (Sehling 11, p. 713),
  Frankfurt 1530 (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 9, p. 497).
- **Bread at one side, cup at the other.** The orders differ on which side:
  - the Palatinate (1546): the communicants "receive the sacrament of the body of Christ on the
    left side of the altar, and the sacrament of the blood on the right side"
    (Sehling 14, p. 97);
  - Hatzkerode (1534) has it the other way round: the body "on the right side from the hand of
    the pastor", the blood "on the left side from the deacon", with silk cloths held under on
    both sides (Sehling 2, p. 587);
  - Neckarbischofsheim (1560): the communicants "go round the altar on the right side to the
    pastor, to receive the blood of the Lord" (Sehling 16, p. 684);
  - Marienhafe 1593: bread at one end, cup at the other (above).
- **At the cross-altar.** Heilbronn (1530): after the creed "the preacher turneth over the cross
  altar with his two deacons in surplices toward the people" and proclaims the Lord's death
  (Sehling 17/1, p. 285).

#### <a id="s2-15-9"></a>2.15.9 The Peace, the kiss and incense

**The kiss of peace replaced by a reading.** Luther made the Pax an absolution ([§2.8](#s2-8)). Strasbourg
(Moderate Reformed) replaced the kiss with a text. **Strasbourg, *Gottesdienstordnung*, 1542**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, p. 330):

<!-- doc 1311 -->

Then, since among the ancients at the distribution of the Lord's Supper the kiss of peace was in
use as a sign of mutual reconciliation, let the minister in the stead of it read some text of
brotherly reconciliation, admonishing [them].

No order keeps a pax-board.

**Incense.** None of the orders prescribes incense at the Mass:
- the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) leaves lights and incense at the gospel free (Sehling 1, p. 5);
- Hannover (1536) lets go of "censing" with the other unneeded gestures (Sehling 6/2, p. 1007).

**Ablutions.** In the sick communion of Brandenburg (1540) and Pfalz-Neuburg (1543) the priest
rinses his fingers over the chalice and gives the ablution to the sick person
(Sehling 3, p. 80; 13, p. 88). The Latin ablution prayers of the Mass are in
[Chapter 7](#ch7), [§7.12.8](#s7-12-8).

#### <a id="s2-15-10"></a>2.15.10 Summary

| Gesture | Prescribed | Rejected or absent |
|---|---|---|
| Sign of the cross | over bread and cup (Allstedt 1523, Radical Reformation); at the greeting and blessing (Strasbourg 1524, Moderate Reformed); at the Pax and blessing (Hof 1592); over the elements in the Latin canons | "so many crosses" let go (Hannover 1536); "without all papistical crossing" (Danzig 1557); "rites and gesticulations" avoided (Nassau 1575, Philippist) |
| Genuflection | none | *flexis genibus* (on bended knees) means kneeling |
| Kneeling | priest at the preparation, the Kyrie and after communion; people at the Kyrie (Hall 1527), the Lord's Prayer (Hall 1535, Palatinate 1563 (Reformed)), the whole communion (Hatzkerode 1534), the thanksgiving (Heilbronn 1543, Lützelstein 1605); communicants at the altar; boys at *Da pacem* (Give peace), the litany, *Veni sancte* | folded hands and kneeling "as to an idol" (Nassau 1575, Philippist); kneeling at prayer struck out (Palatinate 1601, Reformed); sitting at communion forbidden (Petrikau 1578) |
| Bowing | at the elevation and the ablution prayer (Brandenburg 1540, Pfalz-Neuburg 1543); boys' foreheads to the step at "born man" (Mansfeld, later report) | no bow at the name of Jesus |
| Head | men bareheaded, women covered (Hesse 1566, Moderate Reformed) | no rubric for the celebrant's cap |
| Hands | raise the hand at the bread (Allstedt, Radical Reformation); the chalice with both hands (Brandenburg); bread and cup held in turn (Transylvania) | no *orans*, joined hands or extended hands |
| Turning | to the altar for collects and creed, to the people for readings, salutation, Pax and exhortation (Wittenberg 1533 and most); everything toward the people (Döber 1525) | no direction of turn, no right shoulder |
| Places | men right, women left; bread and cup at two sides or ends | no epistle or gospel horn |
| Kiss | a text on reconciliation in its place (Strasbourg 1542, Moderate Reformed) | no kiss of altar, book or deacon; no pax-board |
| Incense | free at the gospel (*Formula missae*) | "censing" let go (Hannover 1536); prescribed nowhere |

## <a id="ch3"></a>Chapter 3. Mass Preliminaries


This chapter covers the parts of the evangelical Mass that are neither Ordinary nor Proper, in the
church orders of the sixteenth century printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen
Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century). It asks:

- **Opening versicles and preliminaries.** What stood before the Introit, and into what families
  do the orders fall?
- **The exhortation.** Where does the exhortation to the communicants fall, and what does it
  say?
- **The *Confiteor*, *Misereatur*, *Indulgentiam* and absolution.** Where are they? Does the
  priest say them alone, with his ministrants or sexton, or with the people? Are they said
  privately before Mass, at the beginning of Mass, or in the communion rite? Are the old texts
  kept or new ones written? Is the absolution optative, declaratory or indicative, and how does
  it compare with the modern Common Service?
- **Before and after the service.** Do the vesting prayers survive? Are the *Benedicite* (Bless ye) and Ps
  150 appointed after Mass, and who says them? Are there prayers before and after the sermon, on
  entering or leaving church, or for the communicants?

**How the chapter is laid out.**
- [§3.1](#s3-1) summarizes the findings, and [§3.2](#s3-2) sets out the scope and sources.
- [§3.3](#s3-3) covers the opening versicles and preliminaries, by family.
- [§3.4](#s3-4) covers the confession and absolution: placement, the chancel party, old and new texts, the
  form of the absolution, and the descent of the Common Service's confession.
- [§3.5](#s3-5) covers the exhortation to the communicants: where it falls, and the families of text, each
  collated against its archetype, which is printed in full with a translation.
- [§3.6](#s3-6) covers what comes before and after the service: vesting, the priest's private prayers, the
  *Benedicite* and Ps 150, prayers about the sermon, and prayers on entering church and at
  communion.
- [§3.7](#s3-7) is a table by order, and [§3.8](#s3-8) a concordance of every order quoted.

The Canon, the Words of Institution and the prayers around communion are treated in
[Chapter 7](#ch7). Several texts printed there are only
cross-referenced here: Kantz 1522, Döber's exhortation, the Kiel Mass and Bugenhagen's
preparatory prayer.

**Related chapters.** Several subjects are treated more fully elsewhere and are only cited here:
- the whole order of the Mass, and where the preliminaries fall in it:
  [Chapter 2](#ch2), §§[2.4](#s2-4)–[2.5](#s2-5);
- private confession and absolution, and the examination of communicants:
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.17](#s13-17);
- the hymns at the opening of the service: [Chapter 8](#ch8),
  [§8.4](#s8-4);
- the prayers and notices around the sermon: [Chapter 11](#ch11), [§11.10](#s11-10);
- confession and communion as duties of the laity:
  [Chapter 15](#ch15), [§15.8.3](#s15-8-3);
- fasting before communion: [Chapter 12](#ch12),
  [§12.13.6](#s12-13-6);
- vestments: [Chapter 14](#ch14), [§14.7](#s14-7).

### <a id="s3-1"></a>3.1 Summary of findings

1. **The Roman preparation was broken up.** No evangelical order keeps the whole of the priest's
   preparation: *Introibo* (I will go in), Ps 43 *Iudica me* (Judge me), *Confiteor* (I confess), *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy), *Indulgentiam* (Pardon) and
   *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us). The one order that keeps most of it is Müntzer's Allstedt Mass (1523/1524;
   Radical Reformation): Ps 43 said by priest and people, then the *Confiteor*, the
   *Misereatur*, *Deus, tu conversus* (O God, thou wilt turn again) and *Aufer a nobis*, all in German and aloud; *Introibo*
   survives there only as a verse of the psalm ([§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)). Elsewhere *Iudica me* disappears, and
   *Aufer a nobis* survives only in the *Cellische Ordnungen* (Celle orders) of 1545 (after the sermon) and, on
   the editor's reading, at Regensburg
   1542. *Adiutorium nostrum* (Our help; Ps 124:8) is the one versicle that survives widely. The German
         missals' *Confitemini Domino quoniam bonus* (O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good) survives in Döber and Mecklenburg 1540
         ([§3.3.1](#s3-3-1)).
2. **The preliminaries fall into seven families** ([§3.3.1](#s3-3-1)):
   - **A.** The priest's private *Confiteor* at the altar during the Introit
     (Brandenburg-Nürnberg, Brandenburg, Pfalz-Neuburg, Hohenlohe, Regensburg, Amberg,
     Buxtehude, Bergedorf, Schleswig-Holstein).
   - **B.** Bugenhagen's kneeling prayer with the sexton: the Our Father and *Domine, non
     secundum* (O Lord, deal not with us; Wolfenbüttel, Hildesheim).
   - **C.** The public confession of Döber (Nürnberg 1525), carried north to Lippe, Kiel and
     Mecklenburg and back south to Amberg, Pfalz-Zweibrücken and Pfalz-Veldenz. Amberg 1555 puts
     the confession in the plural, "We poor sinful men" ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)).
   - **D.** The medieval *Offene Schuld* (open confession) of the preaching service moved into the Mass (Kantz,
     Bremen 1525, Volprecht, Naumburg, Nördlingen).
   - **E.** The Strasbourg and Reformed opening: confession and comfortable word (Strasbourg
     1537, Moderate Reformed; Palatinate 1563, Reformed).
   - **F.** A hymn, a German psalm, or *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) with its versicle and collect, the
     last a recasting of the medieval *accessus* as a preparation of the congregation (Luther
     1526, Amberg 1544, Verden 1606, Transylvania 1547).
   - **G.** Müntzer's German *Stufengebet* (prayers at the foot of the altar) at Allstedt (Radical Reformation), with Ps 43 said by
     priest and people ([§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)).
3. **The confession stands in four places** ([§3.4.1](#s3-4-1)): privately before the Introit; publicly
   before the Introit; after the sermon (Bugenhagen 1528, Amberg 1550, the Palatinate); and in
   the communion rite after the exhortation (Kantz, Württemberg 1536, Nürnberg after 1569).
   Mecklenburg 1552 and Nördlingen 1544 have it twice.
4. **The chancel party** ([§3.4.2](#s3-4-2)):
   - **Families A and B.** The priest prays alone or with his ministrants (Brandenburg 1540,
     Pfalz-Neuburg), or with the second ministrant in dialogue (Regensburg). In the north the
     sexton is the server: he kneels with the priest (Bugenhagen, Mecklenburg 1540), says the
     *Misereatur* (Kiel), or reads the absolution (Kiel, Hadeln).
   - **Family C.** In Mecklenburg 1552 and Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 "another minister or the
     custos" kneels beside the priest and says the prayer for forgiveness, and the choir answers
     the versicle.
   - **The people** keep silence and confess in their hearts (Mecklenburg), repeat the words
     after the priest (Döber, Bugenhagen's pulpit confession, Amberg's weekday prayer), or
     answer "Yes" (Palatinate 1563, Reformed).
5. **Before Mass.** The priest's *Confiteor* is said at the altar, not in the sacristy. The
   communicant's real preparation is private confession on the Saturday or before the service.
   The Brandenburg and Pfalz-Neuburg orders forbid a "gemeine beicht" (common confession) in its
   place ([§3.4.6](#s3-4-6)).
6. **No Roman text is kept in public.** The Latin *Confiteor* survives only as the priest's
   private prayer, unprinted (Hohenlohe: "the pure Confiteor in Latin"). Every public
   confession is a new text, in five families of wording ([§3.4.3](#s3-4-3)). The *Misereatur* survives by
   name at Kiel; as a prayer for "us" in Döber; and as the second minister's collect in
   Mecklenburg 1552. The *Indulgentiam* survives in Kantz's "The almighty, merciful God forgive you your sins!" and in Döber's "The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us".
7. **Five kinds of absolution** ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)):
   - **optative** ("vouchsafe to have mercy upon us");
   - **declaration of grace** in the first person plural ("hath had mercy upon us … God grant this unto us all");
   - **indicative** ("I declare you free, quit and loosed"; "I forgive you"; "I loose you");
   - **conditional declaration** with retention (Strasbourg 1537, Moderate Reformed; Palatinate
     1563, Reformed);
   - **none**, only a word of comfort (Bugenhagen 1528).

   At the beginning of Mass the declaration of grace prevails; in the communion rite, the
   indicative.
8. **The Common Service descends from Mecklenburg** ([§3.4.5](#s3-4-5)). The Common Service's preparation is
   Döber's 1525 sequence by way of Mecklenburg 1552 and Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557. That sequence is
   the address "Beloved in the Lord", *Adiutorium* (Our help), the confession "by nature sinful and
   unclean", the prayer "O most merciful God", and the declaration "Almighty God … hath had
   mercy upon us … Grant this, O Lord, unto us all". The prayer "O most merciful God" was the
   second minister's *Misereatur*; the declaration is a declaration of grace, not an indicative
   absolution. The indicative form of later American books ("Upon this your confession … I
   forgive you all your sins") has its counterpart in Naumburg 1537.
9. **The exhortation** ([§3.5](#s3-5)) falls in six places:
   - after the sermon, from the pulpit or altar (Luther 1526, left free);
   - at the altar before the Verba (Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, moved there at Luther's
     suggestion; Württemberg; the Palatinate 1563, Reformed);
   - before the Preface, as the "true Preface" (Bugenhagen);
   - after the Preface and Sanctus (Mecklenburg 1552; Naumburg 1537 before the Sanctus);
   - after the Verba and Our Father (Nürnberg 1524–1525, Osiander's original place);
   - after communion (Memmingen 1528, Moderate Reformed; Marienhafe 1593).

   There are eleven families of text, each collated word by word against its archetype ([§3.5.2](#s3-5-2)):
   Luther 1526; Osiander 1524, with the Braunschweig recension of the north;
   Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533; Württemberg 1536, revised 1553; Bugenhagen 1528, in Low and High
   German; Naumburg 1537; Mecklenburg 1552, which contains an absolution; the Palatinate 1563
   (Reformed), with its Lower Rhine recension (Reformed); Pfalz-Veldenz 1574; the Basel text
   (Reformed) of Memmingen 1528 (Moderate Reformed) and Neckarbischofsheim 1560; and Strasbourg
   1525 (Moderate Reformed). Augsburg 1530 (Moderate Reformed), Buxtehude 1565 and Micron
   (Reformed) each have an exhortation of their own ([§3.5.14](#s3-5-14)). Every archetype is given in full
   with a translation.
10. **No vesting prayers** ([§3.6.1](#s3-6-1)). None of the prayers in the Lutheran Missal Project's *Vesting
    Prayers* occurs in any order: the preparatory psalms, the antiphon *Ne reminiscaris* (Remember not), the
    *preces* and collects, and the prayers at the washing of hands and at each vestment.
    Vestments are "indifferent". The priest vests in silence, at Hadeln during the *Te
    Deum* (We praise thee, O God) "not as needful". The *Stufengebet* alone of the medieval priest's
    three preparations survives. The *accessus* survives only as the congregation's *Veni Sancte
    Spiritus*.
11. **After Mass** ([§3.6.3](#s3-6-3)). The *Benedicite* (Bless ye) and Ps 150 are never appointed after Mass. They
    occur only as the canticle and psalms of Sunday Lauds, sung by the schoolboys under the
    cantor or by the canons (Pomerania 1535, Schleswig-Holstein 1542, Ansbach 1533). The
    priest's private thanksgiving survives only at Hildesheim 1544 and in Schleswig-Holstein
    1542: he unvests during the closing hymn, kneels, and "thanketh God secretly for himself", with no text given.
12. **Sermon, church door and communion** (§§[3.6.4](#s3-6-4)–[3.6.5](#s3-6-5)):
    - The sermon is framed by a bidding to prayer, the Our Father or a hymn of the Holy Ghost,
      and the general prayer after it. All are led by the preacher, with the people praying and
      the schoolboys singing.
    - No order prints a prayer for the worshipper on entering or leaving church, or private
      prayers for the communicant. Their place is taken by the opening hymn "when one cometh into the church" (Sayn 1590), the prayers the minister says for the communicants
      (Pfalz-Veldenz 1574), and the hymns during the distribution.
    - The nearest thing to a hymnal devotion is the Pfalz-Zweibrücken *Gesangbuch* (hymnal) of 1571/1587,
      which prints the Mecklenburg confession and absolution for the people's use "before the sermon on Sunday".

---

### <a id="s3-2"></a>3.2 Scope, sources and method

**Scope.** The chapter covers the evangelical (Lutheran, Upper German and Reformed) orders printed
in Sehling's volumes 1–24. It deals with what the orders set before the Introit, the confession
and absolution wherever they fall, the exhortation to the communicants, and the prayers before
and after the service. It does not treat:
- the Ordinary and Propers (see [Chapter 4](#ch4));
- the collects (see [Chapter 5](#ch5));
- the general prayer (see [Chapter 6](#ch6));
- the Canon and the communion devotions (see
  [Chapter 7](#ch7));
- private confession (see [Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.17](#s13-17)).

**Sources.** The quotations come from the [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) database. Candidate passages were found by
searching the whole corpus for:
- the Latin incipits *Confiteor* (I confess), *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy), *Indulgentiam* (Pardon), *Introibo* (I will go in), *Adiutorium* (Our help),
  *Confitemini* (O give thanks), *Ne reminiscaris* (Remember not), *Quam dilecta* (How amiable), *Benedicite* (Bless ye) and *Laudate*;
- the German and Low German words for open confession and absolution (*offene beicht*, *offene
  schuld*, *gemeine beicht*, *bicht*, *absolutio*);
- the words for the exhortation (*vermanung*, *vormaninge*, *exhortatio*, *ermanung*), together
  with the address formulas ("Mein allerliebsten", "Lieben freunde", "Myne allerlevesten", "Ir
  geliebten");
- the words for vesting, the sacristy and the preparation (*ornat*, *messgewand*, *angekledet*,
  *praeparatio ad missam*, *Rüsthandlung*);
- prayers before and after the sermon, on entering church, and before and after communion.

Each hit was read in context. Editor's notes that identify a source or a medieval model are
quoted where they bear on the question.

**Method and limits.**
- **Pages.** Each order is cited by Sehling's running head. Pages were checked against the page
  markers in the database.
- **Dates.** Some orders are dated differently in the database's record headings. Hadeln is
  printed by Sehling as the "Hadelner Kirchenordnung von 1526" (Hadeln church order of 1526) within a record headed 1590.
  Verden's order is the *Kirchenordnung* (church order) of 1606 within a record headed 1612. Döber's Mass of
  1525 lies within the record of the Nürnberg parish churches of 1524.
- **Coverage.** The exhortations were found by scanning every document in the corpus for wording
  shared with a known exhortation, and every witness found was collated against the archetype of
  its family ([§3.5.2](#s3-5-2)).
- **Negative findings.** That a form "does not occur" (vesting prayers, *Ne reminiscaris*,
  prayers on entering church) means that searches of the whole corpus for its Latin incipits and
  German equivalents found nothing. OCR damage can hide a passage, so such findings are strong
  but not absolute.

---

### <a id="s3-3"></a>3.3 Opening versicles and preliminaries

#### <a id="s3-3-1"></a>3.3.1 What the Roman Mass had, and what became of it

**The medieval preparation.** Before the Introit, the Roman Mass of the later Middle Ages had
three layers of preparation for the priest:
1. **The *accessus*** (Akzess): a private office of psalms and prayers said before Mass.
2. **The *praeparatio ad missam*** in the sacristy: the washing of hands and a prayer at the
   putting on of each vestment.
3. **The prayers at the foot of the altar** (*Stufengebet*), said by the priest and server in
   dialogue:
   - the invocation, and *Introibo ad altare Dei* (I will go in unto the altar of God) with Ps 43 *Iudica me* (Judge me);
   - *Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini* (Our help is in the name of the Lord; Ps 124:8);
   - the *Confiteor* (I confess), said first by the priest and then by the server;
   - the *Misereatur* ("May almighty God have mercy upon thee …"), said by each for the other;
   - the *Indulgentiam* ("May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us pardon, absolution and
     remission of our sins");
   - the versicles *Deus, tu conversus* (O God, thou wilt turn again), and the prayers *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us) and *Oramus te* (We pray thee).

Many German diocesan missals also had the versicle *Confitemini Domino quoniam bonus* (O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good) / *Quoniam
in saeculum misericordia eius* (For his mercy endureth for ever; Ps 118:1) before the *Confiteor*.

**What became of it.** No evangelical order in Sehling keeps the whole of this. One order keeps
a large part of it: Thomas Müntzer's German Mass for Allstedt (1523, printed 1524; Radical
Reformation). There Ps 43 *Iudica me* is said by the priest and the whole people, and is
followed by German forms of the *Confiteor*, the *Misereatur*, *Deus, tu conversus* and *Aufer a
nobis*. *Introibo ad altare Dei* survives there only as the fourth verse of the psalm, not as an
antiphon ([§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)). Elsewhere only fragments remain:
- *Aufer a nobis* is sung in Latin after the sermon in the *Cellische Ordnungen* (Celle orders) of 1545, and
  Sehling's editor takes the collect after the *Confiteor* at Regensburg 1542 to be the same
  prayer ([§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)).
- The Mass form of the *Confiteor* is said by the priest with a deacon or fellow minister at
  Regensburg 1542 and Nördlingen 1544 ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2), [§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)).
- Sehling's editor prints the Bremen missal's *Stufengebet*, with *Introibo* (I will go in) and *Iudica*, as
  the background to the pastor's kneeling prayer at Buxtehude and Bergedorf ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)).

What survives falls into the families set out below:

| Family | Form | Who says it | Where | Orders (§) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | The priest's own *Confiteor* (or "what his devotion bids") at the altar, while the choir sings the Introit | The priest, sometimes with a ministrant or a fellow minister | Before or during the Introit | Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, Brandenburg 1540, Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, Hohenlohe 1553, Regensburg 1553, Amberg 1550, Buxtehude 1552, Nördlingen 1544, Schleswig-Holstein 1542 ([3.3.2](#s3-3-2)) |
| B | Bugenhagen's kneeling prayer: Our Father and the tract *Domine, non secundum* (O Lord, deal not with us) | The priest and the sexton, alternately | During the opening psalm | Wolfenbüttel 1543, Hildesheim 1544 ([3.3.3](#s3-3-3)) |
| C | A public confession in the people's hearing, with *Adiutorium* (Our help) and *Confitemini* (O give thanks), a recast *Misereatur* and a declaration of grace | The priest kneeling, with the sexton or a second minister; the people silently or repeating | At the very beginning of Mass | Döber 1525, Lippe [1525–1538], Kiel [after 1526], Mecklenburg 1540 and 1552, Amberg 1555, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557, Pfalz-Veldenz 1574, Hadeln ([3.3.4](#s3-3-4)) |
| D | The *Offene Schuld* (open confession) moved into the Mass, with an indicative absolution | The priest to the people | Before the Introit, or before the Sacrament | Kantz 1522, Bremen 1525, Volprecht 1524, Naumburg 1537, Nördlingen 1544 ([3.3.5](#s3-3-5)) |
| E | The Upper German and Reformed opening of the preaching service: confession of sins and a comfortable word | The minister for the congregation | At the beginning of the service, or after the sermon | Strasbourg 1537 (Moderate Reformed), Palatinate 1563 (Reformed), Wertheim 1524 (3.6; and [§3.4](#s3-4)) |
| F | A hymn, a German psalm, or *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) with its versicle and collect | Choir, schoolboys or congregation; the priest the collect | Before the Introit | Luther 1526, Amberg 1544, Verden 1606, Transylvania 1547, Buxtehude 1552, Mecklenburg villages, Sayn 1590 ([3.3.7](#s3-3-7)) |
| G | Ps 43 *Iudica me*, the *Confiteor*, the *Misereatur*, *Deus, tu conversus* and *Aufer a nobis*, in German | The priest and the whole people | Before the Introit | Müntzer, Allstedt 1523 and 1524 (Radical Reformation) ([3.3.8](#s3-3-8)) |

**The versicles that survive.**
- *Adiutorium nostrum* (Our help; Ps 124:8) is the one Roman versicle that survives widely: Kantz 1522,
  Döber 1525, Lippe, Mecklenburg 1540 and 1552, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 and Poullain's French
  liturgy at Frankfurt (Reformed; Sehling 9, p. 563) all have it.
- *Confitemini Domino quoniam bonus* (Ps 118:1) survives in Döber, Lippe and Mecklenburg 1540,
  but is dropped in Mecklenburg 1552.
- In Verden 1606 the versicle is *Emitte Spiritum tuum* (Send forth thy Spirit; Ps 104:30), which belongs with *Veni
  Sancte Spiritus*.

#### <a id="s3-3-2"></a>3.3.2 Family A: the priest's own *Confiteor* at the altar

The commonest form in the south and in Brandenburg is a private preparation of the priest. He
comes to the altar in his vestments, kneels and says the *Confiteor* (I confess) or some other prayer of his
own while the choir sings the Introit. The people take no part, and the text is not printed. The
model is the Brandenburg-Nürnberg order. **Brandenburg-Nürnberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1533**
(Sehling 11, p. 188):

<!-- doc 270 -->

Order of the Mass, how the same shall be held. First, when the priest cometh to the altar, he
may say the Confiteor, or what his devotion putteth him in mind of, and thereafter read the
Introit, provided that it be taken out of the holy Scripture. Meanwhile the scholars, where
there is a school, shall also sing the Introit in Latin. But where, as in villages, there were
not people for such Latin singing, a Christian German hymn shall be sung, according to the
occasion of each place.

The Mark Brandenburg adds the ministrants. **Brandenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1540**
(Sehling 3, pp. 67–68):

<!-- doc 1746 -->

First, the priest that holdeth the Mass, together with his ministrants, in their accustomed
church ornaments, according to the custom of each church, shall go to the altar and at the
beginning say the Confiteor. Thereafter shall be sung the accustomed Introit, then the Kyrie
eleison, as occasion serveth, and upon that the Gloria in excelsis, which together with the Et
in terra belongeth to the Kyrie.

Pfalz-Neuburg copies Brandenburg, but makes the priest kneel and allows a penitential psalm
instead. **Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 13, p. 70):

<!-- doc 386 -->

First, the priest that will hold the Mass, together with his ministrants (where and when they
are wont to be used), shall go to the altar in their accustomed church ornaments, according to
the custom of each church, and at the beginning, kneeling before it, say the Confiteor or a
goodly penitential psalm.

Hohenlohe insists on the Latin text of the Missal. **Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553**
(Sehling 15, p. 68):

<!-- doc 539 -->

First, the parson shall come before the altar in his ornament and church vesture, kneel down,
and pray the pure Confiteor in Latin. Meanwhile the schoolmaster with the scholars shall sing
the Introit *de tempore* (of the season) in Latin, but only those that are agreeable to the holy Scripture.

**Editor's note** (p. 68). "The Confiteor is the confession of sins that is part of the prayers at the foot of the altar. Here the piece from the Mass itself is meant, whereas the Brandenburg-Nürnberg order of 1533 required only a corresponding piece." What "pure" is
meant to exclude is not said; presumably the invocation of the Virgin and the saints.

At Regensburg the *Confiteor* is said in dialogue with the second of two ministrants.
**Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung* under Justus Jonas, 1553** (Sehling 13, pp. 419–420):

<!-- doc 440 -->

then cometh the priest (that is, the minister who, as is said above, is hebdomadary) together
with two ministrants or deacons before the altar, and prayeth thus with the one ministrant (who
is for that time the second) the Confiteor kneeling. Meanwhile the choir singeth the Introit *de
tempore* in Latin and the Kyrie eleison three times.

At Amberg the choir sings an antiphon of the season or *Veni Sancte* (Come, Holy [Spirit]) over the priest's
*Confiteor*, and the priest then sings a collect. **Amberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1550**
(Sehling 13, p. 285):

<!-- doc 411 -->

The Mass is held with us almost throughout as it hath come down of old, with the accustomed
vesture, lights, chants and other ornaments, most seemly; for first the priest prayeth the
Confiteor kneeling before the altar. During this the choir singeth *Haec est dies* (This is the day) or *Veni
Sancte*, and the priest thereupon *Oremus* and the collect. Thereupon the choir singeth the
Introit of the Sunday and of the ordinary feasts that fall.

**Editor's note** (p. 285): "Probably not the *Confiteor* of the Mass said in alternation with the ministrant, but, as also in 1533, a silent prayer."

In the north the same private prayer appears at Buxtehude. **Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552**
(Sehling 7/1, p. 74):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

During the Introit the priest, clad in the accustomed Mass vestment, shall go before the altar
and at the altar's foot make his prayer and confession.

Sehling's editor sets this against the Bremen missal of 1511. **Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*,
1552, editor's note** (Sehling 7/1, p. 74):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

The pastor's prayer at the foot of the altar, appointed there before the Introit because the
pastor must sing the Introit with [the choir], is mentioned by Aepinus in his Bergedorf church
order of 1544. […] The prayers at the foot of the altar according to the Bremen missal of 1511:
Before the altar let the priest say: *Introibo ad altare Dei* (I will go in unto the altar of God) [Psalm 43:4]. The psalm *Iudica me Deus* (Judge me, O God) [Psalm 43], etc.
Then let him say the confession. *Et introibo* (And I will go in), etc.

The Bergedorf order to which the note refers has the same private prayer, before the opening
psalm or Introit. **Bergedorf, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544** (Sehling 5, p. 387):

<!-- doc 1950 -->

In the Mass this order shall be kept. The pastor, clad in the accustomed Mass vestment or
clothes, shall first kneel down at the foot before the altar and make his prayer to God; when he
standeth up, he shall begin and sing with a German psalm, or on the feasts with a Latin Introit
of the Trinity or of the Holy Ghost (if he have help, that can also sing).

Neither order says what the prayer is. Nothing in Sehling shows that *Introibo* (I will go in) and *Iudica*
were said there; the editor gives the missal's form for comparison.

In Schleswig-Holstein 1542 the priest falls on his knees before the altar and reads the
*Confiteor* "to himself", with an intercession for the preachers, the king and the
duchies
(Sehling 23, p. 89; quoted in full in [Chapter 7](#ch7)
[§7.15.3](#s7-15-3)).

**Nördlingen 1544: the private and the public confession side by side.** Kaspar Löner's order
keeps both. The celebrant first receives absolution from a fellow minister on his own
*Confiteor*, while two choirs, the school and the people, sing *Kum, heiliger Geist* (Come, Holy Ghost) or *Nun
bitten wir* (Now pray we) in alternation. Then he turns to the people and says the open confession and the
absolution for them. **Nördlingen, *Kirchenordnung* of Kaspar Löner, 1544**
(Sehling 12, pp. 311–312):

<!-- doc 372 -->

On high feasts the pastor himself shall hold the high office, but on the others and on Sundays
the old pastor shall come before the altar in his due vesture, and there receive the absolution
from one of his fellow ministers upon his Confiteor. Meanwhile two choirs, the one of the
school, the other of the people, shall on high feasts sing *Kum, hailiger Geist* (Come, Holy Ghost) in turn, all
three stanzas out; but on other feasts and Sundays *Nun bitten wir den Heiligen Gaist* (Now pray we the Holy Ghost) with all
its stanzas. When that is out, the celebrant shall turn to the people, or, if they would needs
remain in the choir, come out before the altar, and there say before the people the Confiteor or
open confession, and thereupon the absolution.

**Editor's notes** (pp. 311–312). On the celebrant's *Confiteor* (p. 311):

<!-- doc 372 -->

What is meant here, then, is a preparation appointed only for the clergyman and his ministrant,
as in Brandenburg 1540 and Pfalz-Neuburg 1542, or, restricted to the clergyman, in
Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 and in V. Dietrich's *Agendbüchlein* 1543. Whether it refers only to
the Confiteor and the Misereatur together with the Indulgentiam in the narrowest sense, or
whether the whole prayers at the foot of the altar of the Mass are meant (which, moreover, are
not contained in the missals before 1570, but must have been known from elsewhere), cannot be
decided.

On the open confession to the people (p. 312):

<!-- doc 372 -->

The Open Confession is here a general preparatory service of worship for the congregation, as
also with Volprecht and Döber; not a substitute for confession, or its repetition, as with Kantz
or in Nürnberg.

**What family A shows.**
- **No text.** The orders do not print the *Confiteor* they mean. Brandenburg-Nürnberg leaves
  the choice to the priest's "devotion"; Hohenlohe alone demands the "pure" Latin *Confiteor* of
  the Missal.
- **Who.** The priest alone (Brandenburg-Nürnberg, Hohenlohe, Amberg, Buxtehude,
  Schleswig-Holstein), with his ministrants (Brandenburg 1540, Pfalz-Neuburg), with the second
  ministrant in dialogue (Regensburg), or with a fellow minister who absolves him (Nördlingen).
- **When.** At the altar, kneeling, during the Introit or the opening hymn. It is never said in
  the sacristy, and never before the bells.
- **The people** do not hear it. It is the evangelical remnant of the *Stufengebet* (prayers at the foot of the altar).

#### <a id="s3-3-3"></a>3.3.3 Family B: Bugenhagen's kneeling prayer with the sexton

Bugenhagen's later orders replace the *Confiteor* (I confess) with the Our Father and the tract *Domine, non
secundum peccata nostra* (O Lord, deal not with us after our sins; Ps 103:10; Ps 79:8–9). The priest kneels with the sexton and prays
"for himself and for the people and for all the need of Christendom". The sexton answers each versicle. This is the form in
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1543 (Sehling 6/1, pp. 54–55) and Hildesheim 1544
(Sehling 7/2.1, p. 852). Both texts, with translations and the full versicles, are in
[Chapter 7](#ch7) §§[7.15.1](#s7-15-1)–[7.15.2](#s7-15-2).

**Note.**
- The prayer is said aloud but at the altar, during the opening German psalm, so that in
  practice the people would not have followed it.
- The versicle *Domine, ne memineris iniquitatum nostrarum antiquarum* (O Lord, remember not our former iniquities; Ps 79:8) is the nearest
  thing in the corpus to the antiphon *Ne reminiscaris* (Remember not) of the Missal's preparation (Tobit 3:3),
  which does not occur ([§3.6.2](#s3-6-2)).

#### <a id="s3-3-4"></a>3.3.4 Family C: Döber and the Mecklenburg public confession

**The form.** This is the most important family, because it is the source of the modern Lutheran
confession of sins ([§3.4.5](#s3-4-5)). It keeps the shape of the Roman *Stufengebet* (prayers at the foot of the altar) but speaks it aloud, in
German, in the people's hearing:
1. an address to the people: "My dearly beloved in God, open your hearts …";
2. the priest kneels; *Adiutorium nostrum* (Our help) and *Confitemini Domino*;
3. a new confession in the first person singular ("I, poor sinful man …"), said by the priest
   for all;
4. a prayer for forgiveness in the plural, in the place of the *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy);
5. a declaration of God's mercy, in the place of the *Indulgentiam* (Pardon), ending "God grant this unto us all".

It begins in Nürnberg with Andreas Döber's Mass for the New Hospital. **Nürnberg, Andreas Döber,
*Von der evangelischen meß … im Newen Spital*, 1525** (Sehling 11, p. 51):

<!-- doc 249 -->

First, when the priest cometh to the altar and hath taken the chalice out of the bag, he turneth
to the people and speaketh aloud, as hereafter followeth (and so also all the words that are in
the whole Mass), so that he may yet be understood of the hearers: My dearly beloved in God, open
your hearts, and let us confess our sins unto God, and say after me with hearty desire, in the
name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost! Amen. Therewith the priest kneeleth
down before the altar and saith full slowly as hereafter followeth. Our help be in the name of
the Lord, who hath made heaven and earth! Confess unto the Lord, for he is good, and his mercy
is everlasting. And I, poor sinful man, confess unto God almighty, my Creator and Redeemer, that
I have sinned not only in thoughts, words or works, but was also conceived and born in sins, so
that all my nature and being is before his righteousness punishable and damnable. Therefore I
flee unto his bottomless mercy, seek and pray for grace. Lord, be merciful to me a poor sinner!
The merciful God vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and forgive us our sins, and give us the Holy
Ghost, that through him we may fulfil his divine will and receive everlasting life. Amen. The
absolution. The priest saith: Incline your heart to God! The almighty, merciful God hath had
mercy upon us, and hath given his only Son unto death for our sins, and for his sake forgiven
us; and to all them also that believe on his holy name he hath given power to become the
children of God, and hath promised the Holy Ghost. He that believeth and is baptized shall be
saved. God grant this unto us all. Amen. And unto every one be it done according to his faith!
As he saith: Pray God for me, the same will I also do for you! he standeth up before the altar
and saith for the people (and the people also may pray with him) thus: Come, Holy Ghost, fill
the hearts of thy faithful and kindle in them the fire of thy divine love, who through divers
tongues hast gathered the peoples of the whole world in the unity of the faith! God be praised!

**Note.**
- **The Roman skeleton.** *Adiutorium* (Our help) and *Confitemini* (O give thanks) are the versicles of the German
  missals. "The merciful God vouchsafe to have mercy upon us …" is the *Misereatur*, now in the plural
  ("us") and said by the priest for priest and people together. "The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us …" stands where the *Indulgentiam* stood, and its
  opening words echo it.
- **The *Orate fratres*.** "Pray God for me; the same will I also do" is the Roman
  request for the people's prayers, moved here from the offertory.
- **The absolution** is a declaration in the perfect tense ("hath had mercy") that ends in a wish ("God grant this unto us all"). It is
  neither the indicative "I absolve you" nor the optative *Misereatur*; see [§3.4.4](#s3-4-4).
- **Sehling's editor** notes that the *Form und Ordnung einer christlichen meß* (Form and order of a Christian Mass)
  (Sehling 11, pp. 56 ff.) takes over this beginning, headed "The Confiteor".

The Low German Mass of Lippe follows Döber. The choir sings the Introit or *Veni Sancte
Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) while the priest reads the confession. **Lippe, *Deutsche Messe*, [c. 1525–1538]**
(Sehling 22, p. 565):

<!-- doc 1549 -->

First the priest readeth the Confiteor. The Confiteor. Our help be in the name of the Lord, who
hath made heaven and earth. Confess unto the Lord, for he is good, and his mercy is everlasting.
And I, poor sinful man, confess unto God almighty, my Creator and Redeemer, that I have sinned
not only in thoughts, words or works, but was also conceived and born in sins, so that all my
nature and being is before his mercy punishable and damnable; therefore I flee unto his
bottomless mercy, seek and pray for grace. Lord, be merciful to me a poor sinner. The
absolution. The almighty, merciful God, who for our sins hath given his only Son unto death,
vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for his sake forgive us our sins, and grant the Holy Ghost
unto all that believe on him, that through him we may fulfil his divine will and receive
everlasting life, amen. […] But while the priest readeth the Confiteor, the choir singeth the
Introit of the Mass.

**Note.** Here the optative prayer ("vouchsafe to have mercy") is
itself headed "The absolution". Döber's declaration is missing.

The Kiel Mass takes Döber's address and confession, but its absolution is Kantz's indicative
form, and it is read by the sexton. **Schleswig-Holstein, *Deutsche Messe* (Kiel), [after
1526]** (Sehling 23, p. 55):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

The Confiteor. My dearly beloved in God, open your hearts and let us confess our sins unto God,
and say after me with desirous heart: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy
Ghost. Amen. I, poor sinful man, confess myself unto God almighty, my Creator and Redeemer, that
I have sinned not only in thoughts, words or works, but was also conceived and born in sins, so
that all my nature and being is before his righteousness punishable and damnable. Therefore have
I refuge unto his bottomless mercy, seek and desire grace: Lord, be merciful to me a poor
sinner. The merciful God vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and forgive us our sins, and grant the
Holy Ghost, that through him we may fulfil his divine will and receive everlasting life. Amen.

There follow the *Misereatur*, read by minister and sexton, and an absolution read by the
sexton: "And I, by the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ, say unto you … free, quit and loosed of all your sins" (Sehling 23, p. 55; full text in [Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.11.1](#s7-11-1)). "I have refuge" is the reading that Mecklenburg and the later orders keep.

**Mecklenburg 1540: the country Mass.** The Low German *Ordeninge der misse* (Order of the Mass) puts the confession
at the head of every communion Mass. The sexton, "or another Christian", kneels with the priest
and says the prayer for forgiveness. **Mecklenburg, *Ordeninge der misse*, 1540/1545**
(Sehling 5, pp. 150–151):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

A common Mass for them that will be communicated shall be held on Sundays and other feast days
in the accustomed Mass vestment, upon an altar that shall be prepared and covered for the
purpose. The priest, when he hath vested himself, let him turn about before the altar and say to
the people: My dearly beloved in God, open your hearts, let us confess our sins unto God, and
say after me with hearty desire. In the name of the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Ghost,
amen. Then let him fall upon his knees before the altar, and the sexton or another Christian by
him; then let the parson say aloud: Our help be in the name of the Lord. Answer: Who hath made
heaven and earth. The priest: Confess unto the Lord, for he is good. Answer: And his mercy is
everlasting. The priest: And I, poor sinful man, confess unto God almighty, my Creator and
Redeemer, that I have sinned not only in thoughts, words or works, but was also conceived and
born in sins, so that all my nature and being is before his righteousness punishable and
damnable. Therefore I flee unto his bottomless mercy, seek and desire grace; Lord, be merciful
to me a poor sinner. The minister answereth this prayer: The almighty, merciful God, who for our
sins hath given his only Son unto death, vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for his sake
forgive us our sins, and grant the Holy Ghost, that through him we may fulfil his divine will
and receive everlasting life, amen. The priest saith hereafter this absolution: The merciful God
hath had mercy upon us, and hath given his only Son unto death for us, and for his sake forgiven
us our sins; and to all them also that believe on his holy name he hath given power to become
the children of God, and hath promised the Holy Ghost. Whoso believeth and is baptized, he shall
be saved. God grant this unto us all, amen. When this confession is spoken by the priest, the
whole church shall be still and hear this confession, and also confess their sins with the
priest in like manner, and learn the prayer with the absolution, [to say it] at that time, and
also otherwise right often before God. Hereafter in the towns the cantor or schoolmaster shall
begin the Introit in Latin, or sing at times a German psalm.

The church order of 1552 puts the same form into High German and makes it the beginning of every
Mass. The wording of the confession changes here into the form the later orders keep.
**Mecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 5, pp. 197–198):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

Mass or communion. The same shall be begun, as heretofore ordained and in use in this land, with
the common or public confession, prayer and absolution, by the priest; namely thus. The priest
shall turn about before the altar toward the people, and say: My dearly beloved in God, open
your hearts, let us confess our sins unto God, and pray for forgiveness in the name of our Lord
Jesus Christ. Say after me with hearty desire unto God, in faith in the Lord Jesus Christ,
through the Holy Ghost. Then the priest kneeleth down before the altar, and another minister of
the church or the custos beside him, and the priest saith with a loud voice: Our help standeth
in the name of the Lord. The choir answereth: Who hath made heaven and earth. The priest: I,
poor sinful man, confess before thee, O almighty God, my Creator and Redeemer, that I have
sinned not only in thoughts, words and works, but that I am also by nature sinful and unclean,
conceived and born in sins. But I have refuge unto thy bottomless mercy, seek and desire grace,
for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake. Lord, be merciful to me a poor sinner. The other minister
answereth this prayer: O almighty, merciful God, who hast given thine only-begotten Son unto
death for us, vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for the sake of the same thy beloved Son
forgive us all our sins; and also give us thy Holy Ghost, who may kindle and increase in us true
knowledge of thy divine being and will, and thereto true obedience toward thee; to the end that
we may obtain everlasting life through thy grace, for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake, amen. The
priest saith hereafter this absolution: The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us,
forgiveth us truly all our sins for the sake of his dear Son, whom for our sakes he hath given
unto death, and hath given power to become the children of God to all that believe on his name,
giveth us moreover his Holy Ghost; he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved. God grant
this unto us all, amen. While this confession, prayer and absolution is spoken, the whole church
shall be still and hear it, and also with the priest likewise confess, pray, and take the
absolution to heart, learn it well, and often say the like before God. After this the choir
singeth the Introit *de dominica* (of the Sunday) or *de festo* (of the feast).

**Note.**
- **"as ordered heretofore in this land"** points back to 1540.
- **What changes from 1540.**
  - The *Confitemini* versicle is dropped. The choir, not the sexton, answers *Adiutorium*.
  - The confession turns from the third person ("confess unto God") to the second
    ("confess before thee, O almighty God").
  - It adds "by nature sinful and unclean" and "But I have refuge unto thy bottomless mercy".
  - The second minister's prayer becomes a collect with a relative clause ("thou who …") and asks
    for "true knowledge … and true obedience".
  - The absolution gains "forgiveth us truly all our sins", in the present tense.
- **The people.** In 1540 and 1552 the people are told to keep silence, confess with the priest
  in their hearts, and learn the text. They do not say it aloud, despite the "Say after me"
  (say after me) of the address. The address keeps the phrase from Döber.
- **Pfalz-Zweibrücken** copies 1552 word for word (below).

**Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 and Pfalz-Veldenz 1574: the Mecklenburg form in the Palatinate.** The
Zweibrücken order prints the 1552 form whole, after an opening hymn to the Holy Ghost sung
"until the church gathers". **Pfalz-Zweibrücken, *Kirchenordnung*, 1557** (Sehling 18, p. 187):

<!-- doc 967 -->

When, then, the Supper of Christ is purposed to be held in the church on a Sunday or other holy
day, there shall first be sung the hymn *Komm heyliger Geyst* (Come, Holy Ghost), etc., *Nun bitten wir den
heyligen Geyst* (Now pray we the Holy Ghost), etc., or else a German psalm or spiritual song, especially one agreeable to the
season, until the church cometh together. […] Then the priest kneeleth down before the altar,
and another minister of the church or the custos beside him, and the priest saith with a loud
voice: Our help standeth in the name of the Lord. The choir answereth: Who hath made heaven and
earth.

**Editor's notes** (p. 187). The section from here to the Words of Institution is "from the Mecklenburg church order of 1552". The Zweibrücken hymnal of 1571/1587 reprints it under the heading "Confession, prayer and absolution before the sermon on Sunday", that is, as the opening of every Sunday service, communion or not.

Pfalz-Veldenz takes over the Zweibrücken text with one change that matters: the second minister
has gone, and the minister says the confession, the prayer for forgiveness and the absolution
himself, kneeling for the first two and standing for the third. **Pfalz-Veldenz,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1574** (Sehling 18, pp. 498–499):

<!-- doc 1011 -->

When they are assembled together to hold the Supper, the table of the Lord, which is otherwise
called the altar, shall first be covered with a clean white cloth and be made ready with bread
and wine; then they begin to sing, kneeling: *Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist* (Now pray we the Holy Ghost), or *Khom,
heiliger Geist* (Come, Holy Ghost), etc. Thereupon the pastor exhorteth to the confession of sins and to hearty
prayer for the forgiveness of the same, about with such words: My dearly beloved in the Lord,
let us confess our sins unto God and pray for forgiveness in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ;
open therefore your hearts and say after me with hearty desire unto God, in faith in the Lord
Christ, through the Holy Ghost. […] Then the minister kneeleth down and saith before the people
with a loud voice: I, poor sinful man, confess before thee, O almighty God, my Creator and
Redeemer, that I have, alas, sinned much, not only in thoughts, words and works, but that I am
by nature sinful and unclean, conceived and born in sins. But I have refuge unto thy bottomless
mercy, seek and desire grace for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake; Lord, be merciful to me a poor
sinner. Almighty, merciful God, who hast given thine only-begotten Son unto death for us,
vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for the sake of the same, thy beloved Son, forgive us all
our sins; also give thy Holy Ghost, who may kindle and increase in us true knowledge of thy
divine being and will, and thereto true obedience toward thee, to the end that we may pass this
our life according to all thy good pleasure, and hereafter obtain everlasting life through thy
grace, for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake, etc. The absolution is spoken by the minister when he
hath stood up: The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us, forgiveth us truly all our
sins and misdeeds for the sake of his beloved Son, whom for our sakes he hath given unto death,
and hath given power to become the children of God to all that believe on his name, giveth us
moreover his Holy Ghost, who enlighteneth us and leadeth us into all truth, that we may be
saved; God grant this unto us all, through Jesus Christ, our Saviour. Amen.

**Amberg 1555: the confession in the plural.** The Amberg order of 1555 takes the Mecklenburg
form for its Mass on feast days. Sehling's editor notes that the section is taken "wholly from Mecklenburg 1552". But it changes the priest's confession from the singular to the plural, so
that it is no longer "I, poor sinful man" but "We poor sinful men". **Amberg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1555** (Sehling 13, p. 290):

<!-- doc 412 -->

First shall the choir sing the *Veni, Sancte*, and afterward the priest, in the accustomed
vestment, *Adjutorium nostrum in nomine* (Our help is in the name) [Ps 124:8]. Thereupon the choir respondeth *Qui fecit
celum et terram* (Who made heaven and earth) [Ps 124:8]. Then shall he turn before the altar toward the people and say with
a loud voice: My dearly beloved in God! Open your hearts, let us confess our sins before God and
pray for forgiveness in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ! Say after me with hearty desire unto
God, in faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, through the Holy Ghost! Then let the priest kneel down
before the altar, and another minister of the church beside him, and say with a loud voice: We
poor, sinful men confess before thee, O almighty God, our Creator and Redeemer, that we have
sinned not only with thoughts, words and works, but that we are also by nature sinful and
damned, conceived and born in sins. But we have refuge unto thy bottomless mercy, and seek and
desire grace for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake. Lord, be merciful to us poor sinners! The other
minister of the church answereth this prayer: O almighty, merciful God, who hast given thine
only-begotten Son unto death for us! Vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for the sake of the
same, thy beloved Son, forgive us all our sins, and give us also thy Holy Ghost, who may kindle,
increase and preserve in us true knowledge of thy divine being and will, and thereto true
obedience toward thee, that we may obtain eternal life through thy grace, for the Lord Jesus
Christ's sake! Amen. Let the priest then stand up and thereafter speak this absolution toward
the people, and the other minister of the church shall remain kneeling the while: The almighty,
merciful God hath had mercy upon us, forgiveth us truly all our sins for his dear Son's sake,
whom for our sakes he hath given unto death, and hath given power to become the children of God
to all that believe on his name, and giveth us moreover his Holy Ghost. He that believeth and is
baptized shall be saved. God grant this unto us all! Amen. And while this confession, prayer and
absolution are spoken, the whole church shall be still and hear it, and also with the priest so
confess, pray and take the absolution to heart, learn it well, and often say the like before
God.

**Note.** The plural confession and the instruction that the church shall "with the priest so confess" bring Amberg nearer than any other sixteenth-century
witness to the Common Service, whose confession begins "Almighty God, our Maker and Redeemer, we
poor sinners confess unto Thee" ([§3.4.5](#s3-4-5)). Sehling's apparatus shows that the text it calls the
*Bericht* (report) reads "unrein" (unclean), as Mecklenburg does, where the order of 1555 has "verdamt"
(damned).

**Hadeln: the confession sung, the sexton absolving.** The Hadeln order, which Sehling dates
1526, has the priest vest during the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) at the end of Matins and kneel for *Veni Sancte
Spiritus*. He then sings the confession on the same tone, and the sexton answers and reads the
absolution. **Hadeln, *Kirchenordnung* "of 1526"** (Sehling 5, pp. 467–468):

<!-- doc 1955 -->
