While the Te Deum is being sung, the priest shall clothe himself with the accustomed Mass
vestment, not as needful, but as a seemly and honest ornament, and not seek salvation therein.
Likewise one or two wax lights shall be lit (since it is the Lord's Supper) and be let burn upon
the altar until the Mass is out. When then the collect of Matins hath been sung, the priest
shall go humbly to kneel upon his knees and sing with the choir *Veni sancte spiritus* in Latin
or German. The collect being ended, the priest remaineth kneeling and beginneth aloud the
confession on the same tone, and the sexton by him answereth and readeth the absolution. Then a
psalm is sung before the Introit, of the Sunday or of the Trinity or of the Holy Ghost or of
Easter, or whatever is not contrary to Scripture.

**Note.** One manuscript (Sehling's VIII, 65) adds the remark: "Nota bene: the Confiteor with the sexton's absolution has fallen [away]" (Sehling 5, p. 468). The sexton's absolution was given up at some later date.

#### <a id="s3-3-5"></a>3.3.5 Family D: the *Offene Schuld* moved into the Mass

**The *Offene Schuld*.** The late medieval *Offene Schuld* ("open guilt") was a general
confession, with a declaratory absolution, recited by the preacher after the sermon in the
vernacular preaching service. It was never part of the Mass. The first evangelical Masses carry
it into the Mass, as an absolution of the communicants. Sehling's editor sets out the
development under Volprecht 1524 (Sehling 11, p. 39):

<!-- doc 247 -->

As already the German Mass of Kaspar Kantz in Nördlingen 1522, the Strasbourg German Mass 1524,
and Döber's Mass, after the medieval model, first in the preaching service, but then also after
the sermon in the Mass. In this passage out of the preaching service into the Mass, however, the
Open Confession was changed, as this use of it shows, in the feeling of the people from an
appendage of the sermon into a preparation for the Sacrament.

**Kantz, Nördlingen 1522.** The earliest form opens with an exhortation, then gives the
absolution with no confession text at all: "The almighty and merciful God forgive you your sins! And I, by the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Church, pronounce you free, quit and loosed of all your sins …" (Sehling 12, p. 285). Sehling's editor calls it a
fusion of the *Indulgentiam* (Pardon) with the absolution of private confession. The full text, with
*Adiutorium* (Our help) and the recast *Orate fratres*, is in
[Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.2.1](#s7-2-1).

**Bremen 1525.** The Low German *Evangelische Misse* (Evangelical Mass) printed at Bremen in 1525 translates
Kantz's address and absolution: "The almighty, merciful God forgive you your sins. And I, by the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Church, proclaim you to be free, quit and loosed of all your sins" (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 405). It heads the priest's request
for the people's prayer "the priest's confession", and keeps Kantz's
*Adiutorium* and *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit). The address is printed in [§3.5.14.1](#s3-5-14-1).

**Volprecht, Nürnberg 1524.** The prior of the Augustinians at Nürnberg says an *offene beicht* (open confession)
"in place of the Confiteor" before the Introit, addressed to God and to "brothers and sisters". The
absolution that follows is headed "Absolution, the Misereatur". **Nürnberg, *Deutsche Messe* of
the prior Volprecht, 1524** (Sehling 11, pp. 39–40):

<!-- doc 247 -->

When the priest will read a German Mass, he saith beforehand the open confession instead of the
Confiteor: I, poor, wretched, sinful man, confess myself unto God my heavenly Father and unto my
Lord Jesus Christ my Saviour, unto you, brothers and sisters, and unto the whole Christian
congregation, that I have, alas, often and much sinned against God my Lord with unbelief and
mistrust, not loved him above all things, and my neighbour as myself. That is sore and grievous
unto me from the bottom of my heart. O Lord God, almighty Father, I, a poor sinner, put thee in
mind of thy gracious pledge and promise, wherein thou promisest forgiveness of sins through the
blood of thy Son Jesus Christ, who died for us and shed his blood for us for the forgiveness of
sins. The same my Lord Jesus Christ hath also spoken by his holy mouth: where two or three are
gathered together in his name, there is he in the midst of them; and what they ask of thee in
his name, that shall be granted them. So we pray for the pardon of our sins in his name. Lord
God, say unto us: According to thy faith be it unto thee! Go in peace! Sin no more! Thy sins are
forgiven, pardoned and remitted thee. Absolution, the Misereatur: My dear brother and sister,
God hath had mercy upon us, and hath pardoned us all our sins, and will give us everlasting
life. Amen.

**Note.**
- **"you brothers and sisters"** keeps the *Confiteor*'s "and to you, brethren", with the saints left out.
- **The absolution** is in the first person plural ("us"), so the priest includes
  himself; it is a declaration, not a sentence of loosing.

**Naumburg 1537: an indicative absolution at the start of Mass.** At St. Wenzel's in Naumburg
the choir sings *Kom heiliger geist herre gott* (Come, Holy Ghost, Lord God), and the priest then reads "the Confiteor to the people". It is a bidding to prayer, a confession said by all, and an absolution in the first
person singular. **Naumburg, *Kirchen-Ordnung* for St. Wenzel's, 1537** (Sehling 2, pp. 77–78):

<!-- doc 1219 -->

Thereupon the priest readeth the Confiteor to the people, as followeth. Dear friends, forasmuch
as we are now all gathered in the service of God the almighty to hear his holy, godly word, we
will first call upon the Lord for his grace and pray him that he would open our hearts to the
true understanding of his divine word […] But forasmuch as we are all sinners, let us first
confess our sins and beg pardon for the same of God the almighty, and say: I, poor sinner,
confess unto thee, O almighty God and merciful Father, before this whole congregation all my
sins and misdeeds, whereby I have so manifoldly provoked thee to wrath; and I pray thee, through
thy bottomless mercy and through the bitter passion and death of thy dear Son JESUS CHRIST, that
thou wouldest be gracious to me, poor sinner. Absolution. Upon this your confession, by the
command of the Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Christian Church, I forgive you all
your sins, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. The peace of
the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen. Thereupon the whole choir singeth the Kyrie
eleison.

**Note.** "Upon such your confession … in the stead of the holy Christian church I forgive you all your sins" is the formula of private confession, used here over the whole congregation.
Compare the Brandenburg and Pfalz-Neuburg prohibitions of a "gemeine beicht" (common confession; [§3.4.6](#s3-4-6)).

#### <a id="s3-3-6"></a>3.3.6 Family E: the Upper German and Reformed opening

In Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed, before the Interim) and the Reformed orders the service begins
with the minister's call to confession, a prayer of confession in the first person plural, and a
comfortable word as absolution. This is the *Offene Schuld* (open confession) of the preaching service, kept at
its head. **Strasbourg, *Agende*, 1537/1541** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, p. 270):

<!-- doc 1302 -->

The Confiteor or open confession: Confess unto God the Lord, and acknowledge with me, every one,
his sins and misdeeds: Almighty, everlasting God and Father, we confess and acknowledge unto
thee that we were conceived in iniquities, and are full of sin and transgression in all our
life, as they that neither believe thy word perfectly nor follow thy holy commandments. We pray
thee, look upon thy goodness, and for thy name's sake be gracious and pardon our misdeed, which,
alas, is great. An absolution or comfortable word, 1 Timothy 1: This is a true saying and a
precious word: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. Let every one confess himself
in truth with Saint Paul in his heart, and believe in Christ; so I promise you in his name the
pardon of all your sins, and pronounce you loosed of the same on earth, that ye may be loosed of
them also in heaven for ever, Amen. Sometimes he taketh other sayings that comfort us with the
pardon of sins and Christ's payment for our sins, as John 3: God so loved the world, that he
gave his only Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.

**Note.**
- **The name.** "The Confiteor or open confession": in Strasbourg (1537, Moderate Reformed) the
  open confession *is* the *Confiteor* (I confess).
- **The absolution** is conditional on each one's confession and faith ("Let each one confess … and believe … so I promise you"). Further comfortable words follow: John 3:35–36, Acts
  10:43 and 1 John 2:1–2 (p. 271).
- **A second Confiteor** follows: "Almighty, everlasting God and Father, we confess and acknowledge that we were, alas, conceived and born in sins, and therefore inclined to all evil and slothful to all good …; p. 271". The Palatinate editor names this "other Confiteor" among
  the sources of the Palatinate prayer below.

**The Palatinate 1563** (Reformed). The Reformed order of Elector Frederick III opens the Sunday
morning service with a prayer of confession before the sermon, and puts the confession,
absolution and retention after the sermon ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)). The prayer before the sermon begins
**Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563** (Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 388):

<!-- doc 504 -->

Before the sermon, especially on Sundays and holy days in the morning, and on days of prayer,
this following prayer shall be spoken before the people, wherein the Christian congregation is
expressly reminded of man's misery, and the wholesome grace of God is desired, to the end that
hearts may be made ready unto humility and receive the word of grace the more desirously. Grace,
peace and mercy, etc. Heavenly Father, eternal and merciful God, we confess and acknowledge
before thy divine majesty that we are poor, wretched sinners, conceived and born in all
wickedness and corruption, inclined to all evil, unprofitable to any good, and that with our
sinful life we transgress thy holy commandments without ceasing

**Note.**
- **The opening** is the apostolic greeting "Grace, peace and mercy" in the place of the versicles. The prayer ends with the Our Father (p. 389).
- **The editor** traces the prayer to Geneva 1563 and Frankfurt 1555 (both Reformed) and
  "Strasbourg … (the other Confiteor)", the second Strasbourg confession above (Moderate
  Reformed).
- **Poullain and Micron** (both Reformed). The French stranger church at Frankfurt opens with
  *Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini* (Our help is in the name of the Lord) and a *Confessio peccatorum* (confession of sins), "O Lord God, eternal Father …" (Sehling 9, p. 563). Micron's Dutch order for London, also used at Emden, has an
  open confession with a conditional declaration (Sehling 7/1, p. 602).

**Wertheim 1524: the confession after the sermon.** The earliest report of a Mass after the
sermon is Franz Kolb's letter to Luther. **Wertheim, Franz Kolb to Luther, 27 August 1524**
(Sehling 11, p. 707):

<!-- doc 322 -->

First we all come together to the sermon; the sermon being done, straightway, the ornaments
hitherto used being laid aside, bread and wine being made ready, with knees bowed before the
altar, I say with a loud voice and in German a very short Confiteor, then the Pater noster,
thirdly the Credo in Deum; straightway I rise, consecrate the bread with the bare words of
Christ, and the cup, and without any exhortation communicate my brother the chaplain with the
other brethren and sisters.

#### <a id="s3-3-7"></a>3.3.7 Family F: a hymn, a psalm or *Veni Sancte Spiritus* at the beginning

**Luther.** The *Formula missae* (1523) begins with the Introit. The *Deutsche Messe* (1526)
begins with a German hymn or psalm, followed directly by the Kyrie. **Wittenberg, Luther,
*Deudsche messe und ordnung gottis diensts*, 1526** (Sehling 1, p. 14):

<!-- doc 3 -->

But at the beginning we sing a spiritual song or a German psalm in the first tone, after the
manner as followeth: "I will bless the Lord at all times" (Psalm 34:1–23). Thereupon Kyrie
eleison, also in the same tone, three times and not nine times.

Luther's Mass has no confession and no versicles before the Introit or the opening psalm.

**The Holy Ghost before the Introit.** Several orders recast the medieval *accessus* as a
congregational preparation of the Holy Ghost. At the Amberg hospital church the schoolmaster and
boys sing *Veni Sancte* (Come, Holy [Spirit]), and the priest sings a German collect with the versicle. **Amberg,
*Ordnung der kirchen* … *im spital*, 1544** (Sehling 13, p. 282):

<!-- doc 410 -->

First, when the priest in his habit, according to the old use of the church, goeth up to the
altar, our schoolmaster singeth with the boys the Latin *Veni, Sancte …*; thereupon the priest a
German collect together with the versicle, praying for the grace of the Holy Ghost. Afterward
the choir singeth the Introit of the Mass of the Holy Trinity, or else *de tempore* (of the season).

**Editor's note** (p. 282). This is "a preparation for the congregation in place of the prayers at the foot of the altar, with the Confiteor", probably a form of the *accessus*. The note is
quoted in full in [§3.6.1](#s3-6-1). The collect is presumably the Pentecost collect *Deus, qui corda
fidelium* (O God, who didst teach the hearts of the faithful), and the versicle *Cor mundum crea in me, Deus* (Create in me a clean heart, O God), which Luther used at his ordinations
(WA 38, 424).

At Verden the choir sings *Veni Sancte Spiritus*, the priest sings *Emitte Spiritum tuum* (Send forth thy Spirit), and
the collect *Deus, qui corda fidelium* follows. **Verden, *Kirchenordnung*, 1606**
(Sehling 7/1, pp. 155–156):

<!-- doc 2090 -->

First, when the priest or pastor hath stepped before the altar, the choir shall begin the
antiphon *Veni, sancte Spiritus*. Thereafter the priest shall sing: *Emitte Spiritum et
creabuntur* (Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created). The choir shall answer: *Et renovabis faciem terrae* (And thou shalt renew the face of the earth) […] Further the priest shall
sing: *Oremus. Deus, qui corda fidelium* (Let us pray. O God, who didst teach the hearts of the faithful). Thereupon shall be sung the Introit *de tempore*,
Kyrie eleison, Gloria in excelsis Deo, and Et in terra pax.

**Editor's note** (p. 155): "Our liturgy up to the Introit is a *praeparatio ad missam*. In the later Middle Ages the private preparatory office of the priest, the *accessus*, had sometimes been made into an hour of the clergy, as it were an 'office of the Holy Ghost".

The same pattern stands in other orders:
- **Kantz 1522** and **Döber 1525**: *Veni Sancte Spiritus*, said by the priest for the people
  after the absolution ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)).
- **Buxtehude 1552**: on weekdays a German psalm before the Introit, "such as Come, Holy Ghost"
  (Sehling 7/1, p. 74).
- **Naumburg 1537**, **Nördlingen 1544**, **Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557** and **Pfalz-Veldenz 1574**:
  *Kom heiliger geist herre gott* (Come, Holy Ghost, Lord God) or *Nun bitten wir den heiligen Geist* (Now pray we the Holy Ghost), sung by the choir or
  congregation, at Pfalz-Veldenz kneeling.
- **Hadeln**: *Veni sancte spiritus*, priest kneeling with the choir ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)).
- **Hof 1592**: *Veni Sancte Spiritus* "before the Introit" at the Monday office in the monastery
  church, sung in three parts (Sehling 11, p. 464).

**The Benedictus at Hermannstadt.** The Transylvanian order sings Zechariah's canticle in German
before the Introit on Sundays, in place of the abolished procession. **Transylvania,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1547, Latin version** (Sehling 24, p. 223):

<!-- doc 1669 -->

On Sundays, in place of the abolished procession, before the Introit, there is sung in German
the canticle of Zacharias, *Benedictus Dominus* (Blessed be the Lord); or, if the litany please any better at that
time; in Eastertide, *Salve festa dies* (Hail, festal day). On other feast days we leave these out, taking the
beginning of the Mass from the Introit *de tempore* or another like it, if it be not contrary to
Scripture.

**In the villages.** Where there was no Latin choir, a German psalm or hymn stood in place of
the Introit:
- Mecklenburg 1540: "in the villages a German psalm shall always be sung before the Introit" (Sehling 5, p. 151).
- Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533: "a Christian German song" ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)).
- Sayn 1590: "First, when one cometh into the church, a German psalm shall be sung; thereafter the pastor shall read a collect" (Sehling 19/1, p. 412).

#### <a id="s3-3-8"></a>3.3.8 Family G: Müntzer's Allstedt Mass; *Iudica me* and *Aufer a nobis* elsewhere

**Müntzer keeps the *Stufengebet*.** Thomas Müntzer's German Masses (Radical Reformation) for Allstedt are the one
place in Sehling where Ps 43 *Iudica me* (Judge me) survives as the preparation for Mass. In the order of
1523 the Mass begins "when the general confession has first been made before the altar" (Sehling 1, p. 504). The *Deutsch evangelisch Messe* (German Evangelical Mass) of
1524 prints it. Ps 43 (the Vulgate's 42nd) is said by the priest and the whole people; it
includes, as its fourth verse, the *Introibo ad altare Dei* (I will go in unto the altar of God) that the Roman Mass uses as its
antiphon. Then come the priest's confession, the people's *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy), the versicle *Deus, tu
conversus* (O God, thou wilt turn again), and the prayer *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us), all in German, all aloud, and all before the
Introit. **Allstedt, Thomas Müntzer, *Deutsch evangelisch Messe*, 1524** (Radical Reformation; Sehling 1, p. 499):

<!-- doc 51 -->

The Office of the Incarnation of Christ our Saviour. The 42nd psalm is said with the whole
people, before the general confession is made. 1. O God, judge me and sever me from the ungodly
kind, and deliver me from the deceitful knave. 2. For thou art the God of my strength. Why hast
thou forsaken me? I went as one that mourneth, when the ungodly man oppressed me. 3. Send out
thy light and truth, that they may lead me to the holy hill and to thy dwelling. 4. There will I
come to the altar of God, to God, who maketh glad my youth. O God, my God, there will I confess
thy praise upon the harp. 5. O my soul, why art thou cast down? Why makest thou me sad? Wait for
the Lord; for I confess him. He is the health of my countenance, and he is my God. 6. Glory be
to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Ghost. As it was in the beginning, is now and ever,
and from eternity to eternity. Then the common people answer: Amen. The priest maketh the
confession with clear words before all the people, saying: O mild God, Father, I confess to thee
and to thy tender Son, Jesus Christ, and to the Comforter, the Holy Ghost, before all them that
fear God, that I, a wretched sinner, have all my life long done against thy will (which is
declared by the law), and with negligent confidence, unexercised faith and unstudious love have
given place to sins, and have not turned them away in desire, words and works through God's work
and word. Therefore I pray you, the chosen friends of God that stand about, to help to pray for
me with all your heart, mind and strength, that the secret of the divine covenant may be opened
through my speech and through your hearing. The common people saith thereupon: God be gracious
unto thee, and teach thee from day to day to heed all his will and work for our good, in doing
and in leaving undone. The priest saith thereupon: Amen. And straightway he saith this verse: O
God, turn thee unto us as a faithful instructor. The people answer thereupon: That we, thy
people, may be joyful in thee. Thereafter the priest saith: O Lord, not unto us, not unto us.
Answer: But give the glory unto thy name. The priest saith: Let us pray: O Lord, take from us
our iniquity, that with an upright mind we may wait upon thy holy, divine power in the witness
of the words to come, through Jesus Christ, our Lord. Amen.

**What Müntzer keeps, and what he changes.**

| Roman *Stufengebet* (prayers at the foot of the altar) | Müntzer 1524 |
|---|---|
| *Introibo ad altare Dei* (I will go in unto the altar of God; antiphon) | Not said as an antiphon; kept only as verse 4 of the psalm, "Then will I come unto the altar of God" |
| Ps 43 *Iudica me*, priest and server in alternation, with *Gloria Patri* | Ps 43 in German, "with the whole people", with *Gloria Patri*; the people answer *Amen* |
| *Adiutorium nostrum* (Our help) | Not present |
| *Confiteor* (I confess) of the priest, asking the bystanders to pray for him | A new confession by the priest "before all the people", asking "you chosen friends of God that stand about" to pray for him |
| *Misereatur* of the server | "God be gracious unto thee, teach thee from day to day …", said by the people |
| *Confiteor* of the server and the priest's *Misereatur* and *Indulgentiam* (Pardon) | Not present; there is no absolution |
| *Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos* (O God, thou wilt turn again and quicken us) / *Et plebs tua laetabitur in te* (And thy people shall rejoice in thee) | "O God, turn thee unto us as a faithful instructor" / "That we, thy people, may be joyful in thee" |
| (not in the Roman form) | "O Lord, not unto us, not unto us" / "But unto thy name give the glory" (Ps 115:1) |
| *Aufer a nobis* | "O Lord, take from us our misdeeds …", recast to look forward to the "words to come" |

The Roman versicles *Ostende nobis* (Show us) and *Domine, exaudi* (O Lord, hear), the *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) and *Oramus te* (We pray thee)
are gone. The server's part has passed to the whole congregation.

**Elsewhere, *Aufer a nobis* alone.** Outside Allstedt the prayer *Aufer a nobis* appears in one
order for certain, and in another by the editor's conjecture:
- **The *Cellische Ordnungen* of 1545** sing it in Latin after the sermon, as the first of three
  verses during which the people kneel and pray "in place of the offertory". Its petition to enter "into the holy of holies" here leads
  into the Preface. **Albertine Saxony, *Die Cellischen Ordnungen*, 1545** (Sehling 1, p. 300):

<!-- doc 33 -->

After the sermon. One shall first sing the *Dominus vobiscum*, and thereafter begin these three
verses. 1. Take away from us, O Lord, all our iniquities, that we may be worthy to enter with
pure minds into the holy of holies. Alleluia. 2. Have mercy, have mercy, have mercy upon thy
people, whom thou hast redeemed, O Christ, with thy blood, that thou be not angry with us for
ever. Alleluia. 3. Hear, hear, hear, O Lord, our prayers, O Jesus Christ; make intercession for
us. Alleluia.

- **Regensburg 1542.** During the litany, before the Introit, "the priest, together with the gospeller, prayeth the *Confiteor";
  after the litany the priest sings "a collect in the name of the whole church" (Sehling 13, pp. 391–392). Sehling's editor takes this collect to be
  "probably the prayer *Aufer a nobis* of the Mass, but no longer the *Oramus te* that follows it, which was impossible for evangelicals". He adds that of the south
  German orders only Regensburg kept a prayer at this place, apart from the early Amberg form
  (Sehling 13, p. 392); but at Amberg 1550 he judges the collect "hardly the prayer *Aufer a nobis* that still belongs to the *Confiteor*" (Sehling 13, p. 285).

**The Mass form of the *Confiteor*.** On Regensburg 1542 the editor also notes that
Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, Dietrich's *Agendbüchlein* (agenda booklet) of 1543 and Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 knew "only a 'Confiteor, or what his devotion bids him', said by the clergyman alone", whereas Regensburg's
priest says it with the deacon; and that "in a similar way as at Regensburg, however, the Mass *Confiteor* was also used in 1544 at Nördlingen" (Sehling 13, p. 391). For Nördlingen see [§3.3.2](#s3-3-2).

**The verdict.** *Introibo* (I will go in) as an antiphon and Ps 43 as the priest's preparatory psalm disappear
from every order in Sehling except Müntzer's (Radical Reformation). *Aufer a nobis* survives at
the beginning of Mass only at Allstedt and, if the editor is right, at Regensburg 1542; in the
*Cellische Ordnungen* (Celle orders) it moves to the offertory. Ps 43 itself remains in the Lutheran orders as
the Introit of Judica Sunday (e.g. Nördlingen 1579, Sehling 12, p. 379).

---

### <a id="s3-4"></a>3.4 Confession and absolution: what the orders did with the *Confiteor*

#### <a id="s3-4-1"></a>3.4.1 Where it falls

The confession of sins stands in four different places in the orders, and a few orders have it
in two:

| Place | Form | Orders |
|---|---|---|
| **Before the Introit, privately** | The priest's *Confiteor* (I confess) or other prayer at the altar, during the Introit | Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, Brandenburg 1540, Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, Hohenlohe 1553, Regensburg 1542 and 1553, Amberg 1550, Buxtehude 1552, Bergedorf 1544, Schleswig-Holstein 1542, Nördlingen 1544; Bugenhagen's kneeling prayer at Wolfenbüttel 1543 and Hildesheim 1544 (§§[3.3.2](#s3-3-2)–[3.3.3](#s3-3-3)) |
| **Before the Introit, publicly** | Address, confession and absolution in the people's hearing | Müntzer 1523/1524 (Radical Reformation; with Ps 43, no absolution; [§3.3.8](#s3-3-8)); Volprecht 1524, Döber 1525, Lippe, Kiel, Mecklenburg 1540 and 1552, Amberg 1555, Naumburg 1537, Nördlingen 1544, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557, Pfalz-Veldenz 1574, Hadeln; Strasbourg 1537 (Moderate Reformed); Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; prayer before the sermon) (§§[3.3.4](#s3-3-4)–[3.3.6](#s3-3-6)) |
| **After the sermon** | Open confession from the pulpit, or at the altar before the Sacrament | Bugenhagen, Brunswick 1528; Wertheim 1524 ([§3.3.6](#s3-3-6)); Kurpfalz 1556; Palatinate 1563 (Reformed); Amberg 1550 ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)) |
| **In the communion rite** | Confession and absolution after the exhortation, before the Verba | Kantz 1522 and Bremen 1525; Augsburg 1530 (Moderate Reformed; the absolution inside the second exhortation); Regensburg c. 1544 and 1567; Hohenlohe 1553 (from the pulpit); Württemberg 1536 and its followers, among them Kurpfalz 1556 and Hanau-Lichtenberg 1573; Nürnberg after 1569; Mecklenburg 1552 (the absolution inside the exhortation); Marienhafe 1593 (a prayer of confession without absolution) (§§[3.4.4](#s3-4-4), [3.5](#s3-5)) |

**Mecklenburg 1552** has it twice: the public confession at the beginning of every Mass ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)),
and an absolution inside the exhortation before communion ([§3.5.9](#s3-5-9)). **Nördlingen 1544** has it
twice at the beginning: the celebrant's own *Confiteor*, absolved by a fellow minister, and then
the open confession to the people ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)).

**The Palatinate** moves it. Kurpfalz 1556 sets the order "the sermon, open confession and common prayer" (Sehling 14, p. 165). In 1563,
now Reformed, the confession and absolution follow the Sunday morning sermon, and the Supper has
its own examination by questions ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

#### <a id="s3-4-2"></a>3.4.2 Who says it, and does the chancel party pray it together?

- **The priest alone.** In family A the priest says the *Confiteor* (I confess) by himself at the altar,
  silently or "for himself" (Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, Hohenlohe 1553, Amberg 1550,
  Schleswig-Holstein 1542).
- **The priest and the ministrants.** Brandenburg 1540 and Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 have the priest go
  to the altar "together with his ministrants". At Regensburg 1553 the priest prays the *Confiteor*
  kneeling with "the one ministrant (who at that time is the second)", that is, in the Roman
  dialogue with the server.
- **The priest and the sexton.** In the north the sexton is the server:
  - Bugenhagen's prayer is said by the priest kneeling "with the sexton" (Wolfenbüttel) or "with the sexton" (Hildesheim), who answers each versicle.
  - In Mecklenburg 1540 the sexton "or another Christian" kneels with
    the priest and says the prayer for forgiveness.
  - At Kiel the sexton reads the *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy) and the absolution, and the priest says "Amen".
  - At Hadeln the sexton answers the priest's sung confession and reads the absolution. One
    manuscript notes that this "has been given up".
- **The priest and a second minister.** Mecklenburg 1552 and Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557: "another minister of the church, or the custos" kneels beside the
  priest; "the other minister" says the prayer for forgiveness; the choir answers *Adiutorium* (Our help). At
  Nördlingen 1544 a fellow minister absolves the celebrant.
- **The people.** The people take one of four parts:
  - They say it **after the priest**: "say after me" (Döber 1525) and "say the confession with me" (Bugenhagen 1528).
  - They **confess silently** with him: Mecklenburg 1540 and 1552, "the whole church shall be still … and also confess likewise with the priest".
  - They **confess in their hearts**: Strasbourg 1537 (Moderate Reformed), "let every one confess himself … in his heart".
  - They **answer "Yes"** to questions: Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; [§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

**Is it done privately before Mass?** In two senses, yes:
- **The priest.** His *Confiteor* (family A) is private, but it is said at the altar at the
  beginning of Mass, not in the sacristy beforehand.
- **The communicants.** The usual Lutheran preparation was not a general confession at all, but
  each communicant's private confession, examination and absolution on the Saturday or before
  the service. The general confession was never allowed to replace it in Brandenburg ([§3.4.6](#s3-4-6); the
  private rite is treated in [Chapter 13](#ch13)
  [§13.17](#s13-17)).

#### <a id="s3-4-3"></a>3.4.3 Old texts or new?

**The Latin *Confiteor*.** No evangelical order in Sehling prints the Roman *Confiteor* (I confess). Where
it is kept it is the priest's private prayer, and the text is assumed ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)). Hohenlohe 1553
wants "the pure Confiteor in Latin"; Brandenburg-Nürnberg
allows "the Confiteor, or what his devotion puts him in mind of".

**New confessions.** Every public confession in the corpus is a new text. There are five
families of wording:

| Family | Incipit | Orders |
|---|---|---|
| Döber–Mecklenburg | "And I, poor sinful man, confess unto God Almighty, my Maker and Redeemer, that I have sinned not only with thoughts, words or works …" | Döber 1525, Lippe, Kiel, Mecklenburg 1540, 1552, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557, Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 |
| Volprecht | "I, poor, wretched, sinful man, confess myself unto God my heavenly Father … you brothers and sisters …" | Volprecht 1524 |
| Naumburg | "I, poor sinner, confess unto thee, O almighty God and merciful Father, before this whole congregation all my sins and misdeeds …" | Naumburg 1537 |
| Württemberg | "I, poor sinner, confess myself unto God, my heavenly Father, that I have, alas, sinned grievously and manifoldly, not only with outward, gross sins, but much more with inward, inborn blindness …" | Württemberg 1536; Kurpfalz 1556; Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; in the second person, "before thee, my God and Maker") |
| Strasbourg | "Almighty, everlasting God and Father, we confess and acknowledge unto thee that we were conceived in unrighteousness …" | Strasbourg 1537 (Moderate Reformed); Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; prayer before the sermon); Poullain and Micron (Reformed) |

Bugenhagen's Brunswick confession of 1528 is a sixth, unique form: a confession against the
Creed and the two tables of the law, with a pause for each to name his own sin ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

**The confession's two points.** The Döber family confesses actual sin "in thoughts, words or works: the *cogitatione, verbo et opere* of the *Confiteor"
*and* original sin, "conceived and born in sins". Württemberg
confesses "inward inborn blindness, unbelief, doubt". Both make original sin and unbelief the matter of the confession.

**What became of the *Misereatur*.** The Roman "Almighty God have mercy upon thee" is said by the server for the priest and by the priest for the server. In
the orders:
- **Kept by name.** At Kiel: "the minister reads the Misereatur; the sexton reads the Misereatur". The text is not given.
- **Recast as a prayer for us all.** Döber: "The merciful God vouchsafe to have mercy upon us …". Lippe heads this same prayer "The absolution".
- **Given to the second minister.** In Mecklenburg 1540 "the minister answereth this prayer", as the server answered the priest's *Confiteor* with the
  *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy). In 1552 it becomes a full collect, "O almighty, merciful God, who hast given thine only-begotten Son unto death for us, vouchsafe to have mercy upon us …".
- **The name given to a declaration.** Volprecht heads his absolution "Absolution, the Misereatur" ([§3.3.5](#s3-3-5)).

**What became of the *Indulgentiam*.** The Roman "May the almighty and merciful Lord grant us pardon, absolution and remission of our sins" is a wish in the first
person plural. Two orders keep its opening words:
- **Kantz 1522**: "The almighty and merciful God forgive you your sins!", in the second person, followed by the indicative
  absolution.
- **Döber 1525**: "The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us …", recast as a declaration in the perfect tense.

#### <a id="s3-4-4"></a>3.4.4 Optative, declaratory or indicative?

The absolutions fall into five types. The modern Common Service declaration of grace is type 2.

| Type | Formula | Orders |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Optative** (a wish or prayer) | "The merciful God vouchsafe to have mercy upon us and forgive us our sins …" | Döber 1525 (the *Misereatur* [May almighty God have mercy]); Lippe and Kiel; Mecklenburg 1540; Mecklenburg 1552 and Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 (as the second minister's prayer) |
| **2. Declaration of grace** (first person plural, no "I") | "The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us … God grant this unto us all" | Döber 1525; Mecklenburg 1540 and 1552; Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557; Pfalz-Veldenz 1574; Volprecht 1524 ("God hath had mercy upon us") |
| **3. Indicative** (the minister, by Christ's command, looses) | "I, by the commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Church, pronounce you free, quit and loosed" | Kantz 1522; Kiel (read by the sexton); Naumburg 1537; Württemberg 1536; Nürnberg after 1569; Mecklenburg 1552 (in the exhortation) |
| **4. Conditional declaration, with retention** | "As many of you as … to them I declare … But as many among you as still have pleasure in their sins …" | Strasbourg 1537 (Moderate Reformed; without retention); Micron and Palatinate 1563 (Reformed) |
| **5. No absolution**, only a word of comfort | "Jesus Christ is our salvation for ever" | Bugenhagen, Brunswick 1528; Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; Supper examination) |

**Type 2 and type 3.** The declaration of grace (type 2) is the commonest form at the
*beginning* of the Mass. The indicative (type 3) is the commonest form in the *communion rite*,
where it comes out of private confession. The orders do not argue over the difference.
Württemberg 1536 offers both, and in the second person singular.

**Württemberg 1536: the open confession and three absolutions.** After the exhortation the
pastor says the confession for all, then one of three absolutions; the congregation then sings
the Our Father "as a public confession". **Württemberg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1536** (Sehling 16, pp. 108–109):

<!-- doc 651 -->

After the exhortation he shall say before them the public confession, and afterward the public
absolution, about after this manner: I, poor sinner, confess myself unto God my heavenly Father,
that I have, alas, grievously and manifoldly sinned, not only with outward, gross sins, but much
more with inward, inborn blindness, unbelief, doubting, faint-heartedness, impatience, pride,
evil lusts, secret envy and hatred, grudging, etc., as my Lord God knoweth of me, and I, alas,
cannot so perfectly know; therefore they repent me and are grievous unto me; I desire grace of
God. Absolution: The almighty God hath had mercy upon thee, and through the merit of the most
holy passion, death and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, his beloved Son, he forgiveth
thee all thy sins; and I, as an appointed minister of the Christian Church, declare unto thee,
by the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, such forgiveness of all thy sins, in the name of the
Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Go in peace; be it unto thee as thou
believest. Or thus: The almighty and merciful God forgiveth thee thy sin, and I, by the command
of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Church, pronounce thee free, quit and loosed
of all thy sins, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Go, and
sin no more, but amend thyself without ceasing; God help thee thereto. Or thus: In the
institution of the preaching office of the holy Gospel, Jesus Christ said to his apostles: He
that heareth you heareth me; and whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted, and whose soever
ye retain, they are retained. By virtue of these words and command of Christ I declare unto you
that all your sins are atoned through Jesus Christ, and I remit you, as an ordained minister of
the holy Gospel, all your misdeeds, in the name of the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Ghost,
Amen. Thereupon let the church sing the Our Father in German, for it is a singularly hearty
prayer, and therewith also a public confession.

**Note.**
- **The second person singular.** The first two absolutions are in the singular ("thee"),
  as in private confession. Sehling's editor refers both to the absolution of private confession
  in Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 (Sehling 11, p. 187). Only the third is in the plural.
- **The confession** passes, almost word for word, into the Kurpfalz order of 1556 and from it
  into the Reformed Palatinate order of 1563 (below).
- **The Our Father** sung after the absolution is called "a public confession" because of its
  fifth petition.

**Nürnberg after 1569: the *Offene Schuld* appended to the exhortation.** Veit Dietrich's
*Agendbüchlein* (agenda booklet), in the editions from 1569, ends the exhortation with an invitation to confess
and an absolution that is both conditional and indicative. **Nürnberg, Veit Dietrich,
*Agendbüchlein*, edition of 1569, from Sehling's apparatus** (Sehling 11, p. 498):

<!-- doc 297 -->

And forasmuch as we have all sinned and have need of the grace of God, humble your hearts before
God the Lord, confess your sins and infirmities with hearty love and desire of his divine grace
and help, with firm faith and trust in his gracious promise, and forgive from the heart every
one his neighbour, that your heavenly Father may also forgive your sins and misdeeds! If ye do
this, I loose you, in the stead of the holy Christian Church and by the command and promise of
our Lord Jesus Christ, when he said, "Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them"
(John 20:23), from all your sins, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy
Ghost. Amen.

**Editor's note** (p. 498, note 5). The *Offene Schuld* (open confession) "had been appended in the winter of 1524/25 on the model of the medieval preaching service". Osiander left it out when the
exhortation was taken into the church order of 1533; "at the congregation's wish" it was quickly taken back, and "Osiander now waged a hot but vain battle against it". The
wording disputed in 1533 came from Wenzel Linck.

**Bugenhagen, Brunswick 1528: the confession from the pulpit.** After the sermon the preacher
leads the people in the Creed and a confession of sins, without an absolution. The general
prayer follows. **Brunswick, *Christlike ordeninge* of Johannes Bugenhagen, 1528**
(Sehling 6/1, p. 443):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

Exhortation or admonition on the pulpit after the sermon: Dear friends in Christ, say the Creed
with me. I believe in God the Father almighty, etc. Say the confession with me, and confess your
sins unto God, that God may be gracious unto us. God be merciful to me a poor sinner. I fail in
faith, in that I love not God my Lord with my whole heart, nor rely wholly upon him in
temptations and in all need of body and soul. I should fear God alone and have him before mine
eyes in all things; now I fear the people that can do me evil for righteousness' sake. I fear to
lose my goods, honour, friendship and life. I am careful for my living unchristianly, and seek
in all things mine own and not what is God's. Also I set not my salvation wholly in Jesus
Christ, his only-begotten Son, given for us. I fail also in love, in that I love not my
neighbour as myself, but deal against him with evil suspicions, with backbiting, with words,
with works, and cannot suffer one word from him against me. Much more I keep silence, and cannot
forgive him from the heart, and yet am bound so to do. In especial I have a burdened conscience
in this temptation: N., in this sin: N. (Let every one complain to God of his secret grievous
sin, for amendment.) Therefore, almighty God, dear Father, forgive me all my sins, and enlighten
my heart with thy truth, that I may hold thee for my gracious Father and my neighbour for my
brother, without all offence, according to thy word, through our Lord Jesus Christ. (Say:) Amen.
Jesus Christ is our salvation for ever. (Say:) Amen.

**Note.**
- **"N."** marks a silent pause in which each hearer names his own temptation and sin to God.
- **The ending.** There is no absolution: the preacher's "Jesus Christ is our salvation for ever" stands in its place.

**Amberg 1550: the open confession with the general prayer.** In the Upper Palatinate the open
confession follows the sermon on Sundays, together with the general prayer, and comes before the
offertory and the exhortation. At weekday morning prayer the people say it after the priest.
**Amberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1550** (Sehling 13, pp. 286–287):

<!-- doc 411 -->

Thereupon followeth the sermon, which is commonly begun with the Creed or with another German
psalm or hymn of the high feasts. After the sermon there is always spoken the open confession
and the common prayer for spiritual and temporal [estates], and else for all the pressing need
of the Christian Church. […] The priest readeth before the altar, toward the people, a whole
chapter out of the Bible, with a short summary or exposition; thereafter the open confession and
the common prayer, with the morning blessing, which the people [say] after him; lastly a collect
and a German psalm.

**The Palatinate 1563: confession, absolution and retention after the sermon.** The Reformed
order puts the confession after the Sunday morning sermon. Its confession is Württemberg's, and
its absolution is a conditional declaration with a retention of sins. **Palatinate,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1563** (Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 389):

<!-- doc 504 -->

On Sunday after the morning sermon the minister of the church shall say: Ye beloved in the Lord,
forasmuch as we see in the commandments of God, as in a glass, how great and manifold our sins
are, whereby we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, let us confess the same from the heart
unto our faithful Father; say therefore with me thus: I, poor sinner, confess before thee, my
God and Creator, that I have, alas, grievously and manifoldly sinned against thee, not only with
outward gross sins, but much more with inward inborn blindness, unbelief, doubting,
faint-heartedness, impatience, pride, evil covetousness, secret envy, hatred and grudging, and
other evil tricks, as thou, my Lord and God, knowest of me, and I, alas, cannot sufficiently
know; they repent me and are grievous unto me, and I desire grace from the heart, through thy
dear Son Jesus Christ. Thereupon he shall declare unto the faithful the forgiveness of sins, and
unto the impenitent the judgment of God, and speak thus: Now hear the sure comfort of the grace
of God, which he promiseth to all the faithful in his Gospel. Thus saith the Lord Christ, John
3: God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him
should not perish, but have everlasting life. As many of you, then, as have displeasure in
themselves and in their sins, and trust that they are wholly and altogether forgiven them
through the merit of Jesus Christ alone, and have the purpose more and more to abstain from sins
and to serve the Lord in true holiness and righteousness, to them (since they believe in the Son
of the living God) I declare by the command of God that they are loosed in heaven from all their
sins (as he promiseth in his holy Gospel) through the perfect satisfaction of the most holy
passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ, Amen. But as many among you as still have pleasure
in their sins and shame, or persevere in sins against their conscience, to them I declare by the
command of God that the wrath and judgment of God abideth upon them, and that all their sins are
retained in heaven, and that they cannot be loosed from eternal damnation until they be
converted.

**Note.**
- **The editor's sources.** "almost word for word from Kurpfalz 1556" for the confession, and London 1565 (à Lasco and Micron's order, Reformed) for
  the address.
- **John 3:16** is the Strasbourg *Trostspruch* (1537, Moderate Reformed; [§3.3.6](#s3-3-6)). Kurpfalz 1556
  uses it as the absolution in the communion of the sick (Sehling 14, p. 171).
- **The verbs.** "I declare … that they are loosed in heaven" is a declaration, not a loosing: the minister announces what God
  has done, as in type 2, but to a defined class of hearers, with a retention for the rest.

**The Palatinate's Supper examination.** Before the Supper the Reformed Palatinate (1563) puts
three questions (on sin, redemption and thankfulness), each answered "Yes", and closes with an
assurance in place of an absolution. **Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563**
(Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 383):

<!-- doc 504 -->

All, then, that find this in their heart, let them not doubt that through the holy passion and
death of Christ they already have the forgiveness of all their sins and surely keep it, so long
as they persevere in this purpose, notwithstanding that there are yet many remaining infirmities
in them, which nevertheless are covered with the same passion and death of Jesus Christ.
Thereupon let every one that desireth this from the heart say: Amen. Kneel down and pray as the
Lord hath taught us: Our Father, etc. After the prayer let the minister of the church say: The
God of peace sanctify you wholly, and your whole spirit, soul and body be preserved blameless
unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it,
Amen.

#### <a id="s3-4-5"></a>3.4.5 The public confession and the modern Common Service

The Common Service of 1888, and the American Lutheran books that followed it, open the service
with a confession of sins and a declaration of grace. Their texts descend directly from the
Mecklenburg family ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). The English below is quoted from the Common Service as printed. It is
not in Sehling, and is given here for comparison only, so it is not set as a verified quotation.

| Mecklenburg 1552 / Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 | Common Service (1888) |
|---|---|
| "My dearest in God, open your hearts; let us confess our sins unto God, and pray for forgiveness in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." | "Beloved in the Lord! Let us draw near with a true heart, and confess our sins unto God our Father, beseeching Him, in the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to grant us forgiveness." |
| "Our help standeth in the name of the Lord. *The choir answereth.* Who hath made heaven and earth." | "Our help is in the Name of the Lord. *R.* Who made heaven and earth." |
| (Döber, Mecklenburg 1540: "Confess unto the Lord, for he is good. *Answer.* And his mercy is everlasting.") | "I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord. *R.* And Thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." (Ps 32:5) |
| "I, poor sinful man, confess before thee, O almighty God, my Maker and Redeemer, that I have sinned, not only with thoughts, words and works, but that I am also by nature sinful and unclean … But I have refuge unto thy bottomless mercy, and seek and desire grace, for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake." | "Almighty God, our Maker and Redeemer, we poor sinners confess unto Thee, that we are by nature sinful and unclean, and that we have sinned against Thee by thought, word, and deed. Wherefore we flee for refuge to Thine infinite mercy, seeking and imploring Thy grace, for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ." |
| *The other minister:* "O almighty, merciful God, who hast given thine only-begotten Son unto death for us, vouchsafe to have mercy upon us, and for the sake of the same thy beloved Son forgive us all our sins; and give us also thy Holy Ghost, who may kindle and increase in us true knowledge of thy divine being and will, and true obedience toward thee; that we may attain eternal life through thy grace …" | "O most merciful God, who hast given Thine Only-begotten Son to die for us, have mercy upon us, and for His sake grant us remission of all our sins; and by Thy Holy Spirit increase in us true knowledge of Thee, and of Thy will, and true obedience to Thy Word, to the end that by Thy grace we may come to everlasting life; through Jesus Christ our Lord." |
| *The priest:* "The almighty, merciful God hath had mercy upon us, forgiveth us truly all our sins for his dear Son's sake, whom he hath given unto death for our sake, and hath given power to become the children of God to all that believe on his name; he giveth us thereto his Holy Ghost; whoso believeth and is baptized shall be saved. God grant this unto us all" | "Almighty God, our Heavenly Father, hath had mercy upon us, and hath given His Only Son to die for us, and for His sake forgiveth us all our sins. To them that believe on His Name, He giveth power to become the sons of God, and bestoweth upon them His Holy Spirit. He that believeth, and is baptized, shall be saved. Grant this, O Lord, unto us all." |

**What the comparison shows.**
- **The order** of the Common Service preparation (address, *Adiutorium* [Our help], a second versicle,
  confession, prayer for forgiveness, declaration of grace) is Döber's order of 1525, by way of
  Mecklenburg.
- **The prayer for forgiveness** ("O most merciful God …") is the old *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy). In
  Mecklenburg 1552 it belonged to the *second minister* or custos kneeling beside the priest.
  That is the server's place in the Roman *Stufengebet* (prayers at the foot of the altar).
- **The declaration of grace** ("Almighty God … hath had mercy upon us … Grant this, O Lord,
  unto us all") is type 2 ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)): God's mercy declared in the third person, with no "I absolve",
  and closed with a wish. It is not an indicative absolution, and not the optative *Misereatur*
  either. Its final wish goes back to Döber's "God grant this unto us all".
- **The confession** passes from the priest's "I, poor sinful man" to "we poor sinners".
  The step is already taken at Amberg in 1555, where the priest, kneeling with another minister,
  says "We poor, sinful men confess before thee, O almighty God, our Creator and Redeemer" (Sehling 13, p. 290; [§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). Marienhafe in East Frisia has a plural prayer of confession too,
  "we poor, sinful men confess and lament unto thee with sorrowful hearts our manifold sins and misdeeds" (Sehling 7/1, p. 712), but it comes from another line, the
  *Offene Schuld* (open confession) of the Engerhafe liturgy, and stands before communion. In the
  sixteenth-century orders the priest says it alone while the people keep silence and confess in
  their hearts; the Common Service gives it to the congregation.
- **The second versicle.** The Common Service's second versicle (Ps 32:5) is not in Sehling's
  Mecklenburg texts. Its place is taken in Döber and Mecklenburg 1540 by *Confitemini Domino*.

**The indicative absolution in American Lutheran books.** The other common form in American
Lutheran books, "Upon this your confession, I, by virtue of my office, as a called and ordained
servant of the Word, announce the grace of God unto all of you, and in the stead and by the
command of my Lord Jesus Christ I forgive you all your sins …", has its sixteenth-century
counterpart in Naumburg 1537: "Upon such your confession, by the commandment of the Lord Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Christian church, I forgive you all your sins" ([§3.3.5](#s3-3-5)). Its confession is
also close to the one that goes with this absolution in those books: "O almighty God, merciful
Father, I, a poor, miserable sinner, confess unto Thee all my sins and iniquities … and I pray
Thee of Thy boundless mercy and for the sake of the holy, innocent, bitter sufferings and death
of Thy beloved Son, Jesus Christ, to be gracious and merciful to me". Compare Naumburg's "pray thee, by thy bottomless mercy and by the bitter sufferings and death of thy dear Son JESUS CHRIST, that thou wouldest be gracious unto me, poor sinner". Württemberg's "as an appointed minister of the Christian Church" is the sixteenth-century form of "a called and ordained servant of the Word".

#### <a id="s3-4-6"></a>3.4.6 General confession against private confession

The Brandenburg-Nürnberg tradition was wary of the general confession. The Brandenburg order
forbids the people to replace private confession with a confession said together. **Brandenburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 60):

<!-- doc 1746 -->

Likewise the abuse that hath been taken up in some places, that several persons together in a
crowd make a common confession and receive a public absolution, and let it rest there, shall not
be suffered; but every one shall be heard and absolved severally, as need requireth. And that it
may now go orderly and rightly, and all abuses be prevented as far as possible, the people shall
be told that whoso will receive the holy sacrament shall [announce himself] the evening before,
or, where that could not be by reason of the distance of the way or other chances, in the
morning before the time of Mass, to the pastor […].

Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 repeats the rule: the pastors shall "not suffer many of them to make a common confession together, but every one shall make his confession for himself and desire absolution" (Sehling 13, p. 57).

**The point of the prohibition.** It is not aimed at a confession in the Mass. Brandenburg 1540
itself has the priest's *Confiteor* (I confess) at the altar ([§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)). It is aimed at groups of communicants
confessing together on the Saturday and taking that for private confession. In the Nürnberg
tradition, the general absolution in the Mass was itself contested in 1533 ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)). Where both
exist, as in Mecklenburg, the public confession at the start of the Mass is a preparation for
all, and the private confession on the Saturday is the condition of admission to communion.

---

### <a id="s3-5"></a>3.5 The exhortation to the communicants: the families collated

#### <a id="s3-5-1"></a>3.5.1 Where it falls, and what it is for

**What it is.** Every Lutheran order with a communion rite has an exhortation (*Vermahnung*,
*vormaninge*, *exhortatio*) addressed to the communicants. Bugenhagen calls it "the true Preface, that is, a foreword" (Brunswick 1528, Sehling 6/1, p. 440). It does four things:
- it teaches what the Sacrament is;
- it calls the communicants to examine themselves (1 Cor 11:28);
- it rehearses or paraphrases the Words of Institution;
- it calls for thanksgiving and love of the neighbour.

It never replaces the Words of Institution, which are always sung or said after it. In Nürnberg,
where the exhortation itself rehearsed the Verba, Sehling notes that once the Verba were sung
aloud the exhortation "doubled" them.

**Placement.** The exhortation stands in five places:

| Place | Orders |
|---|---|
| **After the sermon, in the pulpit or at the altar, before the Our Father and Verba** | Luther, *Deutsche Messe* 1526 (pulpit or altar left free); Saxony 1539 and 1580; Mansfeld 1562; Grubenhagen 1581; Henneberg 1582 |
| **At the altar after the sermon, before the Verba** | Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 (moved there "at Luther's suggestion"); Württemberg 1536 and its family; Pfalz-Neuburg 1543; Hohenlohe; Verden 1606; Palatinate 1563 (Reformed; at the table) |
| **At the altar after the sermon, before the Preface** (as its "true" form) | Bugenhagen, Brunswick 1528, Hamburg 1529, Wolfenbüttel 1543, Hildesheim 1544; Kantz 1522 |
| **After the Preface and Sanctus, before the Our Father and Verba** | Mecklenburg 1552 ("if there is time"); Osnabrück 1543; Naumburg 1537 (before the Sanctus) |
| **After the Verba and Our Father, before communion** | Nürnberg 1524, Döber 1525, *Form und Ordnung* 1525 (Osiander's original place) |
| **After communion** | Memmingen 1528 (Moderate Reformed) and Marienhafe 1593 (a short exhortation to love and thanksgiving) |

**Editor's note on the move.** Sehling's editor comments on Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533
(Sehling 11, p. 195): "the transposition, compared with 1524, to before the beginning of the sacramental part goes back to Luther's suggestion in his *Deutsche Messe".

**Who reads it.** The priest, facing the people, from the altar (most orders), or the preacher
from the pulpit (Luther's option; Bugenhagen's pulpit exhortation; Micron, Reformed). In
Nürnberg 1525 "the priest or the minister" may read it.

#### <a id="s3-5-2"></a>3.5.2 The families and their witnesses

**How the collation was made.** Every exhortation in the corpus was located by scanning all
2,368 documents for passages that share wording with a known exhortation. The match tolerates
the spelling differences between High German, Low German and the several regional spellings.
Each witness found was then aligned word by word against the archetype of its family, and every
difference longer than a spelling variant was listed and read. Sehling's apparatus and
footnotes, which the database prints inside the running text, were set aside by hand.

**What "archetype" means here.** For each family the archetype is the earliest full text printed
by Sehling from which the others descend. Where a later recension was copied more widely than
the archetype (Württemberg 1553, the Braunschweig recension of Osiander), its changes are set
out in full.

**The families.** There are eleven families with more than one witness, and a handful of
exhortations that occur in one order only:

| § | Family (archetype) | Incipit | Witnesses in Sehling |
|---|---|---|---|
| [3.5.3](#s3-5-3) | **Luther**, Wittenberg 1526 | "Dear friends of Christ, forasmuch as we are here gathered together …" | Saxony 1539 (abridged in print), Prussia 1544 and 1568 (in place of the Preface), Albertine Saxony 1580, Mansfeld 1562, Grubenhagen 1581, Lindau 1573, Wertheim c. 1555 (as a prayer), Frankfurt 1543 and the French church at Frankfurt 1585 (Reformed; paraphrase only), Henneberg 1582 (admonition only, rewritten) |
| [3.5.4](#s3-5-4) | **Osiander**, Nürnberg 1524 | "Ye dearly beloved in God! Forasmuch as we will now … the supper …" | Volprecht 1524, Nürnberg parish churches 1524, Döber 1525, *Form und Ordnung* 1525; the Braunschweig recension: Lüneburg 1564, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1569, Buxtehude 1565 (Low German, cited), Lippe 1571, Lüneburg 1575 (cited), Verden 1606, Waldeck (revised text B) |
| [3.5.5](#s3-5-5) | **Brandenburg-Nürnberg** 1533 | "Dearly beloved in God, forasmuch as we will now … the holy Supper …" | Brandenburg 1540, Calenberg-Göttingen 1542, Regensburg c. 1544 (rewritten 1567), Dietrich's *Agendbüchlein* 1543 (cited), Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, Schwäbisch Hall 1543, Hohenlohe 1553 and 1578, Strasbourg 1553 (Marbach), Nassau-Dillenburg 1575 (Philippist; cited), Erbach 1587, Ysenburg-Birstein 1588 |
| [3.5.6](#s3-5-6) | **Württemberg** 1536, revised 1553 | "Dearly beloved in Christ Jesus, forasmuch as we will now … the gracious Supper …" | 1536 text: Worms 1560. 1553 text: Kurpfalz 1556, Worms 1560, Leiningen-Westerburg 1566, Lindau 1573, Hanau-Lichtenberg 1573, Nassau-Weilburg 1576 (in its Agende of 1618), Ysenburg-Ronneburg 1582, Strasbourg 1598, Isny c. 1600, Solms-Laubach 1603, Wild- und Rheingrafschaft 1603 |
| [3.5.7](#s3-5-7) | **Bugenhagen**, Brunswick 1528 | "My dearly beloved, it is continually set before us by the preaching of the Gospel …" | Low German: Hamburg 1529, Lübeck 1531 (cited), Hadeln (cited), Wolfenbüttel 1543, Osnabrück 1543 (cited), Hildesheim 1544 (cited), Buxtehude (cited), Hamburg 1556 (cited). High German: Frankfurt 1543 (free paraphrase), Lüneburg 1564, Hildesheim 1561 (cited), Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1569, Lippe 1571 (twice), Verden 1606, Osnabrück 1613 (abridged) |
| [3.5.8](#s3-5-8) | **Naumburg** 1537 | "Dear friends, forasmuch as ye are now … the testament of our dear Lord Jesus Christ …" | Nördlingen 1579 (and, according to Sehling's editor, Nördlingen 1544) |
| [3.5.9](#s3-5-9) | **Mecklenburg** 1552 | "Dear friends, ye that as Christian men have been instructed beforehand concerning God …" | Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557, Nassau-Weilburg 1576, Sayn 1590 (abridged); its prayer in Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 |
| [3.5.10](#s3-5-10) | **The Palatinate** 1563 (Reformed) | "Ye beloved in the Lord Jesus Christ, hear the words of the institution …" | Ysenburg-Birstein 1598; the Lower Rhine recension: Moers 1581, Bentheim-Tecklenburg 1588/1619 (all Reformed) |
| [3.5.11](#s3-5-11) | **Pfalz-Veldenz** 1574 | "Ye beloved in the Lord Christ. It is well known to you as Christians, out of God's word …" | Lützelstein 1605 |
| [3.5.12](#s3-5-12) | **Zürich and Basel** (Reformed) | "Dear brethren! Ye have heard the unspeakable mercy of God …" | Memmingen 1528 (Moderate Reformed; from Zürich 1525), Neckarbischofsheim 1560 (from Basel 1526) |
| [3.5.13](#s3-5-13) | **Strasbourg** (Moderate Reformed) | "Dear brothers and sisters, ye will every one consider with himself …" | the early Strasbourg agendas; its second half in Memmingen 1528 (both Moderate Reformed) |

The exhortations that belong to no family (Kantz 1522 and the Bremen Mass of 1525, Augsburg 1530
(Moderate Reformed), Buxtehude 1565, Micron 1554/1565 (Reformed), Marienhafe 1593, and the
Saturday exhortations of Hohenlohe 1578) are treated in [§3.5.14](#s3-5-14).

**Not reproducible.** Mecklenburg 1540/45 has three Low German exhortations, "one of these three exhortations to be read at a time".
Sehling does not print them: "There follow three exhortations to the Supper, the second of which is freely shaped after the only one in the Low German edition of the Brandenburg-Nürnberg order" (Sehling 5, p. 154.) Weißenburg 1528 meant to print the Nürnberg exhortation but, as the
editor notes, "it was then forgotten to include it" (Sehling 11, p. 659).
#### <a id="s3-5-3"></a>3.5.3 The Luther family: Wittenberg, *Deutsche Messe*, 1526

Luther joins a paraphrase of the Our Father to a short admonition on the testament, and leaves
it free whether it is read from the pulpit or at the altar. **Wittenberg, Luther, *Deudsche
messe und ordnung gottis diensts*, 1526** (Sehling 1, p. 15):

<!-- doc 3 -->

After the sermon shall follow a public paraphrase of the Our Father and an admonition to them
that will go to the sacrament, after this or a better manner, as followeth: Dear friends of
Christ, forasmuch as we are here gathered together in the name of the Lord to receive his holy
testament, I admonish you first that ye lift up your heart to God, to pray with me the Our
Father, as Christ our Lord hath taught us and hath comfortably promised us a hearing. That God
our Father in heaven would mercifully look upon us his wretched children on earth, and grant
grace that his holy name may be hallowed among us and in all the world, through the pure and
upright teaching of his word and through the fervent love of our life; would graciously turn
away all false teaching and evil life, whereby his worthy name is blasphemed and put to shame.
That his kingdom also may come and be increased; that he would bring all sinners, the blinded,
and them that are taken captive by the devil in his kingdom, to the knowledge of the right faith
in Jesus Christ his Son, and make the number of Christians great. That we also may be
strengthened with his Spirit to do and to suffer his will, both in life and in death, in good
and in evil, always breaking, offering up and slaying our own will. That he would also give us
our daily bread, keep us from covetousness and care for the belly, but let us look to him for
enough of all good things. That he would also forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,
that our heart may have a sure and joyful conscience before him, and never fear nor be afraid of
any sin. That he would not lead us into temptation, but help us by his Spirit to subdue the
flesh, despise the world with all its ways, and overcome the devil with all his wiles. And
lastly, that he would deliver us from all evil, both bodily and spiritual, temporal and eternal.
Whoso earnestly desire all this, let them say from the heart: "Amen", believing without all
doubt that it is yea and heard in heaven, as Christ promiseth us: "What ye ask, believe that ye
shall have it, and it shall be done." Amen. Secondly, I admonish you in Christ that ye give heed
with right faith to the testament of Christ, and above all hold fast in your heart the words
wherein Christ giveth us his body and blood for forgiveness; that ye remember and give thanks
for the bottomless love which he hath shown us, when he redeemed us by his blood from God's
wrath, sin, death and hell; and thereupon take outwardly unto you the bread and wine, that is,
his body and blood, for assurance and pledge. Accordingly we will, in his name and by his
command, through his own words, so handle and use the testament. But whether this paraphrase and
admonition be done in the pulpit straight after the sermon, or before the altar, I leave free to
every one's choice. It seemeth that the ancients have done it hitherto in the pulpit, whence it
hath still remained that the common prayer is made in the pulpit, or the Our Father said before
[the people]. But the admonition hath become a public confession.

**Note.**
- **The two parts.** The paraphrase is a prayer, said by the minister, to which the people
  answer "Amen". The admonition proper is the second paragraph.
- **The pulpit.** Luther's last sentences give the history: the medieval pulpit office (*Prone*)
  had a bidding prayer, the Our Father, and an admonition that "has become a public confession", the *Offene Schuld* (open confession) of [§3.3.5](#s3-3-5).

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form |
|---|---|---|
| Saxony (Albertine), *Kirchenordnung*, 1539 | 1, p. 274 | Full, but Sehling prints only incipit and explicit, "Dear friends of Christ, forasmuch as we are here gathered … so handle and use the testament"; headed "Vermanung zum gebet vor der communio" (Exhortation to prayer before the communion). The Our Father and Verba may be sung in its place. |
| Prussia, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544 | 4, p. 65 | Read "in place of the Preface, which shall be done away"; paraphrase as Luther, only lacking "grace"; admonition rewritten (below) |
| Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und ceremonien*, 1568 | 4, pp. 81–82 | The 1544 form, printed in full, again in place of the Preface |
| Wertheim, *Kirchenordnung*, c. 1555 | 11, pp. 713–714 | Paraphrase turned into a prayer to God in the second person (below) |
| Mansfeld, *Kirchenordnung*, 1562 | 2, p. 227 | Verbatim; optional |
| Lindau, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573 | 12, pp. 209–210 | Verbatim, modernized optatives ("wölle" for "wolte"); said at the altar after the Württemberg exhortation from the pulpit ([§3.5.6](#s3-5-6)) |
| Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573 | 7/2.1, pp. 1090–1091 | Verbatim; "before the altar", or a Latin Preface instead |
| Albertine Saxony, *Kirchenordnung*, 1580 | 1, pp. 368–369 | Verbatim; headed "Vermanung zum gebet vor der communion", read "before the altar" |
| Grubenhagen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1581 | 6/2, p. 1075 | Verbatim, with "his holy, precious" added in the admonition |
| Henneberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1582 | 2, p. 308 | Admonition only, rewritten (below) |
| Frankfurt, *Agende* for baptism and the communion of the sick, 1543 | 9, pp. 521, 553 | Paraphrase as a prayer ("we thy wretched children on earth pray thee"); new admonition |
| Frankfurt, French Reformed church, *Diakonieordnung*, 1585 (Reformed) | 9, p. 497 | Paraphrase only, from the draft of the order |

**The significant variants.**
- **No witness changes the paraphrase in substance** except by turning it into a direct prayer.
  The textual tradition of the paraphrase is stable: Saxony, Mansfeld, Oldenburg, Lindau,
  Albertine Saxony and Grubenhagen differ from Wittenberg only in spelling and in single words.
- **The paraphrase as a prayer.** Wertheim c. 1555 and Frankfurt 1543 recast Luther's indirect
  wishes ("that God our Father in heaven would …") as a
  prayer addressed to God. **Wertheim, *Kirchenordnung*, c. 1555** (Sehling 11, p. 713):

<!-- doc 323 -->

O God, our heavenly Father, vouchsafe mercifully to look upon us, thy poor, wretched children on
earth, and grant grace that thy holy name may be hallowed among us and in all the world, through
the pure and upright teaching of thy word and through the fervent amendment of our life.

  Wertheim also reads "amendment of our life" for Luther's "love of our life".
- **Prussia: a declaration of forgiveness in the admonition.** The Prussian order keeps the
  paraphrase but opens the admonition with a conditional declaration of forgiveness and adds a
  sentence on personal appropriation. **Prussia, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544** (Sehling 4, p. 65):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

Secondly, dear friends of Christ: forasmuch as ye hunger and thirst after the mercy of God and
heartily desire the forgiveness of your sins, our Saviour Christ hath given his body and blood
for you on the cross, that your sins shall be washed away, as many of you as believe it;
therefore I admonish you in the Lord that ye give heed with right faith to the rich and holy
testament of Christ, and above all rightly hold fast in your heart, by pure faith, the words
wherein our Lord Christ giveth us his body and his precious blood for the forgiveness of sin;
that ye remember his passion and death and thank him from the heart for the bottomless love
which he hath shown us, when he redeemed us by his own blood from God's wrath, sin, death and
hell; and thereupon take outwardly unto you the bread and wine, that is, his body and blood, for
assurance and pledge; for even as each one receiveth it for himself, so also hath he to comfort
himself with the Gospel and with a gracious, reconciled God, and to take them to himself.

  The order of 1568, which prints the whole paraphrase, reads "heiliger name" for Luther's
  "werder name" (Sehling 4, p. 82).
- **Henneberg: the admonition alone.** The Henneberg order drops the paraphrase. It rewrites the
  admonition with a stronger statement of the presence ("his true body for a meat and his own blood for a drink, a phrase of the Württemberg exhortation") and the Johannine "that so Christ may live in you, and ye in Christ, for ever". **Henneberg, *Kirchenordnung* of Georg Ernst, 1582**
  (Sehling 2, p. 308):

<!-- doc 1247 -->

Dear friends in Christ, forasmuch as we are here gathered in the name of the Lord to celebrate
and receive the gracious Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, I admonish you that ye give good heed
with right earnestness and faith to the testament of Christ, and above all well consider in your
heart the words (Take, eat, this is my body; drink, this is my blood) wherein Christ ordaineth
us his true body for a meat and his own blood for a drink, and therewith giveth and reacheth
forgiveness of sins, and hold them fast with faith; and thereafter humbly and devoutly thank the
Lord Christ for the bottomless love which he hath shown us, when by the shedding of his blood
and his death he redeemed us from God's wrath, sin, death and hell; and thereupon receive the
bread and wine, that is, his body and blood, for a sure assurance, pledge and witness, that so
Christ may live in you and ye in Christ for ever. Accordingly we will, in his name and by his
command, through his own words, so handle and use the testament.

- **Use and option.** Mansfeld 1562 makes the whole text optional: "that whoever will may use it", and allows it to be dropped in towns when the
  singing and organ make the service too long (Sehling 2, p. 227). Saxony 1539 allows the Our
  Father and Verba to be sung instead. Oldenburg allows the Latin Preface instead.
#### <a id="s3-5-4"></a>3.5.4 The Osiander family: Nürnberg, 1524

**The archetype.** Andreas Osiander's exhortation was printed in the Nürnberg provosts' *Grundt
und ursach* (1524). Sehling takes it as the base text of the order of the Nürnberg parish
churches of 1524, with the variants of Volprecht (V), the parish churches (P) and Döber (D) in
his apparatus. Osiander declared himself its author on 22 September 1533. It stood after the
Verba, which were then still said in Latin, and served to "open" them to the people. **Nürnberg,
*Gottesdienstordnung der Pfarrkirchen* (base text of *Grundt und ursach*), 1524**
(Sehling 11, pp. 48–49):

<!-- doc 249 -->

Ye dearly beloved in God! Forasmuch as we will now consider and keep the supper of our Lord
Jesus Christ, wherein his flesh and blood are given us for meat and for drink, not of the body
but of the soul, we ought rightly with great diligence every one to examine himself, as Paul
saith, and so to eat of this bread and drink of this cup. For none but a hungry soul, which
knoweth its sin, feareth God's wrath and death, and is hungry and thirsty after righteousness,
ought to receive this holy sacrament. But when we examine ourselves, we find nothing in us but
sin and death, and can in no wise help ourselves out thereof. Therefore hath our dear Lord Jesus
Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sakes is become man, that he might fulfil the law for us
and suffer that which we had deserved with our sins. And that we might steadfastly believe this
and joyfully rely thereupon, he took after the supper the bread, gave thanks, brake it, and
said: Take and eat! This is my body, which is given for you; as if he would say: That I am
become man, and all that I do and suffer, that is all your own, done for you and for your good.
For a sure token thereof I give you my body for meat. Likewise also the cup, and said: Take and
drink ye all of this! This is the cup of the new testament with my blood, which is shed for you
and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby! As
if he would say: Forasmuch as I have taken your cause upon me and laden your sins upon myself, I
will offer myself unto death for sin, shed my blood, obtain grace and forgiveness of sins, and
so set up a new testament, wherein sin shall be remembered no more for ever. For a sure token
thereof I give you my blood to drink. Whosoever now eateth thus of this bread and drinketh of
this cup, that is, whosoever firmly believeth these words which he heareth and these signs which
he receiveth, he dwelleth in the Lord Christ and Christ in him, and so liveth for ever. Hereby
shall we remember his death, give him thanks therefor, every one take up his cross and follow
him, and above all love one another, as he also hath loved us; for we being many are one bread
and one body, who are all partakers of one bread and drink of one cup.

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form |
|---|---|---|
| Volprecht, *Deutsche Messe*, Nürnberg 1524 (V) | 11, p. 48, apparatus | Full |
| Nürnberg parish churches, 1524 (P) | 11, p. 48, apparatus | Full |
| Döber, *Deutsche Messe*, Nürnberg 1525 (D) | 11, p. 54 (cited) | Full; text in [Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.8.7](#s7-8-7) |
| *Form und Ordnung einer christlichen Messe*, Nürnberg 1525 | 11, p. 57 (cited) | Incipit only, "My dearly beloved in God etc." |
| Weißenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528 | 11, p. 659 | Intended but left out by the printer |
| Lüneburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1564 | 6/1, pp. 546–547 | Braunschweig recension, with a closing bidding to the Our Father |
| Buxtehude, *Agende*, 1565 | 7/1, p. 125 | Low German, "My dearly beloved in God", given as "Another" after Buxtehude's own exhortation ([§3.5.14.3](#s3-5-14-3)); not printed by Sehling, who gives only the closing wish "God grant us all this, that we receive it worthily" |
| Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1569 | 6/1, pp. 146–147 | Braunschweig recension, with the bidding |
| Lippe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571 | 21, pp. 412–413 | Braunschweig recension, with Döber's closing wish |
| Lüneburg (city), *Kirchenordnung*, 1575 | 6/1, p. 659 | Incipit only: "as is further to be found in Dr. M. Luther's hymnal" |
| Verden, *Kirchenordnung*, 1606 | 7/1, pp. 158–159 | Braunschweig recension, with the bidding |
| Waldeck, *Kirchenordnung*, revised text (B) | 9, pp. 247–248, apparatus | Braunschweig recension, "if he have time"; the base text of 1556 has no exhortation |

**The Nürnberg variants, 1524–1525.**
- **The address.** V, P and D all read "Mein allerliebsten" (My dearly beloved) for "Ir allerliebsten" (Ye dearly beloved).
- **Small differences.** V reads "high diligence" for "great". V, D read
  "pardon" for "forgiveness" of sins. V, P, D read "hold dear" for "love".
- **The closing wish.** D adds "God grant us all this, that we may receive it worthily. Amen". V adds "God grant it blessedly, amen".
- **The Offene Schuld.** In the winter of 1524/25 an open confession with absolution was added
  at the end; it was the subject of Osiander's dispute of 1533 ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

**The Braunschweig recension.** The Lower Saxon orders do not copy Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533.
They go back to the 1524 text in a recension first attested in Lüneburg 1564 and taken into the
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel order of 1569. Lüneburg 1575 shows how it circulated: it was printed
with Luther's hymnals. The recension changes the archetype in
these places:
- **"forasmuch as we now [keep] the Supper of our dear Lord"** for "now the evening meal of our Lord".
- **"wherein his flesh is given us for a meat and his blood for a drink, not of the body but of the soul"**, restructuring "flesh and blood for meat and for drink".
- **"For none shall, but only a hungry soul"** for "For it shall not, but only a hungry soul".
- **"for a token thereof"**, dropping "sure" both times.
- **The Verba.** "do it in remembrance of me" for "ye shall remember me thereby".
  Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, Lippe and Waldeck B read the cup-word in the Pauline form, "this cup is
  the new testament in my blood".
- **"offer for sin"**, dropping "unto death".
- **"he abideth in Christ"**, dropping "the Lord" after it.
- **The ending.** "give him thanks from the heart, each take his cross upon him and follow the Lord, and
  above all things love one another, even as Christ hath loved us. For it is one bread and we, being
  many, one body, who are made partakers of one bread and all drink of one cup".
- **The bidding.** Lüneburg 1564, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1569 and Verden 1606 add a bidding
  to the Our Father (below). Lippe 1571 instead ends with Döber's "God grant us all this, that we receive it worthily. Amen".

**Lüneburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1564** (Sehling 6/1, p. 547):
