<!-- doc 2003 -->

But that we may all together, according to the teaching and exhortation now heard, worthily
receive the holy sacrament in right true faith and penitence, we will call upon God the Father
in the name of Christ, and from the bottom of our heart say a devout Our Father.

**Where it stands.** In the Braunschweig recension the exhortation is read after the sermon and
the general prayer, before the Preface (Lüneburg) or before the Our Father and Verba (Verden).
In Lüneburg, Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, Lippe and Verden it is followed by Bugenhagen's
exhortation as "another exhortation", to be used in its place ([§3.5.7](#s3-5-7)).
#### <a id="s3-5-5"></a>3.5.5 The Brandenburg-Nürnberg family, 1533

**The archetype.** The Brandenburg-Nürnberg order of 1533 revised Osiander's text ([§3.5.4](#s3-5-4)) and
moved it before the Verba. This revised text is the most widely copied exhortation in the
corpus. **Brandenburg-Nürnberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1533** (Sehling 11, pp. 195–196):

<!-- doc 270 -->

Order of the Lord's Supper. When the priest will hold the Supper of the Lord (if he have
communicants at all), he shall straightway make the following exhortation to the people, and
then sing the words of the Supper, where the Mass is sung, about after the following manner and
according to the notes set down hereafter; or, if he readeth the Mass, read them with loud and
intelligible words, that they that stand about may hear them. The exhortation followeth. Dearly
beloved in God, forasmuch as we will now consider and keep the holy Supper of our Lord Jesus
Christ, wherein he hath given us his flesh for a meat and his blood for a drink, therewith to
strengthen faith, we ought rightly with great diligence every one to examine himself, as the
holy Paul exhorteth us; for this holy sacrament is given for a special comfort and strength to
poor troubled consciences, which confess their sins, fear God's wrath and death, and are hungry
and thirsty after righteousness. But when we examine ourselves, and every one goeth into his own
conscience, as the holy Paul teacheth us, we shall surely find nothing else than all manner of
horrible sins, and death, which we have deserved with sin, and yet can in no wise help ourselves
out thereof. Therefore hath our dear Lord Jesus Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sins' sake
is become man, that he might fulfil the law and all the will of God for us and for our good, and
take upon himself and suffer death and all that we had deserved with our sins, for us and for
our deliverance. And that we might steadfastly believe this, and through faith live joyfully in
his will, he took after the supper the bread, gave thanks, brake it, and said: Take and eat!
This is my body, which is given for you. That is: that I am become man, and all that I do and
suffer, is all your own, done for you and for your good. For a sure token and witness thereof I
give you my body for meat. Likewise he took also the cup and said: Take and drink ye all of
this! This is the cup of the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you and for many for
the forgiveness of sins. As oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby. That is: forasmuch
as I have taken your cause upon me and laden your sins upon myself, I will offer myself unto
death for sin, shed my blood, obtain grace and forgiveness of sins, and so set up a new
testament, wherein sins are forgiven and shall be remembered no more for ever. For a sure token
and witness thereof I give you my blood to drink. Whosoever now eateth thus of this bread and
drinketh of this cup, and firmly believeth these words which he heareth from Christ, and these
signs which he receiveth from Christ, he dwelleth in the Lord Christ and Christ in him, and
shall live for ever. Hereby shall we now remember him and show forth his death, namely that he
died for our sins and rose again for our justification, and give him thanks therefor, every one
take up his cross and follow him, and according to his commandment love one another, as he hath
loved us: for we are all one bread and one body, forasmuch as we are all partakers of one bread
and drink of one cup.

**What 1533 changes in Osiander's text.**
- **"holy Supper"** for "supper", and "wherein he hath given us his flesh for a meat and his blood for a drink, therewith to strengthen faith" for "not of the body but of the soul".
- **The comfort of consciences.** "this holy sacrament is given for a special comfort and strength to poor troubled consciences" replaces the rule that only a hungry soul "shall … receive".
- **Self-examination expanded:** "and every one go into his own conscience" and "all manner of horrible sins".
- **The work of Christ:** "fulfil the law and all the will of God", "for our deliverance".
- **"as if he would say"** becomes **"That is"** (That is) before each
  gloss.
- **"token and witness"** for "sign".
- **The ending.** "show forth his death, namely that he died for our sins and rose again for our justification" is added from Rom 4:25. Döber's closing wish is
  dropped.
- **No confession or absolution.** The Nürnberg editions from 1569 append the *Offene Schuld*
  ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Brandenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1540 | 3, pp. 69–70 | Verbatim except for a spelling of "now", and "the Supper" for "the holy Supper". Read after the consecration ([Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.12.6](#s7-12-6)). |
| Calenberg-Göttingen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542 | 6/2, pp. 790–791 | Read on Saturdays and the eves of feasts "after confession has been made and absolution received", so it begins "forasmuch as we will tomorrow keep the Supper". "this sacrament is … given to poor, troubled and fainthearted consciences". |
| Regensburg, *Ein Christenliche vermanung, wie die zu Regenspurg alwegen vor der communion verlesen wird*, c. 1544 | 13, pp. 403–404 | "his body for meat" for "his flesh for a meat"; the cup-word in the Pauline form ("this cup … this do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me"); "according to his command" for "commandment". Printed as the exhortation "that is made every Sunday before the communion". Followed by an open confession, "God be merciful to me a sinner", and an indicative absolution ("I declare unto you such forgiveness"). The order of 1553 has it read at the altar by the second minister after the Creed, citing this text (Sehling 13, p. 420). |
| Regensburg, *Vermanung vor der communion*, 1567 | 13, pp. 404–405 | A new text on the same opening, "Ye beloved in God! Forasmuch as we will now keep the holy Supper of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ …", rewritten in three points (sin, Christ's fulfilment of the law, the bodily union with Christ in the Supper). It ends with the plural confession "God be merciful to us poor sinners" and the absolution "God hath had mercy upon you … which forgiveness I hereby declare unto you". |
| Nürnberg, Veit Dietrich, *Agendbüchlein*, 1543 and later editions | 11, p. 498 | Not reprinted: "word for word from the church order of 1533". From 1569 the *Offene Schuld* with an indicative absolution is appended to it ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)) |
| Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543 | 13, pp. 72–73 | "that feel and confess their sins"; the cup-word lacks "which is shed for you and for many for the remission of sins". Text in [Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.14.1](#s7-14-1). |
| Schwäbisch Hall, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543 | 17/1, pp. 136–137 | South-western subgroup (below) |
| Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553 | 15, pp. 69–70 | "will keep and receive the holy, most worthy sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ" for "the holy Supper … consider and keep"; "these words … and these gifts which he receiveth" for "these signs". The manuscript lacks the transition to the open confession. |
| Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung* of Marbach, 1553 | 20/1, p. 412 | South-western subgroup; begins "Dear friends, forasmuch as we will now, by means of divine grace, keep the holy Supper"; read from the altar on Sundays between the psalms |
| Nassau-Dillenburg, *Agende*, 1575 (Philippist) | 10, p. 151 | Incipit only, "Ye dearly beloved in God etc." |
| Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1578 | 15, pp. 286–287 | Verbatim (but "have" for "had") |
| Erbach, *Kirchenordnung*, 1587 | 9, pp. 436–437 | South-western subgroup; "his body and blood for a spiritual meat and drink"; "supper" for "sacrament"; followed by the open confession |
| Ysenburg-Birstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1588 | 10, pp. 626–627 | Verbatim ("with all diligence" for "with great diligence") |

**The south-western subgroup.** Schwäbisch Hall 1543, Strasbourg 1553 and Erbach 1587 share a
set of changes that mark them as one recension:
- "forasmuch as we will now keep the Supper …", dropping "consider and";
- "his body" for "his flesh";
- "and every one goeth into his conscience", dropping "as Saint Paul teacheth us";
- "the law … fulfilled for us and for our good", dropping "and all the will of God";
- "he took the bread in the Supper" for "after the Supper";
- "and according to his commandment love one another, as he hath loved us, also …" and "are partakers of one bread".

  Württemberg 1553 also reads "in the Supper", where Württemberg 1536 had followed
  Brandenburg-Nürnberg's "after the Supper" ([§3.5.6](#s3-5-6)).
#### <a id="s3-5-6"></a>3.5.6 The Württemberg family, 1536 and 1553

**The archetype.** Württemberg 1536 takes the Brandenburg-Nürnberg text and expands it. It adds
Augustine's sacraments as "visible words", a stronger statement of the
presence ("my true, essential body"), and the Didache's figure of
the grains and grapes. After it come the open confession, one of three absolutions, and the Our
Father sung by the church ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)). **Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1536**
(Sehling 16, pp. 107–108):

<!-- doc 651 -->

Dearly beloved in Christ Jesus, forasmuch as we will now celebrate and keep the gracious Supper
of our dearest Saviour, wherein he hath given us his true body for a meat and his own blood for
a drink, therewith to strengthen faith, we ought rightly with great diligence and fervent
devotion to examine ourselves, as Saint Paul exhorteth; for forasmuch as poor feeble consciences
may be comforted and strengthened, by means of the Holy Ghost, as well through the gracious
sacraments, which are called by Saint Augustine visible words, as through the word, so far as it
entereth in, therefore the gracious Supper is given for a special comfort and strength to
troubled spirits and broken hearts, which confess their sins, fear and feel God's strict wrath
and dreadful death, and are hungry after righteousness. But when we examine ourselves, and every
one shall go into his own conscience, as the holy apostle here teacheth us, we shall surely find
nothing else than all manner of great and perilous sin, and terrible death, which we have
deserved with sin, and yet can in no wise help ourselves out thereof. Therefore hath our dear
Lord Jesus Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sins' sake is become man, that he might fulfil
the law and all the will of God for us, and take upon himself and suffer death, and also all
that we had deserved with our sin, for us unto eternal redemption. And that we might steadfastly
believe this, and through faith live joyfully and gladly in his will, he took after the supper
the bread, gave thanks, brake it, and said: Take and eat, this is my body, which is given for
you; (that is) that I am become man, and all that I do and suffer, is all your own, done for you
and for your good; for a sure sign, seal and witness thereof I give you here with the bread my
true, essential body. Likewise he took also the cup and said: Take and drink ye all thereof,
this is the cup of the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the
forgiveness of sins; as oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby; that is, forasmuch as I
have taken your cause upon me and laden your sins upon myself, I will offer myself unto death
for sin, shed my blood, obtain grace and forgiveness of sins, and so set up a new, everlasting
testament, wherein sins are forgiven and shall never more be remembered for ever. For a sure
pledge and everlasting witness thereof I give you my own essential and true blood to drink.
Whosoever now eateth thus of this bread and drinketh of this cup, and firmly believeth these
words which he here heareth from Christ and these signs which he receiveth from Christ, he
dwelleth in the Lord Christ and Christ in him, and shall live for ever. Hereby shall we now
remember him and show forth his death, namely that he died for our sins and rose again for our
justification, and give him thanks therefor, every one take up his cross and follow him, and
according to his commandment love one another, as he hath loved us; for we are all one bread and
one body, forasmuch as we are all partakers of one bread and drink of one cup. For in like
manner as out of many grapes pressed together one wine and one drink floweth and is mingled
together, and out of many grains one meal is ground, and one bread and cake is baked, so shall
we all, that are incorporated into Christ by faith, through brotherly love, for the sake of
Christ our dearest Saviour, who first loved us so highly, become all one body, drink, cake and
bread, and show the same faithfully one toward another, not only with empty words that come not
from the heart, but in deeds and in truth, as John teacheth, without all guile, Amen.

**The revision of 1553.** The Württemberg order of 1553 revised the text, and nearly every later
witness follows the revision. It moves the text back toward Brandenburg-Nürnberg in some places
and adds Johannine clauses in others:
- **Dropped:** the Augustine clause ("forasmuch as the poor, weak consciences … may be comforted and strengthened"); "essential" and "own, essential and true" with the body
  and blood; "seal"; "severe" and "cruel"; "and kindly".
- **Restored from Brandenburg-Nürnberg:** "this holy Sacrament is given for a special comfort and strength to poor troubled consciences"; "for us and for our good"; "for our deliverance".
- **Added:**
  - "that feel their sins in the heart and confess them";
  - "for the wages of sin is death, as Paul saith" (Rom 6:23);
  - with the bread: "and that ye may always abide and live in me and I in you" (John 6:56);
  - with the cup: "and for the strength and furtherance of my life in you";
  - "and receiveth this Sacrament for the remembrance and confirmation of his faith", replacing
    "these word-signs which he receiveth of Christ";
  - "say to him everlasting praise and thanks therefor";
  - the closing doxology "The almighty, merciful God and Father of our dear Lord Jesus Christ help us thereto through his Holy Ghost, Amen".
- **Changed:** "paid" for "suffered"; "in the Supper"
  for "after the Supper"; "in deed and truth" for "by works and truth".
- **The editions of 1555 and after** (and Mömpelgard 1560, 1571) restore after "one bread and one body" the clause "forasmuch as we are all partakers of one bread and drink of one cup" (Sehling 16, p. 253, apparatus). All the later witnesses have it.

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Worms, *Agendbüchlein*, 1560 | 19/1, pp. 176–177 | The **1536** text, but without the Augustine clause and without "essential"; "Ye dearly beloved in God"; "with right devotion" for "more fervently"; "troubled and grieved hearts"; ends at "are partakers of one bread and drink of one cup", without the grains and grapes, and goes straight to the open confession |
| Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553 | 16, pp. 252–253 | The revision |
| Kurpfalz, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556 | 14, pp. 148–149 | 1553 text; drops "faithfully" at the end |
| Leiningen-Westerburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566 | 19/1, pp. 251–252 | 1553 text; "find nothing else"; "thank" for "give thanks" |
| Lindau, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573 | 12, p. 208 | 1553 text; "remember him"; "betrug" for "trug". Luther's paraphrase follows at the altar ([§3.5.3](#s3-5-3)). |
| Hanau-Lichtenberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573 | 20/2, pp. 64–65 | 1553 text; "for our sake" for "for our sins' sake" |
| Nassau-Weilburg, *Agende*, 1618 | 10, p. 275, apparatus | 1553 text recast for the **communion of the sick**: "Dear friend in Christ, forasmuch as ye desire at this time to receive the gracious Supper … ye should rightly … examine … yourself"; the cross and love of neighbour in the second person ("Ye shall also take your cross upon you with patience") |
| Ysenburg-Ronneburg, *Agende*, 1582 | 10, pp. 579–580 | 1553 text, shortened at the end: after "not only with words but in deed and truth" it closes with "forasmuch as we are all partakers of one bread", without the grains and grapes |
| Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598 | 20/1, pp. 611–612 | 1553 text; drops "a drink floweth and mingleth together" |
| Isny, *Agende*, c. 1600 | 17/1, pp. 459–460 | 1553 text; a later hand notes "see the Ulm church order" |
| Solms-Laubach, *Kirchenzuchtordnung*, 1603 | 9, pp. 361–362 | 1553 text with scriptural glosses added: "as he himself saith in the sixth chapter of John"; "as Saint Paul saith, 1 Corinth. 10"; "his neighbour" for "one another" |
| Wild- und Rheingrafschaft, *Kirchenordnung*, 1603 | 19/2, pp. 618–619 | 1553 text, taken by way of Kurpfalz 1556 (editor's note) |
| Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1610 | 16, p. 620 | Incipit only, followed by "the exhortation to public confession" |

**What the revision means.** The 1553 reviser removed both the Augustinian language of signs and
seals ("visible words", "word-signs", "seal") and the strongest realist word
("essential body"). In their place came the Johannine clauses of mutual indwelling and the
Sacrament received "for the remembrance and confirmation of his faith". The orders that took the
text over did not change it on either point.
#### <a id="s3-5-7"></a>3.5.7 The Bugenhagen family: Brunswick, 1528

**The archetype.** Bugenhagen's exhortation is read at the altar to the communicants, after the
pulpit exhortation with its Creed, confession and general prayer ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)). **Brunswick,
*Christlike ordeninge* of Johannes Bugenhagen, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, pp. 443–444):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

Exhortation or admonition before the altar concerning the sacrament, to the communicants. My
dearly beloved, it is continually set before us by the preaching of the Gospel of Christ that we
of ourselves are ignorant, poor and lost sinners. And forasmuch as we of ourselves are no more
than flesh and blood, therefore we can by no understanding or power of ours loose ourselves out
of the strict judgment of God and from the power of the devil, wherein we are fallen through the
transgression of the commandments and of the will of God. So God hath known our impotence better
than we, and hath given for us, as a gracious Father, his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, that
we might be enlightened through his Gospel, and redeemed from our sins through his death, and
through him be children of God, eternally saved, if we believed it. This he letteth be preached
to us continually: whoso believeth it, he hath surely eternal life; upon such faith and unto
such salvation are we also baptized; therein shall we abide continually; so abide we in Christ
and Christ in us. So eat we continually without ceasing, spiritually with faith, the body of
Christ and drink his blood; that is, we are incorporated into Christ, that we become one with
him, in that we believe that he hath given his body into death for us and shed his blood for us
on the cross; thereupon we rely for salvation against all false teaching, all sin, temptation
and need. Out of which benefit of Christ we also learn what love and patience we shall exercise
toward our neighbour, yea, toward our enemy. What would we more? Yet that we might not forget
nor grow slack (as, alas, we do) in such faith in the incarnation and death of Christ, he hath
also commanded us a special remembrance or showing forth of his death, as oft as we will, that
we shall also in the outward sacrament, hidden from reason, known to faith alone out of the word
of Christ, eat and drink his body and blood; that we may in no wise doubt that his death and
shedding of blood on the cross is our sure salvation; thereof shall we sing, read, preach, hear,
as we do in the Mass, and afterward also speak thereof and show it forth among one another, for
our comfort and for the salvation of many, according to the command of Christ: This do in
remembrance of me. Whoso now will worthily eat and drink this sacrament, he shall do two things:
he shall believe what Christ saith, and do what he commandeth. He saith: This is my body, which
is given for you. This is my blood, which is shed for you for the forgiveness of sins. That
shall ye believe. But he commandeth: Take and eat. Drink ye all thereout, and remember me. That
shall ye do according to his gracious word and command. Amen.

**Note.**
- **"two things"**, believing and doing, is the whole doctrine of worthy reception.
- **Two kinds of eating.** "so eat we continually … spiritually with faith" is the spiritual eating of John 6. The Sacrament is given in addition,
  "in the outward sacrament", so that we "may in no wise doubt".

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1529 | 5, pp. 530–531 | Low German, verbatim but for spelling |
| Lübeck, *Kirchenordnung*, 1531 | 5, p. 530, apparatus | As Hamburg (variants in the Hamburg apparatus) |
| Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Christlike kerken-ordeninge*, 1543 | 6/1, pp. 55–56 | Low German; "through the transgression of the commandments" (dropping "and of the will of God"); "and also speak thereof among ourselves and to our children and household"; also offers Luther's paraphrase |
| Osnabrück, city and diocese, 1543 | 7/1, pp. 224, 258 | Incipit only, "My dearly beloved etc.", read after the Sanctus |
| Frankfurt, *Agende* for baptism and the communion of the sick, 1543 | 9, pp. 517–518 | A free High German paraphrase for the sick, "Ye most beloved in Christ our Lord! God causeth it to be preached to us continually through his holy word …" |
| Hildesheim, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544 | 7/2.1, p. 854 | Incipit, with the editor's reference to Wolfenbüttel |
| Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552 | 7/1, p. 75 | Incipit "My dearly beloved in Christ, by the preaching of the Gospel it is continually …" |
| Hadeln, *Kirchenordnung* "of 1526" | 5, p. 468 | Incipit only, "My dearly beloved etc.", read by the priest to the communicants after the sermon, before the Preface |
| Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556 | 5, p. 562 | Incipit "My dearly beloved, it is continually set before us by the preaching of the Gospel etc." |
| Hildesheim (Steuerwald and Peine), *Kirchenordnung*, 1561 | 7/2.1, p. 782 | Incipit, "Pomeranus's exhortation, set down in the Brunswick church order" |
| Lüneburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1564 | 6/1, pp. 547–548 | **High German translation**, "Another exhortation" after the Osiander text ([§3.5.4](#s3-5-4)) |
| Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1569 | 6/1, p. 147 | High German, as Lüneburg |
| Lippe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571 | 21, p. 413 | High German, as Lüneburg, but skipping by homoeoteleuton from "judgement of God" to "so hath God" |
| Lippe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571, communion of the sick | 21, pp. 428–429 | High German, ascribed to "D. Mart. Lutheri" (Dr. Martin Luther's); "of the holy Gospel … set forth"; drops "also toward our enemies"; "external" for "outward" |
| Verden, *Kirchenordnung*, 1606 | 7/1, p. 159 | High German, as Lüneburg |
| Osnabrück (city), *Kirchenordnung*, 1613 | 7/1, p. 269 | High German, **abridged and recast** (below) |

**The High German recension.** Lüneburg 1564 translates the Low German text closely: "My dearly beloved, it is continually set before us by the preaching of the gospel of Christ, that we of ourselves are ignorant, poor sinners and lost …" (Sehling 6/1, p. 547).
Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel 1569, Lippe 1571 and Verden 1606 copy the Lüneburg translation, not
the Low German.

**Osnabrück 1613: the abridgement.** The Osnabrück order of 1613 cuts the exhortation to half
its length. It drops the passage on spiritual eating ("So eat we continually without ceasing, spiritually …") and replaces the account of sacramental eating with a statement of oral reception.
**Osnabrück (city), *Kirchenordnung*, 1613** (Sehling 7/1, p. 269):

<!-- doc 2100 -->

My dearly beloved, forasmuch as we of ourselves are nothing but flesh and blood, and cannot
loose ourselves out of the strict judgment of God, into which we are fallen, God as a gracious
Father hath given for us his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, that through his death we might be
redeemed from eternal death and so through him become children of God, eternally saved, if we
believe on him. Upon such faith and unto such salvation are we baptized; thereof also is
continually preached unto us. And that we may not forget nor grow slack in faith, love and
patience, as, alas, we often do, he hath commanded a special remembrance and showing forth of
his death: that in the outward sacrament, at Christ's command, we should eat with our bodily
mouth, by means of the blessed bread, in a high mystery hidden from reason, the body of our Lord
Jesus Christ, which he hath given into death for us, and drink out of the blessed cup his blood,
which he hath shed for us; and should sing, read, preach and hear of his death and shedding of
blood, according to the command of Christ: This do in remembrance of me.

The ending, "Whoso now will eat and drink this sacrament worthily, he shall do two things …",
follows Bugenhagen's text. Sehling's editor: "It is in essence Bugenhagen's exhortation … but here it is more tightly summarized and shortened".

**What the family shows.** Bugenhagen's text was transmitted in two languages, but the High
German form is a single translation, made once (Lüneburg 1564) and copied. Only Osnabrück 1613
rewrote its doctrine, replacing the spiritual eating of John 6 with the oral eating "with our bodily mouth by means of the blessed bread".
#### <a id="s3-5-8"></a>3.5.8 The Naumburg family, 1537

**The archetype.** The order for St. Wenzel's at Naumburg has a short exhortation of its own,
read while the choir sings and the communicants gather in the choir, and followed by the German
Sanctus. **Naumburg, *Kirchen-Ordnung* for St. Wenzel's, 1537** (Sehling 2, p. 80):

<!-- doc 1219 -->

And while the whole choir thus singeth, the communicants shall gather in the choir, and then the
priest shall make an exhortation to them, as followeth. Dear friends, forasmuch as ye are now
gathered to keep and receive the testament of our dear Lord Jesus Christ, I admonish you that ye
would take good heed of the precious gifts and graces which our dear Lord Jesus Christ hath
bequeathed and given us herein, consider them with high diligence and give him thanks therefor;
and that every one would examine himself herein, that he may worthily eat and drink of the bread
and cup, which is the Lord's body and blood, so that he may know that this is given him by the
Lord for the forgiveness of his sins and for the comfort and strength of his faith; and that
thereafter he would go forth and, to the praise and thanks of Christ our dear Lord and God,
serve his neighbour in true love and faithfulness according to all his power, even as Christ
hath served us herewith, in that he hath redeemed us from eternal death by his holy, bitter
passion and death, and made us children of eternal life. Upon this exhortation the whole choir
singeth the Sanctus.

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Nördlingen, *Kirchenordnung* of Kaspar Löner, 1544 | 12, p. 312 | Prescribes "a short exhortation" to the communicants, followed by the German Sanctus, as at Naumburg, but does not print it. The editor of Nördlingen 1579 takes it to be the Naumburg text, "brought to Nördlingen already by Löner". |
| Nördlingen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1579 | 12, pp. 369–370 | Full (below) |

**Nördlingen 1579.** The text is read "before the altar on which the Supper is distributed", after the Our Father. Sehling's editor:
"Not from Württemberg 1553, where the Nürnberg exhortation is given, but from the Naumburg church order". Its changes:
- **The address** "Beloved in Christ Jesus!" for "Lieben freunde" (Dear friends).
- **"the Lord's body and blood"** in parentheses, and "that he may become worthy".
- **"redeemed from sins and eternal death"**.
- **A transition to the Verba**, sung in German after it: "But how Christ kept his Supper, and what he hath commanded us to believe and to do therein, ye shall further learn from the following words" (Sehling 12, p. 370).
#### <a id="s3-5-9"></a>3.5.9 The Mecklenburg family, 1552

**The archetype.** The Mecklenburg order makes the exhortation a short summary of repentance and
faith, with a conditional, indicative absolution, a call to thanksgiving and intercession, and a
long prayer in the first person singular for each communicant to make his own. It is read after
the Preface and Sanctus, "if there is time". **Mecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*,
1552** (Sehling 5, pp. 202–204):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

Exhortation: absolution, thanksgiving and prayer before the communion. Dear friends, ye that as
Christian men have been instructed beforehand concerning God, concerning God's earnest will and
law, concerning the creation of man's nature, and thereafter concerning our sin, and concerning
the redemption through the Saviour Jesus Christ, and concerning all the articles of the faith,
and truly believe the same, appear here and come to this high comfort which the Lord Christ
giveth us in the eating of his body and blood. Now ye know the oath of the almighty, eternal
God, wherein he saith: As I live, I will not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted
and have life. This oath God hath confirmed with the blood, death and resurrection of his
only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, and both are comprehended therein, conversion and forgiveness of
sins. God hath sworn that it is his will that we shall not remain in sins against conscience,
but shall turn to him, be terrified before his righteous wrath, and have hearty sorrow for our
disobedience and our unthankfulness and dreadful contempt toward him. Whoso now bringeth such a
heart (as God himself saith, he will dwell in the broken hearts and in them that fear his word),
the same shall consider, desire and receive the great grace which is given us for the Lord
Christ's sake, and shall firmly believe that all sins are forgiven them for the Lord Christ's
sake, of grace, without our merit, if they receive this comfort with faith and trust in the Lord
Christ; and shall not remain stuck in doubt, but truly conclude that they so receive forgiveness
of sins, and are pleasing to God and heirs of eternal blessedness, and that the Lord Christ will
surely give them his Holy Ghost, and that God will graciously dwell in them, govern and preserve
them unto eternal blessedness; and they shall so henceforth be in obedience to him in faith and
good conscience. All this ye shall consider daily, and especially when ye come to the eating of
the body and blood of our Lord Christ; there our Lord Christ putteth us in mind of both, namely
that God's wrath against our sin is so great that he could not be reconciled otherwise than only
by the obedience and death of his dearest Son, and also that he surely receiveth graciously all
that are converted and trust in the Son. And for a sure witness of this his unchangeable will
the Lord Christ hath instituted this ordinance, that with these outward visible things he surely
giveth us his true body and blood, and confirmeth herewith his promise that our sins are surely
forgiven us for the sake of his passion, and that he will truly be with us and work in us, as he
saith: I am in them, and I give them eternal life. Therefore unto all that so appear here, that
turn to God, and are terrified before God's wrath against their sin, and believe that their sins
are forgiven them for the Lord Christ's sake, and have the purpose to leave off sins against
conscience, unto them I declare forgiveness of sins, according to the words of Christ, Whose
soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; therefore by the command of the Lord Christ I
speak unto you this absolution, that your sins are forgiven you for the Lord Christ's sake; and
this voice of the Gospel ye shall receive, and have true comfort in the Lord Christ, and
henceforth be obedient to God in faith and good conscience. And for a witness that this grace is
given and applied to you yourselves, ye shall receive the body and the blood of the Lord Jesus
Christ, and know that the Lord Christ hath been a sacrifice for you on the cross, and hath given
his body for you and shed his blood for you, and that the Lord Christ maketh you his members and
will be mighty in you. Here ye shall also give thanks to the almighty God, the Father of our
Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Lord Jesus Christ, for such great graces, and have comfort and joy
in the Lord Christ, for he will be with you, govern and preserve you; ye shall also here make
your hearty prayer for the common Church and government, for yourselves and for your little
children. Almighty, true God, eternal and only Father of our Saviour Jesus Christ, together with
thine only Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost, Creator of all creatures, who art wise, true,
good, just, chaste and a judge, and art wroth against sin: I confess that I, alas, have much sin
in me, and have moreover done much sin, knowingly and unknowingly, and it is heartily grievous
unto me that I have angered thee, the true God; and I pray thee that thou wouldest forgive me
all my sins through thy great mercy, for the sake of thy dearest Son Jesus Christ, be gracious
unto me, and make me righteous and well-pleasing unto thee for the Lord Christ's sake and
through him, and enlighten, cleanse and govern me with thy Holy Ghost. I believe also thy holy
Gospel and thy gracious promise, wherein thou promisest us forgiveness of sins, righteousness
and eternal life for the sake of thy dear Son Jesus Christ, and I pray thee that thou wouldest
strengthen my heart in faith and in the knowledge of thy dear Son. I thank thee also, almighty
God, for all benefits, and especially that thou hast graciously revealed thyself to us, and hast
ordained thy dear Son to be mediator and propitiator for us, and through him hast rescued us
from eternal wrath and received us again unto eternal blessedness. And I pray thee that for thy
Son Jesus Christ's sake thou wouldest be gracious unto us poor, wretched, weak men, and gather
unto thyself evermore among us an eternal Church, and preserve these lands and this government,
and give us peace and blessed rule, and graciously govern and keep me and my poor little
children, amen. I thank thee also, almighty only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, that out of
great love toward the poor human creature thou hast prayed for us, and hast taken human nature
upon thee, that men might not be wholly cast away for ever, but through thee be rescued again
from sins and brought to eternal righteousness and eternal life; and hast turned the great,
unspeakable wrath of the divine majesty against our sins from us weak men upon thyself, in all
thy obedience, passion and death, and art risen again from death, and abidest mediator and
intercessor for us, and gatherest unto thyself an eternal Church through thy Gospel and Holy
Ghost, and art Emmanuel, that is, God with us, givest eternal blessedness to all that are
converted to thee and believe that God is gracious to them for the sake of thy passion and thy
intercession, and wilt surely preserve these poor weak men in thy Church. I pray thee with
hearty sighs that thou wouldest be gracious unto me, and forgive all my sins, and pray thine
eternal Father for me, and give me thy Holy Ghost, govern and preserve me against thine enemies,
namely against the blasphemous, lying, unclean devils. And mayest thou, almighty Son of God,
Jesus Christ, who didst die on the cross and on the third day didst rise again alive, and art
just, true, chaste and merciful, gather unto thyself evermore among us an eternal Church, and
preserve this land and this government, and give us peace and blessed rule, and graciously
govern and keep me and my poor little children, amen.

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Pfalz-Zweibrücken, *Kirchenordnung*, 1557 | 18, pp. 189–190 | Verbatim, under the same heading. The Zweibrücken hymnal of 1571/1587 prints the section for the people and introduces the prayer with "if one can have it in the time, one may also add the following prayer". |
| Nassau-Weilburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1576 | 10, pp. 264–266 | Verbatim in 1576; replaced in the *Agende* of 1618 (below) |
| Sayn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1590 | 19/1, pp. 406–408 | Taken from Pfalz-Zweibrücken (editor's note); a second "Christian" added to "Christian men"; ends after the call to thanksgiving, with the rubric for the Our Father and Verba in place of the prayer |
| Pfalz-Veldenz, *Kirchenordnung*, 1574 | 18, p. 501 | The prayer only, turned into the first person plural ("We confess indeed, Lord, that we have many sins upon us, are by nature sinful and unclean …"), after Pfalz-Veldenz's own exhortation ([§3.5.11](#s3-5-11)) |

**Nassau-Weilburg 1618: the abridged recension.** The Nassau-Weilburg *Agende* of 1618 replaces
the text with a shorter form. It is addressed to those "who announced yourselves yesterday", recalls "the exhortation made to you yesterday", and keeps the conditional absolution. It then adds a
passage on the Words of Institution and ends with the *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts). **Nassau-Weilburg,
*Agende*, 1618, from Sehling's apparatus to the order of 1576** (Sehling 10, p. 264):

<!-- doc 198 -->

That ye lay hold of these words with right, true faith and doubt not, but firmly believe: as
surely as the Son of God, according to his own promise, feedeth you in the Supper and giveth you
to drink with his own body and blood, so surely and truly doth he also deliver to you and to
every one in particular all the spiritual benefits which he hath merited and obtained for his
dear Christendom by the offering of his body and the shedding of his precious blood, such as
forgiveness of sins, the righteousness that availeth before God, and after this life the
eternal, blessed life. Lastly ye shall also here make your prayer to God for the need of all
Christendom, for your dear government, for yourselves and for your little children. Lift up
therefore your hearts unto God, our Lord, for it is meet and right, and also wholesome, that we
should in all places and at all times call upon our heavenly Father and holy God through Jesus
Christ, our Saviour.
#### <a id="s3-5-10"></a>3.5.10 The Palatinate family, 1563

**The archetype.** The Reformed Palatinate order of Elector Frederick III (1563) has the longest
exhortation in the corpus. It is read "at the table" after the sermon and the
Sunday prayer. It follows Geneva 1563 (Reformed) almost word for word at the beginning, and
draws on London 1565 (à Lasco and Micron, Reformed) for the threefold examination and the
fencing of the table, and on Kurpfalz 1556 (the Württemberg text) for the grains and grapes.
**Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1563** (Reformed; Sehling 14, pp. 383–386):

<!-- doc 504 -->

Ye beloved in the Lord Jesus Christ, hear the words of the institution of the holy Supper of our
Lord Jesus Christ, which the holy apostle Paul describeth to us in the first epistle to the
Corinthians, in the eleventh chapter [1 Corinthians 11:23–29]: I have received of the Lord that which I delivered unto
you. For the Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, gave thanks, brake
it and said: Take, eat, this is my body, which is broken for you. This do in remembrance of me.
After the same manner also the cup after the supper, and said: This cup is the new testament in
my blood. This do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as ye eat this
bread and drink this cup, ye shall show the Lord's death till he come. Whosoever now shall eat
this bread unworthily or drink of the cup of the Lord, he is guilty of the body and blood of the
Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of this bread and drink of this cup. For
he that eateth and drinketh unworthily eateth and drinketh judgment to himself, in that he
discerneth not the Lord's body. That we may now keep the Lord's Supper to our comfort, it is
needful for us above all things, first, that we rightly examine ourselves beforehand; secondly,
that we direct it to that end for which the Lord Christ ordained it, namely to his remembrance.
The true examination of ourselves standeth in these three parts. First, let every one consider
by himself his sin and curse, that he may be displeased with himself and humble himself before
God, forasmuch as the wrath of God against sin is so great that, rather than let it go
unpunished, he hath punished it in his dear Son Jesus Christ with the bitter and shameful death
of the cross. Secondly, let every one search his heart whether he also believe this sure promise
of God, that all his sins are forgiven him only for the sake of the passion and death of Jesus
Christ, and that the perfect righteousness of Christ is imputed and given him as his own, as if
he himself in his own person had paid for all his sins and fulfilled all righteousness. Thirdly,
let every one search his conscience whether he be also minded henceforth to show himself
thankful to God the Lord with his whole life and to walk uprightly before the face of God;
whether he also renounce from the heart, without all hypocrisy, all enmity, envy and hatred, and
have an earnest purpose hereafter to live in true love and unity with his neighbour. They now
that are so minded, them God will surely receive into grace and acknowledge for worthy
table-companions of his Son Jesus Christ. But on the other hand, they that feel not this witness
in their heart eat and drink judgment to themselves. Therefore we also, according to the command
of Christ and of the apostle Paul, warn away from the table of the Lord all that know themselves
laden with the following vices, and declare unto them that they have no part in the kingdom of
Christ: as are all idolaters; all that call upon departed saints, angels or other creatures,
that worship images; all sorcerers and soothsayers, that bless cattle and people and other
things, and they that give credence to such blessing; all despisers of God and of his word and
of the holy sacraments; all blasphemers; all that seek to make division and mutiny in the Church
and in the temporal government; all perjurers; all that are disobedient to their parents and
rulers; all manslayers, brawlers, quarrellers, that live in envy and hatred against their
neighbour; all adulterers, whoremongers, drunkards, thieves, usurers, robbers, gamblers,
covetous, and all they that lead an offensive life. All these, so long as they persevere in such
vices, shall take heed and abstain from this meat, which Christ hath ordained for his faithful
alone, lest their judgment and damnation be the heavier. But this is not set before us, dear
Christians, to make the broken hearts of the faithful faint-hearted, as though none might go to
the Supper of the Lord but they that were without all sin. For we come not to this Supper to
bear witness thereby that we are perfect and righteous in ourselves, but on the contrary,
because we seek our life outside ourselves in Jesus Christ, we confess that we lie in the midst
of death. Therefore, although we yet find much infirmity and misery in us, as namely that we
have not a perfect faith, that we do not give ourselves to serve God with such zeal as we are
bound to do, but have daily to strive with the weakness of our faith and the evil lusts of our
flesh; nevertheless, since by the grace of the Holy Ghost such infirmities are grievous to us
from the heart, and we heartily desire to resist our unbelief and to live according to all the
commandments of God, we shall be sure and certain that no sin nor infirmity which yet remaineth
in us against our will can hinder God from receiving us into grace and so making us worthy
partakers of this heavenly meat and drink. Secondly, let us now also consider to what end the
Lord hath instituted his Supper for us, namely that we do it in remembrance of him. And we shall
remember him herein thus: first, that we wholly trust in our heart that our Lord Jesus Christ,
according to the promises which were made to the patriarchs from the beginning, was sent by the
Father into this world, took our flesh and blood upon him, bore for us the wrath of God, under
which we should have sunk for ever, from the beginning of his incarnation to the end of his life
on earth, and fulfilled for us all obedience to the divine law and righteousness; chiefly when
the burden of our sins and of the wrath of God pressed out from him the bloody sweat in the
garden; when he was bound, that he might loose us; then suffered countless reproach, that we
might never be put to shame; was condemned to death innocent, that we might be acquitted before
the judgment seat of God; yea, let his blessed body be nailed to the cross, that he might nail
thereto the handwriting of our sins, and so took the curse upon himself from us, that he might
fill us with his blessing; and humbled himself to the very deepest shame and hellish anguish of
body and soul on the tree of the cross, when he cried with a loud voice: My God, my God, why
hast thou forsaken me [Matthew 27:46], that we might be taken to God and never be forsaken of him; and finally
by his death and shedding of blood sealed the new and everlasting testament, the covenant of
grace and reconciliation, as he said: It is finished [John 19:30]. But that we might firmly believe that we
belong to this covenant of grace, the Lord Jesus in his last Supper took the bread, gave thanks,
brake it, gave it to his disciples and said: Take and eat, this is my body, which is given for
you; this do in remembrance of me. Likewise after the supper he took the cup, gave thanks and
said: Take and drink ye all of it; this cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for
you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. This do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of
me. That is, as oft as ye eat of this bread and drink of this cup, ye shall thereby, as by a
sure memorial and pledge, be reminded and assured of this my hearty love and faithfulness toward
you: that for you, who must otherwise have died the eternal death, I give my body unto death on
the tree of the cross and shed my blood, and feed and give drink to your hungry and thirsty
souls with the same my crucified body and shed blood unto eternal life, as surely as this bread
is broken before the eyes of every one and this cup is given him, and ye eat and drink them with
your mouth in remembrance of me. From this institution of the holy Supper of our Lord Jesus
Christ we see that he directeth our faith and trust to his perfect sacrifice, once made on the
cross, as to the only ground and foundation of our salvation, in that he is become the true meat
and drink of eternal life to our hungry and thirsty souls. For by his death he hath taken away
the cause of our eternal hunger and misery, namely sin, and hath obtained for us the quickening
Spirit, that through the same Spirit, which dwelleth in Christ as the head and in us as his
members, we might have true fellowship with him and become partakers of all his goods, of
eternal life, righteousness and glory. Moreover, that through the same Spirit we might also be
bound together one with another, as members of one body, in true brotherly love, as the holy
apostle saith: It is one bread, so are we, being many, one body, forasmuch as we are all
partakers of one bread [1 Corinthians 10:17]. For as out of many grains one meal is ground and one bread baked, and
out of many grapes pressed together one wine and drink floweth and is mingled together, so shall
we all, that are incorporated into Christ by true faith, through brotherly love, for the sake of
Christ our dear Saviour, who first loved us so highly, be all together one body, and show the
same one toward another not only with words but in deed. The almighty, merciful God and Father
of our Lord Jesus Christ help us thereto through his Holy Ghost, Amen.

**What follows.** A prayer for the right use of the Supper ("Merciful God and Father, we pray thee that in this Supper … thou wouldest work in our hearts through thy Holy Ghost …"), the Our Father and the Apostles' Creed, and then the call to lift up the heart: "let us not cleave with our hearts to the outward bread and wine, but lift up our hearts and faith on high into heaven, where Christ Jesus is" (Sehling 14, p. 386). It is the Reformed form of the *Sursum
corda*.

**The witnesses.**

| Order | Sehling | Form and significant variants |
|---|---|---|
| Moers, *Kirchenordnung*, 1581 (Reformed) | 22, pp. 197–199 | Lower Rhine recension (below); the manuscript is supplemented by the editor from the Palatinate print where it has gaps |
| Bentheim-Tecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1588/1619 (Reformed) | 22, pp. 271–274 | Lower Rhine recension; drops "and those that put faith in such charms" from the list of the excluded |
| Ysenburg-Birstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598 (Reformed) | 10, pp. 651–653 | Verbatim; the editor: the whole chapter, prayers included, "comes word for word from the Palatinate order of 1563" |
| Palatinate, *Kirchenordnung*, 1585 (later edition) (Reformed) | 14, p. 384, apparatus | Allows the passage marked off in the margin to be left out "as the cold of winter or other need requireth" |

**The Lower Rhine recension.** Moers and Bentheim (both Reformed) share a set of changes:
- **A new transition after the Pauline text**, which recalls the opening of Micron's exhortation
  (Reformed)
  ("Ye have heard, dear brethren, from this doctrine of the holy apostle Paul, who is the institutor of the Supper …", Sehling 7/1, p. 631).
  **Moers, *Kirchenordnung*, 1581** (Reformed; Sehling 22, p. 197):

<!-- doc 1502 -->

From this teaching of the holy apostle Paul ye hear, dear Christians, that our Lord and Saviour
Jesus Christ instituted and kept the holy Supper with his disciples, and that he hath commanded
us so to keep the same.

- **The first point of the examination expanded:** "his sin which he hath done against God and his holy law and against his neighbour, and then the curse and righteous wrath of God against sin".
- **The second point:** "all his sins, original as well as actual", forgiven "of grace".
- **The third point:** thankfulness "for his unspeakable grace and mercy, and especially for the gracious forgiveness of all our sins", "all the time of his life"; "all enmity, hatred, envy".
- **The excluded:** those that persevere in the vices "and purpose to continue therein".
- **The Spirit:** "hath obtained for us the quickening Spirit by his intercession" for "merited".
- **Moers** reads "grape-berries" for "berries".
#### <a id="s3-5-11"></a>3.5.11 The Pfalz-Veldenz family, 1574

**The archetype.** The Pfalz-Veldenz order has an exhortation of its own, read by the pastor
after the Sanctus ("Esaja, dem Propheten, das geschach") and before the communion. It closes
with a call to confession and prayer that leads into the Mecklenburg prayer, turned into the
plural ([§3.5.9](#s3-5-9)). **Pfalz-Veldenz, *Kirchenordnung*, 1574** (Sehling 18, pp. 500–501):

<!-- doc 1011 -->

Ye beloved in the Lord Christ. It is well known to you as Christians, out of God's word and
daily experience, that we were all together conceived and born in sins, and also still sin daily
and continually and transgress God's commandments, and that we are thereby subject to the heavy
wrath of God and to eternal damnation. Now out of so great a need we could be helped in no other
way than only by the bitter and most holy death and joyful resurrection of our Lord and Saviour
Jesus Christ, the eternal and only Son of God. He out of immeasurable love and compassion hath
laden the heavy burden of our sins upon himself, fastened it to the cross and buried it in the
earth, and so by the shedding of his precious, innocent blood hath paid for sin and redeemed
mankind from sins and eternal damnation. This his precious merit, and all that he hath obtained
and gained thereby, he giveth and bestoweth on us poor sinners freely, out of pure grace and
mercy; we are not worthy of it, neither can we merit it nor add anything thereto; only we should
heartily take it to ourselves, rejoice and comfort ourselves with firm faith and whole trust.
Whoso doeth that, he enjoyeth and is made partaker of the merit of Christ, is set free from sins
and death, and is an heir of eternal life. But forasmuch as it is very hard for human nature,
especially when a man knoweth not and feeleth not his sin, truly to believe this, that the
only-begotten Son of God suffered such a shameful, bitter death for us poor sinners, and that
the heavenly Father will forgive us all sins and give us eternal life only for his sake, out of
pure grace and mercy, therefore our faithful Saviour Christ Jesus hath not only richly promised
and pledged us such great grace in his holy word, but also confirmed and sealed it with outward,
visible signs, and especially instituted for this end this holy Sacrament of his body and blood,
that thereby our weak faith may be strengthened, our fainthearted consciences comforted, and
wholly assured of his promised grace. Since he himself is here present, and in the eating of
these outward, visible things, bread and wine, giveth us his true body and blood for meat and
drink, as sure pledges and seals, to assure us thereby that he hath as surely and truly given
his holy body for us and shed his innocent blood for our sins, and that our sins are surely
forgiven us for the sake of his passion and death; that he also will be with us, dwell and work
in us, and as living members of his body at last raise us from death and give us eternal life.
Such glorious, sweet comfort have we in this his holy Supper. Therefore, as oft as we feel that
we are weak and fainthearted in faith, sinful and frail in life, we shall betake ourselves to
this comfortable, heavenly table and Supper, that we may be made sure of our reconciliation with
God and of the forgiveness of our sins through the death of Christ, and so be strengthened and
comforted in faith in the Lord Christ. But that we may use and enjoy this Sacrament rightly and
worthily, to our comfort and the salvation of our souls, we must first examine ourselves
according to the teaching of the holy apostle Paul: and first acknowledge and confess our sins
before God with hearty pain, repentance and sorrow; then secondly firmly believe that our sins
are forgiven us only of pure grace for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake; and lastly have a true
purpose to forsake sins, to amend our life with God's help, and henceforth to walk in Christian
love. For our Lord God will not the death and destruction of the sinner; but therewith he
requireth also true conversion, as is declared in the precious oath which he hath sworn by the
prophet: As I live (saith God), I will not that the sinner die, but that he be converted and
have life. Therefore, my beloved, forasmuch as our dear Lord God hath pleasure in sinners that
humble themselves before him and turn to him, and the Lord Christ also inviteth and biddeth to
this his meal such guests as hunger and thirst after righteousness, let us also lift up our
hearts to God with earnestness, heartily lament and confess to him our misery and our frail and
sinful life, and in the name of his dearest Son, our only Redeemer Jesus Christ, pray for the
pardon of all our sins and misdeeds; heartily thank him also for his glorious graces and
benefits which he hath shown to us and to all Christendom in the same his beloved Son Jesus
Christ; and then further pray for the strengthening of faith, the amendment of our sinful life,
and all other need of all Christendom. Say therefore with me from your whole heart:

**What follows.** "confession and common prayer at the communion": the Mecklenburg prayer in the plural, "Almighty, merciful God, eternal and only Father of our Lord Jesus Christ … We confess indeed, Lord, that we have many sins upon us, are by nature sinful and unclean …" (Sehling 18, p. 501). The exhortation itself
draws on Mecklenburg 1552 for the oath of Ezekiel 33:11 and the call to conversion.

**The witness.** Lützelstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1605 (Sehling 18, pp. 603–604) copies the text;
the editor marks the section "from the Pfalz-Veldenz church order". It drops "truly to believe",
"richly promised" and "and biddeth", and ends "say therefore humbly with me".
#### <a id="s3-5-12"></a>3.5.12 The Basel family: Memmingen 1528 and Neckarbischofsheim 1560

**The archetype.** The Memmingen order of 1528 (Moderate Reformed) has an exhortation read
*after* communion. Sehling's editor notes that it is not in the Zürich order, which Memmingen
otherwise follows. Neckarbischofsheim 1560 has the same text, which its editor traces to
Oecolampadius's Basel order, *Form und gstalt* (Form and manner; Basel 1526, Reformed). **Memmingen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 12, p. 245):

<!-- doc 364 -->

After the eating, when every one hath eaten and drunk, followeth the exhortation hereafter
following. Dear brethren! Ye have heard the unspeakable mercy of God. The heavenly Father hath
given his only-begotten Son for us into the most shameful death. The shepherd hath died for the
sheep. The innocent hath suffered for the sinner, the head for the members. The high priest hath
offered himself up for us to the Father as a burning sacrifice, out of unspeakable love, and
with his blood hath sufficiently assured and sealed our covenant with God the Father. Therefore
let us keep the benefits in everlasting, fresh remembrance! His blood touch our heart! To him be
praise for evermore! Now henceforth we will not be our own, but the Lord's servants and the
servants of his servants. Now we will live to Christ and not to ourselves, and desire so to be
incorporated into him as the members that are redeemed by his blood and cleansed from sins.

**What follows at Memmingen.** The deacons say Ps 113 in alternation ("Praise the Lord, ye servants!"), and the leader then gives the second exhortation, which comes from Strasbourg
(Moderate Reformed; [§3.5.13](#s3-5-13)), ending with the Ten Commandments and the dismissal "Now go in the peace of God".

**The witness.** Neckarbischofsheim, *Kirchenordnung*, 1560 (Sehling 16, pp. 682–683). Its form:
- **Placement.** The pastor reads it at the altar *before* communion, as "the communicants' exhortation or reminder of the passion and death of Jesus Christ, with an appended exhortation".
- **The opening.** Before it stands Isaiah 53, introduced: "Beloved friends and chosen children of God, forasmuch as in the receiving of the holy Supper the chief point and the whole matter is to consider with hearty thanksgiving his bitter passion and death, hear and consider how the holy prophet Isaiah foresaw it in the spirit long ago".
- **The common text** follows with "Here ye hear openly, beloved children of God" for "Ye have heard"; "His blood sprinkle and touch our hearts" (Heb 10:22); "To him be praise, honour and glory for ever"; "thereto servant and minister of his servants".
- **An addition on the Supper**, leading to the Words of Institution. **Neckarbischofsheim,
  *Kirchenordnung*, 1560** (Sehling 16, p. 683):

<!-- doc 742 -->

Wherefore we also are mindful with thanksgiving of the benefits of his body and blood, which he
truly giveth us to enjoy in the power of faith in his word, figured in the bodily meat and drink
of the hallowed bread and wine of his Supper, which he himself instituted and ordained us to
keep in remembrance of his bitter passion and death.

#### <a id="s3-5-13"></a>3.5.13 The Strasbourg family, 1525

**The archetype.** The early Strasbourg agendas (Moderate Reformed) leave the exhortation to the
pastor, "on the content of the prayer and generally according to the matter of the sermon preached", and print
one as an example. It was given at St. Peter the Younger, Wolfgang Capito's church, on
Reminiscere Sunday, 12 March 1525, after a sermon on 1 Cor 1 (the word of the cross) and John 8
(Christ the light of the world). It is read after the Our Father and leads into the Words of
Institution. **Strasbourg, *Die frühen Agenden*, 1525**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, pp. 158–159):

<!-- doc 1279 -->

Dear brothers and sisters, ye will every one consider with himself with what hearty desire the
Lord Jesus did his suffering for us, and how great longing he had to eat the passover lamb with
his disciples before he suffered; and how he commanded that this his remembrance should be had
as oft as his Supper is kept, as the old Christians nearly did in their assemblies, and as we in
some measure show on the Sunday, in that some of you eat with me. And yet I hope that ye all
consider it in firm faith, and eat as fruitfully in the spirit as they that come forward; for
the outward eating would bring us much disorder and trouble if every one would also eat bodily
every time; for in all things we should not practise the outward deeds of the Lord, but the
chief part inwardly, which here is the remembrance of our redemption, which may well be with all
of you that stand about. Therefore I exhort you that ye let yourselves be taken by the word of
the cross, which to you that are saved is the power of God, as to the damned world it is
foolishness and to the pious hypocrites an offence. Receive Christ, the light of the world, and
walk no more henceforth in darkness, that is, after the manner of flesh and blood, which is full
of strife, quarrelling and discord. For if ye take upon you, and by your eating or presence
falsely pretend, faith in Christ and love toward your neighbour, and yet stood in grudge against
your brethren, know that ye lie to God the Holy Ghost, that ye are hypocrites, and that ye are
at the Lord's Supper unworthily, or eat to yourselves judgment and damnation. Let us pray God,
therefore, that he would uncover to us the hidden Adam in us, and show his salvation, which he
hath wrought through Christ Jesus.

**Note.** The exhortation assumes that only some will commune ("In that some of you eat with me"), and that the rest "eat in the spirit". It then turns to the
invitation: "Ye that will receive the Lord's Supper with me, and have announced yourselves, come now hither" (Sehling 20/1, p. 159).

**The witness.** Memmingen 1528 (Moderate Reformed) takes the second half, from "that ye let the word of the cross lay hold upon you", as the exhortation of the leader after Ps 113 and after
communion (Sehling 12, pp. 245–246). It reads "after the manner of the evil, poisoned nature of blood and flesh", turns the warning
into the past ("would have received the Lord's Supper unworthily"), and ends with a prayer that God lead us "out of ourselves and all creatures to his only-begotten Son",
followed by the Ten Commandments.
#### <a id="s3-5-14"></a>3.5.14 Exhortations outside the families

The exhortations below belong to none of the families in §[3.5.3](#s3-5-3)–[3.5.13](#s3-5-13). Four are printed in full;
the rest are summarized.

##### <a id="s3-5-14-1"></a>3.5.14.1 Kantz 1522 and the Bremen Mass 1525

Kantz's Nördlingen Mass of 1522 leaves the exhortation free: "an exhortation of the Sacrament, or else something comforting out of the holy Gospel, as the Spirit of God giveth him". It then gives only a short address to the bystanders, "Dearest in Christ! That ye may receive with joyful, desirous heart …", which leads at once into the
absolution. That address and absolution are printed in [Chapter 7](#ch7) [§7.2.1](#s7-2-1), and
summarized in [§3.3.5](#s3-3-5) here.

The Low German *Evangelische Misse* (Evangelical Mass) printed at Bremen in 1525 has the same rubric and a
translation of the same address. **Bremen, *Eyne evangelysce Misse*, 1525**
(Sehling 7/2.2, p. 405):

<!-- doc 2216 -->

First shall the priest, or another chosen thereto, make an exhortation of the Sacrament, or else
somewhat comforting out of the holy Gospel, and say what the Spirit of God giveth him. Therefore
shall he exhort the bystanders with these or the like words: Dearest in Christ, that ye may
receive with joyful and desirous hearts the precious treasure and the testament of the flesh and
blood of Christ Jesus, our Saviour, humble your hearts before God and confess to him your sins
and failings with hearty desire, striving after his godly grace and help. So will I now read you
the absolution.

**The differences.** Bremen has "the precious treasure and the testament of the flesh and blood" for Kantz's "the tender body and rose-coloured blood". It drops "your chosen priest", and it heads the priest's request for prayer "the priest's confession". The absolution keeps Kantz's indicative form ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

##### <a id="s3-5-14-2"></a>3.5.14.2 Augsburg, St. Anna, 1530

The order of the Supper (Moderate Reformed) "as it was kept by the ministers of the Gospel at St. Anna's" prints
two exhortations. The first, the longer, is a sermon on 1 Cor 11:28 in three heads: why Christ
died, the love of God in his death, and the example of love it leaves. **Augsburg, *Form und
ordnung des Herren nachtmal*, 1530** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 12, pp. 40–41):

<!-- doc 334 -->

Beloved! St. Paul exhorteth us, 1 Cor 11[:28], that we should first prove ourselves and then go
to God's table. Therefore shall your love first see wherein the proof standeth, that none eat
and drink the judgment. So must we now consider with earnestness what is done here, what is
here, and what shall be sought here. One shall first look at what Christ hath done and commanded
us to do, namely: we shall remember him and show forth his saving death till he come. Here is no
belly-meal, but a meat and drink unto a new life, wherein Christ will feed us with his true body
and give us to drink of his true blood, which are present here for his word's sake, as he fed
his disciples and gave them to drink in the first Supper; through which body and his blood he
hath bought us on the cross by his death from eternal death, purchased remission of sin, and set
up and confirmed the covenant of grace between God the Father and us, that through Christ and in
Christ we should become children of God, and God be our Father. Therefore we seek here no
earthly, perishable things, but eternal. We are sick and seek the medicine of life. We are
hungry and thirsty and seek the living bread that cometh from heaven: Jesus Christ, the well of
eternal life. Whoso trusteth in him shall be satisfied and have eternal life. That trust is,
that we shall not doubt that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, of the gracious will of his and our
heavenly Father, hath died for us poor sinners and hath reconciled us again to the heavenly
Father. That is the right Christian faith. Whoso looketh not for such from Christ, namely, that
he is our Saviour, who will and can help us out of all evil (for he is true God, and for our
sakes is made man), he were an unbeliever and eateth judgment to himself. Therefore we shall see
that here not the bodily but the spiritual hunger and thirst is to be stilled. So Christ now
commandeth us that we shall keep the Supper in remembrance of him, and Paul saith that we shall
show forth the Lord's death till he come. Here must we now take three things before us: first,
to see the cause why Christ died; secondly, to take to heart the love and grace of God in the
death of his only-begotten Son; thirdly, to consider how Christ hath not only redeemed us by his
death, but also left an example, whereby we learn what faithfulness and love every Christian
oweth to his fellow man. If we can now rightly call ourselves to mind in these three points, and
find ourselves ready thereto, or at the least desirous, that we would gladly walk in faith and
love, then the proof standeth whereof St. Paul speaketh [1 Cor 11:28].

First, mark that Christ died for our sins' sake. It must verily be no small cause, that God's
Son should himself come from heaven into this world and give himself into the despised death of
the cross. Hereby we mark the greatness and heaviness of our sin, which might not be atoned
unless such an infinite person took it upon himself, Isaiah 53[:4f.]. How terrible is the
judgment of God upon sin and sinners! How murderous is the harm of our sin, that the
only-begotten, dearest Son of God should become a curse and die, that we might be redeemed from
the eternal curse and death! Since then Christ himself dieth, that he may make satisfaction for
us and reconcile the Father again, and purchase the Spirit of God, whereby we are enlightened,
cleansed and made ready to be children of God, verily we should form in our heart the precious
death of Christ, this unmeasurable cost, and hate and flee the damned sin, which was a cause of
death to Christ, as hellish poison and death, and set ourselves to a penitent life. Here let
every one go into himself, whether he repent that he hath so often and so manifoldly sinned
against God, wherefore he is worthy of eternal damnation, and whether he desire by God's grace
to be rid of sins and to lead a Christian life! If not, he standeth ill.

Secondly, consider the great grace and love of God, who spared not his only-begotten Son, but
gave him into death for us. So loved he the world, that he sent his only-begotten into the
world, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Where hath such
love ever been heard of? While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us; while we were yet
enemies, we are reconciled to God by the death of his Son, Romans 5[:10]. If your great sin and
the righteous judgment of God have before terrified you, as is meet, so be comforted again! Our
sins lie no more upon us, if we believe, but upon the unspotted lamb of God. He hath atoned
them, abolished death, brought life again; and Christ is given us of the Father, that he may be
our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Of this we all have good need, since
we in ourselves were fools, unrighteous, unholy, poor, captive sinners of the evil enemy. Such
great things belong to us and become our own, if we doubt not of the love of God, that he hath
given us his Son Jesus Christ, that we may live through him. Not that we loved him before; but
he loved us first, and so sent his Son to be a reconciler for our sin, 1 John 4[:9]. There ye
hear such things in the Supper, how Christ hath given his body and blood for us. If we believe
these words, we overcome sin, death, hell, receive peace, joy and assurance of conscience, so
that we become thankful, to do and to suffer willingly for such goodness what Christ layeth upon
us. For this sacrament is also called *eucharistia*, that we thereby should praise and extol
God's mercy and give thanks for his unspeakable love. Where we always remember his death, and
therein his fatherly faithfulness, we become humble and thankful, grow in trust toward God
through Christ, become heedful, and order ourselves to a new life, which then shall and must be,
or we shall be called titular Christians only.

Thirdly, the Supper putteth us in mind of Christian love and unity; for if Christ hath died for
us, it is a token that we have fellowship in his passion and death; and as the head hath
suffered death for his members and laid the highest love upon them, we also shall not despise
one another; for we are children of God through the merit of Christ, among whom such great goods
are dealt out; and this love of Christ shall be an example to us, that we be so minded one
toward another as Christ toward us, namely, that one serve another with all that he is and hath,
as in the natural body one member serveth another. Ill will, backbiting, hatred and all other
vices must be put away; for what wouldest thou do at the common Supper of the Lord, if thy
neighbour were not well commended to thee, for whom Christ hath died, and who shall enjoy all
his goods with all the elect? Thou showest thyself outwardly as a fellow member, who
acknowledgeth Christ for his redeemer and the others for his fellow heirs and brethren, and yet
thou despisest thy neighbour and grudgest him all good. If thou wilt be no member of the body of
Christ, in that thou mayest not suffer the other fellow members, love them and serve them, take
their need upon thee as were it thine own, then thou hatest also the head, Christ, and belongest
therefore not in this fellowship.

Therefore look to yourselves! It is no child's play to go to the Lord's Supper. Rude, insolent,
heedless folk, to whom it is nothing whether they sin or not, let them stay away. But
spiritually poor folk, that have a burdened conscience and would fain be godly, although they be
yet very imperfect, yet if they have a displeasure at their own sin, they shall come and receive
the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Supper; for God is gracious to the humble.

**The second exhortation.** After the Words of Institution the order gives a shorter text,
"used at the late Diet [of 1530] for brevity's sake, and afterwards commonly on Sunday, together with other Christian exhortations out of divine scripture". It contains an indicative general absolution. **Augsburg, *Form und
ordnung des Herren nachtmal*, 1530** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 12, p. 42):

<!-- doc 334 -->

Beloved! Ye know that we have commandment from Christ, our Lord and God, that we should so
preach and minister the holy sacraments, preach forgiveness of sins and forgive all sins in the
stead of God and of our Lord Christ, to all them that desire such and believe it; for thus it is
written [John 20:23]: Whose sins ye remit, they shall be remitted unto them, and whose ye
retain, they shall be retained. Therefore will I first proclaim to you forgiveness of sins in
the stead and on the behalf of God and of our Lord Christ, as Christ our Lord hath made
satisfaction for all our sins by his death, and reconciled God, and purchased grace without our
merit, and commanded that for his sake such be preached in all the world, and sins be rebuked
and forgiven. Therefore I pronounce you all, and each one in particular that desireth it, free
from your sins, and they shall be forgiven you of grace for Christ's sake, by divine
commandment, in the name of God the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. The peace of
God be with you! Amen.

And ye shall also believe this absolution as God's word and commandment, no less than if ye
heard God's voice sound from heaven; and know that ye receive grace and forgiveness of sins
through this faith alone, and that this faith is the highest and right Christian service of God,
that ye give God the honour of holding him true, that he will keep his promise, will be
gracious, as he hath promised, will also hear and help, if ye seek help of him; and ye shall
exercise such faith in all need, that ye may learn by experience that God is wont truly to show
grace and help to them that call upon him and in him, and that this faith may ever increase, so
that one hope all good of God and seek it of him. For this also is the holy sacrament
instituted, to remember that our Lord Christ died for us for sin's sake and rose again, that he
might give us grace, the Holy Ghost and eternal life. Therefore ye shall so receive the holy
sacrament that ye truly believe that grace and forgiveness of sins is offered you herein; for
Christ our Lord giveth us his body and his blood, that we may indeed believe and truly hold that
he will be with us and impart to us his life, his Holy Ghost and his goods. Amen.

**Notes.**
- **The absolution.** "Therefore I declare you all, and each one in particular that desireth it, free of your sins" is indicative, like Kantz's, and grounded in John 20:23. It belongs
  with the forms in [§3.4.4](#s3-4-4).
- **The order of parts.** The first exhortation stands before communion; the minister then
  rehearses the Words of Institution ("before the minister communicates the congregation with the Gospel, he repeats the words of the Supper").
- **Other exhortations.** Sehling's editor, citing Fille (1895), notes that "some other such exhortations also, mostly by Urban Rhegius" were once kept: "but they are now lost" (Sehling 12, p. 40).

##### <a id="s3-5-14-3"></a>3.5.14.3 Buxtehude, *Agende*, 1565

The Buxtehude *Agende* prints, after the Latin Prefaces, a "exhortation before the receiving of the Sacrament". It builds on the Words of
Institution, which it rehearses in full, and draws four lessons from them: what the Sacrament
is, who instituted it, what it is for, and who receive it to salvation. It ends with a prayer
said by all. **Buxtehude, *Agende*, 1565** (Sehling 7/1, pp. 124–125):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

My dear Christians, all that will consider and keep this holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ
fruitfully to their salvation, it is highly needful that before all things they know firmly the
words of the institution of this Supper, as the holy evangelists and Paul have written them,
which run thus: Our Lord Jesus Christ, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread,
gave thanks, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take, eat; this is my body,
which is given for you; this do in remembrance of me. After the same manner also he took the cup
after supper, gave thanks, gave it them, and said: Drink ye all of it; this cup is the new
testament in my blood, which is shed for you for the remission of sins; this do, as oft as ye
drink it, in remembrance of me.

Whoso considereth these words diligently, he findeth therein all that a godly Christian needeth
to know of this holy sacrament, as: First, what this holy sacrament is, namely the true body and
the true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is given us under bread and wine to eat and to
drink, to sustain therewith not the body but the soul. Secondly, these words teach who hath
instituted and ordained this sacrament, namely no emperor, kings, man or angel, but our Lord
Jesus Christ himself, the emperor of all emperors, king of all kings, the Lord of the angels and
of all creatures, the redeemer of mankind, the only-begotten Son of God, who is with the Father
and the Holy Ghost of like power and truth, whose will and words come truly to pass and deceive
no man, though it seemed to our reason incomprehensible and impossible. Thirdly, these words
teach whereto the holy sacrament is profitable and useful to us, namely, first, that we thereby
are incorporated into our Lord Christ in faith, and he become one with us and we one with him,
unto eternal life, as he himself saith, John 6[:56 and 54]: Whoso eateth my flesh and drinketh
of my blood dwelleth in me and I in him, and I will raise him up again at the last day.
Secondly, it serveth us also thereto, that we thereby assure our faith in the promises of the
gospel of the forgiveness of sins, as with a pure, divine, undeceiving seal and pledge. Thirdly,
that we show forth the death of our Lord Christ until his coming again, that is, that we thank
him all the days of our life for the redemption, which hath come to pass not through gold or
silver (as Peter saith), but through his precious sacrifice and bloodshedding. Lastly, these
