words teach who they are that receive the holy sacrament savingly to the forgiveness of their
sins, namely not the hypocrites, who appear penitent only before men and yet think not to amend
their sinful life, but remain after as before full of unchastity, hatred, envy, usury,
falsehood, deceit and the like; these eat and drink (as Paul saith) judgment to themselves. But
they that repent of their sins from the heart, and firmly believe the forgiveness thereof
through the passion, death and bloodshedding of Christ, and earnestly think to amend their life,
and so receive this holy sacrament hungry and thirsty for grace and mercy, as oft as they do it,
they are here assured by Christ that their sins are forgiven them and shall not be remembered.

That we may now receive the holy sacrament worthily, pray with me thus: Lord God, merciful
Father, we beseech thee, help us yet to a true repentance, and cover our sins and unworthiness
with the worthiness of thy dear Son Jesus Christ, our Lord, and grant that we may receive this
holy sacrament to the strengthening of our faith in the forgiveness of sins, and grow and
increase in a new life, that we, thus clothed with the worthiness of thy Son, may be eternally
saved, through the same thy Son, our Lord Christ. Amen.

**What follows.** "another": the editor notes that the order then gives the
exhortation "My dearly beloved in God", which Lüneburg 1564 also has in High German, that is,
the Braunschweig recension of Osiander ([§3.5.4](#s3-5-4)), and that Buxtehude adds the wish "God grant this to us all, that we receive it worthily. Amen" (Sehling 7/1, p. 125). Buxtehude is thus also a witness of [§3.5.4](#s3-5-4).

##### <a id="s3-5-14-4"></a>3.5.14.4 Micron, London 1554, German 1565

Micron's order for the Dutch stranger church at London (Reformed), in the German version of 1565
(with the Norden Dutch variants), has the minister read the institution from 1 Cor 11 from the
pulpit and then exhort the congregation to examine itself "before it sit at the table of the Lord". **Micron, *Ordinancien* (1554), German 1565**
(Reformed; Sehling 7/1, pp. 631–633):

<!-- doc 2116 -->

Ye have heard, dear brethren, out of this doctrine of the holy apostle Paul, who is the
institutor of the Supper, namely Christ Jesus, and how it shall be kept, unless one will fall
into great danger of the soul. For they that receive it unworthily become guilty of the body and
blood of Christ, and eat and drink judgment to themselves. That we then may flee this danger and
enjoy the Supper of the Lord worthily, let us, before we sit at the table of the Lord, hear
diligently wherein (according to the holy scripture) the right eating of the Supper lieth. The
same doth the apostle Paul here set forth in our proving and in the discerning of the body of
the Lord, so that every one that sincerely proveth himself and discerneth the body of the Lord
goeth worthily to the Supper of the Lord to his soul's comfort and salvation. But this proving
and discerning of the body of the Lord, or of his sacrifice, whereby he hath given his body into
death for us, lieth chiefly in three points. First, that we confess and bewail from the heart
our sins, which we have done against God and our neighbour, and truly reconcile ourselves (so
far as it be possible) with all those with whom we have aught at variance. Secondly, that in the
knowledge of our sins and in the feeling of the wrath of God against us we become not
faint-hearted for our sins' sake, nor fall into despair of his goodness toward us, nor yet take
our refuge in human merits, but shall firmly believe that all our sins are forgiven us only out
of pure grace, freely, through the only merit of the death of Christ, even as if we ourselves
had suffered the death in our own person on the tree of the cross. Thirdly, the right proving of
our conscience lieth herein, that we simply, without hypocrisy, purpose a sincere amendment of
life according to the holy will of God. Herein then shall every one diligently search his own
heart and conscience, how he findeth himself prepared toward God and his neighbour; for whoso
will remain stiff-necked in his sins, as in idolatry, blasphemy, covetousness, stealing, lying,
deceiving, quarrelling, drunkenness, uncleanness and the like, or who confesseth his sins and
yet trusteth in any other than in Jesus Christ and in the merit of his death, or who purposeth
not with his whole heart, without hypocrisy, to lead a better life, the same shall not now make
haste to come to the Supper of the Lord. But if any should deal otherwise herein, however
secretly the same be done, he shall yet before the face of God be guilty of the death of Christ,
whom he thus dishonoureth and despiseth.

Yet we say not this, dear brethren, as though we would make the broken hearts of the faithful
faint, as if none might go to the Supper of the Lord but he that is free from all uncleanness of
sins and perfect in all holiness. For Christ the Lord hath not instituted his Supper for a
witness of our holiness or perfection, but much rather for a witness of our imperfection and
unrighteousness, which he taketh from us by the sacrifice of his body, and reckoneth to us his
righteousness and honour, yea, giveth us the same. And therefore the faithful come to the table
of the Lord, not that they may boast of their righteousness and godliness, but much rather to
testify that of themselves they are nothing else than children of wrath, sold under sin, and
unworthy to lift up their eyes to heaven, whose righteousness, perfection and holiness is Christ
alone, who hath taken all our sickness upon himself through his cross, and poureth into us
through the Holy Ghost a right desire for righteousness.

Therefore, as many of us as will sit at the table of the Lord for the comfort of their
conscience with the wedding garment: Let us accuse ourselves with our whole heart for our sins,
and firmly believe that they are not imputed to us, only for Christ's sake. Let us also purpose
an earnest amendment of life. And that we may mightily feel and enjoy in our hearts the
sweetness of the merit of the death of Christ in the use of the Supper, we shall not remain
cleaving to the outward exercise or to the elements of bread and wine, but, admonished thereby,
we must lift up our senses, hearts and understanding into heaven, where Jesus Christ alone is
according to the body, a faithful advocate for us; and thereby we shall be assured without doubt
that we are fed unto eternal life through the spiritual communion of the body and blood of
Christ much more surely than our mortal bodies are daily sustained by meat and drink, and than
we eat bread and wine in the Supper of the Lord according to the commandment of Christ. God, our
heavenly Father, give us his grace, that we may truly taste the true food of our souls, Jesus
Christ, in our conscience unto eternal life. Amen.

**Notes.**
- **The place.** It is read after the Verba, from the pulpit; the minister then goes down to the
  table and announces 1 Cor 5:7f.
  ("after this exhortation the minister goeth from the pulpit and standeth with the other ministers by the table; Sehling 7/1, p. 633").
- **Sources.** Sehling's editor compares the second point, on the forgiveness won "on the gallows of the cross", with the third exhortation of Gellius Faber of Emden
  (Reformed) (Sehling 7/1, p. 632).
- **The *Sursum corda* turned to a doctrine.** "we must lift up our senses, hearts and understanding into heaven, where Jesus Christ alone is according to the body" is the Reformed reading of *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts).
- **Moers** (Reformed). The Lower Rhine recension of the Palatinate exhortation ([§3.5.10](#s3-5-10)) opens
  with Micron's words: "Out of this doctrine of the holy apostle Paul ye hear …".

##### <a id="s3-5-14-5"></a>3.5.14.5 Three short notes

- **Marienhafe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1593.** After communion "the preacher maketh a short exhortation of the love of the neighbour", on 1 Cor 10:17 and the figure of many grains and grapes made into one bread and
  one wine. It turns into the thanksgiving: "so lift up now your hearts to God, beloved, and let us joyfully give thanks" (Sehling 7/1, p. 713).
  The image of grains and grapes is the one that closes the Palatinate exhortation of 1563
  (Reformed; [§3.5.10](#s3-5-10)). Sehling's editor also describes the Low German Nürnberg hospital Mass, "De
  düdesche Misse" (The German Mass) of a Hamburg hymnal of 1558, which has both the Nürnberg and the Bugenhagen
  exhortations after the *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God; p. 714).
- **Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1578.** Besides the Brandenburg-Nürnberg exhortation at the
  altar ([§3.5.5](#s3-5-5)), the order appends "exhortations of the holy Supper, to be read at Saturday Vespers to the penitents and communicants" (Sehling 15, p. 327).
  They are a cycle of eight teaching homilies with a common opening, "Dear friends of Christ, forasmuch as we purpose to keep tomorrow the most worthy and holy Supper",
  which begins with the words of Luther's address ([§3.5.3](#s3-5-3)). The editor traces them to the Saturday
  sermons of Johann Hofmann (pp. 243, 328).
- **Mecklenburg 1540/45.** Its three Low German exhortations are not printed by Sehling ([§3.5.2](#s3-5-2)).

---

### <a id="s3-6"></a>3.6 Before and after the service

#### <a id="s3-6-1"></a>3.6.1 Vesting prayers

**No vesting prayers survive.** None of the evangelical orders in Sehling prints or appoints a
vesting prayer, or any of the other prayers in the Lutheran Missal Project's *Vesting Prayers*:
- the psalms of preparation (84, 85, 86, 116, 130) with the antiphon *Ne reminiscaris* (Remember not);
- the Kyrie, Our Father and *preces*;
- the collects;
- the prayers before vesting, at the washing of the hands, and at the amice, alb, cincture,
  maniple, stole, tunicle, chasuble and mitre.

The searches covered the Latin incipits (*Ne reminiscaris*, *Quam dilecta*, *Benedixisti*,
*Inclina, Domine*, *Credidi*, *De profundis* in a preparatory setting), *praeparatio ad missam* (preparation for Mass),
*amictus*, *indue me*, and the German and Low German words for vesting. The psalms occur only in
the Office and the Introits.

The only mention of the medieval prayers is an editor's note. Sehling's editor, on the Amberg
hospital order of 1544, distinguishes the three preparations of the priest before Mass.
**Amberg, *Ordnung der kirchen* … *im spital*, 1544, editor's note** (Sehling 13, p. 282):

<!-- doc 410 -->

What is here set before the Introit, in this noteworthy attempt, as a preparation for the
congregation instead of the prayers at the foot of the altar (with the Confiteor), which are a
preparation of the celebrating clergyman, is probably a form of the *accessus*. This is the
first of the three prescribed preparations of the clergyman. It was not, like the *Praeparatio
ad missam* (preparation for Mass) that followed it (with, among other things, the prayers at the putting on of the
several parts of the Mass vesture), and that which then came within the Mass itself in the form
of the prayers at the foot of the altar, exactly prescribed in its form in the Missal, and could
therefore differ quite widely by place and person, and could also take the form of a devotion
with which priests prepared themselves together for the celebration of Mass.

**What the orders do say about vesting.** The orders mention vesting only as a rubric, and only
to say that it signifies nothing. The vestments themselves are indifferent. **Brandenburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 65):

<!-- doc 1746 -->

The other additions of outward bodily things, as Mass vestment, altar cloth, silver and golden
vessels, lights, etc., are altogether free; they give and take nothing to faith and conscience.
Therefore, since they were there before and have been provided, they shall be kept and used,
especially the vestments, because the ministers of the church are not always so furnished in
their own clothes that they might serve the congregation therein worthily and honourably.

The rubrics on vesting say no more than this:
- **The moment of vesting.** At Hadeln the priest vests during the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) at the end of
  Matins, "not as needful, but as a seemly and honest ornament, and not seeking salvation therein" ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). In Mecklenburg 1540 the priest turns to the people "when he hath vested himself" ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). In both, vesting is done in silence, in
  the church or sacristy, with no prayer.
- **The *Stufengebet***, the third of the medieval preparations, is the only one that survives
  (§[3.3.2](#s3-3-2)–[3.3.4](#s3-3-4)). The *accessus* survives, recast, only as the congregation's *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit)
  ([§3.3.7](#s3-3-7)).

#### <a id="s3-6-2"></a>3.6.2 The psalms and the *Ne reminiscaris*

None of the five preparatory psalms of the Missal's *praeparatio* is appointed as a private
preparation of the minister, and the antiphon *Ne reminiscaris* (Remember not; Tobit 3:3) does not occur.
- **The nearest thing** is Bugenhagen's *Domine, ne memineris iniquitatum nostrarum antiquarum* (O Lord, remember not our former iniquities)
  (Ps 79:8), said with the sexton at the altar step ([§3.3.3](#s3-3-3)). It is the same plea for the
  forgetting of old sins, but taken from the Lenten tract.
- **Penitential psalms.** Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 allows "a goodly penitential psalm" in place of the *Confiteor* (I confess; [§3.3.2](#s3-3-2)). Ps 130 *De profundis* (Out of the depths) appears as a hymn, Luther's
  *Aus tiefer Not* (Out of deep distress), sung as the Introit in Lippe ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)) and often elsewhere.
- **The psalms themselves** occur in the corpus only as Introits, Office psalms, or proof texts.
  Ps 84 *Quam dilecta* (How amiable) is the dedication psalm at Hof 1592 (Sehling 11, p. 422), and Lüneburg
  1564 cites it in defence of public worship (Sehling 6/1, p. 541).

#### <a id="s3-6-3"></a>3.6.3 After the Mass

**The priest's private thanksgiving.** The medieval *gratiarum actio post missam*, the thanksgiving after Mass (the canticle
*Benedicite* [Bless ye], Ps 150 *Laudate Dominum in sanctis eius* [Praise ye the Lord in his sanctuary], and collects, said by the priest while
unvesting) survives in only one form. In Bugenhagen's Hildesheim order of 1544 and the
Schleswig-Holstein order of 1542, the priest unvests during the closing hymn, kneels again
before the altar, and "thanketh God secretly for himself" (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 855; Sehling 23, p. 91). No text is given. Both are quoted with
translations in [Chapter 7](#ch7) §§[7.15.2](#s7-15-2)–[7.15.3](#s7-15-3).

**The Benedicite and Ps 150.** Neither is appointed after Mass in any evangelical order. Both
occur only as the canticle and psalm of **Sunday Lauds**, sung in the choir by the schoolboys or
the canons. Pomerania prescribes the weekday canticles of Lauds after the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God).
**Pomerania, *Pia ordinatio caeremoniarum*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 349):

<!-- doc 1857 -->

After the third responsory, which is sung with the Gloria Patri, etc., let the Te Deum follow,
etc. Next let the cantor begin some antiphon, according to whose tone there shall be sung only
one of the prophetic psalms, which are called canticles: on the Lord's Day, *Benedicite omnia* (O all ye works, bless ye),
etc.; on Monday, *Confitebor tibi, Domine, quoniam iratus* (I will praise thee, O Lord, though thou wast angry), etc.; on Tuesday, *Ego dixi*, etc.;
on Wednesday, *Exultavit* (hath rejoiced), etc.; on Thursday, *Cantemus* (Let us sing), etc.; on Friday, *Domine, audivi* (O Lord, I have heard),
etc.; on Saturday, *Audite coeli* (Hear, O heavens), etc.

The Schleswig-Holstein order of 1542 has the same scheme in Low German, "on Sundays: *Benedicite omnia*" (Sehling 23, p. 141). At the Ansbach
collegiate churches Sunday Lauds keeps both the *Benedicite* and the *Laudate* psalms.
**Brandenburg-Ansbach, *Ordnung singens und lesens bei den Stiften*, 1533**
(Sehling 11, p. 313):

<!-- doc 276 -->

On Sunday they sing the Te Deum laudamus; thereafter the psalms *Dominus regnavit* (The Lord reigneth), *Jubilate
Deo omnis terra* (Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands), *Deus, Deus meus* (O God, my God), *Benedicite omnia opera* (O all ye works, bless ye), *Laudate Dominum de coelis* (Praise ye the Lord from the heavens), with
the antiphon *Indutus est* (He is clothed); the *Benedictus Dominus* (Blessed be the Lord), etc., as is otherwise customarily held on
Sunday.

**Who sings them.** At Ansbach, "they": the canons and vicars of the collegiate foundations. In
Pomerania and Schleswig-Holstein, the cantor and the schoolboys in the choir. The people are not
present at Lauds. The *Laudate* psalms (Pss 148–150) are sung under the one heading "Laudate
Dominum de coelis".

**What the orders do appoint after Mass.** In place of the priest's private thanksgiving, the
evangelical Mass ends with a public thanksgiving by all:
- a postcommunion collect, usually Luther's "Wir danken dir, allmächtiger Herr Gott" (We give thanks to thee, almighty Lord God);
- the Aaronic blessing;
- a hymn or psalm sung by the schoolboys and people while the communicants return, or at the
  very end. At Hildesheim it is "a short German psalm" begun by
  the schoolmaster.

In Kantz 1522 and in Nürnberg the *Nunc dimittis* is sung after communion. The collects and
thanksgiving prayers are treated in [Chapter 5](#ch5), and the hymns in
[Chapter 8](#ch8).

#### <a id="s3-6-4"></a>3.6.4 Prayers before and after the sermon

**The pattern.** Every Lutheran order surrounds the sermon with prayer. The preacher calls the
people to prayer before he begins, and they pray, usually the Our Father in silence or aloud, or
sing a hymn to the Holy Ghost. At the end of the sermon he calls them again to thanksgiving and
to intercession for the Church, the government and all need, and leads the general prayer. The
Lüneburg order puts it most fully. **Lüneburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1564**
(Sehling 6/1, pp. 544–545):

<!-- doc 2003 -->

But before the sermon the priest is to exhort the people to Christian prayer, that the dear God
would give them his Holy Ghost, to handle his holy word profitably and to take it into the
heart, that they may amend their sinful life, obtain comfort and strengthening of their faith,
and henceforth live christianly and blessedly. Thereupon an Our Father shall be said, or *Nu
bitten wir den heiligen Geist* (Now pray we the Holy Ghost) sung; about Christmas, *Ein kindelein so löbelich* (A little child so praiseworthy), etc.; about
Easter, *Christ ist erstanden* (Christ is arisen), etc. At the end of the sermon the people shall again be exhorted
to prayer and thanksgiving toward God, and [shall pray] together for the preservation of the
Church of God and right doctrine, and thereto of faithful, true teachers, and that God would
send faithful labourers into his harvest; for the government, for temporal peace and the
increase of the fruits; and in sum for the need of all Christendom and of particular persons
that desire the Christian prayer.

**Other orders.**
- **Luther 1526**: "that the common prayer is made in the pulpit, or the Our Father said before [the people]",
  remains from the old pulpit office ([§3.5.3](#s3-5-3)).
- **Mecklenburg 1552**: at the end of the sermon the people are "exhorted to prayer and thanksgiving", and the preacher is to bid them "that they remain in the church at the communion"
  (Sehling 5, p. 198). Lüneburg copies it.
- **Hadeln**: the preacher "shall first exhort the people to diligent calling upon the help of God". After
  the sermon he again exhorts to prayer, recites the Small Catechism, and prays for the prince,
  the preachers "and all needs" (Sehling 5, p. 468).
- **Buxtehude 1552**: the chaplains "shall begin all their sermons with a hymn, to pray God for his grace" (Sehling 7/1, p. 72).
- **Hanau-Lichtenberg 1573**, weekday sermons: "before the sermon sing a psalm; then follow an Our Father and the sermon; lastly close the sermon with hymn, prayer and blessing" (Sehling 20/2, p. 53).
  In the villages without a school the pastor sings a German psalm, then "let him recite the open confession, absolution and epistle" (ibid.).
- **Palatinate 1563** (Reformed): the prayer of confession before the sermon, ending in the Our
  Father, said by the minister ([§3.3.6](#s3-3-6)); the confession, absolution and the long general prayer
  after it ([§3.4.4](#s3-4-4)).

The pulpit prayers, the greeting and the notices are treated more fully in
[Chapter 11](#ch11) [§11.10](#s11-10).

**Who prays.** The preacher bids and leads; the congregation prays the Our Father with him or
silently, and answers "Amen". The schoolboys and choir sing the hymn. No order gives a private
prayer for the preacher to say before going up into the pulpit. Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 has him begin
the sermon "with the prayer, as is customary" (Sehling 18, p. 499), and leaves the text to custom.

#### <a id="s3-6-5"></a>3.6.5 On entering and leaving church; the communicants' own prayers

**On entering church.** No order in the corpus prints or appoints a prayer for the worshipper to
say on entering or leaving the church. The modern hymnal's "prayer on entering church" has no
sixteenth-century church-order counterpart. What the orders appoint "when one comes into church"
is a hymn:
- **Sayn 1590**: "First, when one cometh into the church, a German psalm shall be sung; thereafter the pastor shall read a collect" (Sehling 19/1, p. 412).
- **Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557**: an opening hymn of the Holy Ghost is sung "until the church cometh together" ([§3.3.4](#s3-3-4)).
- **Amberg 1550**, weekday morning prayer: the priest begins *Deus in adiutorium* (O God, make speed to save me), and the choir
  sings one or two Latin psalms "until the people come together" (Sehling 13, p. 287).

The orders regulate behaviour instead: the people are not to stand about in the churchyard or
run in and out during the sermon. The village ordinance of Obereisenheim (Castell) of 1579 wants
each to go into church when the bell is rung, to "hear God's word, wait upon the sermon, and finish his prayer with the whole congregation quietly and still" (Sehling 11, p. 688).

**The communicants' prayers.** The orders print no private prayers for the communicant to say
before or after receiving. What the communicant does is set out in three ways:
1. **Private preparation** by confession and examination on the Saturday ([§3.4.6](#s3-4-6)).
2. **Prayers said for them by the minister**:
   - Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 has a "Prayer before the Supper", read by the minister to the people
     after the absolution. It asks "that thou wouldest graciously give unto all of us that shall eat and drink of this thy holy Supper the blessed communion of thy body and blood" (Sehling 18, p. 499).
   - Micron's Dutch order (Reformed) has a "prayer before the Supper",
     said by the minister from the pulpit while all kneel (Sehling 7/1, p. 630).
   - Ysenburg 1588 prints more than one prayer after communion, all collects of the minister
     (Sehling 10, p. 627).
3. **Hymns sung during the distribution.** *Jesus Christus unser Heiland* (Jesus Christ our Saviour), *Gott sei gelobet* (God be praised),
   the German *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God): the hymns are the people's prayer during communion. Mecklenburg 1552
   tells the communicants "ye shall also here make your hearty prayer", and gives the prayer in the first person, to be made their own
   ([§3.5.9](#s3-5-9)).

**The hymnal.** The nearest thing to the modern hymnal's printed devotions is the
Pfalz-Zweibrücken *Gesangbuch* (hymnal) of 1571/1587. It reprints the Mecklenburg confession, prayer and
absolution as "Confession, prayer and absolution before the sermon on Sunday", so that the people had the text in their hands
(Sehling 18, p. 187, apparatus).

**A note on "Benedicite".** In the household sections of the orders, "Benedicite" (Bless ye) and "Gratias" (Thanks)
are the grace before and after meat of Luther's Small Catechism ("The eyes of all wait upon thee, O Lord" and "O give thanks unto the Lord, for he is good"). It is not the canticle of the three
children. Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557 heads it "How a householder shall teach his household to say the Benedicite and Gratias" (Sehling 18, p. 180).

---

### <a id="s3-7"></a>3.7 Table by order

The table gives, for each order discussed in [§3.3](#s3-3) and [§3.4](#s3-4) and for the orders with an exhortation of
their own ([§3.5.14](#s3-5-14)), what stands before the Introit, how the confession is said and absolved, and
where the exhortation falls. Every cell has been checked against the text of the order. "—"
means the order has nothing of the kind; "not stated" means the order mentions the item but
gives no text or form. "A"–"G" are the families of [§3.3.1](#s3-3-1); absolution types 1–5 are those of [§3.4.4](#s3-4-4).
The orders that appear only as witnesses to an exhortation are listed in the witness tables of
§[3.5.3](#s3-5-3)–[3.5.13](#s3-5-13).

| Müntzer, Allstedt 1523 and 1524 (Radical Reformation) | Ps 43 with priest and people; priest's confession; people's *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy); *Deus, tu conversus* (O God, thou wilt turn again); *Non nobis* (Not unto us); *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us) (G) | Priest, aloud "before all the people"; the people answer | — | — | [3.3.8](#s3-3-8) |

## <a id="ch4"></a>Chapter 4. The Propers of the Mass


This chapter follows the **propers of the Mass**, the parts that change with the day, through the
evangelical church orders printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI.
Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century). The propers covered are the introit, the prophecy or Old Testament lesson, the
epistle, the gradual, the alleluia and tract, the gospel, the offertory, the Proper Preface and
the communion chant. For each it asks:
- Was it **kept**, and where?
- **Who sang or read it**: the cantor and the school choir, the celebrant, the congregation, the
  organ? Was it sung in alternation?
- Was it in **Latin or German**?
- Were the **historic tunes** kept, cut, or replaced with new music: new tones, polyphony?

For the **Proper Prefaces** it asks also:
- On which days of the season, feast or saint were they used?
- Which Prefaces did each order have?

**[Appendix 4.A](#s4-a)** renders every Proper Preface in the corpus:
- in the original language, Latin and German or Low German;
- with a formal-equivalence translation in the idiom of the Authorized Version;
- with the list of the orders that carry each text.

Where the corpus has both the Latin and a German translation, both are given. The English is
then made from the Latin, with notes on where the German shortens, adds to or changes it.

**How the chapter is laid out.**
- [§4.1](#s4-1) summarizes the findings, and [§4.2](#s4-2) sets out the method and cautions.
- [§4.3](#s4-3) describes the three ways the orders dealt with the propers.
- §§[4.4](#s4-4)–[4.9](#s4-9) take the propers in turn: introit, lessons, gradual, offertory, Preface, communion.
- [§4.10](#s4-10) deals with the music.
- [§4.11](#s4-11) is a table by order, and [§4.12](#s4-12) a concordance.

### <a id="s4-1"></a>4.1 Summary of findings

**1. Three models, often combined.** The orders handle the propers in one of three ways ([§4.3](#s4-3)):
- **Keep them in Latin**, sung by the school choir: the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) line.
- **Translate them into German prose**, sung to the old tones: Müntzer 1524 (Radical
  Reformation), Erfurt 1525, Calenberg-Göttingen 1542.
- **Replace them with German hymns** sung by the congregation: the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) line.

Most territorial orders allowed all three by place and day:
- Latin "where there is a school", "in the towns", "on the feasts";
- German psalms "in the villages" and on ordinary Sundays.

The constant condition is that a proper must be **from Scripture and "pure"**. In practice this
meant ***de tempore*, not *de sanctis*** ([§4.3.1](#s4-3-1), [§4.6.2](#s4-6-2)).

**2. The introit was the most widely kept proper** ([§4.4](#s4-4)).
- **Luther's approval.** Luther approved the Sunday and festal introits "if taken from
  Scripture" (1523).
- **Who sang it.** The **school** sang it in Latin, under the cantor or schoolmaster, while the
  priest read it quietly. Villages sang a German psalm instead.
- **Fallbacks.** Where boys could not learn every Sunday's introit, they repeated *Benedicta sit
  sancta Trinitas* (Blessed be the holy Trinity) or *Spiritus Domini* (The Spirit of the Lord; Hatzkerode, Heilbronn, Kurpfalz, Hamburg 1556).
- **German introits.** These appear in Müntzer (Radical Reformation), Erfurt and Hof 1592.
  Wittgenstein 1555 allows the festal introits to be sung in German in the villages.
- **Organ and polyphony.** By the later century the introit was often played by the organ in
  alternation with the choir, or sung *figuraliter* (in figured music; Nördlingen 1579, Hof 1592).

**3. No Old Testament "prophecy" before the epistle survives as a regular lesson** ([§4.5.1](#s4-5-1)).
- **At the Mass.** The prophetic lessons that remain are the historic epistles taken from a
  prophet (Hof 1592). On some feasts a chapter of the feast's history is read instead
  (Pfalz-Neuburg 1543).
- **At the office.** Old Testament lessons belong to Matins and Vespers. They were read in the
  old **prophecy tone**, whose cadence is written out in solmization (Hamburg 1529, Pomerania
  1535, Wittenberg 1533).

**4. The epistle and gospel of the day were kept everywhere, and read toward the people**
(§[4.5.2](#s4-5-2)–[4.5.3](#s4-5-3)).
- **Exceptions.** Müntzer (Radical Reformation), and Nürnberg and Brandenburg-Nürnberg in the
  1520s–30s, read whole chapters in sequence.
- **Three practices of language and tone:**
  - **German in new tones.** Luther's *Deutsche Messe* has the epistle in the eighth tone and
    the gospel in the fifth. The Saxon orders send pastors to copy "the tone and accent
    customary at Wittenberg".
  - **German read without notes**, for intelligibility (Mecklenburg).
  - **Latin chanted "in the old customary melody", then read in German** (Schwäbisch Hall 1526,
    Hamburg 1556, Brieg 1592). Brandenburg's visitors required this in 1573.

**5. The gradual and alleluia survived as a Latin choir piece, cut short** ([§4.6](#s4-6)).
- **Cut short.** Luther limited the gradual to two verses, and kept the alleluia in Lent as "the
  perpetual voice of the church". Bugenhagen's northern orders cut off the jubilus, "the many
  notes which one was wont to hang on behind".
- **Replaced.** In villages, and where the text was "not pure", a German psalm took the place.
- **German graduals.** Müntzer (Radical Reformation) and Erfurt have them. Nürnberg sang its
  gradual "in a tone made for it".

**6. The offertory chant was the proper most often dropped** ([§4.7](#s4-7)).
- **Dropped.** It went with the offertory prayers as part of the "abomination" of sacrifice
  (Luther 1523). Volprecht says it is "never said, because Christ was once offered for our
  sins".
- **Kept.** A few orders kept the Latin offertory as a Scripture text sung by the choir:
  Wittenberg 1525, Brandenburg 1540, Ansbach 1548, Amberg 1550.
- **Translated.** Müntzer (Radical Reformation) and Erfurt translated it.
- **Replaced.** Most replaced it with a German psalm or the creed hymn.

**7. The Proper Preface survived chiefly on the feasts, in Latin, to the Missal tones** ([§4.8](#s4-8)).
- **Cut.** Luther cut the Preface short in 1523 and dropped it in 1526. Prussia abolished it
  outright.
- **The usual rule.** Most orders from Duke Henry's Saxon order of 1539 on adopted the rule:
  **the Latin Preface on the feasts, the exhortation on ordinary Sundays**.
- **The feasts.** The proper Prefaces were those of the feasts of Christ: Christmas, Epiphany,
  Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, Trinity.
- **Ordinary Sundays.** Bugenhagen's northern orders chose the **Trinity Preface** "made against
  the Arians" (Hamburg 1529, Wolfenbüttel 1543, Herford 1532, Wittenberg 1533). Wolfenbüttel
  1543 dropped even the common Preface as "needless".
- **Saints' days.** Sanctoral Prefaces were excluded as impure. The exceptions are:
  - **Michaelmas**, with the common Preface (Hoya, Osnabrück, Lippe);
  - the **Marian and Apostles' Prefaces** in Dortmund's Low German set of 1554, the Apostles'
    made to speak of the apostles' "doctrine";
  - Müntzer's rewording (Radical Reformation) of the Marian Preface for Advent.
- **Who sang.** The priest sang the Preface at the altar; the choir answered and sang the
  Sanctus.
- **Language.** In Lippe 1571 and Mecklenburg the towns had Latin and the villages German.

**8. The communion chant was optional from the start and was mostly replaced by hymns** ([§4.9](#s4-9)).
- **Optional.** Luther says "If one will sing the communion, let it be sung".
- **Kept in Latin.** Volprecht, Ansbach 1536 and Brandenburg 1540 kept it.
- **German.** Müntzer (Radical Reformation) and Erfurt translated it.
- **Polyphony.** In the larger churches festal motets "*sub communione*" (during the communion) took its place, among
  them Clemens non Papa's *Pascha nostrum* (Christ our passover) at Hof.

**9. The old melodies were kept, trimmed, and supplemented** ([§4.10](#s4-10)).
- **Kept.** The Latin propers kept the plainchant of the old books, standardized in **Lossius's
  *Psalmodia***. Rostock made it binding around 1560, and Hof used it in 1592.
- **Trimmed.** They were trimmed by verse and melisma.
- **New tones.** German texts got new or adapted tones.
- **Polyphony.** From the 1530s the feasts brought **polyphonic** introits, Masses and motets:
  "choraliter or figuraliter". Hof 1592 names Senfl, Lassus, Clemens, Victoria, Walter, Isaac
  and Josquin.
- **Organ.** The organ alternated with the choir in the introit and the ordinary.

**10. [Appendix 4.A](#s4-a) gives every Proper Preface in the corpus.**
- **Latin.** The Latin set (Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, Trinity, common)
  belongs to the Lower Saxon and Westphalian orders, Lüneburg 1564 to Verden 1606.
- **German translations of the Latin:**
    - **Müntzer's** (1524, Radical Reformation), carried on by Erfurt, Calenberg-Göttingen and
      the Lippe villages;
    - **Strasbourg's** (1524, Moderate Reformed);
  - **Dortmund's** Low German (1554), which alone translates the whole Roman series, Lent,
    Cross, the Virgin and the Apostles included.
- **New German Prefaces.** There are four:
  - Grubenhagen's Isaiah 53 Preface for Maundy Thursday (1581);
  - Lippe's Michaelmas Preface on the forgiveness of sins (1571);
  - Kurland's Christmas and Pentecost Prefaces (1570), built on the Easter Preface.
