us with the gifts of thy graces, that we may stand constantly against every kind of temptation,
and so go on in this spiritual combat that at the last, having obtained full victory, we may
triumph in thy kingdom together with our Captain and Head and highest and only Protector, the
Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

#### <a id="s6-20-r3-10"></a>R3.10 Creed

**Rubric.** To this prayer the Creed is immediately added; which being recited, the
precentor straightway beginneth a psalm, to which the people then sing to the end; which being
sung, the pastor dismisseth the people with this good wish.

---

### <a id="s6-21"></a>6.21 Family R4: à Lasco/Micron (London stranger church)

The London Dutch stranger church's prayer after the sermon (German version for East Frisia),
still praying for the King of England and the city of London.

- **Earliest witness (archetype):** London 1554 (à Lasco/Micron).
- **Tradition:** Reformed.
- **Language:** German.
- **Form:** continuous prayer + Our Father.
- **Place in the service (London 1554 (Micron)):** Sunday morning after the sermon, the prayer
  for the fruit of the Word, the Decalogue, confession, declaration of loosing and binding, and
  the Creed; then the Our Father, and baptism, the Supper or marriage; a psalm and the blessing
  with a charge to remember the poor. “The great prayer for the common need” is said after
  every sermon.

| Year | Witness | Territory | Sehling | Form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1554 | London, Dutch stranger church: Marten Micron, Christlicke Ordinancien (1554; German edition 1565) (Reformed) | London Dutch refugee church (edition for East Frisia) | Sehling 7/1, IV/Ostfriesland Nr. 23 (Microns Ordinancien 1554/1565), pp. 603–604 | continuous prayer + Lord’s Prayer |

**Sequence:** R4.1 Thanksgiving > R4.2 The Church > R4.3 Civil authority > R4.4 The present
congregation > R4.5 The present congregation > R4.6 The erring & unbelievers > R4.7 The
persecuted > R4.8 The afflicted > R4.9 Lord's Prayer > R4.10 Special intercessions.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-1"></a>R4.1 Thanksgiving

**Rubric.** After this confession the minister beginneth the common prayer for all
manner of need of the Christian congregation after this manner:

**Prayer.** O almighty, heavenly and merciful Father, forasmuch as it hath pleased
thee of thine infinite mercy to deliver us out of the darkness of ignorance and of the Roman
idolatry, and, among others, to reveal unto us the mystery of the holy Gospel of thy dear Son,
for which we give thee thanks with our whole heart: we humbly beseech thee that thou wouldest
strengthen us by the grace of thy Spirit, that we may keep the true Christian faith unto the end
of our life and order our life thereafter.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-2"></a>R4.2 The Church

**Prayer.** We pray thee also, most holy Father, for the common Church of thy dear Son
Jesus Christ, which is scattered throughout the whole wide world, wherein the godly doctrine of
thy Son is taught and maintained (the abomination and idolatry of the Roman Antichrist being
rooted out). Keep from her all false shepherds and teachers, and send godly, faithful and
earnest labourers into thine harvest, which seek not their own honour, but thine honour only and
the edifying of thy congregation.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-3"></a>R4.3 Civil authority

**Prayer.** And first we pray, most gracious Father, for the congregation of this
realm of England and for all its ministers, and especially for our most gracious lord King N.
N.: preserve and keep him and govern him with thy Spirit, that he may rule his people under our
common Head Jesus Christ, that we may lead under him a quiet and still life in all godliness and
honesty according to thy word by thy grace. We pray also for the King’s Majesty’s household and
the nobility, and for all lords and magistrates of the whole kingdom, and chiefly for the right
wise high council of the King’s Majesty: endue it with the spirit of counsel, of strength and of
constancy. Give them also the spirit of unity and of peace, that in their government they may
follow all that is right and good, and so help to further and maintain a Christian quiet and
peace in this realm.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-4"></a>R4.4 The present congregation

**Prayer.** Endue also the whole people of this realm with thy Spirit, that it may
willingly hear the voice of thy prophets, and take heed to the doctrine of thy Son Jesus Christ,
and increase therein more and more from day to day; and that it may abide constant in the true
obedience which it oweth to the King’s Majesty and his officers, to the welfare of this realm
and the edifying of the Christian congregation. We pray further thy divine grace for this city
of London, that thou wouldest turn away from it all manner of plagues (which we daily deserve),
and preserve it in all godliness, peace and common quiet. Govern also the magistrates thereof
with thy Spirit, that they may perform their office faithfully and wisely in thy fear.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-5"></a>R4.5 The present congregation

**Prayer.** Especially we pray thee, O most gracious Father, for this our stranger
congregation, that thou wouldest henceforth so show thy favour toward her, as thou hast planted
her here by thy wonderful grace, that, being defended by thy power and mercy from all worldly
tyranny and false doctrine, she may increase daily more and more in all godliness and true unity
of hearts.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-6"></a>R4.6 The erring & unbelievers

**Prayer.** We pray thee also humbly for all kings, princes, magistrates and peoples
which (being blinded with the antichristian idolatry) have not yet been able to know the voice
of thy Son, and through ignorance persecute as enemies the living members of thy Son (whom they
know not): that thou wouldest bring them, with all other persons blinded or (through any
weakness) led astray, to the true light and the right way, that we all, gathered into one
sheepfold under the one Shepherd of our souls, Christ Jesus, may praise thee with one mind for
ever.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-7"></a>R4.7 The persecuted

**Prayer.** Lastly we pray also for all our brethren scattered over the whole earth,
which for the right confession of thy Son and his doctrine are oppressed under the cross by
Antichrist; and especially wilt thou comfort with thy Holy Spirit N. N., and so strengthen their
hearts from above with thy divine power in the right faith, that they may bear all that thou
sendest them patiently, manfully and with thanksgiving; and that without fear they may
steadfastly confess gloriously before men thy name and the name of thy Son and make it great, be
it by life or by death, as thou knowest it to serve to thine honour.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-8"></a>R4.8 The afflicted

**Prayer.** Especially we pray also for all the brethren whom thou hast justly tried
and exercised with sickness, poverty, imprisonment, banishment or other misery of spirit or
body, that thou wouldest not forsake them in their need, but mitigate their cross according to
thy fatherly mercy, or give them strength and patience to bear steadfastly all that thou sendest
them according to thy good pleasure; that they may understand by their chastisement that they
are proved of thee, as their merciful, dear Father, for the trial of their faith, and so be
converted unto thee.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-9"></a>R4.9 Lord's Prayer

**Prayer.** All these things we desire of thee, most gracious Father, through thy
fatherly grace and favour which thou hast shown toward us in thy Son. And in this undoubted hope
we humbly call upon thy name through the same thy beloved Son Jesus Christ, as we are taught of
him, saying: Our Father, which art in the heavens, etc.

#### <a id="s6-21-r4-10"></a>R4.10 Special intercessions

**Rubric.** Here it is to be noted that other prayers are oftentimes added here before
the Our Father is said, especially when any special concern cometh upon the congregation.

## <a id="ch7"></a>Chapter 7. The Roman Canon in German Evangelical Masses (1522–1544)


This file gives the offertory and eucharistic rites of the orders in the Sehling corpus
that keep pieces of the Roman Canon and of the priest's prayers of the Ordinary, or that
put a prayer of their own in the Canon's place. They were found by a search of the whole
corpus ([§7.1.3](#s7-1-3)) and are printed in order of date.

### <a id="s7-1"></a>7.1 Summary of findings

The orders printed here run from Kantz's Nördlingen Mass of 1522 to Bugenhagen's
Hildesheim order of 1544. Between them they show what the first generation of evangelical Masses kept
of three things:

- the Roman Canon (*Te igitur* to the doxology *Per ipsum*);
- the prayers of the Ordinary around it: the offertory prayers, the embolism, the priest's
  prayers before and after communion, and the words of distribution;
- the rites that go with them: elevation, fraction, the Peace.

[§7.1.1](#s7-1-1) summarises the findings in the order of the Mass. [§7.1.2](#s7-1-2) gives the concordance tables.
[§7.1.3](#s7-1-3) says how the corpus was searched and which orders were examined but not printed.

#### <a id="s7-1-1"></a>7.1.1 Findings

**The offertory.**

- **The offertory prayers.** Luther rejected everything that "sounds of oblation" ([§7.3.1](#s7-3-1)). No
  order keeps *Suscipe, sancte Pater* (Receive, O holy Father), *Offerimus tibi* (We offer unto thee) or *Suscipe, sancta Trinitas* (Receive, O holy Trinity).
- **What does survive:**
  - **the offertory chant**: Latin in Brandenburg 1540 ([§7.12.1](#s7-12-1)); Müntzer's German *Ad te levavi* (Unto thee have I lifted up)
    ([§7.4.1](#s7-4-1); Radical Reformation); a German hymn "for the offertory" in Lippe ([§7.10](#s7-10)) and
    Calenberg-Göttingen 1542 ([§7.13.1](#s7-13-1));
  - **a rubric for preparing the chalice**: Döber ([§7.8.1](#s7-8-1)), Volprecht ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)), Bugenhagen's orders
    ([§7.15.1](#s7-15-1));
  - **the *Orate fratres*, recast** as a request for prayer: Worms (Moderate Reformed; "my prayer and yours", [§7.6.1](#s7-6-1)), Kantz and Bremen ([§7.2.1](#s7-2-1), [§7.9.2](#s7-9-2)), and Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed), where
    it becomes a bidding on Rom 12:1 to offer "our bodies" ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1), [§7.5.3](#s7-5-3));
  - ***Veni, sanctificator* replaced** by the Whitsun antiphon *Veni, Sancte Spiritus* and a
    collect: Kantz ([§7.2.2](#s7-2-2)), Bremen, Kiel ([§7.11.1](#s7-11-1));
  - **the Secret's closing *Per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen***, sung before the Preface
    dialogue: Müntzer ([§7.4.1](#s7-4-1); Radical Reformation), Lippe ([§7.10](#s7-10)), Göttingen ([§7.13.1](#s7-13-1)).
- **One prayer over the gifts.** Only Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 has one: Osiander's prayer "We bring … these thy gifts" ([§7.14.2](#s7-14-2)). It borrows from *Quam oblationem* (Which oblation), *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful) and
  *Supplices* (We humbly [beseech]), and asks for the Spirit. Sehling's editor, after P. Graff, calls it the first
  Lutheran order with a kind of epiclesis (Sehling 8, p. 45, n. 12).

**The Preface and Sanctus.**

- **The common Preface in German:** Worms (Moderate Reformed), Kantz, Bremen.
- **Proper Prefaces in German:** Müntzer (Radical Reformation; Blessed Virgin, reworded so that
  God, not Mary, is praised), Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed; Cross), Lippe (Trinity), Kiel and
  Göttingen (Easter).
- **Luther's short Preface.** Luther cut the Preface off at *per Christum Dominum nostrum* (through Christ our Lord) and
  joined the Verba to it ([§7.3.2](#s7-3-2)). The Nürnberg Latin Mass ([§7.7.1](#s7-7-1)), Döber ([§7.8.2](#s7-8-2)) and Volprecht
  ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)) follow him.
- **The Sanctus after the Verba:** Luther, Döber, Volprecht and Pfalz-Neuburg.

**The Canon.**

- **The only continuous Canon is Worms 1524** (Moderate Reformed; §[7.6.3](#s7-6-3)–[7.6.9](#s7-6-9)). It runs from *Te
  igitur* (Thee therefore) to *Supplices te rogamus* (We humbly beseech thee) in German, abridged:
  - there are no saints in *Communicantes* (In communion; only its closing clause), no *Memento* of the dead,
    no *Nobis quoque* (To us also) and no *Per ipsum* (Through him);
  - the sacrificial nouns become "bread and wine" and "our prayer";
  - emperor and king replace pope and bishop.
- **Elsewhere single Canon prayers survive:**
  - ***Quam oblationem***, recast as a petition that the bread and wine "may become unto us" the
    body and blood: Kantz ([§7.2.4](#s7-2-4)). Bremen changes it to a prayer that "we may firmly believe"
    this ([§7.9.3](#s7-9-3)).
  - ***Unde et memores***, as a thanksgiving "after the elevation": Strasbourg ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1); Moderate
    Reformed). A later hand wrote the Worms text of the prayer into the Strasbourg manuscript.
- **The Canon's intercession** (the petitions of *Te igitur* and the *Memento*) survives in
  three ways:
  - **in the Canon's own place after the Sanctus:** Strasbourg ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1); Moderate Reformed); an
    optional prayer in Döber taken from Strasbourg ([§7.8.11](#s7-8-11)); four collects in Brandenburg
    ([§7.12.2](#s7-12-2)); three in Pfalz-Neuburg ([§7.14.4](#s7-14-4)); one in Göttingen ([§7.13.1](#s7-13-1));
  - **as one long prayer "in place of the Canon":** Strasbourg 1525 ([§7.5.2](#s7-5-2); Moderate Reformed);
  - **as the general prayer after the sermon,** which Bugenhagen calls "our Canon" ([§7.15.4](#s7-15-4)).
- **The Canon critique.** The Brandenburg-Nürnberg order of 1533, repeated in Brandenburg 1540
  and Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, demands that the offering clauses of the Canon be replaced by "We remember the sacrifice of thine only Son" ([Appendix 7.A](#s7-a)). Sehling's register points to this
  critique under "Embolismus" (11:183, 13:65), because his note there explains the Würzburg
  embolism's added saints.

**The words of institution.**

- **Scripture or Canon.** Most orders read the Verba from 1 Cor 11 or a harmony of the Gospels.
  A distinct line keeps the Canon's own *Qui pridie* (Who the day before): *elevatis oculis* (with eyes lifted up), *benedixit* (blessed), *novi et
  aeterni testamenti* (of the new and eternal testament), sometimes *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith). The line runs through Kantz, the Nürnberg
  Latin Mass, Schwarz at Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed), Müntzer (Radical Reformation), Bremen,
  Lippe and Kiel.
- **Where Müntzer's wording travelled.** Müntzer's wording (Radical Reformation) reached Lippe,
  Kiel and Göttingen's proper Masses through the Erfurt *Kirchenämter* (church offices) of 1525–26 ([§7.10](#s7-10), [§7.13](#s7-13)).
- **The elevation** is kept by Luther (at the *Benedictus*), Worms (Moderate Reformed), the
  Nürnberg Latin Mass, Müntzer (Radical Reformation), Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed; cup only),
  Brandenburg and Pfalz-Neuburg. Kantz moves it to the communion ("Behold …"). Schleswig-Holstein
  1542 permits it.

**The Our Father and the embolism.**

- ***Praeceptis salutaribus moniti*** is recast in German almost everywhere, e.g. "Let us pray, as the Lord Christ Jesus hath commanded us …".
- **The embolism *Libera nos, quaesumus*.** Luther struck it out. What remains elsewhere:
  - **its conclusion only** ("Through our Lord Jesus … liveth and reigneth"): Worms
    (Moderate Reformed), Kantz, Bremen, Lippe;
  - **its sung ending *Per omnia saecula*** ("through all eternity of eternity"): Müntzer
    (Radical Reformation), Lippe;
  - **one line of its body** ("O Lord, deliver us from all visible and invisible enemies …"): Döber (p. 54; Sehling: "remnant of the embolism") and Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed).

**The fraction.**

- **Forbidden.** Luther forbids the fraction and commixture: "let the host not be broken nor mixed into the chalice" ([§7.3.3](#s7-3-3)). Worms (Moderate Reformed) repeats the prohibition ([§7.6.11](#s7-6-11)).
- **Kept in two orders only**, at the Roman place (the close of the embolism, before the Peace),
  and neither with the commixture:
  - the 1524 edition of Kantz's Mass, "Here let the priest take the bread and break it, as much as he needeth" ([§7.2.5](#s7-2-5));
  - Müntzer's Allstedt order (Radical Reformation), where the priest "for the communicants' sake divideth the sacrament" ([§7.4.3](#s7-4-3)).
- **The *Deutsche Messe*** (1526) has no fraction.
- **Reformed breaking of bread.** Every other mention of breaking the bread in the corpus comes
  from Reformed orders from the 1550s on (à Lasco, the Palatinate, Anhalt, the Upper Palatinate,
  Hessen-Kassel). There the bread is broken at the distribution on the ground of 1 Cor 10:16 and
  Acts 2:42. It is a new rite, not a survival.

**The Peace and the *Agnus Dei*.**

- ***Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum*** survives widely: Worms (Moderate Reformed), Luther (as a
  "public absolution"), the Nürnberg Latin Mass, Müntzer (Radical Reformation), Volprecht,
  Brandenburg, Pfalz-Neuburg, Lippe and Göttingen. Kantz moves it into the communion.
- **The *Agnus Dei*** is kept in German or Latin by nearly all. Luther has it sung during
  communion.

**The priest's prayers before communion.**

- **All three kept.** *Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti*, *Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei
  vivi* (O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God) and *Perceptio Corporis tui* (Let the receiving of thy Body) stay in Latin in Brandenburg ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)) and Pfalz-Neuburg
  ([§7.14.6](#s7-14-6)). Volprecht has all three in German ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)).
  - The "Libera nos" (Deliver us) in these orders is the petition inside *Fili Dei vivi* (Son of the living God; "deliver us by this thy most holy body and blood"), made plural. It is not the embolism.
- ***Fili Dei vivi* alone** is kept in German by:
  - Kantz and Bremen, abridged. Bremen changes "by this thy holy body and blood" to "by thy
    bottomless mercy".
  - Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed), prayed by all.
  - Döber and Kiel, said by the people line by line after the priest ([§7.8.8](#s7-8-8), [§7.11.3](#s7-11-3)).
- ***Domine, non sum dignus*** appears once, in German, in Kiel ([§7.11.3](#s7-11-3)).
- ***Qui dixisti*** becomes the closing collect of the Mass in Göttingen ([§7.13.3](#s7-13-3)).

**The words of distribution.**

- **The *custodiat*** ("The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life") is the most widespread survival. It appears in about thirty orders of the corpus,
  from Worms (Moderate Reformed) and Volprecht (1524) to 1609:
  - Worms (Moderate Reformed), Döber, Kantz, Bremen, the Nürnberg *Form und Ordnung*, Göttingen
    and many later orders;
  - most in the wording of the Albertine Saxon Agenda of 1539, "The body of our Lord Jesus Christ, given into death for thee, strengthen and preserve thee in the faith unto everlasting life";
  - Brandenburg 1540 uses it only for the communion of the sick (Sehling 3, pp. 79–80).
- ***Calicem salutaris accipiam*** (Ps 116:13) survives in Worms (Moderate Reformed), Kantz,
  Bremen and Volprecht.

**After communion.**

- ***Quod ore sumpsimus* and *Corpus tuum, Domine*.** Luther made these two ablution prayers the
  postcommunion ([§7.3.5](#s7-3-5)). Brandenburg and Pfalz-Neuburg keep them in Latin; Volprecht has both in
  German; Strasbourg (Moderate Reformed) has *Quod ore* (What with our mouth) as its *complenda* (completion).
- **Roman postcommunions and collects reused:**
  - Döber's *Largire sensibus nostris* (Wednesday in Holy Week). Sehling thought Döber's prayer
    newly composed; the identification is new here.
  - the Trinity *Proficiat* (May [the receiving] profit): Volprecht, Lippe;
  - the collect *Protector in te sperantium* (Protector of them that trust in thee): Kantz.
- **The priest's final *Placeat tibi, sancta Trinitas*** survives in Kantz, the sacrifice turned
  into "our praise and thanksgiving" ([§7.2.7](#s7-2-7)).
- **The *Nunc dimittis*** follows communion in Worms (Moderate Reformed), Döber, Kantz and
  Bremen.

**The priest's preparation and thanksgiving.**

- **Bugenhagen's preparatory prayer** is the evangelical counterpart of the prayers at the
  foot of the altar ([§7.15](#s7-15)):
  - in Wolfenbüttel 1543 and Hildesheim 1544, the priest kneels with the sexton and prays
    the *Pater noster* and the versicles *Domine, non secundum peccata nostra … Adiuva nos,
    Deus* (O Lord, deal not with us after our sins … Help us, O God);
  - in Schleswig-Holstein 1542 he says the *Confiteor* (I confess) privately and prays for preachers,
    king and realm.
- **After Mass,** Hildesheim and Schleswig-Holstein have him kneel again and "thank God
  secretly for himself".

**How the orders are related.**

- **Kantz** → Bremen (a Low German version) and the opening prayers of Kiel.
- **Müntzer** (Radical Reformation) → (Erfurt *Kirchenämter*) → Lippe, Kiel, Göttingen.
- **Strasbourg** (Moderate Reformed) → Worms (Moderate Reformed; the same Mass) and Döber's
  optional intercession.
- **Luther's *Formula missae*** → the Nürnberg Latin Mass, Döber, Volprecht, Brandenburg.
- **Nürnberg 1533** → the exhortation and Canon critique of Brandenburg 1540 and Pfalz-Neuburg
  1543.
- **Brandenburg 1540** → Calenberg-Göttingen 1542.

#### <a id="s7-1-3"></a>7.1.3 Method, and orders examined but not printed

The corpus ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb), all volumes of Sehling) was searched with regular expressions for:

- the priest's prayers *Qui dixisti* (Who saidst), *Fili Dei vivi* (Son of the living God), *Perceptio*, *Domine non sum
  dignus* (Lord, I am not worthy), *Corpus … custodiat* (The body … preserve), *Quod ore sumpsimus* (What we have taken with our mouth) and *Corpus tuum* (Thy body);
- Canon incipits and the Canon form of the Verba ("hub auf seine augen", "neuen und
  ewigen");
- offertory language and blessing of the gifts;
- the fraction ("breche", "teilet", *frangatur*, *fractio*);
- the embolism;
- Sehling's register entries *Offertorium* (Offertory), *Kanongebet* (Canon prayer), *Messkanon*, *canon missae* (canon of the Mass),
  *Epiklese* (epiclesis), *Konsekration* (consecration) and *Postcommunio* (postcommunion).

Every hit was read in context. The following orders were examined and are not printed:

| Order | Why not printed |
|---|---|
| Luther, *Deutsche Messe*, 1526 (Sehling 1, doc 3) | No Canon or Ordinary prayers (see [§7.3.6](#s7-3-6)). |
| Homberg, *Reformatio ecclesiarum Hassiae*, 1526 (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, doc 2247, pp. 44–45) | Rules only: "Let that Canon of the Mass, and all the prayers in which the word sacrifice or victim is found, be said by no one any more at this Supper". Luther's German Mass is prescribed. |
| Braunschweig 1528, Hamburg 1529 / Lübeck 1531, Pomerania 1535 (Bugenhagen) | Latin Preface and Sanctus on feasts only, otherwise as [§7.15](#s7-15). |
| Heilbronn 1530 (Sehling 17, doc 770, pp. 276–277) | Quotes *Te igitur* (Thee therefore), *Quam oblationem* (Which oblation) and *Supra quae* (Upon which) only to refute them. |
| Transylvania, Honterus, 1543/47 (Sehling 24, docs 1669–1670) | "the Canon being rejected": Preface, Sanctus, Our Father and Verba, with the Saxon *custodiat* (1547). |
| Corvinus, *Kirchenordnung* 1542 (Sehling 21, doc 1460) | Luther's paraphrase and the Verba. The distribution "Take, eat and remember …" is Strasbourg's "Gedenckent, glaubent" (Remember, believe) type ([§7.5.2](#s7-5-2); Moderate Reformed), not the *custodiat* (preserve). |
| Schwäbisch Hall 1543 (Sehling 17, doc 762) and its communion of the sick, 1537 (doc 761) | *Custodiat* (Preserve) only ("The body of our Lord Christ preserve thee unto everlasting life"). |
| Later Upper German orders, e.g. Sehling 16, V, 1560 (doc 742), after Basel 1526 (Reformed) | A prayer before communion that echoes the *Perceptio*: "that we may receive thy Supper not unto judgement, but unto everlasting life". |
| Reformed orders (Kurpfalz from 1563, Anhalt, Hessen-Kassel, à Lasco) | No Canon prayers; the breaking of bread is a new rite ([§7.1.1](#s7-1-1)). |

### <a id="s7-2"></a>7.2 Nördlingen, Kaspar Kantz, *Von der Evangelischen Mesß*, 1522

*Von der Evangelischen Mesß. Mit schönen Christlichen Gebetten vor und nach der empfahung
des Sacraments. Durch Caspar Kantz von Nördlingen.* (Of the Evangelical Mass. With fine Christian prayers before and after the receiving of the Sacrament. By Caspar Kantz of Nördlingen.) Sehling 12, VIII.1, pp. 285–288
([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 369). Sehling's base text is the print of 1522. The apparatus gives the
changes of the second edition, *Die rechte evangelische und apostolische Mesß*, 1524
("II").

This is the earliest German evangelical Mass in the corpus. It is the source of the
Bremen Mass of 1525 ([§7.9](#s7-9)), and its opening prayers reappear in the Kiel Low German Mass
([§7.11](#s7-11)). The Mass has no offertory. In its place Kantz puts:

- an address and absolution;
- a recast *Orate fratres*;
- the *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) antiphon.

Then comes the common Preface and Sanctus. The Canon is cut down to one prayer, a recast
*Quam oblationem* (Which oblation) that flows into *Qui pridie* (Who the day before). The rubric in front of it says: "Only now
does the evangelical Mass begin".

#### <a id="s7-2-1"></a>7.2.1 Address, absolution and the recast *Orate fratres*

*First the priest, or another, shall make an exhortation concerning the sacrament, or else
say somewhat comfortable out of the holy Gospel, as the Spirit of God giveth it him, etc.
Thereafter he may address them that sit by with such or other words:*
Dearly beloved in Christ! That ye may with joyful and desirous hearts receive the tender
body and rose-coloured blood of our Saviour Jesus Christ, humble your hearts before God,
confess unto him your sins and infirmities with hearty desire, and long after his divine
grace and help!
So will I now, your chosen priest, impart unto you the holy absolution, and pray God for
you.
The almighty and merciful God forgive you your sins! And I, by the commandment of our Lord
Jesus Christ, in the stead of the holy Church, pronounce you free, quit and loosed of all
your sins, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen.
But forasmuch as I also am burdened with manifold infirmities, pray God faithfully for me,
that I may diligently perform and finish this his service to his praise, to your comfort
and mine, and to our salvation.
Psalm 123: Our help shall be in the name of the Lord, who hath made heaven and earth.

**Note.**

- **The absolution.** Sehling's note: it is put together from the *Indulgentiam* (Pardon) at the
  beginning of the Mass and the absolution of private confession.
- **The request for prayer.** "But forasmuch as I also am burdened … therefore pray God faithfully for me" is, in Sehling's words, a "free recasting of the *Orate, fratres*".
  The Roman request is "that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable". Here the priest
  asks for help to perform "this his service".
- **The versicle.** *Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini* (Our help is in the name of the Lord; Ps 124:8, numbered 123 in the
  Vulgate) belongs to the prayers at the foot of the altar.
- **The 1524 edition** drops the lay minister ("or another") and the psalm verse, and
  heads the absolution "The absolution".

#### <a id="s7-2-2"></a>7.2.2 *Veni Sancte Spiritus* and collect (in place of *Veni sanctificator*)

*Thereafter the priest shall kneel down and say:*
Now let us pray; say ye all secretly with me:
Come, Holy Ghost, fill the hearts of thy faithful, and kindle in them the fire of thy
divine love, who through the diversity of tongues hast gathered the peoples of the whole
world in the unity of the faith. Alleluia.
O Lord, almighty God, grant that thy Holy Ghost may be and dwell with us, that he may
enlighten us and teach us all truth, and defend and strengthen us in all adversity;
through Christ our Lord! Amen.

**Note.**

- **The antiphon.** This is the Whitsun Vigil antiphon *Veni, Sancte Spiritus, reple
  tuorum corda fidelium* (Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of thy faithful). Sehling notes that the diocese of Augsburg prayed it in the Mass
  in place of the offertory prayer *Veni, sanctificator*. The rubric keeps the posture of
  the offertory prayers (kneeling, "secretly") but has the whole congregation say them.
- **The collect.** This is not a Roman offertory prayer. It resembles the Whitsuntide
  collect "May the power of the Holy Spirit be present with us, we beseech thee, O Lord, … and defend us from all adversities", with "teach all truth" from John 16:13. The same collect opens the Bremen
  ([§7.9](#s7-9)) and Kiel ([§7.11](#s7-11)) Masses.

#### <a id="s7-2-3"></a>7.2.3 Preface and Sanctus

*The Preface, or foreword of the Mass:*
Lift up your hearts unto God, and let us give thanks unto God our Lord; for that is meet
and right! Yea, verily it is meet and right, and also wholesome, that we should in all
places and at all times give thanks unto thee, O Lord, holy Father, almighty, everlasting
God, through Christ our Lord, through whom all angels and the heavenly powers worship,
honour and praise thy glorious majesty. With the same, we beseech thee, vouchsafe to admit
and receive our voice, that we also may praise thee and say without end:
*Sanctus:*
Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; heaven and earth are full of thy glory. Hosanna in
the highest! Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Luck and salvation in the
highest!

**Note.**

- **The dialogue.** It is reduced to the priest's words, with the responses run in: *Sursum
  corda … Gratias agamus … Dignum et iustum est* (Lift up your hearts … Let us give thanks … It is meet and right).
- **The Preface.** This is the common Preface ("It is very meet … through Christ our Lord. Through whom the Angels praise thy majesty, the Dominions adore … with whom we pray thee that thou wouldest bid our voices also to be admitted"). The ranks of angels are merged into "all angels and the heavenly powers".
- **The Sanctus.** The second *Hosanna* is rendered "luck and salvation" (Ps 118:25, "O Lord,
  send now prosperity").

#### <a id="s7-2-4"></a>7.2.4 *Quam oblationem* and *Qui pridie*

*Here beginneth first the evangelical Mass.*
O most gracious Father, merciful, everlasting God, grant that this bread and the wine may
become and be unto us the true body and the innocent blood of thy most dear Son, our Lord
Jesus Christ; who on the day before his passion took the bread into his holy hands, looked
up to heaven unto thee, his almighty Father, gave thanks, blessed, and brake the bread, and
gave it to his disciples, saying: Take, and eat! This is my body, which is given for you.
Likewise after the supper he took the cup into his holy hands, gave thanks, blessed, and
gave it to his disciples, and said:
Take, and drink ye all of it! This is the cup of the new and everlasting testament in my
blood, which is shed for you and for many for the remission of sins. As oft as ye do this,
do it in remembrance of me!

**Note.**

- **The rubric.** "Now first beginneth the evangelical Mass": everything before is
  preparation. The Canon proper begins here, with the one Canon prayer that is kept.
- **The recast *Quam oblationem*.** Sehling calls it "the prayer after the conclusion of the
  Canon prayer *Quam oblationem*". The Roman text is "Which oblation do thou, O God, vouchsafe, we beseech thee, in all things to make blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable and acceptable, that it may become for us the Body and Blood of thy most beloved Son our Lord Jesus Christ". Kantz
  keeps the petition *ut nobis … fiat* (that for us … it may become) and the superlative *dilectissimi* (most beloved). He drops the
  oblation and its five adjectives. The object becomes "this bread and the wine".
- ***Qui pridie*** keeps *elevatis oculis in caelum ad te Deum Patrem suum omnipotentem* (with eyes lifted up to heaven unto thee, God, his almighty Father)
  ("he looked up to heaven unto thee, his almighty Father"), both *benedixit* (blessed), and *novi et
  aeterni testamenti* (of the new and eternal testament). It drops *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith).
  - "for you and for many" is *pro vobis et pro multis* (for you and for many).
  - "As oft as ye do this, so do it in my remembrance" is *Haec quotiescumque feceritis, in
    mei memoriam facietis* (As often as ye shall do these things, ye shall do them in remembrance of me).
- **The 1524 edition** has "supper" for "evening meal", and "into his worthy hands, but giveth thanks, blesseth it" (*venerabiles manus*).

#### <a id="s7-2-5"></a>7.2.5 Our Father with the conclusion of the embolism; *Agnus Dei*; *Fili Dei vivi*

Let us pray:
Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come! Thy will be done,
as in heaven, so in earth! Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as
we forgive our debtors! And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil! Through
our Lord Jesus, thy Son, who with thee and the Holy Ghost, one true God, liveth and
reigneth for ever. Amen.
*Agnus Dei:*
O thou Lamb of God, that bearest the sin of the world, have mercy upon us and give us thy
peace! Amen.
*A devout prayer before the receiving of the sacrament:*
O Lord Jesu Christ, thou everlasting Word of the Father, thou Saviour of the world, thou
true, living God and man, deliver us by this thy holy body and rose-coloured blood from all
sins! Help us that we may fulfil thy commandments at all times, and never be parted from
thee for ever! Amen.

**Note.**

- **The end of the embolism.** As at Worms ([§7.6.10](#s7-6-10); Moderate Reformed), the Our Father runs
  straight into the conclusion of *Libera nos, quaesumus* (Deliver us, we beseech thee; "Through the same Jesus Christ our Lord, thy Son, who liveth and reigneth with thee in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God"). The body
  of the embolism is gone.
- **The fraction, in the 1524 edition only.** The 1524 edition adds the doxology "for thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever. Amen." It then adds a rubric before
  the conclusion:

  *Here let the priest take the bread and break it, as much as he needeth, and say:*

  - **Where the rubric falls.** Sehling's note 7 points out that the Roman fraction came at
    these same words, at the end of the embolism. There the priest broke the host in
    three and dropped one piece into the chalice. In 1524 the conclusion "Through our Lord …" stands isolated after the doxology's *Amen*, so the breaking marks the old
    place.
  - **Was it new in 1524?** Sehling judges (notes 7–9) that the 1522 edition did not know
    the fraction. There the priest shows "a host", any host, while in 1524 he shows
    "the [host]", the host just broken.
  - **No commixture.** Neither edition drops a piece into the cup.
- **The *Agnus Dei*.** It is sung once, with *dona nobis pacem* (grant us peace).
- ***Fili Dei vivi*.** The prayer before communion is an abridged "O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, … deliver me by this thy most holy Body and Blood from all mine iniquities and from all evils, and make me always to cleave to thy commandments, and suffer me never to be separated from thee".
  - The opening clause (*qui ex voluntate Patris …*, who by the will of the Father …) gives way to a string of titles.
  - The prayer is plural throughout.
  - The 1524 edition heads it "Oratio" (Prayer).

#### <a id="s7-2-6"></a>7.2.6 Communion, with the *custodiat* and *Calicem salutaris*

*After this prayer let the priest receive the sacrament, if he be otherwise prepared
thereto, and then take a host in his hand, show or point it to the communicants, and say
thus:*
Behold, dearly beloved, this is verily the holy body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which
suffered for you the bitter death. Take and eat it, that it may feed, nourish and preserve
you unto everlasting life! Amen. Peace be with you all!
*When he hath now communicated them all with the holy body of Christ, let him say thus:*
Let us also drink the cup of salvation and call upon the name of our Lord!
*And when he hath drunk, he shall turn him to them with the chalice or cup, and say thus:*
Behold, this is verily the precious treasure of the costly blood of our Lord Jesus Christ,
wherewith ye are bought. Take it, and divide it among you, to the washing away of your
sins!

**Note.**

- **"Behold …".** The showing of the host with "Behold" takes the place of the elevation
  (Sehling: "The elevation, which Kantz has thus moved from the act of consecration into the communion"). It also recalls the *Ecce Agnus Dei* (Behold the Lamb of God) of the late-medieval communion of the people.
- **"… that he feed, nourish and preserve you unto everlasting life"** is the *custodiat* (preserve) formula
  ("The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life"), spoken to
  all at once.
- **"The peace be with you all".** The *Pax Domini* (The peace of the Lord) has moved from before the *Agnus
  Dei* (Lamb of God) to the communion. The 1524 edition makes it "The peace be with thee!", said to each
  communicant.
- **"Let us also drink the cup of salvation …"** is the priest's *Calicem salutaris
  accipiam, et nomen Domini invocabo* (I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord; Ps 116:13), from his prayers at the sumption. It
  is turned into a plural invitation.
- **The cup.** "divide it among you" echoes Luke 22:17.

#### <a id="s7-2-7"></a>7.2.7 Thanksgiving: *Nunc dimittis*, *Te Deum*, collects

*When that is done, the priest shall kneel down and give thanks:*
O Lord, now lettest thou thy servants depart in peace according to thy word; for our eyes
have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples, a light
to lighten the Gentiles, and to be the glory of thy people Israel. Unto thee be praise,
honour and thanks, O thou holy, blessed, glorious Trinity, God the Father, Son and Holy
Ghost! Amen.
*Item, for thanksgiving one may say:*
Te Deum laudamus. We praise thee, O God; we acknowledge thee to be the Lord. […]
Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word […]. Glory be to
the Father, etc., as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end.
Amen.
O gracious and merciful God, the strength of all that hope in thee, help us so to walk
through things temporal that we lose not the things eternal; through Christ our Lord.
Amen.
O thou holy Trinity, let our praise and thanksgiving be well-pleasing unto thee! Make firm
and steadfast the work which thou hast wrought in us! Grant that it may be fruitful and
profitable unto us unto everlasting life! Amen.

**Note.**

- **The *Nunc dimittis*.** Made plural ("thy servants", "our eyes"). Sehling notes it
  was among the priest's silent prayers at this point in some German churches.
- **The first collect.** Sehling identifies it as the collect of the third Sunday after
  Pentecost, "O God, the protector of all that trust in thee … that we may so pass through things temporal that we lose not the things eternal", not a postcommunion.
- **The Trinity prayer is the *Placeat*.** Sehling thought it "probably composed by Kantz".
  It is in fact the priest's last prayer of the Roman Mass, said before the blessing:
  "May the homage of my bounden duty be pleasing to thee, O holy Trinity; and grant that the sacrifice which I, unworthy, have offered in the sight of thy majesty may be acceptable to thee, and through thy mercy be a propitiation for me and for all those for whom I have offered it".
  - "let our praise and thanksgiving be well pleasing to thee" is *placeat tibi … obsequium* (may the homage … be pleasing to thee).
  - The sacrifice offered becomes "the work which thou hast wrought in us": God's work in
    us, not ours before him.
  - "fruitful and profitable … unto everlasting life" takes the place of *propitiabile* (a propitiation).
- **What follows.** The order ends by permitting the Latin *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) and the Magnificat
  "for thanksgiving". There is no blessing.

---

### <a id="s7-3"></a>7.3 Wittenberg, Luther, *Formula missae et communionis*, 1523

Sehling 1, Martin Luther's Ordnungen Nr. 4, pp. 4–9 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 2; the database dates
the document 1889, the year of Sehling's volume). The order is in Latin. It is included
because it is the model the German Masses answer to. Brandenburg 1540 ([§7.12](#s7-12)) takes its Latin
communion prayers from the permissions given here. The Nürnberg Latin order of 1524 ([§7.7.1](#s7-7-1))
takes its shortened Preface from it.

Luther states the rule first: everything that "sounds of oblation", with the whole Canon,
is to go. What is "pure and holy" stays. The paragraphs below are numbered as in the
print.

#### <a id="s7-3-1"></a>7.3.1 The rule, and the preparation of bread and wine

Eighthly, there followeth all that abomination, to which everything that went before in
the Mass was forced to serve, whence also it is called the offertory. And from here on
almost everything soundeth and savoureth of oblation. […] Therefore, all those things being
rejected which sound of oblation, together with the whole Canon, let us retain those things
which are pure and holy, and so begin our Mass.
I. During the Creed, or after the canon [*sermon*], let bread and wine be made ready for the blessing
in the accustomed manner; save that I have not yet determined with myself whether water be
to be mixed with the wine, though I incline to this, that pure wine rather be prepared
without the mixture of water […]. Yet I will not bring in a superstitious law against
liberty.

**Note.**

- **"post canonem" (after the canon).** This is Sehling's reading. The Weimar edition (WA 12, 211) reads
  *post concionem*, "after the sermon". That fits the paragraph before, which lets the
  vernacular sermon come after the Creed.
- **What goes.** The offertory prayers (*Suscipe, sancte Pater*; *Offerimus tibi*; *Veni,
  sanctificator*; *Suscipe, sancta Trinitas*), the *Orate fratres*, the Secret and the
  whole Canon, as all "sounding of oblation".
- **What stays** is set out in §§II–VIII below.

#### <a id="s7-3-2"></a>7.3.2 Preface, Verba, Sanctus with elevation

II. The bread and wine being made ready, let him straightway proceed after this manner:
"The Lord be with you"; answer, "And with thy spirit". "Lift up your hearts"; answer, "Let
us lift them up unto the Lord". "Let us give thanks unto the Lord our God". Answer: "It is
meet and right. It is very meet and right, fitting and wholesome, that we should at all
times and in all places give thanks unto thee, O Lord, holy Father, almighty, everlasting
God, through Christ our Lord".
III. Then: "Who the day before he suffered took bread, giving thanks, brake it, and gave it
to his disciples, saying: Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you. Likewise also
the cup, after he had supped, saying: This cup is the new testament in my blood, which
shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins. As oft as ye shall do these
things, ye shall do them in remembrance of me."
These words of Christ I would have recited, after a short pause interposed after the
Preface, in that tone of voice in which the Lord's Prayer is otherwise sung in the Canon,
so that they may be heard by them that stand about; although in all these things let
godly minds have liberty to recite those words either silently or aloud.
IV. The blessing being ended, let the choir sing the Sanctus, and during the singing of the
Benedictus let the bread and cup be elevated after the rite hitherto kept, chiefly for the
sake of the weak, who might perhaps be offended by a sudden change of this more notable
rite in the Mass, especially where they have been taught by sermons in the vulgar tongue
what is sought by that elevation.

**Note.**

- **The Preface.** It is cut off after *per Christum Dominum nostrum* (through Christ our Lord). The Verba follow as a
  relative clause on *Christum* (Christ; "Qui pridie …"). This is the form Nürnberg took up in 1524
  ([§7.7.1](#s7-7-1)) and the German orders of Volprecht ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)) and Döber ([§7.8.2](#s7-8-2)) translated.
- ***Qui pridie*** is reduced to the Gospel and Pauline wording.
  - Gone are *in sanctas ac venerabiles manus suas* (into his holy and venerable hands), *elevatis oculis* (with eyes lifted up), *benedixit* (blessed),
    *aeterni* (eternal) and *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith).
  - "which is given for you" (Luke 22:19) and "this cup is the new testament in my blood"
    (1 Cor 11:25) come from Scripture, not the Missal.
- **"benedictio" (blessing).** Luther calls the recitation of the Verba the "benedictio".
- **The Sanctus and elevation.** The Sanctus, which in the Roman Mass comes before the
  Canon, is moved after the Verba. The elevation is kept "with the rite kept hitherto", during
  the *Benedictus*.

#### <a id="s7-3-3"></a>7.3.3 Our Father; no embolism, no fraction; the Peace as absolution

V. After these things let the Lord's Prayer be read, thus: "Let us pray. Taught by
wholesome precepts, etc.", the prayer following, "Deliver us, we beseech thee", being
omitted, with all the signs that are wont to be made over the host and with the host over
the chalice; and let the host not be broken, nor mixed into the chalice. But straightway
after the Lord's Prayer let there be said "The peace of the Lord, etc.", which is a kind of
public absolution from the sins of the communicants, a voice plainly evangelical,
announcing remission of sins, that one and most worthy preparation for the Lord's table,
if it be laid hold on by faith, no otherwise than as spoken from the mouth of Christ.
Wherefore I would have it announced with the face turned to the people, as bishops are
wont to do, which is the only trace of the ancient bishops left in our bishops.

**Note.**

- **The embolism** ("Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord, from all evils …", Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord, from all evils …) is struck out, with its
  signs of the cross made over the host and the chalice with a fragment.
- **The fraction and commixture are forbidden.** "let the host not be broken nor mixed into the chalice". Worms 1524 (Moderate Reformed) repeats this in German ([§7.6.11](#s7-6-11)). Of the evangelical
  orders in the corpus, only Kantz's second edition (1524, [§7.2.5](#s7-2-5)) and Müntzer's Allstedt order
  ([§7.4.2](#s7-4-2); Radical Reformation) break the bread at this point.
- **The Peace.** *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you) is reinterpreted as a public absolution. Worms
  (Moderate Reformed) and Brandenburg keep it in that sense.

#### <a id="s7-3-4"></a>7.3.4 Communion: *Agnus Dei*, *Fili Dei vivi*, *custodiat*

VI. Then let him communicate first himself, then the people; meanwhile let the Agnus Dei be
sung. But if he will pray before the sumption that prayer, "O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the
living God, who by the will of the Father, etc.", he shall not pray amiss, only changing
the singular number into the plural, "our" and "us" for "my" and "me". Likewise also that
other: "The body of the Lord, etc., preserve my soul, or thy soul, unto life eternal". And
"The blood of our Lord preserve thy soul unto life eternal".

**Note.**

- **What is permitted.** Of the three prayers before the priest's communion, only
  *Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi* (O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God) is allowed, and it is made plural. *Domine Iesu
  Christe, qui dixisti* (O Lord Jesus Christ, who saidst) and *Perceptio corporis* (Let the receiving of [thy] body) are not mentioned. Brandenburg 1540
  nevertheless kept all three ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)).
- **The *custodiat*.** It serves both for the priest ("meam") and for each communicant
  ("tuam").
- **The *Agnus Dei*.** It is sung during communion, not before it.

#### <a id="s7-3-5"></a>7.3.5 Communion chant; *Quod ore sumpsimus* and *Corpus tuum* for the postcommunion;
*Benedicamus*; blessing

VII. If it please them to sing the communion, let it be sung. But in the place of the
complenda or last collect, because they almost all sound of sacrifice, let that prayer be
read in the same tone: "What we have taken with our mouth, O Lord". That other also may be
read: "Thy body, O Lord, which we have received, etc.", the number being changed into the
plural. "Who livest and reignest, etc." "The Lord be with you, etc." In the place of "Ite,
missa est" (Go, it is the dismissal) let there be said "Let us bless the Lord", with Alleluia added (where and when it
pleaseth) in its own melodies; or let the Benedicamus be borrowed from Vespers.
VIII. Let the accustomed blessing be given. Or let that of Numbers 6 be taken, which the
Lord himself appointed, saying: "The Lord bless us and keep us, show us his face and have
mercy upon us; the Lord turn his face unto us and give us peace." Or that of Psalm 96
[67]: "God, even our own God, bless us; God bless us, and let all the ends of the earth
fear him. Amen."

**Note.**

- **The postcommunion.** The variable postcommunions (*complenda*) are rejected because
  "they almost all sound of sacrifice". The two priest's prayers said at the ablutions
  take their place, read aloud in the collect tone:
  - "What we have taken with our mouth, O Lord, may we receive with a pure mind; and from a temporal gift may it become for us an everlasting remedy";
  - "Thy Body, O Lord, which I have taken, and thy Blood, which I have drunk, cleave unto my inmost parts …", made plural.

  Brandenburg 1540 and Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 kept both in Latin ([§7.12.8](#s7-12-8), [§7.14.8](#s7-14-8)). Volprecht ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2))
  and Strasbourg ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1); Moderate Reformed) turned *Quod ore* (What with our mouth) into German.
- ***Benedicamus Domino*** replaces *Ite, missa est*.
- **The blessing.** Luther's use of Numbers 6 is the origin of the Aaronic blessing at the end
  of the Lutheran Mass.

#### <a id="s7-3-6"></a>7.3.6 The *Deutsche Messe* of 1526 (for comparison)

Luther's German Mass (Sehling 1, Nr. 8; doc 3) keeps none of the Canon or of the priest's
prayers:

- **In place of the Canon** stands a public paraphrase of the Our Father, with an
  admonition to the communicants: "After the sermon shall follow a public paraphrase of the Our Father and an admonition to them that will go to the sacrament …".
- **The Verba.** Luther suggested giving the bread straight after the bread-word, "before the cup is blessed", and the cup after the cup-word.
- **The elevation** is kept: "The elevation we will not do away but keep, because it agreeth well with the German Sanctus …".
- **No fraction, no *Pax*.**
- **The thanksgiving** is a new collect, "We give thanks to thee, almighty Lord God, that thou hast refreshed us through this salutary gift …". Bugenhagen's orders ([§7.15](#s7-15)) and Brandenburg
  1540 ([§7.12.8](#s7-12-8)) carry it.

This is why most Lutheran orders after 1526 have no Canon remnants. The orders in this file
are those that, like the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass), kept something of the old text.

---

### <a id="s7-4"></a>7.4 Allstedt, Thomas Müntzer, *Deutsch evangelisch Messe*, 1524, and *Ordnung des teutschen ampts*, 1523/24

- **The Mass.** *Deutsch evangelisch messze, etwan durch die Bebstischen pfaffen im latein
  zu grossem nachteil des Christen glaubens vor ein opffer gehandelt …* (German evangelical Mass, formerly handled by the papist priests in Latin as a sacrifice, to the great harm of the Christian faith …) Sehling 1, Nr. 46,
  pp. 497–503 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 51). It gives five Masses (Advent, Christmas, Passion, Easter,
  Whitsun) with their propers set to the old chant. The ordinary is printed in full with
  the first, the Advent Mass, on pp. 500–501. It is given here.
- **The commentary.** *Ordnung und berechnunge des teutschen ampts zu Alstadt*, 1523,
  printed at Allstedt 1524. Sehling 1, Nr. 47, pp. 504–506 (doc 52). It explains the Mass
  item by item and gives the rubrics the Mass itself lacks.

Müntzer was no Lutheran but a leader of the Radical Reformation; yet his German Mass is the most
conservative in the corpus in wording. It keeps:

- the offertory chant, with the Secret's *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (World without end);
- the full proper Preface;
- the Roman *Qui pridie* (Who the day before) with *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith);
- the end of the embolism, with the fraction (per the *Ordnung* [order]);
- *Pax Domini* (The peace of the Lord).

His wording was taken over in the Lippe Mass ([§7.10](#s7-10)), the Kiel Low German Mass ([§7.11](#s7-11)) and,
for the Preface dialogue, Calenberg-Göttingen 1542 ([§7.13](#s7-13)).

#### <a id="s7-4-1"></a>7.4.1 Offertory, Preface, Sanctus (Advent)

O Lord, unto thee have I lifted up my soul; O God, my God, in thee I trust, and shall not
be put to shame, that mine enemies mock me not; world without end. Amen. The Lord be with
you. And with thy spirit. Our hearts on high. We have them unto the Lord. We give thanks
unto the Lord our God. It is worthy and it is right. Verily it is meet and right and it is
wholesome that we should at all times and in all places give thanks unto thee, O Lord,
holy Father, almighty, everlasting God. For thou hast received thy holy manhood of the
Virgin Mary by the overshadowing of the Holy Ghost, that she with unblemished chastity
brought forth unto the world the everlasting light, Jesus Christ our Lord. Through whom the
angels praise thy glory, and the angels in whom thou reignest do thee honour; the mighty
angels tremble; and the heavens and the powers of the heavens and the holy seraphim praise
thee without ceasing with one accord of joy. Therefore we beseech thee, O Lord, that thou
wouldest let our voices be admitted with them, that we may praise thee with true
confession without end, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth. Heaven and earth are
filled with thy praise. Hosanna in the highest. Blessed be he that cometh in the name of
the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.

**Note.**

- **The offertory chant.** "O Lord, unto thee have I lifted up my soul …" is the offertory
  chant of the first Sunday of Advent, *Ad te, Domine, levavi animam meam: Deus meus, in
  te confido, non erubescam: neque irrideant me inimici mei* (Unto thee, O Lord, have I lifted up my soul: O my God, I trust in thee; let me not be ashamed, neither let mine enemies triumph over me; Ps 25:1–2). The *Ordnung* (order) says
  "We hold no sacrifice in the secret of God": the offertory prayers are gone, but not the
  chant.
- **"through all eternity of eternity. Amen."** This is *Per omnia saecula saeculorum.
  Amen*, the audible end of the silent Secret, which led into the Preface dialogue. The
  Secret itself is gone; its last words remain. The same place in Lippe ([§7.10](#s7-10)) has it as the
  first words of the "Prefatio" (Preface), and Göttingen 1542 ([§7.13](#s7-13)) has "God be praised from eternity to eternity. Amen."
- **The Preface** is the Preface of the Blessed Virgin, not the Advent or Christmas
  Preface. Its text is "And on the [feast] of the blessed Mary ever Virgin to praise thee … who conceived thine only-begotten Son by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and, the glory of her virginity remaining, shed forth upon the world the eternal light, Jesus Christ our Lord. Through whom the Angels praise thy majesty, the Dominions adore, the Powers tremble. The heavens and the Virtues of the heavens and the blessed Seraphim celebrate it together with joy".
  - Müntzer takes out the praise of Mary. God himself becomes the subject: "thou [hast] received thy holy humanity …".
  - The Virgin's *virginitatis gloria permanente* (the glory of her virginity remaining) becomes "with unbroken chastity".
  - The ranks of angels are rendered one by one: *Dominationes* (Dominions) "the angels, wherein thou reignest"; *tremunt Potestates* (the Powers tremble) "the mighty angels were astonished".
- **"with true confession"** is *supplici confessione* (with humble confession).

#### <a id="s7-4-2"></a>7.4.2 The Verba, the Our Father, the end of the embolism, the Peace, *Agnus Dei*

The day before, when Jesus would suffer, he took the bread into his holy hands, and lifted
up his eyes to heaven unto thee, God, his almighty Father, and gave thanks unto thee, and
blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take, and eat thereof. This
is my body, which is given for you. In like manner, when they had eaten, he took the cup
into his holy and worthy hands, and gave thanks unto thee, and blessed it, and gave it to
his disciples, saying: Take, and drink ye all thereof. This is the cup of my blood of the
new and everlasting covenant, a mystery of faith, which is shed for you and for many for
the forgiveness of sins. As oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby. Therefore let
us all pray, as Jesus Christ, the Son of God, hath taught us, saying: Our Father, which art
in the heavens, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, as in heaven, so
on earth. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we forgive our
debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen. World without
end. Amen. The peace of the Lord be alway with you. And with thy spirit. O Lamb of God,
which beareth the sin of the world, have mercy upon us. O Lamb of God, which beareth the
sin of the world, give us thy peace.

**Note.**

- **The Verba are the Roman *Qui pridie*, not the Scriptural text.** "One day before, when Jesus would suffer" is *Qui pridie quam pateretur* (Who the day before he suffered). The following are all kept:
  - *in sanctas ac venerabiles manus suas* ("into his holy [worthy] hands");
  - *elevatis oculis in caelum ad te Deum Patrem suum omnipotentem* ("lifted up his eyes to heaven unto thee, God his almighty Father");
  - *tibi gratias agens* ("gave thanks to thee"), still addressed to the Father in the second
    person;
  - *benedixit* ("blessed it");
  - *Accipite et manducate ex hoc omnes* ("eat thereof");
  - *novi et aeterni testamenti* ("of the new and eternal covenant");
  - ***mysterium fidei*** ("a mystery of the faith");
  - *Haec quotiescumque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis* (As often as ye shall do these things, ye shall do them in remembrance of me).

  Only "which is given for you" (Luke 22:19) is added. The *Ordnung* (order; below) has the
  same text, with crosses at the two blessings.
- **"Therefore let us all pray, as Jesus Christ … hath taught us, saying"** is
  *Oremus: Praeceptis salutaribus moniti, et divina institutione formati, audemus
  dicere* (Let us pray: Admonished by saving precepts and formed by divine institution, we make bold to say).
- **"Through all eternity of eternity. Amen."** after the Our Father is *Per omnia
  saecula saeculorum. Amen* (World without end. Amen), the sung ending of the embolism *Libera nos* (Deliver us). The embolism is
  gone and its ending stays. The *Ordnung* puts the fraction here ([§7.4.3](#s7-4-3)).
- **"The peace of the Lord be always with you. And with thy spirit"** is *Pax Domini sit
  semper vobiscum. Et cum spiritu tuo* (The peace of the Lord be always with you. And with thy spirit), with the Roman response.
- **The *Agnus Dei*** is printed twice in the Mass and three times in the *Ordnung*.

#### <a id="s7-4-3"></a>7.4.3 The Allstedt *Ordnung* on the Sacrament: Verba, elevation, fraction

Ninthly: Then is sung the form of the consecration, or of the supper, in the tone of the
Preface, according to these words following: The day before, when Jesus would suffer, he
took the bread into his holy and worthy hands, and lifted up his eyes to heaven unto thee,
God, his almighty Father, gave thanks unto thee, and blessed ✠ it, and brake it, and gave
it to his disciples, saying: Take, and eat ye all thereof. *Lifting it up with his hand he
saith:* This is my body, which is given for you. *The minister turning, and taking the cup,
saith before the people:* In like manner, when they had eaten, he took the cup into his holy
and worthy hands, and gave thanks unto thee, and blessed ✠ it, and gave it to his
disciples, saying: This is the cup of my blood, of the new and everlasting testament, a
mystery of faith, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. *Turning
again to the altar he saith:* As oft and often as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby,
etc.
Tenthly. Soon after the elevation one singeth straightway in the same tone thus: Therefore
let us all pray, as Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, hath taught us, saying: Our Father,
which art in the heavens, etc.; and all the people sing thereupon: Amen. Thereafter it
becometh still a little while, to take breath, during which time the priest divideth the
sacrament for the sake of the communicants, and singeth: World without end. Then the
common people answer: Amen. The priest again: The peace of the Lord be alway with you.
Then the people answer: And with thy spirit. Soon after this, that a mystery of God, the
death and resurrection of Christ, may be considered, and to explain the same further, all
the people sing the witness of John the Baptist of Christ three times: O Lamb of God, which
takest away the sin of the world, etc.; thereto is sung out of the Gospel, Luke 17: Have
mercy upon us; and at the last: Give us thy peace. […] Upon such faith the people are then
given the most worthy sacrament under the Agnus Dei, without the popish hypocritical
confession.

**Note.**

- **The fraction.** "during which time the priest, for the communicants' sake, divideth the sacrament and singeth: Through all eternity of eternity". This is exactly the
  Roman place and manner: the priest broke the host during the last words of the embolism
  and sang *Per omnia saecula saeculorum* (World without end) over the broken host before the *Pax*.
  - **The reason is new.** The priest breaks "for the communicants' sake", for the sake of
    the communicants, to share the bread. It is not a rite of the Mass for its own sake.
  - **No commixture** is mentioned.
  - Luther had forbidden the fraction in the same year ([§7.3.3](#s7-3-3)).
- **"termung".** This is Müntzer's word for the consecration ("the words of the termung";
  "the consecration a termung, which happeneth not by one alone but by the whole assembled congregation"). Sehling does not gloss it.
- **The elevation.** The bread is elevated at the bread-word ("Elevando manu"). The cup is
  shown to the people ("coram vulgo").
- **Communion** is given during the *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God), "without the papist, hypocritical confession".
  The *Ordnung* (order) adds that after communion "one giveth thanks to God over the people and blesseth the Lord etc.": the postcommunion and the *Benedicamus* ([§7.4.4](#s7-4-4)).

#### <a id="s7-4-4"></a>7.4.4 Postcommunion and *Benedicamus* (Advent Mass)

O Lord God, stand hard by us, that we may make renunciation of our grievous vices,
forasmuch as we have bound ourselves irrevocably unto thee through the spirit of Christ,
thy Son, by this holy sign of his tender flesh and precious blood; who with thee liveth
and reigneth in the unity of the Holy Ghost, etc.
Let us bless the Lord. Thanks be to God for ever.

**Note.**

- **The postcommunion.** It is not a Roman text. The sacrament as a "holy sign" of
  a covenant bond fits Müntzer's teaching. "Tender flesh and precious blood" are the
  vocabulary of late-medieval eucharistic devotion (compare Kantz's "tender body and rose-coloured blood", [§7.2.1](#s7-2-1)).
- ***Benedicamus Domino / Deo gratias*** replaces *Ite, missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal), as in the *Formula
  missae* (Form of the Mass).
- **The Whitsun postcommunion.** The other Masses have their own postcommunions. The Whitsun
  one ("O Lord, grant us the grace of the Holy Ghost, that the dew of thy goodness may make the ground of our hearts fruitful by its sprinkling", Sehling 1, 504) renders
  the Roman Whitsun postcommunion *Sancti Spiritus, Domine, corda nostra mundet infusio: et
  sui roris intima aspersione fecundet* (May the infusion of the Holy Spirit, O Lord, cleanse our hearts, and make them fruitful by the inward sprinkling of his dew). Calenberg-Göttingen 1542 took it over ([§7.13.4](#s7-13-4)).

---

### <a id="s7-5"></a>7.5 Strasbourg, the early German Masses, 1524–1525

Sehling 20, Straßburg, Nr. 3 "Die frühen Agenden" (The early agendas), pp. 120–162 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 1279). These are
Moderate Reformed orders: Strasbourg's Reformation under Bucer and Capito stood between
Wittenberg and Zurich until the Interim. Sehling prints six forms:

| | Form | Pages |
|---|---|---|
| a | Theobald (Diebold) Schwarz's manuscript agenda, "Anfang der evangelischen meß", 1524 | 120–123 |
| b | *Teutsche Meß und Tauff, wie sye yetzund zu Straßburg gehalten werden*, 1524 | 130–134 |
| c | *Ordenung und inhalt Teutscher Mess*, Augsburg reprint, 1524 | 135 |
| d | *Teutsch Kirchenampt mit lobgsengen*, 1524/25 | 136–141 |
| e | *Ordnung des Herren Nachtmal, so man die mesß nennet*, 1525 | 142–150 |
| f | *Straßburger kirchen ampt*, 1525 | 151–162 |

The Worms Mass ([§7.6](#s7-6)) is the Strasbourg Mass of 1524 in use at Worms. Its Canon prayers
(*Te igitur* to *Supplices*) are not in Schwarz's text. A later hand added one of them,
the *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful), to the manuscript, along with *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith; noted in [§7.5.1](#s7-5-1)). Döber took his optional intercession from
Strasbourg ([§7.8.11](#s7-8-11)).

Across these six forms the Canon is replaced step by step:

- **a–d:** a single intercession in the place of *Te igitur*, with the Verba and a short
  prayer after the elevation.
- **e (1525):** one long prayer "in place of the Canon" after a shortened common Preface and
  Sanctus. The Verba are read afterwards as a lesson, and there is no elevation.
- **f:** the same prayer, revised, with no Preface or Sanctus at all.

#### <a id="s7-5-1"></a>7.5.1 Schwarz's Mass, 1524 (form a)

*Turned toward the people let him say:* Dear brethren and sisters, pray God the Father,
through our Lord Jesus Christ, that he send us the Holy Ghost, the Comforter, that he may
make our bodies a living, holy, well-pleasing sacrifice, which is the reasonable service of
God that pleaseth God. May this befall us all, Amen.
*Toward the people, still standing, let him say:* The Lord be with you.
*The Preface*
Lift up your hearts. Let us give thanks unto the Lord our God. It becometh us truly, and is
meet, right and wholesome, that we should alway and in all places give thanks unto thee, O
Lord, holy, almighty Father, everlasting God, who hast wrought our salvation through the
wood of the cross, that life might come from thence whence death arose, and that the enemy
who by the transgression of the tree had overcome us all in Adam might be vanquished again
by the obedience rendered on the tree; through Christ Jesus our Lord, through whose majesty
and glory the angels and all the heavenly host praise thee, and together with like
exultation extol and magnify thee; with whom we pray thee to receive our voices also, with
humble confession, saying:
*Sanctus*
Sanctus. Holy, holy Lord, God of hosts, the heavens and earth are full of thy glory. Ah,
save us in the highest.
*Benedictus*
Praised be he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Ah, save us in the highest.

**Note.**

- **The bidding replaces the *Orate fratres*.** The Roman request that "my sacrifice and
  yours may be acceptable" becomes a prayer for the Spirit, who makes "our bodies" the
  sacrifice (Rom 12:1). The only sacrifice named is that of the worshippers.
- **The Preface** is the Preface of the Cross (Passiontide): "who didst set the salvation of mankind upon the tree of the Cross, that whence death arose, thence life might rise again, and that he who overcame by the tree might also by the tree be overcome, through Christ our Lord. Through whom the Angels praise thy majesty …". Form b prints further proper Prefaces (Christmas, Epiphany,
  Easter, Ascension, Whitsun) "for when thou hast read … Eternal God".
- **The Sanctus.** "Ah, make us blessed" and "Ah, bless us" translate *Hosanna*.

*Let the hands be washed. Silently. Then standing in the manner of one praying: With hands
lifted up, if it please:*
Almighty, merciful Father, forasmuch as thy Son, our Lord Jesus, hath promised that
whatsoever we ask in his name thou wilt grant us; and moreover, forasmuch as thy Spirit
also hath commanded that we should pray for our rulers: we pray thee from our hearts that
thou wouldest move the minds of the emperor, the princes and lords, and first of all of
our lords and superiors of the honourable Council, to the knowledge of thy goodness and of
the Gospel; and also that thou wouldest make all peoples subject to thy Son through the
Holy Ghost, that they themselves may willingly know, receive and keep his promise. And
above all grant unto this congregation that it may increase in the knowledge of the Gospel
and of his sweet yoke and easy burden. Forasmuch now, almighty, everlasting God, beloved and
merciful Father, —
Who on the next day before his passion took the bread into his holy hands, and gave thanks
unto thee, God, his heavenly Father, blessed it, brake it, and gave it to his disciples,
and said: Take, and eat. This is my body, which shall be given for you.
*At the cup:* Likewise after the supper he took the cup into his holy hands, and gave
thanks, and said: Take, and drink ye all thereof. This is the cup of my blood, of the new
and everlasting testament, which shall be shed for you and many for the forgiveness of
sins.
*The elevation of the cup:* As oft as ye do this, do it in remembrance of me.

**Note.**

- **The *lavabo*.** "Let the hands be washed. Silently" keeps the priest's washing of hands from the
  offertory, moved to after the Sanctus.
- **The posture.** "Levatis … manibus", "per modum orantis" (in the manner of one praying): the priest stands with raised
  hands, as for the Canon.
- **The intercession replaces *Te igitur*.** It stands where *Te igitur* (Thee therefore) stood, and like
  *Te igitur* it prays for the Church and its rulers, with emperor and council in place of
  pope and bishop.
  - It breaks off at "Forasmuch now, almighty, eternal God, beloved and merciful Father," and the relative "Who" of *Qui pridie* (Who the day before) follows. The sentence is left
    unfinished in the manuscript. A second hand added a continuation (Sehling's apparatus
    q, later struck out): "O most gracious Father, thine only Son … which thou hast given to the world through Christ Jesus our Lord." This is the germ of the long 1525
    prayer ([§7.5.2](#s7-5-2)).
  - Döber prints the same intercession as an option "after the Preface or before the Sanctus" ([§7.8.11](#s7-8-11)). Form d calls it "Almighty, merciful Father, forasmuch as thy Son …".
- ***Qui pridie*** keeps "on the next day before his suffering" (*pridie quam pateretur*),
  "blessed it" (*benedixit*) and *novi et aeterni testamenti* (of the new and eternal testament).
  - It adds "which shall be given for you" (1 Cor 11:24).
  - A later hand adds after the cup-word "The mystery of the faith", *mysterium
    fidei* (the mystery of faith).
  - The bread is not elevated. The cup is elevated at *Haec quotiescumque* (As often as).
- **Form b's rubrics.** Form b marks this passage "Beginning of the right, true Mass" and,
  after it, "End of the Mass or of the Supper of Christ, for the words that go before and after are all brought in to move and refresh faith, and not as the chief part of the Mass". That is: only the Verba are the Mass. All that stands before and after is
  there to move and refresh faith, and may be changed or left out.

*After the elevation*
How great is thy goodness, that without any merit of ours thou hast not only forgiven us
our sins, but hast left us for an assurance the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ
under the bread and wine; as thou hast alway witnessed all other promises besides with
outward signs. Therefore have we now great and irresistible assurance of thy grace, and
know that we are thy children, thine heirs and joint-heirs with Christ, and may freely
pray, as thine only-begotten Son hath taught us, and say:
Our Father, which art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be
done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our
debts, even as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from
evil, Amen.
Lord, deliver us from all enemies visible and invisible, from the devil, the world, and
from our own flesh; through Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.
*Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God)
Thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us.
Thou Lamb of God, grant us peace.

**Note.**

- **"Post elevationem" (After the elevation).** The prayer stands where *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful) stood, after the
  consecration. It thanks God for the body and blood left "under the bread and wine" as a
  pledge, and leads into the Our Father like *Praeceptis salutaribus* (Taught by saving precepts; "may freely pray" is *audemus dicere* [we make bold to say]).
- **The later hand at Strasbourg.** At this point it wrote into the margin the German
  *Unde et memores* that Worms prints: "Therefore, Lord, we thy servants, considering the … passion and death of the same thy Son, his resurrection from hell and also the glorious ascension into the heavens of thy divine majesty, offer therewith our humble prayer, whereon thou mayest look with gracious, cheerful eyes …" (compare [§7.6.8](#s7-6-8)).
  - It also corrected "the body and blood" to "the remembrance of the body and blood", and
    "under" to "in".
  - It added the doxology to the Our Father.
- **The embolism.** "Lord, deliver us from all visible and invisible enemies …" is
  the embolism reduced to one line. Döber has the same line ([§7.8.5](#s7-8-5)), and Sehling calls it
  there "remnant of the embolism". There is no fraction.

*A short exhortation to the people. The communion*
Let us pray: Lord Jesu Christ, thou Son of the living God, who by the Father's will and the
working of the Holy Ghost hast through thy death brought the world to life: deliver us by
this thy holy body and blood from all our iniquities and wickednesses, and grant that we
may alway obey thy commandments, and never for ever be separated from thee, Amen.
*The complenda*
Let us pray: What we have taken to us with the mouth, grant us, Lord, that we may receive
the same with a pure mind, and that of the temporal gift there may be made unto us an
everlasting medicine; through Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.
*Or some other which seemeth Christian.*
*To the people:* The Lord be with you.
*The blessing*
The blessing of God, the Father ✠ and the Son ✠ and the Holy Ghost ✠, be with us and remain
alway, Amen.

**Note.**

- ***Fili Dei vivi*** is said aloud as the prayer of all ("Let us pray") before the
  communion. Form b adds the rubric "Here both sacraments, the body and blood of the Lord under bread and wine, are distributed … to the people". Döber ([§7.8.8](#s7-8-8)) and the Kiel Mass ([§7.11](#s7-11))
  have the same German text, said by the people after the priest.
- **The *complenda*** is *Quod ore sumpsimus* (What we have taken with our mouth) in full. It is the "complenda" (completion) Luther had
  recommended ([§7.3.5](#s7-3-5)).
- **The blessing** keeps three crosses.
- **Form d** (the *Kirchenampt* [Church office]) adds after the *Agnus* a rubric for the exhortation: "wherein they press only on the fruitful remembrance and wholesome proclamation of the death of Christ". At the distribution the priest says "only the words of the Supper". Luther's
  "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) follows as the communion hymn, then the Aaronic blessing. The
  *complenda* is gone.

#### <a id="s7-5-2"></a>7.5.2 The *Ordnung des Herren Nachtmal*, 1525 (form e): the prayer "in place of the Canon"

*Thereafter the minister prepareth the chalice, and then speaketh to the people:*
Dear brethren and sisters, pray ye all God our Father that he send us his Holy Ghost, who
may teach us to offer up the sacrifices of God, a broken spirit and a contrite heart; and
that we give our bodies a sacrifice, living, holy and well-pleasing unto him, which is our
reasonable service; that we may also offer up thanks and praise unto God, and he may show
us his salvation. The Lord will hear you all.
So let us now lift up our hearts unto the Lord, and give thanks unto him, our Lord and God.
For it is indeed right, meet and wholesome that we should at all times and in all places
give praise and thanks unto thee, holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God, and that
through Jesus Christ our Saviour, through whom the angels also praise thee and all the
heavenly powers magnify thee; with whom we also pray and beseech thee that thou wouldest
admit our voices also, who with humble confession say:
*Sanctus*
Holy, holy, holy art thou, the Lord and God of hosts; full are heaven and earth of thy
glory. Hosanna, help us, most Highest. Blessed art thou also, that comest in the name of
the Lord, a son of David. Hosanna, ah help us, most Highest, that thy kingdom may increase
and be strengthened.

**Note.**

- **The bidding** is expanded with Ps 51:17 ("the sacrifices of God, a broken spirit")
  and Heb 13:15 ("give thanks and offer up praise"). The *Orate fratres* has become a
  prayer to offer the sacrifices Scripture allows.
- **The Preface** is the common Preface, reduced to its frame. The dialogue is folded into
  one sentence spoken by the minister.

*And instead of the Canon the following prayer is used:*
Almighty God, and Father of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who by the same thy most dear Son,
our Lord, hast promised that whatsoever we ask thee in his name thou wilt grant us, and
hast moreover by thy Holy Ghost commanded us to pray for all rulers and all men: we beseech
thee from our hearts, through the same thy most dear Son, our Saviour, that thou wouldest
enlighten the heart of all princes and lords, and specially of our rulers, the honourable
Council, with the knowledge of thy holy Gospel, that they may acknowledge thee for their
right and only Sovereign, and govern us, the work of thy hands and the sheep of thy
pasture, according to thy will and pleasure. And vouchsafe unto all men to come to the
knowledge of thy truth; and unto this thy congregation, here present and gathered in thy
name, thy Holy Ghost, the Comforter, who writeth thy law in our hearts, that our inborn
blindness and folly may be taken away, whereby we not only cannot know our sin and evil,
but are well pleased with ourselves therein. Therefore, O merciful God, most dear, make our
sin alive in us by thy Holy Ghost, that we may feel it and know its vileness and shame;
and that thence, seeing we find in ourselves nothing but sin, death and hell, we may
obtain a true hunger and thirst for thy grace and mercy, that we may yet in part consider,
receive with rightly-formed faith, and praise with everlasting thankfulness thy
overflowing, unmeasurable grace and goodness, which thou hast shown us in this, that thou
wouldest have thine only-begotten Son become man (that is, like unto us poor sinners),
suffer and die for us, and by his death redeem us from sin, death and hell. Grant us now
therefore, heavenly Father, that we may never let the wholesome remembrance of this death,
whereby we are redeemed from all evil unto everlasting life, go out of our hearts; that we
also with him, our Saviour, may die unto sin and live unto righteousness, in all patience
and love toward our neighbour, with joyful watching, awaiting the blessed hope and coming
of the same our dear Lord and Redeemer. And grant that we may at this time also keep his
holy Supper unto such wholesome and needful remembrance with such a heart that we seek not
