things temporal nor our own, but the rising of thy kingdom, and desire to be loosed from
sin and furthered unto all godliness; that none of us become guilty of the body or the
blood of our Saviour Jesus Christ, nor eat judgement and damnation to himself, if he here
confess himself to be a member of Christ, and believe that alone by the sacrifice which
he once offered up for us on the cross unto thee, O Father, his body and blood, and yet
had not such faith as is active through love toward all, and so made a mockery with the
Supper of our Lord; but that we all herewith in true faith may consider and receive his
death suffered for us; that we may surely believe that thou wilt be our gracious and
merciful Father, who hast taken us to be children and heirs, to be conformed to thy most
dear and first-begotten Son Jesus Christ, although we still live here as in sins, so also
in continual tribulation; that we also may all hold one another as true brethren and thy
children, ready to do good to please thee, also to take up thy rod and trial alway with
all patience, and so to wait altogether willingly for the time when thou shalt deliver us
from the body of sin. This faith, hope and love vouchsafe, heavenly Father, to strengthen
and establish in us, that we may call and pray unto thee in truth and in right spirit, as
our only Master hath taught us, and say:
Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. […] For thine is the kingdom, and the
power, and the glory, for ever, Amen.

**Note.**

- **The rubric.** "And instead of the Canon one useth this following prayer". The heading
  says outright what the prayer is for.
- **How it grows out of Schwarz.** It begins with Schwarz's *Te igitur* (Thee therefore) substitute ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1))
  and continues with the second hand's addition there. It runs into the Our Father, as
  Schwarz's *Post elevationem* (After the elevation) did, but without Verba between.
- **Canon themes, recast:**
  - intercession for rulers and "this thy congregation, here present" (*Te igitur*,
    *Memento … omnium circumstantium*);
  - the remembrance of the Son's death, resurrection and coming ("the wholesome remembrance … of this death", "awaiting … the coming"), which does the work of the *anamnesis* of
    *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful);
  - a petition for a fruitful communion (*Supplices … ut quotquot … sumpserimus*, We humbly beseech thee … that as many of us as … shall receive), turned
    into a warning against eating judgement (1 Cor 11:27–29).
- **The one sacrifice.** The only sacrifice named is Christ's own, "as he once for all offered up to thee, O Father, his body and blood for us on the cross" (Heb 9:28; 10:14). Here the
  critique the Brandenburg-Nürnberg order would make in 1533 is already in the prayer
  itself (see [Appendix 7.A](#s7-a)).
- **No Verba.** This prayer is not followed by the Verba but by the Our Father. The Verba
  come after an admonition (below), read as a lesson from 1 Cor 11. There is no elevation.

*After this prayer the minister exhorteth the people to consider the passion of the Lord,
according to the grace given, and commonly concludeth it thus:*
Let us now hear how the Lord ordained his Supper, and what he hath commanded to be done.
*And he readeth the words of the Supper out of the first Epistle of Paul to the
Corinthians, the eleventh chapter, with earnest words, as here followeth:*
The Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread, and when he had
given thanks, he brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take, and eat. This is
my body, which is given for you. This do in remembrance of me. After the same manner also
the cup, when they had supped at evening, and said: This is the cup, the new testament in
my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the loosing of sin. This do, as oft as ye
drink it, in remembrance of me.
*Thereafter the minister saith to the people:*
Come ye now hither, that will with me keep and receive the Supper of the Lord. May he make
you meet thereto, and grant you to consider his death with right faith and to show it
forth with true thankfulness.
*And in the giving of the bread and of the cup of the Lord he saith thus:*
Remember, believe, and show forth that Christ died for you.

**Note.**

- **The *Pax*.** "Come ye now hither …" takes the place of the *Pax* and the invitation
  to communion.
- **"Remember, believe, proclaim …"** replaces the *custodiat* (preserve). Form f keeps it.

#### <a id="s7-5-3"></a>7.5.3 *Straßburger kirchen ampt*, 1525 (form f)

The last form drops the Preface and Sanctus. After the Creed comes an explanatory rubric
and a still longer bidding:

*After the ending of the Creed, that the unchristian sacrificial Masses may not be a
stumbling-block to the people, and that it may be understood how Christ was once offered
for us for the full satisfaction of our sins, the pastor sometimes speaketh thus:*
Dear brethren and sisters, pray God the Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who was
given into death for the redemption of our souls, that he send us the Holy Ghost, who may
teach us to offer up, not Christ, who offered himself once for us and can be offered by no
man, but the true sacrifices well-pleasing to God, as a broken spirit, a contrite heart;
and that we yield our bodies a sacrifice, living, holy and well-pleasing unto him, which is
our reasonable service, wherein we offer unto God honour, praise and thanksgiving. The Lord
hear you and show you his salvation, Amen.

**Note.**

- **The last trace of the *Orate fratres*.** It is now a polemic against the Mass-sacrifice.
  Sehling refers to Bucer's argument from Hebrews in the same years.
- **What follows.** "The Lord be with you. Let us pray:" introduces the revised
  prayer of form e, "Almighty, merciful God and Father …". It is shorter on the
  magistrates and longer on the unity of the members of Christ's body ("whose members we all are … incorporated through the joints of love, with the bond of peace").
- **The Supper itself.** The Our Father; an exhortation (a specimen from St. Peter the
  Younger, Reminiscere 1525, is printed); the Verba from 1 Cor 11; the invitation; the
  distribution with "Remember, believe and proclaim …".
- **The end of the Canon at Strasbourg.** Nothing of the Roman Canon is left but its
  intercession and its remembrance, both prayed in the congregation's own words.

---

### <a id="s7-6"></a>7.6 Worms, *Deutsche Messe*, 1524

*Form und Ordenung der Evangelischen deutschen Messen, wie sie zu Worms gehalten wird.* (Form and order of the evangelical German Mass, as it is held at Worms.) Sehling
19, III, Nr. 1, pp. 124–129. Like its Strasbourg original, it is a Moderate Reformed order.

The preface says this Mass is kept "at Strasbourg and Worms". This is the Strasbourg
German Mass of 1524 ([§7.5](#s7-5)) in use at Worms, with the Canon prayers that Schwarz's Strasbourg
manuscript lacks.

It keeps more of the Canon than any other order in the corpus. The Canon runs in its
proper order from *Te igitur* (Thee therefore) to *Supplices te rogamus* (We humbly beseech thee), each prayer translated and
trimmed. There are three kinds of change:

- **Sacrificial nouns replaced.**
  - *haec dona, haec munera, haec sancta sacrificia illibata* (these gifts, these presents, these holy unspotted sacrifices) becomes "this thy bread and wine";
  - *hostiam puram* (a pure victim) becomes "our humble prayer";
  - *hanc oblationem* (this oblation) becomes "us and … our prayer".
- **Office-holders replaced.** Pope and bishop give way to emperor, king and rulers.
- **Saints dropped.** The saints, the dead and the doxology *Per ipsum* (Through him) are gone.

The Canon still stands between the Sanctus and the Our Father, where it belongs.

#### <a id="s7-6-1"></a>7.6.1 Preparation of the chalice (*Orate fratres*)

*The preparing of the cup.*
Dear brethren and sisters, pray God that my prayer and yours may be acceptable.
The Lord be with you.
*Answer:* And with thy spirit.

**Note.** This is "Pray, brethren, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to God the Father almighty", with *sacrificium* (sacrifice) replaced by *gebet* (prayer). It follows the Creed
directly. There is no offertory chant and there are no offertory prayers.

#### <a id="s7-6-2"></a>7.6.2 Preface and Sanctus

*The Preface.*
Lift up your hearts unto God.
*Answer:* We lift them up unto God.
Let us give thanks unto God our Lord.
*Answer:* It is meet and right.
Yea, verily it is meet and right, and also wholesome, that we should in all places and at
all times give thanks unto thee, holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, through Christ our
Lord: through whom all the angels and the heavenly powers worship, honour and praise thy
glorious majesty; with the same we beseech thee that thou wouldest admit and accept our
voice, that we also may praise thee and say without end:
Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; full are heaven and earth of thy glory. Hosanna in
the highest. Bless ✠ ed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Prosperity and salvation
in the highest.

**Note.** This is the common Preface. "Through whom the Angels praise thy majesty, the Dominions adore, the Powers tremble … with whom we pray thee that thou wouldest bid our voices also to be admitted" is condensed. The second *Hosanna* is translated as "prosperity and salvation"
(prosperity and salvation). The sign of the cross at *Benedictus* is kept.

#### <a id="s7-6-3"></a>7.6.3 *Te igitur*

Wherefore, most gracious Father, we humbly pray and desire through Jesus Christ thy Son our
Lord, that thou wouldest look upon, bless and ble ✠ ss this thy bread and wine; and also
graciously accept our prayer, which we make in the first place for thy holy Christian
Church, and give peace to the same, keep, unite and govern it throughout the whole compass
of the world, with the emperor, the king and all our rulers, together with all thy faithful
Christians.

**Note.** Compare "Therefore, most merciful Father, we humbly pray and beseech thee, through Jesus Christ thy Son our Lord, that thou wouldest accept and bless these gifts, these presents, these holy unspotted sacrifices, which in the first place we offer thee for thy holy catholic Church, which vouchsafe to keep in peace, to guard, to unite and to govern throughout the whole world, together with thy servant N. our Pope and N. our Bishop, and all the orthodox …"

- **Gifts and offering.** The gifts become "this thy bread and wine". "which we offer thee" becomes the prayer "which we … make".
- **Office-holders.** Pope and bishop give way to emperor, king and "all our rulers".
- **Verbs for the Church.** The four verbs for the Church (*pacificare, custodire, adunare, regere*: to keep in peace, to guard, to unite, to govern) are kept exactly.
- **Blessing.** *Accepta habeas et benedicas* (that thou wouldest accept and bless) is translated twice over ("bless and bene ✠ dict"), as a bless-and-bless doublet.

#### <a id="s7-6-4"></a>7.6.4 *Memento* of the living, with the end of *Communicantes*

O Lord, remember all thy servants and handmaidens, and all that stand round about, whose
faith and devotion is known unto thee, for whose health of soul and body we pray thee; that
we all may be preserved by the help of thy protection; through Jesus Christ our Lord.

**Note.** This is "Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids N. and N., and all here standing round, whose faith is known to thee and whose devotion is manifest".

- **Offering removed.** "For whom we offer unto thee, or who offer unto thee, this sacrifice of praise" becomes "for … we pray thee".
- **Ending borrowed from *Communicantes*.** The ending "that we all may be preserved through the help of thy defence" is the last clause of *Communicantes* (In communion): *ut in omnibus
  protectionis tuae muniamur auxilio* (that in all things we may be defended by the help of thy protection).
- **Saints dropped.** The list of saints between these two points is gone.

#### <a id="s7-6-5"></a>7.6.5 *Hanc igitur*

Wherefore we pray: O Lord, vouchsafe graciously to take unto thee us and all our prayer, and
to order all our days in thy peace, to deliver us from eternal damnation, and to number us
among the flocks of thine elect; through Christ our Lord. Amen.

**Note.** This is "This oblation therefore of our service … we beseech thee, O Lord, graciously to accept, and to order our days in thy peace, and to command us to be delivered from eternal damnation and to be numbered in the flock of thine elect". "*Oblationem*" (oblation) becomes "us and all our prayer".

The same words, "deliver from everlasting damnation", are what the 1533/1543 critique singles
out as sacrificial ([Appendix 7.A](#s7-a)).

#### <a id="s7-6-6"></a>7.6.6 *Quam oblationem*

O most gracious Father, merciful, everlasting God, help and grant that this bread and the
wine may become and be unto us the true body and the innocent blood of thy most dearly
beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

**Note.** This is "Which oblation do thou, O God, vouchsafe, we beseech thee, in all things to make blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable and acceptable, that it may become for us the Body and Blood of thy most beloved Son our Lord Jesus Christ".

"May it become and be for us" renders *nobis … fiat* (that for us … it may become) exactly. The five adjectives of offering are
dropped.

#### <a id="s7-6-7"></a>7.6.7 *Qui pridie*, *Simili modo*, *Haec quotiescumque*

Who, on the day before he suffered, took the bread, gave thanks, bless ✠ ed and brake the
bread, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat, this is my body, which is given
for you.
*The elevation of the Sacrament.*
Likewise after the supper he took the cup, gave thanks, bless ✠ ed, and gave it to his
disciples, and said: Take, drink ye all thereof; this is the cup of the new and everlasting
testament in my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the remission of sins.
This, as oft as ye do it, do it in remembrance of me.
*The elevation of the cup.*

**Note.** The Verba keep the Roman Canon's frame:

- "on the day before he suffered" renders *Qui pridie quam pateretur* (Who the day before he suffered);
- "of the new and eternal testament" renders *novi et aeterni testamenti* (of the new and eternal testament);
- "This, as often as ye do it" renders *Haec quotiescumque feceritis* (As often as ye shall do these things).

Two things are dropped: *elevatis oculis in caelum* and *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith). "Which is given for you", from Luke and Paul, is added to the bread word.

#### <a id="s7-6-8"></a>7.6.8 *Unde et memores* and *Supra quae*

Wherefore, O Lord, we thy servants, considering the passion and death of the same thy Son
our Lord Jesus Christ, his resurrection from hell, and also his glorious ascension into the
heavens, do therewith offer unto thy divine majesty our humble prayer; whereupon thou
wouldest look with a gracious and kindly countenance, and let it be well-pleasing unto
thee; through Jesus Christ our Lord.

**Note.** This is "Wherefore, O Lord, we thy servants … mindful of the blessed passion of the same Christ thy Son our Lord, and also of his resurrection from hell, and of his glorious ascension into heaven, offer unto thy excellent majesty, of thy gifts and bounties, a pure victim …", joined to "Upon which vouchsafe to look with a propitious and serene countenance, and to accept them …".

- **What is offered.** The Canon's *offerimus* is kept ("anbieten"), but what is offered is
  "our humble prayer", not the *hostia* (victim).
- **Literal rendering.** "Resurrection from hell" renders *ab inferis
  resurrectionis* (of the resurrection from hell) literally.
- **Types dropped.** The Old Testament types (Abel, Abraham, Melchizedek) are gone.

#### <a id="s7-6-9"></a>7.6.9 *Supplices te rogamus*

Almighty God, we humbly beseech thee, grant that our prayer and desire may be brought upon
the highest altar before the face of thy divine majesty; that we all, who from this most
holy supper receive the body, flesh and blood of thy Son, may be filled with all divine
blessing and grace. Through the same Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

**Note.** This is "We humbly beseech thee, almighty God, command these to be carried by the hands of thy holy Angel to thine altar on high, in the sight of thy divine majesty; that as many of us as, by this partaking of the altar, shall receive the most holy Body and Blood of thy Son, may be filled with all heavenly benediction and grace. Through the same Christ …"

- **What is carried up.** "*Haec*" (these; the gifts) becomes "our prayer and desire".
- **The angel.** The angel who carries them is dropped.
- **The altar.** *Ex hac altaris participatione* (by this partaking of the altar) becomes "of this most holy Supper".

#### <a id="s7-6-10"></a>7.6.10 Our Father, with the conclusion of the embolism

*Let us pray.*
Out of the admonition of the blessed commandments, and by divine ordinance instructed, we
are bold to say: Our Father, which art in the heavens, etc.
Through Jesus Christ our Lord, thy Son, who with thee and the Holy Ghost, one true God,
liveth and reigneth. Amen.

**Note.** The introduction to the Our Father is *Praeceptis salutaribus moniti, et divina
institutione formati, audemus dicere* (Admonished by saving precepts and formed by divine institution, we make bold to say).

The doxology after it is the ending of the embolism, "Through the same Jesus Christ our Lord, thy Son, who liveth and reigneth with thee in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God". The body
of the embolism ("Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord, from all evils …", with its saints) is
dropped. Only its conclusion remains.

#### <a id="s7-6-11"></a>7.6.11 Fraction forbidden; the Peace as absolution

*The priest may not break the host, nor let it fall into the cup.*
The peace of the Lord be alway with you.
*This is the right evangelical absolution, which proclaimeth unto the faithful the
remission of sin, the only and most worthy preparation for the receiving of the body and
blood of Christ. It may well be spoken by the priest turned toward the people.*

**Note.** The fraction and the commixture (*Haec commixtio …*) are forbidden. Sehling
compares Luther's *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass). *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you) is kept, and the rubric
explains it as a public absolution.

#### <a id="s7-6-12"></a>7.6.12 *Agnus Dei* and communion

*Agnus Dei.*
Thou little Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us. And
grant us peace.
*Here let the priest distribute the body and blood to them that desire it. He himself shall
not partake of it, unless he have a special hunger thereto.*
Behold, dearly beloved, this is verily the holy body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath
suffered for you the bitter death. Take and eat it, that it may feed, nourish and preserve
you unto everlasting life.
The body of the Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life.
*The priest taketh the cup and saith:*
Let us also drink the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.
Behold, this is verily the dear treasure of the precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ,
wherewith ye are bought. Take and divide it among yourselves, unto the washing away of your
sins. Amen.
The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul and my soul unto everlasting life.

**Note.**

- **Communion formulas.** "The body … preserve thy soul unto everlasting life" is *Corpus Domini
  nostri Iesu Christi custodiat animam tuam in vitam aeternam* (The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life). The cup formula is *Sanguis
  Domini nostri …* (The blood of our Lord …) in the same way.
- **The priest's cup verse.** "Let us also drink the cup of salvation" is the priest's
  *Calicem salutaris accipiam, et nomen Domini invocabo* (I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord; Ps 116:13), put into the plural.
- **"Behold".** Each "Behold" (*Ecce*) introduces a showing of the element to the people.
- **"Divide it among you".** This is Luke 22:17.
- **The priest's own communion.** The priest communicates only "if he have a special
  hunger thereto".

#### <a id="s7-6-13"></a>7.6.13 Postcommunion, *Benedicamus*, blessing, *Nunc dimittis*

The Lord be with you.
*Answer:* And with thy spirit.
*Let us pray:*
O Lord Jesus Christ, may thy most holy body which we have partaken, and thy innocent blood
which we have drunk, be unto us neither unto damnation nor unto judgement, but, according
to thy goodness, unto a defence and medicine of the soul and of the body, a furtherance
unto everlasting life; who livest and reignest for ever. Amen.
The Lord be with you.
*Answer:* And with thy spirit.
Let us bless God.
Thanks, praise, honour and glory be to God through Christ our Lord. Amen.
*The Blessing:*
The blessing of Almighty God, Father, Son and Holy Ghost, be with you and remain alway with
you. Amen.
*Nunc dimittis:*
O Lord, let thy servant depart in peace according to thy word; for our eyes have seen thy
salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples, the light to lighten the
Gentiles and to be the glory of thy people Israel. To thee be praise, honour and thanks,
blessed, holy Trinity, God Father, Son and Holy Ghost. Amen.

**Note.**

- **The postcommunion.** It joins two of the priest's communion prayers. The first is
  "Let the receiving of thy Body, O Lord Jesus Christ … not turn to my judgement and condemnation, but through thy goodness profit me for a defence of mind and body and for a healing remedy". The second is *Corpus tuum, Domine, quod sumpsi, et Sanguis, quem
  potavi …* (Thy Body, O Lord, which I have taken, and thy Blood, which I have drunk …). Both are made into a public collect.
- **The dismissal.** "Let us bless God" is *Benedicamus Domino* (Let us bless the Lord), and the response
  is an expanded *Deo gratias*.
- **The blessing.** It is *Benedicat vos omnipotens Deus, Pater et Filius et Spiritus
  Sanctus* (May almighty God bless you, the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost).

---

### <a id="s7-7"></a>7.7 Nürnberg, 1524–1525: the parish churches, Volprecht, and the *Form und Ordnung*

Three Nürnberg orders sit alongside Döber's Mass ([§7.8](#s7-8)):

| Order | Sehling | [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc | Pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Gottesdienstordnung der Pfarrkirchen* (St. Sebald, St. Lorenz), June 1524, Latin | 11, I.5 | 249 | 46–47 |
| *Deutsche Messe des Priors Volprecht* (Augustinians), 1524 | 11, I.3 | 247 | 41–42 |
| *Form und Ordnung einer Christlichen Messe*, 1525 | 11, I.7 | 251 | 57 |

The parish order is Latin and follows the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) closely. Volprecht's German Mass is
the most conservative in the corpus after Worms (Moderate Reformed). It keeps all three of the
priest's prayers before communion and both ablution prayers, translated.

#### <a id="s7-7-1"></a>7.7.1 The parish churches, 1524 (Latin)

*The Creed ended, the offertory and the lesser canon being omitted, the celebrant
beginneth:* The Lord be with you.
Lift up your hearts.
Let us give thanks unto the Lord our God.
It is very meet and right, fitting and wholesome, that we should at all times and in all
places give thanks unto thee, O Lord, holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, through
Christ our Lord.
*Here the Preface endeth.*
*Choir:* Holy, holy.
*But the celebrant addeth, reading:*
Who the day before he suffered took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and with eyes
lifted up to heaven unto thee, God the almighty Father, giving thanks unto thee, blesseth,
brake, gave to his disciples, saying: Take and eat ye all of this! For this is my body.
*The bread is elevated.*
In like manner, after they had supped, taking also this excellent cup into his holy and
venerable hands, again giving thanks unto thee, he blessed, gave to his disciples, saying:
Take and drink ye all of it! For this is the cup of my blood, of the new and everlasting
testament, the mystery of faith, which shall be shed for us and for many unto the
remission of sins.
*The cup is elevated.*
*The Hosanna in excelsis being ended, the celebrant beginneth,* Let us pray: Taught by
wholesome precepts, etc.: Our Father, which art in, etc. *After this the people who are to
receive the sacrament are admonished in these words:* […]
*Then the celebrant addeth:* The peace of the Lord be alway with you. *The choir
answereth.*
*Then let the people begin to be communicated, the officiant offering the bread and the
minister the cup. During the communion the choir singeth the Agnus Dei and the communion.
The sacrament having been administered more slowly or more quickly according to the number
of persons communicating, if anything remaineth it is consumed by the celebrant and the
ministers. Lastly let the office be concluded with the prayer which they call the
complenda.*

**Note.**

- **"offertorio ac canone minore omissis" (the offertory and the lesser canon being omitted).** Sehling explains that the offertory part of
  the Mass was often called the *canon minor*, the Canon proper being the *canon maior* (greater canon).
  Both are left out.
- **The Preface** is cut short at *per Christum Dominum nostrum* (through Christ our Lord), as in the *Formula
  missae* (Form of the Mass; [§7.3.2](#s7-3-2)). But here the Sanctus is sung after it.
- ***Qui pridie*** is the full Roman text, *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith) included. It is read quietly
  ("legendo") during the Sanctus and Benedictus, with the two elevations. Sehling (note 17)
  reads the rubric so: in June 1524 the words were still said in Latin and quietly, as the
  *Formula missae* allowed ("either silently or aloud"). By March 1525 Nürnberg reported that
  they were sung aloud "in the tone or melody of the Preface", with the Sanctus after
  them.
  - The print reads "pro nobis" (for us), where the Roman text has *pro vobis* (for you).
  - "paterctur" and "cafix" are corrected here.
- **The exhortation** is the Nürnberg one printed at [§7.8.7](#s7-8-7).
- ***Pax Domini*** follows the exhortation, as in Döber.
- **No embolism, no fraction.**
- **The postcommunion.** The *complenda* (completion) is the proper postcommunion of the day. Luther had
  rejected the variable postcommunions ([§7.3.5](#s7-3-5)).

#### <a id="s7-7-2"></a>7.7.2 Volprecht, 1524

*Here the priest prepareth the chalice. As soon as it is prepared let him say:*
The Lord be with you!
*Answer:* And with thy spirit!
*Priest:* Lift up the hearts!
*Answer:* We lift them up unto the Lord!
*Priest:* Let us give thanks unto God our Lord!
*Answer:* That is meet and right.
*Preface:*
Verily it is meet and right. It is seemly and wholesome that we should always and at all
times give thanks, thou holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God, through Christ our
Lord; who in the night in which he was betrayed took the bread, gave thanks unto God his
heavenly Father, brake it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Come and eat! This is my
body, which is given for you. This do in remembrance of me!
After the same manner he took also the cup, when they had eaten at evening, gave thanks
unto God his heavenly Father, and gave it to them, saying: Take! Drink ye all of it! This
is the cup, the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the
forgiveness of sins. This do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me!
Holy, holy, holy is God the Lord almighty. Heaven and earth are full of thy glory. Save us
in the highest! Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord! Save us in the highest!

**Note.**

- **The chalice.** "Here the priest prepareth the chalice" is all that is left of the offertory,
  as in Döber ([§7.8.1](#s7-8-1)). It stands after the Creed, where the Roman offertory stood.
- **The Preface and Verba.** The Preface cut off at *per Christum Dominum nostrum* (through Christ our Lord) runs
  into the Verba on the pattern of the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass). Sehling: "an independent translation of the introduction to the account of the institution created by Luther". The Verba
  are from 1 Cor 11 and the Gospels, not from *Qui pridie* (Who the day before).
- **The Sanctus** comes after the Verba. "Make us blessed" translates *Hosanna* (Sehling:
  "Help now!").

*Priest:* Let us pray, admonished by wholesome precepts:
Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come! Thy will be done,
as in heaven, so in earth! Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as
we forgive our debtors! And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil! Amen.
*The priest turneth to the people, saying:*
The peace of the Lord be alway with you!
*Answer:* And with thy spirit!
O thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us!
O thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us!
O thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us and give us
peace!

**Note.**

- **"Let us pray, reminded by wholesome precepts".** This is *Oremus: Praeceptis
  salutaribus moniti*, with *praecepta* ("precepts") read as "gebet" (prayer).
- **The *Pax*** is kept with its Roman response. There is no embolism and no fraction.

O Lord Jesu Christ, thou hast said unto thy disciples: Peace I give unto you; my peace I
leave with you; not as the world giveth, give I it unto you. Wherefore, my Lord, look not
upon our sins, but upon the faith of thy Christian Church, which we believe and see not;
which vouchsafe thou, according to thy divine will, to keep, unite and govern, with thy
heavenly Father and the Holy Ghost, for ever. Amen.
*Another prayer:*
O Lord Jesu Christ, thou Son of the living God, who by the will of thy Father, with the
working together of the Holy Ghost, hast by thy death made the world alive again: deliver
us by the taking of thy body and blood from all our sins and from all evil, and grant us
that we may at all times cleave unto thy divine commandments, and never more be parted
from thee! Who with God thy heavenly Father and the Holy Ghost livest and reignest for
ever. Amen.
*Another prayer:*
Let the receiving of thy flesh and blood, Jesu Christ, which we poor sinners partake unto
the forgiveness of our sins, not be suffered to turn to us unto judgement or damnation, but
be our defence here and there for ever! Amen.

**Note.** These are the priest's three prayers before communion, in German, twenty years
before Brandenburg kept them in Latin ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)). Sehling thought only one of them was meant to
be chosen ("Alia oratio").

1. ***Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti.***
   - John 14:27 is given in full, including "not as the world giveth" (not in the Roman
     prayer).
   - "which we then believe and see not" is added.
   - The Tridentine verbs are *pacificare et coadunare* (to keep in peace and unite). Volprecht's "keep, unite, govern" are instead the *custodire, adunare et regere* (to guard, unite and govern) of *Te igitur* (Thee therefore), as in
     Brandenburg's Latin ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)).
2. ***Fili Dei vivi.***
   - *Per hoc sacrosanctum Corpus et Sanguinem tuum* (by this thy most holy Body and Blood) becomes "through the taking of thy body and blood". The deliverance comes through receiving, not through the
     consecrated elements.
   - *Inhaerere* is kept ("anhangen").
   - The prayer is plural.
3. ***Perceptio Corporis tui.*** The body and blood are named ("flesh and blood").
   - *Praesumo* (I presume) disappears; "in forgiveness of our sins" is added.
   - *Tutamentum mentis et corporis, et ad medelam percipiendam* (a defence of mind and body, and for a healing remedy) is shortened to
     "protection here and there".

*Here he receiveth the body of Christ, saying:*
The body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is given for us, preserve my soul unto everlasting
life! Amen.
Let us also drink the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord!
*Here he receiveth the blood, saying:*
The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is shed for us, preserve my soul unto everlasting
life! Amen.
*Straightway let him say:*
What we have received with the mouth, grant, almighty God, that we may receive it also with
a pure heart, that of a temporal gift it may become unto us an everlasting medicine!
*Another prayer:*
May the body and the blood of the Lord, which we have received, cleave alway inwardly unto
our hearts; and grant, almighty God, that there remain not in us a stain of sin, who hast
fed us with thy holy sacraments!

**Note.**

- **The priest's communion.**
  - ***Custodiat.*** "Preserve my soul unto everlasting life" is *Corpus Domini nostri Iesu
    Christi custodiat animam meam in vitam aeternam* (The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my soul unto everlasting life). "which is given for us" is added.
  - ***Calicem salutaris.*** "Let us also drink the cup of salvation" is *Calicem
    salutaris accipiam* (I will take the cup of salvation; Ps 116:13), plural, as in Kantz ([§7.2.6](#s7-2-6)).
- **The ablution prayers.**
  - ***Quod ore sumpsimus*** is complete: "What we have taken with our mouth, O Lord, may we receive with a pure mind; and from a temporal gift may it become for us an everlasting remedy".
  - ***Corpus tuum*** is made plural: "Thy Body, O Lord, which I have taken, and thy Blood, which I have drunk, cleave unto my inmost parts; and grant that no stain of sin may remain in me, whom pure and holy sacraments have refreshed". "Visceribus" (inmost parts) becomes "inwardly in our hearts".
  - Sehling again thinks only one of the two was meant.
- **No communion of the people is provided for** in the text. The exhortation printed after
  the Mass (the Nürnberg exhortation, [§7.8.7](#s7-8-7)) is for those who "would go to God's table, before or during the Mass".

*Communion:*
We praise the God of heaven, and confess before all that live, that he hath dealt with us
according to his mercy.
*Priest:* The Lord be with you!
*Answer:* And with thy spirit!
*Priest:* Let us pray!
May the receiving of thy sacrament, O Lord our God, which we have taken, come unto us for
the health of body and also of soul, and for the confession of the eternal holy Trinity
and undivided Unity; through our Lord Jesus Christ, thy Son, who with thee liveth and
reigneth in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever and everlastingly! Amen.
*Priest:* The Lord be with you!
*Answer:* And with thy spirit!
*Thereafter the priest speaketh the blessing thus:*
The Lord bless you and keep you! The Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious unto
you! The Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace!
*Answer:* Amen.
*Priest:* Let us give praise and thanks unto the Lord!
*Answer:* Thanks be to God.
*The end of the Mass.*

**Note.**

- **The Mass is that of Trinity Sunday**, from the Bamberg missal. The communion chant is
  "We bless the God of heaven, and before all the living we will confess him, because he hath shown his mercy to us" (Tob 12:6).
- **The postcommunion** is the Roman postcommunion of Trinity Sunday: "May the receiving of this sacrament, O Lord our God, profit us for the health of body and soul, and the everlasting confession of the holy Trinity and of its undivided Unity". Lippe uses it
  too ([§7.10](#s7-10)).
- **The ending.** "Let us give praise and thanks to the Lord / God be thanked" is the
  *Benedicamus Domino / Deo gratias*. The Aaronic blessing (Luther's suggestion, [§7.3.5](#s7-3-5))
  stands before it.

#### <a id="s7-7-3"></a>7.7.3 *Form und Ordnung einer Christlichen Messe*, 1525

*After that the priest beginneth the Preface, in the Sunday tone:*
The Lord be with you! *Choir:* And with thy spirit!
Lift up your hearts, etc., as far as "through Christ our Lord".
*Thereafter he beginneth the Qui pridie, and as soon as the priest hath elevated, the choir
beginneth the Sanctus. After the same the priest singeth the Pater noster, with the
beginning:* Let us pray: Taught by wholesome precepts, etc.
*After the Pater noster the priest or minister readeth the exhortation toward the people:*
My dearly beloved in God, etc.
*When that is ended, the priest turneth toward the people and singeth:* The peace of the
Lord be alway with you! *Choir:* And with thy spirit!
*Thereafter the choir beginneth the Agnus Dei, as followeth hereafter. Meanwhile the priest
communicateth the people and saith first:* The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy
soul unto everlasting life! *Then:* The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul
unto everlasting life!
[…]
*Immediately after the Agnus Dei the choir beginneth a psalm for the communion, or else a
hymn. After the same the priest concludeth the Mass with a collect. Thereafter with the
Benedicamus Domino, in the Sunday tone.*

**Note.**

- **The shape.** This is the Mass of the parish churches ([§7.7.1](#s7-7-1)) as sung by 1525: shortened
  Preface, *Qui pridie* (Who the day before; Sehling: presumably sung in Latin), elevation, Sanctus, *Praeceptis
  salutaribus* (Taught by saving precepts) and the Our Father, the exhortation, *Pax Domini* (The peace of the Lord).
- **What is new** is the German *custodiat* (preserve) at the distribution, in the second person.
- **What follows in the print.** The German Sanctus and *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God) printed after the
  rubrics ("Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world …") are omitted here.

---

### <a id="s7-8"></a>7.8 Nürnberg, Döber's *Deutsche Messe*, 1525

Andreas Döber's German Mass for the Neues Spital, Nürnberg. Sehling 11, I.6, pp. 52–55.

Döber follows the order Luther proposed in the *Formula missae* (1523), as Nürnberg's
parish churches had done in 1524. There is no offertory. A truncated Preface runs straight
into the Verba, and the Sanctus follows the Verba. Of the Canon, only the Verba remain in
place. The Roman prayers after the Our Father survive as three things: a remnant of the
embolism, a German *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God), and the *Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi* (O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God), which is
turned into a prayer for the people to repeat.

#### <a id="s7-8-1"></a>7.8.1 Preparation of the gifts (after the Gradual)

*After the Epistle followeth the Gradual. After the same the priest prepareth the cup
together with the bread.* […]
*After the Alleluia the priest asketh the server whether any have announced himself to
receive the holy sacrament. Thereupon he maketh ready; and when that is done, he turneth
himself to the people, or layeth the book upon the desk, and readeth the Gospel, John 6.*

**Note.** This is all that is left of the offertory: a silent preparation, moved in front
of the Gospel, with no prayers. The Nicene or Apostles' Creed follows the Gospel. The Mass
then goes on at once to the Preface.

#### <a id="s7-8-2"></a>7.8.2 Preface

*After that the priest beginneth the Preface:*
The Lord be with you!
*The people:* And with thy spirit!
*The priest:* Lift up your hearts unto God!
*The people:* We have lifted up our hearts.
*The priest:* Let us give thanks unto God our Lord!
*The people:* It is meet and right.
*The priest:* Yea verily, it is meet and right, and also wholesome, that we should in all
places give thanks unto thee, O Lord, holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, through Christ
our Lord. Amen.

**Note.** This is Luther's shortened Preface from the *Formula missae* (Form of the Mass). It was meant to
end at *per Christum Dominum nostrum* (through Christ our Lord) and to run straight into the relative clause *Qui
pridie* (Who the day before). Sehling notes that Döber's "Amen" breaks that join, and shows that Döber "did not
understand its sense".

#### <a id="s7-8-3"></a>7.8.3 The Verba

*Thereafter the priest saith, and taketh the bread into his hands:*
Who, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread into his holy hands, gave thanks
unto his heavenly Father, blessed it, brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said unto
them: Take and eat! This is my body, which is given for you. This do in remembrance of me!
*And he showeth it to the people.*
*Now he taketh the cup into his hand:*
Likewise also he took the cup into his holy hands, gave thanks unto his heavenly Father,
blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and drink ye all of this! This is
the cup of the new testament with my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the
forgiveness of sins. As oft as ye do this, do it in remembrance of me!
*And he showeth it to the people.*

**Note.** The frame is the Canon's:

- "into his holy hands" renders *in sanctas ac venerabiles manus suas* (into his holy and venerable hands);
- "giveth thanks to his heavenly Father" renders *ad te Deum Patrem suum omnipotentem, tibi
  gratias agens* (unto thee, God his almighty Father, giving thanks to thee);
- "As oft as ye do this" renders *Haec quotiescumque feceritis* (As often as ye shall do these things).

The opening, though, is Paul's "in the night in which he was betrayed" (1 Cor 11:23), not *Qui
pridie* (Who the day before). In the 1524 order of the parish churches (Sehling 11, I.5, p. 47) the Verba were
still said in Latin, *Qui pridie … Hoc est enim corpus meum … mysterium fidei* (Who the day before … For this is my body … the mystery of faith).

#### <a id="s7-8-4"></a>7.8.4 Sanctus

*After this he saith the Sanctus, as followeth.*
*The Sanctus:*
Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth. Full are the heavens and the earth of thy glory and
majesty. Ah, save us in the height! Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord! Save
us in the heights!

**Note.** *Hosanna* is translated by its meaning, "help/save us" ("make us blessed"), as in
Volprecht's Mass of 1524.

#### <a id="s7-8-5"></a>7.8.5 Our Father and the remnant of the embolism

*Thereafter the priest shall say, as it standeth in Matthew the sixth:*
When the disciples came unto the Lord Jesus and besought him that he should teach them to
pray, he said: When ye will pray, ye shall not babble much, as the hypocrites do; for they
think that when they make many words they shall be heard. But say thus, as hereafter
followeth:
Our Father, which art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come unto us! Thy
will be done as in heaven and in earth! Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our
debts, as we also forgive our debtors! And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from
evil! Amen.
*And he saith further:* O Lord, deliver us from all visible and invisible enemies, from the
devil, from the world, from our own flesh; through Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

**Note.**

- **The introduction to the Our Father.** *Praeceptis salutaribus moniti* (Admonished by saving precepts) is replaced by
  Christ's own warrant (Mt 6:7; Lk 11:1). Sehling calls it an "reshaping of the introduction".
- **The embolism.** The prayer after the Our Father is what Sehling calls the "remnant of the embolism". It keeps the *Libera nos … Domine* (Deliver us … O Lord) form and the *Per … Christum* (Through … Christ) ending. The
  "evils past, present and to come", the saints and the petition for peace give way to the
  Lutheran triad of devil, world and flesh.

#### <a id="s7-8-6"></a>7.8.6 Salutation and *Agnus Dei*

*Thereafter the priest turneth to the people and saith:*
The Lord be with you!
*The people:* And with thy spirit!
*After that the priest saith:*
O thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy upon us!
O thou Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, give us peace!

**Note.** *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) stands where *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you) stood.

#### <a id="s7-8-7"></a>7.8.7 The exhortation (Osiander)

*After this the priest turneth to the people and saith the exhortation, as hereafter
followeth.*
My dearly beloved in God! Forasmuch as we will now consider and keep the supper of our Lord
Jesus Christ, wherein his flesh and blood are given us for meat and for drink, not of the
body but of the soul, we ought rightly with great diligence every one to examine himself,
as Paul saith, and so to eat of this bread and drink of this cup. For none but a hungry
soul, which knoweth its sin, feareth God's wrath and death, and is hungry and thirsty after
righteousness, ought to receive this holy sacrament. But when we examine ourselves, we find
nothing in us but sin and death, and could in no wise help ourselves out thereof. Therefore
hath our dear Lord Jesus Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sakes is become man, that he
might fulfil the law for us and suffer that which we had deserved with our sins. And that we
might steadfastly believe this and joyfully rely thereupon, he took after the supper the
bread, gave thanks, brake it, and said: Take and eat! This is my body, which is given for
you; as if he would say: That I am become man, and all that I do and suffer, that is all
your own, done for you and for your good. For a sure token thereof I give you my body for
meat.
Likewise also the cup, and said: Take and drink ye all of this! This is the cup of the new
testament with my blood, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As
oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby! As if he would say: Forasmuch as I have
taken your cause upon me and laden your sins upon myself, I will offer myself unto death for
sin, shed my blood, obtain grace and forgiveness of sins, and so set up a new testament,
wherein sin shall be remembered no more for ever. For a sure token thereof I give you my
blood to drink.
Whosoever now eateth thus of this bread and drinketh of this cup, that is, whosoever firmly
believeth these words which he heareth and these signs which he receiveth, he dwelleth in
Christ and Christ in him, and so liveth for ever. Hereby shall we remember his death and
give him thanks therefor, every one take up his cross and follow him, and above all love one
another, as he also hath loved us; for we being many are one bread and one body, who are all
partakers of one bread and drink of one cup. God grant us all this, that we may receive it
worthily. Amen.

**Note.** Sehling does not reprint the text here. He points to the order of the parish
churches of 1524 (Sehling 11, I.5, p. 48), whose base text is **Osiander's** exhortation
from the provosts' *Grundt und ursach* (1524).

The text above is that base text with **Döber's readings (Sehling's siglum D)** taken from
his apparatus:

- "My dearly beloved";
- "could in no wise [help] ourselves";
- "that he for us";
- "for pardon";
- "shall never be remembered";
- "for a sure token";
- "in Christ" without "the Lord";
- "hold dear";
- the closing sentence "God grant this unto us all …", which p. 54 confirms.

One point is uncertain. For "Thereof for [a] sure token" (the bread) the apparatus
is garbled; it seems to say D lacks *ainem* (a).

In Nürnberg this exhortation stood where the Latin Verba had been read silently. Once the
Verba were sung aloud in German, Sehling notes, the exhortation "doubled" them.

#### <a id="s7-8-8"></a>7.8.8 *Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi*, said by the people

*After this exhortation the priest turneth to the altar and saith to the people: Say after
me:*
O Lord Jesus Christ, thou eternal Word of the Father, thou Saviour of the world, thou true,
living God and man, deliver us by thy holy body and rose-red blood from all sins! Help that
we may fulfil thy commandments at all times, and be not separated from thee for ever! Amen.

**Note.** This is "O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who by the will of the Father, the Holy Spirit working with thee, hast by thy death given life to the world: deliver me by this thy most holy Body and Blood from all mine iniquities and from all evils; and make me always to cleave to thy commandments, and suffer me never to be separated from thee". Sehling calls it "slightly reshaped", as in Volprecht's Mass.

- **Opening.** The Trinitarian opening is replaced by titles of Christ.
- **Number and speaker.** *Me* becomes *uns* (us).
- **Words for body and blood.** *Fronleichnam* (the Lord's body) is the old word for the Lord's body (as in
  *Fronleichnamsfest*, Corpus Christi). *Rosenfarbes blut* (rose-coloured blood) is a late-medieval devotional
  epithet.
- **Who says it.** The priest's private preparation before his communion is now said by the
  people after him.

#### <a id="s7-8-9"></a>7.8.9 Communion

*Now he communicateth the people first, if he will; and when he reacheth them the body of
Christ, he saith unto them:*
The body of Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life!
*The same he saith also when he taketh it himself. And thereafter he taketh the cup and
saith:*
The blood of our dear Lord Jesus Christ, which is shed for me and for you unto the
forgiveness of sins, preserve my soul unto everlasting life!
*And when he hath consumed, he bindeth up the cup.*

**Note.** These are *Corpus Domini nostri Iesu Christi custodiat animam tuam in vitam
aeternam* (The body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve thy soul unto everlasting life) and the priest's *Sanguis Domini nostri Iesu Christi custodiat animam meam …* (The blood of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve my soul …),
with "which is shed for me and for you for the forgiveness of sins" added.

"Let him bind up the chalice" means he wraps the chalice in its bag.

#### <a id="s7-8-10"></a>7.8.10 *Nunc dimittis*, postcommunion, dismissal and blessing

*After the same he saith to the people: Say after me:*
O Lord, now let thy servant depart in peace according to thy word; for our eyes have seen
thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples, a light to lighten
the Gentiles and to be the glory of thy people Israel. To thee be praise, honour and thanks,
O thou holy, blessed, glorious Trinity, God the Father, God the Son and Holy Ghost! Amen.
*After this the priest turneth to the people and saith thus:*
The Lord be with you!
*The people:* And with thy spirit!
*Thereafter he saith the collect to the people:* Let us pray:
O Lord, almighty God, grant unto us in our mind and heart that, through the temporal death
of thy Son, which these worthy mysteries signify, we may trust that thou hast given us
everlasting life; through the Christ our Lord. Amen.
*Last of all he turneth about to the people and saith:*
The Lord be with you!
*The people:* And with thy spirit!
*The priest:* Give thanks unto the Lord!
*The people:* God be praise and thanks!
*The priest:* Incline your hearts unto God, and I will give you the blessing! *And he
saith:*
The Lord bless thee and keep thee, and lighten his countenance upon thee, and have mercy
upon thee, and turn his countenance unto thee, and give thee everlasting peace; in the name
of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost! Amen. Go ye in the peace of the Lord!
*Now the priest goeth away from the altar.*
So have ye the end of this evangelical Mass. God grant us that which is profitable for soul
and body! Amen.

**Note.**

- **The collect.** It follows the Roman postcommunion of Wednesday in Holy Week: "Grant to our senses, almighty God, that through the temporal death of thy Son, which the venerable mysteries witness, we may trust that thou hast given us everlasting life". Sehling calls it
  "apparently newly made"; the Roman source is identified here for the first time. Note that *testantur* ("bear
  witness to") is rendered *bedeuten* (signify).
- **The dismissal.** "Give thanks unto the Lord … To God be praise and thanks" answers to *Benedicamus
  Domino / Deo gratias*. Sehling reads "Go in the peace of the Lord" as a paraphrase of
  *Ite, missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal).

#### <a id="s7-8-11"></a>7.8.11 Optional intercession in the place of *Te igitur*

*There followeth a common prayer, to be said on a feast day when much people is present,
after the Preface or before the Sanctus, as one will.*
Almighty, everlasting God and merciful Father: forasmuch as thy Son our Lord Jesus Christ
hath promised that whatsoever we ask in his name, thou wilt grant it us; and moreover,
forasmuch as thy Spirit also hath commanded that we should pray for our magistrates: we
beseech thee from our hearts that thou wouldest move the minds of the emperor, the princes
and lords, and above all of our lords and superiors of an honourable council, unto the
knowledge of thy goodness and of the Gospel; and also that thou wouldest make all peoples
subject unto thy Son through the Holy Ghost, that they themselves may willingly acknowledge,
receive and keep his promise; and above all grant unto this congregation that it may
increase in the knowledge of the Gospel, and of his sweet yoke and easy burden. Forasmuch
now, almighty, everlasting God, beloved and merciful Father, as thine only Son our Lord
Jesus is come into the world to be a physician of the sick and not of the whole, and yet our
blindness cannot of itself see the present shame of sin nor know it for a sickness, for we
are, alas, poisoned, and please ourselves in our error and transgression, hate the
commandments of God and love vices: we pray thee that thou wouldest, through God the Holy
Ghost, write thy law in our hearts and make the hidden sin alive in us, and so grant us that
we may prove and perceive how impossible it is for us to do good; that we may gain a hunger
and thirst after the grace and righteousness which alone availeth before thee, which thou
hast given to the world through Christ Jesus our Lord.
*After this followeth the Qui pridie. God be praised!*

**Note.** Sehling traces the prayer to the Strasbourg order of 1524 (Moderate Reformed). Its
rubric puts it exactly where *Te igitur* (Thee therefore) stood: after the Preface, before the Sanctus in Döber's
order, and leading into *Qui pridie* (Who the day before). It intercedes for the emperor, princes and council, for
all peoples, and for "this congregation". These are the intentions of *Te igitur* and the
*Memento*, turned into an evangelical prayer for faith and for the knowledge of sin.

---

### <a id="s7-9"></a>7.9 Bremen, *Eyne evangelysce Misse*, 1525 (Kantz in Low German)

*Eyne evangelysce Misse myt etlijke schone gebede …* (An evangelical Mass with some fine prayers …) Bremen 1525. Sehling 7, III, Nr. 1,
pp. 403–407 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 2216).

The Mass itself is Kantz's order of 1522 ([§7.2](#s7-2)) in Low German. Before it stand three
devotional prayers for the communicant. The second is a "meditation at the Mass". Its opening confession of the Real Presence is the nearest thing in
the order to a Canon.

The foreword warns that the prayers are no rule: they are meant to show "what faith and
desire are needed to receive the testament of Christ in a Christian manner".

#### <a id="s7-9-1"></a>7.9.1 The meditation during Mass

*A meditation at the Mass*
Almighty, everlasting God, my Lord Jesu Christ, I believe that in this bread is present thy
holy true body, and in this wine thy precious blood, which thou hast taken upon thee to
redeem Adam and all his posterity from everlasting death. And thou hast left us in this
most worthy Sacrament a sure and certain sign of thy true promise to forgive sins, which
thy words witness that are spoken in the Mass:
Take and eat. This is my body, which is given for you.
Take and drink ye all thereof. This is my blood, which is shed for you for the forgiveness
of sins.
Upon such comfortable promise I desire from my whole heart, in right confidence and good
trust, that thou let me not go hence empty and hungry, unfed, but wilt feed and refresh me
with thy living word, which proclaimeth unto us the forgiveness of our sins through thy
body and blood; that I may be established in true love toward thee and brotherly
faithfulness toward my neighbour.

**Note.**

- **Who is addressed.** The prayer is addressed to Christ as "Almighty, eternal God" and
  confesses the Real Presence "in this bread … in this wine".
- **The Verba** are quoted from "the words spoken in the Mass": the priest's words are
  now heard by the congregation.
- **The Roman background.** It is the priest's private preparation for communion, of the
  kind in the late-medieval *Praeparatio ad missam* (preparation for Mass), given to the laity.

#### <a id="s7-9-2"></a>7.9.2 The Mass: preparation

The preparation follows Kantz (§[7.2.1](#s7-2-1)–[7.2.2](#s7-2-2)) closely:

- the exhortation "Dearest in Christ, that ye may receive with joyful and desirous heart the precious treasure and the testament of the flesh and blood of Christ Jesus …";
- the absolution;
- "The priest's confession", the recast *Orate fratres*: "pray ye also God faithfully for me, that he, forgiving me my sins, make me meet to distribute his signs to you";
- Ps 124:8;
- the *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) antiphon, said "secretly" by all;
- Kantz's collect, "O Lord, almighty God, help that thy Holy Ghost may be and dwell with us …".

#### <a id="s7-9-3"></a>7.9.3 Preface, Sanctus, *Quam oblationem* and *Qui pridie*

*The Preface, or foreword of the Mass*
Lift up your hearts to God, and let us give thanks unto God our Lord. For it is meet, right
and wholesome that we should in all places and at all times give thanks unto thee, O Lord,
holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, through Christ our dear Lord, through whom all
angels and heavenly powers worship, honour and praise thy holy majesty. With the same we
beseech thee, vouchsafe to admit and receive our voice, that we also may praise thee and
say without end:
Sanctus: That is: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts. Full are heaven and earth of thy
glory. Hosanna in the highest. Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord. Luck and
salvation in the highest.
*Here beginneth first the Evangelical Mass*
*A prayer to God beforehand*
O most gracious Father, merciful, everlasting God, grant us that we may firmly believe that
this bread and wine becometh the true body and blood of thy most dear Son, our Lord Jesus
Christ; who on the day before his passion took the bread into his holy hands, looked up to
heaven unto thee, his almighty Father, gave thanks, and brake the bread, and gave it to his
disciples, saying:
Take and eat, this is my body, which is given for you.
Likewise, after the supper, he took the cup into his holy hands, thanked his Father, and
gave it to his disciples, and spake:
Take and drink ye all thereout, this is the cup of the new and everlasting testament in my
blood, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As often as ye do
this, do it in my remembrance.

**Note.**

- **The recast *Quam oblationem*.** Sehling's note: "This prayer corresponds largely to the prayer *Quam oblationem* of the Roman Missal". Kantz's petition "help, that this bread and the wine may become and be for us …" (*ut nobis … fiat*) has become "grant us that we may firmly believe that this bread and wine becometh …". The prayer no longer asks that the bread
  become the body. It asks that we believe that it does.
- **The Verba.** Kantz's two *benedixit* ("blesseth") are dropped.

#### <a id="s7-9-4"></a>7.9.4 Our Father, *Agnus Dei*, *Fili Dei vivi*, communion, *Nunc dimittis*

Let us pray: Our Father, which art in heaven. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come unto
us. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And
forgive us our debt, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but
deliver us from all evil. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, thy Son, who with thee and the
Holy Ghost, one true God, liveth and reigneth for ever.
*Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God)
O thou Lamb of God, that bearest the sin of the world, have mercy upon us and give us thy
peace.
*A prayer before the receiving of the most worthy Sacrament*
O Lord Jesu Christ, thou everlasting Word of thy Father, thou Saviour of the world, living
God, deliver us through thy bottomless mercy from all sins. Help us that we may fulfil thy
commandments at all times, and never be parted from thee for ever.
*Hereafter shall the priest give the most worthy Sacrament to them that desire it with a
hungry, sinful heart, saying thus:*
Be comforted. For behold, this is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which suffered for you
the bitter death. Take and eat, that it may feed you and preserve you unto everlasting life.
*When they have all been communicated with the body of Christ, the priest shall take the
cup with the precious blood of Christ, and say thus:*
Now will we also drink the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Behold, ye
troubled, sinful hearts, and be comforted. For this is the precious, costly treasure of the
blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, wherewith ye are bought. Take this and divide it among
yourselves to the washing away of your sins.
*When all this is done, the priest shall with the whole Christian congregation thank and
praise the Lord with this song of praise, saying:*
O Lord, now let thy servant depart in peace according to thy words, for our eyes have seen
thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people, a light to lighten
the Gentiles and for a glory of thy people Israel. To thee be praise and thanks, O thou
holy, blessed Trinity, God the Father, Son, Holy Ghost.

**Note.**

- **As in Kantz (§[7.2.5](#s7-2-5)–[7.2.7](#s7-2-7)):**
  - the conclusion of the embolism after the Our Father;
  - one *Agnus Dei*;
  - an abridged *Fili Dei vivi* (Son of the living God);
  - the *custodiat* ("feed and preserve unto everlasting life");
  - *Calicem salutaris* (The cup of salvation);
  - the *Nunc dimittis* with a Trinitarian doxology.
- **What changes from Kantz:**
  - ***Fili Dei vivi.*** Kantz's "deliver us by this thy holy body and rose-coloured blood" (*per hoc sacrosanctum Corpus et Sanguinem tuum*, by this thy most holy Body and Blood) becomes "through thy bottomless mercy". Bremen removes the one phrase that ascribed the
    deliverance to the consecrated elements.
  - **The communicants** are "they that desire it with a hungry, sinful heart".
  - **Omitted.** The showing of the host and the *Pax* are gone. No fraction, as in
    Kantz's first edition.
- **What follows.** A German *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God).

---

### <a id="s7-10"></a>7.10 Lippe, *Deutsche Messe*, [1525–1538] (Müntzer in Low German)

Sehling 22, IX (Lippe, Nachtrag), Nr. 1, pp. 565–569 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 1549). It is a
manuscript Mass with notes, for Trinity Sunday.

Its eucharistic part is Müntzer's German Mass ([§7.4](#s7-4); Radical Reformation) in Low German, taken
into a Lutheran order:

- the *Per omnia saecula* (World without end) before the Preface;
- the Roman *Qui pridie* (Who the day before) with "lifted up his eyes" and "a mystery of the faith";
- "Therefore let us all pray as Jesus Christ … hath taught us";
- the *Per omnia saecula* after the Our Father;
- *Pax Domini* (The peace of the Lord).

Its propers are those of Volprecht's Trinity Mass ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)): Rom 11:33–36, John 15:26–16:4,
the Alleluia *Benedictus es, Domine, Deus patrum nostrorum* (Blessed art thou, O Lord God of our fathers), and the *Proficiat* (May [the receiving] profit)
postcommunion.

Müntzer's own German Mass has no Trinity Mass. The Erfurt *Kirchenamt* of 1525, which
reprinted Müntzer's Masses, added one (Sehling 6, III, p. 812 n. 26, to Calenberg-Göttingen 1542,
[§7.13](#s7-13)). An Erfurt print of this kind is the likely source of the Lippe text.

*The offertory*
*For the offertory a spiritual song is sung, that is, a psalm.*
*The Preface*
World without end. Amen.
The Lord be with you.
And with thy spirit.
Our hearts on high.
We have them unto the Lord.
We give thanks unto the Lord our God.
It is meet and right.
Verily it is meet and right, and moreover very wholesome, that we should always and in all
places give thanks unto thee, Lord, holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, who with thine
only-begotten Son and the Holy Ghost art one only God, art one only Lord; not in the oneness
of a person, but in the oneness of a single being. For that which by thine own revelation
we believe of thy glory, even the same we hold, without difference, of thy Son and of the
Holy Ghost; that in the confession of the true and everlasting Godhead, the propriety in
the persons and the unity in the being and the equality in the majesty may be rightly
worshipped; which the angels praise, the archangels honour, and thereto Cherubim and
Seraphim, who without ceasing sing with one accord of voice:
Holy, holy, holy art thou, Lord God of hosts, heaven and earth are filled with thy praise.
Ah, help us, thou that art in the highest. Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the
Lord. Ah, give luck and salvation in the highest.

**Note.**

- **The offertory.** It keeps its name and its place, as a German hymn.
- **"Through all eternity of eternity, amen"** heads the "Prefatio" (Preface). It is the *Per omnia
  saecula saeculorum. Amen* (World without end. Amen) that ended the silent Secret, as in Müntzer ([§7.4.1](#s7-4-1)).
- **The Preface** is the Trinity Preface, rendered fully:
  - "Who with thine only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit art one God, one Lord: not in the singularity of one person, but in the Trinity of one substance …";
  - "… and in the persons propriety, and in the essence unity, and in the majesty equality may be adored. Which the Angels praise and the Archangels, the Cherubim also and Seraphim …".

  "In the oneness of a single being" renders *in unius Trinitate substantiae* (in the Trinity of one substance)
  loosely.
- **The Sanctus.** "Ah, help us" is *Hosanna*.

The day before, when Jesus would suffer, he took the bread into his holy hands, and lifted
up his eyes to heaven unto thee, God, his almighty Father, and said thanks unto thee, and
blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat thereof, this
is my body, which is given for you.
*Here he giveth the sacrament to the people who will be communicated. Thereafter he taketh
the cup in his hand and saith:*
In like manner, when they had eaten, he took the cup into his holy and worthy hands, and
said thanks unto thee, and blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink
ye all thereout. This is the cup of my blood, of the new and everlasting covenant, a
mystery of faith, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As often
as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby.
*Here he giveth the people who are communicated the cup also; meanwhile the hymn "Gott sei
gelobet" is sung, or "Jesus Christus unser Heiland", or the German Sanctus.*

**Note.**

- **The Verba** are word for word Müntzer's *Qui pridie* ([§7.4.2](#s7-4-2)), with *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith).
- **The order of communion.** As Luther proposed in the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass), the bread is
  given after the bread-word and the cup after the cup-word. So the Our Father, the *Pax*
  and the *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God) come *after* communion.

Therefore let us all pray, as Jesus Christ, the Son of God, hath taught us, saying: Our
Father, which art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come. Thy will be done
on earth as in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debt, as we
forgive our debtors, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, amen.
This be done through our Lord Jesus Christ, thy Son, who with thee and the Holy Ghost, one
true God, liveth and reigneth for ever, amen.
World without end. Amen.
The peace of the Lord be alway with you, and with thy spirit.
O Lamb of God, that bearest the sin of the world, have mercy upon us.
O Lamb of God, that bearest the sin of the world, give us thy peace.
*The communion*
*For the communion a psalm or spiritual song of praise is sung. Thereafter the pastor saith
to the people:* The Lord be with you.
*Answer:* And with thy spirit.
O Lord God, let the receiving of the holy Sacrament, and the everlasting confession of the
holy and self-subsistent undivided Trinity, profit us for body and soul; who livest and
reignest one only God, world without end, amen.
Let us bless the Lord; thanks be to God for ever.
The Lord bless thee and keep thee, and make his face shine upon thee, and have mercy upon
thee, and turn his face unto thee and give thee peace, amen.

**Note.**

- **The embolism's two endings.** Lippe has both:
  - Kantz's "That be done through our Lord …", the conclusion *Per eundem Dominum* (Through the same Lord);
  - Müntzer's "Through all eternity of eternity", the chant ending *Per omnia saecula*.

  There is no fraction rubric.
- ***Pax Domini*** is kept with its response. The response is run on in the manuscript.
- **The postcommunion** is the Roman *Proficiat* of Trinity Sunday, as in Volprecht
  ([§7.7.2](#s7-7-2)).
- **The blessing.** "Let us bless the Lord; to God be thanks for ever" is Müntzer's
  *Benedicamus*. The Aaronic blessing follows.

---

### <a id="s7-11"></a>7.11 Schleswig-Holstein, a Low German Mass from Kiel, [after 1526]

Sehling 23, A, Nr. 1, pp. 55–57 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 1576; introduction in doc 1568, p. 39). The
manuscript, with notes, was bound into a book of the Kiel preacher Rudolf von Nimwegen
(† 1542). Sehling's editor dates it after 1526 because it draws on Döber (1525) and on
Luther's *Deutsche Messe* (1526).

The order also draws on:

- **Kantz** ([§7.2](#s7-2)): the *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) and its collect.
- **Müntzer** ([§7.4](#s7-4)): the Roman *Qui pridie* (Who the day before), with "lifted up his eyes".
- **Döber** ([§7.8](#s7-8)): the *Fili Dei vivi* (Son of the living God) said by the people after the priest.

It is the only order in the corpus with a German *Domine, non sum dignus* (Lord, I am not worthy).

#### <a id="s7-11-1"></a>7.11.1 Before the altar: absolution by the sexton, *Veni Sancte Spiritus*, collect

*The minister readeth: Misereatur. The sexton readeth: Misereatur.*
The almighty, merciful God forgive us our sins. And I, by the commandment of our Lord Jesus
Christ, say unto you that trust in God's grace and believe his words, free, quit and loosed
of all your sins. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost.
*The priest:* Amen.
*The priest readeth:*
Come, Holy Ghost, fill the hearts of thy faithful and kindle in them the fire of thy divine
love, who through the diversity of tongues hast gathered the peoples of the whole world in
the unity of the true faith.
*Sexton:* Amen.
*The priest readeth:*
O Lord, almighty God, grant that thy Holy Ghost may be and dwell with us, that he may
enlighten us and teach all truth. Strengthen and defend in all adversity; through Christ
our Lord.
*The sexton:* Amen.

**Note.**

- **The absolution.** "Myseriator" (*Misereatur*) and the absolution are Kantz's ([§7.2.1](#s7-2-1)),
  but read by the sexton. The priest only adds the *Amen*. Sehling's editor points to
  Hadeln 1526 for the same practice.
- **The prayers.** The antiphon and collect are Kantz's ([§7.2.2](#s7-2-2)), said before the priest goes
  to the altar. Then the antiphon is sung again, with notes, and a troped Kyrie follows.

#### <a id="s7-11-2"></a>7.11.2 Preface and the bread-word

The Lord be with you. Our hearts on high. We give thanks unto the Lord our God.
Verily it is worthy and right, meet and wholesome, that we, O Lord, almighty God, should in
all places give thanks unto thee, and specially at this time praise thee, for Christ our
Passover lamb is offered for us. He is the true Lamb of God, which hath taken away the sin
of the world, who by his temporal death hath destroyed our eternal death; and when he rose
again, he hath brought life again.
The day before, when Jesus Christ would suffer, he took the bread into his holy and worthy
hands, and lifted up his eyes to heaven unto thee, God, his almighty Father, and said thanks
unto thee, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, saying:
Take and eat ye all thereof. This is my body, which is given for you for the forgiveness of
sins.
*Now the choir beginneth to sing: "Jesus Christus, unser Heiland". One verse thereof.*

**Note.**

- **The Preface** is the Easter Preface: "To praise thee indeed, O Lord, at all times, but chiefly on this day more gloriously, when Christ our passover was sacrificed. For he is the very Lamb that hath taken away the sins of the world; who by dying hath destroyed our death, and by rising again hath restored our life".
  - The manuscript breaks off before the *Et ideo* (And therefore) and the Sanctus (Sehling: "The text breaks off at this point").
  - "Is offered for us" keeps *immolatus est* (was sacrificed; 1 Cor 5:7).
- **The bread-word** is Müntzer's *Qui pridie* (Who the day before), with "in forgiveness of sins" added to the
  bread.
- **Separate consecration.** Only the bread is consecrated now. The cup is consecrated after
  the communion of the bread ([§7.11.4](#s7-11-4)), as Luther had suggested.

#### <a id="s7-11-3"></a>7.11.3 Exhortation, *Fili Dei vivi*, *Domine non sum dignus*

*Thereafter the priest turneth with the body of Christ to the people. And the communicants
seat themselves all in a row before the altar to receive the sacrament. And the priest
maketh an exhortation and saith, holding the body of Christ in his hand:*
Good friends, Christ our Saviour hath left us at his last departing a glorious jewel, to
wit his body and blood, for a spiritual medicine and food, whereby we shall remember him;
through which body and blood he hath set up for us an only testament of salvation, and
confirmed the same testament of his flesh and blood with his bitter passion. And as often
as we feel ourselves burdened with sins, and hunger and thirst after this food and after
this drink, we shall receive it with a thorough and firm faith. And as often as we take it
unto us, we shall be mindful to give him thanks and praise for his bitter passion, for his
benefit, and that this food may be helpful and comfortable unto us unto everlasting life.
Amen.
Say after me with inward heart:
O Lord Jesu Christ, thou Son of the living God, who by the Father's will, through the
working together of the Holy Ghost, hast by thy bitter death made the world alive again
through faith: deliver us poor children of Adam, by this thy holy body and innocent blood,
from all our iniquities and wickednesses, and grant us that we may at all times follow thy
commandments obediently with desire and love, and never be separated from thee. Amen.
O Lord, I am not worthy by my merit of thy worthy body and blood; but make me worthy by thy
divine promise, make me whole by thy wholesome word. Amen.

**Note.**

- **The priest holds the host** during the exhortation. The exhortation takes the place of
  the Canon's remembrance.
- ***Fili Dei vivi*** is the Strasbourg and Döber German text ([§7.5.1](#s7-5-1), [§7.8.8](#s7-8-8)), said after
  the priest by the communicants. Three phrases are added:
  - "through faith" (the world is made alive through faith);
  - "us poor children of Adam";
  - "with desire and love".
- ***Domine, non sum dignus.*** The Roman text is "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my soul shall be healed" (Mt 8:8). It was said by the
  priest, and by the people before communion. The Kiel text changes it:
  - It drops the centurion's roof.
  - It makes the worthiness a question of merit ("through my merit").
  - It asks that Christ's "divine promise" make the communicant worthy.
  - "make me blessed through thy wholesome word" keeps *sed tantum dic verbo, et sanabitur* (but speak the word only, and [my soul] shall be healed).

#### <a id="s7-11-4"></a>7.11.4 Communion of the bread; the cup-word and communion of the cup; blessing

*Now the priest distributeth the body of Christ to the communicants, and the choir beginneth
the second verse thus: "Dass wir des nimmer vergessen, gab etc." (That we might never forget it, he gave etc.), and singeth so long till
the body of Christ is distributed. Thereafter the choir is silent. And the priest
beginneth further to consecrate the blood of Christ, and saith:*
In like manner, when they had eaten, he took the cup into his holy and worthy hands, and
said thanks unto thee, and blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying:
Take and drink ye all thereout. This is the cup of my blood, of the new and everlasting
testament, which is shed for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. As often as ye
do this, do it in my remembrance.
*Now the priest giveth the communicants the blood of Christ, and the choir singeth "Jesus
Christus unser", or the song of praise "Gott sei gelobet und gebenedeiet", etc., and singeth
so long till the blood of Christ is distributed. Thereafter the priest turneth again to the
people and saith:*
The Lord be with you.
*And concludeth the Mass with a collect. And after the collect the priest saith once more:*
The Lord be with you.
*Thereafter he readeth this blessing written hereafter over the people, and saith, Numbers
the sixth chapter:*
The Lord bless you and keep you.
The Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious unto you.
The Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace, through Christ our Lord.
*The choir answereth:* Amen.
*Thereafter a psalm is sung, wherewith the Mass is concluded.*

**Note.**

- **"to consecrate the blood of Christ".** The rubric calls the cup-word a consecration.
- **The cup-word** is Müntzer's *Simili modo* (In like manner), but "testament" (not "covenant"), and without
  *mysterium fidei* (the mystery of faith).
- **No Our Father, no *Pax*, no *Agnus Dei*.** The Our Father is said with the Creed and
  the Verba on weekdays without communicants, and at the communion of the sick.

---

### <a id="s7-12"></a>7.12 Brandenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1540

Church order of the Elector Joachim II, 1540. Sehling 3, Mark Brandenburg Nr. 3, pp. 67–71.

The order is conservative. The Latin chants stay. The offertory chant stays. The Preface
and Sanctus are sung in Latin. The Verba are sung aloud in German. The prayers the priest
said before communion (*Domine Iesu Christe qui dixisti*, *Fili Dei vivi*, *Perceptio*) and
after it (*Corpus tuum*, *Quod ore sumpsimus*) are kept in Latin.

In the Canon's own place, under the Sanctus, the priest says four new German collects. For
the Pfalz-Neuburg version of these, Sehling notes: "These prayers are set in the place of the intercessory prayers said in the Roman Mass partly before, partly after the consecration".

The order's rationale (p. 67) is given before the Mass:

The words of consecration shall also be sung or spoken openly after the Preface, as this
also hath been customary in the Church of old […]. Whence may be gathered with what ground
such words may be forbidden to the laity: only for this cause, that it was perhaps feared
they might in time become aware thereby, and find out, that the sacrament of the cup
belonged to them as well as to the priests; and perhaps besides discover the unfitness of
their Canon, whereon they have set well-nigh all salvation, and yet read the same secretly
[…].

#### <a id="s7-12-1"></a>7.12.1 Creed, offertory, Preface, Sanctus

*Thereupon the priest shall sing Credo in unum Deum; the Patrem shall be sung in cathedrals
and collegiate churches in Latin, but in the parishes in German, "Wir glauben all an einen
Gott" (We all believe in one God). Thereupon the priest shall sing Dominus vobiscum without Oremus; thereupon the chant
which heretofore was kept for the offertory shall be sung; thereupon the priest shall sing
the customary Preface, and next the Latin Sanctus, all sung in Latin. Under the Sanctus the
priest shall pray the following prayer in German.*

**Note.**

- **The offertory.** "*Dominus vobiscum* without *Oremus*" keeps the greeting before the
