  offertory but drops the *Oremus* that led into the offertory prayers. The offertory chant
  itself survives ("the chant that was formerly kept for the offertory"). No offertory
  prayers are said.
- **In villages.** On p. 71 the order adds that "in the small towns … and in the villages" the offertory "of the Sunday or of the feasts" may be replaced by a German psalm
  after the sermon: "thereupon shall follow the Latin Preface, the Sanctus, the communion and further the conclusion".
- **The Preface.** "The customary Preface" is the Latin Preface of the day. It is not
  printed.

#### <a id="s7-12-2"></a>7.12.2 The four collects under the Sanctus (in place of the Canon's intercessions)

*For the magistrates.*
Merciful heavenly Father, in whose hands standeth all power and authority of men, ordained
of thee for the punishment of evildoers and the protection of the godly, in whose hands also
stand all the rights and laws of all lands: we beseech thee, be gracious unto our lord the
Emperor, all kings and princes, especially unto our prince and lord of the land N., and unto
the council and rulers of this city and all lawful magistrates, that they may rightly bear
the temporal sword which thou hast committed unto them. Overshadow them with the power of
the Highest; enlighten them and keep them in thy divine name; let them love thy divine word
from the heart and hold fast thereto, and in no wise suffer it to be persecuted. Give them,
dear Lord, wisdom and understanding and a peaceable government, that they may rule and
defend all their subjects in the truth and righteousness that is well-pleasing unto thee.
Also, my dear God, prolong their life according to thy will; and forasmuch as the judgement
is thine and they sit in thy stead, give them grace so to rule that thy holy name may be
hallowed and praised through them, from henceforth even for ever. This help them the Lord
Jesus Christ, thy beloved Son. Amen.

*Another.*
O almighty, gracious God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hast earnestly commanded us
that we should pray thee for labourers into thine harvest, that is, for right and true
preachers of thy word: we beseech thy bottomless mercy that thou wouldest send us right and
true teachers and ministers of thy divine word, and give thy wholesome word into their heart
and into their mouth, that they may faithfully perform thy commandment and preach nothing
that is contrary to thy holy word; to the end that we, being by thy heavenly, eternal word
admonished, taught, fed, comforted and strengthened, may do that which is well-pleasing
unto thee and profitable unto us. Give, O Lord, unto thy holy Christian Church thy Spirit and
divine wisdom, that thy word may run and grow among us and be preached with all boldness, as
it becometh, and that thy holy Christian congregation may be bettered thereby; that we may
serve thee with steadfast faith and continue in the knowledge of thy name unto the end;
through our Lord, etc.

*Another.*
Almighty God and everlasting Father, a King of glory and a Lord of heaven and of earth, by
whose Spirit all things are governed, by whose providence all things are ordered; thou art a
God of peace, from whom alone unity cometh unto us: we beseech thee through our Lord Jesus
Christ that thou wouldest forgive us our sins and endue us with thy divine peace and unity,
that we may serve thy name in fear and trembling, and that thou mayest be praised of us
evermore. Amen.

Merciful God and heavenly Father, whose mercy hath no end, who art longsuffering, gracious
and of great goodness and faithfulness, and forgivest all iniquity, transgression and sin:
we have, alas, sinned with our fathers, we have done amiss and dealt wickedly and oftentimes
provoked thee to wrath; against thee only have we sinned and done evil in thy sight. But,
Lord, remember not against us our former iniquities; let thy mercy speedily be great upon
us, for we are brought very low. Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name;
deliver us and forgive us our sins, through thy Son Jesus Christ. Amen.

**Note.** The texts and translations are the same as in [`general_prayers.db`](#repo-prayers) (family L).
Sehling traces the collects for the ministers and for peace to Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533.
The one for the magistrates is an expanded form of the Nürnberg collect. The penitential
fourth, woven from Ps 106:6, Ps 51:4 and Ps 79:8–9, stands where the Canon's prayers for
forgiveness stood (*Hanc igitur*'s *ab aeterna damnatione nos eripi* [that we be delivered from eternal damnation], the *Nobis quoque
peccatoribus* [To us sinners also]).

#### <a id="s7-12-3"></a>7.12.3 The Verba, sung, with elevation

*Thereafter the words of consecration shall be sung in German, and the elevation made, as
followeth:*
Our Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread, gave thanks unto his
heavenly Father, blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and
eat, this is my body, which is given for you; this do in remembrance of me.
*Here, with a slight inclination, lift it up reverently on high. Then take the cup with both
hands, and say:*
Likewise also he took the cup after the supper, gave thanks and blessed it, and gave it to
his disciples, and said: Drink ye all of it, this is my blood of the new testament, which is
shed for you and for many for the remission of sins; this do, as oft as ye drink it, in
remembrance of me.
*Lift the cup on high.*
*After the elevation, in cathedrals and collegiate churches a Latin chant shall be sung, as
the responsory Tua est potentia, etc.; but in the parishes a German song: "Es wolt uns Gott
genädig sein", or "Sei Lob und Dank mit hohem Preis".*

**Note.**

- **The Verba.** They are the Pauline and Lutheran form. "Giveth thanks to his heavenly Father"
  keeps an echo of *tibi gratias agens* (giving thanks to thee). 
- **Rubrics.** The Latin rubrics are those of the missal: *elevat … reverenter* (he elevateth … reverently), *accipit
  calicem ambabus manibus* (he taketh the chalice with both hands).
- **The chant.** The Latin responsory after the elevation takes the place of the
  *Benedictus* sung at the elevation.

The elevation in the order of the Mass is treated in [Chapter 2](#ch2),
[§2.11](#s2-11), and as a mark of the feast in
[Chapter 12](#ch12), [§12.10.6](#s12-10-6).

#### <a id="s7-12-4"></a>7.12.4 Our Father and the Peace

*Thereupon the Pater noster shall be sung in German, as followeth.*
Let us pray, as the Lord Christ Jesus hath commanded us, that out of right confidence and
trust we may be bold to say: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy
kingdom come, thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth; give us this day our daily bread,
and forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors; and lead us not into temptation, but
deliver us from evil: for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever.
*Let all the people say, Amen.*
*Turning himself to the people he singeth:*
The peace of the Lord be with you all.
*Let all the people say, Amen.*

**Note.** "As the Lord Christ Jesus hath commanded us, that we … may say" recasts
*Praeceptis salutaribus moniti … audemus dicere* (Admonished by saving precepts … we make bold to say).

There is no embolism. *Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum* (The peace of the Lord be always with you) is kept, with the people answering
*Amen* where the Roman response is *Et cum spiritu tuo* (And with thy spirit).

#### <a id="s7-12-5"></a>7.12.5 *Agnus Dei* and the priest's three prayers before communion (Latin)

O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us.
O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us.
O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, grant us peace.
*The Agnus Dei shall also be sung in Latin.*
*Bow thyself.*
O Lord Jesus Christ, who saidst unto thine apostles, My peace I give unto you, my peace I
leave with you: regard not my sins, but the faith of thy Church; and vouchsafe to pacify,
keep, help and govern her according to thy will; who with God the Father and the Holy Ghost
livest and reignest God, world without end. Amen.
*Bowing, let him say:*
O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who by the will of the Father, the Holy Ghost
working with thee, hast by thine own death given life to the world: deliver us by this thy
most holy body and blood from all our iniquities and all our evils; and make us ever to obey
thy commandments, and suffer us never to be separated from thy mercy for evermore. Who
livest and reignest God, world without end. Amen.
*Another prayer.*
Let the sacrament of thy body, O Lord Jesus Christ, which we unworthy desire to receive, not
turn to us unto judgement and condemnation; but of thy goodness let it profit us unto the
defence of mind and body, and unto the obtaining of healing; who livest and reignest with
God the Father in the unity of the Holy Ghost, God, world without end. Amen.

**Note.** These are the three prayers the priest said before his communion. Pfalz-Neuburg
1543 (note 20–21) reports that in 1540 two were said, the third being an alternative to the
second.

1. ***Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti.***
   - The two halves of John 14:27 are inverted: "do … relinquo" (I give … I leave), where the Roman text has
     *Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis* (Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you).
   - The verbs "pacificare custodire adiuvare et regere" (to keep in peace, guard, help and govern) are those of the Canon's *Te
     igitur* (Thee therefore; *pacificare, custodire, adunare et regere*), with *adiuvare* (help) for *adunare* (unite).
     The Tridentine text has only *pacificare et coadunare* (to keep in peace and unite).
2. ***Fili Dei vivi.***
   - The Roman singular (*libera me … meis … fac me … inhaerere … a te*) is made plural and
     congregational.
   - *Inhaerere* becomes *obedire*.
   - *A te numquam separari* (never to be separated from thee) becomes *a tua misericordia nunquam in perpetuum separari* (never for ever to be separated from thy mercy).
   - This petition, "Deliver us by this thy most holy body and blood", is not the
     embolism *Libera nos, quaesumus* (Deliver us, we beseech thee).
3. ***Perceptio corporis tui*** appears as *Sacramentum corporis tui* (The sacrament of thy body).
   - It is plural, and *praesumo* (I presume) becomes *cupimus* (we desire).
   - *Tutamen* (defence) stands for *tutamentum* (defence). The stray *tui* (thy) after *indigni* (unworthy) is as printed.

#### <a id="s7-12-6"></a>7.12.6 The exhortation (Osiander, Nürnberg 1533)

*Then turning himself to the people let him read this exhortation.*
Dearly beloved in God, forasmuch as we will now consider and keep the supper of our Lord
Jesus Christ, wherein he hath given us his flesh for a meat and his blood for a drink,
therewith to strengthen faith, we ought rightly every one with great diligence to examine
himself, as the holy Paul exhorteth us; for this holy sacrament is given for a special
comfort and strength unto the poor troubled consciences that confess their sins, fear God's
wrath and death, and are hungry and thirsty after righteousness. But when we examine
ourselves, and every one goeth into his own conscience, as the holy Paul teacheth us, we
shall surely find nothing else but all manner of horrible sin, and death, which we have
deserved with sin; and yet we cannot in any wise help ourselves out thereof. Therefore hath
our dear Lord Jesus Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sins' sake is become man, to the
end that he might fulfil the law and all the will of God for us and for our good, and take
upon himself and suffer death and all that we had deserved with our sins, for us and for our
deliverance. And that we might steadfastly believe this, and through faith live joyfully in
his will, he took after the supper the bread, gave thanks, brake it, and said: Take and eat,
this is my body, which is given for you; that is, that I am become man, and all that I do
and suffer is all your own, done for you and for your good; for a sure token and witness
whereof I give you my body for meat. Likewise he took also the cup, and said: Take and drink
ye all of this, this is the cup of the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you and
for many for the remission of sins; as oft as ye do this, ye shall remember me thereby; that
is, forasmuch as I have taken your cause upon me and laden your sins upon myself, I will
offer myself unto death for sin, shed my blood, obtain grace and forgiveness of sins, and so
set up a new testament, wherein sins are forgiven and shall be remembered no more for ever;
for a sure token and witness whereof I give you my blood to drink. Whosoever now eateth thus
of this bread and drinketh of this cup, and firmly believeth these words which he heareth of
Christ and these signs which he receiveth of Christ, he dwelleth in the Lord Christ and
Christ in him, and shall live for ever. Hereby shall we now remember him and show forth his
death, namely that he died for our sins and rose again for our justification, and give him
thanks therefor; every one take up his cross and follow him, and according to his
commandment love one another, as he hath loved us: for we are all one bread and one body,
seeing we are all partakers of one bread and drink of one cup.

**Note.** This is Osiander's Nürnberg exhortation ([§7.8.7](#s7-8-7)) as revised for Brandenburg-Nürnberg
1533 (Sehling 11, 195). It comes after the Latin priest's prayers and immediately before the
distribution. *Darbei dabei* is a doublet in the print.

#### <a id="s7-12-7"></a>7.12.7 Communion

*Thereupon shall be begun the responsory Discubuit Jesus in Latin; and if the communicants
were many, so that it might not suffice therewith, one shall begin to sing to the people in
German "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) or "Jesus Christus, unser Heiland" (Jesus Christ, our Saviour); one of which songs, even though
the Discubuit suffice, shall nevertheless be sung after the communion.*
*Now the communicants approach, and when the Lord's body is reached to them, let the priest
say:*
Take and eat, this is the body of Christ, which is given for thee.
*At the cup let the deacon say:*
Take and drink, this is the blood of the new testament, which is shed for thy sins.

**Note.** The communion formula is Lutheran, not Roman. *Corpus Domini nostri … custodiat* (The body of our Lord … preserve)
is not used. The Latin responsory *Discubuit Jesus* (Jesus sat at table; from the Maundy Thursday office) serves
as the communion chant.

#### <a id="s7-12-8"></a>7.12.8 Thanksgiving and the two Latin ablution prayers

*Then turning to the people let him read the following thanksgiving.*
Let us pray.
O almighty, everlasting God, we give praise and thanks unto thy divine bounty that thou hast
fed us and given us to drink with the wholesome flesh and blood of thine only Son Jesus
Christ our Lord; and we humbly beseech thee that thou wouldest work in us by thy Holy
Spirit, that as we have received this holy sacrament with the mouth, so we may also with
firm faith apprehend and for ever retain thy divine grace, forgiveness of sins, union with
Christ and everlasting life, which are therein set forth and promised. We thank thee also,
almighty God, that thou hast refreshed us through this wholesome gift of the body and blood
of Christ thy Son; and we beseech thy mercy that thou wouldest let the same prosper in us
unto strong faith toward thee and unto fervent love among us all; through our Lord Jesus
Christ thy Son, who with thee in eternity [*read*: unity] of the Holy Ghost liveth and
reigneth, true God, ever and eternally. Amen.
*Then let him bow and say:*
May thy body, O Lord, which we sinners have received, and the cup which we have drunk,
cleave unto our inward parts; and grant, O almighty God, that no stain of sin may remain
there where thy pure and holy sacraments have entered; through the same Christ our Lord.
What we have received with the mouth, O Lord, may we take with a pure mind, and may it be
unto us an everlasting remedy; through Christ our Lord.

**Note.**

- **The German thanksgiving.** It comes from Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533. "In eternity of the Holy Ghost" is evidently a slip for "in unity"; Pfalz-Neuburg reads *einigkeit* (unity).
- **The two Latin prayers.** They are the priest's prayers at the ablutions.
  - *Corpus tuum* (Thy body) is in the plural, with the wording "that no stain of sin may remain there, where … pure and holy sacraments have entered". The Tridentine text reads "that no stain of sin may remain in me, whom pure and holy sacraments have refreshed".
  - *Quod ore sumpsimus* (What we have taken with our mouth) lacks *et de munere temporali* (and from a temporal gift). Pfalz-Neuburg restores it.
- **The blessing.** Sehling notes that the 1540 and 1542 prints end here. The blessing
  printed in Mylius's edition is not in them.

---

### <a id="s7-13"></a>7.13 Calenberg-Göttingen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542

Church order of Duchess Elisabeth for the principality of Calenberg-Göttingen, drawn up by
Antonius Corvinus, 1542. Sehling 6, III, pp. 813–817 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 2036), with the Masses
for the church year on pp. 819–834 (doc 2037).

The Sacrament is taken from Brandenburg 1540 ([§7.12](#s7-12)), put into German throughout:

- the collect for the magistrates prayed by the priest under the Sanctus;
- the *Pax Domini* (The peace of the Lord);
- the Brandenburg thanksgiving.

To these Göttingen adds a *custodiat* (preserve) at the distribution, which Brandenburg lacks.

Brandenburg's Latin *Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti* (O Lord Jesus Christ, who saidst) becomes a German postcommunion collect.
The proper Masses for the church year take many of their introits, collects, readings and
Prefaces from Müntzer's German Mass ([§7.4](#s7-4); Radical Reformation). Sehling's notes to doc 2037 say
so at each place, e.g. p. 821 n. 84: "Compare the same Preface in Müntzer, German evangelical Mass of 1524". The route is given in Sehling's note 26 (p. 812): "Corvinus has here, by way of the Erfurt church offices, taken over in part the altar chants and liturgical texts of Thomas Müntzer". The Erfurt *Kirchenamt* of 1525 added a Trinity Mass to Müntzer's five, and a
second Erfurt print added the Ascension, the Sacrament and the Apostles.

#### <a id="s7-13-1"></a>7.13.1 Offertory, Preface, Sanctus, and the collect under the Sanctus

*Thereafter the priest goeth again before the altar, and the choir singeth in the meantime:
"Es wollt uns Gott genädig sein", etc., or "Gott der Vater wohn uns bei", etc. Thereafter the
priest singeth:* The Lord be with you! *The choir answereth:* And with thy spirit.
*Thereafter followeth the offertory.*
*In the stead of the offertory a German psalm shall be sung with the congregation.*
Praise be to God from everlasting to everlasting. Amen. The Lord be with you, and with thy
spirit. Lift up your hearts! We lift them up unto the Lord. Let us give thanks unto the
Lord our God! That is meet and is right! Verily this is meet and right and wholesome that
we should give thanks unto thee, holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God, through
Christ our Lord, who is the true Passover lamb; he is verily the Lamb that beareth the sin
of the world, who hath destroyed our death by his dying, and hath won life by his rising
again. Therefore we sing with his angels and archangels a song of praise to thine honour,
saying without end:
*The Sanctus.*
Isaiah the prophet, it befell him that he in the spirit saw the Lord sitting upon a high
throne in bright splendour; the hem of his garment filled all the choir. […] Holy is God,
the Lord of Sabaoth! Holy is God, the Lord of Sabaoth! Holy is God, the Lord of Sabaoth!
His glory hath filled the whole world. […]
*Under the Sanctus let the priest pray one of these prayers or collects.*
*For the magistrates.*
Merciful heavenly Father, in whose hands stand the power and authority of all men,
ordained by thee for the punishment of evil-doers and for the protection of the godly; in
whose hands also stand all the rights and laws of all lands: we beseech thee, be gracious
unto our emperor, all kings and princes, specially unto our sovereign lady and the young
lordship, the council and governors of this city and all orderly authority, that they may
rightly bear the temporal sword which thou hast committed unto them. Overshadow them with
the power of the Most High, enlighten them and keep them in thy divine name! Let them love
thy divine word from the heart and hold fast thereby, and never suffer the same to be
persecuted. Give them, dear Lord, wisdom and understanding and a peaceable government,
that they may govern and defend all their subjects in the truth and righteousness that is
pleasing unto thee. Also, my dear God, prolong their life according to thy will. And
because the judgement is thine and they sit in thy stead, give them grace so to govern
that thy holy name may be hallowed and praised through them from henceforth for evermore.
This help them the Lord Jesus Christ, thy beloved Son. Amen.

**Note.**

- **"In place of the offertory".** The offertory keeps its name and place ("Thereafter followeth the offertory") as a German hymn.
- **"God be praised from eternity to eternity. Amen."** This is *Per omnia saecula
  saeculorum. Amen*, the end of the Secret, sung before the Preface dialogue. Müntzer has it
  in the same place as "through all eternity of eternity. Amen" ([§7.4.1](#s7-4-1)).
- **The Preface** is the Easter Preface. Sehling's note refers it to the Roman Easter
  Preface.
- **The Sanctus** is Luther's German Sanctus (*Deutsche Messe*).
- **The collect** is the first of Brandenburg's four collects under the Sanctus ([§7.12.2](#s7-12-2)),
  adapted to a duchess-regent ("our princess of the land and the young lordship"). As
  there, it stands in the place of the Canon's intercessions. The Masses for the church
  year (doc 2037) repeat it or give other collects "which the priest prayeth under the Sanctus".

#### <a id="s7-13-2"></a>7.13.2 Our Father, Verba, communion with the *custodiat*, the Peace

Let us pray, as the Lord Christ Jesus hath commanded us, that out of right confidence and
trust we may be bold to say: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy
kingdom come, thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth. Give us this day our daily
bread, and forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors! And lead us not into
temptation, but deliver us from evil; for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the
glory, for ever. Amen.
*The words of consecration.*
Our Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread, gave thanks unto his
heavenly Father, and brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat, this
is my body, which is given for you; this do in remembrance of me. After the same manner he
took also the cup after the supper, gave thanks, and gave it to his disciples, and said:
Drink ye all of it, this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for you and for
many for the forgiveness of sins; this do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me!
*Hereafter the priest shall give the sacrament to the people and say:* Take and eat, this
is the body of Christ, which is given for thee; the same preserve thy soul unto everlasting
life. Amen.
Take and drink, this is the blood of the new testament, which is shed for thy sins; the
same strengthen thy soul unto everlasting life. Amen.
*And meanwhile let the Discubuit be sung, or "Jesus Christus unser Heiland", etc., or "Gott
sei gelobet". When the last go up, let the choir close with the same verses. Thereafter
let the priest sing:*
The peace of the Lord be with you!
*The choir singeth:* And with thy spirit!

**Note.**

- **The Our Father.** Brandenburg's recast *Praeceptis salutaribus* (Taught by saving precepts; [§7.12.4](#s7-12-4)) is kept.
- **The *custodiat*.** "who preserve thy soul unto everlasting life" is the *custodiat* (preserve). "that strengthen thy soul" varies it for the cup. Brandenburg's own formula ("Take and eat …") has no *custodiat*.
- **The *Pax Domini*** follows the communion, as a greeting of peace before the
  thanksgiving. The Roman response is kept.
- **The communion chant.** *Discubuit Iesus* is the responsory that Brandenburg also
  prescribes ([§7.12.7](#s7-12-7)).

#### <a id="s7-13-3"></a>7.13.3 Thanksgiving, *Agnus Dei*, and *Qui dixisti* as the final collect

*Hereupon followeth the thanksgiving, which shall be made in all Masses after the communion
is done; and the priest turneth to the people and saith:*
O almighty, everlasting God, we give praise and thanks unto thy divine bounty, that thou
hast fed and given us to drink with the wholesome flesh and blood of thine only Son Jesus
Christ, our Lord; and we humbly beseech thee that thou wouldest work in us by thy Holy
Ghost, that as we have received this holy sacrament with the mouth, so we may also lay
hold on thy divine grace, forgiveness of sins, union with Christ and everlasting life,
which are therein shown and promised, with firm faith, and keep them for ever. We thank
thee also, almighty God, that thou hast refreshed us through the wholesome gift of thy body
and blood; and we beseech thy mercy that thou wouldest let it prosper unto us to strong
faith toward thee and to fervent love toward us all; through our Lord Jesus Christ, thy
Son, who with thee in the eternity of the Holy Ghost liveth and reigneth, true God, ever
and everlastingly. Amen.
Go in peace!
*The Agnus Dei.*
O Lamb of God, unspotted, slain upon the tree of the cross, found patient at all times,
although thou wast despised; all sins hast thou borne, else must we have despaired; have
mercy upon us, O Jesu!
*Hereupon followeth the collect, which the priest singeth.*
O Lord Jesu Christ, who hast said to thine apostles: My peace I give unto you, my peace I
leave with you!, vouchsafe not to remember our sins, but look upon the faith of thy
congregation; which vouchsafe thou to keep in peace, to preserve and to govern; who with
the Father and the Holy Ghost, true God, rulest and reignest for ever. Amen.
*Hereafter followeth the blessing:*
The Lord bless thee and keep thee! The Lord make his face shine upon thee and be gracious
unto thee! The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee and give thee peace!
*The priest singeth:* Let us praise the Lord, alleluia!
*The choir:* Give thanks unto the Lord, alleluia!
*Let him conclude with the Da pacem, "Verleih uns Frieden", etc., with the collect.*

**Note.**

- **The thanksgiving** is Brandenburg's, made of two parts ([§7.12.8](#s7-12-8)). Brandenburg's Latin
  ablution prayers after it are dropped.
- **"Go in peace!"** is *Ite, missa est* (Go, it is the dismissal) in German.
- **The *Agnus Dei*** is Decius' hymn, moved after the thanksgiving.
- **The final collect is *Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti* in German.** It is the priest's
  prayer for the peace of the Church, said in the Roman Mass before the kiss of peace and
  kept by Brandenburg in Latin before communion ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)). Sehling's note: "The following collect is contained in Latin in the church order for the Mark of Brandenburg of 1540 … Compare the Roman Missal … (Ordo Missae, prayer for peace)". Here it becomes a collect sung aloud
  to close the Mass.
  - The verbs "keep, preserve and govern" follow Brandenburg's *pacificare custodire
    … regere* (to keep in peace, guard … govern; [§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)).
  - "the faith of thy congregation" puts "congregation" for *ecclesiae tuae* (of thy Church).
- **The Easter *Benedicamus*.** "Let us praise the Lord, alleluia / Give thanks unto the Lord, alleluia" is the Easter *Benedicamus Domino, alleluia / Deo gratias, alleluia* (Let us bless the Lord, alleluia / Thanks be to God, alleluia).

#### <a id="s7-13-4"></a>7.13.4 From the Masses for the church year

The proper Masses (doc 2037) end with proper collects in the same slot. For Whitsun it is
Müntzer's closing prayer (Sehling: "Collect from Müntzer's German evangelical Mass of 1524"),
which is a German version of the Roman Whitsun postcommunion *Sancti Spiritus, Domine, corda nostra mundet
infusio: et sui roris intima aspersione fecundet* (May the infusion of the Holy Spirit, O Lord, cleanse our hearts, and make them fruitful by the inward sprinkling of his dew; [§7.4.4](#s7-4-4)):

O Lord, grant us the grace of the Holy Ghost, that the dew of thy goodness may make the
ground of our heart fruitful by its sprinkling […].

---

### <a id="s7-14"></a>7.14 Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543

Church order of Count Palatine Ottheinrich, 1543. Sehling 13, I.2, pp. 70–76 (Mass). Canon
critique: pp. 64–65, [Appendix 7.A](#s7-a).

Sehling notes that the Mass follows Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533, with additions from
Brandenburg 1540. Its shape differs from both in three ways:

1. **No Preface.** Osiander's exhortation is moved to *before* the consecration.
2. **A new prayer over the elements.** Before the Verba the priest says Osiander's
   newly written prayer over the hosts and cup. In it he "brings before thy divine majesty
   these thy gifts, bread and wine". It serves as both an offertory and an epiclesis.
3. **The Sanctus after the Verba.** The Sanctus follows the Verba, and the Brandenburg
   collects are said under it.

After the Our Father, the Brandenburg Latin prayers follow. There are two changes to them:
*Fili Dei vivi* (Son of the living God) reads **"hast given life to thy Church"**, and *Sacramentum corporis* (The sacrament of the body) adds
**"and of the blood"**.

#### <a id="s7-14-1"></a>7.14.1 Creed, sermon, and the exhortation before the Lord's Supper

*After the Gospel the priest shall sing the Credo and the choir the Patrem in Latin; or,
where there is no choir, the priest may himself sing or say it, and meanwhile let the people
sing the German song "Wir glauben all an einen Gott".* […]
*Where now one preacheth during the Mass, the priest shall forthwith after the sermon go
again to the altar; and, that the people may the more diligently and devoutly perceive all
that followeth, he, or one of the ministers if there be any, shall read the following
exhortation toward the people.*
*Exhortation before the Supper.*
Dearly beloved in God! Forasmuch as we will now consider and keep the holy supper of our
Lord Jesus Christ, wherein he hath given us his flesh for a meat and his blood for a drink,
therewith to strengthen faith, we ought rightly every one with great diligence to examine
himself, as the holy Paul exhorteth us; for this holy sacrament is given for a special
comfort and strength unto the poor, troubled consciences which feel and confess their sins,
fear God's wrath and death, and are hungry and thirsty after righteousness. But when we
examine ourselves, and every one goeth into his own conscience, as the holy Paul teacheth
us, we shall surely find nothing else but all manner of horrible sin, and death, which we
have deserved with sin; and yet we cannot in any wise help ourselves out thereof. Therefore
hath our dear Lord Jesus Christ had mercy upon us, and for our sins' sake is become man, to
the end that he might fulfil the law and all the will of God for us and for our good, and
take upon himself and suffer death and all that we had deserved with our sins, for us and
for our deliverance.
And to the end that we might steadfastly believe this, and through faith live joyfully in
his will, he took after the supper the bread, gave thanks, brake it, and said: Take and eat!
This is my body, which is given for you; that is: that I am become man, and all that I do
and suffer is all your own, done for you and for your good. For a sure token and witness
whereof I give you my body for meat. Likewise he took also the cup, and said: Take and drink
ye all of this! This is the cup of the new testament in my blood. As oft as ye do this, ye
shall remember me thereby. That is: forasmuch as I have taken your cause upon me and laden
your sins upon myself, I will offer myself unto death for sin, shed my blood, obtain grace
and forgiveness of sins, and so set up a new testament, wherein sins are forgiven and shall
be remembered no more for ever. For a sure token and witness whereof I give you my blood to
drink.
Whosoever now eateth thus of this bread and drinketh of this cup, and firmly believeth these
words which he heareth of Christ and these signs which he receiveth of Christ, he dwelleth in
the Lord Christ and Christ in him, and shall live for ever. Hereby shall we now remember him
and show forth his death, namely that he died for our sins and rose again for our
justification, and give him thanks therefor; every one take up his cross and follow him, and
according to his commandment love one another, as he hath loved us: for we are all one bread
and one body, seeing we are all partakers of one bread and drink of one cup.

**Note.** This is the Brandenburg text ([§7.12.6](#s7-12-6)), which Sehling traces from 1540 back to 1533.
It is moved from before the distribution to before the consecration. There are two changes:

- **The cup word** stops at "in my blood". It lacks "which is shed for you and for many for the remission of sins".
- **The consciences** "feel and confess" their sins .

#### <a id="s7-14-2"></a>7.14.2 Osiander's prayer over the hosts and cup (offertory and epiclesis)

*After this exhortation the priest shall say this following prayer over the hosts and the
cup, which shall be set upon the altar according to the number and occasion of the persons
that will go to the holy sacrament:*
*Prayer.*
Lord Jesus Christ, thou only true Son of the living God, who hast given thy body for us all
into the bitter death, and shed thy blood for the forgiveness of our sins, and hast moreover
commanded all thy disciples to eat the same thy body and to drink the same thy blood, and
therewith to remember thy death: we bring before thy divine majesty these thy gifts, bread
and wine, and beseech thee that thou wouldest, by thy divine grace, goodness and power,
hallow and bless the same, and make that this bread be thy body and this wine thy blood, and
let them prosper unto everlasting life unto all them that eat and drink thereof; who with
God the Father in the unity of the Holy Ghost livest and reignest ever and eternally. Amen.

**Note.** Sehling calls this an offertory prayer newly written by Osiander, and cites
Graff's study of the epiclesis in Reformation orders. Addressed to Christ, not to the
Father, it gathers four parts of the Canon into one prayer said over the elements:

| Osiander 1543 | Roman source |
|---|---|
| "Lord Jesus Christ, thou only true Son of the living God" | *Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi* (O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God) |
| "We bring before thy divine majesty these thy gifts, bread and wine" | *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful): *offerimus praeclarae maiestati tuae de tuis donis ac datis* (we offer unto thy excellent majesty, of thy gifts and bounties); also *Te igitur* (Thee therefore): *haec dona, haec munera* (these gifts, these presents) |
| "that thou wouldest … hallow, bless and make these, that this bread may be thy body and this wine thy blood" | *Quam oblationem* (Which oblation): *benedictam … facere digneris, ut nobis Corpus et Sanguis fiat* (vouchsafe to make … blessed, that it may become for us the Body and Blood) |
| "cause it to prosper unto everlasting life for all that eat and drink thereof" | *Supplices* (We humbly [beseech]): *ut quotquot ex hac altaris participatione … sumpserimus, omni benedictione caelesti et gratia repleamur* (that as many of us as by this partaking of the altar … shall receive may be filled with all heavenly benediction and grace) |

It meets the demand of the critique printed earlier in the same order ([Appendix 7.A](#s7-a)) only half-way.
The verb there objected to, *opfern* (offer), becomes *bringen … fur deine götliche majestat* (bring … before thy divine majesty), and
the gifts are "thy gifts, bread and wine", not the body and blood.

#### <a id="s7-14-3"></a>7.14.3 The Verba, sung, with elevation

*As soon as this prayer is ended he shall begin to sing the words of consecration, or to say
them with a loud, well-audible voice, as he hath aforetime sung or said other chants, as
hereafter followeth; and he shall take care that his gestures agree with the words; that is,
when he singeth "He took the bread …", he shall also take the large host and hold it level
with his breast until the words be ended. Likewise, when he singeth "He took the cup …", he
shall do so with the cup also, as aforesaid.*
Our Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took the bread, gave thanks, and
brake it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat! This is my body, which is
given for you. This do in remembrance of me!
*Here he shall lift up the large host with bowed head and show it to the people; thereafter
take also the cup and hold it, until he sing or say the following words:*
Likewise also he took the cup after the supper, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, and
said: Drink ye all of it! This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for you and
for many for the remission of sins. This do, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me!
*Here he shall lift up the cup also and show it to the people.*

**Note.** The Verba are sung to the Our Father tone, following Luther's suggestion in the
*Formula missae* (Form of the Mass) and the Nürnberg melody of 1533. The large host is kept, a relic of the
Roman fraction host. The elevation is kept, with a bowed head.

#### <a id="s7-14-4"></a>7.14.4 Sanctus with three collects

*Thereafter the choir shall sing the Sanctus in Latin; or, where there is no choir, the
priest may himself sing or say it, and in place thereof let the people sing a good German
spiritual song; and under the same singing he shall meanwhile say these following prayers.*
*There follow the prayers which the priest shall say under or after the Sanctus.*
*For the temporal magistrates.*
Merciful heavenly Father, in whose hands standeth all power and authority of men, ordained
of thee for the punishment of evildoers and the protection of the godly, in whose hands also
stand all the rights and laws of all lands: we beseech thee, be gracious unto our lord the
Emperor, all kings and princes, especially unto our prince and lord of the land N., and unto
the council and rulers of this city and all lawful magistrates, that they may rightly bear
the temporal sword which thou hast committed unto them. Overshadow them with the power of
thy divine Majesty; enlighten them and keep them in thy divine name; let them love thy
divine word from the heart and submit themselves thereto. Give them, dear Lord, wisdom and
understanding and a peaceable government, that they may rule and defend all their subjects
in the truth and righteousness that is well-pleasing unto thee. Also, my dear God, prolong
their life according to thy will; and forasmuch as the judgement is thine and they sit in
thy stead, give them grace so to rule that thy holy name may be hallowed and praised through
them, from henceforth even for ever. Amen.

*For the ministers of the word.*
O almighty, gracious God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath earnestly commanded
us that we should pray thee for labourers into thine harvest: we beseech thy bottomless
mercy that thou wouldest send us right and true teachers and ministers of thy divine word,
and give thy wholesome word into their heart and mouth, that they may faithfully perform thy
commandment and preach nothing that is contrary to thy holy word; to the end that we, being
by thy heavenly, eternal word admonished, taught, fed, comforted and strengthened, may do
that which is well-pleasing unto thee and profitable unto us. Give, O Lord, unto thy holy
Christendom thy Spirit and divine wisdom, that thy word may run and grow among us and be
preached with all boldness, as it becometh, and that thy holy Christian congregation may be
bettered thereby; that we may serve thee with steadfast faith and continue in the knowledge
of thy name unto the end.

*For Christian unity.*
Merciful God and everlasting Father, a King of glory and a Lord of heaven and of earth, by
whose Spirit all things are governed, by whose providence all things are ordered: thou art a
God of peace, from whom all unity cometh unto us. We beseech thee that thou wouldest forgive
us our sins and endue us with thy divine peace and unity, that we may serve thy name in fear
and trembling for ever and ever, and thy divine Majesty be praised of us evermore; through
our Lord Jesus Christ thy Son, who with thee in the unity of the Holy Ghost liveth and
reigneth ever and eternally. Amen.

**Note.** These are Brandenburg's first three collects ([§7.12.2](#s7-12-2)), with two changes to the
collect for the magistrates:

- **"Overshadow them with the power of thy divine majesty"** replaces "with the power of the most High". It removes the Marian echo of Luke 1:35.
- **"Submit themselves to the same"** replaces "hold fast thereto and not suffer it to be persecuted". The magistrates are to *submit* to the Word, not merely protect
  it.

Brandenburg's fourth, penitential collect is dropped. Sehling's note on this passage
explains the placing: "These prayers are set in the place of the intercessory prayers said in the Roman Mass partly before, partly after the consecration. Elsewhere in evangelical church orders they were struck out without replacement, because they are founded on the sacrificial character of the Mass rejected by the Reformation." In other words, elsewhere the
Canon's intercessions were cut without replacement, because they rest on the sacrificial
character of the Mass.

#### <a id="s7-14-5"></a>7.14.5 Our Father and the Peace

*When then the Sanctus or other singing is ended and these prayers are said, he shall sing
the Our Father or say it with a loud voice, as hereafter followeth:*
Let us pray!
Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done,
as in heaven, so in earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we
forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: for thine is
the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever.
*Choir:* Amen.
*Thereafter let him turn to the people.*
The peace of the Lord be with you all!
*Choir:* Amen.

**Note.** Of *Praeceptis salutaribus* (Taught by saving precepts) only *Oremus* is left. There is no embolism.

#### <a id="s7-14-6"></a>7.14.6 *Agnus Dei* and the priest's three prayers (Latin)

*Thereafter the choir, or, where there is no choir, the priest himself shall sing or else say
the Agnus Dei, as the custom is, and meanwhile let the people again sing a good German
spiritual song; and under the same the priest shall also say these following prayers.*
O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us!
O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us!
O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world, grant us peace!
O Lord Jesus Christ, who saidst unto thine apostles, My peace I give unto you, peace I leave
with you: regard not my sins, but the faith of thy Church; and vouchsafe to pacify, keep,
help and govern her according to thy will; who with God the Father and the Holy Ghost livest
and reignest, God, world without end! Amen.
*Another prayer:*
O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who by the will of the Father, the Holy Ghost
working with thee, hast given life to thy Church: deliver us by this thy most holy body and
blood from all iniquities and all our evils, and make us ever to obey thy commandments, and
suffer us never to be separated from thy mercy for evermore; who livest and reignest, God,
world without end! Amen.
*Another prayer:*
Let the sacrament of thy body and blood, O Lord Jesus Christ, which we unworthy desire to
receive, not turn to us unto judgement and condemnation; but of thy goodness let it profit us
unto the defence of mind and body, and unto the obtaining of healing; who livest and reignest
with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Ghost, God, world without end! Amen.

**Note.** These are the Brandenburg prayers ([§7.12.5](#s7-12-5)), with three changes:

1. ***Fili Dei vivi.*** "by thine own death hast given life to the world" becomes **"hast given life to thy Church"**. The phrase about Christ's own death goes, and *the world* becomes *thy
   Church*.
2. ***Perceptio.*** "of thy Body *and Blood*" adds the cup, which fits communion in
   both kinds.
3. **The rubric.** All three may be said, each marked *Alia oratio* (Another prayer).

#### <a id="s7-14-7"></a>7.14.7 Communion

*Thereafter all shall go to the sacrament who have announced themselves beforehand and have
received the absolution; and the priest shall reach them the body of the Lord with these
words:*
Take and eat! This is the body of Christ, which is given for thee.
*Likewise, where there are ministers, the deacon shall reach the cup to them that have
partaken of the body of Christ, and say thus:*
Take and drink! This is the blood of the new testament, which is shed for thy sins.
*But where there are no ministers, the priest shall first reach the body of the Lord to every
one, and only thereafter the cup; and while this is done, the choir shall sing the communion
in Latin, and if it were too short, other good Latin chant more, especially what is de coena
Domini, as the responsory Discubuit Jesus. But where there is no choir, the congregation
shall again be let sing a good German spiritual song, such as "Jesus Christus unser
Heiland …" (Jesus Christ, our Saviour …), or else "Gott sei gelobet und gebenedeiet …" (God be praised and blessed …), or another song that befitteth the
occasion of the time.*
*When now every one hath received the holy sacrament, then shall the priest also receive it.
And although he shall from the beginning take diligent care so to order and heed all things
that nothing of the holy sacrament remain over, yet he shall especially at the end see to it
that it be all distributed and used up, as Christ hath commanded, where he saith, Luke 22:
Dividite inter nos …, that no grievous or offensive unseemliness befall.*

**Note.**

- **The communion chant.** The Latin *communio* (communion) of the day survives as the communion chant.
- **The priest's communion.** It is moved after the people's, so that nothing is left over.
  Sehling gives the background: this began in Nürnberg in 1524, and Luther wished it in
  order to cut short the question of what becomes of Christ's body and blood in the
  remaining elements.
- **The quotation.** "Dividite inter nos" (divide it among us) is as printed; the Vulgate reads *inter vos* (among you).

#### <a id="s7-14-8"></a>7.14.8 Thanksgiving, Latin ablution prayers, *Benedicamus*, blessing

*Thereafter he shall sing these two collects under one conclusion in the accustomed tone, or
say them with an audible voice.*
Let us pray:
O almighty, everlasting God, we give praise and thanks unto thy divine bounty that thou hast
fed us and given us to drink with the wholesome flesh and blood of thine only Son Jesus
Christ our Lord; and we humbly beseech thee that thou wouldest work in us by thy Holy
Spirit, that as we have received this holy sacrament with the mouth, so we may also with
firm faith apprehend and for ever retain thy divine grace, forgiveness of sins, union with
Christ and everlasting life, which are therein set forth and promised.
*Another prayer.*
We thank thee also, Lord Jesus Christ, that thou hast refreshed us through this wholesome
gift of thy body and blood; and we beseech thy mercy that thou wouldest let the same prosper
in us unto a strong faith toward thee and unto fervent love among us all; who with God the
Father in the unity of the Holy Ghost livest and reignest ever and eternally.
*Choir:* Amen.
*Then let him bow and say:*
May thy body, O Lord, which we sinners have received, and the cup which we have drunk,
cleave unto our inward parts; and grant that no stain of sin may remain there where so pure
and holy sacraments have entered.
What we have received with the mouth, O Lord, may we take with a pure mind; and of a temporal
gift may it become unto us an everlasting remedy; through Christ our Lord. Amen.
*Thereafter he or his deacons, both or one, shall sing the Benedicamus Domino in the tone in
which the Kyrie eleison was sung; and the choir shall answer in the very same tone:* Let us
say thanks unto God.
*Thereafter let the priest bless the people with a loud, audible voice thus:*
The Lord bless you and keep you! The Lord lighten his countenance upon you and be gracious
unto you! The Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace! Amen.
*Or thus:*
God be merciful and gracious unto us and give us his divine blessing! May he cause his
countenance to shine upon us and give us his peace! Amen.
*Or thus:*
Bless and keep us God the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost. Amen.
*Or thus:*
The blessing of God the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost be with you and remain
alway with us all! Amen.
*End of the Mass with communicants.*

**Note.**

- **The thanksgiving.** Brandenburg's single German thanksgiving is split into two collects
  "under one conclusion". The second is addressed to Christ.
- ***Corpus tuum.*** It keeps Brandenburg's older wording but reads "so pure and holy"
  and drops "almighty God".
- ***Quod ore sumpsimus.*** It has the full Roman text, with *et de munere temporali* (and from a temporal gift).
- ***Benedicamus.*** *Benedicamus Domino* (Let us bless the Lord) is answered "Deo dicamus gratias" (Let us say thanks to God), the form used
  at Lauds and Vespers.
- **The blessings.** They are Numbers 6:24–26, Psalm 67:1 and two Trinitarian forms.

---

### <a id="s7-15"></a>7.15 Bugenhagen: the preparatory prayer, and "Hic est noster canon"

Johannes Bugenhagen's Masses keep nothing of the Canon. His Braunschweig order of 1528
(Sehling 6, I, pp. 440–442; doc 1983) runs as follows after the sermon:

- the chalice is prepared during a German hymn;
- an exhortation;
- on feasts, a Latin Preface and Sanctus;
- the Our Father, sung;
- the Verba over the bread, then communion of the bread;
- the Verba over the cup, then communion of the cup;
- the German *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God);
- Luther's thanksgiving collect and the Aaronic blessing.

Bugenhagen's own comment on the Preface: "for the exhortation on the sacrament is the true Preface, that is, a foreword". The same order says of the Canon that it is "patched together out of many pieces like a beggar's cloak" (p. 440).

What his later orders do keep is a **preparatory prayer of the priest at the altar step**
(*Stufengebet*). It is the evangelical counterpart of the Roman *Iudica me* (Judge me), *Confiteor* (I confess)
and *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us), and it is what is usually meant by "Bugenhagen's preparatory prayer".
It appears in three forms.

Bugenhagen's northern Mass as a family of ordo is treated in
[Chapter 2](#ch2), [§2.4.2](#s2-4-2).

#### <a id="s7-15-1"></a>7.15.1 Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, *Christlike kerken-ordeninge*, 1543

Sehling 6, I/2, pp. 54–55 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 1972). The order came out of the visitation of
1542 by Bugenhagen, Antonius Corvinus and Martin Görlitz (Sehling 6, I, p. 12). It prints the German Benedictus and a psalm at the beginning of the
Mass. The prayer is said while they are sung.

*During the psalm or hymn the priest goeth before the altar, kneeleth down with the sexton,
and prayeth for himself and for the people and for all the need of Christendom thus:* Our
Father, etc. *The sexton saith:* Amen. O Lord, deal not with us after our sins, etc. *The
sexton:* Neither reward us according to our iniquities, etc. O Lord, remember not, etc.
*The sexton:* Let thy mercies speedily prevent us, etc. Help us, O God, etc. *The sexton:*
And be merciful, etc. *Thereafter the priest standeth up, and goeth before the altar, and
prepareth himself to sing and to read.*

**Note.**

- **The versicles in full.** The versicles and responses are the Lenten tract *Domine, non
  secundum* (O Lord, deal not with us), from Ps 103:10 and Ps 79:8–9, which also stands in the *preces* of the Office:
  - "O Lord, deal not with us after our sins, neither reward us according to our iniquities."
  - "O Lord, remember not our former iniquities: let thy mercies speedily prevent us, for we are brought very low."
  - "Help us, O God of our salvation, and for the glory of thy name, O Lord, deliver us, and be merciful to our sins, for thy name's sake."
- **What it replaces.** The Roman prayers at the foot of the altar were said by the priest
  and server in dialogue: Ps 43 *Iudica me* (Judge me), the *Confiteor* (I confess) and *Misereatur* (May [almighty God] have mercy), the
  versicles *Adiutorium nostrum* (Our help) and *Deus, tu conversus* (O God, thou wilt turn again), and *Aufer a nobis* (Take away from us). Bugenhagen
  keeps the form: kneeling, in dialogue with the sexton as server, during the opening chant.
  He replaces the confession of sin with the Lord's Prayer and the tract's plea for mercy,
  "for himself and for the people and for all the need of Christendom". Sehling's editor calls it
  a "Stufengebet" (prayers at the foot of the altar).

The rest of the Wolfenbüttel Sacrament, for comparison with the orders above:

*After all this the customary sermon taketh place. When it is out, and there are found such
as will be communicated, the priest shall prepare bread and wine according to the number of
his communicants; and they shall betake themselves to the altar and orderly dispose
themselves to the communion, the men on the right, the women and maidens on the candle
side. Then the priest turneth to the people that will be communicated, and readeth them an
exhortation to the sacrament thus:*
My dearly beloved, it is continually set before us by the preaching of the Gospel of Christ
that we of ourselves are ignorant, poor and lost sinners. […] He saith: This is my body,
which is given for you. This is my blood, which is shed for you for the forgiveness of
sins. That shall ye believe. But he commandeth: Take and eat. Drink ye all thereout, and
remember me. That shall ye do according to his gracious word and command. Amen.

**Note.**

- **"the priest shall prepare bread and wine"** is all that is left of the offertory, as in
  Braunschweig 1528 and Schleswig-Holstein 1542.
- **The exhortation** (Braunschweig 1528, pp. 443f.) is Bugenhagen's "true Preface". The
  order also allows Luther's paraphrase of the Our Father to be read before it.
- **What follows.** The sung Our Father, the Verba over the bread, communion, the Verba
  over the cup, communion, the German *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God), Luther's thanksgiving collect ("We give thanks to thee, almighty Lord God …") and the Aaronic blessing.
- **On feasts.** In towns the priest may sing a Latin Preface (Christmas, Easter,
  Whitsun; the Trinity Preface on other feasts; "the daily [Preface] one may simply let lie as unneeded"). The whole congregation then sings a German Sanctus, "Holy is God the Father, holy is God the Son, holy is God the Holy Ghost …". After it the
  exhortation may be left out.

#### <a id="s7-15-2"></a>7.15.2 Hildesheim, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544

Sehling 7, V, pp. 852–855 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 2136). This is the order for the city of
Hildesheim, drawn up by Bugenhagen, Winkel and Corvinus. It has the same prayer, and at the end a private thanksgiving of the priest:

*First one may sing before the introit a German psalm or hymn made out of the holy
Scripture. During the singing the priest goeth before the altar and kneeleth down with the
sexton, prayeth for himself and for the people and for all the need of Christendom thus:*
Our Father, etc. *The sexton saith:* Amen. O Lord, deal not with us after our sins, etc.
*The sexton:* Neither reward us according to our iniquities, etc. O Lord, remember not,
etc. *The sexton:* Let thy mercies speedily prevent us, etc. Help us, O God, etc. *The
sexton:* And be merciful, etc. *Thereafter the priest standeth up and goeth before the
altar, and prepareth himself to sing and to read.*
[…]
*Then the schoolmaster beginneth a short German psalm, or what pleaseth him, and therewith
an end, etc. But while the singing lasteth, the preacher unvesteth and layeth the Mass
vestment together, kneeleth down again before the altar, and thanketh God secretly for
himself.*

**Note.**

- **The sexton** is the "opperman" (sexton; *Opfermann*, the offertory-man).
- **The closing thanksgiving** is the evangelical form of the priest's private
  thanksgiving after Mass (*Gratiarum actio post missam*: *Trium puerorum*, Ps 150 and
  collects), still said kneeling and "secretly".

#### <a id="s7-15-3"></a>7.15.3 Schleswig-Holstein, *Christlyke Kercken Ordeninge*, 1542

Sehling 23, A, Nr. 7, p. 89 ([`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) doc 1576). This is the Low German form of the Danish
*Ordinatio ecclesiastica* (1537), which Bugenhagen drew up. The text is fixed only by
rubric:

*A priest that will hold Mass, let him fall on his knees before the altar and read by
himself the Confiteor. Let him pray for the preachers of the Gospel, for the King and for
the realm, and also for these duchies. Thereafter let him conduct the Mass according to the
old custom; yet so that he defile it not with the title of sacrifice or work, as the
hypocrisy and mockery of the papists hath been heretofore.*
[…]
*But while the singing lasteth, the priest unvesteth and layeth the Mass vestment together,
kneeleth down again before the altar, and thanketh God secretly for himself.*

**Note.**

- **The *Confiteor*** is kept in its Roman place and posture, said privately ("for himself").
- **The intercession** (preachers, king, realm, duchies) gathers into the preparation what
  the Canon's *Te igitur* (Thee therefore) and *Memento* had prayed for.
- **"according to the old custom".** The Mass is to be kept "according to the old custom", but
  without "the title of sacrifice or work".
- **At the Verba.** The Latin *Ordinatio* (Ordinance) allows an elevation at this point, "if it seem good to the minister", with the bells.

#### <a id="s7-15-4"></a>7.15.4 "Hic est noster canon"

Bugenhagen names the evangelical replacement of the Canon in two places. The first is the
*Pia ordinatio caeremoniarum* for cathedral chapters and monasteries. Sehling prints it
among the Pomeranian orders (4, pp. 345–352, doc 1857). Its Danish hymn incipits show it
belongs with the Danish *Ordinatio* (Ordinance). The second is its Low German form in Schleswig-Holstein
1542 (p. 147).

After the word of God let them be admonished to pray for all conditions of all men, for
the Church, for peace, salvation, etc. This is our Canon. But the papists have patched
these serious things together with their lies into that secret Canon of the Mass.

After the sermon the people shall be admonished to pray for all manner of estates of the
world, for the pastors, for peace, for salvation, etc. And that same prayer is our Canon.
But the papists have patched such an earnest thing together with their lies into the secret
Canon of the Mass.

**Note.**

- **The Canon has become the general prayer.** For Bugenhagen, the Church's intercession
  after the sermon *is* the Canon: the prayer "for the church … for peace" that *Te igitur* (Thee therefore)
  had once been. The German Masses of Strasbourg (§[7.5.1](#s7-5-1)–[7.5.2](#s7-5-2)) and Döber ([§7.8.11](#s7-8-11)) put the
  same intercession into the Canon's own place after the Sanctus. Bugenhagen moves it to
  after the sermon, where the general prayers of the later church orders stand.
- **"in ullum"** is Sehling's print, for *in illum*.

---

### <a id="s7-a"></a>Appendix 7.A The Canon critique of 1533/1540/1543

This is Pfalz-Neuburg 1543, Sehling 13, I.2, p. 65. Sehling traces it through Brandenburg
1540 (Sehling 3, 64f.) to Brandenburg-Nürnberg 1533 (Sehling 11, 183f.). These are the
register references 11:183 and 13:65. Sehling's footnotes to the three quotations give the
Canon's own words; they are supplied here in brackets.

And if the adversaries would say (as they are then driven by the scripture alleged, if they
be not altogether hardened) that they offer not, but mean only to make a memorial and
representation of the first sacrifice, then shall one answer them thus: if they take out the
words wherewith they plainly offer (but chiefly these: "which we offer unto thee for thy
holy Christian Church, etc.", and: "We beseech thee that thou wouldest graciously accept this
sacrifice and deliver us from eternal damnation, etc.", and: "We offer unto thy glorious
majesty, etc."), and set in place thereof, "We remember the sacrifice of thine only Son,
etc.", then will we believe that they are in earnest; and they are also bound to do it, and
can well perform it without offence. For if they have set Kilian and Totnan therein for
money's sake, which is of no profit, they should now rightly, for faith's and truth's sake,
change these words where it is needful.

**Note.** The three passages condemned are the offering clauses of *Te igitur* (Thee therefore), *Hanc
igitur* (This [oblation] therefore) and *Unde et memores* (Wherefore, mindful). Sehling's note explains "Kilian and Totnan". The Würzburg
missal (Speciale missarum, Würzburg 1495) added these Würzburg martyrs, with Colonat, and
confessors to the saints of the **embolism** *Libera nos* (Deliver us): "and also with thy holy martyrs Kilian, Colonat, Totnan and thy holy confessors Martin, Nicholas, Burchard, Benedict". The argument is that a Canon already changed for local saints can be changed for
the truth.

The orders in this file answer the demand in two ways:

- **Worms 1524** (Moderate Reformed) had already done what the critique asks. It kept the Canon
  but turned each offering into prayer: "offer our humble prayer" ([§7.6.8](#s7-6-8)); "that thou wouldest accept us and all our prayer …" ([§7.6.5](#s7-6-5)).
- **Osiander's prayer in Pfalz-Neuburg 1543** ([§7.14.2](#s7-14-2)) does it half-way. It "brings" the gifts
  before the divine majesty, but offers bread and wine, not the body and blood.

<div style="page-break-before: always;"></div>

## <a id="ch8"></a>Chapter 8. Hymn Practice


This chapter covers where hymns were sung in the evangelical church orders of the sixteenth
century, as printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century).
It asks four questions:

- In which parts of the Mass, the offices and the occasional rites (baptism, weddings, the sick,
  burial, ordination) did the orders put hymns?
- Which hymns did they assign to each of these places?
- Was a given place filled by one fixed hymn, by a choice among a handful, or by a hymn that
  changed with the season, the feast, the Sunday gospel or the sermon?
- What reasons did the orders give for their choices?

It deals with the slots of the service, not with the propers as such. Where a hymn took the place
of a proper (introit, gradual, alleluia, sequence, offertory, communion), the replacement is
recorded. Troped, farced and paraphrased ordinaries (Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, Agnus Dei)
are treated in full.

This chapter is separate from the hymn database, `hymns.db` ([Introduction](#repo-hymns)), which
holds the per-Sunday and per-feast hymn tables. The tables it holds (Pomerania 1569, Pfalz-Zweibrücken
1565, Hof 1592, Weissenfels 1578, Mansfeld 1580, Hohenlohe 1596, Nördlingen 1579 and Heilbronn
1543) are referred to here but not repeated.

The findings are summarised in [§8.1](#s8-1), and the method is described in [§8.2](#s8-2). [§8.3](#s8-3) sets out the slots in
outline. §§[8.4](#s8-4)–[8.15](#s8-15) follow the slots of the Mass in order. [§8.16](#s8-16) covers the offices (with the
*Benedicamus* and the old festal songs such as *Puer natus in Bethlehem* [A child is born in Bethlehem]), the catechism and the
weekday services, and [§8.17](#s8-17) the occasional rites. [§8.18](#s8-18) gathers the reasons the orders give. [§8.19](#s8-19) is
a concordance of every order quoted. [Appendix 8.A](#s8-a) condenses the "Compare by day" sheet of
[`hymns.xlsx`](#repo-hymns) into one table: the chief hymn (*Hauptlied*) of each Sunday and feast in the old
sources, with its original, literal English and common English titles and its witnesses.

**Related chapters.** Several subjects are treated more fully elsewhere and are only cited here:
- the order of the Mass in which the slots stand: [Chapter 2](#ch2),
  §§[2.4](#s2-4)–[2.5](#s2-5);
- the Latin propers that the hymns replaced: [Chapter 4](#ch4), §§[4.3](#s4-3)–[4.9](#s4-9);
- the organ in alternation with choir and people:
  [Chapter 9](#ch9), [§9.3](#s9-3);
- the offices and the catechism service in which the office hymns were sung:
  [Chapter 10](#ch10), §§[10.7](#s10-7), [10.10](#s10-10);
- the Litany: [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22](#s13-22);
- the feasts and seasons: [Chapter 12](#ch12), §§[12.10](#s12-10),
  [12.12](#s12-12);
- the prayer before the sermon and the sermon itself: [Chapter 11](#ch11),
  [§11.10](#s11-10);
- the rites at which hymns were sung (baptism, marriage, burial and ordination):
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), §§[13.3](#s13-3), [13.7](#s13-7), [13.9](#s13-9), [13.10](#s13-10).

### <a id="s8-1"></a>8.1 Summary of findings

#### <a id="s8-1-1"></a>8.1.1 The main findings

**1. Most hymn slots were fixed.** In nearly every order a given place in the service was
filled by one hymn, or by a choice among two to five. The choice was often exchanged at the high
feasts for a hymn of the feast. Only one slot regularly changed from Sunday to Sunday: the hymn
between the epistle and the gospel. From about 1560 a second slot joined it in some regions: the
hymn after the sermon. The table in [§8.1.2](#s8-1-2) sets out the pattern slot by slot.

**2. The opening of the service was a prayer for the Holy Ghost.** *Veni sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit), in
Latin or in German ("Komm heiliger Geist, Herre Gott", or the prose "Komm, heiliger Geist,
erfülle"), or "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we), was often sung kneeling. The Hessian *Agende* (1574, Philippist)
gives the reason: "that the help and assistance of the Holy Ghost may be prayed for, for the
performing of the whole service" ([§8.4.1](#s8-4-1)). Many orders also say plainly that the opening songs
were sung "until the congregation cometh together" ([§8.4.2](#s8-4-2)). Some northern orders opened with the
German Benedictus or the German Te Deum instead (§§[8.4.3](#s8-4-3)–[8.4.4](#s8-4-4)).

**3. Hymns took the place of the introit, the gradual, the sequence and the offertory.**
- **Introit.** A Scriptural Latin introit could be kept where a school sang it. Otherwise, and
  in the villages always, "a German psalm" was sung "in place of the introit". The usual psalms
  were Ps 67, 51, 130, 12, 124 and 14, or "Komm heiliger Geist" (Come, Holy Ghost), usually rotated ([§8.5](#s8-5)).
- **Gradual, alleluia and sequence.** These gave way to a German psalm or hymn, often chosen by
  season or gospel ([§8.8](#s8-8)).
- **Offertory.** This became a German psalm sung while bread and wine were prepared and the
  communicants came forward ([§8.11.3](#s8-11-3)). In Bugenhagen's orders the creed hymn "Wir glauben all" (We all believe)
  served here, sung after the sermon ([§8.9.2](#s8-9-2)).
- **Communion chant.** This was replaced by the communion hymns ([§8.14](#s8-14)).
- **Particular days.** A hymn replaced the gradual at the Purification ("Mit Fried und Freud"),
  the sequence in Passiontide (Ps 51), and the offertory at Christmas ("Ein Kindelein so
  löbelich") (§§[8.8.5](#s8-8-5), [8.11.3](#s8-11-3)).

**4. The ordinaries were troped and paraphrased in German.**
- **Kyrie.** Troped German Kyries survive in the Low German Mass of Schleswig-Holstein (after
  1526), Naumburg (1537/38), Mecklenburg (1545), Ritzebüttel (1556), Pfalz-Zweibrücken (1557) and
  Hof (1592). They were sung to the melodies of the Latin troped Kyries, the *Fons bonitatis* (Fount of goodness)
  (also called the *summum* [the highest chant]), the *paschale* (Easter [Kyrie]) and the *Magne Deus* (Great God), and graded by season. The
  Latin tropes themselves are named at Nördlingen (1579) and printed in Hof's Holy Week office
  (1592) ([§8.6.4](#s8-6-4)). The Kyrie was also sung in three tongues, Greek, Latin and German
  (Prussia 1525, Riga 1530) ([§8.6](#s8-6)).
- **Gloria.** "Allein Gott in der Höh" (To God alone on high be glory) was sung for, alternately with, or inside the Latin
  Gloria. In the last case the whole German hymn was inserted between *Et in terra pax* (And on earth peace) and
  *Laudamus te* (We praise thee; Wolfenbüttel 1543, Hildesheim 1544, Osnabrück 1543). "All Ehr und Lob" (All honour and praise shall be God’s) was the
  alternative ([§8.7](#s8-7)).
- **Creed.** "Wir glauben all" ([§8.9](#s8-9)).
- **Sanctus.** Luther's "Jesaia dem Propheten" (To Isaiah the prophet) was usual, and a Trinitarian troped Sanctus,
  "Heilig ist Gott der Vater" (Holy is God the Father), was also sung ([§8.12](#s8-12)).
- **Agnus Dei.** "Christe, du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God) and "O Lamm Gottes unschuldig" (O Lamb of God, innocent; [§8.15](#s8-15)).
- **Lord's Prayer and Verba.** No troped or farced Lord's Prayer or Words of Institution was
  found. The congregation sometimes sang Luther's "Vater unser im Himmelreich" (Our Father in the kingdom of heaven; [§8.13](#s8-13)).

**5. At the three high feasts the Latin sequences were farced with German stanzas.** The
pairs were *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks) with "Gelobet seist du", *Victimae paschali* with "Christ lag in
Todesbanden" (or "Christ ist erstanden" [Christ is arisen]), and *Veni sancte Spiritus* with "Nun bitten wir".
Choir and people, or organ and cantor, sang by turns ([§8.8.3](#s8-8-3)). Most other sequences were dropped as
impure ([§8.8.2](#s8-8-2)).

**6. Before the sermon the congregation prayed in song.** The hymn was "Nun bitten wir", often
begun by the preacher from the pulpit, and sung "in place of prayer". At the high feasts the old
pre-Reformation *Leisen* took its place: "Ein Kindelein so löbelich", "Christ ist erstanden",
"Christ fuhr gen Himmel" (Christ went up to heaven), "Gott der Vater wohn uns bei" (God the Father, dwell with us). Some orders sang the Lord's Prayer hymn
in Lent or Advent. Several orders give the whole year as a seasonal table ([§8.10](#s8-10)).

**7. After the sermon the core hymn was "Erhalt uns, Herr, bei deinem Wort".** It was sung as a
prayer for the word against the Pope and the Turk (Prussia 1568: "as after every sermon
always"). Other choices were "Es woll uns Gott genädig sein" (May God be gracious to us) and "Gott der Vater wohn uns bei".
From the 1570s the Hanau-Lichtenberg, Hohenlohe, Öhringen, Reutlingen, Rostock and Marienhafe
orders wanted a hymn that "agreeth with the sermon". Hohenlohe (1596) gave a menu under twelve
doctrinal articles ([§8.11.5](#s8-11-5)).

**8. The communion hymns hardly changed through the century.** The core was Hus's "Jesus
Christus unser Heiland" (Jesus Christ our Saviour), "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised), "Jesaia dem Propheten" and Ps 111, followed by the
German Agnus Dei. What changed was the number of hymns, measured almost everywhere by the number
of communicants. Bugenhagen's orders stopped the song as soon as the distribution ended, "though
a song begun be not sung out" ([§8.14.3](#s8-14-3)). Festal hymns, the Passion, *Discubuit*, *Pange lingua* (Sing, my tongue) and
the Te Deum were added at the margin ([§8.14](#s8-14)).

**9. Hymns covered movements and actions.** Many orders say that the hymn is sung "while" or
"meanwhile":
- the people gather ([§8.4.2](#s8-4-2));
- the priest prays at the altar step ([§8.4.6](#s8-4-6));
- the preacher goes up into or comes down from the pulpit (§§[8.9.3](#s8-9-3), [8.10.5](#s8-10-5), [8.11.2](#s8-11-2));
- the priest "takes a little breath" ([§8.11.2](#s8-11-2)) or puts on his vestments ([§8.11.2](#s8-11-2));
- the bread and wine are prepared ([§8.11.3](#s8-11-3));
- the communicants come into the choir (§§[8.11.4](#s8-11-4), [8.12.1](#s8-12-1));
- the celebrant takes off his vestments ([§8.15.4](#s8-15-4)).

Hof sang at baptism "that two actions may not follow one upon the other without a song" ([§8.17.1](#s8-17-1)).

**10. The rules for choosing a hymn grew stricter over the century.** In broad order, the
reasons given were these:
- The text must be from Scripture and "pure" ([§8.18.1](#s8-18-1)).
- The hymn must "rhyme with the feast" and the season ([§8.18.2](#s8-18-2)).
- On ordinary Sundays it should "rhyme with the gospel". The rule of Pomerania 1542 and
  Mecklenburg 1545 lists hymns for gospels of faith and grace, of Christ's enemies, of good
  works, and of the use of earthly goods ([§8.8.6](#s8-8-6)).
- It should agree with the sermon (§§[8.11.5](#s8-11-5), [8.18.3](#s8-18-3)).
- In the catechism service it should be the hymn of the chief part being taught ([§8.16.6](#s8-16-6)).

Alongside these ran the practical reasons:
- The people should learn a few hymns well, repeated and rotated ([§8.18.4](#s8-18-4)).
- Luther's hymns should come first. Prussia 1568 says no new poet "can hold a candle to Luther"
  ([§8.18.5](#s8-18-5)).
- Private choice by schoolmasters and organists was to be curbed.
- Authorized cantionals were enforced: Spangenberg, Lossius, and an "unfalsified" Luther
  songbook ([§8.18.6](#s8-18-6)).
- There were limits of language, length and organ use (§§[8.18.7](#s8-18-7)–[8.18.9](#s8-18-9)).

**11. The *Benedicamus* was graded, put into German and sometimes replaced, but never troped.**
No order in the corpus prescribes a *Benedicamus* troped with a festal song such as *Puer natus
in Bethlehem* (A child is born in Bethlehem). The *Benedicamus* kept seasonal melodies (*in adventu*, *angelicum*,
*dominicale*, *paschale* with alleluia), and was sung in German ("Let us bless the Lord")
at the end of the Mass or office. It could give way to a figured motet of the feast (Hof 1592)
or to a German hymn, at Christmas "Dank sagen wir alle" (Let us all give thanks to God; Nördlingen 1555, Wolfenbüttel 1569).
*Puer natus in Bethlehem* and the other festal songs were sung next to it: upon the Magnificat
(Naumburg 1537), at the entrance or going out of vespers (Pomerania 1569, Hof 1592), for the
introit, and after the catechism or sermon (§§[8.16.8](#s8-16-8)–[8.16.10](#s8-16-10)).

#### <a id="s8-1-2"></a>8.1.2 The slots compared

"Fixed" means one hymn, or one per grade or feast. "A handful" means a named choice of two to
five, often rotated. "Variable" means the hymn changed with the Sunday, gospel or sermon.

| Slot | Where it falls | Hymns usually named | How fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opening ([§8.4](#s8-4)) | before the introit, or before the sermon in the Württemberg type | *Veni sancte* / "Komm heiliger Geist" (Come, Holy Ghost); "Nun bitten" (Now pray we the Holy Ghost); German Benedictus; German Te Deum; Ps 51 | **fixed** or a handful; graded by feast in some orders |
| For the introit ([§8.5](#s8-5)) | first chant of the Mass | "Es woll uns Gott" (May God be gracious to us; Ps 67), "Erbarm dich mein" (Have mercy on me, O Lord God; Ps 51), "Aus tiefer Not" (Out of deep distress; Ps 130), "Ach Gott vom Himmel" (O God, look down from heaven; Ps 12), "Wär Gott nicht mit uns" (Were God not with us at this time; Ps 124), "Komm heiliger Geist"; festal *Leisen* | **a handful**, rotated; festal exchange |
| Kyrie ([§8.6](#s8-6)) | after the introit or confession | Latin by grade; German plain or troped ("Kyrie, Gott Vater in Ewigkeit", "Ach Vater, allerhöchster Gott", "O Herre Gott", "O Vater allmächtiger Gott") | **fixed by grade and season** |
| Gloria ([§8.7](#s8-7)) | after the Kyrie | "Allein Gott in der Höh" (To God alone on high be glory); "All Ehr und Lob" (All honour and praise shall be God’s) | **fixed**; Latin and German alternate or combine |
| Between epistle and gospel ([§8.8](#s8-8)) | the gradual, alleluia and sequence | farced sequences at the high feasts; German psalm matched to season or gospel; litany-hymn "Nim von uns" (Take from us) | **variable**: Sunday or seasonal tables, gospel rule |
| Creed ([§8.9](#s8-9)) | after the gospel, or after the sermon | "Wir glauben all" (We all believe); sung Apostles' or Nicene Creed | **fixed**; place varies |
| Before the sermon ([§8.10](#s8-10)) | after the creed or prayers; from the pulpit | "Nun bitten"; *Leisen* at feasts; Lord's Prayer hymn | **fixed with seasonal exchange** |
| After the sermon ([§8.11](#s8-11)) | after the sermon and prayers; the offertory place | "Erhalt uns" (Keep us); "Es woll uns Gott"; "Gott der Vater wohn uns bei" (God the Father, dwell with us); any German psalm; sermon-matched hymn | **a handful**, becoming **variable** in later orders |
| Sanctus ([§8.12](#s8-12)) | after the preface or exhortation | "Jesaia dem Propheten" (To Isaiah the prophet); "Heilig ist Gott der Vater" (Holy is God the Father); Latin Sanctus by grade | **fixed** |
| Lord's Prayer and Verba ([§8.13](#s8-13)) | before the distribution | "Vater unser im Himmelreich" (Our Father in the kingdom of heaven; rare) | **fixed** or none |
| Under the communion ([§8.14](#s8-14)) | during the distribution | "Jesus Christus unser Heiland" (Jesus Christ our Saviour); "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised); "Jesaia"; Ps 111; Agnus; extras by number of communicants | **fixed core**; quantity varies |
| Post-communion ([§8.15](#s8-15)) | after the distribution | "Christe, du Lamm Gottes" (Christ, thou Lamb of God); "O Lamm Gottes" (O Lamb of God); "Gott sei gelobet" | **fixed** |
| Close ([§8.15](#s8-15)) | after the blessing | "Verleih uns Frieden" (Grant us peace) / *Da pacem* (Give peace); "Erhalt uns"; "Es woll uns Gott"; "Sei Lob und Ehr" (Praise and honour be to the highest good); "Dank sagen wir alle" (Let us all give thanks to God); festal hymn | **a handful**; festal exchange |
| *Benedicamus* (§§[8.16.8](#s8-16-8)–[8.16.10](#s8-16-10)) | end of vespers, matins, and some Masses | Latin by grade; German "Last uns gesegnen den herren" (Let us bless the Lord); "Dank sagen wir alle" at Christmas; figured motet; festal songs (*Puer natus in Bethlehem*) next to it, not in it | **fixed by grade**; replaced at feasts |
| Office hymn ([§8.16](#s8-16)) | vespers, matins | Latin hymn *de tempore* (of the season), purged; German office hymns | **fixed by season** |
| Catechism service ([§8.16.6](#s8-16-6)) | before or after the catechism sermon | the hymn of the chief part | **fixed by the part taught** |
| Occasional rites ([§8.17](#s8-17)) | baptism, wedding, burial, ordination | "Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam" (Christ our Lord came to the Jordan); Ps 127/128; "Mitten wir im Leben" (In the midst of life we are), "Mit Fried und Freud" (With peace and joy I depart), "Nun lasst uns den Leib begraben" (Now let us bury the body); "Nun bitten", Te Deum | **a handful** per rite |

#### <a id="s8-1-3"></a>8.1.3 How the practice changed over the century

- **1523–1535: Luther and Bugenhagen.** Luther's *Formula missae* (1523) wanted German songs
  near the gradual, Sanctus and Agnus. The *Deutsche Messe* (1526) filled these slots.
  Bugenhagen's orders (Braunschweig 1528, Hamburg 1529, Pomerania 1535) fixed the
  northern pattern:
  - German psalm or Benedictus at the start;
  - farced sequences at three feasts;
  - creed as offertory;
  - Hus's hymn and "Gott sei gelobet" (God be praised) at communion, stopped when the distribution ends;
