going forth, to avoid offence. But before the door there might be sung "In the midst of life we
are," etc., and in the going forth, "As truly as I live, saith thy God," etc., item other songs
of repentance.

At Strasbourg there was no singing unless it was asked for, and then no funeral sermon either.
**Strasbourg, *Gottesdienstordnung*, 1577** (Sehling 20/1, p. 518):

<!-- doc 1336 -->

before and after the sermon is sung either "In the midst of life we are," or "In peace and joy I
now depart," item "Now let us bury the body." But where it is not desired, even as one singeth
not, so one also holdeth no funeral sermon.

The Leiningen order abolished the old "singing over" the dead with holy water, but allowed the
scholars to sing German hymns. **Leiningen-Westerburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566** (Sehling 19/1, p. 267):

<!-- doc 1074 -->

all popish pomp with holy water, singing over [the dead], and other things, etc. [shall] be
done away. For such was set up not only without God's word but also against God's word, as
though it should be furthersome to salvation. Now where there are schools, the scholars may well
sing some German songs, as "In the midst of life we are," "Now lettest thou thy servant depart in
peace," etc.

The Goslar order of 1528 left the whole matter to "a godly, reasonable, learned pastor".
**Goslar, Amsdorf, *Vom teglichen gots dinst*, 1528** (Sehling 7/2.2, pp. 237–238):

<!-- doc 2187 -->

That a chaplain, the sexton and also the scholars go along, I allow to be done, and [that they]
sing in German and Latin *Media vita*, a psalm, etc. All this standeth with a godly, reasonable,
learned pastor to lessen and to increase, that he order it as it shall be best and most
profitable for the people.

#### <a id="s8-17-5"></a>8.17.5 Ordination and installation

The ordination and installation rites of the Württemberg family open with "Nun bitten" (Now pray we the Holy Ghost). The
creed is sung after the sermon, and the service closes with the Te Deum or the German *Grates*.
**Württemberg, *Synodalordnung*, 1547** (Sehling 16, p. 159):

<!-- doc 660 -->

And when the people are assembled in the church, one shall begin and sing "Now pray we the Holy
Ghost," etc. After this song the dean or one of the councillors shall stand up and hold a sermon
of the ministry of the word […]. After the sermon the creed shall be sung.

Lippe (1571) copies the rite, and the superintendent steps before the altar during the creed
(Sehling 21, p. 438):

<!-- doc 1462 -->

when the people are assembled in the church, [they shall] sing at the beginning "Now pray we the
Holy Ghost," etc.; after this song the superintendent or his adjunct [shall] stand up and hold a
sermon of the ministry of the word.

**Lauenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1585** (Sehling 5, p. 408):

<!-- doc 1953 -->

The people, first assembled in the church, shall sing some psalms, and thereafter at the last
there shall follow "Now pray we the Holy Ghost," or "Come, Holy Ghost, Lord God."

The Brandenburg installation adds Psalm 67 and the Te Deum. **Brandenburg, *Visitations- und
Consistorialordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 3, p. 109):

<!-- doc 1748 -->

after the Our Father is spoken the congregation shall sing "Now pray we the Holy Ghost," and
"May God be gracious unto us and give his blessing," etc., item the *Te Deum laudamus* (We praise thee, O God), etc.

The Hessian ordination (Philippist) closes with the Te Deum "where there are schools", or "Dank
sagen wir alle" (Let us all give thanks to God). **Hessen, *Agende*, 1574** (Philippist; Sehling 8, p. 455):

<!-- doc 2272 -->

At the close the congregation shall sing *Te Deum laudamus*, in German, or in Latin where there
are schools, or "Thanks say we all to God our Lord Christ," etc., or another such song of
praise.

The Merseburg draft for Luther's ordinations has *Veni creator* (Come, Creator) sung while ordinator and
ordinands kneel. **Merseburg, *Ordinations-Ordnung*, 1545** (Sehling 2, p. 7):

<!-- doc 1210 -->

*Credo in unum*. The people: "We believe." The choir: *Veni creator*, during which the lord
ordinator together with the ordinands should kneel down together before the altar.

#### <a id="s8-17-6"></a>8.17.6 Days of thanksgiving and extraordinary occasions

Michaelmas in Schleswig-Holstein was a harvest thanksgiving, with the Te Deum after the sermon.
**Schleswig-Holstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542** (Sehling 23, p. 95):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

The day of Michael is a common thanksgiving for all the fruits which we have gathered and
received in the year. Therefore the whole congregation shall, straight after the sermon, sing
for the thanksgiving with great devotion *Te Deum Laudamus* (We praise thee, O God), etc.

Lüneburg kept an annual day for the city's deliverance. On it hymns took the place of the
propers: Psalm 127 (figural) and Psalm 124 after the epistle, and Psalm 124 again with Psalm 3 at
matins. **Lüneburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1575** (Sehling 6/1, p. 663):

<!-- doc 2017 -->

At the Mass: 4. the introit *Benedicite* (Bless ye) of the angels; 5. the Kyrie in figured music, item *Et
in terra pax* (And on earth peace), next "To God alone on high be glory"; 6. after the reading of the epistle, *Nisi
Dominus aedificaverit domum* (Except the Lord build the house); 7. "Were God not with us"; 8. the gospel is sung; 9. "Now pray we
the Holy Ghost"; 10. the holy sermon is held; 11. after the sermon the litany is sung.

At Nördlingen's thanksgiving day on 7 January, Psalm 124 could be sung instead of a figured
piece, "that the congregation also may have cause to thank God". **Nördlingen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1579** (Sehling 12, p. 388):

<!-- doc 375 -->

The choir singeth a piece in figured music; or, that the congregation also may have cause to
thank God, the psalm "Where God the Lord standeth not by us," etc. may be sung.

At an execution in Regensburg the crowd sang "Nun bitten" (Now pray we the Holy Ghost) while the condemned man began to recite
the creed. **Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung* of Justus Jonas, 1553**, with the order for the
condemned (Sehling 13, p. 426):

<!-- doc 440 -->

Then that he openly profess the faith and recite the Apostles' Creed, *Credo in Deum Patrem* (I believe in God the Father),
etc. But at the beginning of it the crowd standing about shall sing the song "Now pray we the
Holy Ghost."

---

### <a id="s8-18"></a>8.18 How hymns were chosen: the reasons given

The orders seldom explain a single choice. They often state the rules by which choices were to
be made. Ten kinds of reason recur. They are gathered here with the quotations not already given
in the sections on the slots.

#### <a id="s8-18-1"></a>8.18.1 From Scripture, and "pure"

The first test is always the text. Anything sung, Latin or German, must come from Scripture or
be proved by it. **Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1529**, section "Of singing" (Sehling 5, p. 516):

<!-- doc 1960 -->

All singing, German and Latin, as hath been said, shall be out of the holy Scripture, or proved
by God's clear words and the Christian faith, as Paul teacheth to sing, Ephesians 5; as also the
old Christian doctors sang and caused to be sung, when men knew nothing of the *Salve regina* and
other unchristian songs.

Buxtehude applies the test to the Latin chants. It keeps those "agreeable to divine Scripture"
and drops the rest. **Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 7/1, p. 77):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

All Latin songs agreeable to divine Scripture which have hitherto been sung in the church at Mass,
matins and vespers at their special time shall be kept, used and sung at their time. But those
that are unserviceable, not agreeable to divine Scripture, and wrong, shall not be sung.

Worms admits hymns as well as psalms, because Paul commended both. But no new hymn is to be
brought in without the superintendent and preachers. **Worms, *Agendbüchlein*, 1560** (Sehling 19/1, p. 208):

<!-- doc 1069 -->

Since the holy apostle Paul hath commended and enjoined to Christians not only the psalms of
David but also other spiritual songs and hymns of praise, we also reject them not, yet so far
as they be Christian and grounded in holy Scripture. Only that no new song be brought into the
church without the counsel and foreknowledge of the superintendents and preachers.

In Württemberg every communion hymn beyond the named ones had to be "examined and admitted" by
the superintendents first. **Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1536** (Sehling 16, p. 109):

<!-- doc 651 -->

or other songs of praise which are pure […] and have been beforehand viewed, examined and
admitted by the superintendents.

#### <a id="s8-18-2"></a>8.18.2 Fitting the feast and the season

The Saxon Visitation Articles of 1528 thought it "unseemly that the songs are quite alike at
all feasts". **Saxony (Ernestine), *Unterricht der Visitatoren*, 1528** (Sehling 1, p. 169):

<!-- doc 9 -->

Since it is also unseemly that the songs are quite alike at all feasts, it were good that on the
most glorious feasts one sang the Latin introits, Gloria [etc.].

Bugenhagen asked the schoolmasters to see that "the songs rhyme finely with the feasts". Where no
proper song existed, they were to take "the most joyful psalms or songs". **Braunschweig,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 442). The same sentence recurs in Mecklenburg (1545):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

The schoolmasters shall see to it that the songs rhyme finely with the feasts. When they have no
songs for them, let them take the most joyful psalms or songs, and see always that the songs be
out of the pure Scripture, and pure and pleasant and understandable for the laity, made out of
God's word.

The Kurpfalz order of 1556 wants the songs to follow "the teaching and the order of the
season", so that the church is reminded of the necessary articles "both with preaching and
singing". **Kurpfalz, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556** (Sehling 14, p. 165):

<!-- doc 480 -->

One shall also be diligent that the songs be ordered after the teaching and the order of the
season: namely, on Christmas Day and the feasts following, of the birth of Christ; at Easter, of
the resurrection of Christ; that the church may be well reminded of the necessary pieces of the
teaching of the Christian faith, both with preaching and singing.

The Sayn *Kirchenzuchtordnung* of 1582 repeats this almost word for word (Sehling 19/1, p. 369).
Hanau-Lichtenberg (1573) opens its three rules with the same point ([§8.11.5](#s8-11-5)).

The Württemberg court church order of 1560 made the court preachers settle the hymns with the
choirmaster, so that the singing followed the season and not "his own nod". **Württemberg,
*Hofkirchenordnung*, 1560** (Sehling 16, p. 428):

<!-- doc 686 -->

The court preachers shall also always agree with the choirmaster what he shall sing, and that
the singing fit the season according to the order above, and be not sung at his own nod, as
hath hitherto been done.

#### <a id="s8-18-3"></a>8.18.3 Fitting the gospel and the sermon

The later orders go further. The hymn is to agree with the gospel and "the chief teaching of the
sermon". **Öhringen, *Kirchen- und Schulordnungen*, 1582**, the German school order (Sehling 15, p. 503):

<!-- doc 592 -->

He shall, according to our church order, be diligent at all times as much as possible to sing
such psalms as agree with the customary gospels and the chief teaching of the sermon. He shall
also on the Sunday speak beforehand with the organist and agree what he will sing, that there be
no confusion and disorder.

The Hohenlohe *Gesangsordnung* of 1596 gives the reason in its closing paragraph. When the
hymns are fitted to the sermons, the common man will feel that the singing is "no superfluous or
vain ceremony" but "a short summary and pleasant instruction". It also forbids cutting psalms off
in the middle. **Hohenlohe, *Schul- und Gesangsordnung*, 1596** (Sehling 15, p. 657):

<!-- doc 628 -->

that the pastors, with good consideration, as much as possible, will direct all songs before and
after to the sermons; that the common man, by means of divine grace, may feel in his heart that
the singing is not a superfluous or vain ceremony, but a short summary and pleasant instruction,
whereby all manner of things necessary to be known for salvation are brought home to our hearts
most fairly and lovely.

The Kassel general synod of 1607 (Reformed) asked for the hymn numbers to be posted on a board
at the church doors, and for an order of hymns "by the seasons of the year and fitted to the
texts that are to be preached". **Hessen-Kassel, *Abschied der Kasseler Generalsynode*, 1607**
(Reformed; Sehling 9, pp. 75–76):

<!-- doc 2287 -->

that the psalms which are to be sung in the assembly be at all times marked with their number by
the bell-ringer or sexton (who should first inquire of the psalm from him that is to hold the
sermon) upon a little board at the doors of the church, or as it might otherwise be fitly done
according to the condition of the church.

<!-- doc 2287 -->

that it were not unserviceable that the psalms and other Christian songs be drawn up into a
certain order according to the seasons of the year, and accommodated to the texts which should
be preached, and communicated to the pastors, especially in the country.

#### <a id="s8-18-4"></a>8.18.4 That the people may learn them: few, familiar, often repeated

A second group of reasons concerns the congregation's knowledge. The fewer the hymns, the sooner
they are learned. The Sponheim order uses the longest hymns before the sermon and the shortest
after it. It also prints a short list of hymns to be used "often and before others".
**Hintere Grafschaft Sponheim, *Kirchen- und Zensurordnung*, 1590/91** (Sehling 18, p. 657):

<!-- doc 1021 -->

In towns and market towns where there are schools, the songs and psalms that are found in the
church order may for the most part be used in the churches; yet with this common direction, that
at the beginning and before the sermon the longest, but after the sermon the shortest be sung.
And that the common people be not burdened with many songs, but the sooner learn to sing, it is
needful that some chief psalms and songs be used oftener and before others, [rather than] hard
songs unfit for them. And accordingly the following songs shall be used often and before others;
yet where a congregation hath already learned more songs contained in the church order, these
shall hereby not be forbidden.

Danzig wanted the same hymns used "two [Sundays] running", especially those that contained the
parts of the catechism. **Danzig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1557**, as summarised and quoted by Sehling
(Sehling 4, p. 168):

<!-- doc 1844 -->

A psalm, two or three, "according to the occasion of the season, which the whole church also
shall learn and sing along; and therefore the same songs shall often be used some two [times]
one after another, namely those in which the pieces of the catechism are orderly comprised."

Mecklenburg sang German hymns before and after the weekday sermons "that they may become known
and common to the people, and hearts be thereby stirred to prayer". **Mecklenburg,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 5, p. 201):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

On such days German spiritual songs shall be sung before and after the sermon, that they may
become known and common to the people, and hearts be thereby stirred up to prayer; as especially
"Our Father in the kingdom of heaven," "Were God the Lord not with us," "A mighty fortress,"
etc.

Reutlingen listed the psalm-hymns that had once been "common and known in the church" and wanted
all of them brought back. The feast hymns it did not list, "for they are otherwise known well
enough". **Reutlingen, *Ordnung der Schule und des Kirchengesangs*, 1565/1566** (Sehling 17/2, p. 51):

<!-- doc 828 -->

These psalms have all been common and known in the church; they shall therefore all be brought
back into it. The songs for the special high feasts we have not wished to list here, for they
are otherwise known well enough.

Hesse (Moderate Reformed) wanted the sung psalms explained in sermons, "for what one
understandeth not goeth slowly to the heart". **Hessen, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 255):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

But especially it goeth not off without fruit when the psalms are expounded, above all those
that are sung by the whole congregation; for so they understand the better all that is done by
the church in the holy assembly. The minds also are the more kindled to devotion and godly
meditation under the singing; for what one understandeth not goeth slowly to the heart.

**Sayn, *Kirchenzuchtordnung*, 1582** (Sehling 19/1, p. 369):

<!-- doc 1090 -->

the pastors shall exhort the people to learn the Christian songs and psalms and to help praise
and extol our Lord God with the common singing of the church, that through the songs they may be
reminded of God's word that is comprised therein, and thereby be bettered in the right knowledge
of God, in faith, love, patience and all other virtues. And that a good order and uniformity may
be kept in the songs, the songs chiefly that are Doctor Martin Luther's [shall be used] […].

#### <a id="s8-18-5"></a>8.18.5 Luther's hymns first

From the 1560s several orders put Luther's hymns ahead of all others. The Prussian order of 1568
gives the reason: in them "the whole holy catechism" is set out "with rich, fair and mighty
exposition". **Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und Ceremonien*, 1568** (Sehling 4, p. 75):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

But not all manner of German songs shall be sung in the church, in villages as in towns, but
chiefly Luther's psalms shall be kept and used. For in them one hath most fairly the whole holy
catechism with rich, fair and mighty exposition: first, of the Ten Commandments in two songs,
"These are the holy ten commandments," etc., and "Man, wilt thou live blessedly," etc.; secondly,
the articles of our Christian faith in "We all believe in one God," etc.; thirdly, the prayer
in "Our Father in the kingdom of heaven," etc.; the whole treasure of holy baptism in "Christ our
Lord to Jordan came," etc.; and then all needful instruction of the holy Supper in "Jesus Christ
our Saviour," etc., and "God be praised," etc. Whoso then will have the sum of sums, together
with the use and profit thereof, briefly together, let him sing "Now rejoice, dear Christians
all," etc., or Doctor Speratus's most fair psalm, "Salvation now is come to us," etc.

It then turns on the new hymn-writers (Sehling 4, p. 76):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

So that it is not needful to snatch up all manner of new songs and bring them into the churches.
We have them, God be praised, as good as they can be made, and there is lack nowhere, save that
men are weary and tired of the precious treasure and have lust and love to take up something new;
until at last they come away almost wholly from the glorious psalms of Luther, and everyone
bringeth forward his own poem, which yet cannot hold a candle to Luther in the kind of diction
or the weight of matter. Therefore the pastors shall see to it that they suffer not the
schoolmasters to sing at their own pleasure, but take care that the songs above be kept and
diligently used.

Hoya says the same, and warns that where everyone wants to be a poet, error easily takes root.
It also places boys among the people to teach them. **Hoya, *Kirchenordnung*, 1581** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1151):

<!-- doc 2065 -->

The pastors shall diligently keep the psalms that were made by Doctor Luther and that have been
had and sung from the beginning of the gospel, and use them diligently, and bestow great
diligence that the people in the church may always sing the second verse and the choir meanwhile
keep silence. For the furtherance of this a pair of boys may be made to stand or sit among the
people, who sing, so that the people accustom themselves to singing along with them. Other
Christian songs also may well be used, so far as they be pure and agreeable to God's word; yet
let not too much novelty be made, nor the old songs rejected. For it is found that where every
man will be a poet and make and use his own songs, error may easily take root therewith.

**Harlingerland, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573/74** (Sehling 7/1, p. 738):

<!-- doc 2122 -->

The twelfth article, first section: of the songs which shall be used in the church. We ordain
that the psalms which were made by Doctor Luther of blessed memory and are found in the psalm
books shall be sung and used most of all, before others. Yet hereby we will not have rejected the
praiseworthy songs, Latin or German, appointed for the high feast days and grounded in the divine
word.

The same order forbids schoolmasters and sextons to sing hymns "at their pleasure" without the
pastor's knowledge. It forbids songs the people are not used to, and songs "that have the same
tune as worldly songs", at which the common man might take offence (Sehling 7/1, p. 739):

<!-- doc 2122 -->

also command the schoolmasters and sextons that they sing not the psalms at their pleasure
without the foreknowledge of the pastors, [nor such] as the parish folk are not yet used to, nor
otherwise those that have the same tune as worldly songs, whereat the common man might be
offended.

Mansfeld built its seasonal hymn plan from Luther's songbook. It marked with an asterisk the
hymns in that book by "other excellent men". It did not bind other territories to its order.
**Mansfeld, *Kirchen-Agenda*, 1580** (Sehling 2, p. 235):

<!-- doc 1241 -->

We have therefore taken Doctor Luther's German songbook before us, and divided the songs contained
therein among the feasts and common Sundays and otherwise other days, as we suppose in our
simplicity that they should be most fitting to the sermons and best to be impressed upon the
people. But because in Luther's songbook good and spiritual songs of other excellent men also
are incorporated, we would not leave them out, but have set them in at fitting places, and to
distinguish them from Doctor Luther's songs we have marked them with this sign: *.

The same Mansfeld article explains why hymns had spread so fast: "as all men are by nature
inclined to sing and have pleasure in music" (Sehling 2, p. 235):

<!-- doc 1241 -->

As now all men are naturally inclined to sing and have pleasure in music, so have they received
such songs with great desire, and out of them grasped the ground of the truth firmly and
strongly.

At Langenburg in Hohenlohe the question became a dispute in 1592. The pastor there, Mögner,
objected that singing only Luther's hymns would mean giving up long-used songs by Spengler,
Speratus, Kreuziger, Jonas and others. He appealed to the last paragraph of the 1578 order, to
sing "at all times what is serviceable and answerable to the matter" (Sehling 15, p. 625):

<!-- doc 624 -->

so will we, according to the last paragraph on the songs, sing at all times what is serviceable
and answerable to the matter.

#### <a id="s8-18-6"></a>8.18.6 Against private choice and novelty; the authorized books

Hof defended its whole plan against any "unskilled scholar" who might change it at his pleasure.
**Hof, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1592** (Sehling 11, p. 455):

<!-- doc 294 -->

since it will not become every unskilled scholar to overturn at his pleasure our fair and
well-considered church order, and to sing in the congregation of God what seemeth good to him in
his own name; since the old ones were also men, and surely undertook nothing without great
forethought.

Pfalz-Zweibrücken closed its songbook with a ban on novelty, "that constant uniformity be kept,
as well in singing as in preaching". **Pfalz-Zweibrücken, *Kirchenordnung*, 1557**, songbook
(Sehling 18, p. 255):

<!-- doc 968 -->

These church songs set above the pastors and ministers shall use, and bring in no further
novelty, that Christian, constant uniformity be kept as well in singing as in preaching and
daily teaching.

Grubenhagen tied the whole service to Johann Spangenberg's cantional. **Grubenhagen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1581** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1048):

<!-- doc 2058 -->

the same shall be held with due modesty and discretion, orderly and with one voice, and nothing
new be devised or undertaken by anyone. Since, then, the cantional or missal of the old master
Johann Spangenberg hath long been customary in our principality, and the same hath been given to
every church for keeping and use, every one shall diligently order himself by it on the Sundays,
feasts and apostles' days in holding the office, with lessons, singing, collects, introits,
Kyrie, *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), prefaces, hymns and whatever more there is of the like, according to the order of
the season.

Oldenburg required "a right, pure cantional", Spangenberg's or Lossius's, with Luther's German
songbook. **Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1085):

<!-- doc 2149 -->

For the furtherance of which it is needful that in all churches and schools a right, pure
cantional be always at hand, as namely that of the old master Johann Spangenberg or of Lucas
Lossius, together with the German songbook of Doctor Martin Luther.

It adds that the Luther songbook must be one "printed at no suspect place and unfalsified". This
was aimed at the Reformed-leaning printings of the 1560s and 1570s (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1087):

<!-- doc 2149 -->

and before the sermon a German psalm may be sung out of Luther's songbook, [one] that is printed
at no suspect place and is unfalsified.

Rostock required Lossius in every church, and one melody everywhere. **Rostock, *Conformitas
ceremoniarum*, c. 1560** (Sehling 5, pp. 288–289):

<!-- doc 1936 -->

It is thought good and needful that Lucas Lossius's *Psalmodia* be kept in all churches, and the
choir order itself thereby.

<!-- doc 1936 -->

The schoolmasters and cantors also shall be diligent that in all songs one melody be kept.

The Pomeranian *Agenda* ordered every church to buy Lossius's cantional ([§8.8.6](#s8-8-6)).

#### <a id="s8-18-7"></a>8.18.7 Latin and German

The orders agree that the congregation sings in German. They differ on how much Latin to keep,
and why. Bugenhagen defended the Latin chants for the sake of the Latin school children. He
reproved those who would have "all things and singing in German, as though it were wrong to sing
a Latin word". **Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 438):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

We praise not, nor do we chide, but say that they take it a little too strictly who will have all
things and singing in German, as though it were wrong to sing a Latin word or another; since Paul
saith rightly that one shall not forbid to speak with tongues. When the laity have the German
Mass, they shall bear with the Latin children and others, that these sing at times a Latin
*Gloria in excelsis*, an alleluia, Sanctus, Agnus, and special songs, as sequences on the three
great feasts; yet with German sung in among them or beside them.

East Frisia kept the Latin "because we will that the Latin tongue, together with all good arts,
as music, be kept in honour". **Ostfriesland, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 7/1, p. 380):

<!-- doc 2107 -->

For we will that the Latin tongue, together with all good arts, as music, be held in honour in the
churches and schools.

Hohenlohe kept the Latin for the schools and added German "for the unlearned and those
inexperienced in the Latin tongue". **Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553** (Sehling 15, p. 60):

<!-- doc 539 -->

for its sake keep the Latin songs in use, and beside them also the German songs, because of the
unlearned and those inexperienced in the Latin tongue.

Hesse (1574, Philippist) reasoned from 1 Corinthians 14: whoever does not understand cannot say
Amen. It allowed Latin only before the congregation had gathered, and at vespers when few were
there. It also limited the singing before the sermon to half an hour on feast days and a quarter
of an hour on weekdays. **Hessen, *Agende*, 1574** (Philippist; Sehling 8, p. 411):

<!-- doc 2272 -->

But how can one say Amen to that which he understandeth not and knoweth not what is meant
thereby? 1 Corinthians 14. Therefore, as all sermons, prayer and thanksgiving are done in the
known German tongue, so also the singing, when the whole common multitude is together, shall be
German. But since in towns, where there are many kinds of people, many are found who were brought
up in schools and understand Latin, and likewise strangers often come to the common assemblies to
whom this tongue is well known, a Latin psalm or introit may be sung at times at the beginning,
before the whole congregation cometh together, and at vespers, when few people are present
anyway; yet so that in the villages wholly, and in the towns for the most part, only German songs
be and remain in common use. The songs also shall be set as short as may be, and before the
sermon shall not be stretched on feast days over half an hour, and on working days over a quarter
of an hour at the most, that the people be not held up, and be caused to weariness before the
sermon beginneth.

Sayn called Latin singing in the papacy "a special punishment of God", citing Isaiah 28 and
1 Corinthians 14 (Sehling 19/1, p. 369):

<!-- doc 1090 -->

that it hath hitherto happened in the papacy is to be counted a special punishment of God, as
Isaiah 28 and St Paul, 1 Corinthians 14, bear witness. And it hath the appearance that such
church singing, done in an unknown tongue, was supposed by the merit of its work to reconcile
God's wrath.

#### <a id="s8-18-8"></a>8.18.8 Length

Long singing was to be avoided "that such Christian and wholesome ceremonies may remain pleasant
to the people and not become tedious". **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 4, p. 341):

<!-- doc 1856 -->

Long singing, wherein some priests have pleasure, shall for this cause be avoided: that such
Christian and wholesome ceremonies may remain pleasant to the people and not become tedious.

Two, or at most three, pieces of figured music at one service are enough, "that the people also
may have room to praise God with song". **Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 6/1, p. 54):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

Two good pieces, or at the most three, in figured music are enough at one time, that the people
also may have room to praise God with song, especially during the communion, as Christ saith:
"This do in remembrance of me."

Schönburg held weekday singing and preaching together to one hour, "so the people are kept
willing to go to the sermon and can also come home to work". **Schönburg, *Kirchenordnung*,
1542** (Sehling 2, p. 171):

<!-- doc 1235 -->

In sum, that always in the week, on working days, all singing and preaching be done in one hour
and not beyond. So the people are kept willing to go to the sermon, and can also come home to
work.

#### <a id="s8-18-9"></a>8.18.9 The organ

The organ was allowed, "neither commanded nor forbidden". It was not a way of serving God, but
like a trumpet that moves people to pray, hear the word, and come to church. **Bremen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1534** (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 461):

<!-- doc 2217 -->

Organs and music, which are free, neither commanded nor forbidden, may be used; not in order to
serve God therewith and to strengthen idolatry and hinder the right service of God, as the
Papists do; but as a trumpet or else a cry, whereby men are moved and get occasion both to pray
and diligently to hear God's word, even as Elisha prophesied at the harp, and to go into the
church and abide there.

Heilbronn grounded the organ in the Psalms and in the pleasure of melody, which stirs the heart.
**Heilbronn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 17/1, p. 317):

<!-- doc 781 -->

and since God is to be praised in all things, in organs, cymbals and stringed instruments, as is
written in the holy psalms, and the heart of men also is not only gladdened and awakened by such
lovely melody to tell of the divine benefits […].

The organist was to play only after the choir or church had begun, and to agree with the
schoolmaster beforehand. **Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 7/1, p. 78):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

the organist shall play at Mass, matins and vespers that which the choir or the whole church
first beginneth and singeth. The schoolmaster shall always agree beforehand with the organist
touching the singing, to prevent all unseemliness and confusion.

Harlingerland forbade organists to play worldly songs. **Harlingerland, *Kirchenordnung*,
1573/74** (Sehling 7/1, p. 739):

<!-- doc 2122 -->

And since in places where there are organs the organists are found unfaithful and play worldly
songs, whereof offence followeth, although these [organs] are not forbidden in holy Scripture,
but [given] to praise and extol the Almighty therewith, we ordain that the organists attend to
their service earnestly and [play] glorious spiritual pieces, agreeing with holy Scripture.

In polyphonic settings for the court chapel of Württemberg the familiar tune was to be kept in the
tenor or another voice, so the people could recognize it. **Württemberg, *Hofkirchenordnung*,
1560** (Sehling 16, p. 427):

<!-- doc 686 -->

At the close a German psalm shall always be sung, and in the compositions care shall be taken
that the customary, familiar melody be set in the tenor or another voice.

The organ's silence in certain seasons and the limits on what the organist might play are
treated in [Chapter 9](#ch9), §§[9.3.6](#s9-3-6)–[9.3.7](#s9-3-7).

#### <a id="s8-18-10"></a>8.18.10 Freedom

Many orders end their rules on singing with a clause of freedom, or leave the choice to the
pastor, and some say plainly that such ceremonies are not laws. Northeim: "such things must be
free and subject to no law" ([§8.8.1](#s8-8-1)). Goslar (1528) left the burial singing to "a godly, reasonable,
learned pastor" ([§8.17.4](#s8-17-4)). Mansfeld did not bind others to its plan ([§8.18.5](#s8-18-5)). Nördlingen's St
George's order (1555), after Naumburg, lets the Gloria be dropped when the hymns after the epistle
are long, "for such ceremonies shall at all times be free for the pastor to change according to
the people's convenience". **Nördlingen, *Ordnung der ceremonien* at St George's, 1555**
(Sehling 12, p. 322):

<!-- doc 373 -->

One may also well leave out the *Gloria in excelsis* when the songs after the epistle are somewhat
long; for such ceremonies shall at all times be free for the pastor to change according to the
people's convenience.

- **Hymn practice**: a short note on what the order contributes.
- **§**: the sections where the order is quoted.

### <a id="s8-a"></a>Appendix 8.A The chief hymn (*Hauptlied*) of each Sunday and feast in the old sources

This appendix condenses the **Compare by day** sheet of `hymns.xlsx`. That sheet lists every
hymn that any witness in [`hymns.db`](#repo-hymns) assigns to a day, with the number of witnesses for each.
Here the same evidence is cut down in two ways, so that the hymn of each day can be read at a
glance:

- **Only the old sources are counted.** These are the church orders and hymnals of 1543–1694,
  the Leipzig usage of Bach's time, and the modern studies that do nothing but collate those
  older sources. The modern lists, from 1800 onward, are left out.
- **Only the hymns with significant support are given.** A day with one clear hymn shows that
  hymn alone. A day where support is divided shows each hymn with good support, and none of the
  hymns with only a few witnesses.

The word *Hauptlied* is later terminology and does not occur in the corpus (see [§8.8](#s8-8) and
the Introduction, [The hymn database](#repo-hymns)). The tables these witnesses keep are tables for the hymn of the day, which the
orders place between the epistle and the gospel ([§8.8.7](#s8-8-7)) or before the sermon ([§8.10.3](#s8-10-3)).

#### <a id="s8-a-1"></a>8.A.1 The witnesses counted

Of the 48 witnesses in [`hymns.db`](#repo-hymns), 29 are counted as old.

| Group | Witnesses |
|---|---|
| Sehling church orders (8) | Heilbronn 1543; Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1565; Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569; Weissenfels 1578; Nördlingen 1579; Mansfeld 1580; Hof 1592; Hohenlohe 1596 |
| Hymnals collated in Liliencron's *de tempore* (of the season) concordance (15) | Spangenberg 1545; Keuchenthal 1573; Selnecker; Gesius 1601; Leipzig *Geistliche Lieder* 1605; Stiphelius 1607; Augsburg 1619; Liegnitz 1625–30; Helmstedt 1626; Schein 1627; Erhardi, Frankfurt 1659; Schleswig-Holstein 1665; Darmstadt 1687; Goslar 1687; Leipzig *Kirchenandachten* 1694 |
| Other single orders and schemes (4) | Ludecus, *Ordo cantionum Germanicarum*, 1589; Carpzov (the hymns on which he preached); the *de tempore* plan of c. 1700 printed by Graff; Bach's Leipzig usage (the chorales of his Sunday and festival cantatas) |
| Modern studies that collate older sources (2) | Stiller (the Leipzig, Weissenfels and Dresden hymn schedules of Bach's time); Thompson, dissertation, Appendix 2 (Ludecus with twelve other 16th-century lists) |

The other 19 witnesses are modern and are **not counted**. Krusemark explains his own lists on
pp. 95–96 of `Hymns_ABC_Krusemark.pdf`. The modern witnesses are:

- Krusemark's Years A, B and C;
- the lists of Stuckwisch, Reuning, Gehrke, Eckardt, Judisch, Zion (Detroit) and Redeemer;
- the LCMS Synod selections of 2016–17 and the LSB Hymnal Committee;
- *Lutheran Worship* (1982), *Lutheran Service Book* (2006) and the SELK hymnal;
- the Mecklenburg hymnal of 1855;
- two private schemes (MC, SD) and the unattributed entries.

Some of the old witnesses reach `hymns.db` through modern compilations. Carpzov, Bach and the
plan of c. 1700 come through Krusemark or the Hymn of the Day table, and Selnecker through all
three. Each is counted once, as a witness, whichever book it was read from (Introduction,
[The hymn database](#repo-hymns)).

Some of the old witnesses add nothing to the table, for these reasons:

- **Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1565.** Its table is a three-week rotating cycle, not tied to particular
  Sundays, so it falls outside this table.
- **Heilbronn 1543, Nördlingen 1579 and Hof 1592.** They assign Latin office hymns. These count
  among the witnesses for their days but never reach the threshold.

#### <a id="s8-a-2"></a>8.A.2 How the table was made

- **Counting is by witness.** A hymn's figure is the number of old witnesses that assign it to
  the day. "11 of 18" means that 11 of the 18 old witnesses that give any hymn for that day give
  this one.
- **One hymn, one row.** Spellings, Low German forms and English titles of the same hymn are
  joined, as in the workbook. English-only citations from Carpzov, Selnecker, Bach, the plan of
  c. 1700 and Thompson are joined to their German hymns. "The Day Is Surely Drawing Near", for
  example, is joined to *Es ist gewisslich an der Zeit* (It is surely time). The hymn database does this joining
  with its lexicon of hymns and its table of English titles, so [`hymns.db`](#repo-hymns) and the
  workbook group the hymns as this table does.
- **Hymns with the same or a similar opening are kept apart:**
  - Eber's *Herr Gott, dich loben alle wir* (Lord God, we all praise thee), on the angels, is kept apart from Luther's German
    Te Deum *Herr Gott, dich loben wir* (Lord God, we praise thee). Liliencron himself insists on this distinction.
  - Luther's Easter hymn *Jesus Christus, unser Heiland, der den Tod überwand* (Jesus Christ, our Saviour, who overcame death) is kept apart
    from his Communion hymn of the same opening. A source that prints only the opening words for
    an Easter occasion is read as meaning the Easter hymn.
  - *Als Jesus Christus, Gottes Sohn* (When Jesus Christ, the Son of God) is kept apart from *Jesus Christus, wahrer Gottes Sohn* (Jesus Christ, true Son of God).
  - *Mag ich dem Tod nicht widerstahn* (Though I cannot withstand death) is kept apart from *Mag ich Unglück nicht widerstahn* (If I cannot withstand misfortune).
- **Grouped entries are shared out.** An entry for "Lent 1–3" or "Lent 5, Palm Sunday and Good
  Friday" counts for each of the days it names. The last Sundays after Trinity are given
  together, as most of the hymnals give them ("Trinity 25–27"). Entries for a whole season
  ("Advent", "Lent", "Easter season") and the Pfalz-Zweibrücken cycle are not counted.
- **Which hymns are shown.** A hymn is shown for a day when it meets all three of these
  conditions:
  - it has at least three witnesses;
  - it has at least three fifths of the witnesses of the day's leading hymn;
  - it has at least a quarter of the witnesses that give any hymn for that day.

  On Advent 1, *Nun komm, der Heiden Heiland* (Now come, Savior of the heathen) has 20 witnesses and no other hymn more than 7, so
  it stands alone. On Advent 2, *Gott hat das Evangelium* (God has given the gospel) (11), *Es ist gewisslich an der Zeit*
  (8) and *Ihr lieben Christen, freut euch nun* (Ye dear Christians, rejoice now) (8) are shown. *Es wird schier der letzte Tag
  herkommen* (The last day will soon be coming) (6), *Ach Gott, thu dich erbarmen* (Ah God, have mercy) (5) and *Nun komm* (Now come, Savior of the heathen) (4) are not.
- **Days the witnesses leave open.** On Quasimodogeniti, Maundy Thursday, Easter Monday and
  Pentecost Monday no hymn has three old witnesses. For these four days the table gives the hymn
  assigned by the editor of the corpus, marked ‡, with the number of old witnesses that do give
  it. The assignments are kept in a table of their own in [`hymns.db`](#repo-hymns), and flagged "Assigned" in the Compare by day sheet. They are not
  prescriptions and are not counted as witnesses.
- **Titles.**
  - **Original title:** the hymn's standard spelling from the `hymns` lexicon.
  - **Literal English:** a word-for-word rendering of the incipit.
  - **Common English title:** the received English title. Where the hymn has none, the title of
    Matthew Carver's translation is given and marked †. These come from *Walther's Hymnal*
    (2012), which Carver translated, or from his blog *Hymnoglypt* (Introduction,
    [The hymn database](#repo-hymns)). The title is "—" where neither exists.

#### <a id="s8-a-4"></a>8.A.4 Notes on the table

- **Days not in the table.** The saints' days not listed (St Paul, St Mary Magdalene, St
  Lawrence, St Martin, All Saints and others) have one old witness or two.
- **The assigned days.** Quasimodogeniti is the one Sunday the old witnesses leave open:
  Liliencron's concordance records only a single coincidence for it, and no hymn has more than
  two old witnesses. Only two or three old witnesses give a hymn for Maundy Thursday and the
  second feast days of Easter and Pentecost. The hymns assigned to these days (‡) are mostly the
  ones those few witnesses give: Luther's Communion hymn on Maundy Thursday (Carpzov,
  Selnecker), *Ach bleib bei uns* (Abide with us, Lord Jesus Christ) and *Christ ist erstanden* (Christ is arisen) on Easter Monday (Bach's Leipzig),
  and *Komm, Heiliger Geist* (Come, Holy Ghost) on Pentecost Monday (Stiller). *O filii et filiae* (O sons and daughters) on
  Quasimodogeniti has one old witness (Stiller) and is the usual choice of the modern lists.
- **Thin days.** On some days the evidence is divided or sparse, and the "of" figure should be
  read with the count:
  - the Sunday after Christmas;
  - the Sunday after New Year (three witnesses in all);
  - Quinquagesima;
  - Lent 4 and 5;
  - Palm Sunday.
- **One possible double count.** Thompson's column collates Ludecus with twelve other lists and
  cannot be separated from Ludecus's own entries (Introduction, [The hymn database](#repo-hymns)). Where both support a hymn,
  Ludecus may be counted twice. Thompson is kept, because it is a modern study that collates old
  sources. Without it, the leading hymn of every day except Lent 4 and Trinity 7, 15 and 24
  would stay the same, and on those four days the leading hymns are tied or nearly tied. The
  hymns at the margin would change on 15 days. For example:
  - Trinity 4 would lose *Mensch, willst du leben seliglich* (Man, wouldst thou live blessedly);
  - Advent 2 would gain *Es wird schier der letzte Tag herkommen* (The last day will soon be coming);
  - Ascension would gain *Nun freut euch, Gottes Kinder, all* (Now rejoice, all ye children of God).
- **What the table shows.**
  - The core of the old *de tempore* (of the season) scheme is very stable. On 36 of the 64 days whose hymn the
    witnesses choose, one hymn has at least two thirds of the day's witnesses. Examples:
    - Advent 1, *Nun komm* (Now come, Savior of the heathen);
    - Epiphany, *Was fürchtst du, Feind Herodes* (Why dost thou fear so, foe Herod);
    - Easter 5, the Lord's Prayer hymn;
    - Exaudi, *Wo Gott der Herr* (If God the Lord does not stand by us);
    - Pentecost, *Komm, Heiliger Geist*;
    - Trinity Sunday, *Gott der Vater wohn uns bei* (God the Father, dwell with us);
    - Trinity 6 and 13, *Es ist das Heil* (Salvation has come to us);
    - Trinity 8, *Ach Gott, vom Himmel* (O God, look down from heaven);
    - Trinity 10, *An Wasserflüssen Babylon*;
    - the Purification, *Mit Fried und Freud* (With peace and joy I depart);
    - the Annunciation, the German Magnificat.
  - The same hymns return on several Sundays:
    - *Wo Gott der Herr nicht bei uns hält* (If God the Lord does not stand by us) and *Wär Gott nicht mit uns* (Were God not with us at this time) on Epiphany 4, Trinity
      17 and Trinity 23;
    - *Vater unser* (Our Father) and *Warum betrübst du dich* (Why art thou troubled, my heart) together on Trinity 7 and 15;
    - *Aus tiefer Not* (Out of deep distress), *Allein zu dir* (In thee alone, Lord Jesus Christ) and *Erbarm dich mein* (Have mercy on me, O Lord God) among Trinity 3, 11, 19 and 22.

## <a id="ch9"></a>Chapter 9. Organ, Instruments and Bells


This chapter covers instrumental music and sounded signals in the church orders of the sixteenth
century printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century). It
asks:

- **The organ.** Was it kept? Did the organist play a prelude before the service or before a
  hymn, interludes between the verses or the parts of the service, or a postlude after the
  blessing? When was it silent? What might the organist not play?
- **Other instruments.** Were instruments other than the organ played in church? If so, which,
  when, and by whom?
- **Bells.** Which bells were rung: tower bells, a choir bell, a little bell or handbell at the
  altar, a Sanctus bell? When were they rung: before church, at the canonical hours, at the
  consecration and elevation, at the Sanctus, during the Lord's Prayer, at the *Gloria in
  excelsis* on Easter Day, during certain hymns, for the dead, at baptisms and weddings, against
  storms?

**How the chapter is laid out.**
- [§9.1](#s9-1) answers each question in brief, and [§9.2](#s9-2) sets out the scope and sources.
- [§9.3](#s9-3) covers the organ: its defence and its limits, the prelude, the alternation of organ and
  singers, the postlude, the seasons and rites in which it was silent, and the organist.
- [§9.4](#s9-4) covers the other instruments: trombones, town pipers and fiddlers, the carillon and the
  tower-blower, and the minstrels of weddings.
- [§9.5](#s9-5) covers the bells: their purpose, the summons to church, the daily and prayer bells, bells
  within the Mass, bells at hymns and the litany, the dead, baptisms and weddings, storms, and
  the lesser signals of sermon and alms.
- [§9.6](#s9-6) is a table by order, and [§9.7](#s9-7) a concordance of every order quoted.

**Related chapters.** Several passages are treated more fully elsewhere and are only cited here:
- the organ and polyphony at the introit and other propers:
  [Chapter 4](#ch4), §§[4.4.5](#s4-4-5), [4.10.4](#s4-10-4)–[4.10.5](#s4-10-5);
- the organ and figural music at the office: [Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.9.4](#s10-9-4);
- choir, people and organ in the hymns: [Chapter 8](#ch8),
  §§[8.14.7](#s8-14-7), [8.18.9](#s8-18-9);
- figural music, the organ and bells as marks of feast rank:
  [Chapter 12](#ch12), §§[12.10.5](#s12-10-5), [12.10.7](#s12-10-7);
- bell baptism and weather-ringing, and the organist's contract:
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), §§[13.12.3](#s13-12-3), [13.15.5](#s13-15-5);
- the bell-ringer's appointment and pledge:
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.12.2](#s13-12-2);
- the length of the sermon that the sermon glass measured:
  [Chapter 11](#ch11), [§11.7](#s11-7).

### <a id="s9-1"></a>9.1 Summary of findings

**The organ**

1. **Kept by the Lutherans, kept out of the service by the Reformed.** Luther would have "all
   the organs piped" if it served the young (1526). No Lutheran order abolishes the organ.
   Wittenberg's castle church in 1525 limits it to the Sunday *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) and German songs.
   Strasbourg in 1598 defends "singing and organ-playing" against the Reformed, who cast them
   out as "papistical leaven". Reformed Emden (1594) keeps its organ but uses it only before the
   service, while the people gather, and after it, as they leave ([§9.3.1](#s9-3-1)).
2. **Preludes: yes, of two kinds** ([§9.3.2](#s9-3-2)).
   - **A voluntary while the people gather.** At Strasbourg 1598 the organist begins "at the end
     of the last ringing"; at Emden 1594 (Reformed), "before nine o'clock, when the people gather".
   - **Announcing each piece.** The organist begins a chant or plays the first stanza of a hymn,
     and the choir or people take it up (Gelnhausen [1568], Naumburg 1537/38, Nördlingen 1555,
     Schweinfurt 1576, Hof 1592).
   - Strasbourg requires the prelude to be "even that which the congregation shall afterward
     sing", not "strange pieces and motets".
   - The practice of the organist "preambulating" before every item belongs to the seventeenth
     century (Bischofswerda 1676).
3. **Interludes: yes, chiefly as alternation** ([§9.3.3](#s9-3-3)).
   - **The usual form.** The organ plays a verse or stanza in turn with choir and people, and
     the verse it plays is usually not sung (Regensburg 1553, Naumburg, Nördlingen, Prussia
     1568, Pomerania 1569, Hof). At Regensburg's Vespers, though, "all the verses [are]
     nevertheless sung wholly throughout, for the better understanding".
   - **Limits on the organ's share.** Strasbourg allows "once or at the most twice" in a hymn;
     Reutlingen 1574, one stanza after every two sung. At Bergedorf 1544 the people first sing
     the whole psalm. Schleswig-Holstein 1542 has the German hymns sung "without organ".
   - **Pieces between the parts of the service.** These are separate from the alternation
     ([§9.3.4](#s9-3-4)). Schönburg 1542 has them after the epistle, after the Creed, and after the sermon
     "until the priest come to the altar". Schweinfurt 1576 has one in place of the *Et in
     terra* (And on earth).
4. **Postludes: yes** ([§9.3.5](#s9-3-5)).
   - **After the blessing.** Strasbourg allows "other pieces" or Latin motets for those who wish
     to stay.
   - **Elsewhere.** Gelnhausen: "Let the organist close with a little piece". Schönburg: "a good
     piece" after communion. Prussia 1568: a piece after the *Nunc dimittis*. Hamburg 1556:
     "before and after the sermon". Emden 1594 (Reformed): as the people leave.
5. **Silent seasons and rites** ([§9.3.6](#s9-3-6)).
   - **Seasons.** Lent or Passiontide (Hamburg 1529, Nördlingen 1555); Advent II to Christmas
     Eve (Hof 1592); Rogation week (Pomerania 1569); lower feasts (Henneberg 1582).
   - **Rites.** The litany (Henneberg 1582); communion (Wolfenbüttel 1543, Schönburg 1542 except
     on high feasts, Reutlingen 1574); baptism (Thorn 1560–1570).
   - **Forbidden music.** Worldly songs, love-songs, dances and galliards (Calenberg-Göttingen
     1542, Hamburg 1556, Pomerania 1569, Stettin 1573, Emden 1577 (Reformed)) ([§9.3.7](#s9-3-7)).

**Other instruments**

6. **Rare, and tied to figural music, courts, towns and weddings** ([§9.4](#s9-4)).
   - **Trombones.** "Trombones and other such instruments" accompany the psalms at the Ansbach
     court in 1538, and at weddings in church.
   - **Town pipers and fiddlers.** Danzig in 1612 retains the town pipers (three masters, three
     journeymen) and three fiddlers "for the choir", to play whenever there is figural music.
   - **Emden** (Reformed). The organist-town-piper of 1577 serves with "Christian music and other
     instruments" on feast days, tends the carillon and blows from the town-hall tower. The
     editor's notes add trombone-playing "in the organ" (1579), and a tower-watchman's psalms on
     cornett and trombone (1679).
   - **Wedding minstrels.** Pipes, fiddles, drums and trumpets play the bridal party to the
     churchyard (Hamburg 1529). They must not disturb the sermon (Nassau-Dillenburg 1570,
     Herford 1532), and they are withheld from a bride who has lost her honour (Schwäbisch Hall
     1543/1615).
   - **Not found.** No order names a lute, regal, cornett or trumpet in the service itself.

**Bells**

7. **Purpose.** Bells call people to the Word and to prayer, not to "the pomp of the feasts"
   (Wittenberg 1525, Saxe-Lauenburg 1585). Some orders curbed festal chiming (Danzig 1567,
   Bentheim 1601 (Reformed)); most kept more bells for greater days (Altenburg 1533, Danzig
   1612) ([§9.5.1](#s9-5-1)).
8. **Before church.** The usual summons is three signs, the last "together", or three with one
   bell and a little bell last (Gelnhausen [1568], Esslingen 1540 (Moderate Reformed), Bentheim
   1601 (Reformed)). Danzig 1612 names its seven bells and gives the full Sunday and weekday
   ringing ([§9.5.2](#s9-5-2)).
9. **At the canonical hours and through the day** ([§9.5.3](#s9-5-3)).
   - **Morning and evening, and the prayer bell.** The ringing at morning and evening was kept,
     even where no Matins or Vespers was held (Prussia 1544). It was reinterpreted as a bell
     *pro pace*, for peace, government and against the Turk. Many orders also rang at noon or
     eleven (Saxony 1528, Allstedt 1533, Meissen 1540, Wolfenbüttel 1543, Kurpfalz 1546,
     Lüneburg 1564, Hoya 1581, with its prayer). It also served as a time-signal for workers.
   - **The Ave Maria and Salve.** These names were dropped or the ringing recast (Heilbronn
     1532, Coburg 1554/55, Lichtenberg 1579).
   - **The Friday bell for the Passion.** Kept by some (Kurpfalz 1546, Thüngen 1564), abolished
     with the *Tenebrae* ringing by others (Hohenlohe 1582).
10. **At the elevation and consecration** ([§9.5.4](#s9-5-4)).
    - **A sign with the little bell before the consecration.** Prussia 1525, Riga 1530 and
      Kurland 1570.
    - **Ringing at the elevation.** The Danish *Ordinatio* (Ordinance) of 1537 allows it, "the bells
      meanwhile sounding according to custom". The Interim restored it at Ansbach (1548). At Hof
      it lasted until about 1560, "with a threefold pulse of the little bell".
11. **At the Sanctus.** Only Hatzkerode (1534?) rings a bell during the German Sanctus, and that
    is to call the communicants into the choir. There is no "Sanctus bell" in the corpus ([§9.5.4](#s9-5-4)).
12. **During the Lord's Prayer.** Not in the Mass. The Our Father is tied to the bell only in
    the daily prayer bells and the Friday bell ([§9.5.4](#s9-5-4)).
13. **At the *Gloria in excelsis* on Easter.** Not found ([§9.5.4](#s9-5-4)).
14. **During hymns and chants** ([§9.5.5](#s9-5-5)).
    - **The *Te Deum*.** Ringing to call the people to the sermon and Mass (Prussia 1544 and
      1568). All the bells at the Christmas *Te Deum* (Hof 1592).
    - **The litany.** The greatest bell so that those in the field may join in (Hohenlohe 1582),
      or singing "under the ringing" (Regensburg 1567).
    - **Not found.** No order rings during a particular stanza.
15. **For the dead** ([§9.5.6](#s9-5-6)).
    - **Kept as a call to the living.** "That the living also may consider the hour of their own
      dying" (Meissen 1540).
    - **Abolished.** The Saturday ringing "for all faithful souls" (Zwickau 1529, Reuss 1552).
    - **Regulated.** Equality (Ulm, Moderate Reformed), fees by the number of bells (Danzig
      1578), silence during sermons (Herford 1532).
    - **Withheld.** From despisers of the Sacrament (Zwickau 1533) and from unbaptized infants
      (Lippe 1571).
16. **At baptisms and weddings** ([§9.5.7](#s9-5-7)).
    - **Baptism.** A new evangelical custom: a sign with a bell, often the little bell, calls
      the congregation to a baptism held outside the regular service (Heilbronn c. 1529,
      Kurpfalz 1556, Ansbach 1556, Limpurg 1610).
    - **Weddings.** At Hof the bell is rung half an hour later than usual.
17. **Against storms.** Kept as a call to prayer by some, abolished by most ([§9.5.8](#s9-5-8); see
    [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.15.5](#s13-15-5)).
18. **Small bells.** A little bell in the choir calls the scholars (Prussia 1568); a little bell
    calls communicants (Haldensleben 1564); a little bell ends the sermon when the hour-glass
    runs out (Zerbst 1545); and a hand-bell accompanies the alms collection during sermons
    (Brandis 1529). Little bells at the Sacrament were rejected by the Reformed (Micron) and at
    Transylvanian sick-communions (§§[9.5.4](#s9-5-4), [9.5.9](#s9-5-9)).

---

### <a id="s9-2"></a>9.2 Scope, sources and method

**Sources.** The chapter draws on the whole of Sehling's edition as held in [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb): volumes
1–24, including the half-volumes, with the editors' introductions and notes. Passages from an
editor's introduction or note are marked as such, and so are witnesses later than about 1615,
which are cited only for comparison: Bischofswerda 1676, and the Emden tower-watchman of 1679
(Reformed).

**Searches.** The corpus was searched for:
- **The organ and organist**: *orgel* (organ), *orgeln*, *organist*, *organicen*, *organum* (organ),
  *präambulieren* (prelude), *schlagen* (strike [the organ]) near a chant or hymn.
- **Other instruments**: *posaune* (trombone)/*basune* (trombone), *zinke* (cornett), *pfeifer* (piper), *fidler* (fiddler)/*geige* (fiddle), *laute* (lute),
  *trommete* (trumpet)/*trompete* (trumpet), *pauke* (kettledrum), *bunge* (drum), *saitenspiel* (stringed instruments), *spielleute* (minstrels), *instrument*,
  *klockenspil* (chime of bells), *cymbala* (cymbals).
- **Bells**: *glocke* (bell), *glöcklein* (little bell), *schelle* (small bell), *campana* (bell)/*campanula* (little bell), *leuten* (ring)/*läuten* (ring)/*lüden* (ring),
  *beiern* (chime), *puls* (pulse of the bell), *zeichen* (sign), *pro pace* (for peace), *betglocke* (prayer bell), *Ave Maria*, *Salve*, *wetterleuten* (ringing against storms),
  *tenebre* (Tenebrae), *schiedung* (passing bell).

Because *leuten* ("ring") is spelled like *Leute* ("people") in many of the orders, ringing
passages were found by searching for a bell word within a few words of a ringing verb, and of
the Mass item in question (Sanctus, elevation, consecration, *Pater noster*, *Gloria*, *Te
Deum* [We praise thee, O God], litany, baptism, burial, wedding, storm).

**Negative findings.** Several things the chapter reports as "not found" were searched for
directly:
- a "Sanctus bell" (*Sanctusglocke* or any compound), a *Wandlungsglocke*, a hand-bell
  (*Handglocke*);
- ringing during the Lord's Prayer of the Mass;
- ringing at the Easter *Gloria in excelsis*;
- ringing at a named stanza of a hymn;
- a regal, a lute, a cornett or a trumpet in the service.

A passage phrased in an unexpected way may have escaped these searches. The negatives mean only
that no such passage was found.

**What the chapter does not repeat.** The chapter does not repeat what is quoted in full elsewhere;
see the related chapters listed at the head of this chapter.

---

### <a id="s9-3"></a>9.3 The organ

#### <a id="s9-3-1"></a>9.3.1 Kept, and defended

**Luther.** Luther's preface to the *Deutsche Messe* (German Mass) names the organ in the same breath as the
bells, as means that may serve the teaching of the young. **Luther, *Deutsche Messe und ordnung
gottis diensts*, 1526** (Sehling 1, p. 11):

<!-- doc 3 -->

for the sake of such must one read, sing, preach, write and make verses; and where it were
helpful and furthering thereto, I would have all the bells rung thereto, and all the organs
piped, and let sound everything that could sound.

**Wittenberg 1525.** The Wittenberg order for the castle church, a year earlier, is far more
sparing. The bells are a signal, not festal pomp, and the organ, since it is already there, may
sound only at the Sunday *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) and at German songs. **Wittenberg, *Wie es einer zeit mit den
ceremonien der kirchen gehalten wirt*, 1525** (Sehling 1, p. 699):

<!-- doc 147 -->

Item, let them use the bells for a sign, whereby it may be signified when they are to come
together to the singing and when to the hearing of the word of God. But let them not use them
for that pomp of the feasts. The organs (since they are already there) they may use, if they
will, only on the Lord's day at the *Te Deum laudamus* (We praise thee, O God), and whenever they sing German songs.

**The Lutheran norm.** No Lutheran order in the corpus abolishes the organ. Where a church had
one, the orders assume an organist and regulate him. Wolfenbüttel 1543 commends him as "honest,
and good also for the service of the art of music", and lets the pastor, council and treasury
pay him "more or less, according to the worth of his art, for organists are very unequal"
(Sehling 6/1, p. 45).

**Strasbourg 1598 against the Reformed.** By the end of the century the organ had to be
defended. The Strasbourg order of 1598 opens its chapter "Of singing and the organs" against
those who would cast singing and organ out of the church as popish leaven. Sehling's editor
notes that the Reformed are meant. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598**
(Sehling 20/1, pp. 602–603):

<!-- doc 1344 -->

Even as we cannot nor ought to approve the manifold abuse which was practised in the papacy with
singing and organs, so likewise can we not praise nor approve the purpose of those who cast
singing and organ-playing wholly out of the church as mere papistical leaven. […] But as
touching figural music and the organs, experience itself showeth that thereby the hearts and
minds of the hearers are stirred up and refreshed to laud and praise God the Lord the more
joyfully with their mouth and singing also. Yet shall it be in every way looked to, that such
figural music and organ-playing neither hinder nor too long hold up the common singing of the
whole church, nor the rest of the service with preaching and praying.

**The Reformed.** The Reformed orders went the other way. Micron's London order (Reformed)
(German edition 1565) rejects "altars, lights, little bells, vestments" ([§9.5.4](#s9-5-4)). At Reformed
Emden the organ survived in the great church, but it was kept out of the service altogether.
**Emden, *Kirchenordnung*, 1594** (Reformed; Sehling 7/1, p. 489):

<!-- doc 2113 -->

Of the organ there is no use during the singing, nor at the service, save only on Sunday before
nine o'clock, when the people gather, and afterward, when it goeth out of the church again.

The editor adds that the Reformed synods of Dordrecht (1574, 1578) and Middelburg (1581) pressed
for the abolition of organ-playing, and that in some Dutch towns the organ passed to the town
council, which had the organist play at set hours to keep people out of the taverns
(Sehling 7/1, p. 476, editor's note). The Emden order thus gives exactly the two places that
Lutheran orders also gave the organ outside the singing: a prelude while the people gather and a
postlude as they leave.

#### <a id="s9-3-2"></a>9.3.2 The prelude

The orders know two kinds of prelude: a voluntary while the congregation gathers, and the
organist's announcement of each piece before it is sung.

**While the people gather.** Strasbourg has the organist begin as soon as the last bell has
stopped and "a fair congregation" is there, and play nothing but what the people are about to
sing. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598** (Sehling 20/1, p. 603):

<!-- doc 1344 -->

Therefore, when one will use figural music and the organ, it shall be held after the following
manner. First, that the organist begin betimes, at the end of the last ringing, as soon as a
fair congregation is assembled; as likewise the singers shall do at all other sermons, even when
there is no organ-playing or figural music. Secondly, that before and during the singing of the
church he play no strange pieces and motets, but even that which the congregation shall
afterward sing.

The Emden order of 1594 (Reformed; [§9.3.1](#s9-3-1)) has the same voluntary "before nine o'clock, when the
people gather".

**The organ begins each piece.** In the orders that describe the festal service in detail, the
organ begins the hymn or chant and the singers take it up. At Gelnhausen the organist begins the
*Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit), plays the first stanza of the German psalm, and plays "a little piece"
after it. The editor glosses "strike the first stanza" as "plays the first stanza".
**Gelnhausen, *Kirchenordnung*, [1568]** (Sehling 9, p. 652):

<!-- doc 2341 -->

After the first sign hath been rung at seven o'clock, both summer and winter, the second at half
past seven, and [all the bells] together at eight, let the organist (if there be one) begin the
*Veni Sancte Spiritus*; afterward let the choir sing it out. Thereupon let the organist begin a
German psalm, play the first stanza, [and] afterward let the choir sing it out, without
alternation of the organ. After the psalm let the organist play a little piece; thereupon
followeth the collect and lesson; after that let the organist begin sometimes *Nun bitten wir* (Now pray we),
sometimes *Wir glauben all an einen Gott* (We all believe in one God), [and] let the choir sing it quite out. […] Thereupon
followeth the collect and benediction. Let the organist close with a little piece.

Schweinfurt 1576 likewise has "the organist begin to play the Sunday Kyrie, which the choir
singeth after", and at the Sunday introit the organist "beginneth to play the introit, which the
choir singeth after, as is customary" (Sehling 11, pp. 647–648). At Hof the organist "always
first plays the melody" of each verse of the German *Magnificat*
(Sehling 11, p. 429; see [Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.9.4](#s10-9-4)).

**"The organist playeth a prelude".** The fullest late example is not a sixteenth-century order. It
is a service order sent by the council of Bischofswerda to its cantor in 1676, printed by
Sehling in a note. The organist "preambulates" before the Kyrie, after the epistle, after the
Gospel and catechism, and before the blessing; at the noon service before the hymn, before the
sermon hymn and before the hour of prayer (Sehling 2, p. 106). It shows where the practice of
the sixteenth-century orders led, but it is late evidence and is cited here only for comparison.

#### <a id="s9-3-3"></a>9.3.3 Interludes and alternation

**Alternation.** The commonest use of the organ in the orders is *alternatim*: the organ takes a
verse or stanza in turn with the choir or people, and the verse it takes is played, not sung.
Regensburg is explicit. Sehling's editor glosses the first sentence "that is, these pieces are
not sung", and the communion stanzas "as an interlude". **Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung* of Justus
Jonas, 1553** (Sehling 13, p. 421):

<!-- doc 440 -->

But if an organist be present, he playeth the introit together with the *Kyrie eleison*, *Et in
terra* (And on earth), *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), Sanctus and *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God) on the organ, and also under the communion, in the
German songs, one stanza after another. […] And where the organist is present, he playeth [at
Sunday Vespers] one verse after the other on the organ; yet so that all the verses be
nevertheless sung wholly throughout, for the better understanding.

**Three and four choirs.** Naumburg's St Wenzel order sets out the German songs in alternation
of schoolboys and people, each with its own cantor. When the organ plays there are three choirs,
and when the maidens sing, four. **Naumburg, *Kirchen-Ordnung* for St Wenzel, 1537/1538**
(Sehling 2, p. 72):

<!-- doc 1219 -->

And all such songs as are German are sung, when the people is assembled, one choir after the
other: the scholars' choir singeth and beginneth a stanza, and after that the people keepeth the
other choir, which also hath its own cantor. But when the organ is played, three choirs are
kept, and the organ always beginneth, save that at the *Et in terra* the boys begin and after
them the organ, thereupon the choir and then the people. But when the maidens also sing in
choir, four choirs are kept, and the three choirs sing all the stanzas of the German songs, one
verse after the other, and the organist playeth in between in the [same] tone.

The same passage, almost word for word, stands in Caspar Löner's Nördlingen order as revised in
1555 (Sehling 12, p. 320). Hof's three-choir introit with organ, boys, older boys and girls is
quoted in [Chapter 4](#ch4), [§4.4.5](#s4-4-5).

**How much the organ might take.** The orders that care most for the congregation's singing
limit the organ's share:
- **Strasbourg 1598**: after intoning, the organist may play "not more than once or at the most
  twice" amid the church's singing (quoted in [§9.3.5](#s9-3-5)).
- **Reutlingen 1574**: two stanzas sung, then one played, "about as long as one of the sung
  stanzas", so that the young and the people learn the hymns. **Reutlingen, *Artikel der
  Schulvisitation*, 1574** (Sehling 17/2, p. 58):

<!-- doc 830 -->

but on other Sundays and holy days always two verses or two stanzas shall be sung, and thereupon
one (which might last about as long as one of the sung stanzas) shall be played on the organ; to
the end that the Christian church songs may be the better known to the youth and the common
people, and they the more stirred up to sing along with one accord and diligently.

- **Bergedorf 1544**: the organ may play on feast days, but only after the people have sung the
  whole psalm, and only what has been sung. **Bergedorf, *Kirchenordnung*, 1544**
  (Sehling 5, p. 389):

<!-- doc 1950 -->

Where also there be organs in the churches, one may well use them on the holy days, [and] play
the psalms and the aforesaid church song thereon; yet so that the people sing the whole psalms
first, and that on the organs only that be played which hath been sung.

- **Schleswig-Holstein 1542**: in the cathedral and collegiate churches the Latin Gloria
  alternates choir and organ, but the German Gloria, the German hymn in place of the sequence
  and the German Creed are sung by "the whole church" straight through "without organ".
  **Schleswig-Holstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542** (Sehling 23, p. 146):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

But on Sunday or on the feasts, when the priest hath sung *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (Glory to God in the highest), and the
choir and not the organ hath answered *Et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis* (And on earth peace to men of good will), then shall
they stop altogether, that the whole church may afterward sing *Allein Gott in der Höh sei Ehr* (To God alone on high be glory),
etc., which song shall be sung without break to the end, without organ-playing. After that the
choir and organ go on to sing *Laudamus te* (We praise thee), *Benedicimus te* (We bless thee), etc., to the end; after that the
Alleluia. But in the stead of the sequence the whole church shall again sing a German song
without break and also without organ.

**Organ and the people's hymn at communion.** Pomerania's *Agenda* lets the organ play during
the communion hymns, but only three times: once at the beginning, once in the middle and once at
the end. **Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569** (Sehling 4, p. 439):

<!-- doc 1865 -->

When these songs are sung under the communion, the organists shall make their song on the organ
the shorter, and play no worldly, light songs. The pastor shall provide that the organs be so
moderated that the German psalms under the communion be sung with the congregation wholly to the
end, and that the aforesaid songs be sung in turn, the choir and the people singing one verse
after the other, so that they all be alike in use by the scholars and the congregation.
Therefore the organist may play once at the beginning, once in the middle as occasion serveth,
[and] once at the end, before the collect.

**Hamburg 1556** lets the organist play "fittingly in between" the verses of the German psalm
sung in place of the alleluia and sequence, "as elsewhere is customary, or, as the time allows,
close the song with the organ" (Sehling 5, p. 552). Stettin forbids its organists to "fantasize
on the organ while other good Christians sing the psalms with the congregation" ([§9.3.7](#s9-3-7)).

#### <a id="s9-3-4"></a>9.3.4 Organ pieces between the parts of the service

Beside the alternation, some orders give the organ a short piece of its own between the parts of
the service. The fullest list is Schönburg's. **Schönburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542**
(Sehling 2, pp. 170–171):

<!-- doc 1235 -->

Before the introit, [at the] *Kyrie eleison*, the choir shall sing one Kyrie, one Christe and
again one Kyrie, and the organist play thereto. At or before the last he may also play a good
short little piece, etc. […] 3. After the epistle the organist playeth; thereupon the choir
singeth the alleluia, sometimes the sequence, so far as it is pure and Christian; thereupon the
whole church [singeth] a German psalm or Christian song, whichever one will, as is found in the
song-book. 4. After the Gospel [and] the *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), etc., in Latin, the organist playeth; the
church singeth *Wir glauben* (We believe), etc. 5. After the sermon the organist playeth something, until the
priest come to the altar and have prepared the bread and the cup to be offered. […] 7. […] The
organist shall not play under the communion, except on high feasts; but after the communion is
held he may play a good piece.

**Schweinfurt 1576** puts an organ piece in the place of the *Et in terra* (And on earth): "upon the Gloria,
etc., and instead of the *Et in terra*, etc., the organist playeth some music"
(Sehling 11, p. 647). Gelnhausen's "little piece" after the psalm ([§9.3.2](#s9-3-2)) is of the same kind.

#### <a id="s9-3-5"></a>9.3.5 The postlude

**After the blessing.** Strasbourg keeps the organist's freer music, and Latin motets, for the
end of the service, when those who want to listen may stay and the rest may go about their
business. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598** (Sehling 20/1, p. 603):

<!-- doc 1344 -->

And that the organ-playing and singing be not drawn out too long, he shall, after he hath
intoned, play not more than once, or at the most twice, amid the singing of the church, but
leave it its time to perform its singing with common voice and devotion. But when the service is
wholly performed and the blessing given to the people, then may the organist play other pieces
also, or have Latin motets sung; whereat those will without doubt always gladly stay who have
pleasure and liking thereto; and yet the common people, which would rather go after its
business, is not thereby hindered nor held up. When also the songs which the people singeth are
divided, so that either the organist playeth between, or a part of the song is kept until after
the sermon (which latter yet shall be done only with the longer songs), one shall so divide the
songs that what belongeth together in sense and content remain together and be not torn from one
another.

**Other postludes.**
- **Gelnhausen [1568]**: "Let the organist close with a little piece" ([§9.3.2](#s9-3-2)).
- **Schönburg 1542**: "after the communion is held he may play a good piece" ([§9.3.4](#s9-3-4)).
- **Emden 1594** (Reformed): the organ only "when it goeth out of the church again" ([§9.3.1](#s9-3-1)).
- **Prussia 1568**: at Vespers the organist plays alternate verses of the *Magnificat*, and
  "after the *Nunc dimittis*" plays a piece. **Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und Ceremonien*, 1568**
  (Sehling 4, p. 75):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

Where there is an organist, he playeth one verse after the other, so that after the *Magnificat*
the choir singeth the German antiphon, and the organist after the *Nunc dimittis* playeth a
piece. Thereupon they close with the versicle, collects and *Benedicamus Domino* (Let us bless the Lord).

- **Hamburg 1556**: the organists are to play "before and after the sermon" on holy days and
  working days, and at Vespers on all holy eves and days. **Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556**
  (Sehling 5, p. 547):

<!-- doc 1963 -->

That organists well skilled in their art and honest men be taken on. These shall play on the
organs, both on holy days and working days, in the churches where there is preaching at eight
o'clock, before and after the sermon, also at Vespers on all holy eves and days, according to
the direction of the choir's *ordinarius*. The organists shall agree with those in the choir
about the singing, and play on the organs in accord with what they begin in the choir. The
organists shall refrain from playing worldly, scurrilous and unseemly songs in the churches.

#### <a id="s9-3-6"></a>9.3.6 When the organ was silent

**Seasons.**
- **Lent and Passiontide.** Hamburg 1529 lets the organ "rest for a time, especially the
  fortnight over, when the Passion is preached" (Sehling 5, p. 513). Nördlingen 1555 lets the
  organ "remain out" in Lent until Easter, except on the Annunciation (Sehling 12, p. 320).
- **Advent.** Hof suspends the organ from the second Sunday of Advent to Christmas Eve. **Hof,
  *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1592** (Sehling 11, p. 432):

<!-- doc 294 -->

Note. On this Sunday the organs are suspended until the vigil of the Nativity of Christ.

- **Rogation week.** Pomerania 1569 has "no figural song nor organ" in Rogation week, except on
  the Ascension and its vigil
  (Sehling 4, p. 466; quoted in [Chapter 12](#ch12), [§12.10.5](#s12-10-5)).
- **Lower feasts.** Henneberg 1582 keeps the lower feasts "without organ", and Aschersleben 1575
  sings the Vespers of apostles' days "without the organist" (cited in
  [Chapter 12](#ch12), [§12.10.5](#s12-10-5)).

**Rites.**
- **The litany.** On the Henneberg prayer day of 1582 the German litany is sung "without organ
  or figural music" (Sehling 2, p. 311).
- **The communion.** Wolfenbüttel forbids the organ after the sermon in the Mass, so that the
  Supper may be attended to "in remembrance of Christ". **Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543**
  (Sehling 6/1, p. 45):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

Otherwise the organist may play every Sunday at the pastor's will. But in the Mass one shall not
make it long, that the sermon be not hindered, and that the laity also have room there to praise
Christ with German song. Yet after the sermon in the Mass one shall not play on the organs, but
attend only to the Supper of Christ there, in remembrance of Christ.

Schönburg 1542 likewise keeps the organ silent under the communion except on high feasts ([§9.3.4](#s9-3-4)),
and Reutlingen 1574 drops the organ "wholly" on communion days because the service is then
longer (Sehling 17/2, p. 58).
- **Baptism.** At Thorn baptism is to be held when the church is quiet, not under the singing or
  the organ. **Thorn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1560–1570** (Sehling 4, p. 230):

<!-- doc 1844 -->

Baptism shall be held when it is still in the church, not under the singing or organ-playing,
with all devotion and reverence, and not with the idle chatter of the bystanders
