thanksgiving, with great devotion, *Te Deum laudamus* (We praise thee, O God), etc. But the whole day through, as well
in the morning as in the afternoon, one shall preach of the angels, that every man may
understand what good we have received from God through their service, that we also may thank God
therefor.

In Braunschweig the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) is sung before the Gospel. **Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*,
1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 397):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

Then shall a preacher, when the epistle is read, before the Gospel, exhort the people to thank
God for all benefits, and especially for the fruits of this year which he hath given us to
gather in […] he shall let *Te Deum* be sung, etc., before the Gospel is read.

**Note.** Michaelmas's rank still varies from place to place:

- **A chief feast**: the fourth *Vierzeitenfest* (four-times feast) in Braunschweig, Hamburg, Lübeck, Grubenhagen,
  Mecklenburg, Hoya, Lippe, Oldenburg and Waldeck.
- **Preached "before and after noon"**: in Mecklenburg, where it formally stands in the second
  rank.
- **A whole day with Te Deum**: in the Brunswick orders.
- **A half day**: in Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1561 ([§12.6.2](#s12-6-2)) and Nassau-Weilburg 1609.
- **A sermon day only**: in Wied 1564 (Reformed; [§12.4.5](#s12-4-5)).
- **A "small feast", though with three sermons**: in Danzig 1612 ([§12.5.6](#s12-5-6)).

#### <a id="s12-8-6"></a>12.8.6 John the Baptist

The Nativity of John the Baptist (24 June) is kept by nearly every order, usually in the second
rank. The reason given is either the Gospel history of his birth or the office of preaching: "to the honour of the holy office of preaching the Gospel of Christ". The
Pomeranian order of 1535 counts him with the feasts of Christ: "the feast belongeth also to Christ"
([§12.5.4](#s12-5-4)). The Wolfenbüttel order of 1543 gives his day a polemical theme.

**Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 6/1, pp. 62–63):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

On the day of John the Baptist one shall preach of the outward ministry of the divine Word
against the Anabaptists, who […] stand upon the saying, They shall be all taught of God;
wherewith they would lay all the schools waste.

#### <a id="s12-8-7"></a>12.8.7 Trinity

The feast of the Trinity falls on a Sunday. It is usually listed at the end of the feasts of
Christ with the note that it "falleth on the next Sunday after Whitsunday" (Saxony 1539, Mecklenburg 1552). Its rank is shown in four ways:

- **The Kyrie.** It shares the *Kyrie summum* with Pentecost at Nördlingen and Buxtehude ([§12.4.2](#s12-4-2)).
- **The Latin Mass.** It is one of the "high feasts of Christ" with a Latin Mass in
  Schleswig-Holstein 1542 ([§12.10.1](#s12-10-1)).
- **The Athanasian Creed.** It is read on the day and its vigil in the Thüngen lessons of 1587.
- **Solemnity.** It is kept "hochfeyerlich" in Verden 1606.

The Brandenburg-Ansbach chapter order of 1533 notes only that its office "is pure" ([§12.4.4](#s12-4-4)).

#### <a id="s12-8-8"></a>12.8.8 Mary Magdalene, the Conversion of Paul, the Beheading of John: kept for their Gospels

Three days that are not apostles' days are often ranked with them, because they have a story in
the New Testament. These are the Conversion of Paul (25 January), Mary Magdalene (22 July, Luke
7:36–50) and the Beheading of John the Baptist (29 August). Where they are not holy days, the
orders keep their Gospels on the nearest weekday or Sunday.

**Mecklenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552** (Sehling 5, p. 201):

<!-- doc 1922 -->

When such holy days fall as are not wont to be kept holy, and yet their histories are written in
the Gospel, as is the day of the Conversion of Paul, Mary Magdalene, St John's beheading, etc.,
the preachers may read and handle the same text and histories in the sermon on such working day,
namely Wednesday or Friday, as is next to such holy day.

Solms-Laubach gives a reason for keeping the Beheading of John. **Solms-Laubach,
*Kirchenzuchtordnung*, 1603** (Sehling 9, p. 356):

<!-- doc 2311 -->

The day of John's beheading may be laid on a common week-day sermon day (since the same hath a
glorious history and witness how the world is wont to reward godly preachers), as also the
Gospel of Mary Magdalene, since it containeth a profitable and comfortable history.

In Prussia Mary Magdalene's Gospel is given a fixed Sunday. **Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und
Ceremonien*, 1568** (Sehling 4, p. 87):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

The Gospel of Mary Magdalene, Luke 7, shall ordinarily and henceforth yearly be read and
preached on the seventh Sunday after Trinity

#### <a id="s12-8-9"></a>12.8.9 Corpus Christi, the Holy Cross, local and new feasts

**Corpus Christi.** Most orders abolish it, and some order it to be explained so that people
will know why it has gone.

**Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1096):

<!-- doc 2150 -->

The feast of Corpus Christi shall be done away according to God's Word, and the preachers shall
on the Sunday before remind the people what great abuse and idolatry hath been practised
therewith, which every Christian ought to shun according to the earnest commandment of God.

Two early orders keep it: Northeim for civic reasons, and Nassau-Dillenburg to teach the right
use of the Sacrament.

**Northeim, *Kirchenordnung*, 1539** (Sehling 6/2, p. 935):

<!-- doc 2047 -->

The day of the Lord's true Body men have had to let stand for special political, that is, civil
causes; yet so that the procession, with all other unchristian ceremonies, be done away, and
only God's Word and the Lord's Supper be suffered to be handled and held thereon.

**Nassau-Dillenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1537** (Sehling 10, p. 74):

<!-- doc 169 -->

Our Lord's Body day, called Corpus Christi, shall be retained to this end, that one may rightly
teach and preach thereon of the right use and fruit of the high holy Sacrament of the body and
blood of Christ. But the Sacrament shall be neither set out nor carried about, on that nor on
any other day in the year

**The Holy Cross.** Luther's "Let the feasts of the Holy Cross be anathema" ([§12.3.1](#s12-3-1)) is echoed in Sayn 1582,
"the two days of the cross, the Finding and the Exaltation of the Cross" ([§12.5.5](#s12-5-5)). No order keeps them.

**Local and civic feasts.** Some towns kept days of their own, and the orders treat them in
different ways:

- **Braunschweig.** St Autor had been honoured with a civic procession under a vow. It was
  turned into alms and a Sunday thanksgiving (Sehling 6/1, p. 398).
- **Wied 1564** (Reformed). Patronal feasts are kept with a sermon ([§12.4.5](#s12-4-5)).
- **New days.** Some towns added days of their own: a day of penance for the Osnabrück fire of
  1613 ([§12.6.2](#s12-6-2)); a thanksgiving in Nördlingen for the town's deliverance from a planned surprise
  attack in 1440 (Sehling 12, pp. 387–388); and in Regensburg a dedication festival in October
  for the beginning of evangelical preaching in 1542 (Sehling 13, p. 475).

**A new feast of Christ.** Bugenhagen proposed a feast the medieval calendar did not have.

**Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 380):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

It is a wonder that there hath been no feast of the baptism of Christ, seeing there have been so
many unprofitable feasts, to the destruction of body and soul. […] So that the Shrovetide Sunday
may with us be called the feast of the baptism of Christ; one may then name it as one will.

**Note.** Wolfenbüttel 1543 keeps this "feast of the baptism" on the Sunday before Lent, with
the Gospel of Matthew 3 preached "all day long" (Sehling 6/1, p. 62).

---

### <a id="s12-9"></a>12.9 The *Vierzeiten*: the four chief feasts and the four offerings

In north and central Germany the highest rank of feasts had a name that came from church
finance, not liturgy. These were the *vier Zeiten* (four times; Low German *veer tide* [the four times]), or the four
*Hochzeiten* (high tides). They were the four feasts on which the "four-times penny" (*Vierzeitenpfennig*,
*veertide pennink*) or offering was paid to the pastor or the church chest. Three of the four
were fixed: Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide. The fourth varied by region, as the editors'
notes show. It was most often the Assumption (so at Minden, Sehling 21, p. 138). The Bergedorf
order names St John the Baptist's day instead
(Sehling 5, p. 389, cited by the Buxtehude editor, Sehling 7/1, p. 79). At St John's in
Halberstadt the penny was collected quarterly, on John the Baptist's day, Michaelmas, and the
Tuesdays of Christmas and Easter (Sehling 2, p. 488).

The Lutheran orders kept the payment, and with it the rank. Most of them replaced the Assumption
with Michaelmas, which fell in the same season (after the harvest) and had a lawful Gospel theme
(the angels). The *Vierzeiten* (the four times) are the Lutheran north's equivalent of the *summa festa* (highest feasts). A
*Vierzeitenfest* (four-times feast) is a whole holy day, often with first vespers and a sermon on the eve, and with
a Latin Mass.

#### <a id="s12-9-1"></a>12.9.1 The four times named

Bugenhagen's Lübeck order describes the treasure-chest. **Lübeck, *Kirchenordnung* (Bugenhagen),
1531** (Sehling 5, p. 362):

<!-- doc 1949 -->

Into this chest shall come the four-times penny out of all the parishes. The four times are
Easter, Whitsuntide, Michaelmas, Christmas. Then shall a great basin stand in all churches on
the altar before the choir. Two churchwardens shall have an eye thereon and not be far from it;
and all folk of twelve years and above, young and old, shall bring thither the times-penny.

A pre-Reformation police ordinance of Waldeck names the four *Hochzeiten* (high tides) first among the days
on which attendance at Mass is enforced. **Waldeck, *Landordnung*, 1525** (Sehling 9, p. 179):

<!-- doc 2300 -->

We also set, ordain and will, earnestly commanding, that every one of our subjects that is come
to his years of discretion shall, on the four high-tide feasts and Sundays, and also on all our
Lady's and apostles' days, hear in his parish church the office of the holy mass and the holy
Gospel from their parson

The Pomeranian order sets out the due itself. **Pomerania, *Kerckenordeninge*, 1569**
(Sehling 4, p. 414):

<!-- doc 1862 -->

The four-times penny, every quarter, from every person above twelve years, a farthing, shall be
given either to the pastor or to the church, as is the custom in every place.

The same dues are found in the lower Rhineland, in the Erasmian Catholic order of Jülich-Cleves,
where they are called the "four high-tide offerings". **Jülich-Cleves-Berg,
*Visitationsinstruktion*, 1559** (Roman Catholic humanist; Sehling 21, p. 87):

<!-- doc 1425 -->

yet so that to every one the four high-tide offerings and loaves be given, as heretofore
ordained

#### <a id="s12-9-2"></a>12.9.2 Michaelmas in the Assumption's place

The replacement was made by Braunschweig 1528 ("Item, Michaelmas for a four-times feast", [§12.5.4](#s12-5-4)) and
Hamburg 1529. It became standard through Mecklenburg 1552 ([§12.5.2](#s12-5-2)) and the visitation of 1557
([§12.8.3](#s12-8-3)). The later orders write it into their feast lists.

**Lippe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571** (Sehling 21, pp. 391–392):

<!-- doc 1462 -->

The day of Michael, which in the stead of the feast of the Assumption of Mary is kept solemnly
in our churches as a feast of the four times […] and whereon the needful comfortable doctrine of
the dear holy angels is set forth and handled to the congregation of God. On these feasts it
shall be done, as touching the order of the lessons, chants, sermons and communion, as on the
common Sundays; only that the introits and sequences, and on the four-times feast days the
prefaces *de tempore* (of the season), item the old German feast-songs, as above mentioned and customary with
us, be sung.

**Note.** Lippe ranks the *Vierzeiten* (the four times) above the other feasts of Christ by one liturgical mark,
the proper preface. The same order calls them "the glorious, fair, holy, chiefest four-times feasts" (p. 392).

**Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 7/2.1, pp. 1096–1097):

<!-- doc 2150 -->

The day of Michael, which is kept as a feast of the four times in the stead of the feast […] of
the Assumption or Ascension of Mary, whereon the doctrine of the holy angels shall be set forth
to the people. Likewise also on the same feast, after the epistle is read, a common thanksgiving
shall be made for the fruits received, and the *Te Deum laudamus* (We praise thee, O God) be sung thereto.

In the Harlingerland order the payment is the reason given for Michaelmas taking the place.
**Harlingerland, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573/74** (Sehling 7/1, p. 735):

<!-- doc 2122 -->

We ordain therefore that the last and fourth high feast-tide shall be St Michael's day. And the
parishioners shall on the same day render kindly to the pastor their offering, due duty and
land-rent, and give and pay it without hindrance.

#### <a id="s12-9-3"></a>12.9.3 The *Vierzeiten* as a liturgical rank

At Wolfenbüttel a sermon at first vespers is allowed only on the four. The same words stand in
Hildesheim 1544 (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 858). **Wolfenbüttel, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543**
(Sehling 6/1, p. 62):

<!-- doc 1972 -->

On the greatest feasts, or four times, Christmas, Easter, Whitsuntide and Michaelmas, one may
preach for an hour at the first vespers. On the other feasts it is not needful.

Hoya has the Mass in Latin throughout. **Hoya, *Kirchenordnung*, 1571** (Sehling 6/2, p. 1151):

<!-- doc 2065 -->

VI. Of the four-times feasts. On the four-times feasts one shall hold the office of the mass in
our churches, where it can be had, throughout in Latin, with the introit, Kyrie eleison, *Gloria
in excelsis*, collects, epistles, sequences, Gospels, etc.; yet so that the wonted German psalms
which are appointed for the feasts (that the church also may sing) be not forgotten.

In Lauenburg the *hohe Vierzeitenfeste* (high four-times feasts) are the days for the alms collection, and the meal the
pastor used to give the churchwardens on those days is abolished. **Lauenburg, *Kirchenordnung*,
1585** (Sehling 5, p. 421):

<!-- doc 1953 -->

Fourteenthly, they shall on all Sundays, and on the holy days and the high four-times feasts,
diligently gather the collection from the people during the sermon, write it down and lay it by
[…] And lastly there shall be wholly done away on the high four-times feasts the collation and
feasting which the pastor hath hitherto had to give the churchwardens on such feasts.

In the Neumark the churchwardens are to take the collection plate round on the high feasts
generally, not only on the four. **Neumark (Brandenburg), instruction of Margrave Johann for the
visitors, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 36):

<!-- doc 1745 -->

The same churchwardens shall also go about in the church with the plate on all high holy feasts,
not only on the four times

**Note.** Grubenhagen 1544 defines its first rank of feasts by this payment ("the four chief feasts, on which the four-times penny is gathered", [§12.5.5](#s12-5-5)). Henneberg 1582 has four chief
feasts, but they are Christmas, Easter, Ascension and Whitsuntide ([§12.6.3](#s12-6-3)). It shows that "four
chief feasts" could be understood liturgically as well as fiscally.

---

### <a id="s12-10"></a>12.10 Keeping the feast in church: ceremonial marks, abolished ceremonies and the seasons

Beyond whole and half holy days, the orders mark the higher feasts with a set of ceremonial
additions. None of them is new. Each carries on, in reduced form, a feature of the medieval
feast grades. Listed from the commonest to the rarest:

| Mark | Higher feasts | Lower feasts and ordinary days | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sermons | two or three, sometimes four; a sermon at first vespers | one sermon, in the forenoon | [§12.6.3](#s12-6-3); Wolfenbüttel 1543 ([§12.9.3](#s12-9-3)); Danzig ([§12.5.6](#s12-5-6)) |
| Latin chant | introit, *Gloria*, Alleluia, sequence, *Patrem* (the Nicene Creed), preface, Sanctus, *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God) in Latin | German hymns | [§12.10.1](#s12-10-1) |
| Kyrie grade | *summum* (the highest [chant]), *paschale* (Easter [Kyrie]), *festivale* | *dominicale* (Sunday [Kyrie]), *angelicum* (angelic [Kyrie]), *apostolicum* (apostles' [Kyrie]), *feriale* | [§12.4.2](#s12-4-2), [§12.10.2](#s12-10-2) |
| Proper preface | preface of the feast (*de tempore*, *solemnis*) | common preface, exhortation, or none | [§12.10.3](#s12-10-3) |
| Sequence | kept on the great feasts | dropped | [§12.10.4](#s12-10-4) |
| Figural music and organ | figural music, organ | plain-song or German; no organ | [§12.10.5](#s12-10-5) |
| Vestments, elevation | mass vestment, elevation | choir robe or none | [§12.10.6](#s12-10-6) |
| Bells | more bells, chiming (*beiern*) the day before | one bell | [§12.10.7](#s12-10-7) |
| Creed and *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) | *Athanasianum* (Athanasian Creed), Latin *Te Deum* | — | [§12.10.8](#s12-10-8) |
| Communion | communion and first vespers with confession | no communion on apostles' days | [§12.10.9](#s12-10-9) |
| Civil marks | no weddings, markets or guild feasts | — | [§12.11.3](#s12-11-3) |

#### <a id="s12-10-1"></a>12.10.1 Latin chant on the high feasts

The Saxon *Unterricht der Visitatoren* (Instruction of the Visitors) of 1528 set the pattern. Latin is kept for the higher
feasts "because it is unseemly always to sing one song".

**Saxony (Ernestine), *Unterricht der Visitatoren*, 1528** (Sehling 1, pp. 165 and 169):

<!-- doc 9 -->

On high feasts, as Christmas, Easter, the Ascension, Whitsuntide, or the like, it were good that
certain Latin chants, agreeable to Scripture, were used at the mass. For it is an unseemly thing
evermore to sing one song. […] With the feasts also it shall be done peaceably: that where
certain plain holy days have fallen away, men make not much strife thereof. And forasmuch as it
is also unseemly that the chants be all alike on all feasts, it were good that on the most
glorious feasts there were sung the Latin introits, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (Glory to God in the highest), Alleluia, the pure
sequences, Sanctus, *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God).

In Ernestine Saxony the rule depends on the place as well as the day. **Saxony (Ernestine),
*Gemeine Verordnung*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 192):

<!-- doc 14 -->

In towns and market towns, where there are boys' schools and folk that understand Latin, one may
hold mass in Latin on high feasts, otherwise in German; but in the villages, where no man
understandeth Latin, one shall hold mass in German throughout […] Note: even when mass is held
in Latin on high feasts, yet the epistle, the Gospel, the words of the Sacrament and the Lord's
Prayer are all read in German and aloud

In Schleswig-Holstein the high feasts are named, and Trinity is one of them.
**Schleswig-Holstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542** (Sehling 23, p. 91):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

On the high feasts of Christ, which are Christmas, Easter, Whitsuntide and Trinity, one shall
sing in the towns in Latin the introits, *Gloria in excelsis*, Alleluia with pure sequences;
item Latin prefaces, which the priest beginneth thus: *Dominus vobiscum* (The Lord be with you), etc., *Sursum corda* (Lift up your hearts),
etc.; thereafter the Sanctus; lastly the *Pater noster* with the words of the Supper, yet these
always in the German tongue

At Buxtehude the *Gloria* follows the rank. **Buxtehude, *Kirchenordnung*, 1552**
(Sehling 7/1, p. 74):

<!-- doc 2082 -->

Next shall be sung the Kyrie eleison as occasion serveth, *Gloria in excelsis* and the *Et in
terra* (And on earth): on the high feasts always in Latin, on the Sundays and otherwise in German or in Latin,
as the time will allow.

Thorn has the reverse rule. On Sundays the chants before the sermon are in Latin, but the small
feasts are wholly German. **Thorn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1575** (Sehling 4, p. 238):

<!-- doc 1844 -->

Otherwise the chants, collects and lessons before the sermon are all held in Latin. On the
apostles' days and other small feasts, which are wont to be kept with half solemnity, the whole
office is held in German, both in the Old and the New Town

#### <a id="s12-10-2"></a>12.10.2 Chant on the apostles' days

The lower feasts have their own marks in several orders. They are enough to set them off from
working days without matching Sundays.

The Pomeranian *Agenda* gives the rule for the apostles' days. **Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569**
(Sehling 4, p. 469):

<!-- doc 1865 -->

These following apostles' days one shall keep holy before noon. On the Sunday before, the
preachers shall bid them and exhort every man to come to church on these days. On the evening
before one shall ring or chime *festivaliter*, and hold vespers; in the morning likewise ring
*festivaliter*, preach at seven or eight, yet deal out no testament [no communion]; but one may
hold the office before the altar before the sermon, read the *Gloria*, collect, epistle and
Gospel with the tone, that there may be a difference between these days and the common working
days. When church is out, every man goeth to his work.

The Aschersleben agenda sets out the apostles' day Mass and vespers. **Aschersleben,
*Kirchen-Agenda*, 1575** (Sehling 2, p. 480):

<!-- doc 1260 -->

Of vespers on the apostle's eve. Vespers shall be held as on the Saturday, yet so that one sing
*de festo* (of the feast) and read the collects *de festo* also. Of the mass on the apostles' days. 1. After
the ringing, which shall be done as on a working day, the cantor straightway beginneth the
introit.
2. Thereupon followeth the *Kyrie apostolicum* (apostles' Kyrie). 3. Then is sung the German "Allein Gott in der
   Höh" (To God alone on high be glory), etc. 4. The collect of the feast of the apostle, and thereafter the epistle is read.
   […] Of vespers on the apostles' days. Vespers are sung without the organist, as otherwise on
   a working day, since no sermon is held.

The Riga order gives the melody of the Kyrie. **Riga, *Kirchenordnung*, 1530**
(Sehling 5, p. 15):

<!-- doc 1897 -->

After the introit one singeth the Kyrie eleison with few notes (save on the high feasts, when
one may take the paschal note)

#### <a id="s12-10-3"></a>12.10.3 Proper prefaces

Proper prefaces belonged only to the great feasts, and the orders use them to mark those days.

The same text is in Hamburg 1529 (Sehling 5, p. 528). **Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528**
(Sehling 6/1, p. 441):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

Thereafter he turneth him to the altar, and on the great feasts which have special prefaces, and
else, when he will, on certain Sundays with the preface of the Trinity (which was made against
the Arians, as was the Nicene Creed also), he shall begin in Latin the preface *Dominus
vobiscum* (The Lord be with you) and sing it to the end; whereupon let the choir sing a Latin Sanctus.

In Ottheinrich's order the preface itself has two grades. **Pfalz-Neuburg, *Kirchenordnung* of
Ottheinrich, second printing 1547** (Sehling 14, p. 109):

<!-- doc 473 -->

But for certain high feasts, the feast of Easter, the Ascension, Whitsuntide, Trinity, etc.,
there are special prefaces, two for each feast, a *solemnis* and a *dominicalis*; these a priest
may note out or write out, and have always on the desk beside the church order

**Note.** The *solemnis* and *dominicalis* tones of the preface are the melodic grades of the
medieval preface: the festal tone for the feast itself, the ferial or Sunday tone for the days
within its season. The order prints the Trinity preface as its example.

At Hatzkerode there is an exhortation on ordinary days and the preface on the great feasts.
**Hatzkerode (Harzgerode, Anhalt), *Kirchenordnunge*, 1534(?)** (Sehling 2, p. 587):

<!-- doc 1263 -->

Then shall the priest turn him about and read unto them the exhortation, as it standeth in the
agenda. But on the great feasts, in the stead thereof, the preface of the feast shall be sung,
with the wonted Sanctus in Latin.

**Thorn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1575** (Sehling 4, p. 237):

<!-- doc 1844 -->

After the sermon followeth a German hymn; thereupon the priests on high feasts sing the preface
*de tempore* (of the season) to the wonted notes; but on the common Sundays and holy days [the priest], without
the same, turneth to the people straightway after the German hymn

Kurland allows German proper prefaces for the high feasts, "for variety". **Kurland,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1570** (Sehling 5, p. 89):

<!-- doc 1907 -->

But where one will sing on the high feasts, for a change (as is done at the prince's court),
these prefaces hereafter set down and noted, instead of the daily one, it shall be free to every
minister

**Note.** Saxony 1539 prints Latin prefaces for Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Ascension,
Pentecost and Trinity, and a *Praefatio quotidiana* (daily Preface) for all other days
(Sehling 1, p. 274, editor's summary). The Mecklenburg family allows "prefaces of the season" on
the feasts of Christ ([§12.5.2](#s12-5-2)). Lippe 1571 restricts them to the *Vierzeiten* (the four times; [§12.9.2](#s12-9-2)).

#### <a id="s12-10-4"></a>12.10.4 Sequences

In Schleswig-Holstein sequences are dropped except on the three great feasts, and each great
feast keeps its own sequence. **Schleswig-Holstein, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542**
(Sehling 23, p. 90):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

The sequences and proses shall all be left off and not be sung, save on the three great feasts
of Christ: as from Christmas unto Candlemas, *Grates nunc omnes* (Let us all now give thanks), with its German song; from
Easter unto Whitsuntide, *Victimae paschali*, with its German song; then in Whitsuntide, *Veni,
Sancte Spiritus*, with its German song.

**Note.**

- **Seasons, not days.** The sequence is kept through the whole season of each great feast, from
  Christmas to Candlemas and from Easter to Whitsuntide.
- **Aschersleben 1575.** The cantor "the Sundays after these feasts sing the sequences in the church".
- **The Mecklenburg family.** Sequences are "de tempore" (of the season) on the feasts of Christ ([§12.5.2](#s12-5-2)).

#### <a id="s12-10-5"></a>12.10.5 Figural music and the organ

**Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556** (Sehling 5, p. 551):

<!-- doc 1963 -->

Also the figural song shall on the chiefest feasts be orderly observed and sung in one parish as
well as in the others.

The Hof order gives the title of its collection of polyphonic music in the table of contents;
the collection itself begins on p. 456. **Hof, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1592**
(Sehling 11, p. 477):

<!-- doc 294 -->

XVI. An order of the sweetest and best songs, chosen out of the most excellent masters both old
and new, which are sung in figural music under the leading of the cantor, directed to the chief
feasts of the whole year

In the Pomeranian *Agenda* there is no figural music or organ in Rogation week, except on the
Ascension and its vigil. **Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569** (Sehling 4, p. 466):

<!-- doc 1865 -->

On this Sunday and in the week one shall sing no figural song, nor play the organ, save the day
of the Ascension of the Lord, with its vigil

**Other examples:**

- **Anhalt 1568**: figural music on the first two days of the high feasts, Latin chorale on the
  third ([§12.7.1](#s12-7-1)).
- **Regensburg 1567**: figural music at the vespers before, and the communion on, the feasts of
  Christ (p. 475).
- **Henneberg 1582**: lower feasts are kept "one orgeln" ([§12.6.3](#s12-6-3)).
- **Schwarzburg 1587**: the organ is used on the apostles' days in the forenoon
  (Sehling 2, p. 137).
- **Aschersleben 1575**: the vespers of apostles' days are sung "without the organist" ([§12.10.2](#s12-10-2)).

The seasons and rites in which the organ was silent are treated in
[Chapter 9](#ch9), [§9.3.6](#s9-3-6).

#### <a id="s12-10-6"></a>12.10.6 Vestments and elevation

In Prince Bernhard's Anhalt order the elevation of the Sacrament is kept only on the high
feasts. **Anhalt, *Kirchenordnung* of Prince Bernhard, 1568** (Sehling 2, p. 570):

<!-- doc 1262 -->

Forasmuch as the elevation of the most worthy Sacrament of the true body and blood of Christ
hath fallen away in one church but not in another, the ministers shall elevate on high feasts;
beyond these the said Prince Bernhard is content that it be left off. Likewise on Sunday the
choir robe shall be used at all three sermons, and through the week it may be left off.

**Note.**

- **Grimma 1529.** The mass vestment is required on the three-day high feasts ([§12.7.1](#s12-7-1)).
- **Querfurt.** According to Sehling's account of the visitation, mass vestments were worn at
  communion and, for a time, in the pulpit on the three chief feasts (Sehling 2, p. 460).

#### <a id="s12-10-7"></a>12.10.7 Bells

**Altenburg, castle chapter, *Verordnung der ceremonien*, 1533** (Sehling 1, p. 516):

<!-- doc 56 -->

Thirdly, one shall also henceforth keep this difference: that on common working days one ring to
the holy office of the sermon with one great bell, and on Sundays and other feasts with more
bells, to distinguish the time.

The fullest bell-code is the Danzig one of 1612 ([§12.5.6](#s12-5-6)). It names five bells:

- Osanna;
- Apostolica;
- Dominical;
- Ferial;
- Sybilla.

The great feasts are rung in with the great bell and the three larger bells chimed together
(*beiern*). The small feasts are chimed "with the Osanna".

The bells in general, their signs and their uses, are treated in
[Chapter 9](#ch9), [§9.5](#s9-5).

#### <a id="s12-10-8"></a>12.10.8 The Athanasian Creed and the *Te Deum*

The Mecklenburg convent order gives the rule for the convents' matins. **Mecklenburg,
*Klosterordnung*, 1572** (Sehling 5, p. 258):

<!-- doc 1926 -->

On the high feasts, as Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, Ascension, Whitsuntide and Trinity, the
Athanasian Creed shall be sung in German straightway after the Benedictus.

For the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) in Latin "on the greater feasts" see Transylvania 1547 ([§12.4.3](#s12-4-3)). For the *Te Deum*
as the Michaelmas thanksgiving see [§12.8.5](#s12-8-5).

#### <a id="s12-10-9"></a>12.10.9 Communion and confession

The orders do not give the Supper by rank as such. Communion is held whenever there are
communicants. But rank shows in the preparation and in the days on which communion is normally
held.

- **Regensburg 1567.** Communion and vespers on the eve go with every feast of Christ, but not
  with the third day of the great feasts ([§12.7.1](#s12-7-1)).
- **Pomerania 1569.** No communion on apostles' days ([§12.10.2](#s12-10-2)).
- **Stade, *Kirchenordnung*, c. 1620/22** (Sehling 7/1, p. 54). On the three high feasts
  confession is heard after the afternoon sermon of the first day, and the Supper is given on
  the second day, "which is not done on the first and the last feast day".
- **First vespers.** The vespers of the eve of the higher feasts were also the time for private
  confession of the next day's communicants (for example Leiningen 1584, p. 278: "on the high feast days a vespers the evening before").

#### <a id="s12-10-10"></a>12.10.10 Festal ceremonies abolished

**The plays and processions of the year.** The late-medieval feasts had their own acted
ceremonies:
- the Palm Sunday ass;
- the crucifix laid in the "grave" on Good Friday;
- the image of the risen Christ carried round on Easter Day;
- the figure of Christ drawn up through the church roof on Ascension Day;
- the dove let down on Whitsunday;
- the rocking of the Christ-child's cradle at Christmas;
- processions round the church with holy water, crosses and the sacrament.

The south German orders abolish them by name. They also abolish the blessings of the year: water
and salt on Sundays, candles at Candlemas, ashes on Ash Wednesday, palms on Palm Sunday, and the
Easter candle, font and fire on Holy Saturday. **Hohenlohe, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553**
(Sehling 15, p. 77):

<!-- doc 539 -->

In like manner shall also be left off all spectacles and shows which have been practised with
images: as on Palm Sunday with the ass, on Good Friday with the crucifix and the grave, on
Easter Day with the carrying about of the image of the resurrection of Christ, on Ascension Day
with the drawing up of the same, on Whitsunday with the letting down of the dove, on Christmas
Day with the rocking of the little child, and whatever more of the like hath been in use. Item,
all processions and goings about the church with holy water and crosses, and also with the
carrying about of the holy sacrament in the monstrance, etc.

The same list stands in Pfalz-Neuburg 1543 (Sehling 13, pp. 95–96) and the Palatine *Bedenken
zur Reformation der Stiftskirchen* (Opinion on the reformation of the collegiate churches) of 1546 (Sehling 14, p. 93). The Corpus Christi procession
went with the feast itself ([§12.8.9](#s12-8-9)).

**What stayed.** What the orders keep for the feasts is the reading and preaching of the feast's
history, its hymns and sequences, its proper preface, and in many places its Latin chant
(§[12.10.1](#s12-10-1)–[12.10.4](#s12-10-4)). The *Leisen* sung from the pulpit at the high feasts are treated in
[Chapter 8](#ch8) [§8.10.2](#s8-10-2).

#### <a id="s12-10-11"></a>12.10.11 Seasonal changes in the service

**Advent and Lent.** Some orders mark the penitential seasons by plainer chant and by leaving
out the *Gloria*. The Pomeranian order of 1542 gives the old Kyrie grades by season:
*dominicale* (Sunday [Kyrie]) in Advent and Lent, *paschale* (Easter [Kyrie]) from Easter to Whitsun, *summum* (the highest [chant]) on the higher
feasts. In Lent the *Gloria* may be left out altogether. **Pomerania, *Kirchenordnung*, 1542**
(Sehling 4, p. 356):

<!-- doc 1859 -->

Thereupon the Kyrie *dominicale*; or one may also on the Sundays sing the Kyrie *angelicum* (angelic [Kyrie]), *de
martyribus* (of martyrs), or *confessoribus*, or *virginibus*, as they have been named; the *dominicale* in
Advent and in Lent, the *paschale* between Pentecost and Easter, the *summum* on the higher
feasts, or the *minus summum* (the lesser summum). Thereupon the priest singeth the *Gloria in excelsis* […] in Lent
one may well leave out the *Gloria* altogether, or when it will be too long.

Other seasonal changes in the orders:
- **The Creed in Advent.** At Schweinfurt "Wir glauben all" (We all believe) replaces "Nun bitten wir" (Now pray we) on the
  three Sundays of Advent (Sehling 11, p. 646).
- **The Litany.** Days kept "plainly, *dominicaliter*, as in Advent and Lent" may have the Latin
  Litany (Pomerania, *Karcken ordening* [church order], Sehling 4, p. 354).
- **Hymns.** The hymn tables change with the seasons: Advent, Christmas to Candlemas, Easter to
  Whitsun (see [Chapter 8](#ch8) [§8.7.5](#s8-7-5) for the *Gloria* in
  Advent and Lent, and [§8.10.3](#s8-10-3) for the seasonal hymns before the sermon).
- **Luther's warning.** Luther himself would not have Lent, Holy Week or Good Friday shown off
  "with other rites" than the rest of the year ([§12.12.1](#s12-12-1)).

---

### <a id="s12-11"></a>12.11 Keeping holy days in common life

The orders kept the calendar by law as much as by liturgy. A holy day was a day on which work,
trade and amusement were restricted, and the restrictions were enforced by the magistrate. This
section covers the rest from work ([§12.11.1](#s12-11-1)), its enforcement ([§12.11.2](#s12-11-2)), weddings, guild feasts and
markets ([§12.11.3](#s12-11-3)), the folk festivals of the year ([§12.11.4](#s12-11-4)), and one feast created to replace them
([§12.11.5](#s12-11-5)). Harvest exemptions are treated in [§12.6.4](#s12-6-4).

#### <a id="s12-11-1"></a>12.11.1 Rest: the whole day, the forenoon, or the time of the sermon

**Not a commandment, but good order.** The first Saxon visitors already gave the principle. The
ceremonies of the church, the holy days among them, are not commanded by God. They are kept "for
the sake of good order and peace", as each parish has the custom. **Ernestine Saxony,
*Unterricht der visitatoren an die pfarrherrn*, 1528** (Sehling 1, p. 164):

<!-- doc 9 -->

For such things are more needful than to eat flesh on Friday and the like, although that is
right before God and in the conscience. Yet the people shall nevertheless be taught to speak
modestly of such church orders; for some church orders are made for the sake of good order and
peace, as St Paul saith in the first to the Corinthians, the fourteenth: Let all things be done
in order in the church. Therefore the holy days, as Sunday and some more, shall be kept, as is
the custom of each parish.

**Degrees of rest.** In practice the orders set three degrees:
- **Sunday and the high feasts**: no work all day;
- **the half holy days**: no work until noon, or until the sermon was over ([§12.6.1](#s12-6-1));
- **the other holy days**: no work during the service only.

A visitation recess for an Oldenburg parish states the difference between Sunday and the other
holy days in one sentence. It lists the work forbidden: carting turf, hay and sheaves,
ploughing, harrowing, mowing and digging. The penalty is that the offender's horses are
unharnessed until he pays. **Oldenburg, *Visitationsabschied für Bardenfleth*, 1609**
(Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1201):

<!-- doc 2151 -->

that on Sundays wholly, but on the other holy days during the sermon, there be refraining from
carting turf, hay [and] sheaves, from ploughing, harrowing, mowing, [and] digging, and in other
ways from handiwork; also that during divine service no one tap beer or wine; and that the
wilful transgressors be punished as is due by unharnessing of the horses until [the fine be]
paid […]

**Work allowed after the sermon.** Pfalz-Zweibrücken allowed field work on all holy days except
Sunday and the three high feasts, "especially in harvest and autumn", on condition that the
people had first heard the sermon. The reason given was that "some holy days hinder working
people in their living", while giving the idle occasion "to feast, carouse and drink wine".
**Pfalz-Zweibrücken, *Generalartikel*, 1560** (Sehling 18, p. 293):

<!-- doc 971 -->

And whereas the subjects in the country have also brought forward complaint hereupon, that some
holy days hinder working folk in their living, but give to others, who without that seek
occasion for idleness, opportunity to gorge, carouse and drink wine, we are content that, apart
from the three high feasts and the holy Sunday, on the other holy days, especially in harvest
and autumn time, our subjects may attend to their necessary field and other work; yet so that on
that same day they have first attended God's word and the sermon.

**"Loose holy days".** Where the lesser feasts had been kept by halves, the people treated them
as working days altogether. A Henneberg pastor complained that on the days "which the common man
is wont to call loose holy days" the villagers did their road-mending and timber-carting, and
went hunting after the early sermon. **Wasungen, *Kirchen-Ordnung*, 1566**
(Sehling 2, pp. 356–357):

<!-- doc 1250 -->

for because in other places these holy days have been in part abolished, and the cry hath gone
forth that they shall soon fall altogether, men have undertaken on such holy days, which the
common man is wont to call loose holy days, all manner of common and private work, as making the
common ways, going to the land-defences, carting building timber and more of the like […]. Early
a sermon is done; thereafter one hunteth, or every man worketh what he will.

#### <a id="s12-11-2"></a>12.11.2 Enforcement: gates, fines and taverns

**The town gates shut.** The Brandenburg visitors told town councils to shut the gates on
holy-day mornings, so that no one could go out to work in the fields. **Cölln on the Spree,
*Visitations-Abschied*, 1540** (Sehling 3, p. 194):

<!-- doc 1759 -->

It hath come credibly before the visitors that there are many disobedient people who profane the
holy day with carting and working, and otherwise also; therefore the honourable council shall
keep the gates shut on the holy day before noon, [and] suffer no one [to go] out of them to work

The same order recurs in the visitation recesses for Salzwedel 1579 and Stendal 1578
(Sehling 3, pp. 285, 300, 331).

**Fines.** The town mandates fix the fine. Strasbourg (1534, Moderate Reformed) forbade every
kind of handiwork on Sunday: stacking wood, unloading wood or sand, bucking and washing. The
fine was thirty shillings. Milk and bread might be sold, and in Lent fish, until the last bell
for the sermon. **Strasbourg, *Mandat zur Sonntagsheiligung*, 1534**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 20/1, p. 246):

<!-- doc 1296 -->

First, since Sunday is ordained for the hearing of God's word, that no one in the city of
Strasbourg or its precincts shall on Sunday, without special weighty [and] honest cause or
pressing need, do any handiwork whatsoever, be it with stacking wood, unloading wood or sand,
bucking or washing, or other works, whatever they be, on pain of thirty shillings pfennig.

The discipline orders of the Wetterau counts set fines for each offence: for walking in the
fields during the sermon, for trading, for sitting in the wine-house or working in the field
(Hanau-Münzenberg, *Reformationsmandat für das Amt Rodheim*, 1596, Reformed, Sehling 10, p. 414; see
[Chapter 11](#ch11) [§11.12](#s11-12) for the fines for absence and for disturbing the
sermon). Taverns were to stay shut during divine service on Sundays and holy days alike.

#### <a id="s12-11-3"></a>12.11.3 Weddings, guild feasts and markets

Wedding feasts, guild banquets and markets were moved away from the high feasts, so that they
would not draw people from the sermon. The closed seasons for weddings in Advent and Lent are
treated in [§12.12.6](#s12-12-6).

**Mansfeld, *Kirchen-agenda*, 1580** (Sehling 2, p. 240):

<!-- doc 1241 -->

Of weddings at the chief feasts. Forasmuch as it is very unmeet that wedding-feasts be held at
the chief feasts, the same shall henceforth be wholly stayed at such feasts: and at Christmas,
eight days before, and until the Sunday after the Three Kings; likewise at Easter until the
Sunday Quasimodogeniti; and at Whitsuntide until the Sunday Trinity, no wedding shall be allowed

**Hadersleben, *Zuchtordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 23, p. 244):

<!-- doc 1599 -->

The guild-feasts also shall no more be held on the high feasts, and especially on Whitsunday,
but be put off to another day.

**Brandenburg, *Visitation- und Consistorialordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 3, p. 129):

<!-- doc 1748 -->

The magistrates also shall ordain that the weekly markets which fall on high feasts be put off
until after noon, or to the next day following, that God's Word be not hindered thereby.

#### <a id="s12-11-4"></a>12.11.4 Fastnacht, Kirchweih, May Day and Midsummer

**"Heathen" festivals.** The folk festivals of the year were attacked as "heathen" in mandate
after mandate:
- Shrovetide (*Fastnacht*) with its masks, dances and begging for eggs and meat;
- the church-dedication fair (*Kirchweih*, *Kirmes*);
- May Day and Walpurgis night, with the May-tree;
- Whitsun ales, the *Pfingstbier*;
- the Midsummer fires of St John's Eve;
- the *Hagelfeier*, a day of processions against hail.

The Hessian *Reformationsordnung* of 1572 (Philippist) forbids "Sunday dances, especially during
the sermon and the catechism", and all such "frivolous wantonness". **Hesse,
*Reformationsordnung*, 1572** (Philippist; Sehling 8, p. 401):

<!-- doc 2272 -->

So also shall the Sunday dances, especially during the sermon and the catechism, and also all
other frivolous wantonness which is practised and undertaken by the common man after heathen
manner at Shrovetide, Walpurgis, Whitsuntide, St John's day and at other times more through the
year, be wholly forbidden; and the transgressors shall each time be earnestly punished by our
officers according to the form of the wantonness practised, and the fine brought in to us. But
when there are weddings, one may dance modestly

The same list recurs in Nassau-Weilburg 1576
(with the "*Hagel* holy days" and the Walpurgis and St John's fires, Sehling 10, p. 310), Solms
1603 (Sehling 9, p. 351) and Ysenburg (Sehling 10, p. 707). Separate *Fastnacht* mandates were
issued in Waldeck (1547, 1563, 1589/90), Ysenburg (1590, 1612, Reformed) and Baden (1610)
(Sehling 9, pp. 222, 297, 301; 10, pp. 593, 693; 16, p. 572). Kurpfalz banned church-dedication
fairs, Shrovetide and mummery outright in its police legislation
(Sehling's introduction, Sehling 14, p. 66), and Waldeck abolished the *Kirchweih* in 1583
(Sehling 9, p. 299). The Franconian order of Thüngen named Corpus Christi and the *Hagelfeier*
together as feasts "whereby God is blasphemed" (Sehling 11, p. 737).

#### <a id="s12-11-5"></a>12.11.5 Shrove Sunday turned into a feast of baptism

**A new feast in place of an old one.** Bugenhagen's Hamburg order turned the Sunday before
Lent, the beginning of Shrovetide, into a day for preaching on baptism. The Gospel was the
baptism of Christ (Matthew 3). He remarks that there had never been a feast of Christ's baptism,
though there had been "so many useless feasts". **Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1529**
(Sehling 5, p. 507):

<!-- doc 1959 -->

Therefore it is thought good to use the Shrove Sunday especially for preaching of baptism. In
the morning there shall be preached in all the parish churches the Gospel of Matthew 3, how
Christ was baptized in the Jordan by St John. That is a comfortable and gracious history of the
Lord Christ, which surely shall not be kept silent. It is a wonder that there hath not been a
feast of the baptism of Christ, whereas there have been so many unprofitable feasts, to the ruin
of body and soul.

The Schleswig-Holstein order of 1542 has the same rule (Sehling 23, p. 94). The Pomeranian
*Agenda* of 1569 explains its purpose: the people are to be reminded of their baptism, "that by
God's Spirit they may be the more led away from the heathenish, unchristian Shrovetide doings"
(Sehling 4, p. 473).

---

### <a id="s12-12"></a>12.12 The seasons of the year

The evangelical orders kept the shape of the church year: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Holy Week,
Easter, Ascension, Whitsun and the Trinity season. What they changed was what each season meant
in practice. Lent lost its fast ([§12.13](#s12-13)) but kept its preaching. The seasons with the most extra
services were Lent and Holy Week. Their additions were sermons and catechism, not Masses. This
section covers Luther's starting point ([§12.12.1](#s12-12-1)), Advent ([§12.12.2](#s12-12-2)), Lent ([§12.12.3](#s12-12-3)), Holy Week ([§12.12.4](#s12-12-4)),
Rogation week and the catechism seasons ([§12.12.5](#s12-12-5)), the closed seasons for weddings ([§12.12.6](#s12-12-6)) and the
Ember days ([§12.12.7](#s12-12-7)).

#### <a id="s12-12-1"></a>12.12.1 Luther: no special show for Lent

**The *Formula missae*.** Luther would not mark Lent, Holy Week or Good Friday with rites that
set them apart from the rest of the year. To do so, with the half-Mass of the Presanctified and
the denial of the cup, would be "to mock and laugh at Christ". **Luther, *Formula missae et
communionis*, 1523** (Sehling 1, p. 5):

<!-- doc 2 -->

Further, the Lenten graduals and the like, which exceed two verses, let whosoever will sing at
home. In the church we will not have the spirit of the faithful quenched with tedium. Neither is
it meet to display Lent itself, or the Greater Week, or the Friday of the Passion, with other
rites than any other [days], lest we seem to wish to mock and laugh at Christ any longer with a
half-Mass and with one part of the sacrament. For the Alleluia is the perpetual voice of the
church, even as the memory of his passion and victory is perpetual.

In 1526 he said the same of Holy Week, which "shall be even as other weeks", with the Passion
preached an hour a day (*Deutsche Messe*, Sehling 1, p. 16; see
[Chapter 11](#ch11) [§11.4.4](#s11-4-4)). The later orders did not all follow him in the
chant. Some left the *Gloria* out in Lent and used the plain Kyrie ([§12.10.11](#s12-10-11)).

#### <a id="s12-12-2"></a>12.12.2 Advent

**The coming of Christ.** Advent is kept as a season of preaching on the prophecies of Christ's
coming and on the Last Day. The Pomeranian *Agenda* gives weekday sermons for it. **Pomerania,
*Agenda*, 1569** (Sehling 4, p. 463):

<!-- doc 1865 -->

But how one shall preach in Advent on the working days, the prophecies of the coming of Christ
and the Lord Christ's sermons of the Last Day, that followeth hereafter.

Advent was also a season for the catechism. At Allstedt (1533) the pastor was to examine the
children "three times in the year, in Advent, in Lent and after the harvest"
(Sehling 1, p. 511). The Niederwildungen catechism order of 1533 (Waldeck) held the catechism
three days a week in Advent (Sehling 9, p. 191).

#### <a id="s12-12-3"></a>12.12.3 Lent: repentance, the Passion and the catechism

**Preaching.** Lent kept its old name, *die Fasten* (Lent) or *Quadragesima* (Lent), but its content became
preaching. The Württemberg order sets the themes: repentance through Lent; on Palm Sunday the
whole Passion read to the young people in three parts; on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday the
Passion expounded. **Württemberg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1553** (Sehling 16, p. 267):

<!-- doc 671 -->

In Lent, called *Quadragesima*, there shall be preaching of right Christian repentance. On Palm
Sunday it is profitable, beside the history of Palm Sunday, to read to the young people the
history of the whole Passion, divided into three times, namely morning, afternoon and at Vesper
time; and thereafter to expound the same history to the common church on Maundy Thursday and
Good Friday, and to explain its profit and use with special earnestness and diligence.

The same text stands in Pfalz-Neuburg 1554, Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1557, Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 and
Kurpfalz 1556 (Sehling 18, pp. 207, 520; 14, p. 163). The division of the Passion into a series
of Lenten sermons is described in [Chapter 11](#ch11) [§11.4.4](#s11-4-4).

**More weekday sermons.** In Lent the weekday sermons were increased. In the Corvey village of
Bruchhausen there was a sermon one day a week through Lent and two in the week before Easter.
**Corvey, *Kirchenordnung für das Corveyer Stiftsdorf Bruchhausen*, 1603** (Sehling 21, p. 243):

<!-- doc 1455 -->

Over and above these holy days and prayer days now named, there shall also in Lent be preaching
weekly one day in the week, but before Easter two days, the Thursday and Friday, and the history
of the Passion of Christ be set before the people.

**Daily catechism instead of the *Salve Regina*.** The commonest daily service of Lent was the
catechism, held at the hour when the *Salve Regina* had once been sung. **Gotha, *Artikel durch
die hern visitatores einem erbarn rathe zu Gotha zugestellet*, 1555** (Sehling 1, p. 569):

<!-- doc 88 -->

Every day in Lent, beginning straightway on the first Sunday, [at the hour] when in the papacy
the idolatrous *Salve Regina* was sung, the catechism is held with the children every day until
Palm Sunday. A psalm is sung, as the 8th, 16th, 22nd, 69th, 110th etc., which remember the
Passion of Christ, beside the part of the catechism which is to be handled; thereafter a lesson
is read out of Sirach, the Proverbs of Solomon, or whatever other lesson is appointed by the
pastor

Calenberg 1542 gives the same rule (Sehling 6/2, p. 804). The Upper Lusatian orders of Zittau
and Herwigsdorf had the catechism preached every weekday in Lent "at Salve time"
(Sehling 3, p. 379).

**The Easter communion and the examination.** Lent ended in the Easter communion, which drew the
young people "in great number" (Regensburg 1572, Sehling 13, p. 509). The catechism was
therefore examined on the Sundays of Lent. **Albertine Saxony, *Ordnung* of Duke August, 1580**
(Sehling 1, p. 424):

<!-- doc 44 -->

Secondly, the pastor shall proclaim to the congregation on the Sunday *Esto mihi*, etc., that
henceforth on the Sundays in Lent, after the midday sermon, the examination shall be held with
the children and household servants; wherefore the parents shall send and hold their children
and servants thereto, that they may give account of their faith out of their catechism.

There was no daily Lenten Mass. The orders hold the Supper when there are communicants ([§12.10.9](#s12-10-9)).
In Lent the extra services are sermons, catechism and examination.

The Lenten catechism course is treated in
[Chapter 15](#ch15), [§15.11.1](#s15-11-1), and the catechism
service in [Chapter 10](#ch10), [§10.10](#s10-10).

#### <a id="s12-12-4"></a>12.12.4 Holy Week

**Maundy Thursday and Good Friday.** The two days kept their themes: the institution of the
Supper and the Passion. In Hamburg the morning service on Maundy Thursday was held "as on a
Sunday, with the ceremonies", with a sermon on the sacrament. On Good Friday the Passion was
preached. **Hamburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556** (Sehling 5, p. 544):

<!-- doc 1962 -->

In Lent, on Maundy Thursday, every pastor shall preach at eight o'clock of the sacrament of the
body and blood of the Lord Christ; for in the forenoon it shall be held in the church as
otherwise on a Sunday, with the ceremonies, as hath been done until now. On Good Friday every
pastor shall preach the Passion of the Lord at eight o'clock; yet it shall be free to every
pastor to begin the same in Lent, when he pleaseth, to treat it long or short.

Most orders keep Maundy Thursday and Good Friday as holy days, at least in the forenoon ([§12.6.2](#s12-6-2)).
The old Holy Week ceremonies (palms, the ass, the grave, the Easter fire) were abolished
([§12.10.10](#s12-10-10)). Weddings were not held in Holy Week ([§12.12.6](#s12-12-6)).

#### <a id="s12-12-5"></a>12.12.5 Rogation week and the catechism seasons

**Processions abolished.** The Rogation processions through the fields (*Kreuzgänge*,
*Bittgänge*) went with the other processions ([§12.10.10](#s12-10-10)), and the *Hagelfeier* (hail holiday) against hail was
condemned ([§12.11.4](#s12-11-4)).

**The week kept for the catechism.** Bugenhagen kept Rogation week (*Krützeweke*) as one of four
seasons for preaching the catechism through in eight sermons, by the superintendent and his
adjutor. During these weeks the other preachers rested from their weekday sermons.
**Braunschweig, *Kirchenordnung*, 1528** (Sehling 6/1, p. 378):

<!-- doc 1983 -->

In Advent two weeks, on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday. In the first two full weeks of
Lent likewise. In Rogation week with the week following likewise, except the Lord's Ascension
Day. Two weeks after the harvest, before the hops are taken down, likewise. Therefore the two
preachers must frame the catechism briefly and understandably for the simple, that it can be
preached through in the eight sermons.

Hamburg 1529 and Lübeck 1531 repeat the plan (Sehling 5, pp. 505, 352). The four catechism
seasons stand where the Ember weeks had stood ([§12.12.7](#s12-12-7)).

#### <a id="s12-12-6"></a>12.12.6 Closed seasons: no weddings in Advent and Lent

**The old rule kept.** Most orders kept the medieval closed seasons for weddings: Advent, Lent
(often from mid-Lent) and the high feasts. They gave a new reason: the wedding feast would draw
people from the sermon. **Schwäbisch Hall, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 17/1, p. 155):

<!-- doc 762 -->

Weddings shall not be laid and held on the high feasts, as on Christmas, Easter, Whitsuntide,
etc., nor yet in Advent and in Lent, especially after mid-Lent, that the people be not thereby
led away from the preaching of God's word and the holy service

Strasbourg states the closed seasons exactly and adds that "we do not distinguish the times
after the popish, superstitious manner". **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1598**
(Sehling 20/1, p. 636):

<!-- doc 1344 -->

Although we do not distinguish the times after the popish, superstitious manner, yet, because
everything hath its time, and the devotion of the greater number shall not be hindered by the
joy and pastime of a few, it is the custom with us that from the third Sunday of Advent until
the first Sunday after New Year's day no weddings are accepted to be proclaimed or blessed;
likewise also not from *Laetare* or mid-Lent until Easter.

The same ban, with dispensations "for great causes", is in Saxony 1580, the Upper Palatinate
1579, Grubenhagen 1581, Lüneburg 1575, Stendal 1551, Marienhafe (East Frisia) 1593 and Oldenburg
(Sehling 1, p. 436; 13, p. 316; 6/2, p. 1065; 6/1, p. 672; 3, p. 316; 7/1, p. 718; 7/2.1, p. 1180).
Mansfeld extended it to the octaves of the high feasts ([§12.11.3](#s12-11-3)). Hoya forbade weddings and other
feasting through Lent and Holy Week, "that every one may prepare himself by a sober, moderate
life" for the memory of Christ's passion (Sehling 6/2, p. 1200).

#### <a id="s12-12-7"></a>12.12.7 The Ember days: from fast days to quarter days

**The fast gone, the date kept.** The Ember days (*Quatember*, *Fronfasten*, Low German
*quatertemper*) were the Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after Invocavit, Whitsunday, Holy Cross
(14 September) and St Lucy (13 December). The orders do not keep them as fasts ([§12.13](#s12-13)). They keep
them as the four quarter days of the church year. Their uses in the orders:
- **Payments.** The communicants' offering penny was paid "every Ember time", as were
  schoolmasters' fees, salaries and poor-relief accounts. This is the commonest use by far.
- **Catechism sermons.** The catechism was preached through in each Ember season. **Torgau,
  *Ordnung der Visitatoren*, 1529** (Sehling 1, p. 676):

<!-- doc 139 -->

The catechism shall be preached four times a year, namely in the four Ember seasons. Each Ember
season two or three weeks shall be taken for it, and while the catechism lasteth the other
sermons shall rest.

- **The Litany.** Albertine Saxony had the Litany sung "on the four Ember seasons for a week"
  (Sehling 1, p. 272), and Mansfeld "especially on the four Ember days, when the people are
  together" (Sehling 2, p. 239).
- **Ordinations.** In Pomerania candidates were examined and ordained "at the time of the Ember
  days, especially in Lent and at Michaelmas, when the catechism is repeated", so that the
  ordinands might hear how the catechism was preached. **Pomerania, *Kerckenordeninge*, 1569**
  (Sehling 4, p. 395):

<!-- doc 1862 -->

The examination in doctrine shall be done out of the *Examen ordinandorum*, the *loci communes*,
the catechism and the text of holy Scripture, and that at the time of the Ember days, especially
in Lent and at Michaelmas, when the catechism is repeated, that the ordinands may straightway
hear the form of preaching the catechism.

- **Ordinances read from the pulpit.** The forbidden degrees of marriage and the list of
  offences to be reported were read from the pulpit at every Ember season in Nassau
  (Sehling 10, pp. 95, 115). The Pfalz-Neuburg edicts were to be read "four times a year at the
  Ember times" (Sehling 13, p. 115).
- **Marriage sermons.** Henneberg 1582 held a half-hour sermon on marriage on the Sunday after
  each Ember season (Sehling 2, p. 314).

---

### <a id="s12-13"></a>12.13 Fasting

The medieval Church kept about 160 fast and abstinence days a year (Sehling's note, Sehling 11,
p. 92):
- the forty days of Lent, on the weekdays from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday;
- the Friday abstinence, and in many places the Saturday;
- the Ember days;
- the vigils of the great feasts.

On these days meat, and in Lent also eggs and dairy, were forbidden on pain of mortal sin. The
evangelical orders removed the obligation, kept the praise of fasting, and replaced the fixed
fasts with occasional days of fasting and prayer. This section covers the principle ([§12.13.1](#s12-13-1)), the
call to voluntary fasting ([§12.13.2](#s12-13-2)), the orders that kept the old fasts ([§12.13.3](#s12-13-3)), fasts kept for
civil reasons ([§12.13.4](#s12-13-4)), the days of fasting and prayer ([§12.13.5](#s12-13-5)) and fasting before communion
([§12.13.6](#s12-13-6)).

#### <a id="s12-13-1"></a>12.13.1 Not a law, and not a merit

**Fasting set among human ordinances.** The visitors of 1528 list "appointed fasts, eating no
flesh on Friday" among the ordinances made "to earn grace for sins", which may therefore "be let
fall" (see [Chapter 10](#ch10) [§10.3.4](#s10-3-4) for the passage). Eating meat on Friday
is "right before God and in the conscience", and less needful to preach than the commandments
([§12.11.1](#s12-11-1)).

**Fasting good in itself.** The Lüneburg articles of 1527 put the evangelical teaching in one
sentence. Fasting is "useful and good, to tame the body". But it is not to be kept so that
anything is earned "by difference of food on appointed days". No pastor is to compel anyone "to
a difference of times or of food"; the people are to be led to "a willing fasting and a moderate
life". **Lüneburg, *Artikelbuch*, 1527** (Sehling 6/1, p. 500):

<!-- doc 1996 -->

The eighth article. How one shall conduct himself in fasting. Forasmuch as fasting is useful and
good to tame the body, yet not to be so kept that by difference of food on appointed days
anything special be merited, or God's displeasure incurred if one kept it not; but since Christ
and his apostles, and also for a long time thereafter the common Christian church, left it free,
[it is ordered] that every pastor compel no one to a difference of times or of food, but rather
instruct them in the will of God, that it is left free to them to eat in the name of the Lord
what God granteth them; yet, with constant urging of God's word, he shall meet ignorance and
wantonness, that they fall not into excess, but rather take up a willing fasting and a moderate
life.

**"Who ever taught that Christians should not fast?"** The Calenberg order of 1542 answers the
charge that the evangelicals "teach nothing but to gorge on flesh". The answer has four points.
Fasting is to last the whole of life, not to be bound to fixed times. It is not to be drawn into
justification. It is not to be commanded on pain of mortal sin. And the difference of foods is
not to be suffered, "because Christ hath freed us from such ordinances". **Calenberg-Göttingen,
*Kirchenordnung*, 1542** (Sehling 6/2, p. 772):

<!-- doc 2033 -->

for who hath ever taught or written that Christians should not fast? We teach what right fasting
is; item, that according to the doctrine of Paul such fasting is not bound to any fixed time,
but shall last the time of our life; item, that such a work must not be drawn into
justification, nor be commanded on pain of a mortal sin, to ensnare the consciences therewith;
item, that the difference of food cannot be suffered here, because Christ hath freed us from
such ordinances

The Mecklenburg *Klosterordnung* of 1572 and the Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel *Klosterordnung* of
1569 explain the old fish days as a piece of the monastic "house order", which had wrongly been
turned into "a special service of God" (Sehling 5, p. 252; 6/1, p. 307).

#### <a id="s12-13-2"></a>12.13.2 Fasting exhorted, but free

**The transitional orders.** The earliest orders of the 1520s and 1530s keep the old fast days
as a recommended custom. They tell the preachers to exhort the people to keep them, and to live
moderately every day, but they forbid any command under the ban or mortal sin.
**Brandenburg-Ansbach-Kulmbach, *Landtagsabschied*, 1526** (Sehling 11, pp. 92–93):

<!-- doc 259 -->

Of fasting and eating flesh. The pastors and preachers shall exhort the people that they live
not only in the forty days' fast, the Ember days and the other fast days kept hitherto, but
daily in moderation and abstinence, or without excess of eating and drinking, that they may tame
their fleshly bodies and make them fit to fulfil and practise God's will and work […]. And
whereas, by the ordinance of certain holy fathers and councils, men have for a long time
abstained on the appointed fast days from flesh, eggs and other things, to the praise and honour
of God, although without doubt it was not the meaning of the same holy fathers and councils
thereby to put any one in danger of his soul or body, or to lay a snare of sin, or to make a new
mortal sin, but rather therewith to further men to Christian chastening of their body

Nassau-Dillenburg 1537 and Jülich-Kleve 1525 (Roman Catholic humanist) have the same text
(Sehling 10, p. 77; 21, p. 71).

**Before the Supper.** Oldenburg 1573, following Urbanus Rhegius, asks why Christians will not
fast "once or twice in the year" before coming to the Lord's table, when "the first godly
Christendom a thousand years ago kept the forty fast days, each according to his occasion".
**Oldenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 1573** (Sehling 7/2.1, p. 1081):

<!-- doc 2149 -->

Also, when he will ask anything earnest of God, or will prepare himself for an earnest
thanksgiving in the Lord's Supper, he will beforehand, by the moving of the Spirit of Christ,
fast, or live moderately and soberly. If he do it not, he is yet wholly carnal and a Christian
in name. The first godly Christendom a thousand years ago kept the forty fast days, each one
according to his occasion. What manner of Christians are we, that we will not fast once or twice
in the year, when we are to go to God's table?

#### <a id="s12-13-3"></a>12.13.3 Orders that kept the old fasts

**Waldeck 1528 and Baden.** A few orders kept the fasts as before. The articles for the Waldeck
synod at Mengeringhausen in 1528 say "all fast days shall be kept as hitherto", with abstinence
from meat "at the forbidden times". **Waldeck, *Beschlüsse für die Synode von Mengeringhausen*,
1528** (Sehling 9, p. 185):

<!-- doc 2300 -->

All fast days shall be kept as hitherto. One shall abstain from eating flesh at the forbidden
times. Sunday, the apostles' days, Our Lady's days, etc., shall be kept holy for the Word's
sake, but yet in the time of harvest, etc., no one's conscience shall be burdened.

The Margrave Philipp of Baden, in his mandate of 1531, still required "the forty days and other
fast days brought down in the common Christian church, together with the Fridays and Saturdays",
with abstinence from meat except in need or bodily weakness (Sehling 16, p. 507). The Colmar
council, still Catholic (the city's Reformation came in 1575), complained in 1560 that the
Lenten fast and "other fast days through the year" were kept with little discretion "among young
and old, sick and healthy" (Sehling's introduction, Sehling 20/2, p. 481).

#### <a id="s12-13-4"></a>12.13.4 Fasting by police order

**Meat days for the price of meat.** Where a magistrate ordered abstinence, the reason given was
economic, and the order says so. The Nordhausen police order of 1549 forbids meat on Fridays,
Saturdays and in Lent because the price of meat was rising. The old, the sick, hard labourers,
young children and women in childbed are exempt. It declares that no one is to think it a sin.
**Nordhausen, *Polizei-Ordnung der Stadt Nordhausen*, 1549** (Sehling 2, p. 396):

<!-- doc 1254 -->

Of eating flesh and of Lent. And whereas we find that the buying of flesh groweth ever more into
great dearness, we will that every one abstain from eating flesh two days in the week, Fridays
and Saturdays, and also in Lent; excepted old [and] sick people, hard labourers, young children,
women in childbed, or those to whom it is allowed at the bidding of the physicians; yet so that
no wantonness or abuse be sought herein. Yet shall this article be understood by no one as
though it were sin and forbidden by God not to eat flesh at the aforesaid time, which is in no
wise meant by us; but we will let all that the Lord God hath left free and without sin to be
used remain free and without sin, and herein have sought and meant nothing else than obedience
and good order, police and moderation.

**The fish market.** Strasbourg's Sunday mandate (1534, Moderate Reformed) lets milk and bread
be sold before the sermon, "and in Lent the fish" (Sehling 20/1, p. 246; [§12.11.2](#s12-11-2)). Lent still
governed the market.

#### <a id="s12-13-5"></a>12.13.5 Days of fasting and prayer

**The new fast day.** In place of the fixed fasts, the orders appoint days of fasting and prayer
(*Buß-*, *Bett-* and *Fasttage*) in times of war, plague, dearth and threat to the church. Some
were monthly, some extraordinary. On them feasting and weddings were stopped, and the people
were called to fasting as well as prayer. The Palatine mandate of 1610 (Reformed), issued as the
Catholic League formed, tells the preachers to teach that "at dangerous, sorrowful times even
permitted joys are to be laid aside". It also tells them to correct the false idea that "with
the popish superstitious fasting the rightful Christian fasting also was done away". **Kurpfalz,
*Mandat zu den Bußtagen*, 1610** (Reformed; Sehling 19/2, p. 971):

<!-- doc 1204 -->

1. How that at dangerous, sorrowful times even the permitted joys are to be laid aside. 2. Of
   the custom of the church of God, to prepare itself by fasting and chastening of the body for
   earnest prayer; wherein the false conceit is to be taken from them, as though with the popish
   superstitious fasting the rightful Christian fasting were also done away.

A Nassau-Weilburg text printed with the order of 1576 makes the monthly prayer days fast days,
on which betrothal feasts, guild banquets and all weddings in the week were stopped
(Sehling 10, p. 239). Hesse (Moderate Reformed) and Schleswig-Holstein ordered prayer days with
fasting in the 1550s and 1560s (Sehling 8, p. 263; 23, p. 270). Kurland mentions extraordinary
"fast days" set by edict in time of war (Sehling 5, p. 92).

**Fasting at the choice of ministers.** The Hessian order of 1566 (Moderate Reformed) and the
Reformed orders follow Acts 13 and 14: the church is to prepare "with fasting and prayer" for
the election of a superintendent or minister. **Micron, *Christliche Ordinancien* (1554; German
edition 1565)** (Reformed; Sehling 7/1, p. 588):

<!-- doc 2116 -->

When the congregation is in need of one minister or more, then, according to the ordinance of
God, a common, certain fast day is appointed by the elders, which day is thereafter proclaimed
from the pulpit to the whole congregation

The Hessian rule (Moderate Reformed) is at Sehling 8, p. 203, and the same provision is in
Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 (Sehling 18, p. 560).

The prayer-day sermons are treated in [Chapter 11](#ch11), [§11.4.5](#s11-4-5), and the
Litany days in [Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.22.4](#s13-22-4).

#### <a id="s12-13-6"></a>12.13.6 Fasting before communion

**Sober for the sacrament.** The one fast the orders still expected regularly was the
communicant's. The Hessian order of 1566 (Moderate Reformed) defends receiving the sacrament
fasting with Augustine: "it hath pleased the Holy Ghost that, in honour of this most worthy
sacrament, the body of the Lord should enter the Christian's mouth before other food"
(Sehling 8, p. 309). The Saxon order of 1580 forbids banquets on the eves of Sundays and feasts,
so that the household might come to the sacrament sober. **Albertine Saxony, *Ordnung* of Duke
August, 1580** (Sehling 1, p. 430):

<!-- doc 44 -->

They shall therefore not only do away with all banquets on the eves of Sundays and high feasts,
but also every householder shall hold his whole household to a sober life, chiefly when they go
to the most worthy sacrament, that they may hear God's word soberly, with delight and devotion,
on the following Sunday or feast day, [and] use the communion worthily

**Who fasted, and how.** The orders give no general fasting rules for clergy or laity. What they
show:
- **Communicants.** Communicants were expected to come fasting and to keep the eve soberly
  ([§12.13.6](#s12-13-6) above).
- **Everyone on prayer days.** The whole congregation was called to fast on the appointed days
  of fasting and prayer, and to give up feasts and weddings ([§12.13.5](#s12-13-5)).
- **Under police orders.** Where the magistrate ordered abstinence for economic reasons, the
  old, the sick, labourers, children and women in childbed were exempt ([§12.13.4](#s12-13-4)).
- **No separate clergy fast.** No order lays a separate fast on the clergy. The monastic fasts
  went with the monastic rules: Württemberg's convent order of 1535 counts the bonds of human
  ordinances "in fasting, silence, confessing, wearing cowls and tonsures" among what is cast
  off (Sehling 16, p. 79).

Confession and communion as a duty of the laity are treated in
[Chapter 15](#ch15), [§15.8.3](#s15-8-3).

---

### <a id="s12-14"></a>12.14 Occurrence and transfer

The medieval rubrics had detailed tables of "occurrence" (two feasts on the same day) and
"concurrence" (the vespers of one feast meeting the first vespers of the next). A feast of
higher grade displaced one of lower grade, which was commemorated or transferred. The Lutheran
orders keep the principle, but apply it to three practical cases:

- a feast that falls on a Sunday;
- the Annunciation in Holy Week;
- a lesser feast that falls on a Saturday, or in the same week as another.

Their rules show how the ranks of [§12.5](#s12-5) were understood: Sunday against feast, feast of Christ
against Passiontide, apostle against working week.

#### <a id="s12-14-1"></a>12.14.1 A feast on a Sunday

The general rule is that a feast of Christ displaces the Sunday Gospel, while an apostles' day
yields to it.

**Rostock, *Conformitas ceremoniarum*, c. 1560** (Sehling 5, p. 288):

<!-- doc 1936 -->

But if great feasts fall on the Sunday, as Christmas, St Stephen, St John the Evangelist, New
Year's, the Three Kings, the Purification of Mary, the Annunciation of Mary, John the Baptist,
the Visitation of Mary and Michaelmas, one shall keep the Gospels of the feasts. […] 7. But when
the apostles' feasts fall on the Sunday, one shall keep the Sunday Gospels, and preach the
Gospels that fall on the apostles' feasts in the afternoon.

**Note.** St Stephen and St John count here as "great feasts", as days of Christmas, while the
apostles do not.

Mansfeld sets out the apostles' days by the day of the week on which they fall. **Mansfeld,
*Kirchen-agenda*, 1580** (Sehling 2, p. 240):

<!-- doc 1241 -->

If an apostle's day fall on a Sunday, it may be kept as it falleth; yet so that in the towns, in
the churches where there is preaching two or three times on Sunday, the Sunday Gospel also be
expounded in one of the same sermons. If an apostle's day fall on a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday,
Thursday or Friday, it may be kept in the towns on the day whereon it falleth, as is customary;
but where it is customary to remove it to the next following day whereon the week-day sermons
are otherwise held, it may abide by that custom. But if an apostle's day fall on a Saturday, it
shall be removed to the next following Sunday, and kept thereon.

**Note.**

- **Wintzingerode.** The order (Sehling 2, p. 256) has the same rules. There the apostle's
  Gospel goes to the Sunday afternoon.
- **Thorn 1575.** Small feasts falling near a Sunday go to its vespers ([§12.5.6](#s12-5-6)).
- **Danzig 1612.** A small feast falling on a Sunday is rung like a great one ([§12.5.6](#s12-5-6)).
- **Nördlingen 1579.** A local thanksgiving day falling on a Sunday is to be kept "solemnly, as other high feasts" (Sehling 12, p. 388).

#### <a id="s12-14-2"></a>12.14.2 The Annunciation in Holy Week

The Annunciation (25 March) often falls between Palm Sunday and Low Sunday. The orders count it
as a feast of Christ. It cannot simply be dropped, and it may not displace the Passion and
Easter. The orders give at least six solutions:

| Solution | Orders |
|---|---|
| The Saturday before Palm Sunday (*Palmabend*) | Hadersleben 1528; Schleswig-Holstein 1542; Merseburg 1544; Anhalt 1568; Pomerania 1569; Sayn 1582 |
| Palm Sunday itself, in the forenoon | Aschersleben 1575; Schwarzburg 1587; Wintzingerode (only if it falls Wednesday to Saturday, "per anticipationem" [by anticipation]) |
| A weekday of the week before Palm Sunday | Waldeck 1556 (Wednesday after Judica); Hoya 1571 and Harlingerland 1573/74 (Thursday after Judica) |
| The Sunday after Easter ("according to old custom") | Prussia 1526, 1544 and 1568 |
| Maundy Thursday | Burzenland chapter, 1573 (a proposal of the dean for that year) |
| Omitted that year | Ysenburg 1582 |
| A convenient day agreed with the neighbouring churches | Thorn 1575 |

**Hadersleben, *Artikel*, 1528** (Sehling 23, p. 64):

<!-- doc 1576 -->

Our Lady's Annunciation day (and when it falleth on Maundy Thursday or thereafter, it shall be
kept with one accord on the Saturday before Palm Sunday; otherwise it shall not be transferred)

**Merseburg, *Synodalunterricht*, 1544** (Sehling 2, p. 20):

<!-- doc 1211 -->

But as touching the removing of the feasts: that the Annunciation of Mary, if it should fall in
the week of the Passion, be laid on the eve of Palm Sunday. The removing of the other feasts
shall be determined by the consistory, and shown to the parsons in the synods by the
superintendent.

**Pomerania, *Agenda*, 1569** (Sehling 4, p. 469):

<!-- doc 1865 -->

When the day of the Annunciation of Mary falleth in the still week, be it what day it be, one
shall lay the feast on the eve of Palm Sunday, and bid the same beforehand on the Sunday Judica.

**Wintzingerode (Gericht Bodenstein), *Kirchen-Ordnung*** (Sehling 2, p. 256):

<!-- doc 1243 -->

If the feast of the Annunciation of Mary fall in the week of the Passion on a Monday or Tuesday,
it shall be kept on the same. But if it fall on the Wednesday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday or
Easter Eve, one shall keep it holy (as the ancients call it) *per anticipationem*, back upon
Palm Sunday.

**Note.** *Per anticipationem* (By anticipation) is the old term for moving a feast back, before its date. "As the
ancients call it" shows that the orders knew they were using the medieval rules of transfer.

**Schwarzburg, *Ordnung der fest und feiertage*, 1587** (Sehling 2, p. 137):

<!-- doc 1230 -->

But if the feast of the Annunciation, as sometimes happeneth, fell in the week of the Passion,
it shall be laid on Palm Sunday and kept solemnly in the forenoon, but the Gospel of the same
Sunday be preached in the afternoon

**Waldeck, *Kirchenordnung*, 1556** (Sehling 9, p. 272):

<!-- doc 2300 -->

But this feast shall be kept (to avoid offensive inequality) on the Wednesday after Judica, when
it falleth on Palm Sunday or in Palm week; otherwise it shall be kept on the day whereon it
cometh

**Prussia, *Kirchenordnung und Ceremonien*, 1568** (Sehling 4, p. 87):

<!-- doc 1833 -->

When the day of the Conception of Christ or the Annunciation of Mary falleth on Palm Sunday, or
in the week before Easter, or in the same following week in the Easter days, it shall be kept on
the next Sunday after Easter, and be transferred according to the former church order; that the
same time may be preached, without hindrance and as need requireth, of the riding in of the Lord
Christ and his holy Passion, together with the history of the resurrection.

**Note.** The rule goes back to the Prussian order of 1526 (Sehling 4, p. 38). That order keeps
the day after Easter "according to old custom", after the old custom, which is the medieval
practice of transferring the Annunciation to the week after Low Sunday.

In 1573 Easter fell on 22 March, so the Annunciation fell on the Wednesday after Easter. The
dean of the Burzenland chapter writes. **Burzenland chapter (Transylvania), resolutions of 25
February 1573** (Sehling 24, p. 371):

<!-- doc 1694 -->

6. In the old reckoning of the Church the feast of the Annunciation of Mary, or Conception of
   Christ, is assigned to the 25th of March, which falleth on the Wednesday after Christ's
