  almoners", elected per 1 Timothy 3:8. They collect the alms on Sundays and distribute them,
  and are confirmed "with the knowledge and will of the pastors and appointed seniors". No
  laying on of hands is mentioned. **Bentheim-Tecklenburg, *Bentheim-Tecklenburger
  Kirchenordnung*, 1588/1619** (Reformed; Sehling 22, p. 276):

<!-- doc 1508 -->

[…] pious and godly men, whom men call Deacons or Almoners, be chosen, and confirmed with the
knowledge and will of the Pastors and the appointed Seniors, according to the doctrine and use
of the holy Apostles […]

- **Nassau-Dillenburg (1582)** (Reformed). Here the deacon is the fourth of four offices: ministers,
  doctors, seniors and deacons. The presbytery elects the seniors, the deacons of the poor and
  the sextons (*aeditui*), and the classis confirms them. The minister alone receives
  "confirmation or ordination". **Nassau-Dillenburg, *Kirchenordnung*, 23 January 1582**
  (Reformed; Sehling 10, p. 160):

<!-- doc 184 -->

The offices are fourfold: some of ministers, some of doctors, some of seniors, some of deacons.
[…] 4. Let the calling of ministers be made by the judgement of the classis and of some seniors;
whereunto pertain these four: election, examination, approbation, and confirmation or
ordination. […] 5. As touching the choosing of seniors, deacons of the poor and sextons, let the
power of choosing be with the presbytery; who afterward shall be confirmed by the vote of the
classical assembly and be diligently admonished of [their] office.

**The Bohemian Brethren** (Hussite). Their deacon is something else: an ordained **clerical**
grade between acolyte and minister. The deacons are "older acolytes", preparing for the
ministry. The order defends the grade as kept "constantly in the primitive church", which must
not be cast out though Antichrist abused it. **Bohemian Brethren, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1576**
(Hussite; Sehling 4, p. 276):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

Deacons are the older acolytes, now presently preparing themselves for the future ministry.
These the ministers of the brethren have for assistants or helpers, after the example of the
apostles, Acts 6:2 and Philippians 1:1. For although they were ordained by the apostles
primarily to the ministry of tables, yet it is certain that they both preached and baptised (as
Stephen, Acts 6:10, and Philip, Acts 8:5, 12, 35, 38) and were promoted to a higher grade,
namely of the ministry or presbytery, 1 Timothy 3:13. Therefore this grade of the diaconate was
constantly kept in the primitive church, as appeareth from the canons of the councils. Which
therefore, although it hath been drawn into abuse by the antichrist with the rest, it is not
fitting to cast out of the church.

What the Brethren's deacons did (same page):
- study theology;
- teach the young the rudiments;
- practise preaching;
- baptise "as often as the pastor shall command".

At a crowded communion they help distribute both the bread and the cup, but with one limit: only
a minister "having the power of the keys" pronounces the absolution and recites the words of
institution. **Bohemian Brethren, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1576** (Hussite; Sehling 4, p. 276):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

As often as the holy supper is administered in a more numerous assembly, and sufficient
ministers are not present, the deacons also are employed to distribute not only the cup but also
the bread; yet so that none but a minister having the power of the keys announce the absolution
to the people and solemnly set forth before the words of institution.

They are ordained before the synod, with an examination by the seniors, a vow, prayer and the
**laying on of hands**, "Acts 6:6". **Bohemian Brethren, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1576,
"Ordination of deacons"** (Hussite; Sehling 4, p. 279):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

3. They bind themselves to Christ and the church by a vow. 4. Prayers are made for them, and the
   ordainer confirmeth them by the laying on of hands, Acts 6:6. 5. The new deacons offer to the
   seniors and ministers the right hand of holy obedience; and the former deacons [offer] to
   them [the right hand] of fellowship. 6. The act is closed with a blessing.

#### <a id="s16-5-4"></a>16.5.4 Divine right or human right?

**The question as the church orders put it.** No order asks whether the diaconate is a separate
*order* by divine right in the Roman sense. The orders ask two other questions:
1. Is there one ministry of the word, of which bishop, pastor and deacon are grades?
2. Is the deacon of the poor a lasting institution of the apostles?

**One ministry; grades by human right.** The orders consistently say that bishop, presbyter and
pastor are one office:
- Homberg 1526 (Moderate Reformed): "bishops, or presbyters" ([§16.3.2](#s16-3-2)).
- Bugenhagen 1528: "bishops or preachers (which is all one thing)" ([§16.5.2](#s16-5-2)).
- Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1539. It describes the ancient Church as installing a minister "by one or
  two of the nearest bishops, whom men also call pastors". It says that it now has "certain of
  the nearest pastors or elders" lay hands on the new minister. **Pfalz-Zweibrücken,
  *Kirchenordnung „Form und Ordnung“*, 1539** (Sehling 18, p. 63):

<!-- doc 965 -->

[…] that the congregation chose one, who was set in office and confirmed by one or two of the
nearest bishops, whom men also call pastors or parsons. […] Those then which were found apt for
this office in doctrine and life, upon them have certain of the nearest pastors or elders in the
congregation of God, as aforesaid, laid hands upon the head, and prayed that the Holy Ghost
would enlighten and preserve the ministers of the word in christian doctrine and life.

Where distinctions within the ministry are defended, they are defended as **human order for the
sake of good order**. Melanchthon's *Wittenberg Reformation* (1545) keeps bishops "as a grade
above other priests" so that, "so far as human foresight can consider", there may be a lasting
order. **Ernestine Saxony, *Wittenbergische Reformation*, 1545** (Sehling 1, p. 217):

<!-- doc 20 -->

[…] among these curates of souls there must nevertheless be an order; they have not all like
gifts, they cannot all be judges in weighty articles of doctrine; they cannot all order and hold
the courts. […] and the same places must be so provided with persons and maintenance that there
be, so far as human foresight can consider, a lasting order. Therefore must there be bishops, as
a grade above other priests […]

The same text sets "divine and eternal right" apart from "human, transitory ordinance of things
indifferent" (Sehling 1, p. 218). The Lutheran *Diaconus* (deacon), the *Subdiaconus* and the
superintendent all stand on the second footing. Electoral Saxony can therefore dispense a
candidate from the diaconate altogether ([§16.5.1](#s16-5-1)). Its ordination rite also calls the laying on of
hands a ceremony of "christian liberty", while it calls the ministry itself a "divine command
and ordinance".

**The deacon of the poor as apostolic.** The lay deacon of the poor is, by contrast, defended as
apostolic in origin:
- **Homberg** (1526, Moderate Reformed; [§16.3.2](#s16-3-2)) knows only "bishops, or presbyters, and deacons of
  the poor".
- **Strasbourg** (1539, Moderate Reformed; [§16.3.1](#s16-3-1)) says the deacon alone of the lower grades was
  instituted "by the Holy Ghost through the Apostles". Its list of the three ministries that
  every church needs "even today" includes "the care of the poor".
- **Hesse 1566** (Moderate Reformed) and **Micron** (Reformed) cite Acts 6 and 1 Timothy 3. They
  say the Holy Ghost "himself hath shewed" what men should be chosen, and they ordain deacons as
  the apostles did.
- **The Bohemian Brethren** (Hussite) hold that the diaconate "was constantly kept in the
  primitive church" and must not be cast out. In practice, though, they treat it as a
  probationary step towards the presbyterate.

Of Bugenhagen, the editors of the Hildesheim volume write
(Sehling 7/2.1, p. 811, editor's introduction):

<!-- doc 2132 -->

It is noteworthy that Bugenhagen, in his Schleswig-Holstein church order of 1542 and in his
Wolfenbüttel church order of 1543, reckoneth the maintenance of the ministers of church and
school, and also of the poor, to the divine order, over against which he setteth the human
order. From this, by its function, the office of deacon must accordingly be of divine right. It
standeth in the divine order of right beside the office of preaching!

**Lay deacons.** In this sense **every** Lutheran deacon of the common chest, and every Reformed
deacon, was a **lay deacon**. He was a man who kept his trade and served a term, elected by
council and congregation or by the presbytery, and he had no part in preaching or the
sacraments. The Lutheran *Diaconus*, by contrast, was never a layman. The Bohemian deacon was a
cleric in training.

---

### <a id="s16-6"></a>16.6 Elders

**Two kinds of elders.** Almost every order that speaks of governing elders starts from 1
Timothy 5:17, "the elders that rule well […] especially they who labour in the word and
doctrine". From that verse it distinguishes two kinds of elder (*presbyter*, *senior*,
*Eltester*):
- those who **labour in the word**: the ministers;
- those who **only govern**: the lay elders.

**Lineage.** The lay elder came into the German orders through Bucer, at Strasbourg and in Hesse
(both Moderate Reformed). It was then generalised in the Reformed orders of East Frisia,
Kurpfalz, Nassau and the Wetterau counties.

**In the Lutheran orders** "elder" is either a churchwarden without spiritual jurisdiction or a
senior pastor ([§16.6.5](#s16-6-5)).

#### <a id="s16-6-1"></a>16.6.1 Strasbourg: the disciplinary *seniores*

The Strasbourg examination order of about 1539 (Moderate Reformed) already speaks of a second
"order of presbyters", those "employed only for the discipline of the church" ([§16.3.1](#s16-3-1)). Its
authority is twofold:
- the elders of the synagogue;
- Ambrose on 1 Timothy 5. Ambrose complains that such elders had lapsed through "the sloth or
  rather the pride of the teachers, who alone wish to seem something".

Marbach's Lutheran church order of 1553 identifies the city's *Kirchenpfleger* (churchwardens) with those
*seniores*. They are elected to oversee the "whole householding of the church", which the
preachers cannot manage alone. It reads the "church" of Matthew 18 as these elected men, not the
whole assembly. **Strasbourg, *Kirchenordnung* of Johannes Marbach, 1553, "Of the churchwardens and their office"** (Sehling 20/1, p. 441):

<!-- doc 1321 -->

Out of the Acts of the Apostles it is to be seen that in the first christian church, beside the
apostles which preached the gospel, certain were chosen and ordained thereto by the
congregation, which should have a special oversight, that everywhere house might be rightly
kept, that none might neglect to live godly according to his calling, and so good order be kept
in the church as in the house of God; whom they named seniores and presbyteri. […] Therefore the
Lord Christ, Matthew 18[:15–18], biddeth that the impenitent and obstinate be told to the church, that
they may be rebuked by it and admonished to true conversion. But by the church the Lord
understandeth not the whole congregation as it cometh together to hear the word, but those which
in orderly wise are chosen and given thereto by such assembly, to treat in the name and on
behalf of the church all manner of church matters that fall out […]

#### <a id="s16-6-2"></a>16.6.2 Hesse: elders elected, "sanctified" and finally ordained

**The Ziegenhain discipline order (1539)** (Moderate Reformed), written under Bucer's influence,
introduces elders into every Hessian congregation. They are chosen by the church "according to
the canon of Paul", as the ministers are. It would be good, the order says, to confirm them
publicly "with prayer and exhortation" and so to "sanctify their office". The civil authority is
to uphold their office as the most necessary "after the office of teaching". **Hesse,
*Ziegenhainer Zuchtordnung*, 1539** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 103):

<!-- doc 2252 -->

These elders shall every church choose, as also the ministers of the word, with faithful regard
to the canon of Paul. And it were good also that they should be confirmed in the church with
public prayer and exhortation (to them, the elders, to attend diligently to their office; to the
congregation, to obey the same elders heartily in the Lord), and their office so be sanctified.
Whose office and service the magistracy also shall faithfully exalt and uphold, as the most
necessary and wholesome service and office that may be in the church after the office of
teaching.

**The Hessian church order of 1566** (Moderate Reformed) makes the elders a permanent college in
every parish. The superintendent's instructions open with this (Sehling 8, p. 195):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

The first is, that in all churches of your district seniors, that is, elders, be chosen and
ordained, which may be helpful both to you in this place and to the other pastors in their
churches with counsel and deed and all their power; with whom ye may also take counsel of all
matters which fall out in the government of the church, and advisedly treat of all things with
all speed. Thereof saith Luke thus (Acts 14:23): They ordained elders here and there in the
congregation, prayed and fasted, and commended them to the Lord on whom they believed.

**Election and qualifications.** The order appeals to Ambrose for the antiquity of the office.
The ministers, together with men of the council and the congregation, elect the elders by vote
(Acts 14:23). The elders must be of the same zeal and life as preachers, "only that they need
not be so excellently learned". **Hesse, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566, "How the elders shall be chosen and ordained for the government of the church"** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 207):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

Therefore in every church the ministers of the same congregation, together with certain
appointed thereto both from the council and from the congregation, shall choose these elders. Of
the form and manner of the election it is found in Acts 14 that it was done commonly by
suffrages and voices. But to this office one must choose and have even such people, so far as
concerneth zeal and life, as for the office of preaching; save only that they need not be so
excellently learned.

**Their charge.** The ordination address sets the elders "beside the bishops", placed by the
Holy Ghost to rule the church. They are to assist the ministers as councillors assist a
burgomaster. Above all they are to guard against falsification of doctrine, whether by the
public preachers or by "false teachers and wolves". **Hesse, *Kirchenordnung*, 1566**
(Moderate Reformed; Sehling 8, p. 208):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

Ye have heard, my beloved in the Lord, that beside the bishops elders also are set by the Holy
Ghost for the government of the church of God. Therefore it will behove you that ye take
especial great care and be diligent how the church may be well ruled, and that ye be furthersome
in all things to the other ministers which labour in the word with faithful counsel and help,
even as valiant and wise councillors also behave themselves toward the burgomaster where a good
order is to be set up in the common weal. (1) But above all things ye shall, together with the
other ministers of the church, with highest diligence prevent that no falsifying of doctrine be
brought in, whether by those which preach publicly in the church, or by false teachers and
wolves which secretly creep in beside and will craftily deceive […]

**Ordination.** After the prayer the pastor and the other ministers lay hands on the elders, "as
also before said", using the rite of the ministers' ordination (Sehling 8, p. 209):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

Thereafter shall the pastor and the other ministers lay their hands upon them, as is also said
before, etc. (9) After all this, the ordinands shall be set in the midst, and the church
committed to them to care for and to govern with such words: So we commit unto you this church,
in which ye have been chosen to be elders […]

**Elders at the ordination of ministers.** The traffic also runs the other way. At the
ordination of a new minister of the word, the elders lay on hands with the superintendent and
the ministers (Sehling 8, p. 205):

<!-- doc 2257 -->

After the prayer the superintendent, together with the other ministers of the word and elders,
shall lay hands upon the ordinands […]

The editor of the Hessian volume notes that Johannes a Lasco (Reformed) also knew an ordination
of the governing elders and of the deacons (Sehling 8, p. 208, note 97).

#### <a id="s16-6-3"></a>16.6.3 The Reformed orders: four offices, elders who govern with the ministers

**Micron's *Ordinancien*** (London 1554, printed for Norden 1565; Reformed) gives the classic
Reformed account. There are two "kinds" (*geschlechte*) of elders. Some labour in word and
doctrine, and are called bishops, shepherds and teachers. Others "minister not the public
service of the word and sacraments", but are helpers of the ministers. Paul calls these
"governments" (1 Corinthians 12:28). One of the elders presides, and the king's charter calls
him the superintendent. **Micron, *Ordinancien* (1554) 1565** (Reformed; Sehling 7/1, pp. 587–588):

<!-- doc 2116 -->

[…] and the other elders, although they minister not the public service of the word and of the
sacraments, yet are they helpers of the other ministers, and stand by them with all earnestness,
with counsel and help, that the congregation of God may be ruled and preserved in all godliness,
holiness, peace, order and honesty according to the word of God; wherefore they are also called
by Paul governments. Among these two kinds of elders one out of their number is the chief,
orderly chosen thereto, that by his authority an accordant agreement may be held among all in
all things according to the word of God. And he is called by the king's majesty in their
privilege superintendent, that is, overseer. But the deacons take care for the poor of the
congregation.

The elders are confirmed after questions and prayer by **laying on of hands**, "by the other
ministers and by the minister of the word" (Reformed; Sehling 7/1, p. 596). The words are nearly those
later used in Kurpfalz, given below.

**Kurpfalz** (Reformed). The elders of the Electoral Palatinate were set up by the edict of
1570, after the dispute with Erastus. Sehling's editors describe that dispute in their
introduction (Sehling 14, p. 53, editors' introduction):

<!-- doc 468 -->

What was in dispute was not the exercise of discipline as such, but the question by whom, in
what cases and in what manner it was to be handled. The advocates of the Calvinist church
discipline stood on the line of the Catechism and the church order, and underlined the divine
right of the presbyteries, the necessity of exclusion from the supper of false teachers and of
sinners unwilling to amend, by this [presbytery], and in principle the sharp separation of a
temporal and an ecclesiastical power of punishment.

The decision fell in 1569, with opinions by Beza, Ursinus and Zanchi against Erastus. On 13 July
1570 the edict set up church discipline and the classical assemblies. The editors add that
Erastus still won concessions, including the involvement of the magistrate in excommunication
(same page).

Under Frederick IV a new form for installing the elders was issued, dated 9 December 1592; the
editors say the new elders were installed at the end of the New Year's service. Its title is
"Form, how the elders which labour not in the word are confirmed in the congregation". The
elders are questioned:
- whether they feel the witness of the Spirit;
- whether Scripture contains all that is needful to salvation;
- whether they will assist the ministers and accept correction themselves.

The congregation prays, and then hands are laid on them. **Kurpfalz, *Einführung der Senioren*,
9 December 1592** (Reformed; Sehling 19/2, pp. 789–790):

<!-- doc 1155 -->

Form, how the elders which labour not in the word are confirmed in the congregation, etc. […]
Thereafter hands are laid upon them by the other ministers and by the minister of the word, who
speaketh with a clear voice thus: God and our heavenly Father, which hath called and separated
you with us to the government of this his congregation (according to the doctrine of his word),
enlighten you also by his Holy Spirit and strengthen you with the power of his invincible hand,
that ye may fulfil your service faithfully and constantly, to the honour of his name and the
edifying of his congregation. Amen. […] Lastly he turneth his speech to the elders received, and
admonisheth them that they regard not the contempt and hatred of the world, respect no person,
but that they admonish, amend and rebuke every one without respect of person according to the
use of christian rebuke; that they also take earnest heed to the doctrine, manners, yea, to the
whole life of all ministers of the word; [and] ward off the wolves from the flock of the
congregation together with the ministers of the word […]

The editors of the volume stress the point: "it is especially noteworthy that they are
**ordained by laying on of hands** by the minister of the church and the individual elders
continuing in office" (Sehling 19/2, p. 695, editors' introduction). The same form was adopted
in Ysenburg-Ronneburg in 1592 (Reformed) (Sehling 10, p. 601).

**Kurpfalz about 1601** (Reformed). The Palatine *Presbyterordnung* of about 1601 defines the
presbytery as "certain persons chosen yearly" beside the ministers, "as elders and overseers",
to deal with offences in doctrine and life. Their sanctions:
- admonition, once, twice and three times;
- for the obstinate, being "quietly" warned off the sacraments.

The order grounds the office on Christ's own institution in Matthew 18. **Kurpfalz,
*Presbyterordnung*, about 1601** (Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 595):

<!-- doc 518 -->

[…] that by the presbytery or council of elders nothing else is to be understood than this: that
beside the ministers of the church in every place certain particular persons are chosen yearly
to be elders and overseers of the christian congregation, which in the stead of the whole
congregation come together at certain times, as need requireth, and confer together how the
offences which arise in doctrine and life in the congregation may be amended and done away; and
also make admonitions out of the word of God, according to the order of the Lord Christ, the
first, second and third time […] and, if one would wilfully continue in open sins and offence,
warn him off from the holy sacraments quietly, with christian discretion, until he promise and
shew amendment. Now that this order is grounded in God's word, and that Christ himself hath
ordained and commanded it, the following sayings of holy scripture clearly shew.

These elders take a handfast vow (*angeloben*) to the published order. They are "confirmed" and
announced from the pulpit on New Year's Day, then "confirmed through the common christian
prayer". There is no laying on of hands. **Kurpfalz, *Presbyterordnung*, about 1601**
(Reformed; Sehling 14, p. 598):

<!-- doc 518 -->

[…] thou shalt cause them to vow by handfast, and so confirm them and receive them under
obligation. Afterward they shall be proclaimed to the congregation from the pulpit on New Year's
day, and confirmed through the christian common prayer, with diligent admonition that every man
acknowledge them for orderly elders and governors of the congregation, hold them in due honour,
and render them obedience.

**Hanau-Münzenberg (1609)** (Reformed) copies this procedure. It adds that the minister must
teach the congregation "that the office of elders is of God". This is said partly to comfort the
elders, partly so that the people will not "exempt themselves" from their rebukes.
**Hanau-Münzenberg, *Presbyteriumsordnung*, 1609** (Reformed; Sehling 10, p. 508):

<!-- doc 211 -->

[…] shall be taken under handfast vow. Whereupon on the following Sunday after a short sermon
the elders shall be proclaimed again to the congregation, and so, after diligent admonition made
that every man acknowledge them for orderly elders and governors of the congregation, hold them
in due honour and render them obedience, be confirmed through the christian common prayer. But
at such proclamation and confirmation it is needful that the minister of the church shew the
congregation plainly out of the word of God, 1. that the office of elders is of God, from the
testimonies of holy scripture set down above: for the elders' good, that they may take such
office upon them as a divine calling […]; next, for the congregation's sake, that they set not
themselves against such office nor exempt themselves from it […]

**Pfalz-Veldenz (1574)** calls its elders "censors". They are presented to the assembled
congregation, "commended" from the pulpit with prayer and "set into this high office", "as we
see that the apostles ordained the Elders and commended them to the congregation, Acts 14;
likewise also the Deacons, Acts 6". **Pfalz-Veldenz, *Kirchenordnung*, 1574, "Order of the elders"** (Sehling 18, p. 573):

<!-- doc 1011 -->

Those which are chosen to this high office shall thereafter, upon a set day when the
congregation is assembled together (which also shall be admonished to appear diligently and to
call upon God), be called and set before the congregation, and so publicly with prayer from the
pulpit by the Pastor be commended to the whole Congregation and set into this high office […]
even as we see that the apostles ordained the Elders and commended them to the congregation,
Acts 14; likewise also the Deacons, Acts 6.

**Solms (1594)** (Reformed), in the discipline order of Count Johann Albrecht of
Solms-Braunfels, binds its elders by an **oath**, "so help us God and his only Son", to watch
over all offence and idolatry. They are to admonish offenders and, if admonition fails, report
them to the proper authority. **Solms, *Kirchenzuchtordnung*, 1594, "The elders' oath"**
(Reformed; Sehling 9, p. 338):

<!-- doc 2311 -->

We swear and vow that, according to the tenor of our high office, we will have diligent
oversight upon all offensive dealing in the church, all idolatry, blasphemy, levity and other
things which strive against the honour of God and the holy gospel; that we will hinder the same
so far as is possible for us, and admonish the transgressors, howsoever the occasion may be, to
a better life; but if such admonition will not profit, that without envy, hatred, friendship
[or] enmity we will bring such impenitent dealing to the proper place, and from thence await
help, counsel and support […] so help us God and his only Son.

Similar sworn **censors** are found in the **Wild- and Rhinegraviate** (1603). They are chosen
by the pastor and the old censors and confirmed "under oath" by the superintendent and officials
(Sehling 19/2, p. 600).

**Nassau-Dillenburg (1582)** (Reformed) counts the seniors as the third of the four offices.
They are elected by the presbytery and confirmed by the classis ([§16.5.3](#s16-5-3)).

#### <a id="s16-6-4"></a>16.6.4 The Bohemian Brethren: lay presbyters and *presbyterae*

The Bohemian Brethren (Hussite) have lay *presbyteri politici*. These are "political presbyters" or
"censors of manners", who oversee the life of the congregation and sit in a place of honour in
church. The men of the congregation elect them by free vote after a visitor's admonition. They
bind themselves "by voice and by hand given" to the bishops, the pastor and the church. The same
is done for the **women elders** (*presbyterae*), with only women present. There is **no laying
on of hands**. **Bohemian Brethren, *Ordo ecclesiasticus*, 1576, "Presbyterorum politicorum
ordinatio"** (Bohemian Brethren; Sehling 4, p. 289):

<!-- doc 1846 -->

The ordination of presbyters, when there is need, is performed with this rite. All the men are
bidden to present themselves early before the evening sermon; and there, an admonition having
first been given by the visitors, they choose by free votes those whom they judge worthy of that
office. Those therefore which are designated by the most votes are called forth by the visitor
when the evening sermon is ended, and the duties of this office are read to them (the whole
assembly hearkening); and they bind their faith and diligence by voice and by hand given to the
bishops of the unity, to the pastor, and to their church. And that they may also discharge the
office of overseers in the church, they are honoured with a peculiar place of sitting (for the
more convenient view of the people). The like is done when presbyteresses are chosen, except
that the matter is performed with the female sex alone present.

Like the acolytes ([§16.3.4](#s16-3-4)), these presbyters are said to be "ordained", but by a handfast vow
alone. This sets them clearly apart from the deacons and ministers, on whom hands are laid
([§16.5.3](#s16-5-3)).

#### <a id="s16-6-5"></a>16.6.5 The Lutheran orders: churchwardens and clerical seniors

**Churchwardens.** In the Lutheran orders the lay officers of the parish are the churchwardens,
called *Kirchenväter* (churchwardens), *Kirchgeschworene* (church jurors), *Kastenherren* (chest-wardens) or *Kirchenpfleger* (churchwardens). They administer
church goods, buildings and alms, often with the council. They are not given spiritual
jurisdiction. Memmingen's discipline order (1532, Moderate Reformed) does give its
*Kirchenpfleger* a wide advisory role over worship, schools, alms and the ban. But it expressly
denies them any temporal jurisdiction, "so that two temporal authorities arise not again in our
city". **Memmingen, *Zuchtordnung*, 1532** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 12, p. 248):

<!-- doc 365 -->

For we give such churchwardens no temporal jurisdiction in our city, neither think to give [any]
hereafter, to the end that two temporal authorities arise not again in our city […]

Dinkelsbühl's twelve *Kirchenpfleger* fill their own vacancies "together with the pastor, who
shall bring the Bible or the church order with him" (*Kirchenpflegeordnung*, 1574; Sehling 12,
p. 131). In Augsburg the *Vergleichsartikel* of 1591 provide six *Kirchenpfleger* of the
Augsburg Confession: three appointed by the council and three chosen by the evangelical
citizens. They take part in the examination of new ministers (Sehling 12, pp. 109–110). The
orders give no rite of installation for any of these wardens.

**Clerical seniors.** Where Lutheran orders speak of *seniores*, they usually mean **senior
clergy**:
- In Brandenburg-Ansbach each dean, with the counsel of the whole chapter, chooses "two seniors,
  the fittest among all his subordinates", as assessors and definitors. They administer the
  superintendency in a vacancy and join him in visitation (*Kapitelsordnung*, 1565/78; Sehling
  11, pp. 347, 350).
- Pomerania and the Silesian duchies (Liegnitz) use *seniores* in the same sense. The Pomeranian
  synod of 1574 bids the younger ministers honour the *seniores*, and has the superintendent
  punish unruly ministers with the counsel of the provosts and seniors (Sehling 4, p. 489).

**"Elders" meaning the pastors.** The ordination rite of the Erbach church order (1560) reads
Titus 1:5 of the pastors themselves. Christ commanded his apostles "to choose and set elders in
all his congregations, which shall preach his gospel pure and unfalsified, dispense the most
worthy sacraments, and diligently provide and perform all cure of souls and shepherd's service".
**Erbach, *Erbacher Kirchenordnung*, 1560, ordination rite** (Sehling 9, p. 446):

<!-- doc 2316 -->

[…] and also commanded his own through his Apostles to choose and set Elders in all his
congregations, which shall preach his Gospel pure and unfalsified, dispense the most worthy
Sacraments, and diligently provide and perform all cure of souls and shepherd's service.

**No ruling elders in the Lutheran orders.** In short, a Lutheran order that speaks of "elders"
is speaking of the pastors, of the senior pastors, or of the churchwardens. The **ruling elder**
with a share in the power of the keys belongs to the Bucerian and Hessian (Moderate Reformed)
and the Reformed orders.

The oaths of churchwardens and stewards are treated in
[Chapter 13](#ch13), [§13.12.4](#s13-12-4).

---

### <a id="s16-7"></a>16.7 Sacristans, altar care, deaconesses and the religious life

This section treats six groups that stood beside the clergy without being clergy:
- the **sacristan**, who kept the vessels, vestments and font ([§16.7.1](#s16-7-1));
- the people who cared for the **altar**, the nearest thing in the corpus to an altar guild
  ([§16.7.2](#s16-7-2));
- **deaconesses** and the women who served the sick ([§16.7.3](#s16-7-3));
- **monks** ([§16.7.4](#s16-7-4)) and **nuns** ([§16.7.5](#s16-7-5));
- **beguines**, **tertiaries**, the **Brethren of the Common Life** and the lay
  **confraternities** ([§16.7.6](#s16-7-6)).

How each of them was received or installed is set out with the full forms in
[Chapter 13](#ch13) §§[13.12.2](#s13-12-2) and [13.12.6](#s13-12-6)–[13.12.10](#s13-12-10), and
summarised in the table of [§16.8](#s16-8) below.

#### <a id="s16-7-1"></a>16.7.1 Sacristans

**No separate office.** No evangelical order has a sacristan distinct from the sexton. The
medieval sacristan (*sacrista*, *custos*, *Sigrist* [sexton], *Mesner* [sexton]) and the bell-ringer, sweeper and
doorkeeper were one lay servant, called *Küster* (sexton), *Custos*, *Kirchner*, *Glöckner* (bell-ringer), *Opfermann* (sexton),
*Mesner* or *Sigrist* according to region. The porter's keys passed to him ([§16.3.5](#s16-3-5)). So did the
sacristan's charge: the chalices, the vestments and linen, the font and its water, the bread and
wine, and the lights. In most villages he was also the schoolmaster.

**Anhalt 1594: the sacristan's duties** (Philippist). The appointment of the sexton of Törten in
Anhalt is printed by Sehling as a "sexton's ordinance". It lists the sacristan's work with the
rest: ringing, singing, opening and shutting the church, sweeping, "preparing the altar and
font", and "vesting and unvesting the pastor". The post was granted for one year at a time.
**Anhalt, *Ordnung für den Küster zu Törten*, 8 November 1594**
(Philippist; Sehling 2, pp. 579–580):

<!-- doc 1262 -->

The sexton shall not only perform in general, with highest and faithful diligence, all that
pertaineth and belongeth to him in ringing, singing, opening and shutting the church, sweeping,
preparing the altar and font, [and] vesting and unvesting the pastor, nothing excepted; but also
in particular every day in the week, as is customary in schools, before and after noon, two
hours each time […] keep school for boys and maidens (the harvest excepted) […] all on pain of
losing the service, which shall be promised to every sexton for one year only; and he shall be
bound, shortly before Michaelmas, to sue anew for it with the pastor.

**The keeper of the vessels.** Because the vessels and vestments were in his keeping, the sexton
had to be of known honesty or give surety. **Sayn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1590**
(Sehling 19/1, p. 438):

<!-- doc 1090 -->

Forasmuch also as the chalices, the church's ornaments and other things which are to be kept in
the church are entrusted to the bell-ringers, none shall be received as bell-ringer unless he be
well known or have a warrantor or surety; that if anything be taken away from the church through
his negligence or unfaithfulness, the church may recover the loss suffered again from him.

The Heidelberg bell-ringer of 1572 (Reformed) likewise received "the cloths, silver and vessels
for the Supper and baptism" by inventory
([Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.12.2](#s13-12-2)).

**At the altar and the font.** The sacristan's liturgical tasks recur across the orders:
- **The sick.** In Hohenlohe the pastor called to the sick takes "with him, together with his
  sexton, the particles, chalice, corporal, surplice" (Sehling 15, p. 73). Württemberg's
  German-school order of 1559 bids schoolmasters who also held the *Meßnerei* (sexton's office) go with the pastor
  to the sick "and carry the chalice" (Sehling 17/1, p. 585).
- **The font.** The Lippe sexton was to "fill the font often with clean, fresh water"
  (Sehling 21, p. 447). Baden in 1601 told the *Sigristen* to bring fresh water, "yet not too
  cold", and not to let it stand for weeks in the font (Sehling 16, p. 551).
- **Bread and wine.** Veit Dietrich forbade pastors to set hosts and wine on the altar without
  measure and leave the rest "to the sexton for his use at home" (Sehling 11, p. 531). In the
  Schönburg lordships in 1542 the sexton was no longer to buy the communion wine with his own
  money; the church was to pay and he to fetch it (Sehling 2, p. 176).

**Not women.** At Heilbronn in 1543 the council reserved the sacristan's office at the font to
the sexton, and forbade it to women and maids, lest "the holy act of baptism be mocked by wicked
people". **Heilbronn, *Kirchenordnung*, 1543** (Sehling 17/1, p. 315):

<!-- doc 781 -->

Moreover an honourable, wise [and] provident council will have it that the sextons, and not
women or maids, open and shut the font, or reach the towel to the pastor [and] his deacon to dry
the hands; but he shall do it himself, that the holy act of baptism be not mocked by wicked
people.

**The old abuses.** The sacristan's access to the font water and the hosts made him suspect of
the old "sorcery". Electoral Saxony in 1580, copied by Brandenburg-Ansbach in 1594
(Sehling 11, p. 391), ordered the pastors to stop it. **Electoral Saxony, *Kirchenordnung* of
Elector August, 1580** (Sehling 1, p. 426):

<!-- doc 44 -->

Forasmuch as in some places there yet remaineth of the papistical sorcery, that the bell-ringers
sell the baptismal water left over, as also some deal in the hosts left over, which are
afterward used for sorcery, the pastors shall earnestly admonish the bell-ringers thereof, that
they put it away; and if it happen again afterward, it shall be sharply punished.

**Appointment.** The sacristan was appointed, not ordained. In Strasbourg (1531, Moderate
Reformed) the vacant offices of "helpers or *Sigristen*" were filled "by the pastors and parish
churchwardens, and not otherwise" (Sehling 20/1, p. 226). Elsewhere the council, the patron or
the pastor with the parish chose him, and he bound himself by pledge, oath or written *Revers* (pledge)
([§16.8](#s16-8)).

**In the convents.** The one sacristan with a distinct title is a woman: the **custorin** among
the "spiritual or church offices" of the evangelical convent of Keppel ([§16.7.5](#s16-7-5)).

#### <a id="s16-7-2"></a>16.7.2 Altar care: no altar guild

**No guild.** The corpus knows no altar guild: no society of women or laymen charged with
washing the altar linen, baking the hosts or adorning the altar. The care of the altar fell to
three others:
- the **sexton** or sacristan ([§16.7.1](#s16-7-1));
- the **lay churchwardens**, deacons of the chest or *Altarleute*, who bought the bread, wine
  and candles and kept the church's ornaments;
- in the convents, the sisters who held the church offices ([§16.7.5](#s16-7-5)).

**The deacons of the church keep the altar.** The Pomeranian synodal statutes of 1574 charge the
lay *diaconi ecclesiae et pauperum* (deacons of the church and of the poor; [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2)) with the altar and its ornaments. **Pomerania,
*Statuta synodica*, 1574** (Sehling 4, p. 491):

<!-- doc 1868 -->

Let the pastors also watch that the deacons neglect not the fabric of the church, but that in
the churches they keep the altar with its ornament, the pulpit, the font, the seats, and all
things honestly and decently, and take care that the churchyards be honestly fenced.

In Pfalz-Neuburg it was the churchwardens who received a florin "for the buying of hosts and
wine" (Sehling 13, p. 208).

**The confraternities dissolved.** Before the Reformation the lights and adornment of many
altars were kept by lay confraternities. These were dissolved, and their goods went to the
common chest. The first such order, Leisnig's, names the brotherhoods of the Kaland, of St Anne
and of the shoemakers' journeymen. **Leisnig, *Ordnung eines gemeinen Kastens*, 1523**
(Sehling 1, p. 599):

<!-- doc 102 -->

Whatsoever in ready money, bought rents, jewels, silver plate, stores and movable goods hath
been gathered hitherto for the said brotherhoods, of the Kaland, of St Anne and of the
shoemakers' journeymen, and belongeth to the same, together with the deeds, inventories and
registers, is altogether cast into and ordained for this common chest, there to remain.

**Women at the altar.** No order gives women a role at the altar. Heilbronn forbade them even to
open the font or hand the towel ([§16.7.1](#s16-7-1)).

#### <a id="s16-7-3"></a>16.7.3 Deaconesses, sick-women and *Seelfrauen*

**The word.** The word *diaconissa* (deaconess) occurs once in an order of the corpus, at Keppel in 1570,
for the sister "who distributeth the alms" ([§16.7.5](#s16-7-5)). There is no order of deaconesses and no rite
for them. But three kinds of women did work that the early Church had given to deaconesses and
widows:
- the **convent almoner** at Keppel;
- the **women elders** (*presbyterae*) of the Bohemian Brethren (Hussite), elected by the women
  of the congregation and bound by handfast vow ([§16.6.4](#s16-6-4));
- the **sick-women** (*Seelfrauen*, *Krankenwärterinnen*), appointed by the council or the
  pastor to nurse and comfort the sick and dying. Some had been beguines.

**Keppel 1570: the deaconess as almoner.** **Nassau-Dillenburg, *Ordnung für das Kloster
Keppel*, 1570** (Sehling 10, p. 141):

<!-- doc 181 -->

The spiritual or church offices are: the lecturess or prioress; the precentress; the deaconess,
that is, she who distributeth the alms; […] the catechists; […] the sacristaness. The temporal
offices are: the cellaress, the church-mistress, the kitchen-mistress, the granary-mistress, she
that keepeth the plate, [and] they that teach the children to sew, embroider and weave […]

**The *Seelfrauen*.** In the Franconian and Bavarian towns the *Seelfrauen* were the inmates of
the *Seelhäuser* (soul-houses), foundations for poor widows and single women who nursed the sick and prayed
for the dying (Sehling 11, p. 320, editors' note). The orders kept them, but under the pastor
and the word:
- **Brandenburg-Ansbach 1536.** The visitors asked for oversight "of the *Seelfrau* and other
  such women who may serve the sick", that they serve for a reasonable wage
  (Sehling 11, p. 320).
- **Regensburg 1543.** The order appointed *Seelfrauen*, and men also, to attend the sick and
  dying, and prescribed what they were to say. **Regensburg, *Kirchenordnung des Noppus*, 1543**
  (Sehling 13, p. 410):

<!-- doc 436 -->

That besides there be appointed *Seelfrauen*, and men also, who shall let themselves be used for
the sick where they are desired, and attend upon the dying. And such shall have a christian
understanding, that they point the dying to the merit of Christ alone, not to their own merit or
the intercession of the saints; [that they] say the Lord's Prayer and the Creed before them,
and, where there is time, well-grounded psalms and songs, as: *Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu
dir* (Out of deep distress I cry to thee), etc., *In Fried und Freud ich fahr dahin* (With peace and joy I depart), *Nun freut euch, lieben Christen gmein* (Now rejoice, dear Christians together), [the
hymns] of baptism [and] of the sacrament of the body and blood, etc.; not old, erroneous prayers
and sayings.

- **Nördlingen 1544.** Kaspar Löner asked that the women whom the council had appointed to tend
  the sick be sent to him, so that he might examine their faith and understanding and teach them
  what they did not know (Sehling 12, p. 315). Sehling's editors note that this had been the
  task of the *Seelnonnen* of the town's beguine house, closed in 1536.
- **Wolfstein 1574.** Women who served the sick were to visit them often (Sehling 13, p. 582);
  the editors compare the Nuremberg *Seelfrauen*.

**Beguines turned sick-visitors.** Heilbronn in 1531 gathered its beguines into one house and
charged them, as their service, to visit the sick and instruct them by God's word ([§16.7.6](#s16-7-6)).

**Hospital nurses.** The later Reformed orders put the sick-nurse under the hospital master. The
Heidelberg hospital order of 1594 (Reformed) lets the hospital master engage "fit sick-nurses"
(*kranckenwärterin*) and dismiss them for misconduct, with the advice of the inspectors,
preacher, physician and surgeon (Sehling 19/2, p. 827). Here the office is a domestic service,
without any churchly character.

#### <a id="s16-7-4"></a>16.7.4 Monks

**Profession ended.** Every evangelical territory ended new professions. The monks were offered
three choices:
- to leave, marry or take up a trade, with their goods or a pension;
- to stay for life in a house set apart for them, with maintenance;
- in a few great abbeys, to live under an evangelical rule as teachers and students for the
  ministry.

**Württemberg 1535.** The first Württemberg monastery order forbade all new admissions, to the
monasteries and to the houses of beguines and Lollards alike, and sent the unprofessed novices
home. **Württemberg, *Klosterordnung*, 1535** (Sehling 16, p. 79):

<!-- doc 647 -->

Henceforth also no persons shall be received into the cloisters, nor likewise into the houses of
the beguines and Lollards. And where there be now novices which have not yet made profession,
they shall be sent home to their parents or kinsfolk without delay, with reasonable provision
for the way.

Those who left received back what they had brought in, or forty florins a year for life. The few
remaining mendicant friars were gathered into one house, the old and weak to be cared for "that
they may so die in peace" (Sehling 16, pp. 79–80). In 1552 Duke Christoph forbade the abbots to
"entangle" boys with "superstitious ceremonies and vows" to remain in the cloister
(Sehling 16, p. 199).

**Esslingen 1535: the friars who stayed** (Moderate Reformed). Esslingen's order for the
remaining Franciscans let any friar marry with a settlement from the council. Those who stayed
received board and a yearly allowance. **Esslingen, *Ordnung für die Konventualen im
Barfüßerkloster*, 6 September 1535** (Moderate Reformed; Sehling 17/2, p. 382):

<!-- doc 882 -->

Whosoever among the persons of the order would betake himself to another honest, christian
estate and enter into the estate of matrimony, which shall be permitted to every one to
undertake to the praise of God and the health of his soul, the same shall be set out and
provided for by an honourable council, as the magistrate, according to the revenue of each
cloister, with reasonable maintenance, as it shall please an honourable council. And those
persons of the order which come not out, but purpose so to remain in the cloister, shall be
provided with reasonable sustenance; and to him that hath been a priest ten florins, and to a
lay brother five florins, shall be given every year for clothing and other bodily necessity.

**Evangelical monasteries.** Where the princes kept the great abbeys, they kept them as schools
for the ministry. Their "conventuals" and "novices" were students under an evangelical abbot:
- **Württemberg.** At Herrenalb in 1556 the first Lutheran abbot agreed statutes by which "the
  conventuals and novices" were to pray morning and evening a Latin prayer for the church, the
  emperor, the duke and the abbot, and to live under discipline and study (Sehling 16, p. 317).
  The installation of the Württemberg prelates is in
  [Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.11.3](#s13-11-3).
- **Pfalz-Simmern.** At the Augustinian house of Ravengiersburg in 1560 no novice or prebendary
  was to be received without the duke's and the prior's knowledge. The young men were to be
  trained for the preaching office, and the convent might sing in Latin. **Pfalz-Simmern,
  *Klosterordnung Ravengiersburg*, 1560** (Sehling 19/2, p. 658):

<!-- doc 1125 -->

Further also no youth or prebendary shall be received without the knowledge and will of us, Duke
George, as prince of the land, and of me, the Father [prior]; and such young lords and scholars
as are now already in the cloister, or shall hereafter be received with our knowledge as
aforesaid, shall be taught, directed and held earnestly to this end, that they may hereafter in
our principality hold and administer the preaching office or some other honourable church
service for which they are found apt.

**No vows.** None of these houses required a vow. Ravengiersburg's scholar who was sent to the
university bound himself only to serve the duke and the house (Sehling 19/2, p. 658).

#### <a id="s16-7-5"></a>16.7.5 Nuns

**The women's houses survived longest.** Many nunneries, above all the noble foundations of the
north, survived the Reformation as evangelical convents or *Stifte*. They became homes and
schools for unmarried women, keeping a rule, a habit of sorts, the hours in German or Latin, and
an elected head (abbess, prioress or *domina*). The orders reformed them on four points:
- **Admission.** No one was to be clothed without the prince's or council's consent. At Goslar's
  convent of Frankenberg (1542) and in Württemberg no one was to be admitted at all.
- **Vows.** The vows of perpetual chastity and the cloister were not binding. A sister might
  leave and marry with her goods.
- **Habit.** The consecrated habit (cowl, scapular, veil and crown) was abolished or made
  optional. Baptism was declared the true clothing.
- **Worship.** The hours and the Mass were reformed. Daily preaching, the catechism and
  schooling for girls were added.

**Goslar 1542: no new nuns, free to marry.** **Goslar, *Ordnung für das Frauenkloster
Frankenberg*, 1542** (Sehling 7/2.2, p. 275):

<!-- doc 2198 -->

5. They shall admit no persons hereafter to the habit of their order; but those which have not
   yet made profession they shall send away from them, with all that they brought to the
   convent. 6. It shall be free and lawful to every person of the convent either to remain in
   the convent all the time of her life, or to enter into matrimony with some honest man.

**Lüneburg 1574: clothing kept, the habit changed.** The Lüneburg houses still received girls,
but under the duke's control. The cowl, scapular, veil and crown were replaced by a plain black
or white gown. **Lüneburg, *Klosterordnung* of Duke William the Younger, 1574**
(Sehling 6/1, p. 622):

<!-- doc 2010 -->

So also no child or maiden shall be clothed without our foreknowledge and command. And whereas
the cowls and scapulars and veils and the cross upon the head, as the persons of the cloister
now wear them, give offence to many godly Christians […] henceforth no maiden shall be clothed
in cowl and with veil and cross; but they shall wear honest black or white gowns of one fashion
and cloth, and upon the head white kerchiefs, as they now have, without side-bands or wrought
hoods, but no veil or cross. […] Also no person of the cloister shall be buried in cowl,
scapular, veil, etc., but in a linen sheet like other Christians.

**Mecklenburg 1572: baptism the true clothing.** The Mecklenburg convent order of 1572 rejects
the blessing of the habit "with certain little prayers" and holy water, and the "superstitious
little books of consecration". **Mecklenburg, *Klosterordnung*, 1572** (Sehling 5, p. 254):

<!-- doc 1926 -->

Likewise it is a superstitious error that the cloister garments, or cowls, scapulars and veils,
consecrated with certain little prayers and sprinkled with holy water, should be spiritual and
more glorious garments than others, whereby they cover their sins before the face of God and are
preserved against the assault of the devil as with a harness, put on Christ, and become Christ's
bride and queens; whereas all Christians alike are clothed in baptism in one spiritual garment,
[and] put on the Lord Jesus Christ […]

On vows the same order teaches that "there is no higher vow than that which we have made in holy
baptism", and that vows against God's command are not to be kept (Sehling 5, p. 255).
Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1569 argues the same at length. In baptism all Christians are clothed
"in a red cowl, which is the most holy rose-coloured blood of our Lord Jesus Christ" and
crowned, so that the sister who lays aside her habit and crown loses nothing
(Sehling 6/1, pp. 324–326). The form of words for laying it aside is in
[Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.12.10](#s13-12-10).

**Admission by the magistrate.** Strasbourg in 1555 took admission to its remaining women's
houses out of the hands of the prioress. The council was to decide, and no girl was to be
received under eight years old (Sehling 20/1, p. 454).

**Keppel 1570: an evangelical clothing.** The fullest evangelical form for receiving a nun is
the Nassau order for the convent of Keppel. It has the following elements:
- a probation of at least two years;
- questions to the parents, the *domina* and the candidate;
- an oath;
- a sermon;
- the clothing in the sacristy;
- *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit) and an exhortation at the altar;
- the *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God).

The exhortation tells the new sister that her vows earn nothing, that the convent is "not a
prison" but "as it were a school", and that she may marry in an orderly way. The full rite is in
[Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.12.7](#s13-12-7).

**The offices of the convent.** Keppel divides the sisters' offices into "spiritual or church
offices" and "temporal offices" (quoted in [§16.7.3](#s16-7-3)):
- *Spiritual.* The lecturess or prioress, the precentress, the deaconess or almoner, the
  catechists and the sacristaness (*custorin*).
- *Temporal.* The cellaress, the church-mistress (*kirchenmeisterin*), the kitchen-mistress, the
  granary-mistress, the keeper of the plate and the needlework teachers.

The *domina* assigned these offices. She herself was proposed by the convent from two or three
names, confirmed by the count and deposable by him, and swore an oath (Sehling 10, pp. 141–142).

**Abbess and prioress.** In Schleswig-Holstein the abbess of Itzehoe and the prioresses of the
other houses were still elected by the convent "according to old custom", under oath in the
provost's presence. The sisters swore obedience to them (Sehling 23, p. 182). At Strasbourg the
"mother or prioress" and six elder "council-mothers" were chosen and gave a promise
(Sehling 20/1, p. 456). Both forms are in
[Chapter 13](#ch13) [§13.12.8](#s13-12-8).

#### <a id="s16-7-6"></a>16.7.6 Beguines, tertiaries, Brethren of the Common Life and confraternities

**Semi-religious communities.** The orders say little about the beguines, the tertiaries of the
mendicant orders, the *Nollharden* or Lollards (lay brothers who nursed the sick and buried the
dead), and the Brethren and Sisters of the Common Life. What they say is of three kinds:
- the houses were closed to new members;
- the existing members were maintained or bought out;
- the communities were turned to the service of the sick or the school.

No order creates a third order or a lay religious community.

**Closed to new members.** Württemberg's order of 1535 shut the "houses of the beguines and
Lollards" with the monasteries ([§16.7.4](#s16-7-4)). The beguines might keep or divide what they had brought
in, and sell the houses they had built themselves, with the duke's knowledge
(Sehling 16, p. 80). Sehling's editors record four houses of tertiary sisters at Reutlingen
before the Reformation (Sehling 17/2, p. 28, editors' introduction). In Württemberg only the
Franciscan tertiaries of Weiler used their right to emigrate, and went as a community to a
convent near Augsburg (Sehling 16, p. 50, editors' introduction).

**Heilbronn 1531: beguines as visitors of the sick.** Heilbronn gathered its beguines into one
house and gave them a service, which comes closest in the corpus to an evangelical diaconate of
women. **Heilbronn, *Instruktion zur Zusammenlegung beider Beginenhäuser*, 8 December 1531**
(Sehling 17/1, p. 298):

<!-- doc 776 -->

Item, when they shall so dwell together, they shall be willing upon request to go to the sick,
and to instruct the sick according to God's word. Item, a council trusteth that they,
considering that a good appearance becometh them, will not […] cleave to a distinct clothing,
but otherwise clothe themselves honestly, and go diligently to hear the word of God.

**Herford: the Brethren of the Common Life.** Herford had both a brothers' and a sisters' house
of the Common Life, and its Brethren were early supporters of the Reformation
(Sehling 21, p. 160, editors' introduction). Its church order of 1532 nonetheless counted the
separate communion of such houses as sectarian. **Herford, *Kirchenordnung*, 1532**
(Sehling 21, pp. 173–174):

<!-- doc 1442 -->

That is surely not called *convenire* [to come together], when one separateth oneself from the
congregation into brothers' houses, sisters' houses and other factions and sects; but [it is] to
gather with the common Christians to the remembrance of the Lord, to the use of the sacrament.

**Confraternities.** The lay brotherhoods (*Bruderschaften*) and the Kalands, which had kept
altars, lights and anniversary Masses, were dissolved and their goods put into the common chest
from Leisnig in 1523 onward ([§16.7.2](#s16-7-2)). Lemgo in 1537 gave the revenues of the brotherhoods and of
the Kaland of Corpus Christi to the schoolmaster and preachers (Sehling 21, p. 302). Nassau in
1537 kept a common meal for its clergy synod, but without the "disorderly feasting … as hitherto
at the Kalands" (Sehling 10, p. 84).

**The answer in brief.** The Reformation in the Sehling corpus kept no third order and founded
none. It turned the surviving beguines and *Seelfrauen* (soul-women) into nurses of the sick under the
pastor. The lay confraternities were dissolved into the common chest, and the Brethren of the
Common Life were absorbed into the parish and the school.

---

### <a id="s16-8"></a>16.8 Ordained or not: how each office was installed

**Words that do not settle the question.** "Ordain" (*ordiniren*, *ordinatio*) is not decisive
in these texts:
- Lippe uses it of appointing deacons of the poor.
- The Bohemian Brethren (Hussite) use it of a handfast vow.
- Hesse (Moderate Reformed) uses it of a full rite with laying on of hands.

**How the table classifies.** The table below therefore classifies by what the rite actually
does, in four degrees, from strongest to weakest:
- **hands**: laying on of hands, with prayer;
- **prayer**: public commendation with prayer, without hands;
- **vow**: a handfast vow (*Handgelübde*, *manu stipulata*) or an oath;
- **none**: appointment only.

| Office | Order | Elected or appointed by | Installation | Section |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pastor or *Diaconus* (deacon; assistant minister) | Electoral Saxony 1580 | Called by the church; examined; confirmed by the synod | **hands** (superintendent), prayer; "by divine command" | [§16.5.1](#s16-5-1) |
| Minister of the word | Pfalz-Zweibrücken 1539 | Congregation | **hands** (neighbouring pastors or "elders") | [§16.5.4](#s16-5-4) |
| Minister of the word | Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed) | — | **hands** (superintendent, ministers **and elders**) | [§16.6.2](#s16-6-2) |
| Minister of the word | Nassau-Dillenburg 1582 (Reformed) | Classis and seniors | "confirmation or ordination", public | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Acolyte | Bohemian Brethren 1576 | Pastor; examined by synod | **vow** (*manu stipulata*), right hand of fellowship, blessing | [§16.3.4](#s16-3-4) |
| Deacon (clerical) | Bohemian Brethren 1576 | Chosen from acolytes; examined by seniors | **hands**, vow, prayer, blessing (Acts 6:6) | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Lay presbyter, *presbytera* (presbyteress) | Bohemian Brethren 1576 | Free vote of the men (or women) | **vow** (*voce et stipulata manu*, by voice and by handfast); place of honour | [§16.6.4](#s16-6-4) |
| Deacon of the poor | Brunswick 1528, Hamburg 1529, Lübeck 1531 | — | **none** described | [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2) |
| *Diaconi* (deacons) | Pyritz 1539 | Council and guilds | **none**; "laden with no oath" | [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2) |
| *Diaconi ecclesiae et pauperum* (Deacons of the church and of the poor) | Pomerania 1574 | Chosen under the pastors' eye | **vow** (oath) | [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2) |
| *Leviten* (levites; deacons of the poor) | Hadeln 1526 | — | **none** described | [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2) |
| *Subdiaconi oder Bittherren* (Subdeacons or bidding-men) | Naumburg 1537 | Council and community | **none** described | [§16.5.2](#s16-5-2) |
| Deacon of the poor | Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed) | Ministers with council and congregation; probation | **hands** and prayer (Acts 6) | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Deacon or almoner | Micron 1554/65 (Reformed) | Congregation | questions, prayer, **hands** | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Deacon or almoner | Kurpfalz 1563, Wittgenstein 1581, Bentheim-Tecklenburg 1588/1619 (all Reformed) | —; confirmed by pastors and seniors | confirmation, rite not described | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Deacon, senior, sexton | Nassau-Dillenburg 1582 (Reformed) | Presbytery; confirmed by classis | confirmation and admonition | [§16.5.3](#s16-5-3) |
| Lay elder | Hesse (Ziegenhain) 1539 (Moderate Reformed) | Each church | **prayer** and exhortation ("sanctify their office") | [§16.6.2](#s16-6-2) |
| Lay elder | Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed) | Ministers with council and congregation | **hands** (pastor and ministers), prayer; "ordained" | [§16.6.2](#s16-6-2) |
| Lay elder | Micron 1554/65 (Reformed) | Congregation | questions, prayer, **hands** | [§16.6.3](#s16-6-3) |
| Lay elder | Kurpfalz 1592 (also Ysenburg-Ronneburg 1592; both Reformed) | Congregation | questions, prayer, **hands** (minister and elders) | [§16.6.3](#s16-6-3) |
| Censor (elder) | Pfalz-Veldenz 1574 | — | **prayer** from the pulpit; "set into this high office" | [§16.6.3](#s16-6-3) |
| Lay elder | Kurpfalz about 1601 (Reformed) | Yearly | **vow** (handfast), **prayer** of the congregation | [§16.6.3](#s16-6-3) |

| Novice or scholar of an evangelical monastery | Ravengiersburg 1560 | Duke and prior | **none**; no vow | [§16.7.4](#s16-7-4) |
| Nun | Keppel 1570 | Count; parents, *domina* and candidate questioned | **vow** (oath with hand on breast), sermon, clothing, *Veni Sancte Spiritus* (Come, Holy Spirit), exhortation, *Te Deum* (We praise thee, O God) | [§16.7.5](#s16-7-5) |
| Nun | Lüneburg 1574 | Duke's foreknowledge and command | clothing in a plain gown; rite not described | [§16.7.5](#s16-7-5) |

| Abbess, prioress | Schleswig-Holstein 1610 | Convent, sworn to choose well, in the provost's presence | **vow** (oath); the sisters swear obedience | [§16.7.5](#s16-7-5) |
| Mother (prioress) and six council-mothers | Strasbourg 1555 | Chosen from the eldest and fittest | **vow** (promise) | [§16.7.5](#s16-7-5) |

**Summary.** Laying on of hands was used for four groups:
- ministers of the word, everywhere;
- deacons of the poor, in Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed) and in Micron (Reformed);
- lay elders, in Hesse 1566 (Moderate Reformed), Micron and Kurpfalz 1592 (Reformed);
- the Bohemian Brethren's clerical deacons (Hussite).

It was not used for:
- sacristans, sick-women, nuns, convent heads or the scholars of the evangelical monasteries;
- Lutheran deacons of the poor or churchwardens;
- the Reformed elders of the Kurpfalz *Presbyterordnung*, Hanau or Solms, and the elders of
  Lutheran Veldenz;
- any minor grade, including the Bohemian acolytes.

**Answer to the question asked.** Were ruling elders ordained? Yes, in Hesse 1566 (Moderate
Reformed), the London-Norden order of Micron and the Palatinate form of 1592 (both Reformed).
Elsewhere they were installed with prayer, a handfast vow or an oath, and none of these used the
language of ordination except Veldenz, which uses it of the apostles.

## <a id="ch17"></a>Chapter 17. Confessional Subscription


This chapter covers how the evangelical church orders of the sixteenth and early seventeenth
centuries bound people to the confessions, as printed in Emil Sehling's *Die evangelischen
Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts* (The Evangelical Church Orders of the Sixteenth Century). It asks five questions:

- Which documents did each order name as its rule of doctrine, its *corpus doctrinae* (body of doctrine) or *norma
  doctrinae*? Was it Scripture alone, the Augsburg Confession, the Apology, the Smalcald
  Articles, Luther's catechisms, Melanchthon's *Loci* (Commonplaces) and *Corpus doctrinae* (body of doctrine), a territorial
  corpus, the Formula of Concord or the Book of Concord, or a local confession?
- How was a minister bound to these documents? By a list of books to buy, a question at the
  visitation, an examination, a written *Revers* (pledge), a sworn oath, a "Yea" at ordination, or a
  subscription with his own hand?
- How did this differ from one territory to another, and how did it change over time? The main
  stages are the 1530s, the Interim years, the age of the territorial *corpora doctrinae* in the
  1560s and 1570s, the Formula of Concord campaign of 1577–1580, and the refusals and Reformed
  reorientations that followed.
- Were lay people ever bound in the same way? This covers the profession and vow at
  confirmation, admission to communion, godparents, admission as a burgher, and magistrates and
  other officials.
- What did the orders say about refusers and dissenters?

The findings are summarised in [§17.1](#s17-1), and the method and its cautions are described in [§17.2](#s17-2). [§17.3](#s17-3) is a
glossary of the documents the orders name. [§17.4](#s17-4) sets out the forms of binding. §§[17.5](#s17-5)–[17.16](#s17-16) go through
the territories region by region, each in date order. [§17.17](#s17-17) covers the laity. [§17.18](#s17-18) is a table by
order, and [§17.19](#s17-19) a concordance of every order quoted.

**Related chapters.** Several subjects are treated more fully elsewhere and are only cited here:
- the rites at which the vows were taken (confirmation, ordination, installation, and the oaths
  of sextons, schoolmasters, churchwardens and magistrates):
  [Chapter 13](#ch13), §§[13.6](#s13-6), [13.10](#s13-10)–[13.13](#s13-13);
- the examination, trial sermon and continuing study of ministers, and the consistories that
  examined them: [Chapter 15](#ch15), §§[15.5](#s15-5), [15.7](#s15-7);
- catechesis before first communion and before marriage:
  [Chapter 15](#ch15), [§15.11](#s15-11);
- how deacons, elders and the other church offices were installed:
  [Chapter 16](#ch16), [§16.8](#s16-8);
- the confessional tradition of every order: [Chapter 1](#ch1),
  [§1.3](#s1-3).

The abbreviations for the confessional writings are listed in the
[Conventions](#conv-abbreviations).

### <a id="s17-1"></a>17.1 Summary of findings

#### <a id="s17-1-1"></a>17.1.1 The main findings

**1. There was no single confessional standard until 1580, and not everywhere after it.** Every
territory had a rule of doctrine, but what that rule held varied a great deal. In outline it
moved through five stages:

- **To about 1540: Scripture and the prince.** The earliest oaths bound a pastor to preach "the
  holy gospel and word of God" purely, together with obedience to his lord.
  Brandenburg-Ansbach's priest's oath of 1528 is the model ([§17.14.1](#s17-14-1)). Heilbronn's council swore in
  1530 to stand together in matters "of the gospel" ([§17.17.5](#s17-17-5)). Confessions are not yet named.
- **About 1540 to 1560: the Augsburg Confession and Melanchthon.** The CA and its Apology become
  the measure of preaching. The orders add Melanchthon's *Loci communes* as the textbook from
  which ministers are examined. This is so in Albertine Saxony in 1540 and 1557 ([§17.5.1](#s17-5-1)),
  Württemberg in 1547 ([§17.13.1](#s17-13-1)), Pomerania ([§17.7.4](#s17-7-4)) and Strasbourg's examination of 1549, issued
  under the Interim ([§17.15.1](#s17-15-1)). The norm is still given chiefly as a list of books a parish must
  buy.
- **The 1560s and 1570s: territorial *corpora doctrinae*.** Princes and cities gathered their
  own bodies of doctrine, which pastors had to own, follow and often subscribe. These were the
  Philippist *Corpus doctrinae* (body of doctrine) of 1560 (adopted in Electoral Saxony, Kurland, Brieg, Oldenburg,
  Bremen and Hesse, the last two Philippist), the Pomeranian, the Prussian (1567), the
  Thuringian, the Wolfenbüttel *Corpus Julium* (1576), the Brunswick city corpus (1571), the
  Ansbach-Nürnberg *norma doctrinae* (1573) and the Hohenlohe corpus (1578). Some local
  confessions also served as corpora: Mansfeld 1565, the Lüneburg Articles of 1561, Danzig's
  *Notel* (note) of 1562, the Strasbourg Concord of 1563 and Ravensburg's local "formula concordiae" (Formula of Concord) of
  1578.
- **1577 to about 1600: the Formula and the Book of Concord.** The FC was put to every minister
  for signature in Electoral Saxony, Brandenburg, Württemberg, Mecklenburg, Henneberg, Mansfeld,
  Pfalz-Neuburg, the Upper Palatinate, Ansbach and many Swabian and Franconian cities, and it
  was written into church orders such as Hoya's (1581). Later orders made signing the BoC a
  condition of admission to office (§§[17.5.3](#s17-5-3), [17.6.2](#s17-6-2), [17.9](#s17-9), [17.13](#s17-13), [17.14](#s17-14)). Ordination questions took the FC
  into the vow itself, answered with "Yea" (Henneberg 1582, Waldeck, Frankfurt 1589 and
  Strasbourg 1598).
- **The refusers and the Reformed turn.** Some refused the FC outright: Anhalt ([§17.6.6](#s17-6-6)), Hesse
  (Philippist), Danzig, Nürnberg and its neighbours, Gottorp and the Danish lands, Colmar
  (Moderate Reformed) and Bremen (Philippist). Pomerania kept its own corpus and took only three
  points of the FC against the Calvinists, in
  1593. Some ceased to require it when they turned Reformed: Kurpfalz after 1583 and the Upper
        Palatinate in 1585. Others kept a pre-1577 norm or replaced the FC with a local formula,
        such as Hohenlohe's *Gründlicher Bericht* (Thorough report) of 1603–1605. Where the Reformed took over,
        the CA *variata* or Scripture alone became the stated norm. The CA was understood in the
        Frankfurt Recess and Naumburg sense, and the Heidelberg Catechism replaced Luther's.

**2. The canon grew by accretion.** The usual sequence of additions to Scripture and the three
creeds was:

- the CA, from 1530;
- the Apology;
- the SA, named increasingly from the 1550s, often "as signed at Smalcald 1537";
- Luther's catechisms;
- then either Melanchthon's corpus or a territorial corpus;
- and finally the FC or the whole BoC.

Many orders show this growth inside their own textual history. Ansbach's 1528 oath carries
apparatus variants for 1570, 1573 and 1588 ([§17.14.1](#s17-14-1)). The Hohenlohe KO of 1578 gained a
handwritten "7. The *formula concordiae*" ([§17.13.3](#s17-13-3)). The Kurpfalz formula of 1556 was rewritten in
1580 and 1586 ([§17.12.1](#s17-12-1)).

**3. "Unaltered" and "in its true sense" are the signs of party.**

- *Gnesio-Lutheran or FC party.* Adjectives such as *unverändert* (unaltered), *ungeändert* (unchanged), *uralt* (most ancient), *wie
  anno 30 übergeben* (as delivered in the year [15]30), "in its right, true sense" and "as explained in the Apology, the SA and
  the catechisms" mark the Gnesio-Lutheran or FC party. Examples are Wolfenbüttel 1569 ([§17.9.1](#s17-9-1)),
  Verden 1606, Osnabrück 1610 and Hoya 1581.
- *Philippist or Reformed party.* Phrases such as "as repeated at Frankfurt and Naumburg", the
  *Corpus doctrinae Philippi* (Philip's body of doctrine) and the *Repetitio* (Repetition; *Confessio Saxonica*) mark the Philippist or
  Reformed party. Examples are Bremen 1572 (Philippist), the Upper Palatinate 1585 (Reformed)
  and Kurland 1570 (Lutheran).

**4. The form of binding hardened.** The forms run from a book list, through a question at the
visitation and a promise, to a sworn oath and a signature in one's own hand. In the oldest
orders the confession appears as books a parish must buy (Ernestine Saxony 1554, Albertine
Saxony 1557). Later orders demand:

- a public confession at admission (Ernestine Saxony 1569, Strasbourg from 1562);
- a written promise or *Revers* (pledge; Nassau-Diez 1564);
- an oath on the confessions (Ansbach, Peine/Gottorp 1574, Wimpfen, Hessen-Darmstadt 1617,
  Transylvania);
- subscription "with his own hand" (Electoral Saxony 1580, Regensburg 1572/88, Hildesheim 1593,
  Wimpfen).

The Kurpfalz (Lutheran and Reformed in turn) and Pfalz-Neuburg *Bestallungen* bind "with fealty
given by the hand in the stead of a bodily sworn oath" ([§17.12.1](#s17-12-1)). [§17.4](#s17-4) gives the forms in full.

**5. Subscription reached beyond the clergy, but not to the common people.** Superintendents,
consistorial assessors and professors were bound as a matter of course. So in some cities were
burgomasters, syndics, physicians and secretaries (Hildesheim 1593), the chamberlain and council
(Regensburg 1572/88), and schoolmasters in many places. **No order requires ordinary lay people
to subscribe the CA or the FC.** The laity were bound in other ways ([§17.17](#s17-17)):

- by the catechism examination before first communion and before marriage;
- by a public profession and vow at confirmation, chiefly in Hesse from 1539 and Strasbourg
  (both Moderate Reformed), the Reformed refugee churches and Electoral Saxony's confirmation of
  the baptismal faith;
- by the confession and exploration required before each communion (Schweinfurt 1543, after the
  CA itself);
- by rules for godparents and for admission as a burgher.

The Reformed orders alone required an explicit "confession of the Reformed doctrine" before the Supper (Nassau-Dillenburg 1582, Reformed, [§17.17.2](#s17-17-2)).

### <a id="s17-2"></a>17.2 Scope, sources and method

#### <a id="s17-2-1"></a>17.2.1 What was searched

The whole of [`eko.db`](#repo-ekodb) was searched for the vocabulary of confessional obligation:

- the names of the confessions, in German and Latin and with their OCR variants (*augspurgische
  confession*, *apologia*, *schmalkaldische artikel*, *catechismus Lutheri*, *formula
  concordiae*, *concordienbuch*, *corpus doctrinae*, *norma doctrinae*, *loci communes*,
  *repetitio*);
- the verbs of binding (*unterschreiben*, *subscribieren*, *schwören*, *geloben*, *angeloben*,
  *verpflichten*, *zusagen*, *Revers*, *Eid*, *Pflicht*, *iuramentum*, *subscribo*, *promitto*);
- the occasions of binding: ordination, examination, vocation, *Bestallung* (appointment), visitation, synod,
  admission to the consistory, and appointment as schoolmaster, superintendent or assessor.

Every hit was read in context. Each was sorted by whether it was the text of an order, Sehling's
introduction or a footnote. For the laity the search covered confirmation, first communion,
admission to the Supper (*exploration*, *verhör*), godparents (*gevattern*, *paten*,
*susceptores*), admission as burgher (*bürger*, *hintersäß*), and oaths of councils and
officials.

#### <a id="s17-2-2"></a>17.2.2 What the chapter does not do

- It does not give the full text of each confession, nor the history of the FC's making. It
  records only what the church orders themselves say.
- It does not list every signature. The great lists of subscribers in the archives are beyond
  the edition. Sehling sometimes reports their numbers, for example 444 signatures in
  Mecklenburg in 1577 (Sehling 5, pp. 142–143), and these are noted where he does.
- **A book list is not a subscription.** Many orders tell a parish to buy the CA, the *Loci* (Commonplaces) or
  a *Corpus doctrinae* (body of doctrine), and tell the pastor to read it. That makes the book a standard of
  preaching, but it is not an oath or a signature. Where an order lists books only, this is
  said.
- **A territorial norm is not always a personal obligation.** A preface may say that "our
  churches" hold the CA without saying how a pastor was bound to it. The chapter marks which kind
  of statement each quotation is.

#### <a id="s17-2-3"></a>17.2.3 Cautions

- **Sehling's introductions and apparatus.** Several of the best statements about subscription,
  such as the Hildesheim decision of 1593 or the Anhalt refusal of the FC (Anhalt was still
  Lutheran), are found only in Sehling's introductions or footnotes, which quote or summarise
  archival sources. They are marked as such.
- **Apparatus variants.** Some orders were reissued, and the editors print the later wording in
  the apparatus. Examples are the Ansbach priest's oath (1528, with forms of 1570, 1573 and
  1588), the Hohenlohe KO of 1578 (with a handwritten addition naming the FC) and the Kurpfalz
  KO of 1556 (with variants of 1577). These are quoted as variants with their dates.
- **Record headings.** The database's record headings sometimes name the first order in a volume
  section rather than the order on the page. So document 1844 is headed "This first Danzig order … 1557", but its p. 234 is the Thorn KO of 1575, and its p. 210 the Danzig KO of 1612.
  Each order is named here from Sehling's running head. Where the running head is itself
  misleading, this is said (as at Anhalt, p. 579, where a passage of the 1588 *Instructio* runs
  onto a page headed with the next order).
- **OCR errors.** OCR errors are quoted as printed. Thus Calenberg's "Gorpus doctrinae Julium"
  is printed as such, and the Kassel KO of 1539 (Moderate Reformed) carries the running head
  "1589".

#### <a id="s17-2-4"></a>17.2.4 How to read the regional sections

Each regional section goes through its orders in date order. For each it says:

- **what the norm was**: which documents the order names, in what order, and with what
  qualifiers ("unaltered", "as delivered in 1530", "in its true sense");
- **who was bound**: ordinands, pastors, superintendents, schoolmasters, assessors, councils;
- **how they were bound**: book list, visitation question, examination, promise, *Revers* (pledge), oath,
  ordination "Yea", or subscription.

The table in [§17.18](#s17-18) gathers these by order.

---

### <a id="s17-3"></a>17.3 The documents the orders name

This glossary gives the documents in the form the orders name them. Where an order's wording
identifies a particular edition or reading (the *invariata* [unaltered] or the *variata*, the first print of
the Apology), this is noted. For dates and contents the standard editions are the
*Bekenntnisschriften der evangelisch-lutherischen Kirche* (Confessional writings of the Evangelical Lutheran Church) (BSLK, BSELK), which the editors of
the later volumes cite in their footnotes.

#### <a id="s17-3-1"></a>17.3.1 The ancient creeds

- **The three creeds** (*drei Hauptsymbola*, *symbola oecumenica*): the Apostles', the Nicene
  and the Athanasian. They come first after Scripture in almost every list.
- **The four councils** (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon). These are named in
  Kurland (1570), the Katzenelnbogen pastors' oath (1598, Philippist, together with Leo's Tome
  to Flavian), Strasbourg (1598) and the Upper Palatinate (1585, Reformed). In Hessen-Kassel and
  the Upper Palatinate they are aimed against the ubiquity doctrine.

#### <a id="s17-3-2"></a>17.3.2 The Lutheran confessions

- **Augsburg Confession (CA), 1530.** Named in nearly every order from the 1530s on. The
